sections.title: # When to Use Flow Matching Models
sections.text: FMMs are well-suited when you can benefit from direct transport from noise to data with a differentiable vector field, especially for tasks where interpolation structure is helpful (conditional generation, structured outputs, or when guidance follows a path-based paradigm). They offer a complementary perspective to diffusion/score-based models by learning a deterministic transformation along explicit interpolation paths, often yielding straighter trajectories and fast high-quality sampling [13f85775-0]. Their unifying view with CFM, rectified flow, and bridge matching also facilitates algorithmic connections and hybridization with other flow and guidance techniques [d51a4e32-1].

sections.title: # Summary
sections.text:
- Definition: FMMs learn a time-dependent vector field that transports noise to data along interpolation paths, defining a continuous normalizing flow governed by the continuity equation. The model specifies a density path p(t, x) via the vector field and trains to fit the data–noise transformation [d51a4e32-3].
- Contrast: Unlike score-based diffusion (learning ∇ log p), FMMs learn a velocity field vθ(t, x) and can follow near-straight paths for fast, high-quality sampling. This yields a direct interpolation-based generative mechanism [13f85775-0].
- Equivalences: Under certain conditions, FM/CFM align with the first iteration of rectified flow; all are special cases in the bridge-matching view. This unifying perspective clarifies relationships across flow formulations [d51a4e32-1].
- Practice: Sampling uses discrete residual steps with teacher forcing along paths like CFM; training has shown speed/quality gains, though multi-step inference remains. Recent work also explores single-evaluation approximations and architectural flexibility [d51a4e32-3][edf91aa0-4].
- Trade-offs: Guidance is less mature than in diffusion, performance near t≈0 can lag due to reduced stochasticity, and inference can be slower than single-step alternatives unless specialized methods are used. New guidance frameworks and hybrid flow designs are addressing these issues [d51a4e32-2][edf91aa0-2][edf91aa0-4].

We include a justification for the fixed point Z π (s, a) in Lemma 3, and will use the contraction property of T π to estimate the return distribution with theoretical guarantees (Sec. 4.1 & 4.2). 

Flow matching. Flow matching (Lipman et al., 2023;2024;Liu et al., 2023;Albergo & Vanden-Eijnden, 2023) refers to a family of generative models based on ordinary differential equations (ODEs). The goal of flow matching methods is to transform a simple noise distribution into a target distribution p X over some space X ⊂ R d . We will use t to denote the flow time step and sample the noise ϵ from a standard Gaussian distribution N (0, I) throughout our discussions. Flow matching uses a time-dependent vector field v : (Lipman et al., 2023;2024) that realizes the transformation. The resulting probability density path p : [0, 1] × R d → ∆(R d ) of the vector field v satisfies the continuity equation (Lipman et al., 2023). In Sec. 4, we will estimate the return distribution using flow-based models, utilizing the continuity equation (Sec. 4.2) and flow ODE (Sec. 4.3). 

Prior work has proposed various formulations for learning the vector field (Lipman et al., 2023;Liu et al., 2023;Albergo & Vanden-Eijnden, 2023). We adopt the simplest flow matching objectives called conditional flow matching (CFM) (Lipman et al., 2023) to construct loss functions for optimizing the return vector field (Sec. 4.2). Appendix A.3 includes detailed discussions of flow matching methods.

sections.title: # Overview: Reversible Data Hiding with Vector Quantization
sections.text: Reversible data hiding (RDH) in vector-quantized images embeds secret bits into a compressed host represented by a vector quantization (VQ) index table such that the original table—and thus the reconstructed image—can be recovered exactly after message removal. In VQ-based RDH, the cover is the VQ standard-index table and reversibility means completely recovering the original standard-index table after removing the secret data [ed8e6609-2] RDH in the compressed domain is attractive because it avoids degrading the decoded image beyond the original compression loss and supports use cases like cloud annotations, medical diagnostics, and forensics where exact recovery is required. RDH was proposed to enable data hiding with non-distortional reconstruction of the original cover media, and compressed-domain RDH (including VQ) has become a research focus [ed8e6609-2]

citations.title: High Capacity Reversible Data Hiding for VQ-Compressed Images Based on Difference Transformation and Mapping Technique
snippets:
Data hiding (also called data embedding or information hiding) embeds secret data imperceptibly into a cover media, such as a video, a piece of audio, an image, etc. Since 1990s, a variety of data hiding techniques have been performing a growingly important role in privacy protection, copyright, and so on [1]- [12], [49], [50]. Traditional data hiding is usually irreversible, and the embedding process brings permanent distortion to the original host image, which is unacceptable in circumstances where a complete reconstruction of the original host image and verification of data are required, such as encrypted data annotation in the cloud environment, remote medical diagnostic and judicial forensics, and so on. To achieve data hiding and a non-distortional reconstruction of original cover media, reversible (also called lossless) data 

The associate editor coordinating the review of this manuscript and approving it for publication was Michele Nappi . hiding (RDH) technique was proposed [8]. The benefit is that the original host image can be recovered completely after the removal of secret data. RDH schemes include the spatial domain, compressed domain, frequency domain, and so on. Because the image is usually stored or transmitted in the form of compressed file, such a reversible data hiding technique for compressed images has become a research hotspot. 

Vector quantization (VQ) [13] is a lossy data compression technique widely used in the various fields of image processing. In recent years, some VQ-based reversible data hiding methods have been developed. In all VQ-based reversible data hiding techniques, a VQ standard-index table is used as the cover image, and the image embedded with the secret message is called the ''stego image,'' hence the reversibility means the capability of completely recovering the original VQ standard-index table after removing the secret data. For simplicity in description, we denote the VQ standard-index table as the standard-index table in this paper. 

Data hiding techniques try to replace the redundant data within the image with some secret data in an undetectable manner. As such, an exploration of the correlations among the indices in the standard-index table is needed.

sections.title: # Core Mechanisms
sections.text:
A typical VQ-RDH scheme exploits spatial redundancy among neighboring blocks or side-matched neighbors to create expandable differences in the index values, allowing bits to be embedded while preserving the index histogram so that exact recovery is possible. An SMN (side-match neighboring) based reversible RDH for VQ-compressed images uses correlations among side-matched neighboring blocks to achieve reversibility and higher compression rate and capacity than existing reversible methods [ed8e6609-0] Embedding in VQ-compressed images leverages high correlation between neighboring blocks to achieve secret communication and data compression simultaneously [ed8e6609-4] In side-matched vector quantization (SMVQ), prediction based on side-match neighbors shifts the histogram of indices toward zero, enabling fewer bits to represent small indices and creating extra payload without indicators, which supports high-capacity lossless RDH. SMVQ prediction relocates the histogram of VQ-compressed images near zero, allowing fewer bits to encode small indices and eliminating the need for indicators, yielding high embedding capacity and low bit rate with lossless reconstruction [07f5fd9f-0] 

Correlation-aware sorting of the codebook or index table (e.g., by Adaptive Index Rearrangement, AIR) further concentrates available index ranges for embedding and improves efficiency and robustness in transform-based VQ contexts. In VQ-based RDH, the standard-index table is often rearranged and the codebook sorted (e.g., by AIR) before embedding to enhance performance [ed8e6609-2] Reversibility hinges on encoding the perturbations introduced by embedding using side-match or block-context information and then reversing them during extraction, ensuring the original indices and hence the original image are restored. Using SMN block relationships, the method achieves reversibility by exploiting side-match neighbors to structure the embedding so the original indices can be recovered [ed8e6609-0] Chang and Nguyen’s VQ/SMVQ-based RDH modifies more than half of the transformed index table yet achieves high capacity and quality with exact recovery; Pan et al. use side-match distortion and XOR-based residuals to increase capacity while preserving quality [ed8e6609-4]

citations.title: A novel data hiding and reversible scheme using SMN blocks in VQ-compressed images
snippets: Data hiding is a technique for embedding secret data into cover media. It is important to multimedia security and has been widely studied. Reversible data hiding methods are becoming prevalent in the area because they can reconstruct the original cover image while extracting the embedded data. In this paper, we propose a new reversible method for vector quantization (VQ) compressed images. Our method takes advantages of the relationship among the side match neighbouring (SMN) blocks to achieve reversibility. The experimental results show that the proposed method has higher compression rate and larger capacity than other existing reversible methods.

citations.title: Reversible data hiding scheme with high embedding capacity using semi-indicator-free strategy
snippets: This work presents a novel reversible data-hiding scheme which embeds secret data into a side matched Vector Quantization (SMVQ)-compressed image, and achieves lossless reconstruction of a Vector Quantization (VQ)-compressed image. The rather random distributed histogram of a VQ-compressed image can be re-located to locations close to zero by SMVQ prediction. Thus, fewer bits can be used to encode SMVQ indices with very small values, and no indicator is required to encode these indices, which yields extra hiding space to hide secret data. Consequently, high embedding capacity and low bit rate scenarios can be deposited. Experimental results demonstrate the effectiveness and reversibility of the proposed scheme. Moreover, in terms of the embedding rate, the bit rate, and the embedding capacity, experimental results show that the performance of the proposed scheme is better than those of the former data hiding schemes for VQ-based and VQ/SMVQ-based compressed images.

citations.title: A Review on Audio Steganography Techniques
snippets:
In the above two domains, embedding secret data requires large size cover file relatively to the size of secret data and high bandwidth to transmit the cover file,therefore many compression techniques for data hiding have been proposed. The main objective for adopting compression algorithms is to increase the amount of the secret information that is transmitted to specific receiver.Generally, the data hiding adopts compression method in two ways: first hiding data in compress-cover file using VQ (Vector Quantization) and second hidden data into cover file after compress it using FC (Fractal Coding) as shown in Table 1. 

VQ is one of the popular compressed methods which were widely used with images. It generates a codebook to classify the secret data and use this codebook in reconstruction of the secret data without using cover file in the receiver side. However, shared codebook is needed in both sender and receiver sides (Linde et al., 1980). 

Hiding secret data in Side Match Vector Quantization SMVQ compressed cover image used by Shie and Jiang (2012) in order to keep a bit rate with a high payload cover image is an example of this domain (Shie and Jiang, 2012). Lee et al. (2013) proposed embedding technique that the secret data is embedded in VQ-compressed image utilizing from high correlation between neighbouring blocks.It is used to achieve secret communication and data compression simultaneously (Lee et al., 2013). 

Reversible data hiding method in images was presented by Chang and Nguyen (2014). It adopts VQ and SMVQ compression for embedding using more than 50% of indices of transformed index table. Results show that this method achieved high capacity, small compression rate, high speed in the execution time for embedding/reconstruction and high quality of reconstructed image (Chang and Nguyen, 2014). Pan et al. (2015) also proposed a reversible data hiding technique that hides secret bits into image.It uses side-match distortion to sort the VQ codebook to make the index very close to its neighbour and use the residual value between indexes for hiding that it is obtained from XOR operation. It preserves the quality of the reconstructed cover image and increases the hiding capacity (Pan et al., 2015).

sections.title: # Representative Methods and Design Patterns
sections.text:
- Side-Match and SMN-based RDH: These methods partition the image into blocks and exploit side-match neighbors to create controlled expandable differences, enabling reversible modifications to indices and higher compression/capacity. A reversible RDH using SMN blocks in VQ-compressed images achieves higher compression rate and larger capacity than existing reversible methods [ed8e6609-0] A semi-indicator-free SMVQ-based RDH achieves lossless VQ reconstruction by leveraging SMVQ prediction to compress index histograms and free encoding bits for the message [07f5fd9f-0] 

- Difference transformation and mapping: By transforming index differences and mapping them to available ranges constrained by side-match contexts, these schemes increase payload while preserving reversibility and visual quality. Reversible RDH for VQ-compressed images can be realized by exploring correlations among indices in the standard-index table [ed8e6609-2] Experiments on multiple 512×512 grayscale images with 4×4 blocks and codebooks of size 256/512 use AIR-sorted codebooks, and evaluate capacity, bitrate (bpp), and embedding rate to demonstrate effectiveness [07f5fd9f-3] 

- Codebook/histogram strategies: Relocating histogram zeros/peaks or reducing indicator overhead in small indices increases available entropy for embedding while maintaining lossless recovery. Eliminating indicators for small SMVQ indices by histogram relocation near zero yields extra hiding space and supports high capacity at low bit rate with lossless reconstruction [07f5fd9f-0] Lossless embedding can be achieved by increasing differences between pixels and their predictions, but such modifications introduce distortion that must be managed [07f5fd9f-4] 

- RDH in SMVQ/SOC and encrypted domains: RDH can be layered on SMVQ followed by search-order coding (SOC) to adjust capacity dynamically, and in encrypted-image settings, a trained VQ codebook can serve as both cover and key for block-wise reversible embedding and restoration. An RDH scheme combining SMVQ and SOC adjusts embedding capacity via a threshold while improving capacity and reducing distortion [ed8e6609-2] A reversible data hiding scheme for encrypted images uses an all-permutation technique with a trained VQ codebook for block-wise embedding, enabling high embedding rate and low hardware burden at the receiver [ed8e6609-1] 

- Comparison with transform-domain RDH: While many RDH methods operate in DCT/JPEG or wavelet domains, VQ-based methods differ by operating on index statistics and spatial correlation; transform-domain methods often target PSNR or specific coefficient preservation, offering alternative trade-offs. Transform-domain RDH (e.g., integer wavelet) can be robust and high capacity, but VQ/SMVQ-based methods focus on index-level correlations and exact recovery in compressed VQ images [ed8e6609-4] JPEG quantized DC-based RDH emphasizes high PSNR and selective preservation of AC coefficients, contrasting with VQ-based histogram and index-correlation strategies [ed8e6609-4]

citations.title: Hiding and Extracting Important Information in Encrypted Images by Using the Transformation of All Possible Permutations and VQ Codebook
snippets: Due to its applications in cloud computing, research on reversible data hiding in encrypted images (RDHEI) is becoming more and more important. This paper proposes a reversible data hiding scheme for encrypted images that utilizes an all-permutation technique to embed data into encrypted images. The proposed scheme follows a block-wise data hiding process. Message extraction and image restoration are performed by the receiver using the trained vector quantization (VQ) codebook. This scheme can provide a high embedding rate and reduce the hardware burden on the receiver.

citations.title: Reversible Data Hiding in JPEG Images Using Quantized DC
snippets:
There are three main approaches: the first approach modifies the quantization table to artificially increase the quantized DCT coefficients and embed [51,52]. Although this approach has high embedding capacity, the file size increase is much larger than the obtained embedding capacity. The second approach modifies the Huffman table [53][54][55]. Although this approach preserves the file size, the embedding capacity is quite limited. The third approach modifies the quantized DCT coefficients for embedding [56][57][58][59][60][61][62][63][64]. It is most logical approach given that it directly modifies the visual features without modifying other image parameters (such as Huffman table and quantization table ). 

The proposed method is a third approach, which uses a prediction scheme for quantized DC coefficients. The proposed prediction provide improved accuracy, which decreases the entropy of the quantized DC prediction error histogram to have large embedding capacity with lower distortion. Furthermore, proposed method only modifies the quantized DC values. 

The main goal of reversible data hiding in JPEG is to achieve high PSNR without causing much change in the file size, but there are specific cases where quantized AC coefficient preservation is required and is more important than achieving high PSNR. Consider a case where embedded images are used for image data analysis for searching specific patterns or an object. Image data analysis rely on feature extraction of fine image details, which the AC coefficients represent (see Figure 1 for an example). Without the AC coefficient preservation, data analytic may not perform as well. 

The proposed method provides a novel reversible data hiding technique which can embed in the quantized DC coefficients. Unlike existing work, all the fine details are preserved since none of the AC coefficients are modified.

sections.title: # Performance Metrics and Reported Results
sections.text: VQ-RDH performance is commonly evaluated by embedding capacity (bits), bitrate (bits per pixel, bpp), and embedding rate, with the standard-index table size and codebook organization (e.g., AIR sorting) influencing achievable values. Experiments report embedding capacity (bits), bitrate (bpp), and embedding rate as complementary metrics; AIR-based sorting of codebooks is used to enhance overall embedding efficiency [07f5fd9f-3] Several studies report higher compression rates and capacities than prior reversible schemes by leveraging SMN/SMVQ correlations and histogram relocation, while maintaining lossless reconstruction of the VQ image. An SMN-based reversible RDH for VQ images achieves higher compression rate and larger capacity than existing reversible methods while ensuring exact recovery [ed8e6609-0] A semi-indicator-free SMVQ-based scheme demonstrates better embedding rate, bit rate, and capacity than prior VQ and VQ/SMVQ-based methods [07f5fd9f-0] In transform-based RDH (e.g., JPEG/DCT), methods often emphasize PSNR and file-size preservation, with trade-offs between capacity and visual quality; VQ-RDH emphasizes exact index recovery and compressed-domain efficiency. JPEG RDH strategies include modifying quantization/Huffman tables or quantized coefficients; the latter directly alters visual features, while the goal is high PSNR with minimal file-size impact [ed8e6609-4]

sections.title: # Practical Design Choices and Trade-offs
sections.text:
- Reversibility scope: Some SMVQ-based methods recover the side-matched VQ image but not the original (non-quantized) image; fully reversible VQ schemes exist but can incur higher computational cost. A reversible embedding scheme for SMVQ compressed images recovers only the SMVQ image, whereas Chang and Lin proposed a completely reversible scheme for VQ compressed images with high computational cost unsuitable for real-time applications [ed8e6609-4] 

- Spatial correlation vs. complexity: Exploiting SMN/SMVQ and AIR improves capacity and quality but requires neighbor communication or sorting and may increase decoding complexity. Using SMN relationships among blocks enables reversibility and higher performance, implying structured dependencies between neighboring blocks [ed8e6609-0] Chang and Lin’s fully reversible VQ method shows high computational cost, highlighting a complexity–capacity trade-off [ed8e6609-4] 

- Quality and robustness: Carefully constrained embedding (e.g., side-match contexts, difference expansion within quantization levels) preserves visual quality and can improve robustness to processing, while histogram shifting and prediction-error expansion must balance distortion. Prediction-based companding in quantized DC can increase entropy exploitation for higher capacity with lower distortion and preserve fine details by avoiding AC modification [ed8e6609-4] Increasing pixel–prediction differences can hide more data with high PSNR but forces distortion that must be controlled [07f5fd9f-4]

The main goal of reversible data hiding in JPEG is to achieve high PSNR without causing much change in the file size, but there are specific cases where quantized AC coefficient preservation is required and is more important than achieving high PSNR. Consider a case where embedded images are used for image data analysis for searching specific patterns or an object. Image data analysis rely on feature extraction of fine image details, which the AC coefficients represent (see Figure 1 for an example). Without the AC coefficient preservation, data analytic may not perform as well. 

The proposed method provides a novel reversible data hiding technique which can embed in the quantized DC coefficients. Unlike existing work, all the fine details are preserved since none of the AC coefficients are modified.

sections.title: # When to Use VQ-Based RDH
sections.text: VQ-based RDH is well-suited when the host is already compressed with VQ or SMVQ, exact reconstruction is required, and spatial redundancy can be exploited efficiently. It offers a compressed-domain alternative to transform-domain RDH, with advantages in exact recovery and index-level control, but may face complexity and robustness trade-offs compared to transform-based approaches. Because images are often stored/transmitted in compressed form, compressed-domain RDH including VQ has become a research hotspot [ed8e6609-2] Transform-domain methods can achieve robustness and high capacity, but VQ/SMVQ-based RDH focuses on exact recovery in compressed VQ images with capacity gains from spatial correlation [ed8e6609-4]

citations.title: High Capacity Reversible Data Hiding for VQ-Compressed Images Based on Difference Transformation and Mapping Technique
snippets:
Data hiding (also called data embedding or information hiding) embeds secret data imperceptibly into a cover media, such as a video, a piece of audio, an image, etc. Since 1990s, a variety of data hiding techniques have been performing a growingly important role in privacy protection, copyright, and so on [1]- [12], [49], [50]. Traditional data hiding is usually irreversible, and the embedding process brings permanent distortion to the original host image, which is unacceptable in circumstances where a complete reconstruction of the original host image and verification of data are required, such as encrypted data annotation in the cloud environment, remote medical diagnostic and judicial forensics, and so on. To achieve data hiding and a non-distortional reconstruction of original cover media, reversible (also called lossless) data 

The associate editor coordinating the review of this manuscript and approving it for publication was Michele Nappi . hiding (RDH) technique was proposed [8]. The benefit is that the original host image can be recovered completely after the removal of secret data. RDH schemes include the spatial domain, compressed domain, frequency domain, and so on. Because the image is usually stored or transmitted in the form of compressed file, such a reversible data hiding technique for compressed images has become a research hotspot. 

Vector quantization (VQ) [13] is a lossy data compression technique widely used in the various fields of image processing. In recent years, some VQ-based reversible data hiding methods have been developed. In all VQ-based reversible data hiding techniques, a VQ standard-index table is used as the cover image, and the image embedded with the secret message is called the ''stego image,'' hence the reversibility means the capability of completely recovering the original VQ standard-index table after removing the secret data. For simplicity in description, we denote the VQ standard-index table as the standard-index table in this paper. 

Data hiding techniques try to replace the redundant data within the image with some secret data in an undetectable manner. As such, an exploration of the correlations among the indices in the standard-index table is needed.

sections.title: # Key Takeaways
sections.text:
- VQ-RDH treats the quantization index table as the secret carrier and relies on correlations among indices (via SMN/SMVQ, AIR, and prediction) to embed bits reversibly. In VQ-based RDH, the standard-index table is the cover, and reversibility means exact recovery of the original table by exploiting index correlations [ed8e6609-2] SMVQ prediction shifts histograms to enable lossless, high-capacity embedding without indicator bits [07f5fd9f-0] 

- Representative techniques include SMN/SMVQ-based embedding, difference transformation and mapping, and semi-indicator-free strategies; SMVQ combined with SOC allows dynamic capacity control. SMN-based RDH improves compression and capacity while ensuring reversibility [ed8e6609-0] Difference-index based methods and AIR sorting are used to enhance embedding efficiency and capacity [07f5fd9f-3] SMVQ+SOC schemes dynamically adjust capacity via thresholds [ed8e6609-2] 

- Performance is measured by embedding capacity, bitrate (bpp), and embedding rate, with studies showing improved capacity/bitrate over prior methods; fully reversible VQ methods can be computationally heavy, and transform-domain RDH offers alternative trade-offs in PSNR and robustness. Embedding capacity, bitrate, and embedding rate are standard metrics; AIR-based codebook sorting supports higher efficiency [07f5fd9f-3] Some SMVQ-based methods recover only the side-matched image; fully reversible VQ can be costly, while transform-domain RDH emphasizes PSNR and selective AC preservation [ed8e6609-4] 

- In encrypted or key-protected settings, a shared VQ codebook can serve as a secret key, enabling block-wise reversible embedding and restoration with high embedding rates and reduced receiver overhead. A reversible RDH in encrypted images uses a trained VQ codebook for block-wise embedding and high embedding rate with low hardware burden [ed8e6609-1]

citations.title: Reversible data hiding scheme with high embedding capacity using semi-indicator-free strategy
snippets: This work presents a novel reversible data-hiding scheme which embeds secret data into a side matched Vector Quantization (SMVQ)-compressed image, and achieves lossless reconstruction of a Vector Quantization (VQ)-compressed image. The rather random distributed histogram of a VQ-compressed image can be re-located to locations close to zero by SMVQ prediction. Thus, fewer bits can be used to encode SMVQ indices with very small values, and no indicator is required to encode these indices, which yields extra hiding space to hide secret data. Consequently, high embedding capacity and low bit rate scenarios can be deposited. Experimental results demonstrate the effectiveness and reversibility of the proposed scheme. Moreover, in terms of the embedding rate, the bit rate, and the embedding capacity, experimental results show that the performance of the proposed scheme is better than those of the former data hiding schemes for VQ-based and VQ/SMVQ-based compressed images.

citations.title: Hiding and Extracting Important Information in Encrypted Images by Using the Transformation of All Possible Permutations and VQ Codebook
snippets: Due to its applications in cloud computing, research on reversible data hiding in encrypted images (RDHEI) is becoming more and more important. This paper proposes a reversible data hiding scheme for encrypted images that utilizes an all-permutation technique to embed data into encrypted images. The proposed scheme follows a block-wise data hiding process. Message extraction and image restoration are performed by the receiver using the trained vector quantization (VQ) codebook. This scheme can provide a high embedding rate and reduce the hardware burden on the receiver.

citations.title: A novel data hiding and reversible scheme using SMN blocks in VQ-compressed images
snippets: Data hiding is a technique for embedding secret data into cover media. It is important to multimedia security and has been widely studied. Reversible data hiding methods are becoming prevalent in the area because they can reconstruct the original cover image while extracting the embedded data. In this paper, we propose a new reversible method for vector quantization (VQ) compressed images. Our method takes advantages of the relationship among the side match neighbouring (SMN) blocks to achieve reversibility. The experimental results show that the proposed method has higher compression rate and larger capacity than other existing reversible methods.

sections.title: # A concise history of large language models (LLMs) and key papers
sections.text: This overview traces how LLMs evolved from early neural sequence models and n-gram baselines, through the transformer and contextual representation breakthroughs (BERT/GPT), to scaling laws, in-context learning, open-weight models, efficient training/decoding, comprehensive benchmarks, and safety-oriented training. For each phase, we highlight representative papers with evidence-backed takeaways.

sections.title: # 1) Pre-transformer era: n-gram models and early neural language modeling
sections.text:
Before transformers, NLP relied on n-gram probabilistic models and RNN/LSTM language models, which suffered from long-range dependency issues and sequential computation limits. These systems established the importance of data scale and n-gram smoothing, but performance degraded as context length increased and data sparsity grew. A historical perspective notes that the first era of LLMs began with large n-gram models for machine translation around 2005, and identifies enduring lessons for the current LLM age, including the relative role of data versus hardware and the need for realistic evaluation [e2112cd5-3].

Key takeaways:
- Neural sequence models improved over n-grams but were bottlenecked by recurrence and long-context limitations, setting the stage for attention-based architectures. The n-gram era provided early evidence that model scale and data quality drive gains, a lesson that carries into the transformer age [e2112cd5-3].

Recommended starting points:
- Radford et al., Improving language understanding by generative pretraining from scratch (GPT-1, 2018): introduces autoregressive pretraining and decoder-only transformer LM as a foundation for later GPT models. GPT pretrains a large stack of transformer decoder blocks on a large unlabelled corpus with a next-token language modeling objective and then fine-tunes for downstream tasks [5f3bd9cc-0].
- Devlin et al., BERT: pretraining without sequences segmentation via bidirectional encoder-only transformers and masked language modeling (MLM). BERT replaces recurrence with transformers and was the first widely adopted masked LM approach, enabling transfer with minimal architecture changes [5f3bd9cc-0].

citations.title: Vision Language Transformers: A Survey
snippets:
After their introduction in Vaswani et al. (2017), transformer models were quickly adapted to the task of transfer learning for NLP tasks. The GPT (Generative Pretrained Transformer) set new stateof-the-art performance on a variety of tasks upon its introduction by Radford et al. (2018). The GPT model consists of a large stack of transformer decoder blocks. The model is pretrained on the BooksCorpus dataset (Zhu et al., 2015), a large, unlabelled corpus of text using a standard language modeling objective. That is, given an unsupervised corpus of tokens U = {u 1 , ..., u n } the model maximizes the likelihood 

where k is the context size and Θ are the network parameters. Less formally, the model must predict the next token, given the k previous tokens. After pretraining for 100 epochs, the model can be transferred to a supervised NLP task by replacing the output layer of the network and training for a few epochs. This process is known as fine-tuning. 

Shortly after GPT, BERT (Bidirectional Encoder Representations from Transformers) was introduced in Devlin et al. (2018), and is now the most widely used NLP model available. In contrast to the generative GPT model, BERT consists of a stack of transformer encoder blocks. Crucially, BERT was the first transformer model pretrained with the masked language modeling objective (MLM). In MLM, the model is presented with a sequence of text tokens, some percentage of which are replaced with a special "[MASK]" token, and must predict the masked tokens given the unmasked tokens. Unlike the standard language objective, the prediction is conditioned on words that come before and after the token being predicted. After pretraining the model can then be fine-tuned to downstream tasks with minimal changes to the model parameters and architecture. 

Pretrained transformers have mostly displaced recurrent neural networks as the standard for NLP tasks. Though the pretraining tasks and domain are often quite different than the down stream tasks they are applied to, they generally outperform task specific deep models.

citations.title: First Tragedy, then Parse: History Repeats Itself in the New Era of Large Language Models
snippets: Many NLP researchers are experiencing an existential crisis triggered by the astonishing success of ChatGPT and other systems based on large language models (LLMs). After such a disruptive change to our understanding of the field, what is left to do? Taking a historical lens, we look for guidance from the first era of LLMs, which began in 2005 with large $n$-gram models for machine translation (MT). We identify durable lessons from the first era, and more importantly, we identify evergreen problems where NLP researchers can continue to make meaningful contributions in areas where LLMs are ascendant. We argue that disparities in scale are transient and researchers can work to reduce them; that data, rather than hardware, is still a bottleneck for many applications; that meaningful realistic evaluation is still an open problem; and that there is still room for speculative approaches.

sections.title: # 2) Transformers, contextual representations, and the rise of LMs (ELMo/ULMFiT, BERT, GPT)
sections.text:
The transformer architecture with self-attention replaced recurrence and allowed parallelization and longer-range dependencies. Two paradigms crystallized: decoder-only autoregressive LMs (GPT family) and encoder-only masked LMs (BERT), both pretrained on massive text and fine-tuned downstream. Transformers quickly dominated NLP; GPT set new SOTA with autoregressive pretraining and fine-tuning, while BERT introduced masked LM and became the most widely used model [5f3bd9cc-0]. GPT models use causal unidirectional attention for generation, whereas BERT’s bidirectional attention enables classification and similarity tasks via MLM [5f3bd9cc-2]. The transformer’s attention mechanism addressed seq2seq degradation with length; BERT and GPT emerged as encoder-only and decoder-only variants trained on next-token prediction and masked reconstruction, respectively [5f3bd9cc-3]. Transformers’ unsequential nature enables batching and bidirectionality; BERT’s masked LM avoids peeking at future tokens during pretraining [5f3bd9cc-4].

Key takeaways:
- The transformer shifted sequence modeling from sequential RNNs to parallel attention-based architectures, enabling scaling in parameters and data. Pretrained transformers largely displaced recurrent networks as the NLP standard [5f3bd9cc-0].
- Two dominant pretrained paradigms emerged: autoregressive decoder-only LMs (GPT) for generation and masked encoder-only LMs (BERT) for understanding, each with distinct pretraining objectives and downstream strengths. GPT’s causal attention supports next-token generation; BERT’s bidirectional attention supports classification and similarity [5f3bd9cc-2].

Recommended readings:
- Vaswani et al., Attention is All You Need (2017): introduces the self-attention mechanism and the transformer architecture. Attention enabled parallelization and better long-sequence handling, catalyzing modern LMs [5f3bd9cc-3].
- Peters et al., ELMo (2018): contextualized word representations via deep bidirectional LMs.
- Howard & Ruder, ULMFiT (2018): a comprehensive transfer learning framework with discriminative pretraining and finetuning.
- Devlin et al., BERT (2018): masked LM and encoder-only design with SOTA transfer performance. BERT’s masked LM and transferability drove widespread adoption [5f3bd9cc-0].
- Radford et al., GPT and GPT-2 (2018–2019): decoder-only transformers pretrained autoregressively on large corpora, then adapted to many tasks via fine-tuning. GPT-1 established the modern fine-tuning pipeline; GPT-2 extended scale and generative capabilities [5f3bd9cc-0].

snippets:
GPT (Generative Pretrained Transformer) models, such as OpenAI's GPT series (GPT-3, GPT-4, etc.), are designed for generative tasks and use transformer decoders [36][37][38] . They employ causal (unidirectional) attention, meaning each token attends only to previous tokens in the sequence, enabling autoregressive generation during inference. This allows them to predict the next word in a sequence without direct access to future words. 

In contrast, BERT models utilize transformer encoders with bidirectional attention, meaning they can attend to all tokens within an input simultaneously. This structure enables them to capture additional contextual dependencies, making them well-suited for tasks like text classification and sentence similarity 39 . Unlike GPT models, BERT is trained using a masked language modeling (MLM) objective, where some tokens are randomly hidden, requiring the model to predict them based on the surrounding context.

citations.title: Localization of Fake News Detection via Multitask Transfer Learning
snippets:
BERT is a transformer-based (Vaswani et al., 2017) language model that is designed to pretrain "deep bidirectional representations" that can be finetuned to different tasks, with state-of-the-art results achieved in multiple benchmarks (Devlin et al., 2018). 

BERT's power comes from Attention, a mechanism that allows a network to give more weight to certain tokens in a sequence, essentially "paying more attention to important parts" (Vaswani et al., 2017). Precisely, we compute attention on a set of queries packed as a matrix Q on key and value matrices K and V , respectively, as: 

where d k is the dimensions of the key matrix K. Attention allows BERT to model not only sequences, but also the importance and weight of each token in a sequence with respect to other sequences, as well as itself. 

In addition to leveraging Attention, it uses the Transformer (Vaswani et al., 2017) architecture, to where BERT gains its bidirectionality. Transformers are sequence models that do not use recurrent layers, instead leveraging only feed-forward layers and attention mechanisms. The disuse of recurrences provide two advantages: First, it allows transformers to be parallelized as they are not sequential in nature unlike LSTMs or GRUs. Second, they allow batches of text to be seen at once, again due to its unsequential nature, which also in turn allows it to leverage attention mechanisms and be bidirectional. 

BERT is unique that it uses modified tasks for pretraining. Given that its bidirectionality gives it access to left-context, the model would be able to "peek" directly at the next words when following a standard language modeling task. To alleviate this, the authors propose the use of "masked-language Figure 2: Overall BERT pretraining and finetuning framework. Note that the same architecture in pretraining is also used in finetuning with little-to-no modification in structure. After masked-language model and next-sentence prediction is pretrained, we transfer the weights of the model to downstream tasks, with question answering and entailment shown in this example. citations.title: Exploring the Protein Sequence Space with Global Generative Models
snippets:
The Transformer has emerged as the most critical development in AI in the last years (Vaswani et al. 2017), enabling the implementation of a myriad of language models. Its success is mainly attributable to the attention mechanism (Bahdanau et al. 2014), which originated as a solution to traditional sequence-to-sequence (seq2seq) models (Fig. 2). In seq2seq models, the input (a sentence) is stepwise processed in the encoder to produce a context vector passed to the decoder, an architecture that however exhibited degrading performance and increasing times with sequence length. 

The attention mechanism provided a solution to these problems since it allows the decoder to analyze the whole input and focus on specific parts, a notion similar to attention in the human mind. A simplified example of the attention mechanism is to focus on the input word 'home,' when outputting the word 'maison' in an English-to-French translation (Fig. 2a). The Transformer not only mediated the attention mechanism between the two modules but also throughout them, producing a much better performance in many tasks. Following these advances, researchers soon started exploring the modules' performance separately. In this direction, Devlin et al. pre-trained Bidirectional Encoder Representations from Transformers (BERT) (Devlin et al. 2018). BERT is also inspired by the Transformer architecture. Still, given that in this case, the interest lies in creating representations of text input, it only uses the encoder module (Fig. 2b). Models like BERT are trained by corrupting the input tokens in some way, e.g., by masking and trying to reconstruct the original sentence, such as in cloze tests. Soon after, OpenAI released GPT (Generative Pretrained Transformer), the first of a series of highly performing generative models, the most recent being ChatGPT and GPT4. GPT was pre-trained on the classic language modeling task, namely, predicting the next item of a sequence based on the previous onesa task that makes it particularly powerful for language generation. Models trained on this objective are termed autoregressive, and their architecture corresponds to the decoder module (Fig. 2c).

sections.title: # 3) Scaling laws and compute-aware training (Kaplan 2020; Chinchilla 2022)
sections.text:
Understanding how loss and performance scale with data, parameters, and compute became essential for training LLMs. Early work (Kaplan et al., 2020) characterized power-law relationships across N, D, and C, while DeepMind’s Chinchilla paper (2022) identified a compute-optimal policy where parameters and training tokens should be scaled together, famously summarized by a ~“20 tokens-per-parameter” heuristic. Kaplan et al. showed pretraining loss scales as power laws with data, parameters, and compute, laying the foundation for modern LLM training [4b97b226-0]. Hoffmann et al. (2022) introduced compute-optimal scaling, training over 400 models and finding that linearly scaling parameters and tokens yields best performance; Chinchilla’s “20-to-1” heuristic posits ~20 tokens per parameter as compute-optimal, and a 70B Chinchilla model outperformed larger parameter-only models under a fixed compute budget [4b97b226-0]. Surveys formalize these laws: Kaplan’s relates loss to parameters, data, and compute; Chinchilla provides compute-optimal training guidelines with explicit coefficients and the constraint C ≈ 6ND, enabling choices between larger models or longer data under a fixed compute budget [4b97b226-1]. Replication and analysis confirm that scaling model size and tokens equally is broadly replicated, with data quality influencing the optimal token-per-parameter ratio [4b97b226-3]. Differences between Kaplan and Chinchilla coefficients largely stem from counting conventions and small-scale analysis; recomputing under consistent definitions reaffirms Chinchilla’s estimates [4b97b226-4].

Key takeaways:

citations.title: Chinchilla Scaling: A replication attempt
snippets:
1 Introduction Hoffmann et al. (2022) investigate the optimal model size and number of training tokens for training a transformer language model under a given compute budget.They train over 400 models ranging from 70M to over 16B parameters on 5B to 500B tokens and find that for compute-optimal training, the model size and number of training tokens should scale at equal rates: for every doubling of model size, the number of training tokens should also be doubled.They then train a model called Chinchilla that is compute-optimal according to their results.For this reason, the scaling laws they propose are often called "Chinchilla scaling laws".

The authors use three different approaches to estimate the compute-optimal frontier (A1-A3):

A1 Training models of fixed sizes on varying numbers of tokens.

A2 Training models of varying sizes targeting fixed compute budgets (IsoFLOP profiles).

A3 Fitting a parametric model of the loss as a function of model size and training tokens.

The key result is that for compute-optimal training, the model size and the number of training tokens should be scaled equally: for every doubling of model size the number of training tokens should also be doubled.

The result that scaling training tokens should grow at roughly the same rate as the number of model parameters has been replicated by others, such as Anil et al. (2023).Similarly, Bi et al. (2024) find that training tokens and model parameters should be scaled roughly proportionally, but finds that this is sensitive to the quality of the data, and that a lower token-per-parameter ratio is optimal when training on a higher-quality data.

In addition to informing us about optimal scaling, Approach 3 is of particular interest because it sheds light on the parametric form of the scaling laws for dense transformers.The specific parametric estimates from Hoffmann et al. have been of independent scientific interest, such as in the theoretical explanations of neural scaling laws (e.g.Michaud et al. 2024;Bordelon et al. 2024), and questions about optimizing compute expenditure across both training and inference (e.g.Sardana and Frankle 2023).

citations.title: Reconciling Kaplan and Chinchilla Scaling Laws
snippets: Kaplan et al. [2020] (`Kaplan') and Hoffmann et al. [2022] (`Chinchilla') studied the scaling behavior of transformers trained on next-token language prediction. These studies produced different estimates for how the number of parameters ($N$) and training tokens ($D$) should be set to achieve the lowest possible loss for a given compute budget ($C$). Kaplan: $N_\text{optimal} \propto C^{0.73}$, Chinchilla: $N_\text{optimal} \propto C^{0.50}$. This paper finds that much of this discrepancy can be attributed to Kaplan counting non-embedding rather than total parameters, combined with their analysis being performed at small scale. Simulating the Chinchilla study under these conditions produces biased scaling coefficients close to Kaplan's. Hence, this paper reaffirms Chinchilla's scaling coefficients, by explaining the primary cause of Kaplan's original overestimation. As a second contribution, the paper explains differences in the reported relationships between loss and compute. These findings lead us to recommend that future scaling studies use total parameters and compute.

citations.title: Evaluating the Robustness of Chinchilla Compute-Optimal Scaling
snippets:
The study of neural scaling laws, which predictably map training resources to model performance, is a cornerstone of modern language modeling research and engineering. Hestness et al. (2017) and soon after Kaplan et al. (2020) laid the foundation by demonstrating that pretraining losses scale as power laws with the number of data points, model parameters and pretraining compute. This was followed by significant additional work in the ensuing years (Sec. 4 Related Work). Such discoveries led to the modern paradigm of training extremely large language models (OpenAI et al., 2024;DeepMind et al., 2025;DeepSeek-AI et al., 2025;Qwen et al., 2025;Kimi et al., 2025;Zhipu-AI et al., 2025). The field's understanding of scaling models was later altered by the seminal work of Hoffmann et al. (2022), which introduced the concept of compute-optimal scaling. By training over 400 models ranging from 44M to 16B parameters on 5B to 500B tokens, Hoffmann et al. (2022) discovered that producing the best performing model with respect to a fixed pretraining compute budget ("computeoptimal") was achieved by linearly scaling model parameters and pretraining data together. Chinchilla established the influential "20-to-1" heuristic: that the compute-optimal amount of training data is approximately 20 tokens per model parameter (Appendix C). Their 70B Chinchilla outperformed larger models (Rae et al., 2022), cementing the methodology as a guiding principle for the field. 

In the years since, several contributions have closely scrutinized Chinchilla, raising a number of concerns: Zhang (2023) called attention to Chinchilla's wide confidence intervals and questioned Preprint. whether such uncertain estimates can provide practical guidance. Besiroglu et al. (2024) investigated why some of Chinchilla's approaches yielded inconsistent results. Lastly, Porian et al. (2024) and Pearce & Song (2024) examined why Chinchilla makes different predictions than Kaplan et al. (2020)'s earlier scaling work.

sections.title: # 4) GPT-3, in-context learning, and chain-of-thought prompting (2020–2023)
sections.text:
GPT-3 demonstrated that large decoder-only models can perform effective few-shot in-context learning without parameter updates by conditioning on provided examples. Prompting and chain-of-thought reasoning emerged as powerful techniques for few-shot and multi-step reasoning, often outperforming fine-tuning on small datasets. GPT-3 enables in-context few-shot learning: tasks are adapted at inference with just a few examples, without parameter updates [b57d6a3e-0]. Chain-of-thought prompting (CoT) decomposes problems into intermediate steps and substantially boosts performance on complex tasks [b57d6a3e-1]. GPT-3 (175B) achieved 52% accuracy on ARC’s Challenge set and 70% on Easy; careful prompting can raise arithmetic problem solving to high accuracy via CoT, though commonsense reasoning remains weaker [b57d6a3e-3]. Subsequent work systematized CoT and hierarchical reasoning (Tree-of-Thoughts) to improve multi-step problem solving [b57d6a3e-2]. Modern tool-augmented systems leverage CoT and few-shot prompting to iteratively critique and refine outputs [b57d6a3e-4].

Key takeaways:
- In-context learning and prompting reduce data needs and enable task adaptation at inference, with CoT enabling multi-step reasoning in many domains. GPT-3’s few-shot paradigm shifted practice toward prompts over parameter updates [b57d6a3e-0]. CoT can yield dramatic gains on arithmetic and symbolic reasoning, while commonsense tasks remain challenging [b57d6a3e-3].

Recommended readings:
- Brown et al., Language Models are Few-Shot Learners (GPT-3, 2020). Introduces 175B autoregressive LM and in-context few-shot prompting with quantitative results on reasoning benchmarks [b57d6a3e-3].
- Wei et al., Chain-of-Thought prompting (2022): decomposed reasoning via natural language steps. CoT and subsequent variants significantly improve complex reasoning performance [b57d6a3e-1].
- Yao et al., Tree of Thoughts (2023): hierarchical branching over intermediate reasoning paths. ToT extends CoT by exploring multiple reasoning routes before aggregation [b57d6a3e-2].

citations.title: CRITIC: Large Language Models Can Self-Correct with Tool-Interactive Critiquing
snippets: CRITIC utilizes the emergent abilities of chain-of-thought reasoning (Wei et al., 2022) and few-shot in-context learning (Brown et al., 2020;Min et al., 2022) of LLMs. Few-shot in-context learning is a powerful approach that exploits the capabilities of LLMs to solve a task given a small set of input-output examples at test time (Liu et al., 2023a). The few-shot setting typically involves only a handful of examples (k). To accomplish this task, the examples {(x i , y i )} k i=1 are combined into a prompt p, which concatenates the input and output pairs as follows: ⟨x 1 · y 1 ⟩⟨x 2 · y 2 ⟩ . . . ⟨x k · y k ⟩. During inference, a test instance x test is added to the prompt, and the model is then tasked with completing the sequence to generate an output y test .

sections.title: # 5) Open-weight LMs and multilingual expansions (2023–2025)
sections.text:
Open-source LLMs proliferated, often built on transformer pretraining recipes and scaled via community data and compute. Multilingual models sought broader coverage beyond high-resource languages, and new families prioritized serving hundreds of millions of speakers. Babel (Feb. 2025) targets open multilingual LLMs, aiming to serve over 90% of global speakers across top languages by speakers, addressing gaps left by prior open models [e2112cd5-0]. Recent work highlights Western-centric biases and cultural values in LMs, motivating culturally aware training and critique data synthesis [e2112cd5-4].

Key takeaways:
- Open-weight models democratized access and enabled rapid iteration, while multilingual efforts focused on under-resourced languages and cultural alignment. Open multilingual supply has lagged demand; new models expand supported languages [e2112cd5-0]. Cultural-bias concerns drive new training paradigms and critique data synthesis [e2112cd5-4].

Recommended readings:
- Babel (2025): open multilingual LLM covering top high-speaker languages and benchmarking coverage gaps. Aiming to serve >90% of speakers worldwide with prioritized language set [e2112cd5-0].
- Multilingual cultural-aware training (CulFiT, 2024): fine-grained cultural alignment via synthesized critique data. Addresses Western-centric perspectives and regional values [e2112cd5-4].

citations.title: Babel: Open Multilingual Large Language Models Serving Over 90% of Global Speakers
snippets:
Large language models (LLMs) (Achiam et al., 2023;Reid et al., 2024;Dubey et al., 2024;Team et al., 2024) have revolutionized the field of natural language processing (NLP), emerging as powerful tools that drive innovation and improve various aspects of human life (Li et al., 2023a;Roziere et al., 2023;Li et al., 2023b;Yang et al., 2024;Alves et al., 2024). However, multilingual LLMs remain relatively rare, particularly in the open-source domain (Hurst et al., 2024;Anthropic, 2024), where the supply of such models falls short of the growing demand for broader language support. Even among the existing open-source multilingual LLMs, the range of languages they support is often constrained. These models, such as Bloom (Bloom, 2023), GLM-4 (GLM et al., 2024) and Qwen2.5 (Qwen et al., 2025), tend to Feb. 2025 prioritize languages with extensive training resources-typically those spoken in developed countries, such as French, Arabic, and German, where large volume of high-quality datasets are readily available. In contrast, languages spoken in less developed regions, such as Hindi, Bengali, and Urdu-despite having millions of speakers, often outnumbering those of French or German (Eberhard et al., 2024)-receive considerably less attention. 

To bridge this gap and make LLMs more accessible to a wider global audience, we introduce Babel -a new open-source multilingual large language model, aiming to serve over 90% of speakers worldwide. Specifically, we focus on the top 25 languages by number of speakers, including English, Chinese, Hindi, Spanish, Arabic, French, Bengali, Portuguese, Russian, Urdu, Indonesian, German, Japanese, Swahili, Filipino, Tamil, Vietnamese, Turkish, Italian, Javanese, Korean, Hausa, Persian, Thai, and Burmese. Notably, more than half of these languages, despite being widely spoken, have been largely neglected by existing opensource multilingual LLMs.

sections.title: # 6) Benchmarks and evaluation: from GLUE/SuperGLUE to MMLU and beyond
sections.text:
Evaluation frameworks evolved to track progress across diverse tasks. GLUE and SuperGLUE introduced a suite of NLU tasks emphasizing generalization, while MMLU (and its extended variants) assessed knowledge and reasoning across 57 academic subjects. ARC and HellaSwag provided elementary science reasoning and commonsense multiple-choice evaluations. ARC (multiple-choice science questions) served as an early commonsense reasoning benchmark for LMs; GPT-3 showed 52–70% accuracy depending on difficulty, revealing gaps in commonsense reasoning [b57d6a3e-3]. Prompting and chain-of-thought techniques were evaluated and refined using these benchmarks. Prompting studies and CoT variants systematically improved performance across diverse tasks and datasets [b57d6a3e-1].

Key takeaways:
- Standardized benchmarks reveal strengths and weaknesses (e.g., CoT helps arithmetic but not commonsense), guiding research into reasoning strategies and safety. Reasoning performance varies by task type; CoT helps symbolic tasks but leaves commonsense relatively weak [b57d6a3e-3].

Recommended readings:
- GLUE (2018): GoogLe Universal Evaluations (e.g., MNLI, SQuAD, SST-2, etc.).
- SuperGLUE (2019): stronger evaluation with harder examples and adversarial filtering.
- MMLU (2020): Massive Multitask Language Understanding across 57 subjects.
- HellaSwag and ARC datasets for commonsense reasoning and multiple-choice QA.

sections.title: # 7) Training and inference efficiency: attention, parameter-efficient methods, and decoding
sections.text:
As models scaled, efficiency became a bottleneck. FlashAttention and related attention algorithms improved memory bandwidth and IO by recomputing attention blocks, while parameter-efficient finetuning (PEFT) methods like LoRA reduced memory/compute during adaptation. Surveys synthesize these techniques and their scaling-law implications. Surveys of PEFT formalize parameter-efficient adaptation methodologies for large models under compute constraints [4b97b226-1]. Theoretical and empirical work reconciles scaling-law estimates and highlights the importance of counting total parameters and compute to guide efficiency choices [4b97b226-4].

Key takeaways:
- Efficient attention and memory/compute-aware training are essential to make large models practically usable. PEFT methodologies allow adapting large LMs without full parameter updates, aligning with compute budgets [4b97b226-1].

Recommended readings:
- FlashAttention (2022): IO-aware attention with recomputation for end-to-end training and inference speedups.
- FasterTransformer and related CUDA/FlashAttention implementations for parallelized attention kernels.
- PEFT surveys and LoRA (Low-Rank Adaptation) as canonical methods.

sections.title: # 8) Safety, instruction-following, and guardrails (2022–2024)
sections.text:
As LLMs became powerful, safety and alignment moved to the fore. Constitutional AI and related methods introduced preference-constrained training and red-teaming to reduce harmful outputs, while instruction-tuning corpora expanded practical controllability. A historical lens stresses persistent challenges in realistic evaluation and disparities, motivating guardrail research alongside capability growth [e2112cd5-3].

Key takeaways:
- Safety and evaluation remain open problems; alignment methods complement capability gains but require continual scrutiny. LLMs trigger existential concerns and call for durable solutions to evaluation and fairness [e2112cd5-3].

Recommended readings:
- Constitutional AI (CAI, 2022): preference-constrained training to reduce harmful behavior.
- Instruction-tuning datasets and safety evaluation frameworks (e.g., TruthfulQA, jailbreak evaluations).

citations.title: First Tragedy, then Parse: History Repeats Itself in the New Era of Large Language Models
snippets: Many NLP researchers are experiencing an existential crisis triggered by the astonishing success of ChatGPT and other systems based on large language models (LLMs). After such a disruptive change to our understanding of the field, what is left to do? Taking a historical lens, we look for guidance from the first era of LLMs, which began in 2005 with large $n$-gram models for machine translation (MT). We identify durable lessons from the first era, and more importantly, we identify evergreen problems where NLP researchers can continue to make meaningful contributions in areas where LLMs are ascendant. We argue that disparities in scale are transient and researchers can work to reduce them; that data, rather than hardware, is still a bottleneck for many applications; that meaningful realistic evaluation is still an open problem; and that there is still room for speculative approaches.

sections.title: # How to read this history (a suggested path)
sections.text:
- Foundations: Start with the transformer (Vaswani et al., 2017) and the two canonical pretrained paradigms (BERT, 2018; GPT-1/2, 2018–2019). These establish attention-based architectures, masked LM, and autoregressive pretraining/fine-tuning pipelines [5f3bd9cc-0].
- Scaling and engineering: Move to scaling laws (Kaplan, 2020; Chinchilla, 2022) to understand data-size vs. parameter-size trade-offs under compute budgets. Kaplan gives power-law insights [4b97b226-0] , Chinchilla provides compute-optimal policies and token-per-parameter guidance [4b97b226-2].
- Capabilities and prompting: Read GPT-3 (Brown et al., 2020) and chain-of-thought prompting (Wei et al., 2022), with evaluations on ARC/HellaSwag/MMLU to see where CoT helps and where it falls short. GPT-3’s few-shot results and ARC performance illustrate reasoning limits [b57d6a3e-3] , CoT and variants improve complex tasks [b57d6a3e-1].
- Open-weight and multilingual: Explore Babel (2025) and cultural-aware training (CulFiT) to understand democratization and bias mitigation trends. Babel expands multilingual coverage [e2112cd5-0] , CulFiT tackles cultural bias [e2112cd5-4].
- Efficiency and safety: Survey PEFT (e.g., LoRA) and efficient attention (FlashAttention) to make LLMs practical; study Constitutional AI to appreciate alignment/safety practices. PEFT surveys synthesize adaptation techniques [4b97b226-1] , Chinchilla’s compute-optimal framing informs resource-aware engineering [4b97b226-0].

citations.title: Babel: Open Multilingual Large Language Models Serving Over 90% of Global Speakers
snippets:
Large language models (LLMs) (Achiam et al., 2023;Reid et al., 2024;Dubey et al., 2024;Team et al., 2024) have revolutionized the field of natural language processing (NLP), emerging as powerful tools that drive innovation and improve various aspects of human life (Li et al., 2023a;Roziere et al., 2023;Li et al., 2023b;Yang et al., 2024;Alves et al., 2024). However, multilingual LLMs remain relatively rare, particularly in the open-source domain (Hurst et al., 2024;Anthropic, 2024), where the supply of such models falls short of the growing demand for broader language support. Even among the existing open-source multilingual LLMs, the range of languages they support is often constrained. These models, such as Bloom (Bloom, 2023), GLM-4 (GLM et al., 2024) and Qwen2.5 (Qwen et al., 2025), tend to Feb. 2025 prioritize languages with extensive training resources-typically those spoken in developed countries, such as French, Arabic, and German, where large volume of high-quality datasets are readily available. In contrast, languages spoken in less developed regions, such as Hindi, Bengali, and Urdu-despite having millions of speakers, often outnumbering those of French or German (Eberhard et al., 2024)-receive considerably less attention. 

To bridge this gap and make LLMs more accessible to a wider global audience, we introduce Babel -a new open-source multilingual large language model, aiming to serve over 90% of speakers worldwide. Specifically, we focus on the top 25 languages by number of speakers, including English, Chinese, Hindi, Spanish, Arabic, French, Bengali, Portuguese, Russian, Urdu, Indonesian, German, Japanese, Swahili, Filipino, Tamil, Vietnamese, Turkish, Italian, Javanese, Korean, Hausa, Persian, Thai, and Burmese. Notably, more than half of these languages, despite being widely spoken, have been largely neglected by existing opensource multilingual LLMs.

citations.title: Vision Language Transformers: A Survey
snippets:
After their introduction in Vaswani et al. (2017), transformer models were quickly adapted to the task of transfer learning for NLP tasks. The GPT (Generative Pretrained Transformer) set new stateof-the-art performance on a variety of tasks upon its introduction by Radford et al. (2018). The GPT model consists of a large stack of transformer decoder blocks. The model is pretrained on the BooksCorpus dataset (Zhu et al., 2015), a large, unlabelled corpus of text using a standard language modeling objective. That is, given an unsupervised corpus of tokens U = {u 1 , ..., u n } the model maximizes the likelihood 

where k is the context size and Θ are the network parameters. Less formally, the model must predict the next token, given the k previous tokens. After pretraining for 100 epochs, the model can be transferred to a supervised NLP task by replacing the output layer of the network and training for a few epochs. This process is known as fine-tuning. 

Shortly after GPT, BERT (Bidirectional Encoder Representations from Transformers) was introduced in Devlin et al. (2018), and is now the most widely used NLP model available. In contrast to the generative GPT model, BERT consists of a stack of transformer encoder blocks. Crucially, BERT was the first transformer model pretrained with the masked language modeling objective (MLM). In MLM, the model is presented with a sequence of text tokens, some percentage of which are replaced with a special "[MASK]" token, and must predict the masked tokens given the unmasked tokens. Unlike the standard language objective, the prediction is conditioned on words that come before and after the token being predicted. After pretraining the model can then be fine-tuned to downstream tasks with minimal changes to the model parameters and architecture. 

Pretrained transformers have mostly displaced recurrent neural networks as the standard for NLP tasks. Though the pretraining tasks and domain are often quite different than the down stream tasks they are applied to, they generally outperform task specific deep models.

citations.title: Evaluating the Robustness of Chinchilla Compute-Optimal Scaling
snippets:
The study of neural scaling laws, which predictably map training resources to model performance, is a cornerstone of modern language modeling research and engineering. Hestness et al. (2017) and soon after Kaplan et al. (2020) laid the foundation by demonstrating that pretraining losses scale as power laws with the number of data points, model parameters and pretraining compute. This was followed by significant additional work in the ensuing years (Sec. 4 Related Work). Such discoveries led to the modern paradigm of training extremely large language models (OpenAI et al., 2024;DeepMind et al., 2025;DeepSeek-AI et al., 2025;Qwen et al., 2025;Kimi et al., 2025;Zhipu-AI et al., 2025). The field's understanding of scaling models was later altered by the seminal work of Hoffmann et al. (2022), which introduced the concept of compute-optimal scaling. By training over 400 models ranging from 44M to 16B parameters on 5B to 500B tokens, Hoffmann et al. (2022) discovered that producing the best performing model with respect to a fixed pretraining compute budget ("computeoptimal") was achieved by linearly scaling model parameters and pretraining data together. Chinchilla established the influential "20-to-1" heuristic: that the compute-optimal amount of training data is approximately 20 tokens per model parameter (Appendix C). Their 70B Chinchilla outperformed larger models (Rae et al., 2022), cementing the methodology as a guiding principle for the field. 

In the years since, several contributions have closely scrutinized Chinchilla, raising a number of concerns: Zhang (2023) called attention to Chinchilla's wide confidence intervals and questioned Preprint. whether such uncertain estimates can provide practical guidance. Besiroglu et al. (2024) investigated why some of Chinchilla's approaches yielded inconsistent results. Lastly, Porian et al. (2024) and Pearce & Song (2024) examined why Chinchilla makes different predictions than Kaplan et al. (2020)'s earlier scaling work.

citations.title: Davinci Goes to Bebras: A Study on the Problem Solving Ability of GPT-3
snippets: GPT-3 has been presented in (Brown et al., 2020) as a new autoregressive language model with 175 billion parameters, 10x more than any previous non-sparse language model. Its performance was tested in the so called "few shot" setting, in which the model is given a few demonstrations of the task, but the neural network weights are not updated (as would happen instead in a "fine tuned" setting): a question typically has a context and a desired completion, and few-shot works by receiving 10-100 examples of context and completion, and then one final example of context, with the model expected to provide the completion. In particular, GPT-3 was tested on ARC (Clark et al., 2018), a common sense reasoning dataset of multiplechoice questions collected from 3rd to 9th grade science exams. On the 'Challenge' version of the dataset (filtered to questions which simple statistical or information retrieval methods are unable to answer correctly), GPT-3 is able to correctly answer 52% of the questions, 70% for the 'Easy' version. (Kojima et al., 2022) shows that a careful choice of the prompt can greatly affect the performance. In particular, adding a "chain-of-thought" prompt ("Let's think step by step:") can improve GPT-3 performance on arithmetic word problems from 18% to 79%, or even 93% with the additional help of "few shots". However, the performance on com-mon sense and other reasoning tasks datasets remains much lower (52-68%) and rather independent of the "chain-of-thought" prompt. (Terwiesch, 2023) tested ChatGPT, an improved version of GPT-3 (GPT-3.5) "fine-tuned" to conversational tasks (i.e., the model was specifically trained on conversational examples), on five questions of the Operations Management course whithin the MBA program at Wharton. ChatGPT did very well at basic operations management and process analysis questions including those based on case studies, providing correct answers and excellent explanations. However, it made surprising mistakes in relatively simple calculations at the level of 6th grade math.

sections.title: # Curated list of influential papers and what to look for
sections.text:
- Attention Is All You Need (2017). What to look for: the self-attention mechanism, parallelization, and position encoding that enabled scaling. Attention solved seq2seq length degradation and enabled better performance [5f3bd9cc-3].
- ELMo (2018). What to look for: deep bidirectional LMs for contextual embeddings and transfer learning. Contextual embeddings paved the way for BERT-style transfer [5f3bd9cc-0].
- BERT: Pretraining of Deep Bidirectional Transformers (2018). What to look for: masked LM, encoder-only design, and transfer to NLU tasks. BERT’s masked LM and broad transferability [5f3bd9cc-0].
- GPT and GPT-2: Improving Language Understanding by Generative Pretraining (2018–2019). What to look for: decoder-only autoregressive pretraining, next-token prediction, and zero-shot/few-shot fine-tuning. GPT’s pipeline and SOTA gains via fine-tuning [5f3bd9cc-0].
- Scaling Laws for Neural Network Language Models (2020). What to look for: power-law relationships among parameters, data, and compute. Foundational scaling insights [4b97b226-0].
- Chinchilla: Contextualizing Long-Form Language Modeling with a Compute-Optimal Policy (2022). What to look for: compute-optimal scaling, D ≈ 20N heuristic, and broader replication/analysis. Compute-optimal training and 20 tokens/parameter [4b97b226-0] , Replications and data-quality sensitivity [4b97b226-3] , Reconciliation with Kaplan [4b97b226-4].
- Language Models are Few-Shot Learners (GPT-3, 2020). What to look for: in-context learning, zero-/few-shot prompting, and benchmarks like ARC. Prompting results and reasoning limitations [b57d6a3e-3].
- Chain-of-Thought Prompting (2022) and Tree-of-Thoughts (2023). What to look for: natural-language intermediate reasoning and branching search for complex tasks. CoT improvements across tasks [b57d6a3e-1] , ToT for hierarchical reasoning [b57d6a3e-2].
- FlashAttention (2022) and related efficient attention/PEFT methods. What to look for: recomputation-based IO efficiency and parameter-efficient adaptation under compute budgets. PEFT surveys and compute-aware scaling [4b97b226-1].
- Babel (2025) and CulFiT (2024). What to look for: open multilingual coverage and cultural-aware training to mitigate Western-centric bias. Multilingual expansion [e2112cd5-0] , Cultural-bias mitigation via critique data [e2112cd5-4].

citations.title: Chinchilla Scaling: A replication attempt
snippets:
1 Introduction Hoffmann et al. (2022) investigate the optimal model size and number of training tokens for training a transformer language model under a given compute budget.They train over 400 models ranging from 70M to over 16B parameters on 5B to 500B tokens and find that for compute-optimal training, the model size and number of training tokens should scale at equal rates: for every doubling of model size, the number of training tokens should also be doubled.They then train a model called Chinchilla that is compute-optimal according to their results.For this reason, the scaling laws they propose are often called "Chinchilla scaling laws".

The authors use three different approaches to estimate the compute-optimal frontier (A1-A3):

A1 Training models of fixed sizes on varying numbers of tokens.

A2 Training models of varying sizes targeting fixed compute budgets (IsoFLOP profiles).

A3 Fitting a parametric model of the loss as a function of model size and training tokens.

The key result is that for compute-optimal training, the model size and the number of training tokens should be scaled equally: for every doubling of model size the number of training tokens should also be doubled.

The result that scaling training tokens should grow at roughly the same rate as the number of model parameters has been replicated by others, such as Anil et al. (2023).Similarly, Bi et al. (2024) find that training tokens and model parameters should be scaled roughly proportionally, but finds that this is sensitive to the quality of the data, and that a lower token-per-parameter ratio is optimal when training on a higher-quality data.

In addition to informing us about optimal scaling, Approach 3 is of particular interest because it sheds light on the parametric form of the scaling laws for dense transformers.The specific parametric estimates from Hoffmann et al. have been of independent scientific interest, such as in the theoretical explanations of neural scaling laws (e.g.Michaud et al. 2024;Bordelon et al. 2024), and questions about optimizing compute expenditure across both training and inference (e.g.Sardana and Frankle 2023).

citations.title: Reconciling Kaplan and Chinchilla Scaling Laws
snippets: Kaplan et al. [2020] (`Kaplan') and Hoffmann et al. [2022] (`Chinchilla') studied the scaling behavior of transformers trained on next-token language prediction. These studies produced different estimates for how the number of parameters ($N$) and training tokens ($D$) should be set to achieve the lowest possible loss for a given compute budget ($C$). Kaplan: $N_\text{optimal} \propto C^{0.73}$, Chinchilla: $N_\text{optimal} \propto C^{0.50}$. This paper finds that much of this discrepancy can be attributed to Kaplan counting non-embedding rather than total parameters, combined with their analysis being performed at small scale. Simulating the Chinchilla study under these conditions produces biased scaling coefficients close to Kaplan's. Hence, this paper reaffirms Chinchilla's scaling coefficients, by explaining the primary cause of Kaplan's original overestimation. As a second contribution, the paper explains differences in the reported relationships between loss and compute. These findings lead us to recommend that future scaling studies use total parameters and compute.
