snippets:
In recent years, few-shot in-context learning has emerged as a pivotal area of research, particularly in the realm of natural language processing.This learning paradigm leverages pre-trained language models to generalize from a limited number of examples, effectively learning new tasks without extensive retraining.A seminal paper by Brown et al. [2020] demonstrated that large language models like GPT-3 could perform a variety of tasks in a few-shot manner by simply providing them with a prompt that includes a few examples of the task at hand.This approach has been further explored in various studies, such as Tam et al. [2021], which investigates strategies for selecting optimal examples to include in the prompt, enhancing the model's performance on the target task.These developments underscore the potential of few-shot learning to adapt large-scale models to specific applications with minimal data, making it a promising direction for resource-constrained scenarios.

The concepts of Chain of Thought (CoT) and Tree of Thought (ToT) represent advanced strategies for tackling complex reasoning tasks.The CoT method, introduced by Wei et al. [2023], involves prompting models to generate intermediate reasoning steps before arriving at a final answer, thereby mimicking human-like problem-solving processes.This approach has shown significant improvements in the model's ability to handle multi-step reasoning questions.Building on this, the Tree of Thought (ToT) framework extends the idea by structuring the reasoning process in a more hierarchical and branching manner, as discussed in Yao et al. [2023].This allows the model to explore multiple reasoning pathways and aggregate these to formulate a more robust conclusion.These methodologies not only enhance the interpretability of model decisions but also contribute to their robustness and accuracy in complex reasoning domains.

Its success is mainly attributable to the attention mechanism (Bahdanau et al. 2014), which originated as a solution to traditional sequence-to-sequence (seq2seq) models (Fig. 2). In seq2seq models, the input (a sentence) is stepwise processed in the encoder to produce a context vector passed to the decoder, an architecture that however exhibited degrading performance and increasing times with sequence length. 

The attention mechanism provided a solution to these problems since it allows the decoder to analyze the whole input and focus on specific parts, a notion similar to attention in the human mind. A simplified example of the attention mechanism is to focus on the input word 'home,' when outputting the word 'maison' in an English-to-French translation (Fig. 2a). The Transformer not only mediated the attention mechanism between the two modules but also throughout them, producing a much better performance in many tasks. Following these advances, researchers soon started exploring the modules' performance separately. In this direction, Devlin et al. pre-trained Bidirectional Encoder Representations from Transformers (BERT) (Devlin et al. 2018). BERT is also inspired by the Transformer architecture. Still, given that in this case, the interest lies in creating representations of text input, it only uses the encoder module (Fig. 2b). Models like BERT are trained by corrupting the input tokens in some way, e.g., by masking and trying to reconstruct the original sentence, such as in cloze tests. Soon after, OpenAI released GPT (Generative Pretrained Transformer), the first of a series of highly performing generative models, the most recent being ChatGPT and GPT4. GPT was pre-trained on the classic language modeling task, namely, predicting the next item of a sequence based on the previous onesa task that makes it particularly powerful for language generation. Models trained on this objective are termed autoregressive, and their architecture corresponds to the decoder module (Fig. 2c).

sections.title: # Perspective and open problems
sections.text:
Historical reviews argue that while LLMs have transformed NLP, enduring challenges include data bottlenecks for under-resourced languages, meaningful realistic evaluation, and fairness/bias. A historical lens across eras emphasizes that scale disparities are transient, data remains a bottleneck, and realistic evaluation is still open [e2112cd5-3]. Multilingual LLMs remain relatively rare in open source, with supply lagging demand for broader language support [e2112cd5-0]. Cultural-bias concerns motivate cultural-aware training and critique data synthesis [e2112cd5-4].

These threads—architectural advances, scaling laws, in-context learning, open-weight and multilingual expansion, efficient training/decoding, robust benchmarks, and safety—constitute the historical arc of LLMs from 2017 to the present, with active areas of research continuing to push capability, efficiency, and responsible deployment.

citations.title: Babel: Open Multilingual Large Language Models Serving Over 90% of Global Speakers
snippets:
Large language models (LLMs) (Achiam et al., 2023;Reid et al., 2024;Dubey et al., 2024;Team et al., 2024) have revolutionized the field of natural language processing (NLP), emerging as powerful tools that drive innovation and improve various aspects of human life (Li et al., 2023a;Roziere et al., 2023;Li et al., 2023b;Yang et al., 2024;Alves et al., 2024). However, multilingual LLMs remain relatively rare, particularly in the open-source domain (Hurst et al., 2024;Anthropic, 2024), where the supply of such models falls short of the growing demand for broader language support. Even among the existing open-source multilingual LLMs, the range of languages they support is often constrained. These models, such as Bloom (Bloom, 2023), GLM-4 (GLM et al., 2024) and Qwen2.5 (Qwen et al., 2025), tend to Feb. 2025 prioritize languages with extensive training resources-typically those spoken in developed countries, such as French, Arabic, and German, where large volume of high-quality datasets are readily available. In contrast, languages spoken in less developed regions, such as Hindi, Bengali, and Urdu-despite having millions of speakers, often outnumbering those of French or German (Eberhard et al., 2024)-receive considerably less attention. 

To bridge this gap and make LLMs more accessible to a wider global audience, we introduce Babel -a new open-source multilingual large language model, aiming to serve over 90% of speakers worldwide. Specifically, we focus on the top 25 languages by number of speakers, including English, Chinese, Hindi, Spanish, Arabic, French, Bengali, Portuguese, Russian, Urdu, Indonesian, German, Japanese, Swahili, Filipino, Tamil, Vietnamese, Turkish, Italian, Javanese, Korean, Hausa, Persian, Thai, and Burmese. Notably, more than half of these languages, despite being widely spoken, have been largely neglected by existing opensource multilingual LLMs.

citations.title: First Tragedy, then Parse: History Repeats Itself in the New Era of Large Language Models
snippets: Many NLP researchers are experiencing an existential crisis triggered by the astonishing success of ChatGPT and other systems based on large language models (LLMs). After such a disruptive change to our understanding of the field, what is left to do? Taking a historical lens, we look for guidance from the first era of LLMs, which began in 2005 with large $n$-gram models for machine translation (MT). We identify durable lessons from the first era, and more importantly, we identify evergreen problems where NLP researchers can continue to make meaningful contributions in areas where LLMs are ascendant. We argue that disparities in scale are transient and researchers can work to reduce them; that data, rather than hardware, is still a bottleneck for many applications; that meaningful realistic evaluation is still an open problem; and that there is still room for speculative approaches.

Digital transformation is no longer a luxury but a necessity for firms that wish to remain competitive. question: Arc fault feature extraction method

sections.title: # 1) Overview and sensing modalities
sections.text: Electrical arc-fault feature extraction typically analyzes voltage or current waveforms from a single phase to detect the distinctive signatures of arcing, especially series arcs that are hardest to detect yet most common in residential and light-industrial wiring. Traditional arc fault detection in photovoltaic systems relies on extracting features from current and voltage signals and classifying them with machine learning or classical detectors [59c679bd-0]. In practice, time–frequency domain analysis of voltage or current is the common feature extraction approach because direct photothermal measurements are usually impractical [37edf46d-0]. Load variability and background noise often mask arc signatures, making general-purpose features elusive and motivating multi-modal sensing and advanced transforms [37edf46d-3]. High-frequency coupling sensors can be used to capture arc-specific high-frequency characteristics for discrimination among different loads [37edf46d-0].

citations.title: A Novel Arc Fault Detector for Early Detection of Electrical Fires
snippets:
Because arc fault features are always hidden in the line currents, many advanced methods have been used to extract them. A Kalman filtering algorithm, artificial neural networks and fuzzy logic algorithms have been separately used to classify arc faults and normal states [40][41][42]. The harmonic components of arc fault currents have been analyzed [43,44]. The reconstructed information entropy of each current frequency band has been calculated to obtain the feature frequency bands of arc faults [45]. Arc fault currents have been decomposed based on the discrete wavelet transform (DWT), where the wavelet transform coefficients were used as fault features [46]. In one study, currents were first de-noised by DWT to improve the signal-to-noise ratio, and the current eigenvectors were then trained through wavelet networks to detect arc faults [47]. The Gabor Transform (GT) has been used to obtain an optimal feature extraction; the extracted GT coefficients of currents were used to identify arc faults [48]. 

However, arc fault currents are always strongly affected by different types of loads. Fault currents produced by certain home appliances do not change noticeably, and arc fault features are usually easily masked by load currents and background noise. It is difficult to find a general fault feature that performs well for all loads. Moreover, the residential electrical standard for single-phase alternating current (AC) is 120 V (60 Hz) in the United States, whereas it is 220-240 V (50-60 Hz) in other countries including China, Germany, Switzerland and Korea. Higher voltages more readily produce electrical fires caused by arc faults [49][50][51][52]. For example, the probability of fire ignition due to arc faults increases from 3.5% for 120 V to 83% for 240 V, and their nominal current levels are both 15 A [49]. Compared to 120 V, the higher voltages from 220 to 240 V are more likely to break down gaps and lead to more arcs [50,51]. Arc currents are usually continuous in higher voltage systems, but they are sometimes intermittent in 120 V systems [49,50]. Thus, higher voltage systems generate larger arc energy and thus provide better conditions for the ignition of electrical fires [50,51].

citations.title: Research on arc fault detection using ResNet and gamma transform regularization
snippets:
In recent years, the researches of arc fault detection are not limited to the arc mathematical model. In fact, some circuit parameters may have a mutation when an arc fault occurs. The purpose of fault detection can be achieved by identifying the circuit parameters as features. In practical application, it is difficult to collect the photothermal physical characteristics of the arc in real time due to the random arc generation. As a result, the common feature extraction method is time-frequency domain analysis of voltage or current. Fast Fourier analysis (FFT) is the main method of frequency domain analysis. In addition, literature (Humbert et al., 2021) realizes the detection of series arc faults of different loads through the change rate of voltage spectral dispersion index (SDI) of low-voltage power line. Literature (Chu et al., 2020) designed a highfrequency coupling sensor to detect the high-frequency characteristics of arc generation, and established a fault identification model according to the different high-frequency characteristics of different loads. In literature (Joga et al., 2021), time-domain information and frequent-domain information are fused by wavelet analysis. The fused features are fed into the convolutional neural network for detection. 

The extraction of time domain features has also changed from the original phase analysis to empirical mode analysis (EMD) or noise processing (Ji et al., 2020;Lala and Subrata, 2020;Cui and Tong, 2021). However, a single feature has great uncertainty in the face of arc faults with many singularities. The fusion of fault feature has become a new challenge in the research of detection method. 

As a time-frequency analysis method, the multi-resolution characteristic of wavelet analysis is efficient in many fields. The fusion of fault features in time-frequency domain ensures the realtime detection (Xiong and Chen, 2020) (Liu and Du, 2017). 

In addition, some statistics of the circuit can also be used as fusion features, such as information entropy wavelet energy entropy and power spectrum entropy of signal (Cui and Li, 2021a) or the fusion of proportional coefficient of arc zero rest time and normalization coefficient of low-pass filter (Zhao and Qin, 2020). These features detect the fault state of the circuit by setting the weight and threshold of parameters.

citations.title: Progress of Photovoltaic DC Fault Arc Detection Based on VOSviewer Bibliometric Analysis
snippets:
Traditional methods employ feature extraction and classifier-based techniques for arc fault detection in photovoltaic systems [45].These methods extract feature parameters from current and voltage signals in the photovoltaic system and train and classify these features using various classifiers to determine the presence of arc faults.

Feature extraction methods include time-domain features, frequency-domain features, and wavelet transform features.Time-domain features analyze parameters such as amplitude, peak value, and mean value of current and voltage signals [16].Frequencydomain features extract spectral characteristics like frequency and amplitude through Fourier transforms or spectrum analysis [46].Wavelet transform features combine information from the time and frequency domains to enhance the representation capability of fault signals [47].

Classifiers, such as support vector machines, artificial neural networks, and decision trees, are commonly used [48].They establish classification models by learning feature data from known faults and normal states, enabling accurate detection of unknown data.However, traditional methods still face challenges.Feature selection and parameter settings during extraction significantly influence the results, and classifier performance is limited by the dataset's size and quality.

sections.title: # 2) Time-domain features and morphological indicators
sections.text: Time-domain features quantify waveform shape and dynamics, capturing arc-specific morphology such as pulse amplitude, asymmetry, and zero-crossing anomalies. Representative time-domain indicators include amplitude, peak value, and mean value of current/voltage [59c679bd-0]. Arc currents exhibit increased randomness and fluctuation, loss of strict periodicity, “zero off” (shoulder) at zero crossings, and multiple pulses per half-cycle that raise high-frequency content [37edf46d-3]. Compared with conventional indicators like kurtosis, skewness, and form factor, the Hurst exponent has been shown to better reflect current characteristics under arcing [37edf46d-2]. Inter-harmonic variance has been selected as a frequency-domain feature that better captures partial changes in signal frequency than centroid or root-mean-square frequency metrics [37edf46d-2].

sections.title: # 3) Frequency-domain features and spectral metrics
sections.text: Spectral features summarize power distribution and can highlight arc-related energy shifts. Fourier-based spectrum analysis yields frequency and amplitude characteristics used as features [59c679bd-0]. Harmonic analysis and FFT are used to characterize current spectra; to suppress low-frequency harmonics and noise, analyses often target 3–40 kHz for AC branch-circuit applications [37edf46d-1]. Reconstructed information entropy of current frequency bands has been computed to identify feature frequency bands of arc faults [37edf46d-3]. Centroid frequency, mean-square frequency, and root-mean-square frequency describe main power-band location but have been found less suitable for arc detection in some applications [37edf46d-2].

sections.title: # 4) Time–frequency features: wavelets, STFT/HHT/EMD, and 3D representations
sections.text: Arc signals are nonstationary with transient pulses and rapidly varying spectra, motivating time–frequency methods. Wavelet transform features combine time and frequency information to enhance representation of fault signals [59c679bd-0]. Wavelet analysis supports multi-resolution feature fusion for real-time detection; convolutional models have been trained on wavelet-domain features [37edf46d-0]. In practice, wavelet-based features include mean/standard deviation of wavelet energy across bands, and multi-scale permutation entropy combined with wavelet packet energy and energy–entropy [37edf46d-2]. Short-time Fourier transform (STFT) can quantify time–frequency energy distributions and support feature selection via 2D time–frequency maps [37edf46d-1]. From STFT time–frequency-energy maps, improved H–I–W three-dimensional features can be extracted as a compact representation for downstream detection [917fa202-0]. Empirical mode decomposition (EMD) and Hilbert–Huang transform (HHT) have been explored to handle nonstationary arcs, and wavelet-based time–frequency features are favored for real-time systems [37edf46d-1].

citations.title: Detection of AC Arc Faults of Aviation Cables Based on H-I-W Three-Dimensional Features and CNN-LSTM Neural Network
snippets: Traditional arc fault detection methods are often used to analyze a certain characteristic of arc signals, but it is difficult to achieve the same detection effect on different types of arc faults with these methods. Therefore, in order to break through the limitations of traditional arc signal feature extraction methods and achieve effective detection of different types of AC arc faults, the time-frequency-energy of the signals is analyzed based on the short-time Fourier transform (STFT) in this section. The two-dimensional distribution of time-frequency-energy provides the basis for the selection of three-dimensional features of arc signals. Then, the H-I-W three-dimensional features are extracted with an improved algorithm and used as the feature data basis for fault detection.

snippets:

snippets: In the time domain, compared with the representative indicators such as kurtosis, skewness, and form factor, the Hurst exponent introduced in this paper can better reflect the characteristics of the current. sections.title: # 5) Energy, entropy, and other statistical features for discrimination
sections.text: Energy and entropy features capture arc pulse structure and irregularity, and are often fused across domains. Wavelet packet/transform energy and entropy are widely used to represent arc pulses [59c679bd-0]. Wavelet stratification with spatial distribution analysis (wavelet energy entropy) contributes to extracting weak arc features [37edf46d-4]. Multi-scale permutation entropy combined with wavelet packet energy and energy–entropy has been integrated to improve robustness across load types [d024b468-2]. Random forests trained on improved multi-scale permutation entropy, wavelet packet energy, and energy–entropy have shown better detection performance than BPNN and LSSVM, and can reduce misclassification during load start/stop transients [37edf46d-4]. Statistical features such as kurtosis, skewness, and form factor are common, but domain-specific evidence (e.g., Hurst exponent) can outperform them under arcing conditions [37edf46d-2].

citations.title: Identification Method for Series Arc Faults Based on Wavelet Transform and Deep Neural Network
snippets:
Qiwei Lu et al. [7] utilize the phase relation between supply voltage and load current, shoulder time, impulse current, randomness, and other characteristics to detect a series arc fault. Hong-Keun Ji et al. [8] designed a band pass filter (BPF) which has a frequency range from 2.4 kHz to 39 kHz, and use arc signal energy and arc pulse count of filtered signals to diagnosis series arc fault. Others combine signal analysis tools with neural networks, support vector machine, and fuzzy logic. There are some reported signal analysis tools, including wavelet transform [9], Fourier transform [10], Hilbert-Huang transform [11], empirical mode decomposition (EMD) [12], and others. Among them, wavelet transform is widely used in feature extraction and fault detection with the ability of providing better local characteristics of the signal. Shiwen Zhang et al. [13] analyzed the high-frequency components of different load current signals by wavelet transform, and extracted the average and standard deviation of wavelet energy as input features of BP neural network. Zhendong Yin et al. [14] constructed arc fault features by improved multi-scale permutation entropy, the wavelet packet energy, and the wavelet packet energy-entropy. However, most of above methods need to extract appropriate characteristic indicators for distinguish arcing and normal state. It is difficult to determine the threshold of different loads. Feature selection is subjective and requires a large amount of work. If the waveforms acquired by experiments are insufficient, the extracted features will be limited, and the detection performance on the new load cannot be guaranteed. Moreover, the characteristic value extracted from wavelet transform coefficients and wavelet transform energy is a one-dimensional vector. [15] presented AlexNet with 1.2 million three-channel images as training sets and a 1000-dimensional vector as output, and became winner in the ImageNet LSVRC-2010 competition.

snippets: Traditional arc fault detection methods are often used to analyze a certain characteristic of arc signals, but it is difficult to achieve the same detection effect on different types of arc faults with these methods. The two-dimensional distribution of time-frequency-energy provides the basis for the selection of three-dimensional features of arc signals. Then, the H-I-W three-dimensional features are extracted with an improved algorithm and used as the feature data basis for fault detection.

sections.title: # 6) Event windowing and preprocessing: zero-crossing, background subtraction, de-noising
sections.text: Robust extraction requires aligning to arc events and suppressing non-arc spectral content and noise. Cycles-based processing uses background subtraction on per-cycle current segments, with 23 time–frequency indices computed per cycle and subsequent Fisher-score-based feature screening to reduce redundancy [37edf46d-1]. Bandpass filtering in the 3–40 kHz band helps suppress low-frequency harmonics and noise for spectral and time–frequency analysis [37edf46d-1]. Event-triggered analysis around breaker operations and high-frequency coupling sensors can isolate arc-specific transients masked by normal load operation [37edf46d-3].

citations.title: A Novel Arc Fault Detector for Early Detection of Electrical Fires
snippets:
Because arc fault features are always hidden in the line currents, many advanced methods have been used to extract them. A Kalman filtering algorithm, artificial neural networks and fuzzy logic algorithms have been separately used to classify arc faults and normal states [40][41][42]. The harmonic components of arc fault currents have been analyzed [43,44]. The reconstructed information entropy of each current frequency band has been calculated to obtain the feature frequency bands of arc faults [45]. Arc fault currents have been decomposed based on the discrete wavelet transform (DWT), where the wavelet transform coefficients were used as fault features [46]. In one study, currents were first de-noised by DWT to improve the signal-to-noise ratio, and the current eigenvectors were then trained through wavelet networks to detect arc faults [47]. The Gabor Transform (GT) has been used to obtain an optimal feature extraction; the extracted GT coefficients of currents were used to identify arc faults [48]. 

However, arc fault currents are always strongly affected by different types of loads. Fault currents produced by certain home appliances do not change noticeably, and arc fault features are usually easily masked by load currents and background noise. It is difficult to find a general fault feature that performs well for all loads. Moreover, the residential electrical standard for single-phase alternating current (AC) is 120 V (60 Hz) in the United States, whereas it is 220-240 V (50-60 Hz) in other countries including China, Germany, Switzerland and Korea. Higher voltages more readily produce electrical fires caused by arc faults [49][50][51][52]. For example, the probability of fire ignition due to arc faults increases from 3.5% for 120 V to 83% for 240 V, and their nominal current levels are both 15 A [49]. Compared to 120 V, the higher voltages from 220 to 240 V are more likely to break down gaps and lead to more arcs [50,51]. Arc currents are usually continuous in higher voltage systems, but they are sometimes intermittent in 120 V systems [49,50]. Thus, higher voltage systems generate larger arc energy and thus provide better conditions for the ignition of electrical fires [50,51].

sections.title: # 7) Advanced and global-feature strategies
sections.text: Some methods move beyond local spectral/temporal indicators to model the global statistical structure of arc signals. Classical feature-based approaches (variance, pulse amplitude, spectral characteristics, DWT) are interpretable and practical but often extract “local” features that are brittle under disturbances [59c679bd-2]. Independent component analysis (ICA) decomposes DC currents; arc-faulty signals decompose into two independent components while non-arc currents do not, enabling a global “independence” feature; dynamic time warping (DTW) then quantifies independence to realize end-to-end detection with improved accuracy and robustness [59c679bd-4]. Feature-space detection constructs a time–frequency–morphology feature vector and maps signals to a feature space for classification, demonstrating feasibility and accuracy with verified anti-interference ability [59c679bd-1].

citations.title: Study on the Feature Space Detection Method of DC Arc Fault for Photovoltaic system
snippets: An arc fault on the DC side of the photovoltaic system is a potential safety hazard and is difficult to detect due to the complexity of photovoltaic systems. The detection method of series arc fault in photovoltaic systems is investigated here. The DC arc fault test platform for a photovoltaic system is established to collect the current signal under normal and fault conditions. In this study, the time domain characteristics, frequency domain characteristics, and time-frequency domain characteristics are compared by analysing the current data from the photovoltaic system in before and after fault states: corresponding feature vectors are used to construct the arc fault feature space of the system, and according to the position of the current signal in the feature space the fault is detected, so as to realise effective arc fault feature information. Then the method of establishing the arc fault feature space is introduced and key parameters of the feature space are determined. Finally, the anti-interference ability of arc fault feature space detection is verified. The results showed that the detection method is both feasible and accurate.

citations.title: Arc Fault Detection for Photovoltaic Systems Using Independent Component Analysis Technique and Dynamic Time-Warping Algorithm
snippets:
Arc fault detection in photovoltaic (PV) systems is crucial, since it may cause incidents like fires and explosions [1][2][3][4]. In general, arc faults can be classified into three categories as follows: (1) series arcs, which appear at the break point of a conductor or the bad connection point at the DC side [5]; (2) parallel arcs, which may occur between conductors with different potentials; and (3) ground arcs, which may occur when a current path is formed through the ground [6,7]. Among the above categories, series arc fault detection is the most challenging task because an arc signal is too small to be easily detected, which has led to extensive research on it [8][9][10][11]. 

So far, most of the series arc fault detection methods can be divided into two categories, namely feature-based and data-based methods. Feature-based methods mainly detect the arc features from the time or frequency domain. For instance, F. Schimpf detected arc faults by investigating the variance of arc current signals [12], Qing xiong et al. used pulse amplitude and spectral characteristics to detect arc faults [13], Wang used discrete wavelet transform (DWT) to detect arc faults [14], and SidhuT. S et al. used arc infrared and electromagnetic radiation to detect arc faults. These methods have high interpretability and can be easily realized in practical situations. However, these methods can only extract an arc's local features, which means such features can only describe part of the arc characteristics. These local features have the limitation of low robustness against disturbances and may lead to failure in arc fault detection. For example, some external disturbances, such as power grid disturbance, may have a similar frequency characteristic as arc signals, resulting in possible failure detection when spectral-based methods are used [15]. 

Another category is data-based detection methods, which typically use machine learning techniques to detect arc faults.

citations.title: Arc Fault Detection for Photovoltaic Systems Using Independent Component Analysis Technique and Dynamic Time-Warping Algorithm
snippets: Arc fault detection in photovoltaic systems is crucial, since it may cause incidents like fires and explosions. So far, most existing methods rely on an arc’s local features and do not characterize arc faults globally, which may lead to detection failure in noisy environments. In this paper, a fundamentally different method is proposed that relies on an arc’s global features instead of local ones. The core idea of the method is that the physical mechanisms of the arc fault signals and the normal signals are so different that they are thought to be generated by two independent sources. Based on this insight, independent component analysis (ICA) is introduced to decompose the photovoltaic system’s DC currents. By using ICA, the DC current signals with an arc fault can be decomposed into two independent signals, while the normal signals without an arc fault cannot be decomposed into two such independent signals. This indicates that arc faults can be detected by using the concept of “independence”. Then, the dynamic time warping algorithm was used to determine the independence level of the ICA outputs so as to realize end-to-end arc fault detection. Experimental results showed that our method has better performance than traditional methods in terms of detection accuracy and robustness against environmental disturbances.

sections.title: # 8) Robustness, multi-sensor fusion, and hardware constraints
sections.text: Robust detection requires addressing load variability, cross-interference, and real-time constraints. Fusion of time, frequency, and time–frequency features and their entropy counterparts improves robustness and real-time performance [37edf46d-0]. Feature redundancy and interference can degrade accuracy and efficiency; Fisher scoring is used to rank and select among 23 cycle-level features [37edf46d-1]. Hardware implementation can be challenging; frequency-domain and time–frequency transforms are computationally intensive and hard to realize in embedded devices, motivating image-convert approaches and efficient wavelet-based pipelines [37edf46d-0]. Multi-sensor fusion (e.g., high-frequency coupling sensors with current sensing) can extract complementary arc features and reduce masking by loads [37edf46d-3]. A lack of unified standards and benchmarks complicates reproducibility and practical deployment; robustness, anti-interference capability, and operational feasibility across environments remain key challenges [59c679bd-3].

sections.title: # 9) Performance and deployment trade-offs
sections.text: Method choice trades off interpretability, robustness, and computational cost. Local time/frequency features are easy to implement and interpretable but lack robustness under disturbances such as grid noise, which can resemble arc spectra [59c679bd-2]. Global-feature approaches like ICA+DTW improve accuracy and robustness in noisy environments compared to traditional methods [59c679bd-4]. Deep models (e.g., CNN, RF) trained on multi-resolution entropy and wavelet energy features have shown improved detection and reduced misclassification during load start/stop events versus classical classifiers [37edf46d-4]. Wavelet-based features enhance representation and real-time detection but require careful basis and level selection [59c679bd-0]. Per-cycle background subtraction with feature screening reduces redundancy and improves efficiency, aiding real-time systems [37edf46d-1]. As datasets grow, parameter-sensitive traditional detectors face real-time and efficiency limits; standardized testing and unified benchmarks are needed to validate reliability across environments [59c679bd-3].

citations.title: Arc Fault Detection for Photovoltaic Systems Using Independent Component Analysis Technique and Dynamic Time-Warping Algorithm
snippets: Arc fault detection in photovoltaic systems is crucial, since it may cause incidents like fires and explosions. So far, most existing methods rely on an arc’s local features and do not characterize arc faults globally, which may lead to detection failure in noisy environments. In this paper, a fundamentally different method is proposed that relies on an arc’s global features instead of local ones. The core idea of the method is that the physical mechanisms of the arc fault signals and the normal signals are so different that they are thought to be generated by two independent sources. Based on this insight, independent component analysis (ICA) is introduced to decompose the photovoltaic system’s DC currents. By using ICA, the DC current signals with an arc fault can be decomposed into two independent signals, while the normal signals without an arc fault cannot be decomposed into two such independent signals. This indicates that arc faults can be detected by using the concept of “independence”. Then, the dynamic time warping algorithm was used to determine the independence level of the ICA outputs so as to realize end-to-end arc fault detection. Experimental results showed that our method has better performance than traditional methods in terms of detection accuracy and robustness against environmental disturbances.

sections.title: # 10) A practical feature extraction workflow
sections.text:
A practical pipeline fuses multiple domains around event-triggered windows and emphasizes robust selection. 
- Sensing and windowing: use per-phase current (and optionally high-frequency coupled voltage) with event triggers (e.g., around breaker cycles or load start/stop); bandpass filter to suppress mains harmonics and line noise. Per-cycle background subtraction segments signals and suppresses low-frequency content [37edf46d-1]. Denoise with wavelet transforms before feature extraction [37edf46d-3].
- Time-domain morphology: compute peak, mean, change rate, similarity, Hurst exponent, zero-crossing/shoulder indicators, and pulse count. Basic statistical time-domain measures capture amplitude/shape [59c679bd-0]. Hurst exponent can better reflect arc-induced singularities than kurtosis/skewness [37edf46d-2]. Zero-crossing “shoulder” and multiple pulses per half-cycle are hallmark arc signatures [37edf46d-3].
- Frequency-domain: FFT-based spectral energy bands, harmonic/inter-harmonic metrics; select discriminatory bands via entropy screening. Fourier spectral features summarize arc frequency content [59c679bd-0]. Inter-harmonic variance has shown better identifiability than centroid/RMS frequency [37edf46d-3].
- Time–frequency: apply wavelet (DWT/WPT) or STFT to quantify multi-resolution energy and entropy; optionally use EMD/HHT for adaptive basis. Wavelets combine time and frequency for fault-representative features [59c679bd-0]. STFT energy maps support selection of 3D H–I–W features [37edf46d-1]. Wavelet packet energy and multi-scale permutation entropy provide compact, robust features [d024b468-2].
- Statistical/entropy fusion: compute wavelet energy, packet energy, permutation entropy, energy–entropy composites; train robust classifiers (RF, CNN, SVM). High-dimensional features from SVD pre-processing, IMPE, and WPT energy/entropy improved detection and avoided start/stop misclassifications [37edf46d-4]. Fusion of time–frequency and entropy features feeds CNNs for real-time detection [37edf46d-0].
- Robustness and validation: perform feature ranking (e.g., Fisher score) to reduce redundancy; evaluate across multiple loads and voltages; consider multi-sensor fusion; follow emerging standards. Fisher scoring reduces redundancy and interference [37edf46d-1]. Higher voltages (220–240 V) are more likely to produce arcs and larger arc energy, affecting feature prevalence and detection emphasis [37edf46d-3]. Standardization and benchmarking gaps complicate cross-study comparisons [59c679bd-3].
- Alternative global models: when local features fail under noise, consider ICA/DTW or HHT-based representations to capture global signal structure. ICA+DTW leverages statistical independence of arc signals to improve detection robustness [59c679bd-4].

citations.title: A Novel Arc Fault Detector for Early Detection of Electrical Fires
snippets:
Because arc fault features are always hidden in the line currents, many advanced methods have been used to extract them. A Kalman filtering algorithm, artificial neural networks and fuzzy logic algorithms have been separately used to classify arc faults and normal states [40][41][42]. The harmonic components of arc fault currents have been analyzed [43,44]. The reconstructed information entropy of each current frequency band has been calculated to obtain the feature frequency bands of arc faults [45]. Arc fault currents have been decomposed based on the discrete wavelet transform (DWT), where the wavelet transform coefficients were used as fault features [46]. In one study, currents were first de-noised by DWT to improve the signal-to-noise ratio, and the current eigenvectors were then trained through wavelet networks to detect arc faults [47]. The Gabor Transform (GT) has been used to obtain an optimal feature extraction; the extracted GT coefficients of currents were used to identify arc faults [48]. 

However, arc fault currents are always strongly affected by different types of loads. Fault currents produced by certain home appliances do not change noticeably, and arc fault features are usually easily masked by load currents and background noise. It is difficult to find a general fault feature that performs well for all loads. Moreover, the residential electrical standard for single-phase alternating current (AC) is 120 V (60 Hz) in the United States, whereas it is 220-240 V (50-60 Hz) in other countries including China, Germany, Switzerland and Korea. Higher voltages more readily produce electrical fires caused by arc faults [49][50][51][52]. For example, the probability of fire ignition due to arc faults increases from 3.5% for 120 V to 83% for 240 V, and their nominal current levels are both 15 A [49]. Compared to 120 V, the higher voltages from 220 to 240 V are more likely to break down gaps and lead to more arcs [50,51]. Arc currents are usually continuous in higher voltage systems, but they are sometimes intermittent in 120 V systems [49,50]. Thus, higher voltage systems generate larger arc energy and thus provide better conditions for the ignition of electrical fires [50,51].

citations.title: Identification Method for Series Arc Faults Based on Wavelet Transform and Deep Neural Network
snippets:
Qiwei Lu et al. [7] utilize the phase relation between supply voltage and load current, shoulder time, impulse current, randomness, and other characteristics to detect a series arc fault. Hong-Keun Ji et al. [8] designed a band pass filter (BPF) which has a frequency range from 2.4 kHz to 39 kHz, and use arc signal energy and arc pulse count of filtered signals to diagnosis series arc fault. Others combine signal analysis tools with neural networks, support vector machine, and fuzzy logic. There are some reported signal analysis tools, including wavelet transform [9], Fourier transform [10], Hilbert-Huang transform [11], empirical mode decomposition (EMD) [12], and others. Among them, wavelet transform is widely used in feature extraction and fault detection with the ability of providing better local characteristics of the signal. Shiwen Zhang et al. [13] analyzed the high-frequency components of different load current signals by wavelet transform, and extracted the average and standard deviation of wavelet energy as input features of BP neural network. Zhendong Yin et al. [14] constructed arc fault features by improved multi-scale permutation entropy, the wavelet packet energy, and the wavelet packet energy-entropy. However, most of above methods need to extract appropriate characteristic indicators for distinguish arcing and normal state. It is difficult to determine the threshold of different loads. Feature selection is subjective and requires a large amount of work. If the waveforms acquired by experiments are insufficient, the extracted features will be limited, and the detection performance on the new load cannot be guaranteed. Moreover, the characteristic value extracted from wavelet transform coefficients and wavelet transform energy is a one-dimensional vector. To some extent, characteristic information of current and voltage signals is lost. 

In 2006, Hinton proposed the concept of deep learning, which using deep neural network to automatically learn high-level feature from big training data. In 2012, Alex Krizhevsky et al. [15] presented AlexNet with 1.2 million three-channel images as training sets and a 1000-dimensional vector as output, and became winner in the ImageNet LSVRC-2010 competition.

citations.title: Research on arc fault detection using ResNet and gamma transform regularization
snippets:
In recent years, the researches of arc fault detection are not limited to the arc mathematical model. In fact, some circuit parameters may have a mutation when an arc fault occurs. The purpose of fault detection can be achieved by identifying the circuit parameters as features. In practical application, it is difficult to collect the photothermal physical characteristics of the arc in real time due to the random arc generation. As a result, the common feature extraction method is time-frequency domain analysis of voltage or current. Fast Fourier analysis (FFT) is the main method of frequency domain analysis. In addition, literature (Humbert et al., 2021) realizes the detection of series arc faults of different loads through the change rate of voltage spectral dispersion index (SDI) of low-voltage power line. Literature (Chu et al., 2020) designed a highfrequency coupling sensor to detect the high-frequency characteristics of arc generation, and established a fault identification model according to the different high-frequency characteristics of different loads. In literature (Joga et al., 2021), time-domain information and frequent-domain information are fused by wavelet analysis. The fused features are fed into the convolutional neural network for detection. 

The extraction of time domain features has also changed from the original phase analysis to empirical mode analysis (EMD) or noise processing (Ji et al., 2020;Lala and Subrata, 2020;Cui and Tong, 2021). However, a single feature has great uncertainty in the face of arc faults with many singularities. The fusion of fault feature has become a new challenge in the research of detection method. 

As a time-frequency analysis method, the multi-resolution characteristic of wavelet analysis is efficient in many fields. The fusion of fault features in time-frequency domain ensures the realtime detection (Xiong and Chen, 2020) (Liu and Du, 2017). 

In addition, some statistics of the circuit can also be used as fusion features, such as information entropy wavelet energy entropy and power spectrum entropy of signal (Cui and Li, 2021a) or the fusion of proportional coefficient of arc zero rest time and normalization coefficient of low-pass filter (Zhao and Qin, 2020). These features detect the fault state of the circuit by setting the weight and threshold of parameters.

sections.title: # 11) Key takeaways
sections.text:
- The most effective arc-fault feature sets combine time-domain morphology (peaks, shoulders, pulse count), frequency-domain spectral indicators, and time–frequency energy/entropy features from wavelets or STFT, often fused across domains. Time-, frequency-, and wavelet-based features each capture complementary aspects of arc signals [59c679bd-0]. Wavelet energy statistics and entropy-based measures are particularly sensitive to arc pulse structure and nonstationarity [37edf46d-2]. Time–frequency-energy maps can be condensed into compact 3D H–I–W features for robust classification [917fa202-0].
- Robustness hinges on event-aware windowing, denoising, and intelligent feature selection; local features alone are brittle to disturbances and load variability. Local spectral and statistical features are prone to false alarms from grid disturbances [59c679bd-2]. Per-cycle background subtraction and Fisher-score ranking mitigate redundancy and interference [37edf46d-1]. Global statistical approaches like ICA+DTW and entropy-rich models (RF, CNN) improve accuracy and reduce misclassification during transients [59c679bd-4].
- Deployment must account for sensing constraints, computational budgets, and standardization gaps; multi-sensor fusion and standardized benchmarks can improve practical reliability. Frequency/time–frequency transforms can be computationally intensive for embedded deployment, motivating efficient wavelet pipelines and image-convert methods [37edf46d-0]. A lack of unified standards and benchmarks remains a barrier to reproducibility and engineering validation [59c679bd-3].

snippets:
Arc fault detection in photovoltaic (PV) systems is crucial, since it may cause incidents like fires and explosions [1][2][3][4]. In general, arc faults can be classified into three categories as follows: (1) series arcs, which appear at the break point of a conductor or the bad connection point at the DC side [5]; (2) parallel arcs, which may occur between conductors with different potentials; and (3) ground arcs, which may occur when a current path is formed through the ground [6,7]. Among the above categories, series arc fault detection is the most challenging task because an arc signal is too small to be easily detected, which has led to extensive research on it [8][9][10][11]. 

So far, most of the series arc fault detection methods can be divided into two categories, namely feature-based and data-based methods. Feature-based methods mainly detect the arc features from the time or frequency domain. For instance, F. Schimpf detected arc faults by investigating the variance of arc current signals [12], Qing xiong et al. used pulse amplitude and spectral characteristics to detect arc faults [13], Wang used discrete wavelet transform (DWT) to detect arc faults [14], and SidhuT. S et al. used arc infrared and electromagnetic radiation to detect arc faults. These methods have high interpretability and can be easily realized in practical situations. However, these methods can only extract an arc's local features, which means such features can only describe part of the arc characteristics. These local features have the limitation of low robustness against disturbances and may lead to failure in arc fault detection. For example, some external disturbances, such as power grid disturbance, may have a similar frequency characteristic as arc signals, resulting in possible failure detection when spectral-based methods are used [15]. 

Another category is data-based detection methods, which typically use machine learning techniques to detect arc faults.

In this paper, a fundamentally different method is proposed that relies on an arc’s global features instead of local ones. The core idea of the method is that the physical mechanisms of the arc fault signals and the normal signals are so different that they are thought to be generated by two independent sources. Based on this insight, independent component analysis (ICA) is introduced to decompose the photovoltaic system’s DC currents. By using ICA, the DC current signals with an arc fault can be decomposed into two independent signals, while the normal signals without an arc fault cannot be decomposed into two such independent signals. This indicates that arc faults can be detected by using the concept of “independence”. Then, the dynamic time warping algorithm was used to determine the independence level of the ICA outputs so as to realize end-to-end arc fault detection. Experimental results showed that our method has better performance than traditional methods in terms of detection accuracy and robustness against environmental disturbances.

question: research on enhancing LLM reasoning ability via critique model

sections.title: # What “critique models” are and why they help
sections.text: Critique models are auxiliary models or procedures that generate feedback on an LLM’s intermediate reasoning or final answer, enabling revision, repair, or policy updates that improve accuracy, robustness, or calibration on reasoning tasks. They can operate as a separate “critic” that scores or explains flaws in a generator’s output, or be embedded into a single model’s objective via self-critique or optimization over critique signals. The core idea is that revising reasoning based on explicit feedback is often easier than producing a perfectly correct solution in one shot, especially when compute is available at inference time or via targeted fine-tuning on critique–refine data. Self-critique pipelines explicitly separate forward reasoning from backward verification by a second LLM that scrutinizes the resulting answer [2aea6196-0] and split-architecture critique models or reward estimators score and refine generator outputs, particularly in math domains [2aea6196-2].

citations.title: Optimizing Multimodal Large Language Models for Detection of Alcohol Advertisements via Adaptive Prompting
snippets: Self-critique is a two-step process designed to improve the output of an LLM by inspecting and criticizing its own initial output. The initial stage involves forward reasoning, where the model utilizes a prompt to address a specific task. In the subsequent backward-verification phase, a second LLM scrutinizes the validity of the initial answer.

citations.title: Double-Checker: Enhancing Reasoning of Slow-Thinking LLMs via Self-Critical Fine-Tuning
snippets:
Long Chain-of-Thought and Slow Thinking. The rise of LLMs has driven extensive research to enhance their reasoning capabilities through various strategies. Early efforts include advancements in pretraining methodologies [5,6], supervised fine-tuning [7,8,9,10,11], and rigorous evaluation techniques [4,12,13]. More recently, RL has emerged as a key paradigm for improving reasoning in LLMs. For instance, [15] demonstrates that RL with verifiable rewards enables models to generate long chains of thought (long-CoT) [17], fostering more structured, multi-step problem-solving skills. This approach has been shown to promote reflective reasoning behaviors, termed as the "aha moments" [18]. These advancements mark significant progress in LLM reasoning [28]. However, our work reveals a critical limitation: while strong reflection-like reasoning allows LLMs to recognize errors or inconsistencies, it does not inherently ensure robust self-improvement [29,30]. Additionally, existing self-improvement methods [29,30] often depend on external tools or explicit feedback mechanisms, making it challenging to guide a single LLM through multiple, reliable rounds of refinement. Addressing these challenges is crucial to unlocking the full potential of self-improvement in LLMs. 

Critique LLMs and Integrated Self-Improvement. A parallel line of research employs critique models or reward estimators to score and refine outputs from a "generator" model, especially in mathematical domains [31,32,33,34]. While effective in principle, this split-architecture strategy requires substantial overhead (running two separate LLMs) or produces numeric feedback that lacks actionable corrections [35]. Other efforts have tried to incorporate critique into a single model's training objective [23] or train on large multi-round self-critique data [19], but with limited gains in iterative refinement. Against this backdrop, our work introduces Double-Checker, which merges critique and generation into a unified "reflect-and-refine" loop within one long-CoT LLM.

sections.title: # Method families and mechanisms
sections.text:
- Split pipelines: Generator + critic. These “critique-and-repair” loops evaluate outputs and trigger edits or re-runs. Critic or reward estimators can provide actionable feedback or numeric signals to drive refinement, though numeric feedback alone can lack actionable corrections [2aea6196-2]. 
- Test-time reflection loops: Single-model iterative self-critique. Methods like Self-Refine and Reflexion prompt the same model to generate, critique, and refine multiple times at inference, leveraging additional compute for reliability without extra training data. Self-Refine uses a single LLM to generate, critique, and refine iteratively; Reflexion extends multi-agent/self-reflective loops to verbal feedback and stored self-critiques guiding future decisions [d54a8a1f-2]. 
- Unified/self-critique training: Integrate critique into one model. Prior attempts to either integrate critique into a single model’s training objective or to train on large multi-round self-critique corpora have shown limited iterative gains, motivating unified reflect-and-refine training such as Double-Checker [2aea6196-2]. Double-Checker probes long-CoT models and finds they often fail to produce informative critiques that improve prior answers, introducing a training scheme combining direct inference and curated critique–refine data (1,730 instances) to enable iterative self-improvement [2aea6196-4]. 
- Optimization from critique: Online learning over feedback. Critique-GRPO learns from both natural language and numerical feedback, showing that critiques are more effective than spontaneous self-reflection for self-correction and that CoT critiques are especially informative [d54a8a1f-4]. 
- Process supervision and verification: Step-level feedback and checkers. Multiplex CoT prompts a second chain of thought that critiques the first, improving accuracy without extra training [d54a8a1f-2]. Self-Check provides zero-shot mechanisms for LLMs to verify multi-step reasoning in math, filtering low-confidence solutions and boosting accuracy on GSM8K, MathQA, and MATH [8b1db788-3]. 
- Self-evolving critique abilities: Training models to critique better. SCRIT improves critique-correction accuracy on PRM800K and ProcessBench across GSM8K, MATH, OlympiadBench, and Omni-Math, approaching o1-mini critique performance [8b1db788-4].

snippets:
However, employing a separate model exclusively for critique introduces additional overhead [22]. Alternatively, [23] proposes integrating critique as a training objective. Nevertheless, the resulting LLMs are unable to leverage self-critique effectively during inference. Furthermore, [19] reports only marginal improvements for Long-CoT LLMs, even after fine-tuning on 100K self-critique examples. These raise an open question: Do Long-CoT LLMs, which demonstrate reflection-like reasoning, possess the capacity to leverage self-critique to enhance performance? If not, how can we equip them with this ability? 

In this paper, we investigate the integration of reflection-like reasoning with self-critique to enhance the reasoning abilities of slow-thinking LLMs. Specifically, we start by examining whether long-CoT LLMs can leverage self-critique to iteratively refine their prior solutions during inference in a probeinduced manner. Our findings reveal that the occurrence of an "aha moment" does not necessarily indicate the presence of a self-critique mechanism (see Sec. 3.1). For instance, as illustrated in Fig. 1, DeepSeek-Distill-Qwen-7B fails to generate informative critiques of its prior solution, ultimately arriving at the same incorrect answer. To address this, we introduce Double-Checker, a novel framework designed to empower LLMs to critique and refine their prior solutions iteratively and adaptively. Through a specialized training process that combines direct inference instances with curated critique-refine data (1,730 instances in total), our Double-Checker equips long-CoT LLMs with an effective self-critique capability. This enables iterative improvements in performance during inference via self-critique. An example of this process is shown in Fig. 1, where Double-Checker successfully resolves a complex math problem using the "reflect-and-refine" approach. 

Our main contributions can be summarized as follows: ❶ We investigate the self-critical behavior of long-CoT LLMs via a probing and find that they are unable to generate informative critiques to improve their prior solutions.

This suggests that critiques can enable both models to successfully correct some persistently failed responses that cannot be resolved through spontaneous self-reflection, as discussed in Section 3.1.

The effectiveness of CoT critiques can be attributed to their richness: by providing a step-by-step explanation of the reasoning along with targeted guidance on the correct solution approach, they offer substantially more informative feedback than simpler alternatives. 

Binary correctness signals alone can provide refinement benefits. citations.title: Unveiling the Latent Directions of Reflection in Large Language Models
snippets: Most prior work aims to improve reflection rather than explain how it works. A prominent line explores multi-agent reflection [6,7], where an actor-critic setup lets one model generate reasoning while another critiques and suggests revisions. Reflexion [8] extends this idea, with agents interacting with an environment, verbally reflecting on feedback, and storing self-critiques for future decisions. Another strand focuses on long chain-of-thought (Long CoT) reasoning [9,10], where multiple reasoning paths are intertwined with explicit reflection phases, often marked by cues like Wait or Alternatively. Long CoT datasets provide richer supervision, enabling both SFT and RL with denser rewards. Multiplex CoT [11] further prompts a second, alternative chain of thought that critiques the first, improving accuracy without extra training. A different approach is self-refinement, which avoids extra data or fine-tuning altogether: SELF-REFINE [12] uses a single LLM to generate, critique, and refine its own output iteratively. Finally, reflection can also be applied at test time scaling, where extra compute is used to double-check answers. For instance, [17] shows that test-time reflection often corrects earlier mistakes, yielding more reliable results.

sections.title: # Empirical effectiveness
sections.text:
- Single-model iterative critique (Self-Refine). Self-Refine iteratively generates, critiques, and refines outputs without additional training, leveraging test-time compute so that a model can identify and fix errors more reliably than solving from scratch [2fedede6-1]. Human evaluations show Self-Refine outputs are preferred over all k initial outputs in 1-vs-k settings, demonstrating the value of feedback-guided refinement [2fedede6-3]. However, weaker models (e.g., Vicuna-13B) struggle to generate actionable feedback or follow refinement prompts, sometimes repeating outputs or hallucinating dialog—underscoring the importance of model capability for effective critique [2fedede6-3]. 
- Multi-agent/reflective critique (Reflexion). Reflexion frames agents as actors with critics that produce verbal feedback and store reflections for future decisions, improving performance across QA and decision-making environments [d54a8a1f-2]. Surveys report marked enhancements over traditional approaches in tasks such as HotPotQA and HumanEval, indicating broader transfer beyond math [8b1db788-3]. 
- Verifier/zero-shot self-check (Self-Check). Self-Check enables zero-shot verification of multi-step reasoning and significantly boosts accuracy on GSM8K, MathQA, and MATH by rejecting low-confidence solutions [8b1db788-3]. 
- Critique-and-refine with search and multi-rollout (MCTSr-Zero). Monte Carlo Tree Self-refine shows success rates increase with the number of rollouts on GSM8K and GSM-Hard, with stronger gains in simpler problems and plateaus on harder sets—illustrating both the promise and limits of iterative self-refinement on complexity [2fedede6-2]. 
- Unified reflect-and-refine training (Double-Checker). Probing long-CoT models reveals they often fail to generate informative critiques that change answers; Double-Checker’s curated critique–refine data and training enable iterative improvements on complex math problems [2aea6196-4]. 
- Learning from critiques (Critique-GRPO). Incorporating critiques, especially CoT critiques, yields more effective refinements than spontaneous reflection; valid refinement rates are non-zero and higher with richer stepwise feedback, while simple correctness signals provide minimal benefits without explanatory guidance [d54a8a1f-4]. 
- Process-level supervision and self-critique ability evolution (SCRIT). Self-evolving critique (SCRIT) improves locating and correcting error steps across GSM8K, MATH, OlympiadBench, and Omni-Math, achieving a 10% relative gain in critique-correction accuracy over the base model and approaching o1-mini’s critique performance [8b1db788-4]. 
- Calibration-focused critique (CritiCal). Multi-turn self-critique improves calibration in math reasoning (small ECE and AUROC gains) but shows no notable accuracy improvements and can worsen calibration on factuality-related benchmarks, indicating that critique strategies targeting confidence calibration may not uniformly help accuracy [8b1db788-2]. 
- RL with verifiable rewards and long-CoT. RL with verifiable rewards enables long chains of thought and reflective “aha” moments, yet reflection alone does not ensure robust self-improvement; this motivates critic-guided refinement loops [2aea6196-2].

(2023), the Self-Refine framework is inspired by how humans revise a draft: The model first produces an initial answer, then critiques or evaluates that answer, and finally uses the critique to refine the answer. This feedback-refinement loop can be repeated multiple times, progressively polishing the output. In essence, Self-Refine leverages test-time compute to let the model "think twice (or more)" about its answer, leading to higher-quality and more reliable outputs.

snippets:
To comprehensively evaluate Self-Critique performance, we conduct multi-turn Self-Critique exper- iments with 4 models, those have both reasoning and non-reasoning ones, across 6 benchmarks. In each iteration, the model receives the results of all previous iterations as context. Detailed prompt is provided in Appendix A. 

Figure 4 illustrates the standard deviation of multi-turn Self-Critique for each model, focusing on ECE and AUROC to evaluate confidence calibration stability. Figure 5 presents the average performance of all models across three benchmarks, highlighting the impact of Self-Critique on different tasks. The specific variation curves of each model are shown in Figure 12 in Appendix B. Task Analysis. The six benchmarks are catego-rized into three tasks: one-hop factuality (Compar-isonQA and TriviaQA), multi-hop factuality reasoning (StrategyQA and HotpotQA), and math reasoning (MATH500 and MATH-Perturb). As shown in Figure 5, the semi-transparent light gray area represents the average performance of all models with a one-third standard deviation. For accuracy, models exhibit greater stability on one-hop factuality and math reasoning tasks compared to multihop factuality reasoning. However, unlike prior self-improvement studies (Madaan et al., 2023;Welleck et al., 2023), Self-Critique shows no notable accuracy improvements, as it primarily targets confidence calibration rather than accuracy. For ECE and AUROC, Self-Critique exhibits relatively stable performance with slight improvements in math reasoning tasks. In contrast, factualityrelated benchmarks experience negative impacts, with increased average ECE and decreased average AUROC. These findings suggest that Self-Critique has limited effectiveness, significantly worsening calibration for factuality-related tasks while only marginally enhancing it for math reasoning. Thus, prompting-based Self-Critique alone is inadequate for robust confidence calibration. 

Model Analysis. In Figure 4 and Figure 12, LLMs are represented in cool colors, while LRMs are depicted in warm colors. For ECE and AUROC, LRMs demonstrate greater stability on factualityrelated benchmarks, with significantly lower standard deviation than LLMs, whose calibration varies widely.

citations.title: Unveiling the Latent Directions of Reflection in Large Language Models
snippets: Most prior work aims to improve reflection rather than explain how it works. A prominent line explores multi-agent reflection [6,7], where an actor-critic setup lets one model generate reasoning while another critiques and suggests revisions. Reflexion [8] extends this idea, with agents interacting with an environment, verbally reflecting on feedback, and storing self-critiques for future decisions. Another strand focuses on long chain-of-thought (Long CoT) reasoning [9,10], where multiple reasoning paths are intertwined with explicit reflection phases, often marked by cues like Wait or Alternatively. Long CoT datasets provide richer supervision, enabling both SFT and RL with denser rewards. Multiplex CoT [11] further prompts a second, alternative chain of thought that critiques the first, improving accuracy without extra training. A different approach is self-refinement, which avoids extra data or fine-tuning altogether: SELF-REFINE [12] uses a single LLM to generate, critique, and refine its own output iteratively. Finally, reflection can also be applied at test time scaling, where extra compute is used to double-check answers. For instance, [17] shows that test-time reflection often corrects earlier mistakes, yielding more reliable results.

sections.title: # Design patterns and training/inference trade-offs
sections.text:
- Pipeline architecture. Split pipelines offer clearer separation of concerns and can produce actionable feedback, but incur runtime and compute overhead from running two models or generating non-detailed rewards. Running separate generator and critic models adds overhead and numeric rewards may lack actionable guidance, whereas integrating critique into a single model or training on self-critique data has shown limited iterative gains without careful design [2aea6196-2]. 
- Inference-time reflection. Single-model loops like Self-Refine and Reflexion are simple and effective when models are sufficiently capable, but their benefits depend on the quality of self-generated feedback and adherence to refinement prompts. Weaker models often fail to produce or follow feedback, causing stagnation or hallucination during refinement [2fedede6-3]. 
- Unified reflect-and-refine. Training specialized critique–refine data and prompts can harden models to iteratively improve outputs. Curated critique-refine corpora (e.g., 1,730 instances) and probe-guided training enable models to move from weak or off-target critiques to effective self-improvement [2aea6196-4]. 
- Optimization over critique. Online algorithms like Critique-GRPO show that learning from natural language critiques and numeric signals can improve refinement policies and correct persistent failures that spontaneous reflection misses. CoT critiques are particularly effective because they explain reasoning and point to corrective approaches, whereas bare correctness flags yield fewer valid refinements [d54a8a1f-4]. 
- Process supervision. Multiplex CoT and process-labeled datasets (PRM800K, ProcessBench) provide step-level supervision that improves error localization and correction. Multiplex CoT critiques the first chain of thought to improve accuracy without extra training [d54a8a1f-2] and process-focused training improves identifying first-failure steps across multiple math benchmarks [8b1db788-4]. 
- Calibration vs. accuracy. Critique strategies aimed at confidence calibration may improve stability but not accuracy, and can even harm factuality tasks. Self-critique shows limited accuracy gains but modest calibration improvements in math and degraded calibration on factuality benchmarks [8b1db788-2].

snippets: Work on self-improvement provides mechanisms for refining reasoning policies over time. Reflexion leverages verbalized reflection for reinforcement [Shinn et al., 2023], Self-Refine operationalizes a generate-critique-refine loop [Madaan et al., 2023], and evolutionary strategies such as PromptBreeder optimize prompts via self-referential mutation [Fernando et al., 2023]. Complementary views frame reasoning as structured search, externalized in Tree-of-Thoughts [Yao et al., 2023] and Graph-of-Thoughts [Besta et al., 2024]. TextGrad formalizes language feedback as textual gradients for systematic refinement [Yuksekgonul et al., 2025]. A persistent frontier is to develop systems that autonomously improve from sparse, noisy, and unstructured feedback, especially in domains lacking explicit reward signals, where domain-specific intuition must be accrued gradually.

citations.title: Double-Checker: Enhancing Reasoning of Slow-Thinking LLMs via Self-Critical Fine-Tuning
snippets:
Long Chain-of-Thought and Slow Thinking. The rise of LLMs has driven extensive research to enhance their reasoning capabilities through various strategies. Early efforts include advancements in pretraining methodologies [5,6], supervised fine-tuning [7,8,9,10,11], and rigorous evaluation techniques [4,12,13]. More recently, RL has emerged as a key paradigm for improving reasoning in LLMs. For instance, [15] demonstrates that RL with verifiable rewards enables models to generate long chains of thought (long-CoT) [17], fostering more structured, multi-step problem-solving skills. This approach has been shown to promote reflective reasoning behaviors, termed as the "aha moments" [18]. These advancements mark significant progress in LLM reasoning [28]. However, our work reveals a critical limitation: while strong reflection-like reasoning allows LLMs to recognize errors or inconsistencies, it does not inherently ensure robust self-improvement [29,30]. Additionally, existing self-improvement methods [29,30] often depend on external tools or explicit feedback mechanisms, making it challenging to guide a single LLM through multiple, reliable rounds of refinement. Addressing these challenges is crucial to unlocking the full potential of self-improvement in LLMs. 

Critique LLMs and Integrated Self-Improvement. A parallel line of research employs critique models or reward estimators to score and refine outputs from a "generator" model, especially in mathematical domains [31,32,33,34]. While effective in principle, this split-architecture strategy requires substantial overhead (running two separate LLMs) or produces numeric feedback that lacks actionable corrections [35]. Other efforts have tried to incorporate critique into a single model's training objective [23] or train on large multi-round self-critique data [19], but with limited gains in iterative refinement. Against this backdrop, our work introduces Double-Checker, which merges critique and generation into a unified "reflect-and-refine" loop within one long-CoT LLM.

citations.title: Double-Checker: Enhancing Reasoning of Slow-Thinking LLMs via Self-Critical Fine-Tuning
snippets:
However, employing a separate model exclusively for critique introduces additional overhead [22]. Alternatively, [23] proposes integrating critique as a training objective. Nevertheless, the resulting LLMs are unable to leverage self-critique effectively during inference. Furthermore, [19] reports only marginal improvements for Long-CoT LLMs, even after fine-tuning on 100K self-critique examples. These raise an open question: Do Long-CoT LLMs, which demonstrate reflection-like reasoning, possess the capacity to leverage self-critique to enhance performance? If not, how can we equip them with this ability? 

In this paper, we investigate the integration of reflection-like reasoning with self-critique to enhance the reasoning abilities of slow-thinking LLMs. Specifically, we start by examining whether long-CoT LLMs can leverage self-critique to iteratively refine their prior solutions during inference in a probeinduced manner. Our findings reveal that the occurrence of an "aha moment" does not necessarily indicate the presence of a self-critique mechanism (see Sec. 3.1). For instance, as illustrated in Fig. 1, DeepSeek-Distill-Qwen-7B fails to generate informative critiques of its prior solution, ultimately arriving at the same incorrect answer. To address this, we introduce Double-Checker, a novel framework designed to empower LLMs to critique and refine their prior solutions iteratively and adaptively. Through a specialized training process that combines direct inference instances with curated critique-refine data (1,730 instances in total), our Double-Checker equips long-CoT LLMs with an effective self-critique capability. This enables iterative improvements in performance during inference via self-critique. An example of this process is shown in Fig. 1, where Double-Checker successfully resolves a complex math problem using the "reflect-and-refine" approach. 

Our main contributions can be summarized as follows: ❶ We investigate the self-critical behavior of long-CoT LLMs via a probing and find that they are unable to generate informative critiques to improve their prior solutions.

citations.title: CritiCal: Can Critique Help LLM Uncertainty or Confidence Calibration?
snippets:
To comprehensively evaluate Self-Critique performance, we conduct multi-turn Self-Critique exper- iments with 4 models, those have both reasoning and non-reasoning ones, across 6 benchmarks. In each iteration, the model receives the results of all previous iterations as context. Detailed prompt is provided in Appendix A. 

Figure 4 illustrates the standard deviation of multi-turn Self-Critique for each model, focusing on ECE and AUROC to evaluate confidence calibration stability. Figure 5 presents the average performance of all models across three benchmarks, highlighting the impact of Self-Critique on different tasks. The specific variation curves of each model are shown in Figure 12 in Appendix B. Task Analysis. The six benchmarks are catego-rized into three tasks: one-hop factuality (Compar-isonQA and TriviaQA), multi-hop factuality reasoning (StrategyQA and HotpotQA), and math reasoning (MATH500 and MATH-Perturb). As shown in Figure 5, the semi-transparent light gray area represents the average performance of all models with a one-third standard deviation. For accuracy, models exhibit greater stability on one-hop factuality and math reasoning tasks compared to multihop factuality reasoning. However, unlike prior self-improvement studies (Madaan et al., 2023;Welleck et al., 2023), Self-Critique shows no notable accuracy improvements, as it primarily targets confidence calibration rather than accuracy. For ECE and AUROC, Self-Critique exhibits relatively stable performance with slight improvements in math reasoning tasks. In contrast, factualityrelated benchmarks experience negative impacts, with increased average ECE and decreased average AUROC. These findings suggest that Self-Critique has limited effectiveness, significantly worsening calibration for factuality-related tasks while only marginally enhancing it for math reasoning. Thus, prompting-based Self-Critique alone is inadequate for robust confidence calibration. 

Model Analysis. In Figure 4 and Figure 12, LLMs are represented in cool colors, while LRMs are depicted in warm colors. For ECE and AUROC, LRMs demonstrate greater stability on factualityrelated benchmarks, with significantly lower standard deviation than LLMs, whose calibration varies widely.
