sections.title: # Failure modes and best practices
sections.text:
- Weak or mis-targeted critiques. Models may fail to generate actionable or correct critiques, leading to repeated answers or hallucinations during refinement. Probing long-CoT models reveals many cannot produce informative critiques that change outcomes [2aea6196-4] and weaker models produce non-compliant feedback and may repeat outputs [2fedede6-3]. 
- Numeric-only feedback. Scores without explanations are hard to act on. Numeric rewards can lack actionable corrections, motivating richer natural language critiques or integrated objectives [2aea6196-2]. 
- Overhead and scalability. Split pipelines add latency and parameter cost; iterative methods may plateau on very hard reasoning. Gains increase with iterations on GSM8K but plateau on GSM-Hard, indicating capacity and complexity limits [2fedede6-2]. 
- Calibration pitfalls. Critique for calibration may worsen performance on factuality-heavy tasks or require task-specific design. Self-critique can degrade ECE and AUROC on factuality benchmarks while helping only marginally in math [8b1db788-2]. 
- Data and supervision design. Effective critique relies on high-quality feedback and step-level labels. Curated critique–refine data and prompts improve iterative self-critique [2aea6196-4] and process-labeled datasets improve step-localization accuracy across math domains [8b1db788-4]. 
- Model capability matters. Iterative critique benefits stronger base models more than weak ones. Vicuna-13B struggles with structured feedback and refinement despite instruction-tuning, whereas instruction-based models generalize better [2fedede6-3].

sections.text:

citations.title: Unveiling the Latent Directions of Reflection in Large Language Models
snippets: Most prior work aims to improve reflection rather than explain how it works. A prominent line explores multi-agent reflection [6,7], where an actor-critic setup lets one model generate reasoning while another critiques and suggests revisions. Reflexion [8] extends this idea, with agents interacting with an environment, verbally reflecting on feedback, and storing self-critiques for future decisions. Another strand focuses on long chain-of-thought (Long CoT) reasoning [9,10], where multiple reasoning paths are intertwined with explicit reflection phases, often marked by cues like Wait or Alternatively. Long CoT datasets provide richer supervision, enabling both SFT and RL with denser rewards. Multiplex CoT [11] further prompts a second, alternative chain of thought that critiques the first, improving accuracy without extra training. A different approach is self-refinement, which avoids extra data or fine-tuning altogether: SELF-REFINE [12] uses a single LLM to generate, critique, and refine its own output iteratively. Finally, reflection can also be applied at test time scaling, where extra compute is used to double-check answers. For instance, [17] shows that test-time reflection often corrects earlier mistakes, yielding more reliable results.

sections.title: # Open problems and future directions
sections.text:
- Reliable self-critique. Training models to reliably produce actionable critiques remains challenging; unified reflect-and-refine approaches and curated datasets show promise but require broader validation across domains and tasks. Empirical probing reveals many long-CoT models lack informative critique generation without targeted training [2aea6196-4]. 
- Overhead vs. gains. Balancing compute for critique loops and multi-round refinement against latency and cost is an active design problem; hybrid strategies that trigger critique only when uncertainty is high may help. Iteration benefits vary nonlinearly with problem complexity [2fedede6-2]. 
- Richer feedback formats. Numeric-only signals underperform without explanatory guidance; integrating CoT-style critiques and process labels can improve effectiveness but increases data and supervision complexity. CoT critiques outperform indicative-only signals in producing valid refinements [d54a8a1f-4]. 
- Task-specific calibration. Critique strategies that improve calibration on math may need adaptation for factuality-heavy QA; joint objectives balancing accuracy and calibration merit exploration. Task-dependent calibration effects suggest domain-specific tuning [8b1db788-2]. 
- Unified training for critique. Moving beyond two-model pipelines to single-model architectures that maintain critique capacity at inference remains an open area, with evidence that naive integration is insufficient without careful objective and data design. Integrating critique as a training objective or training on large self-critique corpora has shown limited iterative gains without specialized design [2aea6196-2].

citations.title: Double-Checker: Enhancing Reasoning of Slow-Thinking LLMs via Self-Critical Fine-Tuning
snippets:
Long Chain-of-Thought and Slow Thinking. The rise of LLMs has driven extensive research to enhance their reasoning capabilities through various strategies. Early efforts include advancements in pretraining methodologies [5,6], supervised fine-tuning [7,8,9,10,11], and rigorous evaluation techniques [4,12,13]. More recently, RL has emerged as a key paradigm for improving reasoning in LLMs. For instance, [15] demonstrates that RL with verifiable rewards enables models to generate long chains of thought (long-CoT) [17], fostering more structured, multi-step problem-solving skills. This approach has been shown to promote reflective reasoning behaviors, termed as the "aha moments" [18]. These advancements mark significant progress in LLM reasoning [28]. However, our work reveals a critical limitation: while strong reflection-like reasoning allows LLMs to recognize errors or inconsistencies, it does not inherently ensure robust self-improvement [29,30]. Additionally, existing self-improvement methods [29,30] often depend on external tools or explicit feedback mechanisms, making it challenging to guide a single LLM through multiple, reliable rounds of refinement. Addressing these challenges is crucial to unlocking the full potential of self-improvement in LLMs. 

Critique LLMs and Integrated Self-Improvement. A parallel line of research employs critique models or reward estimators to score and refine outputs from a "generator" model, especially in mathematical domains [31,32,33,34]. While effective in principle, this split-architecture strategy requires substantial overhead (running two separate LLMs) or produces numeric feedback that lacks actionable corrections [35]. Other efforts have tried to incorporate critique into a single model's training objective [23] or train on large multi-round self-critique data [19], but with limited gains in iterative refinement. Against this backdrop, our work introduces Double-Checker, which merges critique and generation into a unified "reflect-and-refine" loop within one long-CoT LLM.

snippets:
However, employing a separate model exclusively for critique introduces additional overhead [22]. Alternatively, [23] proposes integrating critique as a training objective. Nevertheless, the resulting LLMs are unable to leverage self-critique effectively during inference. Furthermore, [19] reports only marginal improvements for Long-CoT LLMs, even after fine-tuning on 100K self-critique examples. These raise an open question: Do Long-CoT LLMs, which demonstrate reflection-like reasoning, possess the capacity to leverage self-critique to enhance performance? If not, how can we equip them with this ability? 

In this paper, we investigate the integration of reflection-like reasoning with self-critique to enhance the reasoning abilities of slow-thinking LLMs. Specifically, we start by examining whether long-CoT LLMs can leverage self-critique to iteratively refine their prior solutions during inference in a probeinduced manner. Our findings reveal that the occurrence of an "aha moment" does not necessarily indicate the presence of a self-critique mechanism (see Sec. 3.1). For instance, as illustrated in Fig. 1, DeepSeek-Distill-Qwen-7B fails to generate informative critiques of its prior solution, ultimately arriving at the same incorrect answer. To address this, we introduce Double-Checker, a novel framework designed to empower LLMs to critique and refine their prior solutions iteratively and adaptively. Through a specialized training process that combines direct inference instances with curated critique-refine data (1,730 instances in total), our Double-Checker equips long-CoT LLMs with an effective self-critique capability. This enables iterative improvements in performance during inference via self-critique. An example of this process is shown in Fig. 1, where Double-Checker successfully resolves a complex math problem using the "reflect-and-refine" approach. 

Our main contributions can be summarized as follows: ❶ We investigate the self-critical behavior of long-CoT LLMs via a probing and find that they are unable to generate informative critiques to improve their prior solutions.

sections.title: # Practical guidance
sections.text:
- Start with lightweight self-critique loops on math/symbolic reasoning and multi-step QA, using explicit prompts to elicit actionable critiques and confidence judgments. Self-Refine demonstrates that iterative feedback-driven refinement can outperform single-shot generation when compute is available [2fedede6-1]. 
- For verification-heavy tasks, adopt zero-shot self-checkers to filter low-confidence solutions before accepting answers. Self-Check improves accuracy on GSM8K, MathQA, and MATH [8b1db788-3]. 
- Invest in process-level supervision where possible (PRM800K/ProcessBench) to improve error localization and targeted repair. Step-level accuracy gains across multiple math benchmarks indicate superior critique precision/recall [8b1db788-4]. 
- When using RL or optimization over critique, prefer hybrid signals (natural language + numeric) and CoT-style feedback to guide policy updates, and evaluate both accuracy and calibration. Critique-GRPO shows richer critiques enable more successful refinements than spontaneous reflection [d54a8a1f-4] and calibration-focused critique requires task-aware evaluation [8b1db788-2]. 
- Monitor model capability: weaker models may benefit from simpler critique schemas or external tools, while stronger models can exploit complex multi-round loops. Capability gaps directly affect the ability to generate and act on critiques [2fedede6-3]. 

In summary, critique-based approaches—whether split pipelines, iterative self-reflection, unified training, or optimization over critique signals—consistently enhance reasoning performance across math and QA tasks, with the strongest gains when critiques are actionable, process-aware, and paired with adequate model capability and calibration-aware evaluation. While split-architecture critiques are effective, they incur overhead and require actionable feedback [2aea6196-2] , and single-model iterative refinement is simple and powerful when models can generate useful feedback [2fedede6-1] ; bridging the gap with unified reflect-and-refine training and curated process supervision is an active and promising direction [2aea6196-4].

Self-Refine (Madaan et al., 2023) is an advanced TTS technique that enables an LLM to iteratively improve its own outputs through self-generated feedback. Introduced by Madaan et al. (2023), the Self-Refine framework is inspired by how humans revise a draft: The model first produces an initial answer, then critiques or evaluates that answer, and finally uses the critique to refine the answer. This feedback-refinement loop can be repeated multiple times, progressively polishing the output. Notably, Self-Refine requires no additional training data or fine-tuning -the same pre-trained model acts as the initial answer generator, the feedback provider, and the refiner. For sufficiently powerful models, this self-iteration yields significantly better results, presumably because it is easier for a model to identify and fix errors in a given solution than to produce a perfect solution in one attempt. In essence, Self-Refine leverages test-time compute to let the model "think twice (or more)" about its answer, leading to higher-quality and more reliable outputs.

citations.title: RareAgent: Self-Evolving Reasoning for Drug Repurposing in Rare Diseases
snippets: Work on self-improvement provides mechanisms for refining reasoning policies over time. Reflexion leverages verbalized reflection for reinforcement [Shinn et al., 2023], Self-Refine operationalizes a generate-critique-refine loop [Madaan et al., 2023], and evolutionary strategies such as PromptBreeder optimize prompts via self-referential mutation [Fernando et al., 2023]. Complementary views frame reasoning as structured search, externalized in Tree-of-Thoughts [Yao et al., 2023] and Graph-of-Thoughts [Besta et al., 2024]. TextGrad formalizes language feedback as textual gradients for systematic refinement [Yuksekgonul et al., 2025]. A persistent frontier is to develop systems that autonomously improve from sparse, noisy, and unstructured feedback, especially in domains lacking explicit reward signals, where domain-specific intuition must be accrued gradually.

question: What is the state-of-the-art in automation of detecting road surface cracks?

sections.title: # Scope and Challenges
sections.text: Automated detection of road surface cracks spans image acquisition (overhead, in-vehicle, mobile), preprocessing, and AI-driven analysis (classification, detection, or pixel-level segmentation) to localize and characterize cracks for maintenance workflows. Automated distress detection from pavement images is a challenging problem with inherent challenges including shadows, illumination variation, low contrast between cracks and backgrounds, and interference from other objects like patches and lane markings [8b966abd-0]. Most recent work focuses on crack detection from 2D street-view or pavement images, with a shift from coarse classification to pixel-level detection as data collection moves toward 3D sensing [8b966abd-0]. Deep CNNs have become the dominant approach, with interest in methods that can detect and characterize crack type, extent, and severity from 2D and 3D images [8b966abd-4].

citations.title: Deep Learning in Data-Driven Pavement Image Analysis and Automated Distress Detection: A Review
snippets: Deep learning, more specifically deep convolutional neural networks, is fast becoming a popular choice for computer vision-based automated pavement distress detection. While pavement image analysis has been extensively researched over the past three decades or so, recent ground-breaking achievements of deep learning algorithms in the areas of machine translation, speech recognition, and computer vision has sparked interest in the application of deep learning to automated detection of distresses in pavement images. This paper provides a narrative review of recently published studies in this field, highlighting the current achievements and challenges. A comparison of the deep learning software frameworks, network architecture, hyper-parameters employed by each study, and crack detection performance is provided, which is expected to provide a good foundation for driving further research on this important topic in the context of smart pavement or asset management systems. The review concludes with potential avenues for future research; especially in the application of deep learning to not only detect, but also characterize the type, extent, and severity of distresses from 2D and 3D pavement images.

citations.title: Deep Learning in Data-Driven Pavement Image Analysis and Automated Distress Detection: A Review
snippets:
Automated distress detection from pavement images is a challenging problem that has been actively investigated over the past three decades. The presence of shadows; inhomogeneity of distresses; lack of illumination and sufficient contrast between the distress and the background; presence of other objects such as patches and white lane markings, among others, are some major inherent challenges that are difficult to address. While the application of machine learning approaches to automated pavement distress detection is not new, the recent emergence and success of deep learning approaches in areas like speech recognition and computer vision has attracted the attention of pavement researchers. This paper reviewed some recent applications of deep learning to vision-based automated pavement distress detection. 

Based on a small number of studies that have been reported so far in 2016-2018, it appears that interest in the use of deep learning in vision-based automated pavement distress detection is growing fast. Among the reviewed papers, two were published in 2016, seven in 2017, and three in 2018 (as of March). One of the articles included in the review is not yet published, but is uploaded to the arXiv repository. Most reviewed papers focused on crack detection from 2D pavement images or street view images as cracks are easier to detect compared with other 3D oriented distresses like rutting, pothole, and so on. Similar to other application areas, the convolutional neural networks (and variants) rank at the top in most pavement image classification studies. While some studies have shown that deeper CNNs achieve better performance than shallower networks, it is not clear whether the predictive accuracy can be improved by merely adding more layers to a CNN [34]. It has been demonstrated in image analysis competitions that the top performers are often distinguished from the rest by their ability to incorporate their domain expertise in some way into a deep learning pipeline along with the use of some data warping strategies [50]. Likewise, for automated pavement crack detection, data pre-processing and data augmentation at some level seems to be important for improving predictive accuracy.

sections.title: # Sensing Modalities and Acquisition Pipelines
sections.text:
Overhead imagery from UAVs/satellites and vehicle-mounted cameras/smartphones are the main sources for automated crack detection, with LiDAR increasingly used for geometric robustness. Most reviewed papers focused on crack detection from 2D pavement or street-view images because cracks are easier to detect than 3D distresses like potholes and rutting [8b966abd-0]. Hybrid systems combining 2D LiDAR profiles with RGB images have been proposed to combine robustness to poor conditions with texture cues [1e37becf-3]. Mobile LiDAR mapping systems can detect pavement distress at highway speeds, and studies have validated crack detection and characterization workflows over highway and runway segments [1e37becf-0].

LiDAR-based sensing provides geometric cues and can achieve high precision for crack detection under challenging visual conditions. With mobile laser scanning, road cracks wider than 2 mm can be detected with about 95% precision even at low contrast and lighting, and studies report F1 scores of 96.6% (transverse), 87.1% (oblique), and 81.5% (longitudinal) over a 220 m stretch [1e37becf-2]. Earlier work reported completeness of 96% and correctness of 85% for cracks wider than 2 cm, and reviews note feasibility of TLS for medium/high severity cracks though automation for distress mapping is still developing [1e37becf-2].

sections.title: # Pixel-level segmentation (2D CNNs)
sections.text:
U-Net and its modern variants remain foundational, with enhanced backbones and skip connections to capture multi-scale crack patterns and complex backgrounds. Crack segmentation is predominantly implemented with deep CNNs; U-Net and ResNet-based encoders (e.g., ResU-Net) improved crack detection performance over traditional UNet by enhancing feature extraction [0e0da7ca-0]. Efficient designs (e.g., EGA-UNet with lightweight convolutional blocks) target real-time segmentation of varied crack morphologies [0e0da7ca-0].

Recent specialized architectures report high segmentation accuracy on in-situ datasets captured by vehicle-mounted cameras and smartphones across pavement classes. CrackU-net, a U-shaped CNN, achieved loss=0.025, accuracy=0.9901, precision=0.9856, recall=0.9798, and F-measure=0.9842 on 3,000 images, and claimed to avoid false-positive crack detections [0e0da7ca-3]. CrackU-net was trained on 2,400 images and validated on 600 images, extracting crack information from noisy backgrounds and various crack fragments, outperforming FCN and U-Net in pixelwise detection [0e0da7ca-4]. Comparative evaluations have tested UNet, FPN, and UNet++ with ResNet18/50 and DenseNet-121 encoders on datasets like CrackTree260, CrackLS315, CRKWH100, and Stone331, using augmentation and cosine annealing as baselines [0e0da7ca-1].

citations.title: CrackU‐net: A novel deep convolutional neural network for pixelwise pavement crack detection
snippets: Periodic road crack monitoring is an essential procedure for effective pavement management. Highly efficient and accurate crack measurements are key research topics in both academia and industry. Automatic methods gradually replaced traditional manual surveys for more reliable evaluation outputs and better efficiency, whereas the devices are not available to all functional classes of pavements and different departments considering the high cost versus the limited budget. Recently, the widespread use of smartphones and digital cameras made it possible to collect pavement surface crack images at an affordable price in easier ways. However, the qualities of these crack images are diversely influenced by the noises from pavement background, roadways, and so forth. Thus, traditional methods usually fail to extract accurate crack information from pavement images. Therefore, this research proposes a state‐of‐the‐art pixelwise crack detection architecture called CrackU‐net, which is featured by its utilization of advanced deep convolutional neural network technology. CrackU‐net achieved pixelwise crack detection through convolution, pooling, transpose convolution, and concatenation operations, forming the “U”‐shaped model architecture. The model is trained and validated by 3,000 pavement crack images, in which 2,400 for training and 600 for validating, using the Adam algorithm. CrackU‐net has the performance of loss = 0.025, accuracy = 0.9901, precision = 0.9856, recall = 0.9798, and F‐measure = 0.9842 with learning rate of 10−2. Meanwhile, the false‐positive crack detection problem is avoided in CrackU‐net. Therefore, CrackU‐net outperforms both traditional approaches and fully convolutional network (FCN) and U‐net for pixelwise crack detections.

citations.title: CrackU‐net: A novel deep convolutional neural network for pixelwise pavement crack detection
snippets:
This research proposes a convolutional-deconvolutional-based "U"-shaped deep neural network architecture for pixelwise pavement crack detection, which is called CrackU-net. CrackU-net is trained by pavement crack images collected by high-speed, vehicle-mounted action cameras and smartphones from different functional classes of pavements. In total, 2,400 various types of crack images are randomly selected as the training dataset, and 600 images are validation datasets. The multiscale crack features are extracted to multilevel feature maps from the input images through convolutional layers and the pooling layers. Then the transpose convolution layers use the multiscale crack information to achieve semantic segmentation. Concatenate operations are adopted to better utilize the feature information and improve model training performance. CrackU-net is programmed with TensorFlow platform using GTX 1080Ti GPU. The model achieves the best crack segmentation results when the learning rate equals to 10 −2 . The best performance was achieved with the performance measurements of loss = 0.025, accuracy = 0.9901, precision = 0.9856, recall = 0.9798, and F-measure = 0.9842. Experiments demonstrate that CrackU-net can extract crack information correctly from pavement background, regardless of the noise levels, background conditions, and qualities of the original image as long as the crack points can be recognized by a human. However, traditional methods usually fail to provide satisfactory results when the crack images contain many noises or the many minor cracks fragment. This proved the effectiveness and robustness of the CrackU-net for pixelwise crack detection. 

To the best of the authors' knowledge, CrackU-net requires no preprocessing operations compared with the traditional methods. CrackU-net outperforms both traditional methods and other CNN-based methods such as FCN and Unet for pixelwise pavement crack detection according to the comparative experiments of this research. Although CrackU-net in its current version can obtain satisfactory pixelwise crack segmentation results, it is trained on a large number of pavement crack images, and the calculations of crack width, length, areas, and other parameters have not been addressed.

citations.title: An efficient semantic segmentation method for road crack based on EGA-UNet
snippets: Semantic segmentation of road cracks is predominantly implemented through deep convolutional neural networks (CNNs). In this paper, it is possible to learn the complex relationships between crack pixels in an image and generate a crack prediction map of the same size as the input image by training the network, ensuring that each pixel is assigned a specific category label. Leveraging the advantages of CNN in feature representation, various semantic segmentation techniques for crack image detection have emerged. Cheng et al. 22 proposed an automatic crack detection method based on the U-Net deep convolutional neural network, achieving excellent results. A supervised method 23 based on deep learning was proposed, which had the ability to handle different road surface conditions. However, the encoder of the traditional UNet network had relatively weak feature extraction capabilities and a large number of parameters. This had prompted efforts to enhance the encoder's feature extraction capabilities and to make the entire network more lightweight. Yu et al. 24 proposed a U-shaped encoder-decoder semantic segmentation network that combined UNet and ResNet for pixel-level road surface crack image segmentation, improved crack detection performance. Zhang et al. 25 proposed a customized deep learning model architecture named Efficient Crack Segmentation Network to accelerate realtime pavement crack detection and segmentation without compromising performance. Building upon the work of previous researchers, the algorithm proposed in this paper, named EGA-UNet, integrates efficient lightweight convolutional blocks to quickly and precisely segment topological cracks of varying shapes with complex backgrounds.

citations.title: Texture Analysis to Enhance Drone-Based Multi-Modal Inspection of Structures
snippets: This case study employed a deep learning approach for detecting cracks on paved roads. Similar to the texture segmentation task, a variety of state-of-the art architectures and encoders were tested, including Unet [67], FPN [77] and Unet++ [68] combined with the Resnet18, Resnet50 [69], and DenseNet-121 [78] encoders. The top five models presenting the best results were chosen as possible candidate models. To do so, two main criteria were analysed: (a) the overall quantitative performance on the validation set and (b) the perceived qualitative quality of the predictions on the validation set. All networks were trained and validated using a combination of publicly available datasets containing segmented cracks on pavement [85,86]. Details on the used datasets are presented in the next section. Similar to the previous training recipe, unweighted multi-class cross-entropy loss was employed to train the models on the visible part of the acquired data. This time, the Adam optimizer [87] was selected as the optimization strategy. In order to manage the learning rate during the training, the cosine annealing method [72] was employed again. Trivial augment (TA) [73] was also used as the default augmentation strategy. Additionally, following [86]'s training procedure, the targets were symmetrically dilated by 1 pixel. The hyperparameters for the crack segmentation models are presented in Table 3. The aforementioned parameters serve as a baseline for optimization, and small variations may occur if a given model needs further optimization. The training and validation set were randomly generated following a 80%/20% split ratio from four datasets found in [85,86], named CrackTree260, CrackLS315, CRKWH100 and Stone331. CrackTree260 was the first dataset employed in this study [85]. It contains 260 visible images of paved surfaces at a monotone distance. Two different resolutions are found in this dataset, 800 × 600 and 960 × 720 pixels. CRKWH100 is a dataset collected for pavement crack detection [86].

sections.title: # Object detection (single- and two-stage, and modern YOLO variants)
sections.text:
For localization and moderate detail, object detectors are widely used and can be lighter than full pixel-wise segmenters, with strong real-time potential. As practice moves from classification to pixel-level detection, detectors and segmenters are both used; CNN-based models rank at the top in classification and are effective for crack localization [8b966abd-0]. Two-stage detectors like Faster R-CNN with strong backbones (e.g., ResNet50) and attention modules (SENet) are used for crack detection, but bounding boxes lack fine-grained feature estimation [f322b955-3]. One-stage detectors (e.g., SSD with InceptionV2 or MobileNet) and YOLOv5 have been applied to road crack datasets collected via vehicle-mounted smartphones [f322b955-3].

Recent YOLOv8-based methods show strong improvements via tailored losses, adaptive convolutions, and attention modules, with quantified gains in accuracy, recall, mAP, F1, and computational cost. Flexi-YOLO (on YOLOv8) introduces Wise-IoU loss, DCNv-C2f adaptive sampling, Global Attention, and AKConv to improve crack shape modeling; it reports +2.7% accuracy, +4.7% recall, +5.3% mAP@0.5, +3.9% mAP@0.5–0.95, and F1 improvement from 0.80 to 0.84, while reducing GFLOPs by 0.5 [f322b955-0]. These designs target robustness to complex environments and fine crack details while maintaining lightweight deployment suitability [f322b955-2]. Studies emphasize that YOLOv8’s improved accuracy and efficiency make it compelling for real-time crack detection, and that preprocessing and crack type distribution significantly impact detector performance [f322b955-4].

snippets: Although patch-level classification can generate location information, the results are rough. In order to further improve the accuracy of crack detection, the method based on object detection has attracted the attention of researchers. Object detection is to locate the object with the bounding box in the image and determine the category of the object. Nie et al. [45] put forward a crack detection model based on Faster R-CNN and adopted a transfer learning method with parameter fine-tuning to realize the detection of pavement diseases such as cracks, looseness, and deformation. citations.title: Flexi-YOLO: A lightweight method for road crack detection in complex environments
snippets: This article presents a novel Flexi-YOLO model applied to road crack detection. The model employs DCNv-C2f adaptive convolution sampling positions and AKConv adaptive convolution kernel sizes within its backbone network to enhance its ability to extract crack features, allowing for more accurate and flexible crack identification. By adding a GAM attention mechanism at the neck of the network, the model can comprehensively capture global information and further fuse detailed features with low-level network characteristics to obtain more feature information. The newly designed detection head mitigates the issue of information redundancy caused by the attention mechanism's extensive global information collection and the increased model size due to the high parameter count and computation in the original detection head, making it challenging to deploy on devices with limited computational resources. The Wise-IoU method assigns different weights based on sample quality, effectively reducing the negative impact of low-quality samples on the model. With these improvements, the YOLOv8 model performs better in handling complex information across various road conditions, demonstrating stability against fine details and interference information. The developed model shows outstanding performance across various metrics, specifically a 2.7% increase in accuracy, a 4.7% increase in recall, a 5.3% improvement in mAP@0.5, a 3.9 improvement in mAP@0.5-0.95, a 0.5 decrease in GFLOPS, and an increase in F1 score from 0.80 to 0.84. This data underscores the superiority of Flexi-YOLO in multiple dimensions. Furthermore, practical detection experiments indicate that our model excels in numerical evaluation and real-world road condition detection. This validates the practicality of our model improvements and provides valuable experience and technological advancement for real-world road crack operations, offering reliable solutions for global road aging, safety, and maintenance. Its lightweight design also presents an economically efficient solution for infrastructure maintenance, contributing to global public safety and sustainable development.

citations.title: Flexi-YOLO: A lightweight method for road crack detection in complex environments
snippets: Road crack detection is critical to global infrastructure maintenance and public safety, and complex background environments and nonlinear damage crack patterns challenge the need for real-time, efficient, and accurate detection.This paper proposes a lightweight yet robust Flexi-YOLO model based on the YOLOv8 algorithm. We designed Wise-IoU as the model’s loss function to optimize the regression accuracy of its bounding boxes and enhance robustness to low-quality samples. The DCNv-C2f module is constructed for the transformation and fusion of feature information, allowing the convolutional kernels to adapt to the complex shape characteristics of cracks dynamically. A Global Attention Module (GAM) is integrated to improve the model’s perception of global information. The AKConv convolution operation is employed to adaptively adjust the size of convolutions, further enhancing local feature capturing. Additionally, a lightweight network design is implemented, establishing G-Head (Ghost-Head) as the detection head to optimize the issue of feature redundancy. Experimental results show that Flexi-YOLO achieves an accuracy increase of 2.7% over YOLOv8n, a recall rate rise of 4.7%, a mAP improvement of 5.3%, a mAP@0.5–0.95 increase of 3.9%, a decrease of 0.5 in GFLOPS, and an F1 score improvement from 0.80 to 0.84. Flexi-YOLO offers higher detection accuracy and robustness and meets the industrial demands for lightweight real-time detection and lower application costs, providing an efficient and precise solution for the automated detection of road cracks.

citations.title: Impact of Image Preprocessing and Crack Type Distribution on YOLOv8-Based Road Crack Detection
snippets:
The Pavement Management System (PMS) plays a crucial role in ensuring safety and preventing structural failures. With the advent of Industry 4.0, intelligent and data-driven solutions have rapidly developed across various domains, bringing new opportunities for the PMS. In the PMS, advancements in computer vision and deep learning (DL) have enabled automatic road crack detection based on DL models. By leveraging automated detection, the PMS can promptly acquire road damage information, formulate appropriate maintenance plans, reduce manual intervention, and enhance detection efficiency. Consequently, the maintenance and management of transportation infrastructure are shifting gradually from traditional manual inspections to intelligent automation. 

Crack detection algorithms such as You Only Look Once (YOLO) [1], Faster Regionbased Convolutional Neural Network (Faster R-CNN) [2], and U-Net [3] have emerged in response to this need. YOLO outperforms two-stage detectors such as Faster R-CNN in terms of inference speed and is more suitable for real-time road inspection applications. Meanwhile, U-Net has demonstrated strong feature learning capabilities and often requires significantly higher computational resources. Thus, it is less feasible for real-time crack detection in field conditions. As an evolution of the YOLO framework, YOLOv8 [4] introduces several improvements, including enhanced detection accuracy, an optimized network structure, and better generalization capabilities. Compared to its predecessors, YOLOv8 integrates improved feature extraction and a more efficient loss function, making it particularly suitable for detecting fine-grained structural defects such as road cracks. Recent advancements, such as YOLOv9 [5], have demonstrated a strong performance in object detection tasks. However, YOLOv8 remains a compelling choice for real-time applications due to its efficiency and relatively lower computational cost [6]. Given these advantages, this study employed YOLOv8s as the primary detection model for road crack analysis. 

The performance of YOLO-based models depends largely on the quality of input images and the composition of the dataset. Previous studies have explored various image preprocessing techniques to enhance crack detection performance.

sections.title: # Smartphone + LiDAR fusion for quantitative assessment
sections.text: Smartphone imagery combined with onboard LiDAR enables fully automatic crack segmentation and quantitative measurement (length, thickness) with high accuracy. A U-Net pipeline augmented with morphology and registration to LiDAR color data achieved 95% accuracy in crack length estimation and R²=0.98 for thickness, validated on public and in-house datasets [1e37becf-1]. The method maximizes segmentation accuracy through data augmentation and morphology transforms, then registers image cracks to LiDAR color to estimate crack length and thickness at each pixel [1e37becf-4]. The authors suggest extending with self-supervised learning and richer geometric cues to reduce false detections and improve registration [1e37becf-4].

citations.title: Quantitative road crack evaluation by a U‐Net architecture using smartphone images and Lidar data
snippets: Road cracks are a major concern for administrators. Visual inspection is labor‐intensive. The accuracy of previous algorithms for detecting cracks in images requires improvement. Further, the length and thickness of cracks must be estimated. Light detection and ranging (Lidar), a standard smartphone feature is used to develop a method for the completely automatic, accurate, and quantitative evaluation of road cracks. The two contributions of this study are as follows. To achieve the highest segmentation accuracy, U‐Net is combined with data augmentation and morphology transform. To calculate the crack length and thickness, crack images are registered into Lidar color data. The proposed algorithm was validated using a public database of road cracks and those measured by the authors. The algorithm was 95% accurate in determining crack length. The coefficient of determination for thickness estimation accuracy was 0.98 addressing various crack shapes and asphalt pavement patterns.

citations.title: Quantitative road crack evaluation by a U‐Net architecture using smartphone images and Lidar data
snippets:

sections.title: # Performance, Datasets, and Generalization
sections.text:
Crack detection performance varies with crack type, size, and dataset composition; modern deep models report strong results but remain sensitive to class imbalance and domain shifts. Comparative studies train and validate on multiple crack segmentation datasets (e.g., CrackTree260, CrackLS315, CRKWH100, Stone331), using augmentation and cosine annealing; hyperparameters and splits are tuned to balance performance and generalization [0e0da7ca-1]. Reported segmentation metrics (e.g., F1=0.9842, recall=0.98) reflect performance on curated in-situ datasets captured with vehicle-mounted cameras/smartphones across pavement classes [0e0da7ca-3]. For detectors, YOLOv8-based pipelines show improved real-time performance, but outcomes depend on image preprocessing and the distribution of crack types within training and inference data [f322b955-4].

LiDAR-based pipelines demonstrate robustness to visual degradation and can measure crack geometry with high precision, though comprehensive, standardized benchmarks remain limited. Mobile/terrestrial LiDAR studies report precision around 95% for mm-scale thresholds and F1 scores of 81–97% across crack orientations; however, many studies note incomplete reporting of crack area/volume accuracy and limited coverage of crack types or conditions [1e37becf-2]. Reviews of TLS-based crack detection acknowledge strong feasibility for medium/high severity cracks but highlight that fully automated distress mapping and quantitative accuracy validation are still developing areas [1e37becf-2].

citations.title: CrackU‐net: A novel deep convolutional neural network for pixelwise pavement crack detection
snippets: Periodic road crack monitoring is an essential procedure for effective pavement management. Highly efficient and accurate crack measurements are key research topics in both academia and industry. Automatic methods gradually replaced traditional manual surveys for more reliable evaluation outputs and better efficiency, whereas the devices are not available to all functional classes of pavements and different departments considering the high cost versus the limited budget. Recently, the widespread use of smartphones and digital cameras made it possible to collect pavement surface crack images at an affordable price in easier ways. However, the qualities of these crack images are diversely influenced by the noises from pavement background, roadways, and so forth. Thus, traditional methods usually fail to extract accurate crack information from pavement images. Therefore, this research proposes a state‐of‐the‐art pixelwise crack detection architecture called CrackU‐net, which is featured by its utilization of advanced deep convolutional neural network technology. CrackU‐net achieved pixelwise crack detection through convolution, pooling, transpose convolution, and concatenation operations, forming the “U”‐shaped model architecture. The model is trained and validated by 3,000 pavement crack images, in which 2,400 for training and 600 for validating, using the Adam algorithm. CrackU‐net has the performance of loss = 0.025, accuracy = 0.9901, precision = 0.9856, recall = 0.9798, and F‐measure = 0.9842 with learning rate of 10−2. Meanwhile, the false‐positive crack detection problem is avoided in CrackU‐net. Therefore, CrackU‐net outperforms both traditional approaches and fully convolutional network (FCN) and U‐net for pixelwise crack detections.

snippets: This case study employed a deep learning approach for detecting cracks on paved roads. Similar to the texture segmentation task, a variety of state-of-the art architectures and encoders were tested, including Unet [67], FPN [77] and Unet++ [68] combined with the Resnet18, Resnet50 [69], and DenseNet-121 [78] encoders. The top five models presenting the best results were chosen as possible candidate models. To do so, two main criteria were analysed: (a) the overall quantitative performance on the validation set and (b) the perceived qualitative quality of the predictions on the validation set. All networks were trained and validated using a combination of publicly available datasets containing segmented cracks on pavement [85,86]. Details on the used datasets are presented in the next section. Similar to the previous training recipe, unweighted multi-class cross-entropy loss was employed to train the models on the visible part of the acquired data. This time, the Adam optimizer [87] was selected as the optimization strategy. In order to manage the learning rate during the training, the cosine annealing method [72] was employed again. Trivial augment (TA) [73] was also used as the default augmentation strategy. Additionally, following [86]'s training procedure, the targets were symmetrically dilated by 1 pixel. The hyperparameters for the crack segmentation models are presented in Table 3. The aforementioned parameters serve as a baseline for optimization, and small variations may occur if a given model needs further optimization. The training and validation set were randomly generated following a 80%/20% split ratio from four datasets found in [85,86], named CrackTree260, CrackLS315, CRKWH100 and Stone331. CrackTree260 was the first dataset employed in this study [85]. It contains 260 visible images of paved surfaces at a monotone distance. Two different resolutions are found in this dataset, 800 × 600 and 960 × 720 pixels. CRKWH100 is a dataset collected for pavement crack detection [86].

citations.title: Impact of Image Preprocessing and Crack Type Distribution on YOLOv8-Based Road Crack Detection
snippets:
The Pavement Management System (PMS) plays a crucial role in ensuring safety and preventing structural failures. With the advent of Industry 4.0, intelligent and data-driven solutions have rapidly developed across various domains, bringing new opportunities for the PMS. In the PMS, advancements in computer vision and deep learning (DL) have enabled automatic road crack detection based on DL models. By leveraging automated detection, the PMS can promptly acquire road damage information, formulate appropriate maintenance plans, reduce manual intervention, and enhance detection efficiency. Consequently, the maintenance and management of transportation infrastructure are shifting gradually from traditional manual inspections to intelligent automation. 

Crack detection algorithms such as You Only Look Once (YOLO) [1], Faster Regionbased Convolutional Neural Network (Faster R-CNN) [2], and U-Net [3] have emerged in response to this need. YOLO outperforms two-stage detectors such as Faster R-CNN in terms of inference speed and is more suitable for real-time road inspection applications. Meanwhile, U-Net has demonstrated strong feature learning capabilities and often requires significantly higher computational resources. Thus, it is less feasible for real-time crack detection in field conditions. As an evolution of the YOLO framework, YOLOv8 [4] introduces several improvements, including enhanced detection accuracy, an optimized network structure, and better generalization capabilities. Compared to its predecessors, YOLOv8 integrates improved feature extraction and a more efficient loss function, making it particularly suitable for detecting fine-grained structural defects such as road cracks. Recent advancements, such as YOLOv9 [5], have demonstrated a strong performance in object detection tasks. However, YOLOv8 remains a compelling choice for real-time applications due to its efficiency and relatively lower computational cost [6]. Given these advantages, this study employed YOLOv8s as the primary detection model for road crack analysis. 

The performance of YOLO-based models depends largely on the quality of input images and the composition of the dataset. Previous studies have explored various image preprocessing techniques to enhance crack detection performance.

sections.title: # Robustness to Adverse Conditions and Domain Adaptation
sections.text:
Adverse weather, shadows, and illumination changes remain challenging; recent models incorporate frequency-aware features, context fusion, and adaptive upsampling to improve robustness. CrackNet-Weather targets rain and snow by enhancing frequency information preservation, context-aware feature fusion, and adaptive upsampling to maintain performance under adverse conditions [8b966abd-3]. Prior work with YOLOv5-based detectors shows speed and accuracy gains but notes persistent challenges in complex or visually degraded environments, motivating specialized architectures [8b966abd-3]. Shadow-removal frameworks and dedicated shadow-crack datasets have been proposed to mitigate shadow interference and brightness variation [0e0da7ca-1].

Data augmentation, domain-informed preprocessing, and attention mechanisms are key to improving generalization and robustness. Domain expertise integration into deep learning pipelines and data warping/augmentation are important differentiators for top performers in pavement crack detection [8b966abd-0]. Baseline training recipes include trivial augment, cosine annealing, and symmetric dilations of targets to stabilize and improve segmentation performance across diverse crack shapes and backgrounds [0e0da7ca-1].

citations.title: Deep Learning in Data-Driven Pavement Image Analysis and Automated Distress Detection: A Review
snippets:
Automated distress detection from pavement images is a challenging problem that has been actively investigated over the past three decades. The presence of shadows; inhomogeneity of distresses; lack of illumination and sufficient contrast between the distress and the background; presence of other objects such as patches and white lane markings, among others, are some major inherent challenges that are difficult to address. While the application of machine learning approaches to automated pavement distress detection is not new, the recent emergence and success of deep learning approaches in areas like speech recognition and computer vision has attracted the attention of pavement researchers. This paper reviewed some recent applications of deep learning to vision-based automated pavement distress detection. 

Based on a small number of studies that have been reported so far in 2016-2018, it appears that interest in the use of deep learning in vision-based automated pavement distress detection is growing fast. Among the reviewed papers, two were published in 2016, seven in 2017, and three in 2018 (as of March). One of the articles included in the review is not yet published, but is uploaded to the arXiv repository. Most reviewed papers focused on crack detection from 2D pavement images or street view images as cracks are easier to detect compared with other 3D oriented distresses like rutting, pothole, and so on. As the state-of-the-practice in pavement distress data collection is moving towards 3D vision and measurement systems, more studies are expected to focus on analyzing 3D pavement images and move from overall image classification (crack or no_crack) to pixel-level crack detection [46]. 

Similar to other application areas, the convolutional neural networks (and variants) rank at the top in most pavement image classification studies. While some studies have shown that deeper CNNs achieve better performance than shallower networks, it is not clear whether the predictive accuracy can be improved by merely adding more layers to a CNN [34]. It has been demonstrated in image analysis competitions that the top performers are often distinguished from the rest by their ability to incorporate their domain expertise in some way into a deep learning pipeline along with the use of some data warping strategies [50]. Likewise, for automated pavement crack detection, data pre-processing and data augmentation at some level seems to be important for improving predictive accuracy.

citations.title: CrackNet-Weather: An Effective Pavement Crack Detection Method Under Adverse Weather Conditions
snippets: Many researchers have already undertaken similar work on solving the problem of pavement crack detection [39][40][41]. Gavilan et al. [42] propose an adaptive pavement crack detection framework that leverages pavement classification and multi-stage preprocessing to improve the reliability of automatic road distress assessment. The system utilizes an SVM-based classifier ensemble to tailor detection parameters to different pavement types, effectively reducing false positives from non-crack features and enhancing overall crack detection accuracy. Hu et al. [43] employ YOLOv5-based deep learning models for automatic pavement crack detection, demonstrating superior accuracy and speed over traditional approaches. Their work highlights the effectiveness of deep learning for identifying cracks of varying severity, though challenges persist in more complex or visually degraded environments. Fan et al. [44] propose a shadow-removal-oriented crack detection framework and introduce a dedicated shadow-crack dataset to address the interference of shadows in pavement crack detection. Their method effectively improves detection accuracy in the presence of shadows and varying brightness caused by seasonal and weather changes. Despite significant progress in deep learning-based pavement crack detection, robust and efficient detection under adverse weather conditions remains an open challenge. Existing models often experience degraded performance when dealing with low visibility, background noise, and complex crack morphologies. Motivated by these gaps, this paper presents CrackNet-Weather, a model that systematically enhances frequency information preservation, context-aware feature fusion, and content-adaptive upsampling, aiming to achieve robust pavement crack detection in rain, snow, and other challenging weather scenarios.

sections.title: # Deployment and Operationalization
sections.text:
Industrial deployments emphasize real-time performance, low latency, and cost-effective data capture via smartphones and in-vehicle sensors. A deep learning surveying scheme using mobile-device imagery reported real-time analysis with models achieving F1 52–56% and 10–178 images per second, indicating practical throughput for on-device or edge pipelines [8b966abd-1]. Lightweight YOLOv8-based designs (e.g., Flexi-YOLO) report improved mAP and F1 while reducing GFLOPs, supporting efficient deployment on resource-constrained devices [f322b955-0]. Mobile LiDAR systems have been validated on multi-mile highway and runway segments for automated distress detection and characterization at operating speeds [1e37becf-0].

Hybrid pipelines that fuse camera and LiDAR are increasingly adopted to combine visual context with geometric robustness for both detection and quantitative assessment. Smartphone-image segmentation fused with LiDAR achieves accurate crack length and thickness estimation, enabling quantitative reports for maintenance [1e37becf-1]. Hybrid 2D–3D systems using two LiDARs and RGB images combine profile robustness with texture cues to improve detection under poor conditions [1e37becf-3].

citations.title: An Efficient and Scalable Deep Learning Approach for Road Damage Detection
snippets: Pavement condition evaluation is essential to time the preventative or rehabilitative actions and control distress propagation. Failing to conduct timely evaluations can lead to severe structural and financial loss of the infrastructure and complete reconstructions. Automated computer-aided surveying measures can provide a database of road damage patterns and their locations. This database can be utilized for timely road re-pairs to gain the minimum cost of maintenance and the asphalt’s maximum durability. This paper introduces a deep learning-based surveying scheme to analyze the image-based distress data in real-time. A database consisting of a diverse population of crack distress types such as longitudinal, transverse, and alligator cracks, photographed using mobile-device is used. Then, a family of efficient and scalable models that are tuned for pavement crack detection is trained. Proposed models, resulted in F1-scores, ranging from 52% to 56%, and average inference time from 178-10 images per second. Finally, the performance of the object detectors are examined, and error analysis is reported against various images. The source code is available at https://github.com/mahdi65/roadDamageDetection2020.

citations.title: Quantitative road crack evaluation by a U‐Net architecture using smartphone images and Lidar data
snippets: Road cracks are a major concern for administrators. Visual inspection is labor‐intensive. The accuracy of previous algorithms for detecting cracks in images requires improvement. Further, the length and thickness of cracks must be estimated. Light detection and ranging (Lidar), a standard smartphone feature is used to develop a method for the completely automatic, accurate, and quantitative evaluation of road cracks. The two contributions of this study are as follows. To achieve the highest segmentation accuracy, U‐Net is combined with data augmentation and morphology transform. To calculate the crack length and thickness, crack images are registered into Lidar color data. The proposed algorithm was validated using a public database of road cracks and those measured by the authors. The algorithm was 95% accurate in determining crack length. The coefficient of determination for thickness estimation accuracy was 0.98 addressing various crack shapes and asphalt pavement patterns.

citations.title: Flexi-YOLO: A lightweight method for road crack detection in complex environments
snippets: Road crack detection is critical to global infrastructure maintenance and public safety, and complex background environments and nonlinear damage crack patterns challenge the need for real-time, efficient, and accurate detection.This paper proposes a lightweight yet robust Flexi-YOLO model based on the YOLOv8 algorithm. We designed Wise-IoU as the model’s loss function to optimize the regression accuracy of its bounding boxes and enhance robustness to low-quality samples. The DCNv-C2f module is constructed for the transformation and fusion of feature information, allowing the convolutional kernels to adapt to the complex shape characteristics of cracks dynamically. A Global Attention Module (GAM) is integrated to improve the model’s perception of global information. The AKConv convolution operation is employed to adaptively adjust the size of convolutions, further enhancing local feature capturing. Additionally, a lightweight network design is implemented, establishing G-Head (Ghost-Head) as the detection head to optimize the issue of feature redundancy. Experimental results show that Flexi-YOLO achieves an accuracy increase of 2.7% over YOLOv8n, a recall rate rise of 4.7%, a mAP improvement of 5.3%, a mAP@0.5–0.95 increase of 3.9%, a decrease of 0.5 in GFLOPS, and an F1 score improvement from 0.80 to 0.84. Flexi-YOLO offers higher detection accuracy and robustness and meets the industrial demands for lightweight real-time detection and lower application costs, providing an efficient and precise solution for the automated detection of road cracks.

citations.title: HIGHWAY AND AIRPORT RUNWAY PAVEMENT INSPECTION USING MOBILE LiDAR
snippets: This implies that their approach cannot be applied to mobile mapping systems moving at a considerably high speeds or LiDAR data captured by 3D LiDAR units. Laurent et al. (2008) proposed the use of Laser Crack Measurement System (LCMS) for crack monitoring using two 2D laser units. The system generates transversal profiles throughout the road segment to detect cracking and is reported to have an accuracy of 90% for transverse crack detection when the 3D crack is captured. The scope of this study was to determine if we could effectively map pothole volume and surface area at highway speeds so that patching tables can be derived. This research is focused on proposing a fully automated strategy that is suitable to conduct a two-fold assessment of pavements over highways as well as airport runway strips. The first component consists of detecting and reporting locations that exhibit any form of pavement distress, such as cracking, rutting, and potholes (occurring due to wear-and-tear, pavement patching discontinuity, missing RPMs). Secondly, the detected distress locations are characterized based on their severity, which constitutes the following attributesdepth below road surface, surface area denoting the level of degradation at different depths below road surface, and filling volume of the detected potholes. In order to achieve this end goal, we first start by introducing and comparing two different grades (medium-grade and high-grade) of LiDAR-based mobile mapping systems (MMS) in terms of the relative and absolute accuracy of their acquired point clouds. The qualitative and quantitative accuracy analysis of point clouds from the two MMS validates our choice of using the high-grade MMS for pavement distress monitoring. Finally, the proposed strategy for cracking and pothole detection and characterization is validated by testing it on a 10-mile-long highway segment and two airport runway strips. The results indicate the ability of LiDAR-based mobile mapping systems to accurately detect locations exhibiting pavement distress with varying severity and different causes.

As shown in Fig. 14, the road video frames acquired by a high definition (HD) camera were first utilized to detect (recognize) road potholes. Simultaneously, the same video was also employed for sparse 3-D road geometry reconstruction. By analyzing such multi-modal road inspection results, the potholes were accurately detected. Such a hybrid method dramatically reduces the incorrectly detected road potholes. sections.title: # Open Challenges and Emerging Directions
sections.text:
Despite progress, several challenges persist: fine-width crack detection, crack width/depth estimation, long-tail crack morphologies, and robustness across domains and conditions. Reviews highlight persistent issues with illumination, shadows, and other surface artifacts that confound crack vs. non-crack discrimination [8b966abd-0]. LiDAR-based studies note incomplete or missing quantitative accuracy evaluations (e.g., crack area/volume) and limited type/condition coverage [1e37becf-2]. Future work includes extending with self-supervised or dynamic learning to improve generalization, enriching datasets with appendage/scene context to reduce false positives, and improving registration/fusion workflows [1e37becf-4].

Emerging methods include adaptive convolution, global attention, and tailored losses to better capture crack geometry; transformer-based or attention-augmented detectors and segmenters are being explored for multi-scale crack patterns and fine details. Architectural innovations such as adaptive sampling, adaptive kernels, and global attention improve modeling of complex crack shapes while keeping models lightweight [f322b955-0]. Recent lines of work adapt YOLOv8 backbones and necks (e.g., SPD-conv for small crack enhancement and ASF-YOLO for multi-scale fusion) and refine bounding box regression losses to improve crack localization [f322b955-1].

citations.title: Flexi-YOLO: A lightweight method for road crack detection in complex environments
snippets: Road crack detection is critical to global infrastructure maintenance and public safety, and complex background environments and nonlinear damage crack patterns challenge the need for real-time, efficient, and accurate detection.This paper proposes a lightweight yet robust Flexi-YOLO model based on the YOLOv8 algorithm. We designed Wise-IoU as the model’s loss function to optimize the regression accuracy of its bounding boxes and enhance robustness to low-quality samples. The DCNv-C2f module is constructed for the transformation and fusion of feature information, allowing the convolutional kernels to adapt to the complex shape characteristics of cracks dynamically. A Global Attention Module (GAM) is integrated to improve the model’s perception of global information. The AKConv convolution operation is employed to adaptively adjust the size of convolutions, further enhancing local feature capturing. Additionally, a lightweight network design is implemented, establishing G-Head (Ghost-Head) as the detection head to optimize the issue of feature redundancy. Experimental results show that Flexi-YOLO achieves an accuracy increase of 2.7% over YOLOv8n, a recall rate rise of 4.7%, a mAP improvement of 5.3%, a mAP@0.5–0.95 increase of 3.9%, a decrease of 0.5 in GFLOPS, and an F1 score improvement from 0.80 to 0.84. Flexi-YOLO offers higher detection accuracy and robustness and meets the industrial demands for lightweight real-time detection and lower application costs, providing an efficient and precise solution for the automated detection of road cracks.

sections.title: # Practical Takeaways (SOTA Summary)
sections.text:
- For pixel-level mapping from 2D images, modern CNN-based segmenters with enhanced backbones and skip connections (U-Net/ResU-Net/UNet++-style) are state-of-the-art, achieving high segmentation accuracy on in-situ datasets captured by vehicle-mounted cameras/smartphones, with reported F1 around 0.98 on curated datasets. U-Net and ResNet-based encoders improved crack segmentation performance over traditional UNet [0e0da7ca-0]. CrackU-net reports F1=0.9842, precision=0.9856, recall=0.9798 on 3,000 pavement images [0e0da7ca-3].

- For real-time localization and coarse geometry, YOLO-family detectors with strong backbones and tailored losses (e.g., YOLOv8 variants) deliver high accuracy, recall, and mAP with low latency, making them attractive for deployment; careful preprocessing and dataset balancing are crucial. YOLOv8-based Flexi-YOLO improves accuracy, recall, mAP@0.5/0.5–0.95, and F1 while reducing GFLOPs compared to YOLOv8n [f322b955-0]. Detector performance is sensitive to preprocessing and crack type distribution [f322b955-4].

- For robustness to adverse conditions and quantitative crack characterization, fusion of smartphone imagery with LiDAR is a strong SOTA direction, achieving high accuracy in crack length and thickness estimation via segmentation plus registration to LiDAR color space. Smartphone+LiDAR achieves 95% length accuracy and R²=0.98 for thickness using U-Net with augmentation and morphology transforms [1e37becf-1]. Further gains are expected from self-supervised learning and richer geometric context [1e37becf-4].

- For 3D sensing-only pipelines, mobile/terrestrial LiDAR can detect and characterize cracks with precision around 95% for threshold widths and F1 scores of 81–97% across crack orientations, though comprehensive benchmarking and standardization remain active areas. TLS/MLS studies report ~95% precision for mm-scale thresholds and orientation-specific F1 (96.6%, 87.1%, 81.5%) over multi-hundred meter test stretches [1e37becf-2].

- Across modalities, domain-informed preprocessing/augmentation, attention mechanisms, and adaptive convolutions are key factors differentiating top-performing systems and improving generalization under real-world variability. Incorporating domain expertise and warping/augmentation strategies is important to boost accuracy [8b966abd-0]. Baseline recipes (cosine annealing, trivial augment, target dilation) improve segmentation stability and quality [0e0da7ca-1].

citations.title: CrackU‐net: A novel deep convolutional neural network for pixelwise pavement crack detection
snippets: Periodic road crack monitoring is an essential procedure for effective pavement management. Highly efficient and accurate crack measurements are key research topics in both academia and industry. Automatic methods gradually replaced traditional manual surveys for more reliable evaluation outputs and better efficiency, whereas the devices are not available to all functional classes of pavements and different departments considering the high cost versus the limited budget. Recently, the widespread use of smartphones and digital cameras made it possible to collect pavement surface crack images at an affordable price in easier ways. However, the qualities of these crack images are diversely influenced by the noises from pavement background, roadways, and so forth. Thus, traditional methods usually fail to extract accurate crack information from pavement images. Therefore, this research proposes a state‐of‐the‐art pixelwise crack detection architecture called CrackU‐net, which is featured by its utilization of advanced deep convolutional neural network technology. CrackU‐net achieved pixelwise crack detection through convolution, pooling, transpose convolution, and concatenation operations, forming the “U”‐shaped model architecture. The model is trained and validated by 3,000 pavement crack images, in which 2,400 for training and 600 for validating, using the Adam algorithm. CrackU‐net has the performance of loss = 0.025, accuracy = 0.9901, precision = 0.9856, recall = 0.9798, and F‐measure = 0.9842 with learning rate of 10−2. Meanwhile, the false‐positive crack detection problem is avoided in CrackU‐net. Therefore, CrackU‐net outperforms both traditional approaches and fully convolutional network (FCN) and U‐net for pixelwise crack detections.

citations.title: Deep Learning in Data-Driven Pavement Image Analysis and Automated Distress Detection: A Review
snippets:
Automated distress detection from pavement images is a challenging problem that has been actively investigated over the past three decades. The presence of shadows; inhomogeneity of distresses; lack of illumination and sufficient contrast between the distress and the background; presence of other objects such as patches and white lane markings, among others, are some major inherent challenges that are difficult to address. While the application of machine learning approaches to automated pavement distress detection is not new, the recent emergence and success of deep learning approaches in areas like speech recognition and computer vision has attracted the attention of pavement researchers. This paper reviewed some recent applications of deep learning to vision-based automated pavement distress detection. 

Based on a small number of studies that have been reported so far in 2016-2018, it appears that interest in the use of deep learning in vision-based automated pavement distress detection is growing fast. Among the reviewed papers, two were published in 2016, seven in 2017, and three in 2018 (as of March). One of the articles included in the review is not yet published, but is uploaded to the arXiv repository. Most reviewed papers focused on crack detection from 2D pavement images or street view images as cracks are easier to detect compared with other 3D oriented distresses like rutting, pothole, and so on. As the state-of-the-practice in pavement distress data collection is moving towards 3D vision and measurement systems, more studies are expected to focus on analyzing 3D pavement images and move from overall image classification (crack or no_crack) to pixel-level crack detection [46]. 

Similar to other application areas, the convolutional neural networks (and variants) rank at the top in most pavement image classification studies. While some studies have shown that deeper CNNs achieve better performance than shallower networks, it is not clear whether the predictive accuracy can be improved by merely adding more layers to a CNN [34]. It has been demonstrated in image analysis competitions that the top performers are often distinguished from the rest by their ability to incorporate their domain expertise in some way into a deep learning pipeline along with the use of some data warping strategies [50]. Likewise, for automated pavement crack detection, data pre-processing and data augmentation at some level seems to be important for improving predictive accuracy.

citations.title: An efficient semantic segmentation method for road crack based on EGA-UNet
snippets: Semantic segmentation of road cracks is predominantly implemented through deep convolutional neural networks (CNNs). In this paper, it is possible to learn the complex relationships between crack pixels in an image and generate a crack prediction map of the same size as the input image by training the network, ensuring that each pixel is assigned a specific category label. Leveraging the advantages of CNN in feature representation, various semantic segmentation techniques for crack image detection have emerged. Cheng et al. 22 proposed an automatic crack detection method based on the U-Net deep convolutional neural network, achieving excellent results. A supervised method 23 based on deep learning was proposed, which had the ability to handle different road surface conditions. However, the encoder of the traditional UNet network had relatively weak feature extraction capabilities and a large number of parameters. This had prompted efforts to enhance the encoder's feature extraction capabilities and to make the entire network more lightweight. Yu et al. 24 proposed a U-shaped encoder-decoder semantic segmentation network that combined UNet and ResNet for pixel-level road surface crack image segmentation, improved crack detection performance. Zhang et al. 25 proposed a customized deep learning model architecture named Efficient Crack Segmentation Network to accelerate realtime pavement crack detection and segmentation without compromising performance. Building upon the work of previous researchers, the algorithm proposed in this paper, named EGA-UNet, integrates efficient lightweight convolutional blocks to quickly and precisely segment topological cracks of varying shapes with complex backgrounds.

citations.title: Impact of Image Preprocessing and Crack Type Distribution on YOLOv8-Based Road Crack Detection
snippets:
The Pavement Management System (PMS) plays a crucial role in ensuring safety and preventing structural failures. With the advent of Industry 4.0, intelligent and data-driven solutions have rapidly developed across various domains, bringing new opportunities for the PMS. In the PMS, advancements in computer vision and deep learning (DL) have enabled automatic road crack detection based on DL models. By leveraging automated detection, the PMS can promptly acquire road damage information, formulate appropriate maintenance plans, reduce manual intervention, and enhance detection efficiency. Consequently, the maintenance and management of transportation infrastructure are shifting gradually from traditional manual inspections to intelligent automation. 

Crack detection algorithms such as You Only Look Once (YOLO) [1], Faster Regionbased Convolutional Neural Network (Faster R-CNN) [2], and U-Net [3] have emerged in response to this need. YOLO outperforms two-stage detectors such as Faster R-CNN in terms of inference speed and is more suitable for real-time road inspection applications. Meanwhile, U-Net has demonstrated strong feature learning capabilities and often requires significantly higher computational resources. Thus, it is less feasible for real-time crack detection in field conditions. As an evolution of the YOLO framework, YOLOv8 [4] introduces several improvements, including enhanced detection accuracy, an optimized network structure, and better generalization capabilities. Compared to its predecessors, YOLOv8 integrates improved feature extraction and a more efficient loss function, making it particularly suitable for detecting fine-grained structural defects such as road cracks. Recent advancements, such as YOLOv9 [5], have demonstrated a strong performance in object detection tasks. However, YOLOv8 remains a compelling choice for real-time applications due to its efficiency and relatively lower computational cost [6]. Given these advantages, this study employed YOLOv8s as the primary detection model for road crack analysis. 

The performance of YOLO-based models depends largely on the quality of input images and the composition of the dataset. Previous studies have explored various image preprocessing techniques to enhance crack detection performance.

sections.title: # What’s Next for SOTA
sections.text:
Near-term SOTA advances are likely to come from: (1) stronger multi-sensor fusion (RGB-D, TLS/MLS) for fine-width crack detection and width/depth estimation; (2) adaptive architectures (transformer-based attention, adaptive sampling/kernels) tailored to crack morphology; (3) self-/weakly-supervised and domain adaptation to bridge in-vehicle/UAV/satellite domains; and (4) standardized benchmarks reporting full crack geometry metrics (length, width, area/volume) and robustness across seasons/conditions to enable fair comparisons. Existing laser-based studies often lack complete quantitative accuracy reporting for crack area/volume and cover limited crack types/conditions [1e37becf-2]. Community recommendations include adopting up-to-date self-supervised learning and expanding datasets with appendage/scene context and global geometric features [1e37becf-4].

In sum, the state-of-the-art in automated road crack detection combines modern deep CNNs (segmentation and YOLO-style detection) with adaptive modules and robust preprocessing for 2D imagery, and hybrid 2D–3D pipelines that fuse smartphone images with LiDAR for accurate, quantitative crack mapping; LiDAR-only systems provide strong geometric robustness and precision for crack detection and characterization, with active work ongoing to standardize benchmarks and improve generalization across environments and crack morphologies. Deep CNNs dominate crack detection in images, with enhanced encoders and architectures improving performance [0e0da7ca-0]. YOLOv8-based models with tailored losses and adaptive components show significant accuracy and efficiency gains for crack detection [f322b955-0]. Smartphone+LiDAR fusion enables accurate quantitative crack assessment [1e37becf-1]. LiDAR-based systems achieve high precision and orientation-dependent F1 across real road segments [1e37becf-2].
