question: write a literature review on the topic of Spatial abilities in AI regarding to depth prediction

sections.title: # Spatial abilities in AI: A literature review with a focus on depth prediction
sections.text: Depth prediction is a core component of AI’s spatial abilities: it captures the third dimension, enables metric understanding of scenes, and supports tasks such as navigation, augmented reality, and robotics. In practice, “spatial abilities” in AI can be operationalized through capabilities like geometric consistency across views, scale-aware reasoning, robustness to occlusions and textureless surfaces, and the ability to synthesize novel viewpoints with metric plausibility. These abilities manifest in two closely related families of work: monocular depth estimation and 3D scene representations (e.g., NeRF/3D Gaussian splatting), each with distinct assumptions, strengths, and limitations.

sections.title: # Foundations: from geometric constraints to deep learning
sections.text:
Classical approaches to monocular depth estimation formulated the problem via geometric relationships between consecutive frames, often casting depth prediction as an optimization that leverages motion and photometric constraints. These methods achieved reasonable accuracy but suffered in textureless or varying illumination conditions, and their dense inference cost limited deployment at scale. As deep learning matured, CNN-based architectures learned to predict depth directly from single images, with multi-scale supervision and joint prediction of surface normals and semantics to enforce geometric consistency. Later work emphasized enforcing geometric priors within the network—e.g., planarity and curvature constraints—to improve the consistency of predicted depth and normals, yielding robustness to noise and better 3D feature recovery such as point clouds and surface normals. Monocular depth estimation is a fundamental computer vision task which plays an essential role in many real-world applications such as autonomous driving, robot navigation, and virtual reality. Classical geometric methods resolve this problem by leveraging the geometric relationship between temporally contiguous frames and formulating depth prediction as an optimization problem, while deep learning techniques have reformed the field by training networks to predict depth directly from monocular images; supervised methods perform best but labeling is costly, motivating unsupervised approaches that use backwarping photometric errors [4b9ec87c-0] One of the first papers to report success in monocular depth from perspective images used an MRF with local and global features; with deep learning, CNNs became common, with multi-scale predictions and joint estimation of normals and semantics; later methods enforce geometric consistency within the network, such as using a plane-aware loss derived from principal curvature [4b9ec87c-1] Constructing high-order global geometric constraints (virtual normal) beyond pixel-wise ones improves depth accuracy and recovers high-quality 3D features (point cloud, surface normal) on NYU-Depth V2 and KITTI, demonstrating robustness to noise and strong global constraints [4b9ec87c-3].

Self-supervised monocular depth estimation broadened data access by avoiding pixelwise labels, but introduced new challenges. Photometric reprojection errors enable consistency training, yet are sensitive to illumination changes and moving objects; moreover, the scale ambiguity problem—arising because backwarping-based objectives are invariant to an arbitrary depth–translation scale—remains a fundamental limitation unless addressed by scale-aware losses or post-hoc calibration. Unsupervised monocular depth estimation leverages backwarping photometric errors but suffers from scale ambiguity, requiring median-scale ratios for evaluation that are unavailable in practice; photometric errors are also sensitive to illumination and moving objects, and learning uncertainty for predicted ego-motion is non-trivial [4b9ec87c-0].

citations.title: Towards Scale-Aware, Robust, and Generalizable Unsupervised Monocular Depth Estimation by Integrating IMU Motion Dynamics
snippets:
Monocular depth estimation is a fundamental computer vision task which plays an essential role in many real-world applications such as autonomous driving, robot navigation, and virtual reality [36,20,44]. Classical geometric methods resolve this problem by leveraging the geometric relationship between temporally contiguous frames and formulating depth prediction as an optimization problem [9,29,8]. While geometric methods have achieved good performance, they are sensitive to either textureless regions or illumination changes. The computational cost for dense depth prediction also limits their practical use. Recently deep learning techniques have reformed this research field by training networks to predict depth directly from monocular images and designing proper losses based on groundtruth depth labels or geometric depth clues from visual data. While supervised learning methods achieve the best performance [7,24,11,1,45], the labour cost for collecting ground-truth labels prohibits their use in real-world. To address this issue, unsupervised monocular depth estimation has drawn a lot of research attention [48,14], which leverages the photometric error from backwarping. 

Although unsupervised monocular depth learning has made great progress in recent years, there still exist several fundamental problems that may obstruct its usage in real-world. First, current methods suffer from the scale ambiguity problem since the backwarping process is equivalent up to an arbitrary scaling factor w.r.t. depth and translation. While current methods are usually evaluated by re-scaling each prediction map using the median ratio between the ground-truth depth and the prediction, it is difficult to obtain such median ratios in practice. Secondly, it is well-known that the photometric error is sensitive to illumination change and moving objects, which violate the underlying assumption of the backwarping projection. In addition, though uncertainty has been introduced for the photometric error map under the unsupervised learning framework [21,41], it remains non-trivial to learn an uncertainty measure for the predicted ego-motion, which could further benefit the development of a robust and trustworthy system.

citations.title: Enforcing Geometric Constraints of Virtual Normal for Depth Prediction
snippets: This paper proposed to construct a high-order global geometric constraint (VNL) in the 3D space for monocular depth prediction. In contrast to previous methods with only pixel-wise constraint, our method can not only predict accurate depth but also recover high-quality 3D features, such as the point cloud and the surface normal, eliminating necessities to optimize a new sub-model. Compared with other 3D constrains, our proposed VNL is more robust to noise and can encode strong global constraints. Experimental results on NYUD-V2 and KITTI have proved the effectiveness of our method and the state-of-the-art performance both on large models and light-weight backbones.

citations.title: Pano Popups: Indoor 3D Reconstruction with a Plane-Aware Network
snippets:
There is a significant body of existing research on the task of monocular depth estimation from perspective images. One of the first papers to report success in this task was from Saxena et al. [21], who use a Markov Random Field to infer depth from a blend of local and global image features. With the advent of practical deep learning, more recent methods have focused on applying CNNs to estimate depth. Eigen et al. [7] present a CNN for depth estimation that uses multi-scale predictions to provide coarse and fine supervision for the depth predictions. Eigen et al. [6] built on that work to simultaneously generate surface normal predictions and semantic labels as well. Dharmasiri et al. [4] follow a similar network design but replace semantic label prediction with principal curvature prediction. Our network architecture has some commonalities with the aforementioned, primarily in our use of multi-scale predictions and similar prediction modalities. However, our goal is more aligned with that of Qi et al. [19] who propose a method for enforcing geometric consistency in the network outputs. In that work, the authors use the depth predictions to refine normal predictions and vice versa. In our case, we use a plane-aware loss to make our network predictions geometrically consistent. Our objective is also somewhat similar to that of Liu et al. [16] who predict a planar segmentation of the scene. However, they rely on a separate plane classification branch in their network and are limited to a fixed number of planes. We use a parametric definition of a plane derived from the principal curvature map and are thus unlimited in the number of planes we can predict. 

There have been other recent works in monocular depth estimation that, while interesting and useful, are not currently feasible for our task. Godard et al. [10] use stereo image pairs to train a model for monocular depth estimation using an image reconstruction loss. In our case, we only have access to monocular images. Li and Snavely [15] train a network on a dataset built from large-scale, unordered image collections. Alas, there is not yet such a repository for omnidirectional images.

sections.title: # Datasets and evaluation: what “spatial ability” means in numbers
sections.text:
Depth prediction is typically evaluated on indoor and outdoor benchmarks with domain-specific metrics and clipping ranges. For NYU-Depth V2, common metrics include mean absolute relative error (REL), RMSE, and percentage of pixels satisfying δ thresholds relative to ground truth; for KITTI, evaluations add MAE, inverse RMSE/MAE, squared relative error, and log-depth errors, reflecting metric differences between indoor centimeter-scale scenes and outdoor meter-scale scenes. On NYU Depth V2, RMSE, mean absolute relative error (REL), and δ thresholds are used; on the KITTI DC dataset, RMSE, MAE, and inverse variants (iRMSE, iMAE) follow the benchmark [8afdd02e-0] On KITTI and NYU-Depth V2, predictions are clipped to sensor ranges (e.g., 0.01–80 m for KITTI and 0.01–10 m for NYU), a practice common in prior works; reported results emphasize REL, RMSE, and δ metrics [8afdd02e-1] Standard protocols report REL, RMS, and δ accuracy (δ<1.25, δ<1.25^2, δ<1.25^3), with additional log-depth errors for NYU and KITTI [8afdd02e-2] For NYU V2 and KITTI, evaluations follow prior work reporting REL, RMS, and δ accuracy; full-resolution upscaling and standard cropped regions are used for indoor and outdoor models [8afdd02e-4].

Modern models also report zero-shot transfer and robustness. ZoeDepth combines relative and metric depth training and demonstrates large improvements on both trained (NYU, KITTI) and untrained metric datasets, indicating cross-domain generalization capacity. Evaluations show that combining relative and metric depth enables zero-shot transfer, outperforming state of the art on 7 metric datasets not seen during training with up to 976.4% (∼11×) metric improvements [8afdd02e-3].

sections.title: # From supervised SOTA to diffusion and zero-shot transfer
sections.text:
Supervised CNNs and transformer-based architectures have steadily improved accuracy on KITTI and NYU-Depth V2, with many works emphasizing relative error and δ thresholds. Recent work shows that diffusion models can be effective for depth, following standard REL/RMSE/δ protocols across both indoor and outdoor datasets, and that improved depth priors and consistency can yield better small-depth accuracy with competitive RMSE. On KITTI and NYU-Depth V2, methods report REL, RMSE, and δ metrics; improvements can be observed in relative error and small-depth accuracy (δ1/δ3) while maintaining fewer parameters [8afdd02e-1] Diffusion-based monocular depth follows standard evaluation (REL, RMS, δ) on NYU and KITTI, and reports log-depth errors to capture scale behavior [8afdd02e-2] Diffusion models for monocular depth are evaluated with REL, RMS, and δ, often with full-resolution evaluation protocols established in prior work [8afdd02e-4].

Zero-shot and transfer learning push spatial abilities toward generalization. By jointly training relative and metric depth, models can surpass prior state of the art on both seen and unseen metric datasets, suggesting that combining cues and training signals can enhance spatial reasoning beyond data overlap. A combined relative–metric training setup significantly improves absolute relative error on trained datasets and shows up to ∼11× improvements on several zero-shot metric datasets [8afdd02e-3].

sections.title: # 3D scene representations and spatial reasoning (NeRF/3D Gaussian Splatting)
sections.text:
NeRFs and their successors encode scenes as 5D functions over rays, enabling novel view synthesis with consistent depth and normals; Mip-NeRF/InstantNGP and 3D Gaussian Splatting (3DGS) trade off quality, speed, and memory, and explicitly model geometric properties that underpin spatial abilities. These methods support 6-DoF viewing and, when trained metrically, produce depth and normal maps that reflect scene geometry. NeRF-based methods (e.g., Nerfacto in Nerfstudio) provide NeRF rendering depths and normals for comparison; 3D Gaussian Splatting also provides depth rendering [c4469969-3] 3D Gaussian Splatting offers high-quality, real-time novel view synthesis with less training time than NeRF; extensions like 2DGS incorporate depth distortion and normal consistency for geometric precision, and Mip-Splatting limits Gaussian frequency to reduce aliasing [c4469969-1] On Mip-NeRF 360, methods based on Gaussian splatting and NeRF variants show trade-offs: e.g., Zip-NeRF achieves strong quality but with long inference and training, while Gaussian-based approaches can reach higher PSNR than 3DGS in some indoor scenes and offer faster real-time performance [c4469969-0] Micro-splatting regularizes covariance with isotropy-informed optimization to improve high-fidelity 3D Gaussian Splatting, with ablations on Mip-NeRF scenes showing higher PSNR/SSIM and lower LPIPS, with training time and FPS trade-offs [c4469969-4].

These representations shift spatial abilities from per-pixel depth maps to continuous volumetric or primitive-based encodings, enabling consistency across viewpoints and supporting tasks like 4D reconstructions and interactive environments. Integrated systems (e.g., Nerfstudio) streamline NeRF creation and training, producing depth and normal maps for scene analysis and comparison [c4469969-3] Work on 3D Gaussian-based models tests on diverse datasets (LLFF, Mip-NeRF 360, LERF, 3DGS test scenes), indicating adaptability across indoor and outdoor, complex scenes; evaluation often uses 2D ground truth via SPIn-NeRF when no 3D ground truth exists [c4469969-2].

snippets: Gaussian Splatting. Alongside the widespread application of NeRF, 3D Gaussian Splatting (3DGS) (Kerbl et al. 2023) has emerged as a powerful technique for novel view synthesis. Compared to NeRF, 3DGS requires less training time and enables high-quality, real-time novel view synthesis at high resolution. Yuan et al. (Huang et al. 2024) further proposed a novel approach, 2D Gaussian Splatting (2DGS), which incorporates depth distortion and normal consistency to more accurately model and reconstruct geometrically precise radiance fields. More recently, Yu et al. (Yu et al. 2024) introduced Mip-Splatting, which employs two sampling filters to limit the maximum frequency of Gaussian primitives and approximate the box filter, thereby simulating the physical imaging process. While their approach is innovative in addressing aliasing issues, it diverges from our focus as it does not effectively handle viewpoints that significantly differ from those in the training domain (e.g., close-up views with varying camera orientations).

NeuRBF [6] performs well, similar to our method, but has an infer-ence time of a few seconds per image-about 100x longer than ours (25 FPS on Blender dataset, see Tab. 3)-and does not support the Mip-NeRF360 dataset. Results on the Mip-NeRF 360 Dataset: Regarding Mip-NeRF 360, we provide quantitative results in Tab. 2 and qualitative comparisons in Fig. 2. A general trend is that our approach performs better on most indoor scenes than state-of-the-art methods like Mip-Splatting [2], and slightly worse on outdoor scenes. This may be due to the adaptive control of gaussians strategy, which adapts well in Gaussian Splatting [12] but may perform worse with our approach. Nevertheless, we achieved better overall results than Mip-Splatting and 3D Gaussian Splatting, with an average PSNR of 29.71 dB, +0.56 dB higher than 3D Gaussian Splatting. Zip-NeRF performs slightly better on Mip-NeRF 360 but requires over 7 hours of training per scene and about 1.5 seconds per image for inference, which is significantly higher than our approach (see Tab. 3). 

Performance Analysis: We discuss here results in Tab. 3, which show the performance of our approach compared to Gaussian Splatting. These metrics were obtained using an RTX 4090 GPU with 24GB of RAM on 800x800 pixel images. Our approach has slower training and infer- ence times compared to Gaussian Splatting due to the computational cost of ray casting. Generally, our computation times depend mainly on the number of rays, while Gaussian Splatting's times are influenced by the number of projected primitives. However, our training times remain reasonable (30 minutes per scene on Blender) and real-time inference is achieved on Blender, although slower on Mip-NeRF 360. We also note that our method generates fewer primitives for better visual quality. Thus, Gaussian Splatting likely adds more Gaussians to compensate for splatting artifacts.

sections.title: # Learning regimes, generalization, and robustness
sections.text:
Training paradigms differ in supervision strength and data diversity. Supervised methods achieve best performance but depend on labeled depth; unsupervised/self-supervised methods leverage photometric reprojection and temporal consistency, while large-scale and web-based datasets (e.g., MegaDepth, DIW) provide abundant, diverse imagery with weak or proxy supervision. These regimes shape spatial abilities: supervised models excel in their domains, self-supervised models improve with motion and sequence priors, and web-scale training enhances generalization across viewpoints and conditions. Supervised learning achieves the best performance but requires costly labels, while unsupervised monocular depth estimation leverages backwarping-based photometric errors, introducing scale ambiguity and sensitivity to illumination and motion [4b9ec87c-0] Stereo matching can benefit from imperfect monocular disparity priors; using weakly supervised monocular depth (e.g., DiW, MegaDepth) as synthetic supervision improves stereo performance, indicating cross-task benefits of spatial priors [dce09b5d-2] MegaDepth comprises 130K internet images with COLMAP-derived depths, reflecting noise and missing details under diverse lighting and weather; DIODE provides 100K high-resolution RGB images with accurate dense far-range depth but covers static scenes only, highlighting dataset limitations [dce09b5d-1] MegaDepth uses an hourglass CNN trained on large web-collected image collections and generalizes to datasets like KITTI, Make3D, and DIW, supporting broad spatial generalization [dce09b5d-0].

Robustness and security are active concerns. Self-supervised models are widely adopted in industry due to low data costs and practical performance, but they are vulnerable to adversarial attacks via carefully designed patches that fool depth estimation in both monocular and stereo pipelines. This underscores gaps in uncertainty estimation and robustness in current spatial abilities. Industry uses self-supervised monocular depth (e.g., Monodepth2, Depthhints, ManyDepth) due to low data costs and practical performance; evaluating across objects and networks reveals transferable adversarial patches that attack depth estimation, highlighting robustness limitations [dce09b5d-3].

snippets: The majority of our experiments are performed using monocular depth from MiDaS [50], which itself is trained with a variety of different datasets e.g. flow derived pseudo ground truth and structured light depth. In Table 3 we show that our approach still produces competitive stereo performance when we use alternative monocular networks that have been trained using much weaker supervision. This includes using monocular video only self-supervision on the KITTI dataset (Monodepth2 (M) [23]), pairwise ordinal human annotations (DiW [6]) and multi-view image collections (Megadepth [38]). While the recent MiDaS [50] performs best overall, we observe a consistent performance increase in stereo estimation with better monocular depth. This is very encouraging, as it indicates that our performance may only get better in future as monocular depth networks improve. We also show qualitatively in Fig. 4 how our stereo predictions can recover from errors made by monocular models.

snippets:
Megadepth, as one of the largest datasets used for monocular depth estimation tasks 13 , provides a total of 130 K images. Different from other depth datasets images and depth maps captured by sensor devices, MegaDepth is composed of RGB images sourced from the internet and the corresponding ground-truth depth maps are generated via a modified algorithm based on COLMAP. Therefore, the images generated are always with noise and details missing, particularly under challenging conditions such as diverse lighting and weather conditions. 

DIoDe. DIODE is the first public dataset that obtains RGBD images of indoor and outdoor scenes with one sensor suite 11 , it contains a total of 100 K diverse high-resolution (1204 × 768) RGB images with accurate, dense, far-range depth measurements. Although it covers outdoor and indoor scenes in different cities during day and night, the content of images captured consists of only static objects which unable to fully describe the information of the real world. 

The existing monocular depth driving datasets play a pivotal role in the prosperity of perception algorithms but still have some key limitations. sections.title: # What “spatial abilities” look like in practice: consistency, scale, and geometry
sections.text:
Across methods, several facets of spatial abilities recur. First, geometric consistency—enforcing planarity, curvature, and normal coherence—improves depth quality and downstream tasks like 3D reconstruction and SLAM. Second, scale awareness remains a central challenge; backwarping-based losses yield scale-ambiguous predictions, motivating clipping, re-scaling, and specialized scale-invariant training or evaluation protocols. Third, temporal consistency across frames is critical for applications such as AR/MR, SLAM, and video understanding, yet remains underexplored compared to frame-wise accuracy. Enforcing geometric consistency within networks (e.g., plane-aware losses and curvature/normal relationships) improves depth, normals, and 3D feature recovery [4b9ec87c-1] Self-supervised monocular depth has advanced, but predicting temporally and geometrically consistent depth over multiple frames is mostly unexplored, despite its essential role in reconstruction, SLAM, AR/MR, and autonomous driving [4b9ec87c-2] The scale ambiguity of backwarping makes practical evaluation and deployment challenging, as median scale ratios must often be estimated or assumed [4b9ec87c-0].

Representations also influence spatial abilities. NeRFs and 3DGS encode volumetric geometry, enabling consistent depth and normal predictions across novel viewpoints and approximating physical imaging processes via sampling filters and covariance regularization. These approaches have raised performance bar for 6-DoF view synthesis, but still face trade-offs in training time, inference speed, and handling extreme views or close-ups. 3D Gaussian Splatting reduces training time and enables real-time synthesis; recent variants incorporate depth distortion, normal consistency, and sampling filters to approximate physical imaging and mitigate aliasing [c4469969-1] Comparisons on Mip-NeRF 360 show method-dependent trade-offs: Gaussian-based approaches can outperform 3DGS in PSNR for indoor scenes, while Zip-NeRF offers superior quality at the cost of long training and inference times [c4469969-0] Micro-splatting improves fidelity with higher PSNR/SSIM and lower LPIPS, but introduces its own training/inference trade-offs [c4469969-4].

citations.title: Enhancing Close-up Novel View Synthesis via Pseudo-labeling
snippets: Gaussian Splatting. Alongside the widespread application of NeRF, 3D Gaussian Splatting (3DGS) (Kerbl et al. 2023) has emerged as a powerful technique for novel view synthesis. Compared to NeRF, 3DGS requires less training time and enables high-quality, real-time novel view synthesis at high resolution. Yuan et al. (Huang et al. 2024) further proposed a novel approach, 2D Gaussian Splatting (2DGS), which incorporates depth distortion and normal consistency to more accurately model and reconstruct geometrically precise radiance fields. More recently, Yu et al. (Yu et al. 2024) introduced Mip-Splatting, which employs two sampling filters to limit the maximum frequency of Gaussian primitives and approximate the box filter, thereby simulating the physical imaging process. While their approach is innovative in addressing aliasing issues, it diverges from our focus as it does not effectively handle viewpoints that significantly differ from those in the training domain (e.g., close-up views with varying camera orientations).

citations.title: Towards Scale-Aware, Robust, and Generalizable Unsupervised Monocular Depth Estimation by Integrating IMU Motion Dynamics
snippets:
Monocular depth estimation is a fundamental computer vision task which plays an essential role in many real-world applications such as autonomous driving, robot navigation, and virtual reality [36,20,44]. Classical geometric methods resolve this problem by leveraging the geometric relationship between temporally contiguous frames and formulating depth prediction as an optimization problem [9,29,8]. While geometric methods have achieved good performance, they are sensitive to either textureless regions or illumination changes. The computational cost for dense depth prediction also limits their practical use. Recently deep learning techniques have reformed this research field by training networks to predict depth directly from monocular images and designing proper losses based on groundtruth depth labels or geometric depth clues from visual data. While supervised learning methods achieve the best performance [7,24,11,1,45], the labour cost for collecting ground-truth labels prohibits their use in real-world. To address this issue, unsupervised monocular depth estimation has drawn a lot of research attention [48,14], which leverages the photometric error from backwarping. 

Although unsupervised monocular depth learning has made great progress in recent years, there still exist several fundamental problems that may obstruct its usage in real-world. First, current methods suffer from the scale ambiguity problem since the backwarping process is equivalent up to an arbitrary scaling factor w.r.t. depth and translation. While current methods are usually evaluated by re-scaling each prediction map using the median ratio between the ground-truth depth and the prediction, it is difficult to obtain such median ratios in practice. Secondly, it is well-known that the photometric error is sensitive to illumination change and moving objects, which violate the underlying assumption of the backwarping projection. In addition, though uncertainty has been introduced for the photometric error map under the unsupervised learning framework [21,41], it remains non-trivial to learn an uncertainty measure for the predicted ego-motion, which could further benefit the development of a robust and trustworthy system.

citations.title: Pano Popups: Indoor 3D Reconstruction with a Plane-Aware Network
snippets:
There is a significant body of existing research on the task of monocular depth estimation from perspective images. One of the first papers to report success in this task was from Saxena et al. [21], who use a Markov Random Field to infer depth from a blend of local and global image features. With the advent of practical deep learning, more recent methods have focused on applying CNNs to estimate depth. Eigen et al. [7] present a CNN for depth estimation that uses multi-scale predictions to provide coarse and fine supervision for the depth predictions. Eigen et al. [6] built on that work to simultaneously generate surface normal predictions and semantic labels as well. Dharmasiri et al. [4] follow a similar network design but replace semantic label prediction with principal curvature prediction. Our network architecture has some commonalities with the aforementioned, primarily in our use of multi-scale predictions and similar prediction modalities. However, our goal is more aligned with that of Qi et al. [19] who propose a method for enforcing geometric consistency in the network outputs. In that work, the authors use the depth predictions to refine normal predictions and vice versa. In our case, we use a plane-aware loss to make our network predictions geometrically consistent. Our objective is also somewhat similar to that of Liu et al. [16] who predict a planar segmentation of the scene. However, they rely on a separate plane classification branch in their network and are limited to a fixed number of planes. We use a parametric definition of a plane derived from the principal curvature map and are thus unlimited in the number of planes we can predict. 

There have been other recent works in monocular depth estimation that, while interesting and useful, are not currently feasible for our task. Godard et al. [10] use stereo image pairs to train a model for monocular depth estimation using an image reconstruction loss. In our case, we only have access to monocular images. Li and Snavely [15] train a network on a dataset built from large-scale, unordered image collections. Alas, there is not yet such a repository for omnidirectional images.

citations.title: RayGauss: Volumetric Gaussian-Based Ray Casting for Photorealistic Novel View Synthesis
snippets:
NeuRBF [6] performs well, similar to our method, but has an infer-ence time of a few seconds per image-about 100x longer than ours (25 FPS on Blender dataset, see Tab. 3)-and does not support the Mip-NeRF360 dataset. Results on the Mip-NeRF 360 Dataset: Regarding Mip-NeRF 360, we provide quantitative results in Tab. 2 and qualitative comparisons in Fig. 2. A general trend is that our approach performs better on most indoor scenes than state-of-the-art methods like Mip-Splatting [2], and slightly worse on outdoor scenes. This may be due to the adaptive control of gaussians strategy, which adapts well in Gaussian Splatting [12] but may perform worse with our approach. Nevertheless, we achieved better overall results than Mip-Splatting and 3D Gaussian Splatting, with an average PSNR of 29.71 dB, +0.56 dB higher than 3D Gaussian Splatting. Zip-NeRF performs slightly better on Mip-NeRF 360 but requires over 7 hours of training per scene and about 1.5 seconds per image for inference, which is significantly higher than our approach (see Tab. 3). 

Performance Analysis: We discuss here results in Tab. 3, which show the performance of our approach compared to Gaussian Splatting. These metrics were obtained using an RTX 4090 GPU with 24GB of RAM on 800x800 pixel images. Our approach has slower training and infer- ence times compared to Gaussian Splatting due to the computational cost of ray casting. Generally, our computation times depend mainly on the number of rays, while Gaussian Splatting's times are influenced by the number of projected primitives. However, our training times remain reasonable (30 minutes per scene on Blender) and real-time inference is achieved on Blender, although slower on Mip-NeRF 360. sections.title: # Spatial abilities across domains and failure modes
sections.text:
Indoor vs. outdoor datasets impose distinct geometry and scale regimes. Indoor datasets like NYU-Depth V2 emphasize centimeter-scale structures with strong semantics, while outdoor datasets like KITTI involve vast scale ranges, dynamic objects, and challenging illumination. Models trained on one domain often transfer poorly to the other, motivating joint training, domain adaptation, and robust metrics. Clipping depth to sensor ranges (e.g., 0.01–10 m for NYU vs. 0.01–80 m for KITTI) reflects domain differences and is standard in evaluation [8afdd02e-1] Models trained on specific datasets tend to fail on unseen datasets due to lighting, camera characteristics, and context differences; mixed data and inclusion of severe weather improve generalization [4b9ec87c-4].

Failure modes include textureless surfaces, repetitive patterns, and large-scale variations, where photometric reprojection and scale priors degrade. Large-scale, diverse datasets and weakly supervised signals (e.g., from stereo or LiDAR points) can mitigate some issues through additional consistency losses and completion tasks, but generalization remains a bottleneck. Photometric error sensitivity to illumination and moving objects violates backwarping assumptions, and scale ambiguity hinders robustness without explicit handling [4b9ec87c-0] Using sparse LiDAR points with self-supervised photometric/geometric consistency losses enables depth completion and improves accuracy, though generalization across domains is still limited [dce09b5d-2] DIODE’s static content and MegaDepth’s noisy, missing details under challenging conditions expose limitations of current datasets and highlight the need for more comprehensive, diverse training data [dce09b5d-1].

citations.title: Predicting Depth Maps from Single RGB Images and Addressing Missing Information in Depth Estimation
snippets: Monocular Depth estimation is the task of predicting a Depth map (distance from the camera) from a single RGB image. This is a challenging problem due to the lack of direct Depth cues (like stereo vision or motion) in a single image. Moreover, Many Depth estimation models trained on specific datasets tend to perform well on those datasets but fail when tested on new or unseen datasets due to differences in lighting conditions, camera characteristics, or environmental contexts. This is a significant issue because creating large-scale annotated Depth datasets is resourceintensive. The paper (Ranftl et al., 2020) mixed the data for better generalization, and the severe weather (Chaar et al., 2023;Chaar et al., 2024) has also been included in their data. The authors (Ma et al., 2019) introduced a method for Depth completion, converting sparse LiDAR data into dense Depth maps using RGB images without needing ground-truth Depth annotations. The approach leveraged self-supervised learning through photometric and geometric consistency losses, enabling the model to train effectively by using sparse LiDAR points and monocular images. It also incorporated stereo image pairs to enhance Depth accuracy. This framework achieved robust, high-quality Depth estimation, providing a practical solution for applications like autonomous driving, this methodology works well in specific scenes that are used in training, but it is limited when we generalize it in other data. The paper (Xian et al., 2018) approached predicting relative Depth from a single image using stereo data from the web for weak supervi-sion. Instead of relying on costly ground-truth Depth annotations, the method leveraged geometric cues from stereo images (3600 images) to train a model that can generalize across diverse scenes. This scalable approach pushes the boundaries of monocular Depth estimation, making it effective for real-world applications without requiring extensive labeled data. The paper (Agarwal and Arora, 2023) introduced a monocular Depth prediction using a novel skip attention mechanism. The model leveraged attention layers focusing on important features across different network scales. By incorporating skip connections with attention, the model efficiently combines high-level semantic information with low-level spatial details, improving Depth prediction accuracy.

citations.title: Learning Stereo from Single Images
snippets: The majority of our experiments are performed using monocular depth from MiDaS [50], which itself is trained with a variety of different datasets e.g. flow derived pseudo ground truth and structured light depth. In Table 3 we show that our approach still produces competitive stereo performance when we use alternative monocular networks that have been trained using much weaker supervision. This includes using monocular video only self-supervision on the KITTI dataset (Monodepth2 (M) [23]), pairwise ordinal human annotations (DiW [6]) and multi-view image collections (Megadepth [38]). It is worth noting that even though Megadepth [38] training depth is computed from unstructured image collections, without using any trained correspondence matching, using it to synthesize training data still outperforms the synthetic Sceneflow baseline. This is likely due to the fact that stereo matching is fundamentally different from monocular depth estimation, and even potentially unrealistic disparity information can help the stereo network learn how to better match pixels. While the recent MiDaS [50] performs best overall, we observe a consistent performance increase in stereo estimation with better monocular depth. This is very encouraging, as it indicates that our performance may only get better in future as monocular depth networks improve. We also show qualitatively in Fig. 4 how our stereo predictions can recover from errors made by monocular models.

sections.title: # Applications and the importance of consistent spatial reasoning
sections.text: Depth prediction underpins spatial reasoning in applications that demand 3D consistency: SLAM and reconstruction benefit from temporally consistent depth across frames; AR/MR requires accurate, view-consistent geometry for registration and occlusion; autonomous driving needs reliable metric depth for planning and perception. These application constraints push research toward multi-frame consistency, scale-aware priors, and robustness to real-world variations. Consistency in depth prediction across consecutive frames is essential for reconstruction, SLAM, pose estimation, medical applications, AR/MR, computational photography, and autonomous driving [4b9ec87c-2] Unsupervised monocular depth’s scale ambiguity and sensitivity to environmental changes motivate robust, trustworthy systems with explicit uncertainty and motion handling [4b9ec87c-0] Self-supervised monocular depth is used in production-level autonomous driving (e.g., Tesla and Baidu), underscoring the practical importance of spatial abilities and their robustness considerations [dce09b5d-3].

sections.title: # Limitations and open problems
sections.text: Key challenges include: (1) scale robustness without re-scaling hacks; (2) metric accuracy and scale consistency across scenes; (3) handling occlusions and dynamic objects in self-/unsupervised settings; (4) generalization to long-tail domains (weather, time of day, novel objects) and sensor perturbations; and (5) uncertainty estimation and adversarial robustness. Recent work advances zero-shot transfer and diffusion-based modeling, and 3D representations improve viewpoint consistency, but standardized, scale-invariant evaluation and robust uncertainty remain open areas. Scale ambiguity persists in backwarping-based unsupervised methods, complicating real-world deployment and necessitating better uncertainty for ego-motion and depth [4b9ec87c-0] Zero-shot improvements suggest promise for generalization, yet robustness across diverse, unseen datasets and conditions remains a major challenge [8afdd02e-3] Even large datasets have limitations (e.g., static content in DIODE, narrow conditions in driving datasets), motivating synthetic and perturbed-domain benchmarks like SDCD for robustness [dce09b5d-1] Adversarial vulnerabilities reveal the need for robustness and uncertainty-aware spatial reasoning in deployed systems [dce09b5d-3].

The existing monocular depth driving datasets play a pivotal role in the prosperity of perception algorithms but still have some key limitations. The small-scale training examples (Make3D) and low diversity of driving conditions (DIODE, Scene Flow) lead to the datasets cannot cover driving situations comprehensively in the real world, which makes it difficult to generalization to unforeseen driving conditions 17 . Moreover, the sparse and low-resolution ground-truth depth maps of datasets (KITTI, Make3D) potentially weaken the performance of depth estimation solutions, making the limited understanding of driving scenarios 4,18 . 

A comprehensive dataset is thus needed to meet the requirements of driving scene diversity and the high quality of data. Therefore, to figure out the problems above, we introduce SDCD, a new synthetic dataset, which covers common driving conditions: Sunny, Rain, Snow, Sleet, Overcast and Dust. In addition, the robustness of depth estimation models is explored by considering the detrimental effects of data transmission, including Noise, Blur, Image Compression (JPEG), Colour Quantization, and Pixelation. These adverse perturbations are taken into account to assess the performance and resilience of the models.

MDE models can be either trained with supervised method (using ground truth depth collected by Lidar or depth camera) or unsupervised method (using video frames or stereo image pairs). Unsupervised models are more attractive to industry because one can easily collect a large amount of training data (e.g. videos) with affordable RGB cameras or reuse existing videos at a low cost. Tesla has declared that they use a self-supervised model in monocular depth estimation [7]. Hence, in our evaluation, we use three monocular depth estimation models: Mon-odepth2 [21], Depthhints [59], and Manydepth [58]. We selected these models with the following criteria. 

(1) Representativeness. Among self-supervised monocular depth estimation models, these models are most widely used in many previous research [70,40]. Monodepth2 [21] is one of most successful monocular depth estimation methods. Depthhints [59] is an advanced model that improves performance via additional depth suggestion obtained from stereo algorithms. Manydepth [58] is the stateof-the-art model that uses sequence information from multiple images to achieve better performance. 

(2) Practicality. We focus on self-supervised monocular depth estimation models because they do not require ground truth depth data for training, which is usually collected by high-priced Lidar sensors. In contrast, they require only monocular videos or stereo pairs collected by RGB camera(s), enabling them to collect data and train a model economically and efficiently. These techniques have already been in production-level vision-based autonomous driving systems such as Tesla Autopliot [7] and Baidu Apollo Lite [1]. 

(3) Open Model. The models are publicly available. In our evaluation, we use models trained with both monocular videos and stereo pairs on KITTI dataset [20] and the resolution of input images are 320×1024. These models are publicly available in their project repository on GitHub [5,3,4]   We evaluate the transferability of our adversarial patch in two phases: the transferability across objects and the transferability across networks. For objects, we use three types of vehicles as our target objects.

sections.title: # Linking AI spatial abilities to human spatial cognition
sections.text: Human spatial abilities rely on a mix of egocentric and allocentric representations, geometric priors, and transfer across viewpoints and contexts. AI’s spatial abilities via depth prediction and 3D representations reflect explicit geometric constraints and consistency, but often lack the flexible, viewpoint-invariant and uncertainty-aware reasoning seen in humans. While models like ZoeDepth demonstrate impressive zero-shot transfer and diffusion-based depth shows strong cross-domain metrics, systematic comparisons to human spatial reasoning and transfer capabilities remain sparse in the literature surveyed here. Future work could benchmark AI spatial abilities against human performance on geometry-consistency and viewpoint-transfer tasks, and integrate cognitive insights (e.g., egocentric/allocentric strategies, metric vs. allocentric coding) into learning objectives and evaluation protocols. Zero-shot transfer via combined relative–metric depth shows large improvements on unseen datasets, suggesting strong generalization potential [8afdd02e-3] 3D Gaussian Splatting and related methods encode explicit geometric priors and enable consistent 6-DoF views, aligning with human allocentric spatial reasoning in some respects [c4469969-1].

citations.title: Enhancing Close-up Novel View Synthesis via Pseudo-labeling
snippets: Gaussian Splatting. Alongside the widespread application of NeRF, 3D Gaussian Splatting (3DGS) (Kerbl et al. 2023) has emerged as a powerful technique for novel view synthesis. Compared to NeRF, 3DGS requires less training time and enables high-quality, real-time novel view synthesis at high resolution. Yuan et al. (Huang et al. 2024) further proposed a novel approach, 2D Gaussian Splatting (2DGS), which incorporates depth distortion and normal consistency to more accurately model and reconstruct geometrically precise radiance fields. More recently, Yu et al. (Yu et al. 2024) introduced Mip-Splatting, which employs two sampling filters to limit the maximum frequency of Gaussian primitives and approximate the box filter, thereby simulating the physical imaging process. While their approach is innovative in addressing aliasing issues, it diverges from our focus as it does not effectively handle viewpoints that significantly differ from those in the training domain (e.g., close-up views with varying camera orientations).

sections.title: # Conclusion
sections.text: AI’s spatial abilities in depth prediction have advanced rapidly: from geometrically constrained CNNs and self-supervised reprojection to diffusion models and rich 3D scene representations that support 6-DoF synthesis. These advances enable consistent geometry, cross-viewpoint understanding, and notable zero-shot transfer, yet core challenges remain around scale robustness, metric accuracy, dynamic scenes, and real-world robustness. As benchmarks expand and learning regimes diversify—web-scale data, synthetic perturbations, and adversarial evaluations—AI’s spatial abilities will become more reliable and transferable. Bridging to human spatial cognition will require targeted studies that compare viewpoint transfer, uncertainty handling, and robustness across common spatial tasks. Unsupervised approaches and geometric priors have pushed performance while revealing scale and environmental sensitivity [4b9ec87c-0] Diffusion models now match standard protocols across NYU and KITTI, adding a new toolkit for depth prediction [8afdd02e-2] 3D Gaussian and NeRF families demonstrate how volumetric encodings can elevate spatial abilities to 6-DoF consistency with careful trade-offs in speed and quality [c4469969-0] Diverse, realistic datasets and synthetic robustness suites (e.g., SDCD) are emerging to test generalization under real-world perturbations [dce09b5d-1].

citations.title: Towards Scale-Aware, Robust, and Generalizable Unsupervised Monocular Depth Estimation by Integrating IMU Motion Dynamics
snippets:
Monocular depth estimation is a fundamental computer vision task which plays an essential role in many real-world applications such as autonomous driving, robot navigation, and virtual reality [36,20,44]. Classical geometric methods resolve this problem by leveraging the geometric relationship between temporally contiguous frames and formulating depth prediction as an optimization problem [9,29,8]. While geometric methods have achieved good performance, they are sensitive to either textureless regions or illumination changes. The computational cost for dense depth prediction also limits their practical use. Recently deep learning techniques have reformed this research field by training networks to predict depth directly from monocular images and designing proper losses based on groundtruth depth labels or geometric depth clues from visual data. While supervised learning methods achieve the best performance [7,24,11,1,45], the labour cost for collecting ground-truth labels prohibits their use in real-world. To address this issue, unsupervised monocular depth estimation has drawn a lot of research attention [48,14], which leverages the photometric error from backwarping. 

Although unsupervised monocular depth learning has made great progress in recent years, there still exist several fundamental problems that may obstruct its usage in real-world. First, current methods suffer from the scale ambiguity problem since the backwarping process is equivalent up to an arbitrary scaling factor w.r.t. depth and translation. While current methods are usually evaluated by re-scaling each prediction map using the median ratio between the ground-truth depth and the prediction, it is difficult to obtain such median ratios in practice. Secondly, it is well-known that the photometric error is sensitive to illumination change and moving objects, which violate the underlying assumption of the backwarping projection. In addition, though uncertainty has been introduced for the photometric error map under the unsupervised learning framework [21,41], it remains non-trivial to learn an uncertainty measure for the predicted ego-motion, which could further benefit the development of a robust and trustworthy system.

sections.title: # Summary: What “best” pretrained models look like
sections.text:
For temporal action detection (TAD), the strongest results today come from transformer-based detectors that build on 3D CNN feature backbones (e.g., SlowFast) and exploit dense proposal refinement on challenging, long, and egocentric videos like EPIC-Kitchens-100, with complementary pipelines validated on THUMOS14 and ActivityNet benchmarks. ActionFormer reports strong results on EPIC-Kitchens-100 using SlowFast features and outperforms BMN and G-TAD by over 13.5% absolute mAP points under the standard verb/noun TAL protocol [42355c69-0] A unified temporal action detection framework reports outperforming previous SOTA on THUMOS14 by over 10% and achieving detection performance close to the winning submission on ActivityNet v1.3 at IoU=0.5 [448f809e-1] One-stage boundary-refinement detectors achieve state-of-the-art results on EPIC-KITCHENS-100 by estimating boundary confidence scores and refining boundaries [42355c69-2] Refining Action Boundaries provides detailed comparison protocols across EPIC-Kitchens, ActivityNet-1.3, and THUMOS14 and modifies ActionFormer to enable combined action detection [448f809e-3] Frequency-decoupling for boundary refinement (FDDet) evaluates on THUMOS14, HACS, and ActivityNet-1.3 with mAP reported at IoU thresholds commonly used in the literature [448f809e-4].

For broader “video understanding” (recognition, localization, retrieval, grounded QA, long-form reasoning), current video large vision-language models (LVLMs) such as Qwen2.5-VL, LLaVA-OneVision, and related variants are the most versatile. They provide video encoders capable of transfer to TAD pipelines and achieve strong performance across multiple video benchmarks and QA datasets, especially when scaled to 7B-class parameters and equipped for long-context video inputs. Qwen2.5-VL excels at long-context and dense visual-textual reasoning and supports both short and long video tasks, while Long-LLaVA and LLaVA-OneVision are optimized for multi-frame processing and unified visual tokenization across images and video [7397ebdc-1] LLaVA-OneVision is evaluated on open-ended and multi-choice video benchmarks (ActivityNet-QA, MLVU, EgoSchema, VideoDetailCaption, Video-ChatGPT), with larger LLMs improving performance on reasoning-heavy datasets like EgoSchema [7397ebdc-2] LLaVAction shows that adding EPIC-KITCHENS-100 improves video-based action recognition across multiple benchmarks and transfers well beyond the training set [7397ebdc-0] SurveillanceVQA-589K shows LLaVA-OV-Qwen2 and LLaVA-Video models excel in detection and classification QA, with larger 7B models generally outperforming smaller variants and specialized strengths across task types [7397ebdc-3] VideoChat-R1 uses Qwen2.5-VL-7B for main experiments and evaluates on general video understanding (MVBench, PerceptionTest, VideoMME), temporal grounding (Charade-STA, ActivityNet-Grounding), object tracking (GoT-10k), and QA/captioning (NExTGQA, Dream-1k, VidTAB-QA) [7397ebdc-4].

snippets:
Dataset. EPIC-Kitchens 100 is the largest egocentric action dataset. The dataset contains 100 hours of videos from 700 sessions capturing cooking activities in different kitchens. In comparison to ActivityNet-1.3, EPIC-Kitchens 100 has less number of videos, yet many more instances per video (average 128 vs. 1.5 on ActivityNet-1.3). In comparison to THUMOS14, EPIC-Kitchens is 3 times larger in terms of video hours and more than 10 times larger in terms of action instances. These egocentric videos also include significant camera motion. This dataset thus poses new challenges for TAL. 

Experiment Setup. We used a SlowFast network [24] pre-trained on EPIC-Kitchens for feature extraction. This model is provided by [18]. Our model was trained on the training set and evaluated on the validation set. A window size of 9 was used for local self-attention. For evaluation, we used mAP@[0.1:0.1:0.5] and report the average mAP following [18]. In this dataset, an action is defined as a combination of a verb (action) and a noun (object). As this dataset was recently released, we are only able to compare our methods to BMN [36] and G-TAD [75], both using the same SlowFast features provided by [18]. Again, implementation details are described in the appendix C. 

Results. Table 2 presents the results. Our method achieves an average mAP ([0.1:0.1:0.5]) of 23.5% and 21.9% for verb and noun, respectively. Our results again largely outperform the strong baselines of BMN [36] and G-TAD [75] by over 13.5% in absolute percentage points. An interesting observation is that the gaps between our results and BMN / G-TAD are much larger on EPIC-Kitchens 100. A possible reason is that ActivityNet has a small number of actions per video (1.5), leading to imbalanced classification for our model; only a few moments (around the action center) are labeled positive while all rest are negative. We adapt ActionFormer for EPIC-Kitchens 100 2022 Action Detection challenge.

LLaVA-NeXT-Video: LLaVA-NeXT-Video is an open-source video-language assistant built by fine-tuning the LLaVA-NeXT image model (based on Qwen-1.5 32B) with high-quality video instruction data ( 830K samples) mixed with image data.

sections.title: # Best pretrained models for Temporal Action Detection (TAD)
sections.text:
If your primary goal is TAD on untrimmed videos (ActivityNet, THUMOS14, EPIC-Kitchens), use a transformer-based detector plus strong spatiotemporal features. Two families are currently best:

- Two-stage transformer detectors with SlowFast features: ActionFormer is a strong baseline on EPIC-Kitchens-100, using SlowFast pretraining and transformer attention to localize verb/noun actions, with large gains over BMN and G-TAD. ActionFormer achieves average mAP@0.1:0.1:0.5 of 23.5% (verb) and 21.9% (noun) on EPIC-Kitchens-100 and largely outperforms BMN and G-TAD by over 13.5% absolute percentage points [42355c69-0]. For ensembles and strong generalization across datasets, look for unified frameworks reported to surpass prior SOTA on THUMOS14 and approach winning ActivityNet v1.3 results at IoU=0.5, indicating robust temporal boundary localization and dataset portability. A unified framework outperforms previous SOTA on THUMOS14 by >10% and reaches near-challenge-winning performance on ActivityNet v1.3 at IoU=0.5 [448f809e-1].

- One-stage boundary-refinement transformers: If you need speed and accuracy on dense, egocentric actions, one-stage detectors with boundary heads/refinement are state-of-the-art on EPIC-Kitchens-100 and competitive across benchmarks. They explicitly model action start/end boundaries and show consistent gains in mAP, especially at higher IoU thresholds where boundary precision matters. Refining Action Boundaries achieves SOTA on EPIC-KITCHENS-100 by estimating boundary confidence scores and refining boundaries for temporal actions [42355c69-2] Refining Action Boundaries details evaluation protocols across EPIC-Kitchens, ActivityNet-1.3, and THUMOS14 and compares against SOTA methods, with modifications enabling combined action detection [448f809e-3] FDDet demonstrates boundary refinement via frequency-decoupling and evaluates on THUMOS14, HACS, and ActivityNet-1.3 with standard mAP thresholds [448f809e-4]. An ensemble of one-stage transformers has also reached 21.28% average mAP on EPIC-Kitchens-100 test, illustrating the effectiveness of this design pattern. An ensembled one-stage transformer (OADT) reaches 21.28% average mAP on EPIC-KITCHENS-100 test [448f809e-2].

Practical recommendations:
- Prefer SlowFast as the backbone for EPIC-Kitchens and HACS due to its demonstrated efficacy in TAD pipelines and compatibility with BMN-style proposal generation and proposal-classification decoupling. SlowFast features pre-trained on EPIC-Kitchens are used as the feature extractor in ActionFormer [42355c69-0] TAR and related work use SlowFast, TSP, and I3D features depending on the task (EPIC-Kitchens, ActivityNet-1.3, THUMOS14) [42355c69-3] The pipeline typically decouples background learning from proposal generation/classification, with BMN trained on extracted features for proposals [42355c69-3] For EPIC-Kitchens, features are extracted with SlowFast; for THUMOS14 and ActivityNet-1.3, pipelines adapt feature backbones (I3D, TSP) and evaluation protocols [42355c69-4] Implementation details include SlowFast features for EPIC-Kitchens-100, transformer feature pyramids, and label assignment strategies tailored to TAD [42355c69-3].
- If you target THUMOS14 and ActivityNet, adopt the unified framework reported to exceed prior SOTA on THUMOS14 and match challenge-winning performance at IoU=0.5 on ActivityNet v1.3; adapt detection heads for combined verb-noun action classes rather than separate heads, which is important for fair comparisons on EPIC-Kitchens-100. Unified framework surpasses prior SOTA on THUMOS14 and approaches winning ActivityNet v1.3 performance at IoU=0.5 [448f809e-1] Comparisons emphasize using combined action detection heads for EPIC-Kitchens-100 rather than separate verb/noun heads [448f809e-3].

citations.title: ActionFormer: Localizing Moments of Actions with Transformers
snippets:
Dataset. EPIC-Kitchens 100 is the largest egocentric action dataset. The dataset contains 100 hours of videos from 700 sessions capturing cooking activities in different kitchens. In comparison to ActivityNet-1.3, EPIC-Kitchens 100 has less number of videos, yet many more instances per video (average 128 vs. 1.5 on ActivityNet-1.3). In comparison to THUMOS14, EPIC-Kitchens is 3 times larger in terms of video hours and more than 10 times larger in terms of action instances. These egocentric videos also include significant camera motion. This dataset thus poses new challenges for TAL. 

Experiment Setup. We used a SlowFast network [24] pre-trained on EPIC-Kitchens for feature extraction. This model is provided by [18]. Our model was trained on the training set and evaluated on the validation set. A window size of 9 was used for local self-attention. For evaluation, we used mAP@[0.1:0.1:0.5] and report the average mAP following [18]. In this dataset, an action is defined as a combination of a verb (action) and a noun (object). As this dataset was recently released, we are only able to compare our methods to BMN [36] and G-TAD [75], both using the same SlowFast features provided by [18]. Again, implementation details are described in the appendix C. 

Results. Table 2 presents the results. Our method achieves an average mAP ([0.1:0.1:0.5]) of 23.5% and 21.9% for verb and noun, respectively. Our results again largely outperform the strong baselines of BMN [36] and G-TAD [75] by over 13.5% in absolute percentage points. An interesting observation is that the gaps between our results and BMN / G-TAD are much larger on EPIC-Kitchens 100. A possible reason is that ActivityNet has a small number of actions per video (1.5), leading to imbalanced classification for our model; only a few moments (around the action center) are labeled positive while all rest are negative. We adapt ActionFormer for EPIC-Kitchens 100 2022 Action Detection challenge.

citations.title: Action Progression Networks for Temporal Action Detection in Videos
snippets:
THUMOS14 serves as a benchmark dataset for temporal action detection (TAD), featuring videos across 20 human action classes against temporal backgrounds. The dataset is comprised of 2,756 trimmed videos for training, 200 untrimmed videos for validation, and 212 untrimmed videos for testing, totaling 2,756, 3,007, and 3,358 annotated action instances across the training, validation, and test splits, respectively. Unlike conventional TAD methods, which are typically trained only on the validation split due to their dependency on learning temporal backgrounds, our APN utilizes action frames exclusively. This enables the use of both training and validation splits for model training, leveraging the comprehensive annotations available. 

ActivityNet-1.3 consists of 10,024 training videos (15,410 instances) and 4,926 validation videos (7,654 instances), spanning over 200 action classes. In contrast to THUMOS14, ActivityNet-1.3 often features videos with a single, extensively annotated action instance, presenting a different set of challenges for TAD. 

DFMAD is a part of the DCD dataset [95] aimed at children behavior research. It includes 63 untrimmed, longduration videos from a first-person perspective. Of these, 50 videos are designated for training and 13 for testing. Each video encompasses eight complete (4+2+2) and five incomplete (2+2+1) action instances across three action classes. DFMAD is characterized by (1) precise annotations, exclusively marking complete action instances, distinguishing it from the more common practice in THUMOS14 and ActivityNet of annotating incomplete actions or sequences of multiple action instances, and (2) the extended duration of both videos and actions, averaging 676 seconds and 31 seconds, respectively. These features make DFMAD particularly suited for evaluating the efficacy of TAD methodologies in complex, research scenarios. 

In Fig. 3, sample images from the three datasets are shown. It is evident that the videos have significant variety in terms of camera settings and content, making temporal action detection challenging.

sections.title: # Best pretrained models for General Video Understanding with TAD Transfer
sections.text:
If you need a single model that excels at video understanding (recognition, localization, grounded QA, long-form) and can be adapted for TAD, pick a strong LVLM/Video backbone:

- Qwen2.5-VL (7B): A top open-source LVLM that scales well to video tasks and emphasizes long-context and dense visual-textual reasoning, making it suitable for long untrimmed videos and instruction-driven video understanding. It is widely used as a base for video QA, grounding, and captioning, and pairs well with temporal grounding heads for TAD transfer. Qwen2.5-VL excels in long-context and dense visual-textual reasoning and supports both short and long video tasks [7397ebdc-1] VideoChat-R1 uses Qwen2.5-VL-7B across multiple video benchmarks and tasks, including temporal grounding and QA [7397ebdc-4]. Evidence across benchmarks shows larger models outperform smaller ones on reasoning-heavy video tasks, while unified visual tokenization simplifies transfer across images and video. LLaVA-OneVision uses a unified visual token strategy (AnyRes-9 for images, frame-level pooling for video) and shows at least 5-point gains when scaling the LLM from 0.5B to 7B on many datasets; larger LLMs substantially enhance performance on reasoning-heavy datasets like EgoSchema [7397ebdc-2].

- LLaVA-OneVision (Qwen-2 vision encoder + Qwen-2 LLM): Offers a unified visual token design and strong performance across open-ended and multi-choice video benchmarks, including ActivityNet-QA, MLVU (long video), EgoSchema, VideoDetailCaption, and Video-ChatGPT. It is convenient for projects needing both image and video understanding with a single model family, and you can add a boundary-aware detection head for TAD. LLaVA-OneVision evaluates across diverse video benchmarks and shows improved performance with larger LLMs on complex, reasoning-driven tasks [7397ebdc-2] LLaVA-OneVision excels across single-image, multi-image, and video understanding tasks using a unified visual token strategy [7397ebdc-1]. Studies show that adding EPIC-Kitchens-style action data to LLaVAction improves action recognition across multiple video benchmarks, indicating effective transfer to action-centric tasks—useful when adapting for TAD. LLaVAction demonstrates that training with EPIC-KITCHENS-100 (and replaying a large video corpus) improves performance on five of six additional video benchmarks, supporting generality beyond the training set [7397ebdc-0].

- Long-LLaVA / LLaVA-NeXT-Video: If your videos are long and require cross-frame temporal coherence, these variants incorporate attention and cross-frame mechanisms tailored for long videos, which helps in temporal grounding and QA tasks that underpin TAD pipelines. Long-LLaVA is optimized for efficient multi-frame processing with temporal coherence constraints and cross-frame attention, improving video QA and description [7397ebdc-1] LLaVA-NeXT-Video fine-tunes a Qwen-1.5 32B base with high-quality video instruction data, enabling video-language interactions [7397ebdc-4].

Practical recommendations:
- Start with Qwen2.5-VL (or LLaVA-OneVision) as the video encoder and add a temporal detection head (e.g., BMN for proposals + transformer-based classification/regression, or a one-stage boundary head). These LVLMs provide strong features for action localization and have demonstrated transfer gains when augmented with action-centric data like EPIC-Kitchens. Qwen2.5-VL supports long video inputs and dense reasoning, enabling transfer to video understanding tasks that TAD pipelines rely on [7397ebdc-1] Augmenting with EPIC-Kitchens-100 improves video action recognition across multiple benchmarks, suggesting effective transfer to TAD [7397ebdc-0] Unified visual tokenization and larger LLMs improve performance on complex video reasoning tasks, which are prerequisites for robust TAD [7397ebdc-2].
- For long-form or surveillance scenarios, consider models with explicit long-term memory or sliding-window tokenization (e.g., MovieChat, Kangaroo) when you need to handle hundreds of frames and complex temporal reasoning before grounding into detection heads. MovieChat uses sliding-window tokenization and dual-memory mechanisms (short-term and long-term) for long video understanding; Kangaroo adopts attention and memory-efficient tokenization to process hundreds of frames [7397ebdc-1].

sections.title: # How to choose: fit the model to your task and constraints
sections.text:
- Dense, egocentric, long untrimmed videos (EPIC-Kitchens, HACS): Prefer transformer-based TAD detectors with strong spatiotemporal features. Two-stage ActionFormer with SlowFast features is a robust baseline; one-stage boundary refinement detectors (Refining Action Boundaries, FDDet, OADT ensembles) offer speed and accuracy, especially at higher IoU thresholds where precise boundary localization is critical. ActionFormer with SlowFast features achieves large gains on EPIC-Kitchens-100 over BMN and G-TAD [42355c69-0] Boundary-aware one-stage detectors achieve SOTA on EPIC-Kitchens-100 [42355c69-2] Ensembles of one-stage transformers achieve 21.28% mAP on EPIC-Kitchens-100 test [448f809e-2] FDDet evaluates on THUMOS14, HACS, and ActivityNet-1.3 with standard mAP thresholds [448f809e-4].

- General video understanding plus TAD: Choose a strong LVLM/encoder as backbone and add a detection head. Qwen2.5-VL (7B) and LLaVA-OneVision provide versatile video encoders with strong performance across QA, long-form understanding, and transfer to action tasks; they integrate well with temporal grounding/proposal modules and scale efficiently for production. Qwen2.5-VL excels in long-context and dense visual reasoning for both short and long videos [7397ebdc-1] LLaVA-OneVision demonstrates broad performance across video QA and long-form datasets and benefits from larger LLMs on complex tasks [7397ebdc-2] LLaVAction shows improved generality when pretrained with EPIC-Kitchens-100 and data replay, supporting transfer to action-centric tasks [7397ebdc-0].

- Multi-task or open-ended video QA/localization: Favor models explicitly evaluated on long-form and QA-heavy benchmarks (MLVU, EgoSchema, ActivityNet-QA), such as LLaVA-OneVision and Qwen2.5-VL, and add a temporal grounding head for TAD. Expect larger model sizes (7B) to outperform smaller variants on reasoning-heavy tasks, with unified visual tokenization easing integration with detection heads. LLaVA-OneVision shows at least 5-point improvements when scaling from 0.5B to 7B and excels on reasoning-heavy datasets like EgoSchema [7397ebdc-2] Qwen2.5-VL emphasizes long-context and dense reasoning across videos, aiding multi-choice and open-ended tasks [7397ebdc-1].

Dataset. EPIC-Kitchens 100 is the largest egocentric action dataset. The dataset contains 100 hours of videos from 700 sessions capturing cooking activities in different kitchens. In comparison to ActivityNet-1.3, EPIC-Kitchens 100 has less number of videos, yet many more instances per video (average 128 vs. 1.5 on ActivityNet-1.3). sections.title: # Caveats and gaps
sections.text:
- Dataset shifts matter: EPIC-Kitchens has dense, egocentric actions; ActivityNet-1.3 and HACS offer more general daily activities, while THUMOS14 focuses on sports with shorter actions. A model strong on one may not transfer directly to another without finetuning; ensemble strategies and unified frameworks help bridge gaps. EPIC-Kitchens-100 has many more instances per video than ActivityNet and poses new challenges due to camera motion and density [42355c69-0] ActivityNet-1.3 and THUMOS14 differ in action duration and video length, requiring adaptability across temporal structures [42355c69-4] A unified framework shows adaptivity across THUMOS14 and ActivityNet v1.3, surpassing prior SOTA on THUMOS14 and approaching winning results on ActivityNet v1.3 [448f809e-1].
- Higher IoU thresholds expose boundary errors; methods that explicitly refine boundaries (e.g., boundary heads, frequency-decoupling) tend to fare better at stringent thresholds on dense datasets. Refining Action Boundaries explicitly models boundary confidence and improves localization precision [42355c69-2] FDDet introduces frequency-decoupling for boundary refinement across multiple datasets and IoU ranges [448f809e-4].
- For LVLMs, performance on higher-order causal reasoning and long-form anomaly detection remains challenging; larger models help but may still underperform humans, so task-specific finetuning and detection heads are often needed for production TAD. SurveillanceVQA shows LVLMs struggle on cause/result inference, with larger 7B models generally outperforming smaller ones but still facing challenges on complex reasoning [7397ebdc-3].

citations.title: Action Progression Networks for Temporal Action Detection in Videos
snippets:
THUMOS14 serves as a benchmark dataset for temporal action detection (TAD), featuring videos across 20 human action classes against temporal backgrounds. The dataset is comprised of 2,756 trimmed videos for training, 200 untrimmed videos for validation, and 212 untrimmed videos for testing, totaling 2,756, 3,007, and 3,358 annotated action instances across the training, validation, and test splits, respectively. Unlike conventional TAD methods, which are typically trained only on the validation split due to their dependency on learning temporal backgrounds, our APN utilizes action frames exclusively. This enables the use of both training and validation splits for model training, leveraging the comprehensive annotations available. 

ActivityNet-1.3 consists of 10,024 training videos (15,410 instances) and 4,926 validation videos (7,654 instances), spanning over 200 action classes. In contrast to THUMOS14, ActivityNet-1.3 often features videos with a single, extensively annotated action instance, presenting a different set of challenges for TAD. 

DFMAD is a part of the DCD dataset [95] aimed at children behavior research. It includes 63 untrimmed, longduration videos from a first-person perspective. Of these, 50 videos are designated for training and 13 for testing. Each video encompasses eight complete (4+2+2) and five incomplete (2+2+1) action instances across three action classes. DFMAD is characterized by (1) precise annotations, exclusively marking complete action instances, distinguishing it from the more common practice in THUMOS14 and ActivityNet of annotating incomplete actions or sequences of multiple action instances, and (2) the extended duration of both videos and actions, averaging 676 seconds and 31 seconds, respectively. These features make DFMAD particularly suited for evaluating the efficacy of TAD methodologies in complex, research scenarios. 

In Fig. 3, sample images from the three datasets are shown. It is evident that the videos have significant variety in terms of camera settings and content, making temporal action detection challenging.

In QA tasks involving abnormal video scenarios, LVLMs demonstrate notable performance variations and task-specific capabilities. sections.title: # Bottom line: my picks
sections.text:
- If you want the strongest pretrained option purely for TAD today: a one-stage boundary-refinement transformer built on SlowFast (or a unified two-stage transformer like ActionFormer) trained/ensembled for EPIC-Kitchens/THUMOS/ActivityNet protocols. Expect state-of-the-art mAP on dense, long, and egocentric videos and strong portability across benchmarks. ActionFormer with SlowFast features sets a strong baseline on EPIC-Kitchens-100, outperforming BMN and G-TAD [42355c69-0] Refining Action Boundaries achieves SOTA on EPIC-Kitchens-100 via boundary confidence refinement [42355c69-2] OADT ensembles reach 21.28% mAP on EPIC-Kitchens-100 test [448f809e-2] Unified frameworks surpass prior SOTA on THUMOS14 and approach winning ActivityNet v1.3 results [448f809e-1].

- If you need a single pretrained model that unifies video understanding with transfer to TAD: choose Qwen2.5-VL (7B) or LLaVA-OneVision as your video encoder, and add a temporal grounding/proposal classification head (e.g., BMN + transformer, or boundary head). These models deliver strong features and broad task coverage, and have demonstrated transfer gains when augmented with action-centric data like EPIC-Kitchens. Qwen2.5-VL excels at long-context and dense visual-textual reasoning for videos [7397ebdc-1] LLaVA-OneVision shows strong performance across video QA and long-form datasets, with larger LLMs improving complex reasoning [7397ebdc-2] LLaVAction demonstrates improved generality when pretrained with EPIC-Kitchens-100 and data replay [7397ebdc-0].

If you share your target dataset (e.g., ActivityNet vs. EPIC-Kitchens vs. surveillance/long-form), compute budget, and latency constraints, I can map these picks to specific model releases and provide a concrete finetuning recipe and expected mAP/IoU outcomes.

sections.title: # Overview
sections.text: Kubernetes is an open-source system for automating deployment, scaling, and management of containerized applications across clusters of machines. It provides a higher-level abstraction over the container runtime by organizing apps into declarative, manageable units (such as Pods, Deployments, Services, and Stateful/Job sets) and by running a control plane that ensures the desired state is realized across nodes in the cluster. An overview of the key components that make up a Kubernetes cluster [9c7fc5eb-0] Kubernetes cluster architecture overview and hardening guidance [9c7fc5eb-1].

sections.title: # Control plane and nodes
sections.text:
A Kubernetes cluster has a control plane and worker nodes. The control plane runs on one or more master nodes and contains several services that make up the “brain” of the system: the API server, etcd, the controller manager, and the scheduler. Worker nodes run the applications and host the pods; each node runs kubelet (node agent) and kube-proxy (networking agent). Overview of key components that make up a Kubernetes cluster [9c7fc5eb-0] Cluster architecture overview [9c7fc5eb-1].

- API server: The entry point for programmatic interactions; serializes and deserializes objects and exposes the Kubernetes API. Key component overview [9c7fc5eb-0].
- etcd: A consistent, distributed key–value store that stores the cluster’s desired state and configuration. Cluster architecture overview [9c7fc5eb-1].
- Controller Manager: Runs controllers that continuously reduce the difference between the actual and desired state (e.g., ReplicaSet controller for Deployments, DaemonSet controller). Key component overview [9c7fc5eb-0].
- Scheduler: Assigns newly created pods to nodes based on constraints and resource availability, scoring and selecting a target node. The scheduler finds feasible Nodes for a Pod and then runs a set of functions to score the feasible Nodes and picks a Node with the highest score [9c7fc5eb-2].
- kubelet: The primary node agent that runs pods and manages containers, filesystem, and secrets on the node. Key component overview [9c7fc5eb-0].
- kube-proxy: Network proxy that loads the Services’ rules and maintains network rules on nodes (e.g., iptables/ipvs) so endpoints in pods are reachable. Key component overview [9c7fc5eb-0].

In practice, managed clusters (e.g., GKE, AKS) abstract some of these, such as multi-master control planes and automated etcd backups, while the core behavior and interfaces remain the same. Hardening and architecture guidance for Kubernetes clusters [9c7fc5eb-1].
