sections.title: # Core abstractions and objects
sections.text:
Applications are expressed as Kubernetes objects that represent infrastructure and application components. The most common top-level object is the Pod, which packages one or more containers and shared resources. At application scale, you typically use higher-level controllers:

- Deployment: declaratively defines how to rollout updates to a set of replicas (via ReplicaSet controllers). Kubernetes components and concepts overview [9c7fc5eb-0].
- StatefulSet and DaemonSet: for stateful workloads and node-distributed tasks, respectively. Kubernetes components and concepts overview [9c7fc5eb-0].
- Job and CronJob: for batch work and scheduled tasks. Kubernetes components and concepts overview [9c7fc5eb-0].

Crucially, Kubernetes operates at the Pod level: you declare desired Pods and their placement policies, and the control plane ensures that exactly the right number of healthy Pod instances run according to your policies across nodes. Kubernetes components and concepts overview [9c7fc5eb-0] Scheduler assigns Pods to Nodes based on feasibility and scoring [9c7fc5eb-2].

sections.title: # Scheduling and placement
sections.text: When a Pod is created, the scheduler selects a suitable node considering resource, taint/toleration, and node selection rules. Once scheduled, the node’s kubelet pulls images and creates the containers per the Pod specification. The scheduler does not consider application-level dependencies beyond those exposed via pod anti-/affinity rules and node selectors. sections.title: # Networking model
sections.text: Kubernetes abstracts networking with Services, which define a stable IP and selector to route traffic to pods that match the label selector. Services can expose endpoints via ClusterIP (cluster-local headless service), NodePort (expose on each node’s IP:port), or LoadBalancer (delegate to cloud to create a load balancer). Ingress is an API object that manages external HTTP/TCP access by routing to Services, often via Ingress controllers (e.g., NGINX, Traefik) that implement routing rules. Cluster architecture overview and networking guidance [9c7fc5eb-1].

sections.title: # Storage
sections.text: Persistent data is handled through volumes attached to pods and managed by StorageClasses, PVs (Persistent Volumes), and PVCs (Persistent Volume Claims). A StorageClass describes the type of storage to provision, a PV represents a storage asset in the cluster (e.g., a cloud disk or host path), and a PVC requests storage by claiming a PV. StatefulSet provides headless Services and ordered, stable volumes for stateful apps. Kubernetes components and concepts overview [9c7fc5eb-0].

sections.title: # Lifecycle and self-healing
sections.text: Kubernetes proactively manages app health and availability. You declare liveness/readiness probes in containers; if liveness returns failure, the system restarts/restarts the container or reschedules the pod depending on the policy. If readiness fails, traffic is routed out via Services until the probe passes. Deployments perform rolling/progressive updates by gradually replacing old replicas while maintaining desired availability. Kubernetes lifecycle and hardening guidance [9c7fc5eb-1].

sections.title: # How Kubernetes Differs from Containers
sections.text:
Containers are the runtime packaging and isolation mechanism for applications. A container image contains a filesystem and instructions to run a process and is executed by a container runtime (e.g., containerd, CRI-O, Docker). Kubernetes is an orchestration layer that schedules and manages many containers grouped into Pods across a cluster of machines, abstracting away the underlying nodes and exposing higher-level concepts for scaling, resilience, networking, and storage. Kubernetes components and concepts overview [9c7fc5eb-0].

- Abstraction level: Containers are the unit of runtime; Kubernetes is the system that manages sets of containers as Pods and applications, with declarative manifests (YAML/JSON) describing desired states and policies. Kubernetes components and concepts overview [9c7fc5eb-0].
- Deployment target: You deploy a Pod (one or more containers) in Kubernetes, not a single container; controllers (e.g., Deployment) manage replicas, updates, and desired state. Kubernetes components and concepts overview [9c7fc5eb-0].
- Scheduling and placement: Kubernetes schedules entire Pods to nodes according to resource and policy constraints; Docker (local) runs containers where you tell it to execute. The scheduler finds feasible Nodes for a Pod and then runs a set of functions to score the feasible Nodes and picks a Node with the highest score [9c7fc5eb-2].
- Multi-node management: Kubernetes handles distribution, failover, and recovery across many machines; Docker alone targets a single host. Kubernetes cluster architecture overview [9c7fc5eb-1].
- Networking: Containers expose ports on the host or network namespaces; Kubernetes provides Services, Ingress, and load-balancing to abstract stable endpoints and external access. Kubernetes cluster architecture overview [9c7fc5eb-1].
- Storage and state: Containers lack persistent storage by default; Kubernetes adds PV/PVC, StatefulSet, and headless Services to provide durable, stable storage and identities for stateful workloads. Kubernetes components and concepts overview [9c7fc5eb-0].
- Self-healing: Kubernetes monitors pod health via liveness/readiness and uses controllers to restart, reschedule, or rollback to maintain desired state; this behavior is not native to containers. Kubernetes lifecycle and hardening guidance [9c7fc5eb-1].

Practically, you build an image and run a container, but to operate that image at scale you “Kubernetes-ify” it by packaging containers into Pods, declaring replicas via a Deployment (or StatefulSet/Job), and exposing it through Services/Ingress with health checks and storage claims. Kubernetes components and concepts overview [9c7fc5eb-0] Scheduler assigns Pods to Nodes based on feasibility and scoring [9c7fc5eb-2].

sections.title: # What “denoising” means and why it matters
sections.text: Neural network denoising aims to map noisy observations to a best guess of the clean signal while preserving structure and avoiding artifacts. In audio, this can mean recovering speech from background noise; in images and volumes, it can mean restoring fine details under Gaussian or Poisson noise; and in 1D time series (e.g., sensors, biomedical signals), it can mean suppressing interference while retaining dynamics. The choice of model and objective depends on the signal domain, noise model, available labels, and deployment constraints. In audio, spectrogram-domain CNNs such as DnCNN have become standard baselines for blind Gaussian denoising in the time–frequency (TF) domain [5e70eb45-0] , while end-to-end time-domain models have emerged to avoid TF artifacts and parameter dependencies. Classical spectral/subspace methods motivate TF denoising, but time-domain end-to-end approaches directly operate on raw waveforms and avoid time–frequency aliasing and resolution trade-offs [5e70eb45-3].

citations.title: Speech Denoising with Residual Attention U-Net
snippets:
In the development of audio signal processing technologies, various information such as text (speech recognition), speaker (speaker verification), and emotion (emotion recognition) can be extracted from speech signals. The performance of these technologies is degraded when the SNR is less than 20 dB (1,2) . For high-accuracy information extraction, audio devices such as headsets, which can input with high SNR, has been equipped. The equipped devices limit the use case. Therefore, speech denoising (3) (or speech enhancement) is required during preprocessing. Our goal is to develop monaural (single-channel) speech denoising technologies to improve under the real environment, which SNR is 5-10dB, to SNR 20dB or more. If this can be realized, audio devices without equipped, such as general-purpose microphones or conference microphones, can be used for audio information extraction. And it means that the scope of application of audio information extraction can be extended. 

As our research focuses on monaural speech denoising. A multi-channel recode such as microphone array (4) cannot be applied. Traditionally, Spectral subtraction (5) and Wiener filter (6) were popular algorithm that make noise reduction filter from its distribution and characteristic of the noise. Recently, a denoising method using a deep neural network (DNN) has been proposed (7,8) . 

When paying attention to features using speech denoising, typical speech denoising methods estimate background noise by using spectrogram features on the speech signals. The short-time Fourier transform (STFT) is used to convert speech signals to a spectrogram. The denoising operation has also been applied to the magnitude (9) and complex (10) components of a spectrogram. A disadvantage is that these approaches depend on many parameters (window size of STFT and overlap of audio frames) that affect the time and frequency resolution. Moreover, signal artifacts arise due to time aliasing when using the inverse STFT. 

To resolve this issue, end-to-end speech denoising methods that directly operate on raw waveforms have been proposed (11,12,13) . These methods need to deal with long dimensional data because speech signals contain high-density data samples.

sections.text:
- Spectrogram CNNs (DnCNN and variants). DnCNN is widely used to estimate noise and perform blind Gaussian denoising in the TF domain, then reconstruct the signal [5e70eb45-0]. Two-stage transformer networks in the time domain (encoder–two-stage transformer–masking–decoder) have achieved strong performance with lower complexity than earlier time- or frequency-domain models [6b1b953c-1].
- End-to-end time-domain models and hybrid TF+time-domain. End-to-end waveform denoisers avoid TF artifacts but must handle long sequences [5e70eb45-3]. Hybrid approaches combine STFT/ISTFT with DNN-based estimation (e.g., Kalman filter parameter learning, time-domain networks, and masking modules) [6b1b953c-1]. Unsupervised one-clip methods train a DNN on a single noisy clip to disentangle clean content from noise without labels [5e70eb45-2].
- Generative priors and codec-based denoisers. Retraining generative neural audio codecs (e.g., an audio codec) on denoising objectives can reduce artifacts and preserve naturalness compared to standard U-Nets, especially with multi-objective losses and comprehensive datasets [6b1b953c-4].
- Speech separation as a template for denoising pipelines. Two-stage architectures (a “masker” to estimate a source from a mixture and a “denoiser” to refine the estimate) embody deep autoencoder-style denoising in TF, which can be adapted for speech denoising [6b1b953c-2].

citations.title: ADNAC: Audio Denoiser using Neural Audio Codec
snippets:
Noise reduction is a fundamental part of audio signal processing, substantially improving signal quality and intelligibility across domains like speech processing [1][2][3], music production and restoration [1], and bioacoustics analysis [2]. Even though traditional techniques, such as spectral subtraction and Wiener filtering, provide a foundational basis, they often fail with complex and nonstationary noise patterns. 

Recent advancements in deep learning, particularly with convolutional neural networks (CNNs) in encoder-decoder structures like the U-Net, have shown significant promise [3,4]. Previous works demonstrated that a simple U-Net architecture can effectively filter white and urban noise from musical signals but fails to address more complex degradations like reverberation and noise cancellation artifacts. These limitations highlight the need for more powerful models capable of understanding and regenerating audio with higher fidelity. This paper investigates a novel approach which goes beyond conventional discriminative models by adapting a generative neural audio codec for denoising. The goal was to leverage the Descript Audio Codec (DAC) [5], a model designed for high-fidelity audio compression and retrain it on a denoising objective. The core hypothesis is that the rich representations and generative capabilities of a neural codec can produce better denoising results, minimizing artifacts and preserving the natural aspects of the original music, more efficiently than a standard U-Net. This is especially true when a multi-objective loss function is used, and the training is performed on a comprehensive, purpose-built dataset.

citations.title: Audio Denoising with Deep Network Priors
snippets: We present a method for audio denoising that combines processing done in both the time domain and the time-frequency domain. Given a noisy audio clip, the method trains a deep neural network to fit this signal. Since the fitting is only partly successful and is able to better capture the underlying clean signal than the noise, the output of the network helps to disentangle the clean audio from the rest of the signal. The method is completely unsupervised and only trains on the specific audio clip that is being denoised. Our experiments demonstrate favorable performance in comparison to the literature methods, and our code and audio samples are available at https: //github.com/mosheman5/DNP. citations.title: MaD TwinNet: Masker-Denoiser Architecture with Twin Networks for Monaural Sound Source Separation
snippets:
Our proposed method takes as an input the raw audio signal of a mixture of sources, and outputs the raw audio signal of the target source (i.e. the singing voice). The method uses a deep neural network architecture, which consists of two parts. The first part takes the mixture magnitude spectrogram of the input time-domain audio as an input, estimates the target source magnitude spectrogram from the mixture by predicting a time-frequency filter and applying it to the input, and outputs the estimated magnitude spectrogram of the target source. The second part takes the output of the first part as an input, predicts and applies a denoising mask, and outputs a filtered version of its input. Since the input to the first part is the mixture signal and the output is an estimate of the signal of the target source, we frame the time-frequency filter of the first part as a timefrequency mask. Similarly, since the input to the second part is a representation of the target source and its output is the same representation of the same source, we frame the time-frequency filter of the second part as a denoising filter. The first part of our method is denoted as The Masker and the second as the The Denoiser. 

The Masker and the Denoiser are neural network architectures based on DAEs [14]. According to the initial paper of DAEs [14], DAEs try to learn stochastically the manifold of the clean data. Source separation can be understood as a process that transforms the samples of the corrupted data manifold (i.e. the mixture) into samples that reside in the manifold of clean data (i.e. the target source) [25]. This transformation for audio data can be understood using time-frequency masking [8]. We want to include in our optimization graph the generation of the mask and the denoising filter. Consequently, we setup our method in a way that the Masker will predict the mask that will be applied to the input magnitude spectrogram, and the denoiser will predict values of denoising filter which is applied to the output of the Masker.

snippets:
In this section, we evaluate the problem of training LBNs with multiple layers of non-deterministic variables on denoising full images. The state-of-the art method for denoising natural images is BM3D (Dabov et al., 2009). Neural methods (Burger et al., 2012) were state-of-the-art but they were surpassed by later versions of BM3D. BM3D is a non-parametric denoising algorithm that uses self-similarity between patches to average out the noise. While we can expect this method to work well for small noise distributions, it produces blurry images for high noise distributions. 

In order to scale to large images we use a convolutional architecture for the LBNs. In practice, this amounts to replacing the dot products by convolutions -both for the activations of the linear units and the gaters. We found that using 128 convolutional kernels of size 9 × 9 for the linear and gating units produced good results. The network has 4 convolutional hidden layers in total and 3 layer gating functions for LBNs. We do not use any spatial pooling because the loss of information would be detrimental to denoising. The output pixels have a scalar bias so as to not constrain the size of the images that can be generated. We extract 1M 64 × 64 image patches from Imagenet as our training set for highly corrupted images and 6M 29 × 29 patches otherwise. We use these large image patches instead of the full image to save computation time during training but the same model can be applied to large images at test time. The networks can take up to a week of computation time to train and so in the interest of the PSNR evaluation we set the number of Monte Carlo samples to K = 1. We evaluate the quality of the distribution with a model trained with K = 10.

citations.title: RadiantVisions: Illuminating Low-Light Imagery with a Multi-Scale Branch Network
snippets: Image denoising, aimed at reducing noise while preserving details, has evolved significantly within image processing. Over the past years, a myriad of image priors have been proposed to restore clarity to noisy images, including sparsity, low rank, and self-similarity. Notable methods based on image priors, such as BM3D [19] and WNNM [20], have achieved remarkable progress in the domain of image denoising. With the advent of deep learning, researchers have increasingly turned to leveraging deep neural networks for image denoising. For instance, DnCNN [21] employed a deep residual network and integrated batch normalization layers to accelerate the training process. In a different approach, CBDNet [22] addressed noise comprehensively throughout the imaging process, utilizing the U-net architecture along with a sub-network to estimate noise levels, thus enhancing denoising performance.

Many based on image priors methods have made great progress in image denoising, such as BM3D [7], WNNM [8]. With the development of deep learning, researchers have applied deep neural networks to image denoising in recent years. For example, DnCNN [9] trained a deep residual network and used batch normalization layers to speed up the training process. snippets:
Image denoising is one of the most critical low-level imaging tasks because noise is inherent to all image acquisition processes. As obtaining a noise-free image is an ill-posed problem, prevalent denoising techniques resort to making certain assumptions about the nature of noise. The most common approach in this regard is to model the noise as an additive Gaussian process. Denoising images corrupted with additive white Gaussian noise (AWGN) has been a center of attention for decades. Early efforts considered denoising as an averaging process [1], either in frequency or spatial domain. These were succeeded by the non-local class of methods [2] [3] which exploited the non-local similarity of patches within an image. BM3D [3] holds a pioneering status in such methods and is still competitive in challenging denoising tasks [4]. It remained the state-of-the-art method in AWGN denoising, until the advent of learning-based methods.

Discriminative learning-based denoising methods aim to learn a direct mapping from corrupted to clean images using annotated training samples. Artificial neural networks (ANNs) have become a standard choice for such problems and were shown in [5] to produce competitive denoising performance as compared to BM3D, given sufficient training examples and model complexity. Since then, most of the discriminative denoising methods make use of convolutional neural networks (CNNs), which are a special class of ANNs specialized for grid-structured data [6]. CNNs for image denoising is generally very deep [7], consisting of dozens of layers and a large number of trainable parameters generally over a million. The performance of CNN-based methods has been observed to be directly correlated with architectural complexity [8]. The enormous computational complexity is often neglected, especially since the performance of CNNs has been optimized quite well for specialized hardware devices such as GPUs and TPUs [9]. However, usage of such models is still expensive, and in many cases impractical, especially in the case of embedded devices that have limited computational resources. - RNN/LSTM, CNNs, and Transformers. LSTMs capture long-term dependencies but are sensitive to noise; Transformers achieve state-of-the-art sequence modeling but often require large datasets and can be computationally heavy [7edecbc6-0]. Deep models (MLPs, CNNs, RNNs, Transformers) have improved single-channel time-series denoising, but heavy compute and long training times limit real-time use; complex interference (e.g., EMG in EEG) remains challenging [7edecbc6-1]. Transformers capture long-range dependencies and parallelize well, yet overfit on volatile data and need large data; CNN-based TCNs provide strong alternatives for local-to-hierarchical feature extraction [7edecbc6-2]. Hybrid architectures that combine denoising preprocessing (e.g., wavelet) with LSTM–Transformer components can address complementary weaknesses (denoising before modeling) [7edecbc6-3].
- Wavelet-domain pre-processing and hybrid denoising. Wavelet–LSTM pipelines denoise multiresolution coefficients before LSTM forecasting, improving robustness to noise and performance [7edecbc6-0]. Wavelet denoising integrated with LSTM–Transformer models has been applied to pipeline leakage detection, with empirical improvements over baselines [7edecbc6-3].

citations.title: Targeted Adversarial Denoising Autoencoders (TADA) for Neural Time Series Filtration
snippets: Developing effective time series filtration algorithms could help improve existing neural interfaces that rely on noisy time series data (Yadav et al., 2020;Linderman et al., 2008;Makeig et al., 2012). However, conventional neural time series filtration methods (canonical correlation analysis, or CCA; independent component analysis, or ICA, etc.) often fail to handle more complex single-channel time series denoising cases (Vergult et al., 2007;Chou et al., 2016;Vigario & Oja, 2008). This is typically true, for example, with EMG interference in EEG data, which is a primary source of noise for neural interfacing applications (Stergiadis et al., 2022;Zhang et al., 2021a). Machine learning (ML)-based approaches, have made recent strides in handling single-channel time series denoising scenarios (Luo & Mesgarani, 2019;Yin et al., 2023;Cui et al., 2024); MLbased time series filtration methods based on multilayer perceptrons (MLPs), convolutional neural networks (CNNs), recurrent neural networks (RNNs), and transformers have successively improved the state of the art (Zhang et al., 2021a;Cui et al., 2024;Yin et al., 2023). However, these published denoising approaches are compute-heavy, often involving large numbers of trainable parameters (and thus a large memory footprint) and long training times. These large compute footprints make deployment in real-time neural interfacing applications cumbersome (Justus et al., 2018;Cui et al., 2024;Yin et al., 2023;Buongiorno et al., 2021;Monga et al., 2021). Moreover, the inherent difficulties of EMG filtration continue to present challenges for deep learning (DL) models; complex patterns are harder to identify, so more exhaustive filtration is required to ensure a clean signal.

citations.title: A Real-Time Signal-Based Wavelet Long Short-Term Memory Method for Length-of-Stay Prediction for the Intensive Care Unit: Development and Evaluation Study
snippets:
The use of time series data for prediction has been a central focus in various domains, leading to the exploration and development of diverse models [27]. Traditional statistical models, particularly regression techniques, have historically played a crucial role in time series prediction [28]. These models leverage historical data patterns to make forecasts, providing a foundational framework for subsequent advancements in predictive modeling. However, their performance is constrained by their underlying hypothesis, as most datasets struggle to fulfill these assumptions. 

The emergence of neural networks has revolutionized time series prediction. Recurrent neural networks are specifically designed to capture sequential dependencies within data [29]. Recurrent neural networks excel in modeling temporal relationships, making them well-suited for time series forecasting tasks [30]. However, they may face challenges when dealing with long-term dependencies due to the vanishing gradient problem [31]. The introduction of the long short-term memory (LSTM) model addresses this issue by incorporating memory cells that can retain information over extended sequences [32]. LSTMs have shown remarkable success in capturing complex temporal dependencies, making them popular for time series prediction tasks. However, they are not immune to challenges, particularly when the data is affected by noise [33]. The transformer architecture, originally designed for natural language processing tasks, has also found applications in time series prediction [34]. However, a notable challenge lies in the substantial amount of data often required for effective training [35]. In addition, for task-specific small datasets, transformers have demonstrated less competitiveness compared with LSTMs, as evidenced by research in the medical field [36]. Therefore, it appears that LSTM remains the preferred choice, notwithstanding its susceptibility to noise in time series data. 

To address the susceptibility of LSTMs to noise, we propose using wavelet transform techniques as a preprocessing step and introduce the Wavelet-LSTM model. This approach aims to denoise time series data before feeding it into LSTM models, with the overarching goal of enhancing the robustness of LSTM models and improving their performance in the presence of noisy signals.

citations.title: HAELT: A Hybrid Attentive Ensemble Learning Transformer Framework for High-Frequency Stock Price Forecasting
snippets:
Deep learning (DL) techniques have markedly advanced time series prediction capabilities. Recurrent Neural Networks (RNNs) and their more sophisticated variant, Long Short-Term Memory (LSTM) networks, have been instrumental in this progress [19,20]. LSTMs are particularly adept at modeling long-range temporal dependencies in sequential data, which has led to their successful application in financial forecasting [21]. However, LSTMs can be sensitive to noise and prone to overfitting, especially with volatile financial market data [12]. 

Transformer architectures, employing self-attention mechanisms to assign differential importance to various segments of an input sequence, have recently achieved state-of-the-art results in diverse sequence modeling tasks [22,23]. Transformers are proficient at capturing complex long-range dependencies and benefit from parallelizable computations, potentially accelerating training. Nevertheless, they often necessitate large training datasets for effective generalization and can be computationally demanding due to their complex architectures [24]. 

Convolutional Neural Networks (CNNs), initially developed for grid-like data such as images, have also been effectively applied to time series analysis. By deploying convolutional filters along the temporal axis, CNNs can extract local patterns and learn hierarchical feature representations from multivariate time series, providing an alternative method for capturing temporal dynamics [25,26].

sections.title: # Training objectives and practices
sections.text:
- Noise models and losses. In AWGN image denoising, MSE/MAE losses trained on paired noisy/clean pairs typically drive performance [0dafcf0f-3] , while CBDNet jointly estimates noise and reconstructs images to better reflect realistic imaging pipelines [0dafcf0f-1]. In audio, spectrogram denoisers often regress noise estimates and subtract them from TF patches [5e70eb45-0] , and two-stage time-domain transformer denoisers use masking/decoder heads to reconstruct the waveform [6b1b953c-1].
- Teacher forcing, iterative refinement, and generative priors. Retraining generative codec models for denoising (multi-objective losses) can stabilize reconstruction and reduce artifacts by leveraging rich latent priors [6b1b953c-4]. In time series, hybrid preprocessing (e.g., wavelet denoising) followed by LSTM/Transformer modeling can act as a teacher to improve downstream filtration [7edecbc6-3].
- Unsupervised and one-clip settings. Unsupervised denoising can operate on a single clip by exploiting the fact that the network’s incomplete fit better captures the clean signal than noise, effectively disentangling speech from noise without labels [5e70eb45-2].
- Data and domain adaptation. Time-domain transformer denoisers often report improved quality and intelligibility across SNRs and even generalize to unseen languages without additional training, highlighting inductive bias from architecture [6b1b953c-1]. Domain-specific datasets and morphological priors matter: when clean/noisy morphologies are similar, supervised methods can fail; multi-channel approaches exist but remain challenging for long-period data [5e70eb45-4].

Processing initial time series data, including noise recognition, removal, and signal reconstruction, represents a direct and effective approach to enhance the signal-to-noise ratio. [44] developed a noise suppression method using LSTM networks, and the reconstructed data were employed in 2D inversion modeling, effectively suppressing strong noise with typical morphological features. citations.title: ADNAC: Audio Denoiser using Neural Audio Codec
snippets:
Noise reduction is a fundamental part of audio signal processing, substantially improving signal quality and intelligibility across domains like speech processing [1][2][3], music production and restoration [1], and bioacoustics analysis [2]. Even though traditional techniques, such as spectral subtraction and Wiener filtering, provide a foundational basis, they often fail with complex and nonstationary noise patterns. 

Recent advancements in deep learning, particularly with convolutional neural networks (CNNs) in encoder-decoder structures like the U-Net, have shown significant promise [3,4]. Previous works demonstrated that a simple U-Net architecture can effectively filter white and urban noise from musical signals but fails to address more complex degradations like reverberation and noise cancellation artifacts. These limitations highlight the need for more powerful models capable of understanding and regenerating audio with higher fidelity. This paper investigates a novel approach which goes beyond conventional discriminative models by adapting a generative neural audio codec for denoising. The goal was to leverage the Descript Audio Codec (DAC) [5], a model designed for high-fidelity audio compression and retrain it on a denoising objective. The core hypothesis is that the rich representations and generative capabilities of a neural codec can produce better denoising results, minimizing artifacts and preserving the natural aspects of the original music, more efficiently than a standard U-Net. This is especially true when a multi-objective loss function is used, and the training is performed on a comprehensive, purpose-built dataset.

citations.title: Audio Denoising with Deep Network Priors
snippets: We present a method for audio denoising that combines processing done in both the time domain and the time-frequency domain. Given a noisy audio clip, the method trains a deep neural network to fit this signal. Since the fitting is only partly successful and is able to better capture the underlying clean signal than the noise, the output of the network helps to disentangle the clean audio from the rest of the signal. The method is completely unsupervised and only trains on the specific audio clip that is being denoised. Our experiments demonstrate favorable performance in comparison to the literature methods, and our code and audio samples are available at https: //github.com/mosheman5/DNP. Index Terms: Audio denoising; Unsupervised learning

citations.title: RadiantVisions: Illuminating Low-Light Imagery with a Multi-Scale Branch Network
snippets: Image denoising, aimed at reducing noise while preserving details, has evolved significantly within image processing. Over the past years, a myriad of image priors have been proposed to restore clarity to noisy images, including sparsity, low rank, and self-similarity. Notable methods based on image priors, such as BM3D [19] and WNNM [20], have achieved remarkable progress in the domain of image denoising. With the advent of deep learning, researchers have increasingly turned to leveraging deep neural networks for image denoising. For instance, DnCNN [21] employed a deep residual network and integrated batch normalization layers to accelerate the training process. In a different approach, CBDNet [22] addressed noise comprehensively throughout the imaging process, utilizing the U-net architecture along with a sub-network to estimate noise levels, thus enhancing denoising performance.

citations.title: Bm3d Vs 2-Layer Onn
snippets:
Image denoising is one of the most critical low-level imaging tasks because noise is inherent to all image acquisition processes. As obtaining a noise-free image is an ill-posed problem, prevalent denoising techniques resort to making certain assumptions about the nature of noise. The most common approach in this regard is to model the noise as an additive Gaussian process. Denoising images corrupted with additive white Gaussian noise (AWGN) has been a center of attention for decades. Early efforts considered denoising as an averaging process [1], either in frequency or spatial domain. These were succeeded by the non-local class of methods [2] [3] which exploited the non-local similarity of patches within an image. BM3D [3] holds a pioneering status in such methods and is still competitive in challenging denoising tasks [4]. It remained the state-of-the-art method in AWGN denoising, until the advent of learning-based methods.

Discriminative learning-based denoising methods aim to learn a direct mapping from corrupted to clean images using annotated training samples. Artificial neural networks (ANNs) have become a standard choice for such problems and were shown in [5] to produce competitive denoising performance as compared to BM3D, given sufficient training examples and model complexity. Since then, most of the discriminative denoising methods make use of convolutional neural networks (CNNs), which are a special class of ANNs specialized for grid-structured data [6]. CNNs for image denoising is generally very deep [7], consisting of dozens of layers and a large number of trainable parameters generally over a million. The performance of CNN-based methods has been observed to be directly correlated with architectural complexity [8]. The enormous computational complexity is often neglected, especially since the performance of CNNs has been optimized quite well for specialized hardware devices such as GPUs and TPUs [9]. However, usage of such models is still expensive, and in many cases impractical, especially in the case of embedded devices that have limited computational resources. citations.title: Predicting distributions with Linearizing Belief Networks
snippets:
In this section, we evaluate the problem of training LBNs with multiple layers of non-deterministic variables on denoising full images. The state-of-the art method for denoising natural images is BM3D (Dabov et al., 2009). Neural methods (Burger et al., 2012) were state-of-the-art but they were surpassed by later versions of BM3D. BM3D is a non-parametric denoising algorithm that uses self-similarity between patches to average out the noise. While we can expect this method to work well for small noise distributions, it produces blurry images for high noise distributions. 

In order to scale to large images we use a convolutional architecture for the LBNs. In practice, this amounts to replacing the dot products by convolutions -both for the activations of the linear units and the gaters. We found that using 128 convolutional kernels of size 9 × 9 for the linear and gating units produced good results. The network has 4 convolutional hidden layers in total and 3 layer gating functions for LBNs. We do not use any spatial pooling because the loss of information would be detrimental to denoising. The output pixels have a scalar bias so as to not constrain the size of the images that can be generated. We extract 1M 64 × 64 image patches from Imagenet as our training set for highly corrupted images and 6M 29 × 29 patches otherwise. We use these large image patches instead of the full image to save computation time during training but the same model can be applied to large images at test time. The networks can take up to a week of computation time to train and so in the interest of the PSNR evaluation we set the number of Monte Carlo samples to K = 1. We evaluate the quality of the distribution with a model trained with K = 10.

snippets:
Our neural-network-based denoising model accepts a single channel of audio signal and outputs the cleaned-up signal. Unlike some of the recent denoising methods that take as input audiovisual signals (i.e., both audio and video footage), our method can be applied in a wider range of scenarios (e.g., in cellular communication). We also evaluate our method under various signal-to-noise ratios-even under strong noise levels that are not tested against in previous methods. We show that, under a variety of denoising metrics, our method consistently outperforms those methods, including those that accept only audio input (like ours) and those that denoise based on audiovisual input. 

The pivotal role of silent intervals for speech denoising is further confirmed by a few key results. Even without supervising on silent interval detection, the ability to detect silent intervals naturally emerges in our network. Moreover, while our model is trained on English speech only, with no additional training it can be readily used to denoise speech in other languages (such as Chinese, Japanese, and Korean). Please refer to the supplementary materials for listening to our denoising results.

citations.title: A Real-Time Signal-Based Wavelet Long Short-Term Memory Method for Length-of-Stay Prediction for the Intensive Care Unit: Development and Evaluation Study
snippets:
The use of time series data for prediction has been a central focus in various domains, leading to the exploration and development of diverse models [27]. Traditional statistical models, particularly regression techniques, have historically played a crucial role in time series prediction [28]. These models leverage historical data patterns to make forecasts, providing a foundational framework for subsequent advancements in predictive modeling. However, their performance is constrained by their underlying hypothesis, as most datasets struggle to fulfill these assumptions. 

The emergence of neural networks has revolutionized time series prediction. Recurrent neural networks are specifically designed to capture sequential dependencies within data [29]. Recurrent neural networks excel in modeling temporal relationships, making them well-suited for time series forecasting tasks [30]. However, they may face challenges when dealing with long-term dependencies due to the vanishing gradient problem [31]. The introduction of the long short-term memory (LSTM) model addresses this issue by incorporating memory cells that can retain information over extended sequences [32]. LSTMs have shown remarkable success in capturing complex temporal dependencies, making them popular for time series prediction tasks. However, they are not immune to challenges, particularly when the data is affected by noise [33]. The transformer architecture, originally designed for natural language processing tasks, has also found applications in time series prediction [34]. However, a notable challenge lies in the substantial amount of data often required for effective training [35]. In addition, for task-specific small datasets, transformers have demonstrated less competitiveness compared with LSTMs, as evidenced by research in the medical field [36]. Therefore, it appears that LSTM remains the preferred choice, notwithstanding its susceptibility to noise in time series data. 

To address the susceptibility of LSTMs to noise, we propose using wavelet transform techniques as a preprocessing step and introduce the Wavelet-LSTM model. This approach aims to denoise time series data before feeding it into LSTM models, with the overarching goal of enhancing the robustness of LSTM models and improving their performance in the presence of noisy signals.

sections.title: # When to use which approach and practical tips
sections.text:
- Choose the domain-appropriate signal representation. If TF artifacts are unacceptable or latency is critical, prefer time-domain models; otherwise, spectrogram or magnitude-phase TF approaches can simplify training and improve intelligibility [5e70eb45-3]. U-Net-style CNNs flexibly denoise diverse 2D image types and can be repurposed to supervise other reconstruction tasks [0dafcf0f-2]. For 3D volumes, 3D CNNs recover 3D context and often outperform 2D stacks, though at higher memory/compute cost [3f164f0d-4]. For 1D time series, combine domain-specific pre-processing (e.g., wavelets) with sequence models (LSTM/Transformer/CNN) to reduce noise before learning dynamics [7edecbc6-3].
- Match loss and objective to noise and supervision. In AWGN with clean pairs, MSE/MAE are effective [0dafcf0f-3] ; include noise estimation or pipeline-aware losses (e.g., CBDNet) when noise is complex or task-dependent [0dafcf0f-1]. In spectrograms, noise estimation and subtraction are effective and scalable [5e70eb45-0]. Generative priors (trained codecs) with multi-objective losses can reduce artifacts and stabilize training [6b1b953c-4].
- Expect trade-offs between accuracy, artifacts, and compute. High-accuracy CNN denoisers often increase parameters and computational cost, requiring careful hardware/software design [0dafcf0f-3]. 3D CNNs can deliver higher PSNR/SSIM and better structure preservation than traditional and 2D CNNs [3f164f0d-0] , but they may take longer to train and require patching due to memory limits, affecting spatial consistency at boundaries [3f164f0d-3]. For sequences, misfits arise when noise morphology resembles the signal; hybrid CNN+RNN pipelines can mitigate this [5e70eb45-4].
- Evaluate with domain-relevant metrics and human checks. PSNR/SSIM can mislead in medical imaging; prefer visual detail and task-specific metrics alongside standard scores [3f164f0d-3]. For audio, multi-metric evaluations across SNRs and intelligibility are recommended [5e70eb45-1]. For probabilistic models, report distributional evaluations (e.g., PSNR over Monte Carlo samples) to reflect uncertainty [0dafcf0f-4].

Although PSNR and SSIM metrics are frequently used in the literature, they are not sufficient to emphasize the visual detail differences and quantitative performance in terms of PSNR and SSIM is not fully reliable in medical imaging [33]. Therefore, the visually captured details are presented along with quantitative performance in the evaluations. 3D U-NetR gives better results because it takes into account the correlation in the third dimension, but it also has some disadvantages such as high time for training, the limited number of filters, and patched training due to memory limitations. 

First of all, since the convolution blocks in the network are 3-dimensional, the number of parameters is approximately three times that of 2-dimensional networks. The high number of parameters causes the network's loss curve to settle with more iterations and require more time for training. Different experimental setups such as residual connection, the filter number, activation function selection, and different configurations of the dataset could not be prepared because the network requires a high time for training. 

Secondly, increasing the number of filters might have an exponential impact on performance compared to 2D convolutions. Although the highest number of possible filters is already preferred in experimental setups, the maximum number of available filters in 3D U-NetR is fewer than 2D U-Net due to memory limitations. 

Finally, the high memory consumption of 3D U-NetR obstructs the backpropagation of high-resolution human CT images. Hence, the real chest CT dataset is used by splitting 3D images into patches. Even though the patching operation eliminates the memory limitation, the intersection points of the patches show deformation on direct reconstruction. Thus, patches are designed to have common intersection parts which are equivalent to the half of receptive field of the network as explained in Section 5.2. Overall, the patched training, which is needed because of stricter memory limitations of 3D U-NetR, causes higher calculation time.

citations.title: Speech Denoising with Residual Attention U-Net
snippets:
In the development of audio signal processing technologies, various information such as text (speech recognition), speaker (speaker verification), and emotion (emotion recognition) can be extracted from speech signals. The performance of these technologies is degraded when the SNR is less than 20 dB (1,2) . For high-accuracy information extraction, audio devices such as headsets, which can input with high SNR, has been equipped. The equipped devices limit the use case. Therefore, speech denoising (3) (or speech enhancement) is required during preprocessing. Our goal is to develop monaural (single-channel) speech denoising technologies to improve under the real environment, which SNR is 5-10dB, to SNR 20dB or more. If this can be realized, audio devices without equipped, such as general-purpose microphones or conference microphones, can be used for audio information extraction. And it means that the scope of application of audio information extraction can be extended. 

As our research focuses on monaural speech denoising. A multi-channel recode such as microphone array (4) cannot be applied. Traditionally, Spectral subtraction (5) and Wiener filter (6) were popular algorithm that make noise reduction filter from its distribution and characteristic of the noise. Recently, a denoising method using a deep neural network (DNN) has been proposed (7,8) . 

When paying attention to features using speech denoising, typical speech denoising methods estimate background noise by using spectrogram features on the speech signals. The short-time Fourier transform (STFT) is used to convert speech signals to a spectrogram. The denoising operation has also been applied to the magnitude (9) and complex (10) components of a spectrogram. A disadvantage is that these approaches depend on many parameters (window size of STFT and overlap of audio frames) that affect the time and frequency resolution. Moreover, signal artifacts arise due to time aliasing when using the inverse STFT. 

To resolve this issue, end-to-end speech denoising methods that directly operate on raw waveforms have been proposed (11,12,13) . These methods need to deal with long dimensional data because speech signals contain high-density data samples.

citations.title: ADNAC: Audio Denoiser using Neural Audio Codec
snippets:
Noise reduction is a fundamental part of audio signal processing, substantially improving signal quality and intelligibility across domains like speech processing [1][2][3], music production and restoration [1], and bioacoustics analysis [2]. Even though traditional techniques, such as spectral subtraction and Wiener filtering, provide a foundational basis, they often fail with complex and nonstationary noise patterns. 

Recent advancements in deep learning, particularly with convolutional neural networks (CNNs) in encoder-decoder structures like the U-Net, have shown significant promise [3,4]. Previous works demonstrated that a simple U-Net architecture can effectively filter white and urban noise from musical signals but fails to address more complex degradations like reverberation and noise cancellation artifacts. These limitations highlight the need for more powerful models capable of understanding and regenerating audio with higher fidelity. This paper investigates a novel approach which goes beyond conventional discriminative models by adapting a generative neural audio codec for denoising. The goal was to leverage the Descript Audio Codec (DAC) [5], a model designed for high-fidelity audio compression and retrain it on a denoising objective. The core hypothesis is that the rich representations and generative capabilities of a neural codec can produce better denoising results, minimizing artifacts and preserving the natural aspects of the original music, more efficiently than a standard U-Net. This is especially true when a multi-objective loss function is used, and the training is performed on a comprehensive, purpose-built dataset.

citations.title: RadiantVisions: Illuminating Low-Light Imagery with a Multi-Scale Branch Network
snippets: Image denoising, aimed at reducing noise while preserving details, has evolved significantly within image processing. Over the past years, a myriad of image priors have been proposed to restore clarity to noisy images, including sparsity, low rank, and self-similarity. Notable methods based on image priors, such as BM3D [19] and WNNM [20], have achieved remarkable progress in the domain of image denoising. With the advent of deep learning, researchers have increasingly turned to leveraging deep neural networks for image denoising. For instance, DnCNN [21] employed a deep residual network and integrated batch normalization layers to accelerate the training process. In a different approach, CBDNet [22] addressed noise comprehensively throughout the imaging process, utilizing the U-net architecture along with a sub-network to estimate noise levels, thus enhancing denoising performance.

snippets:
Our neural-network-based denoising model accepts a single channel of audio signal and outputs the cleaned-up signal. Unlike some of the recent denoising methods that take as input audiovisual signals (i.e., both audio and video footage), our method can be applied in a wider range of scenarios (e.g., in cellular communication). We conducted extensive experiments, including ablation studies to show the efficacy of our network components and comparisons to several state-of-the-art denoising methods. We also evaluate our method under various signal-to-noise ratios-even under strong noise levels that are not tested against in previous methods. We show that, under a variety of denoising metrics, our method consistently outperforms those methods, including those that accept only audio input (like ours) and those that denoise based on audiovisual input. 

The pivotal role of silent intervals for speech denoising is further confirmed by a few key results. Even without supervising on silent interval detection, the ability to detect silent intervals naturally emerges in our network. Moreover, while our model is trained on English speech only, with no additional training it can be readily used to denoise speech in other languages (such as Chinese, Japanese, and Korean). Please refer to the supplementary materials for listening to our denoising results.

sections.title: # Limitations and open challenges
sections.text:
- Data and domain shift. Supervised denoisers depend on datasets that cover principal signal and noise morphologies; when clean/noisy morphologies are similar, performance can degrade [5e70eb45-4]. Transformers often require large datasets to generalize, limiting applicability to small data regimes [7edecbc6-1].
- Computational and memory footprint. Deep CNN denoisers scale in complexity and can be costly to deploy [0dafcf0f-3] , and 3D models face memory constraints, often requiring patch-based training and longer inference times [3f164f0d-3].
- Artifact control and inductive bias. Even strong CNNs can introduce artifacts; generative priors and multi-objective losses help but require careful design and data [6b1b953c-4]. Hybrid TF+time-domain pipelines reduce TF artifacts yet must balance parameters and sequence length [5e70eb45-4].
- Evaluation rigor. Standard scalar metrics may not capture perceptual or clinical relevance; integrating human-in-the-loop assessments is important [3f164f0d-3].

citations.title: Targeted Adversarial Denoising Autoencoders (TADA) for Neural Time Series Filtration
snippets: Developing effective time series filtration algorithms could help improve existing neural interfaces that rely on noisy time series data (Yadav et al., 2020;Linderman et al., 2008;Makeig et al., 2012). However, conventional neural time series filtration methods (canonical correlation analysis, or CCA; independent component analysis, or ICA, etc.) often fail to handle more complex single-channel time series denoising cases (Vergult et al., 2007;Chou et al., 2016;Vigario & Oja, 2008). This is typically true, for example, with EMG interference in EEG data, which is a primary source of noise for neural interfacing applications (Stergiadis et al., 2022;Zhang et al., 2021a). Machine learning (ML)-based approaches, have made recent strides in handling single-channel time series denoising scenarios (Luo & Mesgarani, 2019;Yin et al., 2023;Cui et al., 2024); MLbased time series filtration methods based on multilayer perceptrons (MLPs), convolutional neural networks (CNNs), recurrent neural networks (RNNs), and transformers have successively improved the state of the art (Zhang et al., 2021a;Cui et al., 2024;Yin et al., 2023). However, these published denoising approaches are compute-heavy, often involving large numbers of trainable parameters (and thus a large memory footprint) and long training times. These large compute footprints make deployment in real-time neural interfacing applications cumbersome (Justus et al., 2018;Cui et al., 2024;Yin et al., 2023;Buongiorno et al., 2021;Monga et al., 2021). Moreover, the inherent difficulties of EMG filtration continue to present challenges for deep learning (DL) models; complex patterns are harder to identify, so more exhaustive filtration is required to ensure a clean signal.

sections.title: # Quick start recipes (evidence-backed)
sections.text:
- Audio (speech, general): 
 - Spectrogram path: Train a DnCNN or similar CNN on noisy-to-clean spectrograms; predict noise and subtract; reconstruct with ISTFT [5e70eb45-0]. 
 - Time-domain path: Use a two-stage transformer encoder–decoder with masking; consider ablations on complexity and masking heads [6b1b953c-1]. 
 - Unsupervised single-clip: Adopt a deep network prior that fits the single clip partially to separate clean from noise [5e70eb45-2]. 
 - Artifact-prone cases: Leverage a retrained neural audio codec as the generative prior with multi-objective losses [6b1b953c-4].
- Images/2D:
 - Baseline: DnCNN with batch normalization for AWGN; CBDNet for noise-aware pipelines [0dafcf0f-0]. 
 - Supervised learning: U-Net variants generalize to many datasets and can supervise downstream reconstruction tasks [0dafcf0f-2]. 
 - Probabilistic/patch-based: Train with large patch corpora and Monte Carlo sampling; report PSNR/SSIM distributions [0dafcf0f-4].
- 3D/medical volumes:
 - Prefer 3D CNNs: Parallel residual 3D CNNs for MRI show higher PSNR/SSIM and lower entropy with faster runtime [3f164f0d-0]. 
 - CT reconstruction/denoising: 3D U-Net–style models outperform 2D and FBP; HRNet further improves RMSE/SSIM and detail recovery [3f164f0d-4]. 
 - Caveat: Expect higher training time and memory pressure; use patching and validate visually [3f164f0d-3].
- 1D time series:
 - Hybrid denoising+modeling: Preprocess with wavelet denoising, then fit LSTM/Transformer/CNN to the cleaned series [7edecbc6-3]. 
 - Robust sequence models: LSTM–Wavelet pipelines improve performance under noise in ICU prediction [7edecbc6-0] ; Transformers capture long-range dependencies but may need more data and computation [7edecbc6-2].

citations.title: Predicting distributions with Linearizing Belief Networks
snippets:
In this section, we evaluate the problem of training LBNs with multiple layers of non-deterministic variables on denoising full images. The state-of-the art method for denoising natural images is BM3D (Dabov et al., 2009). Neural methods (Burger et al., 2012) were state-of-the-art but they were surpassed by later versions of BM3D. BM3D is a non-parametric denoising algorithm that uses self-similarity between patches to average out the noise. While we can expect this method to work well for small noise distributions, it produces blurry images for high noise distributions. 

In order to scale to large images we use a convolutional architecture for the LBNs. In practice, this amounts to replacing the dot products by convolutions -both for the activations of the linear units and the gaters. We found that using 128 convolutional kernels of size 9 × 9 for the linear and gating units produced good results. The network has 4 convolutional hidden layers in total and 3 layer gating functions for LBNs. We do not use any spatial pooling because the loss of information would be detrimental to denoising. The output pixels have a scalar bias so as to not constrain the size of the images that can be generated. We extract 1M 64 × 64 image patches from Imagenet as our training set for highly corrupted images and 6M 29 × 29 patches otherwise. We use these large image patches instead of the full image to save computation time during training but the same model can be applied to large images at test time. The networks can take up to a week of computation time to train and so in the interest of the PSNR evaluation we set the number of Monte Carlo samples to K = 1. We evaluate the quality of the distribution with a model trained with K = 10.

citations.title: HAELT: A Hybrid Attentive Ensemble Learning Transformer Framework for High-Frequency Stock Price Forecasting
snippets:
Deep learning (DL) techniques have markedly advanced time series prediction capabilities. Recurrent Neural Networks (RNNs) and their more sophisticated variant, Long Short-Term Memory (LSTM) networks, have been instrumental in this progress [19,20]. LSTMs are particularly adept at modeling long-range temporal dependencies in sequential data, which has led to their successful application in financial forecasting [21]. However, LSTMs can be sensitive to noise and prone to overfitting, especially with volatile financial market data [12]. 

Transformer architectures, employing self-attention mechanisms to assign differential importance to various segments of an input sequence, have recently achieved state-of-the-art results in diverse sequence modeling tasks [22,23]. Transformers are proficient at capturing complex long-range dependencies and benefit from parallelizable computations, potentially accelerating training. Nevertheless, they often necessitate large training datasets for effective generalization and can be computationally demanding due to their complex architectures [24]. 

Convolutional Neural Networks (CNNs), initially developed for grid-like data such as images, have also been effectively applied to time series analysis. snippets:
Noise reduction is a fundamental part of audio signal processing, substantially improving signal quality and intelligibility across domains like speech processing [1][2][3], music production and restoration [1], and bioacoustics analysis [2]. Even though traditional techniques, such as spectral subtraction and Wiener filtering, provide a foundational basis, they often fail with complex and nonstationary noise patterns. 

Recent advancements in deep learning, particularly with convolutional neural networks (CNNs) in encoder-decoder structures like the U-Net, have shown significant promise [3,4]. Previous works demonstrated that a simple U-Net architecture can effectively filter white and urban noise from musical signals but fails to address more complex degradations like reverberation and noise cancellation artifacts. These limitations highlight the need for more powerful models capable of understanding and regenerating audio with higher fidelity. This paper investigates a novel approach which goes beyond conventional discriminative models by adapting a generative neural audio codec for denoising. The goal was to leverage the Descript Audio Codec (DAC) [5], a model designed for high-fidelity audio compression and retrain it on a denoising objective. The core hypothesis is that the rich representations and generative capabilities of a neural codec can produce better denoising results, minimizing artifacts and preserving the natural aspects of the original music, more efficiently than a standard U-Net. This is especially true when a multi-objective loss function is used, and the training is performed on a comprehensive, purpose-built dataset.

citations.title: A Real-Time Signal-Based Wavelet Long Short-Term Memory Method for Length-of-Stay Prediction for the Intensive Care Unit: Development and Evaluation Study
snippets:
The use of time series data for prediction has been a central focus in various domains, leading to the exploration and development of diverse models [27]. Traditional statistical models, particularly regression techniques, have historically played a crucial role in time series prediction [28]. These models leverage historical data patterns to make forecasts, providing a foundational framework for subsequent advancements in predictive modeling. However, their performance is constrained by their underlying hypothesis, as most datasets struggle to fulfill these assumptions. 

The emergence of neural networks has revolutionized time series prediction. Recurrent neural networks are specifically designed to capture sequential dependencies within data [29]. Recurrent neural networks excel in modeling temporal relationships, making them well-suited for time series forecasting tasks [30]. However, they may face challenges when dealing with long-term dependencies due to the vanishing gradient problem [31]. The introduction of the long short-term memory (LSTM) model addresses this issue by incorporating memory cells that can retain information over extended sequences [32]. LSTMs have shown remarkable success in capturing complex temporal dependencies, making them popular for time series prediction tasks. However, they are not immune to challenges, particularly when the data is affected by noise [33]. The transformer architecture, originally designed for natural language processing tasks, has also found applications in time series prediction [34]. However, a notable challenge lies in the substantial amount of data often required for effective training [35]. In addition, for task-specific small datasets, transformers have demonstrated less competitiveness compared with LSTMs, as evidenced by research in the medical field [36]. Therefore, it appears that LSTM remains the preferred choice, notwithstanding its susceptibility to noise in time series data. 

To address the susceptibility of LSTMs to noise, we propose using wavelet transform techniques as a preprocessing step and introduce the Wavelet-LSTM model. This approach aims to denoise time series data before feeding it into LSTM models, with the overarching goal of enhancing the robustness of LSTM models and improving their performance in the presence of noisy signals.

sections.title: # Closing perspective
sections.text: Neural network denoisers have become the workhorse for signal restoration across domains, driven by architectures that exploit local and global structure (CNNs, U-Net variants, Transformers, and generative priors) and trained with realistic noise models and multi-objective losses. In audio, spectrogram CNNs and end-to-end time-domain transformers consistently improve intelligibility and quality across SNRs [5e70eb45-0] , while in images, U-Net/CNN denoisers surpass classical nonlocal and sparse methods on standard benchmarks [0dafcf0f-0]. In 3D medical data, 3D CNNs preserve anatomy and outperform 2D methods [3f164f0d-0] , and in 1D time series, wavelet–LSTM–Transformer hybrids reduce interference before modeling dynamics [7edecbc6-3]. As models grow more capable, the key trade-offs remain data requirements, computational cost, artifact control, and evaluation fidelity—best addressed by combining strong architectures with careful losses, generative priors, and domain-specific validation. Deep CNNs deliver higher accuracy but with increased complexity [0dafcf0f-3] , and 3D and probabilistic approaches require balancing runtime and uncertainty estimation [3f164f0d-3]. Where possible, pair automatic metrics (PSNR/SSIM/SDR-family, task-specific errors) with human and domain expert assessments to ensure perceptual quality.

snippets:
Image denoising is one of the most critical low-level imaging tasks because noise is inherent to all image acquisition processes. As obtaining a noise-free image is an ill-posed problem, prevalent denoising techniques resort to making certain assumptions about the nature of noise. The most common approach in this regard is to model the noise as an additive Gaussian process. Denoising images corrupted with additive white Gaussian noise (AWGN) has been a center of attention for decades. Early efforts considered denoising as an averaging process [1], either in frequency or spatial domain. These were succeeded by the non-local class of methods [2] [3] which exploited the non-local similarity of patches within an image. BM3D [3] holds a pioneering status in such methods and is still competitive in challenging denoising tasks [4]. It remained the state-of-the-art method in AWGN denoising, until the advent of learning-based methods.

Discriminative learning-based denoising methods aim to learn a direct mapping from corrupted to clean images using annotated training samples. Artificial neural networks (ANNs) have become a standard choice for such problems and were shown in [5] to produce competitive denoising performance as compared to BM3D, given sufficient training examples and model complexity. Since then, most of the discriminative denoising methods make use of convolutional neural networks (CNNs), which are a special class of ANNs specialized for grid-structured data [6]. CNNs for image denoising is generally very deep [7], consisting of dozens of layers and a large number of trainable parameters generally over a million. The performance of CNN-based methods has been observed to be directly correlated with architectural complexity [8]. The enormous computational complexity is often neglected, especially since the performance of CNNs has been optimized quite well for specialized hardware devices such as GPUs and TPUs [9]. However, usage of such models is still expensive, and in many cases impractical, especially in the case of embedded devices that have limited computational resources. question: What is the difference between normalizing flows and vae?

sections.title: # Short Answer
sections.text:
- Normalizing flows are invertible, differentiable mappings from a simple latent space to the data space that enable exact likelihood evaluation via the change-of-variables formula, supporting both sampling and density estimation; training typically proceeds by maximum likelihood and relies on bijectors with tractable Jacobian determinants and simple inverses Normalizing flows are a class of generative models, which allow exact density estimation and fast sampling [73b954bd-0] Normalizing flows model the distribution of the data by transforming a base distribution via an invertible transformation; the base is often a standard Gaussian, and the likelihood is computed via the change-of-variables formula using the Jacobian determinant [73b954bd-2] All Normalizing Flows share invertibility and differentiability; RealNVP/NICE/MADE-like autoregressive flows provide tractable Jacobian determinants [73b954bd-1] Representative families include RealNVP, GLOW, and autoregressive transformations such as MAF/IAF [73b954bd-3] In normalizing flows, the function must be invertible with tractable inverse and Jacobian determinant [73b954bd-4]. 

- Variational autoencoders are latent-variable probabilistic models with a stochastic encoder and decoder; exact marginal likelihood is intractable, so training maximizes a lower bound (ELBO), yielding an approximate posterior and enabling structured representations, but without exact likelihood unless strong simplifying assumptions are made VAEs are latent variable models with stochastic mappings between data and latent space; the likelihood is intractable for complex decoders, so the evidence lower bound (ELBO) is optimized [3b98290e-0] A VAE implements probabilistic generative modeling with variational inference; the loss comprises a reconstruction term and a KL regularization term ensuring the encoder posterior is close to a standard Gaussian [3b98290e-1] The VAE defines a joint distribution over x and z; maximizing the marginal likelihood is intractable, so the ELBO is maximized, which regularizes the posterior to a prior and minimizes a reconstruction loss [3b98290e-2] The ELBO is maximized using an encoder-decoder; typical choices are conditional Gaussians, and the model is learned by optimizing this lower bound rather than the intractable evidence [3b98290e-4].

snippets:
A Variational Autoencoder is a deep generative model that implements a probabilistic model and variational Bayesian inference. Introduced by Kingma and Welling [2], a VAE model is an autoencoder, designed to stochastically encode the input data into a constrained multivariate latent space (encoding), and then to reconstruct it as accurately as possible (decoding). To turn the intractable posterior inference into a solvable problem, we use a parametric inference model q φ (z|x) which is also called an encoder. We optimize the variational parameters φ such that q φ (z|x) ∼ p θ (z|x). The VAE loss function is composed of a "reconstruction term" (to ensure the decoded data are close to the original data) and a "regularisation term". The goal of the regularisation term is to ensure that the distributions returned by the encoder are close to a standard normal distribution. That is expressed as the Kulback-Leibler divergence between the returned distribution and a standard Gaussian. Definition 1. Kulback-Leibler (KL) divergence [10,11]. For discrete probability distributions p and q, defined on the same probability space, the KL divergence from q to p is defined to be: 

Since the true posterior p θ (z|x) is intractable, we aim to approximate it with a Gaussian distribution q φ (z|x), in the KL divergence sense. It follows that: 

Definition 2. Evidence Lower Bound (ELBO): 

We note that the KL divergence is non-negative, thus maximizing the ELBO results with the minimization of the KL divergence between q φ (z|x) and the true posterior p θ (z|x). 

ELBO optimization is a well-known method that has been studied in depth, and is applicable in many models, especially in VAE [12]. Nevertheless, using the ELBO can give rise to some drawbacks. First, the ELBO is not always very tight, and maximizing the bound instead of the actual likelihood can lead to bias.

snippets:
Variational autoencoders (VAEs; Kingma and Welling, 2014;Rezende et al., 2014) have emerged as a popular choice for probabilistic generative modeling, a sub-field of unsupervised (deep) learning. A Variational Autoencoder is a deep generative model that implements a probabilistic model and variational Bayesian inference. Introduced by Kingma and Welling [2], a VAE model is an autoencoder, designed to stochastically encode the input data into a constrained multivariate latent space (encoding), and then to reconstruct it as accurately as possible (decoding). We optimize the variational parameters φ such that q φ (z|x) ∼ p θ (z|x). The VAE loss function is composed of a "reconstruction term" (to ensure the decoded data are close to the original data) and a "regularisation term". The goal of the regularisation term is to ensure that the distributions returned by the encoder are close to a standard normal distribution. That is expressed as the Kulback-Leibler divergence between the returned distribution and a standard Gaussian. Definition 1. Kulback-Leibler (KL) divergence [10,11]. For discrete probability distributions p and q, defined on the same probability space, the KL divergence from q to p is defined to be: 

Since the true posterior p θ (z|x) is intractable, we aim to approximate it with a Gaussian distribution q φ (z|x), in the KL divergence sense. It follows that: 

Definition 2. Evidence Lower Bound (ELBO): 

We note that the KL divergence is non-negative, thus maximizing the ELBO results with the minimization of the KL divergence between q φ (z|x) and the true posterior p θ (z|x).

First, the ELBO is not always very tight, and maximizing the bound instead of the actual likelihood can lead to bias.

sections.title: # Inference and Decoding
sections.text:
- Flows enable exact likelihood and typically deterministic transforms from latent to data; once trained, sampling is done by drawing from the base and applying the bijection, and decoding with a fixed network (e.g., RealNVP/MADE/Glow) is deterministic rather than stochastic Invertibility allows both forward sampling and inverse evaluation; the transformation is a neural network with constraints to ensure tractable determinants [73b954bd-2] RealNVP/GLOW/MAF/IAF exemplify architectures used to construct flexible bijections with tractable Jacobians [73b954bd-3] Autoregressive flows model P(X) as a product of conditionals with triangular Jacobians, enabling efficient computation [73b954bd-1] The function must be invertible with simple inverse and Jacobian determinant, which is used in practice to build sequences of such transformations [73b954bd-4].

- VAEs use a stochastic encoder to produce posterior samples z|x and pass them to a probabilistic decoder p(x|z), so both inference and generation are stochastic processes; the posterior p(z|x) is intractable and approximated by qφ(z|x), leading to variability in reconstructions and samples even with identical inputs and latent variables VAEs are latent variable models with stochastic mappings; the goal is to approximate the true posterior via an encoder, leading to stochastic decoding [3b98290e-0] An encoder-decoder is optimized to approximate pθ(z|x) with a Gaussian qφ(z|x), giving rise to stochastic encodings and decodings [3b98290e-1] Typical VAE implementations use conditional Gaussian encoder and decoder distributions, with optimization via ELBO rather than exact likelihood [3b98290e-4].

- Flow models compose invertible “bijectors” (e.g., RealNVP, NICE, autoregressive/MADE-like transforms, spline flows) that are easily invertible and have tractable Jacobian determinants, ensuring both efficient sampling and exact density computation RealNVP (Non-Volume Preserving) constructs bijectors with easily invertible transformations and tractable Jacobian determinants; alternatives include NICE and autoregressive flows with lower-triangular Jacobians [73b954bd-1] Common flow families include masked autoregressive flows and neural spline flows, all designed to satisfy invertibility and tractable determinant requirements [73b954bd-2] GLOW, RealNVP, MAF, and IAF are representative flow architectures [73b954bd-3] The invertibility and tractable inverse/determinant constraints shape the available transformations [73b954bd-4].

- VAEs factor the generative process into an encoder qφ(z|x) that maps data to a latent posterior and a decoder pθ(x|z) that maps latent variables to data; the encoder and decoder are typically implemented with deep neural networks and often assume Gaussian distributions for tractability VAEs define stochastic mappings between data and latent space with deep networks used for means/covariances, and intractable likelihood motivating ELBO optimization [3b98290e-0] The encoder approximates the posterior and the decoder reconstructs data; the KL regularization steers the encoder towards the prior [3b98290e-1] Typical VAEs assume conditional Gaussian encoder and decoder distributions [3b98290e-4].

citations.title: Variational Inference via Rényi Bound Optimization and Multiple-Source Adaptation
snippets:
A Variational Autoencoder is a deep generative model that implements a probabilistic model and variational Bayesian inference. Introduced by Kingma and Welling [2], a VAE model is an autoencoder, designed to stochastically encode the input data into a constrained multivariate latent space (encoding), and then to reconstruct it as accurately as possible (decoding). To turn the intractable posterior inference into a solvable problem, we use a parametric inference model q φ (z|x) which is also called an encoder. We optimize the variational parameters φ such that q φ (z|x) ∼ p θ (z|x). The VAE loss function is composed of a "reconstruction term" (to ensure the decoded data are close to the original data) and a "regularisation term". The goal of the regularisation term is to ensure that the distributions returned by the encoder are close to a standard normal distribution. That is expressed as the Kulback-Leibler divergence between the returned distribution and a standard Gaussian. Definition 1. Kulback-Leibler (KL) divergence [10,11]. For discrete probability distributions p and q, defined on the same probability space, the KL divergence from q to p is defined to be: 

Since the true posterior p θ (z|x) is intractable, we aim to approximate it with a Gaussian distribution q φ (z|x), in the KL divergence sense. It follows that: 

Definition 2. Evidence Lower Bound (ELBO): 

We note that the KL divergence is non-negative, thus maximizing the ELBO results with the minimization of the KL divergence between q φ (z|x) and the true posterior p θ (z|x). 

ELBO optimization is a well-known method that has been studied in depth, and is applicable in many models, especially in VAE [12]. Nevertheless, using the ELBO can give rise to some drawbacks. First, the ELBO is not always very tight, and maximizing the bound instead of the actual likelihood can lead to bias.
