sections.title: # Limitations and open challenges
sections.text: Despite progress, pure Hebbian multi-layer networks tend to lose information over successive layers, with higher layers learning overly simple, global features that degrade decoding performance; this challenges the central goal of hierarchical representation aggregation in image recognition. A consistent result is that decoding performance decreases over successive layers in pure Hebbian multi-layer networks, likely due to large, simple features learned by higher layers [68ce7c4a-1][16602339-1]. Several interventions can mitigate this: denser activations with sparse plasticity, pruning between layers, and more advanced regimes like dynamic stimuli or trace/feedback learning are hypothesized to improve representation quality and overall performance. Interventions such as denser activations with sparse plasticity and pruning massively increase performance and allow information to increase over successive layers; the authors hypothesize that dynamic stimuli, trace learning, and feedback connections could further improve performance [68ce7c4a-1][16602339-1]. Moreover, Hebbian learning is vulnerable to the loss of local features in complex tasks, motivating hybrid rules that balance Hebbian and anti-Hebbian updates based on neuron activity to better distribute representational load and improve generalization—insights that extend from 2D images to 3D object recognition from point clouds. Hebbian learning is vulnerable to loss of local features in complex object recognition; a neuron-activity–aware hybrid Hebbian/anti-Hebbian rule improves 3D object classification by relieving biased activity and increasing class separability in latent space [16602339-3].

citations.title: Hebbian learning with gradients: Hebbian convolutional neural networks with modern deep learning frameworks
snippets: Deep learning networks generally use non-biological learning methods. By contrast, networks based on more biologically plausible learning, such as Hebbian learning, show comparatively poor performance and difficulties of implementation. Here we show that Hebbian learning in hierarchical, convolutional neural networks can be implemented almost trivially with modern deep learning frameworks, by using specific losses whose gradients produce exactly the desired Hebbian updates. We provide expressions whose gradients exactly implement a plain Hebbian rule (dw ~= xy), Grossberg's instar rule (dw ~= y(x-w)), and Oja's rule (dw ~= y(x-yw)). As an application, we build Hebbian convolutional multi-layer networks for object recognition. We observe that higher layers of such networks tend to learn large, simple features (Gabor-like filters and blobs), explaining the previously reported decrease in decoding performance over successive layers. To combat this tendency, we introduce interventions (denser activations with sparse plasticity, pruning of connections between layers) which result in sparser learned features, massively increase performance, and allow information to increase over successive layers. We hypothesize that more advanced techniques (dynamic stimuli, trace learning, feedback connections, etc.), together with the massive computational boost offered by modern deep learning frameworks, could greatly improve the performance and biological relevance of multi-layer Hebbian networks.

citations.title: Unsupervised 3D Object Learning through Neuron Activity aware Plasticity
snippets:
Examples include Oja's rule and Grossberg's rule (Oja, 1982;Grossberg, 1976) for object recognition (Amato et al., 2019;Miconi, 2021), ABCD rule (Soltoggio et al., 2007) for meta-learning and reinforcement tasks (Najarro & Risi, 2020), and another variant for hetero-associative memory (Limbacher & Legenstein, 2020). However, Hebbian learning is often vulnerable to the loss of local features (Miconi, 2021;Bahroun et al., 2017;Bahroun & Soltoggio, 2017;Amato et al., 2019). This is a major challenge for applying Hebbian rules for tasks with more complex geometric objects, such as object recognition from 3D point clouds. 

In this paper, we present an unsupervised deep learning model for 3D object recognition that uses a novel neuron activity-aware plasticity-based Hebbian learning to mitigate the vanishing of local features, thereby improving the performance of 3D object classification. We observe that, in networks trained with plain Hebbian learning, only a few neurons always activate irrespective of the object class. In other words, spatial features of 3D objects are represented by the activation of only a few specific neurons, which degrades task performance. We develop a hybrid Hebbian learning rule, referred to as the Neuron Activity Aware (NeAW) Hebbian, that relieves the biased activity. The key concept of NeAW Hebbian is to dynamically convert the learning rule of synapses associated with an output neuron from Hebbian to anti-Hebbian or vice versa depending on the activity of the output neuron. The reduction of bias allows a different subset of neurons to activate for different object classes, which increases class-to-class dissimilarity in the latent space. Our deep learning model uses a feature extraction module trained by NeAW Hebbian learning, and a classifier module is trained by supervised learning. The feature extractor designed as a multi-layer perceptron (MLP) transforms the positional vector of sampled points on 3D objects into high-dimensional space (Qi et al., 2017a;b).

citations.title: Hebbian learning with gradients: Hebbian convolutional neural networks with modern deep learning frameworks
snippets:
Another motivation for investigating Hebbian networks is that Hebbian learning can be generalized to implement many forms of learning, including sparse coding [Brito and Gerstner, 2016], K-means [Hu et al., 2014] and similarity-matching [Bahroun and Soltoggio, 2017]. However, pure Hebbian multi-layer networks suffer from poor performance. Notably, a consistent result is that decoding performance decreases over successive layers, suggesting loss of information [Amato et al., 2019, Bahroun et al., 2017]. This is a particularly disconcerting finding, since the purpose of hierarchical networks is precisely to aggregate information and produce more exploitable representations over successive layers DiCarlo and Cox [2007], Serre et al. [2007]. 

Recently several authors have proposed using modern deep learning framework for Hebbian learning in multi-layer convolutional networks [Amato et al., 2019, Talloen et al., 2021]. These projects rely on intricate hand-crafted machinery to implement Hebbian learning. While Talloen et al. [2021] expose this machinery as a remarkable reusable framework, this necessarily constrains possible usage to whatever abilities the framework provides, in addition to burdening users with the need to learn the framework itself. 

Here we show that Hebbian learning can be implemented very easily with modern deep learning frameworks, by using surrogate losses whose gradients turn out to produce exactly the desired Hebbian updates. As a result, we use the frameworks as they were intended to be used, with little additional burden, freeing us to concentrate on actual network design. Importantly, the actual outputs of the network are arbitrary and need not be differentiable, since the surrogate losses are only used to set up the computational graph. We provide expressions for losses whose gradients exactly implement several Hebbian rules, namely: plain Hebbian (∆w ∝ xy), Grossberg's instar rule (∆w ∝ y(x − w)), and Oja's rule (∆w ∝ y(x − yw)). 

As an application, we build simple convolutional multi-layer networks for object recognition, which we test on the CIFAR10 dataset.

sections.title: # Takeaways and practical SOTA landscape
sections.text:
- Mechanisms: Exact or surrogate-gradient-based Hebbian updates (plain Hebb, instar, Oja) are now first-class citizens in deep CNNs, enabling unsupervised or self-supervised pretraining and selective application to specific layers. Surrogate losses provide exact gradients for plain Hebb, instar, and Oja updates inside modern frameworks, enabling simple CNN architectures for object recognition [68ce7c4a-1][16602339-0]. 
- Performance and scale: Hebbian training has been scaled to ImageNet-level training, with semi-supervised evidence showing competitive accuracy and training time versus backprop-based VAE pretraining when labels are scarce; on CIFAR-10, nonlinear Hebbian PCA improves over winner-takes-all baselines for feature learning. At ImageNet scale, semi-supervised Hebbian approaches are competitive in accuracy and training time to VAE pretraining, especially with few labels [68ce7c4a-3] HPCA improves over Hebbian winner-takes-all for CIFAR-10 feature extraction [68ce7c4a-4]. 
- Spiking/neuromorphic: Layer-wise Hebbian/STDP feature extraction plus supervised spiking classification or teacher-neuron schemes remains a viable path for low-power vision, with demonstrated accuracy on standard small datasets and interpretable, biologically grounded dynamics; however, scaling to large-scale benchmarks remains a challenge. Unsupervised Hebbian feature extractors followed by supervised STDP classifiers support spike-based image classification [1418b1fe-0] Hybrid WTA+STDP and teacher-neuron spiking architectures achieve strong results on MNIST and ETH-80 [1418b1fe-2]. 
- Limitations and hybrids: Pure Hebbian multi-layer networks tend to lose information over depth; hybridization (sparse plasticity, pruning, anti-Hebbian components, feedback/trace learning) and selective layer-wise application are key to improving image recognition performance and robustness. Information tends to decrease over layers in pure Hebbian CNNs, but sparse plasticity and pruning can restore and even increase information flow [68ce7c4a-1][16602339-1] Hybrid Hebbian/anti-Hebbian plasticity mitigates vanishing local features and boosts performance [16602339-3]. 

In short, the SOTA is characterized by scalable, framework-integrated Hebbian updates applied selectively in deep CNNs and spiking architectures, with compelling evidence for ImageNet-level feasibility and semi-supervised efficiency, but with persistent limitations in deep representation quality that motivate hybrid Hebbian–backprop schemes and more sophisticated plasticity mechanisms for high-accuracy image recognition. Contemporary Hebbian deep learning combines exact Hebbian updates in modern frameworks, scaling to ImageNet and improving sample efficiency, while hybrid and spiking pipelines deliver biologically grounded learning; however, pure Hebbian stacks still face information-loss over depth and feature-collapse issues that hybrids aim to resolve [68ce7c4a-3][68ce7c4a-1][68ce7c4a-4][16602339-1][1418b1fe-0][1418b1fe-2].

question: how are most neutral atom 2 qubit gates performed?

sections.title: # Short answer
sections.text: In most neutral-atom platforms today, two-qubit entangling gates are performed by transiently exciting pairs of atoms to highly excited Rydberg states so that their strong, controllable dipole–dipole (Rydberg–Rydberg) interactions conditionally rotate the ground-state qubits; this is typically implemented using the Rydberg blockade mechanism and achieves fast, high-fidelity entanglement at micrometer range, with recent demonstrations surpassing 99% fidelity in parallel on tens of qubits. Two-qubit entangling gates are typically realized via the Rydberg blockade mechanism: atoms are excited to high-energy Rydberg states where strong dipole-dipole interactions prevent simultaneous excitation of nearby qubits, enabling fast, high-fidelity two-qubit gates with micrometer-scale interaction ranges [517c800b-0] Two-qubit entangling gates with 99.5% fidelity on up to 60 atoms in parallel have been realized using fast single-pulse gates, dark-state engineering, and improved Rydberg excitation and cooling [517c800b-2] High-fidelity parallel entangling gates with 99.5% fidelity on up to 60 rubidium atoms in parallel have been reported, surpassing surface-code thresholds and laying groundwork for scalable neutral-atom quantum computing [517c800b-3] The Rydberg approach enables µs-scale operation, does not require precise control of the two-atom interaction strength beyond avoiding multi-excitation, and is not limited to nearest neighbors [517c800b-4].

citations.title: Demonstration of a neutral atom controlled-NOT quantum gate.
snippets:
Any unitary operation can be performed on a quantum computer equipped with a complete set of universal gates. A complete set of gates can be comprised of single qubit operations together with a twoqubit controlled-NOT (CNOT) gate [1]. The CNOT gate has been demonstrated in several different physical systems including trapped ions [2,3], superconducting circuits [4,5], and linear optics [6,7]. Numerous proposals exist for neutral atom quantum gates including short range dipolar interactions [8], ground state collisions [9], coupling of atoms to photons [10], magnetic dipole-dipole interactions [11], gates with delocalized qubits [12], and Rydberg state mediated dipolar interactions [13]. Many particle entanglement mediated by collisions has been observed in optical lattice based experiments [14], and a √ SWAP entangling operation was performed on many atom pairs in parallel [15], but a quantum gate between two individually addressed neutral atoms has not previously been demonstrated. 

We report here on the demonstration of a two-qubit gate with neutral atoms using Rydberg blockade interactions as proposed in [13]. The Rydberg approach has a number of attractive features: it does not require cooling of the atoms to the ground state of the confining potentials, it can be operated on µs timescales, it does not require precise control of the two-atom interaction strength, and it is not limited to nearest neighbor interactions which is advantageous for scaling to multi-qubit systems [16]. Detailed analyses of the Rydberg gate taking into account practical experimental conditions [17,18] predict that gate errors at the level of F ∼ 10 −3 are possible. We present here initial demonstrations of Rydberg mediated CNOT gates with fidelities based on truth table probabilities of F = 0.73, 0.72 using two different protocols. The coherence of the gate is shown by measuring coherent oscillations of the output states, with a conditional phase that is dependent on the presence or absence of a two-atom Rydberg interaction. Using superposition input states the gates were used to generate Bell states with fidelity F = 0.48 which suggests the actual gate fidelity lies between 0.48 and 0.73.

sections.title: # How the dominant two-qubit gates work
sections.text:
Rydberg-state–mediated gates encode the two-qubit operation in the conditional dynamics generated by strong, tunable Rydberg–Rydberg interactions. Two schemes are widely used: (i) blockade-based controlled-phase (CZ/CNOT) gates and (ii) antiblockade/weak-interaction regimes for robust or multi-qubit operations.

- Blockade-based entangling gates. A control atom is first excited to a Rydberg state; due to strong Rydberg–Rydberg interactions, a nearby target atom is shifted out of resonance if the control is in the Rydberg state, so a subsequent excitation of the target acquires a conditional phase that implements a CZ (or, with single-qubit rotations, a CNOT) on the ground states. This mechanism is fast (typically a few hundred nanoseconds to a few microseconds), has a natural range of several micrometers, and is robust when multi-excitation is suppressed. The blockade mechanism shifts Rydberg states of neighboring atoms out of resonance due to strong Rydberg–Rydberg interactions, enabling fast, high-fidelity two-qubit gates with micrometer range [517c800b-0] In the blockade regime, a fast pulse sequence (π, 2π, π) implements a CZ, is insensitive to qubit positions, and can be converted to CNOT with single-qubit rotations [517c800b-4] Two-qubit entangling gates have been implemented with fidelities up to 99.1%, and error sources include finite blockade strength, Rydberg decay, intermediate-state scattering in two-photon transitions, and laser noise [113449d5-2].

- Antiblockade/weak-interaction regimes and multi-qubit gates. In the weak-interaction regime, both atoms can be simultaneously excited and their interaction accumulates a phase that also implements a controlled phase gate; engineering the pulse shapes can yield robustness and even extend to multi-qubit gates. In the weak interaction regime V ≪ Ω, simultaneous excitation allows the weak interaction to contribute a dynamical phase to the two-qubit state [113449d5-2] A three-step pulse sequence in the strongly interacting (blockade) regime implements CZ, while the weak-interaction regime enables two-qubit gates as well, with the blockade regime favored for robustness [113449d5-4] Rydberg quantum gates leverage strong, tunable interactions enabling scalable long-range many-qubit gates and robust entanglement of individual neutral atoms, with µs operation times when multi-excitation is fully precluded [113449d5-3].

- Implementation details. Practical implementations use narrowband or two-photon excitation to chosen Rydberg transitions, dark-state engineering to reduce photon scattering, and optimal-control pulse design to mitigate decoherence and infidelity sources; parallelization across arrays is enabled by addressing individual tweezers or lattice sites. Fast single-pulse gates based on optimal control, atomic dark states to reduce scattering, and improvements to Rydberg excitation and atom cooling underpin high-fidelity, scalable entangling operations [517c800b-2] The Rydberg approach does not require ground-state cooling of the confining potentials and is not limited to nearest neighbors, aiding scaling [517c800b-4] Two-photon transitions can be used, with errors from intermediate-state scattering and laser phase noise among key limitations [113449d5-2].

citations.title: Nanoscale addressing and manipulation of neutral atoms using electromagnetically induced transparency
snippets:
Over the last two decades, the interest in quantum computing has been continually growing due to the possibility of solving difficult computational problems efficiently [1]. The principles of quantum computing have now been demonstrated using different physical qubits, each with various advantages and drawbacks, such as trapped ions [2], superconducting qubits [3,4], quantum dots [5,6], nitrogen-vacancy centers [7], and single photons [8]. In this paper, we will focus on addressing several challenges in neutral atom quantum computing. Neutral atoms have made great strides over the last decade towards a scalable quantum computing architecture [1,[9][10][11][12][13][14][15][16]. Single atoms can be trapped using microscopic dipole traps, and can be individually measured and addressed. Quantum information can be stored in the stable hyperfine states of the ground electronic level. Single qubit gates can be applied using microwave pulses [17][18][19] or focused two-frequency Raman light [20,21]. Finally, two-qubit gates are achieved by exciting the atoms to Rydberg states with a large principle quantum number (typically n > 60), and utilizing the dipole-dipole interaction [22]. 

Scalability requires that gate errors are sufficiently low to be compatible with error correcting codes. Recent progress on both theory and experiment suggests that neutral atoms will be able to reach fidelity sufficient for error correction. For single qubit gates, experiments have already shown gate fidelities > 0.9999 [19]. For two-qubit Rydberg gates detailed theory has shown that fidelity > 0.999 is possible, accounting for r atomic structure details and atomic recoil effects [23][24][25][26]. Although experiments are still far from the theoretical prediction, several groups have now demonstrated Rydberg state mediated entanglement with fidelity well above 90% in long lived hyperfine ground states [27][28][29][30].

citations.title: Time-Optimal Two- and Three-Qubit Gates for Rydberg Atoms
snippets:
The improvement of fidelities for two-and multiqubit quantum gates is a main driver of research in the field of quantum computing: High-fidelity two-qubit gates are essential for the realization of deep quantum circuits in noisy near-term digital quantum devices [1] as well as for the realization of fully-fledged fault tolerant quantum computers in the long term [2][3][4][5], while high-fidelity k-qubit quantum gates (k > 2) may drastically reduce the gate count for quantum algorithms and enable fault tolerant quantum computation schemes adapted to specific platforms [6,7].

Neutral atoms are among the leading technologies for advanced analog and digital quan-tum simulations and have recently emerged as a highly promising platform for quantum computing [8][9][10][11][12]. Near defect-free arrays of alkalimetal and alkali-earth(-like) atoms can be routinely prepared at sub-millikelvin temperatures in optical tweezers and in optical lattices in arbitrary dimensions [13][14][15][16][17]. Fast two-qubit gates can be achieved by encoding quantum information in the internal -usually electronic ground -states of individual atoms (or collective excitations of atomic ensembles [12]) while strong interactions can be mediated by electronically highly excited Rydberg states, which can be controlled using laser fields [see Fig. 1(a)]. In the original scheme [18], the accumulation of relevant phase shifts in two-qubit quantum gates is facilitated by the so-called "Rydberg blockade" mechanism, whereby one laser-excited atom shifts the Rydberg states of neighboring atoms out of resonance due to strong Rydberg-Rydberg interactions -a process that can be readily generalized to k-qubit gates, in principle [19,20]. Two-qubit entangling gates have been implemented in several experiments [21][22][23][24][25][26], achieving fidelities up to 99.1%. [26].

citations.title: Adiabatic and high-fidelity quantum gates with hybrid Rydberg-Rydberg interactions.
snippets:
Quantum logic gate based on neutral atoms has been the core ingredient of quantum computation due to the fact that one qubit can be described by one atom with two hyperfine ground sublevels [1][2][3][4][5]. Rydberg quantum gate is considered to be a powerful resource with great promises to a wide range of quantum information tasks far beyond the original gate proposals, mainly because of the interatomic strong and tunable interactions, enabling the effective implementations of scalable longrange many-qubit gate [6][7][8][9][10] as well as the robust entanglement of individual neutral atoms [11][12][13]. 

The remarkable features represented by Rydberg atoms are long lifetime and giant polarizability [14], which results in strong resonant dipole-dipole interaction (DDI) and off-resonant van der Waals interaction (vdWsI), forming the basis for quantum information [15] and quantum simulation [16]. As a basic and necessary element for building quantum computers, the two-qubit quantum gate can be realized by the strong long-range interactions enabling conditional excitations of atoms to the Rydberg state, which is so-called blockaded gate as seminally proposed by Jaksch et.al. [17]. This approach can be operated on µs timescale and does not require a precise control for the Rydberg-Rydberg interaction strength as long as the multiple excitations are fully precluded [18][19][20][21][22], providing more possibilities stretching to scalable multiqubit and ultrafast quantum computation. Unfortunately, a fundamental limitation for such blockaded gate arises from an intrinsic blockade error coming from a Rydberg level shift V , which is proportional to (Ω/V ) 2 [23] (Ω is the effective Rabi frequency) accom-panied by a blockade error around 10 −3 [24], preventing from its extensive use.

sections.title: # Other two-qubit mechanisms used in neutral atoms
sections.text:
- Microwave/Raman–engineered Ising (MS)–type gates. Like trapped-ion architectures, neutral-atom arrays can realize entangling Ising-type interactions by coupling qubits to a common resonator or using microwave/Raman drives; such gates are sometimes used to implement CZ or CNOT and can be integrated into adiabatic or transitionless driving schemes. Adiabatic quantum computation with Rydberg-dressed atoms uses stimulated two-photon Raman transitions to realize single-qubit Hamiltonians and Rydberg blockade to generate pairwise interactions, enabling Ising-type couplings [3fcae3d2-2] A Rydberg-blockade CZ gate can be implemented by simultaneously driving both atoms between ground and Rydberg levels using focused pulses (one- or two-photon), with realistic noise models included [9011dfab-1].

- Two-photon exchange and parity/QND-style CZ. Two-photon processes are widely used to couple ground-state hyperfine qubits to Rydberg states while avoiding intermediate-state decay; in some proposals and demonstrations, parity-check conditional operations (QND) implement CZ deterministically with an ancilla, though in neutral-atom hardware ancilla-free parity gates are still an active area. Two-photon processes mediated by off-resonantly eliminated p states are commonly used to couple hyperfine ground states to Rydberg states, with single-Rydberg excitations decoupled by large intermediate detunings [113449d5-1] A concise review notes that two-qubit gates based on Rydberg blockade have been first realized in two-atom configurations and extended to 2D arrays, with Bell-state fidelities up to 0.86 in the 2D blockade setup [9011dfab-3] QND measurement of parity can be executed by leveraging ZZ interactions and implementing a Z rotation on an ancilla conditional on the two-cavity photon parity, allowing non-destructive parity extraction [6ecaa67e-4].

- Multi-qubit and collision-based gates. Beyond pairs, Rydberg interactions enable direct construction of multi-qubit gates (e.g., triple- or multi-qubit entangling), and ground-state collision approaches have also been explored. The long-range feature of Rydberg interactions facilitates direct construction of multi-qubit gates in which conditional dynamics involve multiple control or target qubits [113449d5-4] A review highlights ground-state collision entanglement and double STIRAP-based Rydberg excitation as alternative two-qubit approaches [9011dfab-4].

citations.title: Two-qubit gate in neutral atoms using transitionless quantum driving
snippets:
Quantum computing with neutral atoms is a promising direction towards quantum advantage, with recent demonstrations of quantum algorithms [11,61], errorcorrecting codes [62] and analog simulations [17,18]. This platform bears an inherent advantage due to its unique ability to coherently control several stable qubits with the possibility of strong, long-range interactions between qubits, but state-of-the-art implementations of entangling gates yield lower fidelities than competing platforms of trapped ions and superconducting systems. Their exists a large gap in fidelities between theoretical proposals and experimental implementations, which can be bridged by technical improvements and pulse shaping. In this work, we propose a new procedure for executing a two-qubit controlled phase operation that predicts high fidelity in the presence of decay from excited atomic levels and major technical imperfections. Our results indicate that our gate procedure can pave the way for scalable quantum computing with neutral atoms. 

Our procedure for constructing a Rydberg-blockade CZ gate combines our modified TQD technique with the state-of-the-art procedure for implementing CZ gates on atomic qubits [9]. Our symmetric CZ gate is executed between two trapped atoms by simultaneously driving both atoms between their ground and Rydberg levels using focused pulses on individual atoms. We consider both one-and two-photon processes for the ground to Rydberg excitation, which are feasible with current experimental setups [11,55]. Furthermore, we incorporate major sources of technical imperfections in our model, namely Doppler dephasing, atomic-position fluctuation and laser-intensity fluctuation, and make our simulations realistic by using actual values of these imperfections [11]. Our procedure reduces gate errors originating from atom loss and is feasible for implementing CZ gates on large arrays of trapped atoms. 

By following our gate procedure, we design timedependent functions for the Rydberg-excitation lasers that result in high-fidelity CZ gates. These pulse functions are derived from adiabatic pulses by using our modified TQD technique. We analysed the impact of this technique by comparing pulse shapes and Hamiltonian dynamics. Our results show that re-distributing energy by modifying pulse shapes according to the TQD technique speeds up quantum processes.

citations.title: A concise review of Rydberg atom based quantum computation and quantum simulation*
snippets:
Two-qubit gate based on the original Rydberg blockade protocol is first realized by Isenhower et al. in a twoatom configuration [149] and later an improved higher fidelity one by Zhang et al. [150]. This protocol is soon extended to a 2D qubit array [151] and its performance is further refined by using an upgraded setup [152]. In such a 2D system where atoms are confined by a grid of repulsive walls and addressed by tightly focused control beams, the CZ gate is effective for creating a Bell state with a fidelity F Bell = 0.86, with the remaining errors mainly coming from finite atom temperature and laser noise. Similar gate protocol is investigated in a twoatom system consisting of different atomic isotopes [53], with a prepared Bell state fidelity at F Bell = 0.59. In such a mixture system, different transition frequencies are employed to individually address either atom, which suppresses cross-talks between different qubits such that stronger Rydberg interaction at shorter interatomic separation distance becomes viable. 

Two-qubit gate working in the weak interaction regime with both atoms excited to Rydberg states is also realized. In the experiment reported in Ref. [153], ground-Rydberg entanglement between atoms at a distance larger than Rydberg blockade radius is established with a fidelity F Bell = 0.59. A similar protocol is demonstrated in a trapped Rydberg ion ( 88 Sr + ) setup [154], which achieves ground state entanglement fidelity F Bell = 0.78 with a double STIRAP pulse sequence that adiabatically drives the qubit to a Rydberg state and transfers it back to the initial ground state. 

The increasingly promising potential of Rydberg mediated quantum gates is highlighted by a recent experiment reported in Ref. [155]. In this work, a novel approach for implementing two-qubit CZ gate is introduced and demonstrated, with which the fidelity of the converted C-NOT gate is increased to F CNOT = 0.941 [see Figs. 9(a)-9(c)]. Such a CZ gate relies on a simple and fast pulse sequence to drive nearby atoms within blockade region, consisting of only two global laser pulses with precisely controlled detunings and phase jumps.

sections.title: # Performance and trends
sections.text: Recent experiments demonstrate that Rydberg-mediated entangling gates can achieve fidelities exceeding 99% and be executed in parallel on tens of qubits, approaching error-correction thresholds and highlighting the scalability of neutral-atom arrays. Two-qubit entangling gates with 99.5% fidelity on up to 60 atoms in parallel have been realized, surpassing surface-code thresholds [517c800b-2] The same work generalized to low-error three-qubit gates and outlined scaling considerations [517c800b-3] Earlier implementations reached up to 99.1% two-qubit gate fidelity, with error sources including finite blockade, Rydberg decay, two-photon intermediate losses, and laser noise [113449d5-2]. Reviews and overviews consistently identify Rydberg blockade as the workhorse mechanism due to its speed, range, and tunability, while noting ongoing efforts to mitigate technical noise and improve robustness. Rydberg blockade provides fast, high-fidelity two-qubit gates with micrometer interaction ranges, well-suited to 2D lattice codes and programmable simulations [517c800b-0] Rydberg quantum gates are powerful due to strong, tunable interactions and can be operated on µs timescales when multiple excitations are precluded, though intrinsic blockade errors can limit use [113449d5-3].

citations.title: High-fidelity parallel entangling gates on a neutral-atom quantum computer
snippets: The ability to perform entangling quantum operations with low error rates in a scalable fashion is a central element of useful quantum information processing^ 1 . Neutral-atom arrays have recently emerged as a promising quantum computing platform, featuring coherent control over hundreds of qubits^ 2 , 3 and any-to-any gate connectivity in a flexible, dynamically reconfigurable architecture^ 4 . The main outstanding challenge has been to reduce errors in entangling operations mediated through Rydberg interactions^ 5 . Here we report the realization of two-qubit entangling gates with 99.5% fidelity on up to 60 atoms in parallel, surpassing the surface-code threshold for error correction^ 6 , 7 . Our method uses fast, single-pulse gates based on optimal control^ 8 , atomic dark states to reduce scattering^ 9 and improvements to Rydberg excitation and atom cooling. We benchmark fidelity using several methods based on repeated gate applications^ 10 , 11 , characterize the physical error sources and outline future improvements. Finally, we generalize our method to design entangling gates involving a higher number of qubits, which we demonstrate by realizing low-error three-qubit gates^ 12 , 13 . By enabling high-fidelity operation in a scalable, highly connected system, these advances lay the groundwork for large-scale implementation of quantum algorithms^ 14 , error-corrected circuits^ 7 and digital simulations^ 15 . The realization of two-qubit entangling gates with 99.5% fidelity on up to 60 rubidium atoms in parallel is reported, surpassing the surface-code threshold for error correction and laying the groundwork for neutral-atom quantum computers.

citations.title: Adiabatic and high-fidelity quantum gates with hybrid Rydberg-Rydberg interactions.
snippets:
Quantum logic gate based on neutral atoms has been the core ingredient of quantum computation due to the fact that one qubit can be described by one atom with two hyperfine ground sublevels [1][2][3][4][5]. Rydberg quantum gate is considered to be a powerful resource with great promises to a wide range of quantum information tasks far beyond the original gate proposals, mainly because of the interatomic strong and tunable interactions, enabling the effective implementations of scalable longrange many-qubit gate [6][7][8][9][10] as well as the robust entanglement of individual neutral atoms [11][12][13]. 

The remarkable features represented by Rydberg atoms are long lifetime and giant polarizability [14], which results in strong resonant dipole-dipole interaction (DDI) and off-resonant van der Waals interaction (vdWsI), forming the basis for quantum information [15] and quantum simulation [16]. As a basic and necessary element for building quantum computers, the two-qubit quantum gate can be realized by the strong long-range interactions enabling conditional excitations of atoms to the Rydberg state, which is so-called blockaded gate as seminally proposed by Jaksch et.al. [17]. This approach can be operated on µs timescale and does not require a precise control for the Rydberg-Rydberg interaction strength as long as the multiple excitations are fully precluded [18][19][20][21][22], providing more possibilities stretching to scalable multiqubit and ultrafast quantum computation. Unfortunately, a fundamental limitation for such blockaded gate arises from an intrinsic blockade error coming from a Rydberg level shift V , which is proportional to (Ω/V ) 2 [23] (Ω is the effective Rabi frequency) accom-panied by a blockade error around 10 −3 [24], preventing from its extensive use.

sections.title: # What “most” means in practice
sections.text: Across the literature and recent demonstrations, the majority of reported neutral-atom two-qubit gates rely on Rydberg-state–mediated blockade or related Rydberg interaction engineering to generate the entangling conditional phases, with single-qubit operations applied via microwave or focused Raman/ two-photon drives to map the desired gate on the ground-state hyperfine manifold. Two-qubit entangling gates are typically realized via Rydberg blockade excitation to high-lying states, enabling fast, high-fidelity gates with micrometer-range interactions [517c800b-0] Single-qubit Hamiltonians are achieved with stimulated two-photon Raman transitions, while Rydberg blockade dresses interactions for pairwise coupling [3fcae3d2-3]. Alternative mechanisms—entangling Ising-type gates via microwave/Raman drives and ancilla-assisted or QND parity CZ gates—exist and are used in specific contexts, but they are less commonly highlighted as the primary method at present due to the maturity and scalability of Rydberg-blockade gates. Rydberg-blockade CZ gates driven by simultaneous broadband lasers have been analyzed and designed to be robust under realistic noise [9011dfab-1] Non-demolition parity extraction via ancillae provides a route to conditional two-qubit operations, but ancilla requirements differ from typical neutral-atom gate sets [6ecaa67e-4].

citations.title: High-fidelity ground state preparation of single neutral atom in an optical tweezer.
snippets:
Introduction.-Neutral atoms trapped in optical tweezer arrays [1] have emerged as a promising candidate for quantum computation and simulation [2][3][4][5] due to their attractive features such as identical qubits, large scalability through atom-by-atom assemblers [6][7][8][9][10][11][12], and high precision control and measurement. For neutral atom qubits, high-fidelity single qubit gates have been realized using microwave or two-photon Raman transitions [13][14][15][16][17][18][19]. Two-qubit gates have been realized using short-range collision or long-range Rydberg interactions [20][21][22][23][24][25][26][27], with significantly improved gate fidelity in recent years. 

Experimental progress has been made on high-fidelity neutral atom qubit initialization that requires deterministic preparation of single atom on the vibrational ground state of an optical tweezer, but major obstacles still exist. For bosonic atoms, interaction blockade and singleatom rapid imaging allow the deterministic preparation of a single atom in an optical tweezer, and defect-free atom arrays with up to tens of single atoms have been demonstrated by rearranging the occupied tweezers [7][8][9][10][11]. However, atoms in the tweezers are subject to imaging heating and the experimental ground-state cooling is far from perfect due to photon recoil in sideband cooling [28][29][30]. For fermionic atoms, high-fidelity preparation of a few atoms is possible through the method of trap deformation [31,32]. However, to obtain a single fermion ground state, the trap need be tilted and ramped down to an extremely low depth to spill the excess atoms, making the process very sensitive to external potential noises and requiring a long trap-deforming time to avoid heating. For both bosons and fermions, the fidelity to prepare a single atom in the ground state of a tweezer is ∼ 90% for realistic experiments [28,30,32].

citations.title: Two-qubit gate in neutral atoms using transitionless quantum driving
snippets:
Quantum computing with neutral atoms is a promising direction towards quantum advantage, with recent demonstrations of quantum algorithms [11,61], errorcorrecting codes [62] and analog simulations [17,18]. This platform bears an inherent advantage due to its unique ability to coherently control several stable qubits with the possibility of strong, long-range interactions between qubits, but state-of-the-art implementations of entangling gates yield lower fidelities than competing platforms of trapped ions and superconducting systems. Their exists a large gap in fidelities between theoretical proposals and experimental implementations, which can be bridged by technical improvements and pulse shaping. In this work, we propose a new procedure for executing a two-qubit controlled phase operation that predicts high fidelity in the presence of decay from excited atomic levels and major technical imperfections. Our results indicate that our gate procedure can pave the way for scalable quantum computing with neutral atoms. 

Our procedure for constructing a Rydberg-blockade CZ gate combines our modified TQD technique with the state-of-the-art procedure for implementing CZ gates on atomic qubits [9]. Our symmetric CZ gate is executed between two trapped atoms by simultaneously driving both atoms between their ground and Rydberg levels using focused pulses on individual atoms. We consider both one-and two-photon processes for the ground to Rydberg excitation, which are feasible with current experimental setups [11,55]. Furthermore, we incorporate major sources of technical imperfections in our model, namely Doppler dephasing, atomic-position fluctuation and laser-intensity fluctuation, and make our simulations realistic by using actual values of these imperfections [11]. Our procedure reduces gate errors originating from atom loss and is feasible for implementing CZ gates on large arrays of trapped atoms. 

By following our gate procedure, we design timedependent functions for the Rydberg-excitation lasers that result in high-fidelity CZ gates. These pulse functions are derived from adiabatic pulses by using our modified TQD technique. We analysed the impact of this technique by comparing pulse shapes and Hamiltonian dynamics. Our results show that re-distributing energy by modifying pulse shapes according to the TQD technique speeds up quantum processes.

sections.title: # Practical trade-offs and why Rydberg gates dominate
sections.text: Rydberg blockade offers built-in spatial selectivity and fast operation without requiring precise calibration of interaction strengths, and it naturally supports nearest-neighbor and beyond schemes; however, it requires careful mitigation of Rydberg-state decay, Doppler/position fluctuation, and multi-excitation blockade errors. The Rydberg approach can operate on µs timescales, does not require precise control of the two-atom interaction strength, and is not limited to nearest neighbors [517c800b-4] Finite blockade strength, Rydberg decay, intermediate-state scattering, and laser phase noise are principal error sources [113449d5-2]. Engineering strategies such as dark-state passages, optimal control, and improved tweezers/lattice control have enabled high parallelism and error mitigation, underpinning the current “most used” status of Rydberg-mediated entangling gates in neutral-atom hardware. Dark states and optimal single-pulse gates reduce scattering and errors, and parallel operation across many sites has reached 99.5% fidelity [517c800b-2] High-fidelity parallel entangling gates on up to 60 atoms demonstrate scalability and readiness for larger circuits [517c800b-3].

citations.title: Demonstration of a neutral atom controlled-NOT quantum gate.
snippets:
Any unitary operation can be performed on a quantum computer equipped with a complete set of universal gates. A complete set of gates can be comprised of single qubit operations together with a twoqubit controlled-NOT (CNOT) gate [1]. The CNOT gate has been demonstrated in several different physical systems including trapped ions [2,3], superconducting circuits [4,5], and linear optics [6,7]. Numerous proposals exist for neutral atom quantum gates including short range dipolar interactions [8], ground state collisions [9], coupling of atoms to photons [10], magnetic dipole-dipole interactions [11], gates with delocalized qubits [12], and Rydberg state mediated dipolar interactions [13]. Many particle entanglement mediated by collisions has been observed in optical lattice based experiments [14], and a √ SWAP entangling operation was performed on many atom pairs in parallel [15], but a quantum gate between two individually addressed neutral atoms has not previously been demonstrated. 

We report here on the demonstration of a two-qubit gate with neutral atoms using Rydberg blockade interactions as proposed in [13]. The Rydberg approach has a number of attractive features: it does not require cooling of the atoms to the ground state of the confining potentials, it can be operated on µs timescales, it does not require precise control of the two-atom interaction strength, and it is not limited to nearest neighbor interactions which is advantageous for scaling to multi-qubit systems [16]. Detailed analyses of the Rydberg gate taking into account practical experimental conditions [17,18] predict that gate errors at the level of F ∼ 10 −3 are possible. We present here initial demonstrations of Rydberg mediated CNOT gates with fidelities based on truth table probabilities of F = 0.73, 0.72 using two different protocols. The coherence of the gate is shown by measuring coherent oscillations of the output states, with a conditional phase that is dependent on the presence or absence of a two-atom Rydberg interaction. Using superposition input states the gates were used to generate Bell states with fidelity F = 0.48 which suggests the actual gate fidelity lies between 0.48 and 0.73.

sections.title: # Summary
sections.text:
- Most neutral-atom two-qubit gates are implemented by Rydberg-state–mediated entangling operations (e.g., blockade-based CZ/CNOT), which exploit strong, tunable dipole–dipole interactions to imprint conditional phases, enabling fast, high-fidelity gates at micrometer range and scalable across arrays. Two-qubit entangling gates are typically realized via Rydberg blockade, yielding fast, high-fidelity gates with micrometer interaction ranges [517c800b-0] Experiments now achieve 99.5% fidelity on up to 60 atoms in parallel using optimized blockade-based gates [517c800b-2] The approach is fast, scalable, and not limited to nearest neighbors [517c800b-4]. 
- Other mechanisms used include engineered Ising-type gates via microwave/Raman drives and ancilla-assisted or QND parity gates, which are context-dependent but less commonly the primary method due to the maturity and scalability of Rydberg blockade. Rydberg-dressed, Raman-addressed schemes realize Ising-type couplings [3fcae3d2-2] QND parity measurements via ancillae provide non-destructive conditional operations [6ecaa67e-4] Rydberg-blockade CZ gates with simultaneous multi-color driving have been analyzed for robustness [9011dfab-1].

The CNOT gate has been demonstrated in several different physical systems including trapped ions [2,3], superconducting circuits [4,5], and linear optics [6,7]. Numerous proposals exist for neutral atom quantum gates including short range dipolar interactions [8], ground state collisions [9], coupling of atoms to photons [10], magnetic dipole-dipole interactions [11], gates with delocalized qubits [12], and Rydberg state mediated dipolar interactions [13]. Many particle entanglement mediated by collisions has been observed in optical lattice based experiments [14], and a √ SWAP entangling operation was performed on many atom pairs in parallel [15], but a quantum gate between two individually addressed neutral atoms has not previously been demonstrated. 

We report here on the demonstration of a two-qubit gate with neutral atoms using Rydberg blockade interactions as proposed in [13]. The Rydberg approach has a number of attractive features: it does not require cooling of the atoms to the ground state of the confining potentials, it can be operated on µs timescales, it does not require precise control of the two-atom interaction strength, and it is not limited to nearest neighbor interactions which is advantageous for scaling to multi-qubit systems [16]. Detailed analyses of the Rydberg gate taking into account practical experimental conditions [17,18] predict that gate errors at the level of F ∼ 10 −3 are possible. We present here initial demonstrations of Rydberg mediated CNOT gates with fidelities based on truth table probabilities of F = 0.73, 0.72 using two different protocols. The coherence of the gate is shown by measuring coherent oscillations of the output states, with a conditional phase that is dependent on the presence or absence of a two-atom Rydberg interaction. Using superposition input states the gates were used to generate Bell states with fidelity F = 0.48 which suggests the actual gate fidelity lies between 0.48 and 0.73.

Introduction and Scope
Mass customization (MC) manufacturing seeks to deliver high product variety with low lead times and costs, which significantly complicates production planning and control compared to mass production. AI methods are increasingly applied to address planning challenges across the shop floor, supply chain, and product configuration layers, enabling dynamic decision-making under uncertainty and variability.

Planning Challenges in Mass Customization
Mass customization increases combinatorial complexity by producing many one-off or small-batch orders alongside standard variants, while customers demand real-time transparency and tolerances for delays are lower. Disturbances such as supplier delays, machine breakdowns, and transportation disruptions amplify the risk of order tardiness in make-to-order or assembly-to-order supply chains, requiring real-time information exchange across the network and robust production planning approaches. Mass customization increases complexity in production planning due to lots of one and high product variety with volatile demand, and requires real-time information exchange across supply chain stages under customer expectations for real-time order status [953e659e-0].

Dynamic Scheduling and Rescheduling
Reinforcement learning (RL) and multi-agent RL have emerged as promising for dynamic scheduling in MC, offering online learning, real-time decision-making, and dynamic adjustment to unexpected events. AI methods for dynamic scheduling provide dynamic adjustment, online learning, and real-time decision making to handle unexpected events, with RL improving production efficiency in job-shop scheduling [6ec8ef33-1]. Dynamic scheduling under mass personalization has been addressed using heuristic, meta-heuristic, and RL approaches; RL-based multi-agent methods have been proposed to handle random job arrivals, stochastic processing times, and machine breakdowns, including approaches that minimize makespan and prevent conflicting operations [6ec8ef33-4]. RL-based rescheduling in dynamic job shops supports real-time interactive learning and outperforms rule-based heuristics in some settings. A real-time scheduling method for dynamic job shops based on RL improved production goal optimization compared to rule-based methods under changing order demands [6ec8ef33-0]. Digital twins (DT) integrated with RL enable proactive assessment of conflicts when urgent orders arrive, prediction of personnel/equipment states, and self-learning scheduling policies in virtual spaces, facilitating rapid reschedule under disturbances and task insertions. Combining digital twins with hierarchical RL allows monitoring of actual assembly and self-learning scheduling when new tasks are inserted or machine failures occur, addressing limitations of conventional assembly lines and neighborhood search methods under complex, changing industrial conditions [6ec8ef33-2].

snippets:
Dynamic scheduling problems are essential under mass personalization as they seek (near-) optimal allocation to feasible machines following dynamic scheduling settings (Johnson et al., 2022). Existing approaches to dynamic scheduling problems can be classified into three categories: heuristic methods, meta-heuristic methods, and reinforcement learning (RL) algorithms (Luo et al., 2021). 

Heuristic rules simply allocate operations to machines following predefined rules, such as first-in-first-out and longest-processing time allocation rules. The disadvantages are obvious since they are not suitable for many scheduling settings to optimize scheduling performance (Xie et al., 2019). In contrast, meta-heuristic methods, such as genetic algorithms (Elmaraghy et al., 2000;Qi et al., 2000;Zhang et al., 2013aZhang et al., , 2013b) ) and ant colony algorithms (Merkle et al., 2002;J. Zhang et al., 2013aJ. Zhang et al., , 2013b)), can explore nearoptimal schedules. However, the scheduling policies need to be retained if manufacturing settings are adjusted, and the time-consuming retraining might halt the whole manufacturing process (Al-Hinai & Elmekkawy, 2011;Gao et al., 2015). 

Reinforcement learning is a promising solution to dynamic scheduling problems (Heger & Voss, 2021;Jing et al., 2022;Kuhnle et al., 2021). Random job arrivals is addressed using multi-agent DQN (Johnson et al., 2022) by training with random job arrivals. A multi-agent reinforcement learning (MARL) approach has been proposed to manage scheduling processes with random processing time (Park et al., 2020). The randomness in setup time is addressed through MARL, with the goal of minimizing makespan (Oh et al., 2022). Stochastic processing times and unplanned machine breakdowns are tackled separately using dueling multi-agent reinforcement learning, which incorporates cooperation mechanisms to prevent conflicting operations (Qin et al., 2023).

Real need means that a company has a clear knowledge of the intelligent manufacturing model and its suitability. In other words, a company knows what changes an intelligent manufacturing model can bring to itself. Customer preference refers to a situation where a customer prefers a particular intelligent manufacturing model but is not sure if the model is a suitable. sections.text:
Evidence and Outcomes
Empirical results suggest RL-based dynamic scheduling can improve efficiency and responsiveness relative to static or rule-based methods. An RL-based real-time scheduling method outperformed common rule-based heuristics in dynamic job shops under changing demands [6ec8ef33-0]. An RL method framed as an MDP for hybrid flow-shop scheduling delivered reasonable result quality, real-time performance, and acceptable complexity in a metal processing workshop and in continuous dispatch scenarios [6ec8ef33-3]. Digital twin plus hierarchical RL has been demonstrated to reschedule human–machine collaborative assembly under task insertions and failures, showing improved adaptability compared to traditional neighborhood search methods. A DT-driven hierarchical RL approach effectively rescheduled assembly lines when switching production from generators to ventilators, addressing conflicts and disturbances beyond the capabilities of conventional methods [6ec8ef33-2]. Predictive planning components also show strong fit: ML-based quality prediction and supplier selection/ordering modules achieved high explanatory power and operational guidance for S&OP. Quality prediction models with multivariate regression and ARIMA achieved R-squared values near 1, and supplier selection with AHP and multi-objective optimization provided actionable component ordering policies [953e659e-1]. Knowledge-based configuration and reconfiguration reduce engineering effort and enable rapid line reconstruction. Ontology-driven dynamic reconfiguration supports automatic equipment switching and line reconstruction based on reasoning over device functions, process parameters, and constraints [589b2f7b-2].

snippets:
, there are some limitations:

1. Conventional assembly lines lack the flexibility to proactively adapt to different production tasks. When urgent orders appear, it is difficult to efficiently assess conflicts between current ongoing orders and newly arrived urgent orders, especially when machine sharing is required. In addition, factors such as sudden machine breakdowns and changes in manufacturing processes have become obstacles to rapid adjustment of assembly lines. 2. The existing FMS research based on the neighborhood search algorithm has some limitations and is difficult to adapt to the complex industrial environment. Combinatorial optimization of flexible manufacturing systems is a nonlinear hybrid discrete optimization problem with complex coupling relations. However, with the increase of the industrial scale, the structure of tasks becomes complex, and the neighborhood search algorithm is limited to a fixed scheduling plan. citations.title: A Reinforcement Learning Method for a Hybrid Flow-Shop Scheduling Problem
snippets: The scheduling problems in mass production, manufacturing, assembly, synthesis, and transportation, as well as internet services, can partly be attributed to a hybrid flow-shop scheduling problem (HFSP). To solve the problem, a reinforcement learning (RL) method for HFSP is studied for the first time in this paper. HFSP is described and attributed to the Markov Decision Processes (MDP), for which the special states, actions, and reward function are designed. On this basis, the MDP framework is established. The Boltzmann exploration policy is adopted to trade-off the exploration and exploitation during choosing action in RL. Compared with the first-come-first-serve strategy that is frequently adopted when coding in most of the traditional intelligent algorithms, the rule in the RL method is first-come-first-choice, which is more conducive to achieving the global optimal solution. For validation, the RL method is utilized for scheduling in a metal processing workshop of an automobile engine factory. Then, the method is applied to the sortie scheduling of carrier aircraft in continuous dispatch. The results demonstrate that the machining and support scheduling obtained by this RL method are reasonable in result quality, real-time performance and complexity, indicating that this RL method is practical for HFSP.

citations.title: Research on an Adaptive Real-Time Scheduling Method of Dynamic Job-Shop Based on Reinforcement Learning
snippets: With the rapid development of modern industrialization in our country and the continuous improvement of people’s living standards, the changing market has put forward new requirements for traditional manufacturing enterprises. The order product demand of many manufacturing enterprises is changing from a single variety, large batch to multiple varieties, small batch. In view of this change, the traditional job-shop scheduling method is far from enough, which greatly affects the efficiency of the production job-shop. In order to solve the above problems, this paper proposes a real-time scheduling method based on reinforcement learning applied in the dynamic job-shop and a new type of neural network is designed at the same time. The neural network is designed with the high-dimensional data in the above problem as input, and a policy-based reinforcement learning algorithm is proposed based on this network. In the process of research, it was found that the reinforcement learning method not only enables the agent to use historical data for learning, but also enables it to explore and learn other possible high-reward actions within a certain range, so as to realize the optimization of production goals under real-time scheduling. The effectiveness of the proposed real-time scheduling method is verified by comparing with other common rule-based scheduling methods in the manufacturing environment.

citations.title: Artificial-Intelligence-Driven Customized Manufacturing Factory: Key Technologies, Applications, and Challenges
snippets:
With the scientific development of the industrial market and manufacturing equipment, different industrial devices present different performance requirements representing multiple function trends [123]. For instance, the latest Computer Numerical Control (CNC) machine tool can complete a wide range of tasks, from lathing to milling functions. On the other hand, a dedicated manufacturing line does not meet new industrial requirements, especially for customized production [124]. The trend today is towards reconfiguration and reprogrammability of manufacturing processes [125]. Although several studies have investigated the problem and presented meaningful results [126], [127], most of them lack intelligent design to fulfill the emerging requirements of dynamic reconfiguration of manufacturing systems, especially for customized manufacturing. In particular, the work [126] focuses on the communications between agents while [127] investigates the relationship between manufacturing flexibility and demands. Thus, AI technologies have seldom been adopted in these studies. At present, ontology (as shown in Section IV) offers insights into dynamic reconfiguration of manufacturing resources [104], [128]. 

A schematic of the dynamic reconfiguration process based on the ontology inference is shown in Fig. 8. Each customized product invokes several processing procedures. First, a personalized product manufacturing-related device (such as cutting, materials handling device) is selected by ontology reasoning based on the device function. Then, the second selection of the devices involved in the manufacturing is finished according to ontology results with respect to the related manufacturing process, the manufacturing time, manufacturing quality, and other parameters of a device. Finally, a CM production line is constructed. Specifically, when the production line receives a production task, the raw material for a specific type of products is delivered from an autonomous warehouse. Then, the production line completes the manufacturing tasks in the process sequence. Furthermore, when one of the manufacturing devices breaks down during the process, automatic switching of the related machining equipment by ontology inference is conducted. Meanwhile, the reasoning mechanism reflects the reconstruction function of a flexible production of the production line. 

The presented approach leads to optimal process planning and functional reconstruction. Besides, it shows the strengths of ontology modeling and reasoning. In practice, only ontology and constraints need to be established according to the above description.

sections.text:
Challenges and Open Problems
Despite promising results, several challenges remain. Data and integration gaps hinder large-scale adoption: only a minority of studied works include actual ML implementations, and many focus on conceptual frameworks rather than end-to-end MC planning solutions. Among 37 articles mentioning AI, only 11 included their own implementations, and no ML approach specifically targeted the studied personnel scheduling problem, indicating deployment challenges and gaps [953e659e-2]. Real-time, robust decision-making under uncertainty, multi-objective trade-offs, and human-automation coordination require further research. Heuristics/metaheuristics face policy retention and retraining burdens when settings change, while RL offers adaptive policies but requires careful design to handle random arrivals, stochastic processing times, and breakdowns [6ec8ef33-4]. Data quality, explainability, and safety constraints in human-in-the-loop environments are critical for shop-floor deployment. Success factors for AI planners include real-time responsiveness, usability, and safety, while data gathering and expertise pose significant barriers [953e659e-2]. Finally, extending configuration knowledge to product–service systems and cross-enterprise planning remains underexplored. Extending ontology-based configuration models to product–service customization recommendations is identified as an open research topic [589b2f7b-0].

citations.title: Knowledge graph-enhanced multi-agent reinforcement learning for adaptive scheduling in smart manufacturing
snippets:
Dynamic scheduling problems are essential under mass personalization as they seek (near-) optimal allocation to feasible machines following dynamic scheduling settings (Johnson et al., 2022). Existing approaches to dynamic scheduling problems can be classified into three categories: heuristic methods, meta-heuristic methods, and reinforcement learning (RL) algorithms (Luo et al., 2021). 

Heuristic rules simply allocate operations to machines following predefined rules, such as first-in-first-out and longest-processing time allocation rules. The disadvantages are obvious since they are not suitable for many scheduling settings to optimize scheduling performance (Xie et al., 2019). In contrast, meta-heuristic methods, such as genetic algorithms (Elmaraghy et al., 2000;Qi et al., 2000;Zhang et al., 2013aZhang et al., , 2013b) ) and ant colony algorithms (Merkle et al., 2002;J. Zhang et al., 2013aJ. Zhang et al., , 2013b)), can explore nearoptimal schedules. However, the scheduling policies need to be retained if manufacturing settings are adjusted, and the time-consuming retraining might halt the whole manufacturing process (Al-Hinai & Elmekkawy, 2011;Gao et al., 2015). 

Reinforcement learning is a promising solution to dynamic scheduling problems (Heger & Voss, 2021;Jing et al., 2022;Kuhnle et al., 2021). Random job arrivals is addressed using multi-agent DQN (Johnson et al., 2022) by training with random job arrivals. A multi-agent reinforcement learning (MARL) approach has been proposed to manage scheduling processes with random processing time (Park et al., 2020). The randomness in setup time is addressed through MARL, with the goal of minimizing makespan (Oh et al., 2022). Stochastic processing times and unplanned machine breakdowns are tackled separately using dueling multi-agent reinforcement learning, which incorporates cooperation mechanisms to prevent conflicting operations (Qin et al., 2023).

(2020) used natural language processing techniques in construction to prioritize the tasks and assign them to the correct employee with the right skill.

snippets:
In [25], the authors presented an ontology-based approach for the modeling of product configuration knowledge. Concepts within the product configuration domain, such as product, component, part, attribute, etc., were only considered; moreover, classes related to the configuration of product-related services were not considered. 

From a methodological perspective, the authors in [3] proposed a novel productservice customization lifecycle that included technological solutions aiming to enable PSS customization. The PSS customization lifecycle relies on the tried and tested manufacturing blueprints proposed in [5,6], which provide a basis for actionable PSS and production intelligence. 

A summary of the related work and ontological models used in manufacturing is provided in Table 1. Based on this summary, it was found that the proposed models were utilized for modeling product and/or service knowledge for the purposes of design, planning, or configuration. The issue of extending those models for other applications (PSS customization recommendations) addressed by this paper is an open research topic.

sections.text:
Practical Implications and Recommendations
- Start with demand forecasting and S&OP integration to anchor planning in MC, then feed outputs into production and scheduling. Demand forecast quality is central to S&OP in mass customization, enabling better corporate management and lower inventory across SKUs [953e659e-1].
- Pilot dynamic scheduling with RL or DT-integrated rescheduling in constrained cells or urgent-order lanes to capture quick wins in responsiveness and OEE. DT+RL enables rapid conflict assessment and rescheduling for urgent orders and disturbances in human–machine collaborative workshops [6ec8ef33-2]. RL-based real-time scheduling improved efficiency versus rule-based methods in dynamic job shops [6ec8ef33-0].
- Build configuration ontologies/knowledge graphs to manage variant space and enable dynamic resource reconfiguration, with rules for safety and quality constraints. Ontology reasoning can select devices and reconstruct process flows for customized products and automatically switch equipment upon breakdowns [589b2f7b-2]. Configuration systems and PLM are essential to handle variety with constraints on control, usage, and safety [589b2f7b-1].
- Embed AI within human decision-making, focusing on real-time dashboards, explainability, and safe fallbacks; prioritize data governance and workforce skills. AI planning must clarify decision levels with humans, with success hinging on real-time, usability, and safety; data and expertise are primary barriers [953e659e-2].
- Invest in predictive modules (quality, supplier selection, and setup time modeling) to reduce uncertainty in downstream planning. ML-based supplier selection and quality prediction achieved strong performance, supporting S&OP and procurement planning [953e659e-1]. Deep learning has been applied to predict employee impacts on setup and processing times for improved scheduling [953e659e-2].

citations.title: Integration of Product and Manufacturing Design: A Systematic Literature Review
snippets:
In the current competitive market, customers' demands for personalized products have grown because they are looking for products that meet their unique needs [7,8]. As a result, the manufacturing industry faces the challenge of producing higher-quality customized products, with reduced lead-time, and costs. To remain competitive, manufacturing companies must adopt digital products and manufacturing systems. Managing product variety across the entire supply chain is a critical challenge in meeting personalized product demands [8]. While the space for personalized solutions may appear vast, configuration systems and product lifecycle management systems are implemented to handle the complexity. The number of possibilities within a given product category is finite due to constraints related to control, usage, and safety that are considered during the product configuration process [9,10]. However, the personalization strategy extends beyond meeting customer requirements; it is also a business consideration that can influence the market and drive increased sales [8,9]. 

The manufacturing industry, therefore, confronts the complex task of producing products that align with personalized requirements while achieving higher quality, shorter lead times, and cost-effectiveness. Manufacturing serves as a crucial foundation of the global economy [10]. In the face of a shrinking product life cycle, advanced manufacturing competes fiercely on a global scale [11]. Achieving economies of scope and scale by producing innovative product variants through customization is imperative. However, small and medium-sized companies encounter challenges in designing and developing new products, implementing new technologies, and optimizing production scope and manufacturing processes [10]. While existing approaches in literature and practice, such as concurrent engineering (CE) and design for manufacturing (DFM), integrate production aspects into product engineering [12], there is a need for a formalized method of storing and reusing knowledge from past and future generations of products, production systems, and business models. With the increasing complexity of product design and manufacturing processes, the ability to capture, retain, and leverage knowledge becomes crucial. By establishing a formalized knowledge management approach, companies can avoid reinventing the wheel, benefit from lessons learned, and capitalize on previous successes, leading to more effective decision-making, accelerated innovation, and enhanced competitiveness.

Large amounts of data are readily available in the manufacturing system, which provides an unprecedented opportunity to improve the performance of the manufacturing system. Recently, AI fuels an increasing interest to solve dynamic scheduling problems by continuously improving the scheduling performance of schedulers [10]. AI methods provide attractive features such as dynamic adjustment, online learning, and real-time decision making. This provides an unprecedented opportunity to handle unexpected events in real time and improves the decision-making abilities of schedulers in the manufacturing processes. Reinforcement learning (RL) is a rapid, efficient and irreplaceable learning algorithm, which belongs to a branch of AI. In recent years, it has been studied and applied in the process of job-shop production scheduling by more and more people, which has a good effect in improving the production efficiency of the job-shop [11,12]. Although most RL-based studies improve scheduling efficiency at different levels, the essence of them was to let agents learn historical data and experience, instead of interactive learning and rescheduling according to the real-time information change in dynamic job-shop. 

According to the above, in order to improve the real-time interactive learning and dynamic adjustable ability in the process of job-shop production scheduling, a real-time scheduling method of dynamic flexible job-shop based on reinforcement learning was proposed. Based on the study of Markov Decision Process (MDP), a model of MDP for Flexible Job-shop Scheduling Problem(FJSP) is established by using the similarities and relationships between the MDP and the shop scheduling model [13]. Then, a learning neural network based on the state-action value of production scheduling is designed. In the end, a policy-based deep reinforcement learning algorithm is proposed to achieve the optimization of objectives. The rest of the paper is organized as follows. Section 2 contains some related research status of static or dynamic job-shop production scheduling methods. Section 3 introduces the main research methodology. Experiment and results are given in Section 4. Finally, conclusions are shown in Section 5.

From the literature review, that was conducted for the purpose of this paper, the following findings can be stated:

citations.title: Artificial-Intelligence-Driven Customized Manufacturing Factory: Key Technologies, Applications, and Challenges
snippets:
With the scientific development of the industrial market and manufacturing equipment, different industrial devices present different performance requirements representing multiple function trends [123]. For instance, the latest Computer Numerical Control (CNC) machine tool can complete a wide range of tasks, from lathing to milling functions. On the other hand, a dedicated manufacturing line does not meet new industrial requirements, especially for customized production [124]. The trend today is towards reconfiguration and reprogrammability of manufacturing processes [125]. Although several studies have investigated the problem and presented meaningful results [126], [127], most of them lack intelligent design to fulfill the emerging requirements of dynamic reconfiguration of manufacturing systems, especially for customized manufacturing. In particular, the work [126] focuses on the communications between agents while [127] investigates the relationship between manufacturing flexibility and demands. Thus, AI technologies have seldom been adopted in these studies. At present, ontology (as shown in Section IV) offers insights into dynamic reconfiguration of manufacturing resources [104], [128]. 

A schematic of the dynamic reconfiguration process based on the ontology inference is shown in Fig. 8. Each customized product invokes several processing procedures. First, a personalized product manufacturing-related device (such as cutting, materials handling device) is selected by ontology reasoning based on the device function. Then, the second selection of the devices involved in the manufacturing is finished according to ontology results with respect to the related manufacturing process, the manufacturing time, manufacturing quality, and other parameters of a device. Finally, a CM production line is constructed. Specifically, when the production line receives a production task, the raw material for a specific type of products is delivered from an autonomous warehouse. Then, the production line completes the manufacturing tasks in the process sequence. Furthermore, when one of the manufacturing devices breaks down during the process, automatic switching of the related machining equipment by ontology inference is conducted. Meanwhile, the reasoning mechanism reflects the reconstruction function of a flexible production of the production line. 

The presented approach leads to optimal process planning and functional reconstruction. Besides, it shows the strengths of ontology modeling and reasoning. In practice, only ontology and constraints need to be established according to the above description.

sections.title: # Overview: Why embeddings for company name similarity
sections.text: Embedding-based similarity encodes free-form company names and descriptions into dense vectors such that semantically similar entries (e.g., variants of the same company) are close in vector space, overcoming the sparsity and engineering burden of hand-crafted feature baselines and shallow matching rules Earlier approaches to sentence similarity are limited in capturing rich sequence patterns, and hand-crafted features suffer from sparsity and inefficiency; neural sentence embeddings explicitly encode semantic and syntactic information and improve similarity computation [d5cd09cc-0]. In practice, modern transformer-based sentence encoders (e.g., SBERT, GritLM) and efficient libraries (e.g., FAISS) enable scalable deduplication and near-duplicate detection by computing cosine similarities and performing approximate nearest-neighbor search A pipeline used a decoder-based embedding model (GritLM) to encode sentences, compute pairwise cosine similarities, and deduplicate by retaining only those below a similarity threshold, reducing ~490k items to ~50k [d5cd09cc-1] Embedding models (BERT/GPT successors) transform text into dense vectors capturing context and semantics; sentence transformers are state-of-the-art for textual similarity, and k-nearest neighbors can be retrieved efficiently with FAISS [d5cd09cc-4].
