snippets:
We first use NLTK to segment each report into individual sentences. Through analyzing large volumes of reports, we found that many repetitive sentences share similar semantics. To simplify the final dataset and reduce the burden of pairwise similarity computation, we apply extensive deduplication to the sentence-level inputs. To this end, we use GritLM (Muennighoff et al., 2024), a decoder-based embedding model that achieves state-of-the-art performance on the Massive Text Embedding Benchmark (MTEB) and the Reasoning as Retrieval Benchmark (RAR-b), to encode sentences and obtain their vector representations. 

We then iteratively compute pairwise cosine similarities between sentences, retaining those that do not exceed a similarity threshold of 0.8 with previously selected sentences and discarding the rest. Through this deduplication procedure, the number of sentences is reduced from approximately 490,000 to 50,000, substantially lowering computational cost and improving the efficiency of subsequent processing.

citations.title: Sentence-Embedding and Similarity via Hybrid Bidirectional-LSTM and CNN Utilizing Weighted-Pooling Attention
snippets:
In the present era, text understanding and information retrieval research have generated great interest among researchers for analyzing the sentence similarity in natural language processing (NLP). Although computing similarity facilitates many tasks such as plagiarism detection [1], query rank [2], and question answering [3], yet it is still a challenging issue, largely due to the intrinsic ambiguity of various linguistic sequences and the inadequate number of labeled training corpora available. On the other hand, conventional NLP methodologies utilized to operate similarity systems strongly depend on hand-crafted features [4]. Because a word is embedded in a multi-dimensional space with high-dimensional vectors, these features suffer from sparsity, unavoidably resulting in unacceptable complexity and inefficiency. 

Recent advancements in deep neural network (DNN) models have already brought outstanding performance improvements in various artificial intelligence operations related to computer vision, speech recognition, robotics, and NLP. In the last decade, many researchers have presented the effective modeling of words referred to as 'distributed word embedding', which are competent to explicitly encode both the semantic and syntactic information [5]. In this method, a word is embedded in the multi-dimensional vector space, where similar semantics contexts lie close to each other, e.g., the vector (("Madrid" − "Spain") + ("France")) is closer to vector ("Paris") than any other word vector. 

Today, word embedding has become extremely effective and is applied to various applications such as part-ofspeech (POS) tagging [6] and name entity recognition [7]. It has also demonstrated the potential for neural word representations for analogies tasks. 

Moreover, the increasing number of applications of DNNs has diverted the attention from word-level to larger texts, such as sentences embedding. Earlier approaches applied to look for sentence similarity are only able to capture the brief dependencies and similarities among characters, which is indeed not appropriate for finding similarity accurately. Therefore, these traditional approaches have limitations in capturing rich input sequence patterns between their correlations. In short, sentence embedding plays a vital role and is an emerging fundamental parameter in computing similarity.

For multilingual corpora, choose multilingual models and evaluate on multilingual subsets (e.g., MTEB multilingual tasks) to ensure cross-language robustness Multilingual deduplication/semantic text tasks can be evaluated with SBERT and related models on multilingual datasets; cosine-based nearest neighbor retrieval is commonly used [a4e070ca-4].

SBERT provides strong baselines for sentence similarity (STS) and relatedness, with design choices (pooling, concatenation, objective) affecting training and inference; cosine similarity is the standard metric at inference SBERT ablations show pooling and concatenation choices affect performance; at inference, similarity is measured with cosine similarity between sentence embeddings [65af70c1-0] SBERT substantially outperforms using raw BERT outputs and outperforms InferSent and USE on STS Spearman, with details on how different embedding strategies correlate with human judgments [65af70c1-1]. If you need compact vectors for speed or memory, MiniLM and compressed variants are competitive on standard semantic benchmarks and can be paired with a trainable projection layer for downstream tasks MiniLM (all-MiniLM-L6-v2) is a distilled SBERT backbone; freezing the backbone and training a projection layer yields competitive performance on clustering/retrieval and other semantic benchmarks [65af70c1-4].

citations.title: Sentence-BERT: Sentence Embeddings using Siamese BERT-Networks
snippets:
We have demonstrated strong empirical results for the quality of SBERT sentence embeddings. In this section, we perform an ablation study of different aspects of SBERT in order to get a better understanding of their relative importance.

We evaluated different pooling strategies (MEAN, MAX, and CLS). For the classification objective function, we evaluate different concatenation methods. For each possible configuration, we train SBERT with 10 different random seeds and average the performances.

The objective function (classification vs. regression) depends on the annotated dataset. For the classification objective function, we train SBERTbase on the SNLI and the Multi-NLI dataset. For the regression objective function, we train on the training set of the STS benchmark dataset. Performances are measured on the development split of the STS benchmark dataset. Results are shown in Table 6.  When trained with the classification objective function on NLI data, the pooling strategy has a rather minor impact. The impact of the concatenation mode is much larger. InferSent (Conneau et al., 2017) and Universal Sentence Encoder (Cer et al., 2018) both use (u, v, |u − v|, u * v) as input for a softmax classifier. However, in our architecture, adding the element-wise u * v decreased the performance.

The most important component is the elementwise difference |u − v|. Note, that the concatenation mode is only relevant for training the softmax classifier. At inference, when predicting similarities for the STS benchmark dataset, only the sentence embeddings u and v are used in combination with cosine-similarity. The element-wise difference measures the distance between the dimensions of the two sentence embeddings, ensuring that similar pairs are closer and dissimilar pairs are further apart.

When trained with the regression objective function, we observe that the pooling strategy has a large impact. There, the MAX strategy perform significantly worse than MEAN or CLS-token strategy. This is in contrast to (Conneau et al., 2017), who found it beneficial for the BiLSTM-layer of InferSent to use MAX instead of MEAN pooling.

snippets:
We evaluate the performance of SBERT for STS without using any STS specific training data. We use the STS tasks 2012 -2016 (Agirre et al., 2012(Agirre et al., , 2013(Agirre et al., , 2014(Agirre et al., , 2015(Agirre et al., , 2016, the STS benchmark (Cer et al., 2017), and the SICK-Relatedness dataset (Marelli et al., 2014). These datasets provide labels between 0 and 5 on the semantic relatedness of sentence pairs. We showed in (Reimers et al., 2016) that Pearson correlation is badly suited for STS. Instead, we compute the Spearman's rank correlation between the cosine-similarity of the sentence embeddings and the gold labels. The setup for the other sentence embedding methods is equivalent, the similarity is computed by cosinesimilarity. The results are depicted in Table 1.

The results shows that directly using the output of BERT leads to rather poor performances. Averaging the BERT embeddings achieves an average correlation of only 54.81, and using the CLStoken output only achieves an average correlation of 29.19. Both are worse than computing average GloVe embeddings.

Using the described siamese network structure and fine-tuning mechanism substantially improves the correlation, outperforming both InferSent and Universal Sentence Encoder substantially. The only dataset where SBERT performs worse than Universal Sentence Encoder is SICK-R. Universal Sentence Encoder was trained on various datasets, including news, question-answer pages and discussion forums, which appears to be more suitable to the data of SICK-R. In contrast, SBERT was pre-trained only on Wikipedia (via BERT) and on NLI data.

While RoBERTa was able to improve the performance for several supervised tasks, we only observe minor difference between SBERT and SRoBERTa for generating sentence embeddings.

citations.title: Cropping outperforms dropout as an augmentation strategy for training self-supervised text embeddings
snippets:
As the first evaluation suite to assess the sentence representation quality, we used the Massive Text Embedding Benchmark (MTEB) (Muennighoff et al., 2023). It comprises older benchmarks, such as BEIR (Thakur et al., 2021) or STS (Agirre et al., 2012); as well as a wide range of downstream tasks from different modalities, such as clustering, classification, or retrieval. 

We fine-tuned a base transformer (i.e., a model primarily pre-trained with a token-level loss) using the SSL training setup outlined in the previous section and compared two augmentation strategies: cropping and dropouts. We chose MPNet (Song et al., 2020;mpnet-base) as base model, following SBERT (Reimers & Gurevych, 2019; model all-mpnet-base-v2 on HuggingFace). This model has bert-base architecture with 110 M parameters and uses 768 embedding dimensions. We used mean pooling over all tokens to obtain a single 768-dimensional output vector for each input text, but also compared other pooling strategies (Supplementary Figure S1). 

For fine-tuning the base model we used the ICLR dataset (González-Márquez & Kobak, 2024), which consists of 24,347 scientific abstracts of all papers submitted to the ICLR conference within the years 2017-2024. This recently assembled dataset is well-suited for our purposes because it is not part of the MTEB benchmark. 

Fine-tuning on this dataset therefore enables a fair model comparison and avoids evaluation data leakage, which can potentially lead to inflated performance estimates. 

For simplicity, we did not use all MTEB tasks for evaluation, but focused on a subset of tasks from four different modalities: clustering, reranking, retrieval, and STS. Clustering tasks assess the K-means clustering results in the embedding space; retrieval and reranking tasks assess the quality of the nearest neighbors in the embedding space; STS tasks measure how well the embedding represents not only small but also large ground-truth pairwise distances (see Section A.2 for details).

sections.title: # Practical pipeline for company name similarity
sections.text:
- Embed: Encode company names and optionally full descriptions using a high-quality sentence encoder (e.g., SBERT/MiniLM, GritLM). Use mean or CLS pooling as per model; cosine-normalize vectors for similarity SBERT supports different pooling strategies (MEAN, MAX, CLS); cosine similarity is used for inference [65af70c1-0] GritLM embeddings enable efficient deduplication via pairwise cosine similarity and hard thresholding [d5cd09cc-1].
- Search: For large corpora, use approximate nearest neighbors (e.g., FAISS) to find candidates for each name and reduce pairwise comparisons from quadratic to near-linear time Iterative cosine similarity with a threshold reduced items from ~490k to ~50k, cutting computational cost [d5cd09cc-1] k-nearest neighbors can be retrieved with FAISS to scale similarity search [d5cd09cc-4].
- Match and deduplicate: Pairwise cosine thresholds and clustering (e.g., DBSCAN) are effective. Adjust threshold and cluster parameters to balance precision/recall; merge small clusters if needed to avoid noisy labels A cosine threshold of 0.8 retained non-duplicates and pruned near-duplicates efficiently [d5cd09cc-1] DBSCAN can be run on a cosine distance matrix; clusters are formed by semantic similarity, and a threshold-based merging strategy can merge small clusters to improve downstream robustness [878c1538-3].
- Evaluate: For STS-style relatedness, report Spearman correlation between embedding cosine similarity and human labels; for clustering, use V-measure or external indices; for retrieval, use nDCG@k; for deduplication, report precision/recall at thresholds and human review of a sample of matches and non-matches Clustering tasks use V-measure; retrieval and reranking use nearest neighbor quality and nDCG@k; STS measures alignment of pairwise distances [a4e070ca-2] STS evaluation typically uses Spearman rank correlation between cosine similarity and gold labels [65af70c1-1] A multilingual STS setup using SBERT embeddings and FAISS for nearest neighbors followed by cross-encoder labeling illustrates evaluation of semantic similarity [a4e070ca-4] DBSCAN clustering with cosine distance and a threshold-based merge step supports robust deduplication [878c1538-3].

citations.title: Sanitizing Manufacturing Dataset Labels Using Vision-Language Models
snippets:
Note that the DBSCAN algorithm typically calculates distances between points using Euclidean distance by default. However, in this task, cosine similarity was used as the measure to capture the semantic relationships in word embeddings, where the direction of the vectors holds more meaning than their magnitude. Hence, a cosine distance matrix was computed and provided as input to the DBSCAN algorithm. The cosine similarity between two label embeddings e ij and e kl was defined as: 

where e ij , e kl ∈ R d are the embeddings of labels l ij and l kl respectively. The cosine distance, based on this similarity, is defined as: 

A cosine distance of 0 indicates perfect similarity, while values closer to 1 suggest greater dissimilarity. Given the pairwise cosine distance matrix D, where each entry D ij represents the cosine distance between the label embeddings e ij and e kl , the DBSCAN algorithm was applied using D. By setting appropriate values for ε and the minimum number of samples, DBSCAN identified clusters of labels that were semantically similar, while outliers or noise labels that did not fit into any dense cluster were left unclustered. After clustering the labels, the frequency of each label's occurrence across the entire dataset was calculated. Within each cluster, the label with the highest frequency in the dataset was selected as the cluster's representative label. This approach ensures that the representative label is both semantically relevant and statistically dominant within the dataset. Once the representative labels were determined, all labels in the dataset that belonged to the same cluster were replaced with their respective cluster representative. 

Note that, among all the clusters, there were some with a low number of labels, which are considered noise or outliers. Clusters containing very few labels pose challenges for downstream tasks, as they do not provide sufficient examples for a classifier to learn meaningful patterns. To address this, a threshold-based merging strategy was implemented. This process involved identifying clusters with label counts below a predefined threshold and merging them into the closest neighboring cluster based on the cosine distance between their cluster representative label.

Instead, we compute the Spearman's rank correlation between the cosine-similarity of the sentence embeddings and the gold labels. The setup for the other sentence embedding methods is equivalent, the similarity is computed by cosinesimilarity. The results are depicted in Table 1.

The results shows that directly using the output of BERT leads to rather poor performances. Averaging the BERT embeddings achieves an average correlation of only 54.81, and using the CLStoken output only achieves an average correlation of 29.19. Using the described siamese network structure and fine-tuning mechanism substantially improves the correlation, outperforming both InferSent and Universal Sentence Encoder substantially. The only dataset where SBERT performs worse than Universal Sentence Encoder is SICK-R. In contrast, SBERT was pre-trained only on Wikipedia (via BERT) and on NLI data.

citations.title: Cropping outperforms dropout as an augmentation strategy for training self-supervised text embeddings
snippets:
As the first evaluation suite to assess the sentence representation quality, we used the Massive Text Embedding Benchmark (MTEB) (Muennighoff et al., 2023). It comprises older benchmarks, such as BEIR (Thakur et al., 2021) or STS (Agirre et al., 2012); as well as a wide range of downstream tasks from different modalities, such as clustering, classification, or retrieval. 

We fine-tuned a base transformer (i.e., a model primarily pre-trained with a token-level loss) using the SSL training setup outlined in the previous section and compared two augmentation strategies: cropping and dropouts. We chose MPNet (Song et al., 2020;mpnet-base) as base model, following SBERT (Reimers & Gurevych, 2019; model all-mpnet-base-v2 on HuggingFace). This model has bert-base architecture with 110 M parameters and uses 768 embedding dimensions. We used mean pooling over all tokens to obtain a single 768-dimensional output vector for each input text, but also compared other pooling strategies (Supplementary Figure S1). 

For fine-tuning the base model we used the ICLR dataset (González-Márquez & Kobak, 2024), which consists of 24,347 scientific abstracts of all papers submitted to the ICLR conference within the years 2017-2024. This recently assembled dataset is well-suited for our purposes because it is not part of the MTEB benchmark. 

Fine-tuning on this dataset therefore enables a fair model comparison and avoids evaluation data leakage, which can potentially lead to inflated performance estimates. 

For simplicity, we did not use all MTEB tasks for evaluation, but focused on a subset of tasks from four different modalities: clustering, reranking, retrieval, and STS. Clustering tasks assess the K-means clustering results in the embedding space; retrieval and reranking tasks assess the quality of the nearest neighbors in the embedding space; STS tasks measure how well the embedding represents not only small but also large ground-truth pairwise distances (see Section A.2 for details).

citations.title: CompanyName2Vec: Company Entity Matching based on Job Ads
snippets: In this study, we used embedding to create a mathematical representation for a company name that holds the naming semantics. When some object x is said to be embedded in another object y, the embedding is given by some injective and structure-preserving map f : X → Y . We used text embedding, similarly to what Yoshua Bengio proposed in 2001 [34], in the form of a feed-forward neural network language model. Modern methods use a simpler and more efficient neural architecture to learn word vectors, like word2vec [35], [36], and GloVe [37], based on objective functions that are explicitly designed to produce high-quality vectors. Neural embedding learned by these methods have been applied in a myriad of NLP applications, including initializing neural network models for objective visual recognition [38], or machine translation [39], [40], as well as directly modeling wordto-word relationships [35], [41]- [43], Paragraph vectors, or doc2vec, were proposed in 2014 by Quoc Le and Tomas Mikolov [44] as a simple extension to word2vec to extend the learning of embedding from words to word sequences. Doc2vec 1 is agnostic to the granularity of the word sequence, and it can equally be a word n-gram, sentence, paragraph, or document. One of the benefits of using dense and lowdimensional vectors is computational. The main benefit of this dense representation is generalization power. If we believe some features may provide similar clues, it is worthwhile to give a representation that can capture these similarities. We used text embedding to learn company names semantics and to measure similarity.

sections.title: # Robustness to variants, noise, and adversarial settings
sections.text: Neural text embeddings are more robust to paraphrases, missing words, and minor wording changes than n-gram methods, but specialized models can be even more resilient. RETSim demonstrates improved robustness and accuracy over MinHash and standard neural embeddings for near-duplicate detection, adversarial retrieval, and spam clustering, and is designed for multilingual use; it reports SOTA on deduplication and adversarial text retrieval tasks RETSim produces robust metric embeddings for near-duplicate retrieval, clustering, and deduplication, outperforming MinHash and neural baselines and attaining SOTA on deduplication and adversarial retrieval [878c1538-0] RETSim is significantly faster than prior neural embeddings and more robust than n-gram algorithms, and a multilingual W4NT3D benchmark was introduced to evaluate adversarial robustness [878c1538-1]. In financial and other domains, practitioners often hybridize TF-IDF or n-gram similarity (for lexical overlap) with semantic embeddings to improve detection of both exact and semantic duplicates A financial RAG system used TF-IDF for deduplication (cosine-thresholded) to remove redundant segments and BGE-M3 embeddings to store semantic vectors for efficient retrieval [878c1538-2].

Furthermore, we introduced the W4NT3D benchmark, the first multilingual dataset designed to measure the adversarial robustness of near-duplicate text detection algorithms. In this section, we randomly selected a set of false positives and false negatives for RETSim on the NEWS-COPY deduplication dataset to provide further insight into the results.

citations.title: FinSage: A Multi-aspect RAG System for Financial Filings Question Answering
snippets:
Two embedding models are used in this project, each serving a distinct purpose: TF-IDF for text deduplication and BGE-M3 for storing text in the database. 

For the deduplication task, we employ the TF-IDF tool to convert the text into vector representations. This approach helps to identify and remove redundant text segments by comparing their vector similarities. The model uses term frequency and inverse document frequency to generate vectors, which are then compared using cosine similarity to detect high similarity between text segments. Text with similarities above a predefined threshold is removed, reducing redundancy. 

For storing text in the Chroma database, we use the BGE-M3 embedding model. This model, trained on large-scale datasets, transforms text into high-dimensional vectors that capture the semantic meaning of the content. These vectors are then stored in the database, enabling efficient indexing and retrieval for future similarity searches and semantic analysis.

citations.title: RETSim: Resilient and Efficient Text Similarity
snippets: This paper introduces RETSim (Resilient and Efficient Text Similarity), a lightweight, multilingual deep learning model trained to produce robust metric embeddings for near-duplicate text retrieval, clustering, and dataset deduplication tasks. We demonstrate that RETSim is significantly more robust and accurate than MinHash and neural text embeddings, achieving new state-of-the-art performance on dataset deduplication, adversarial text retrieval benchmarks, and spam clustering tasks. We also introduce the W4NT3D benchmark (Wiki-40B 4dversarial Near-T3xt Dataset) for evaluating multilingual, near-duplicate text retrieval capabilities under adversarial settings. RETSim and the W4NT3D benchmark are open-sourced under the MIT License at https://github.com/google/unisim.

sections.title: # Evaluation, thresholds, and clustering details
sections.text:
- STS and relatedness: Report Spearman correlation between cosine similarity and human similarity labels; this aligns with common practice in SBERT and related work SBERT evaluates on STS datasets using Spearman rank correlation between cosine similarity and gold labels [65af70c1-1] STS tasks measure how well embeddings represent small and large ground-truth pairwise distances [a4e070ca-2].
- Clustering: Use external clustering metrics (e.g., V-measure, NMI, RI, F1) when ground truth exists; train mini-batch K-means on embedded space and tune the number of clusters; for open-ended deduplication, DBSCAN with cosine distance can group similar entries and flag outliers Clustering tasks in MTEB use mini-batch K-means and evaluate with v-measure [a4e070ca-4] DBSCAN on a cosine distance matrix clusters semantically similar labels, with a threshold-based merging strategy for small clusters [878c1538-3]. When no labels exist, validate clusters by sampling representative entries and verifying business sense (e.g., cross-check a sample of cluster pairs).
- Retrieval/duplication: For deduplication, set an embedding cosine threshold and inspect false positives/negatives; adaptive thresholds and post-hoc review can calibrate precision/recall for downstream workflows A cosine threshold of 0.8 effectively pruned near-duplicates in a large corpus [d5cd09cc-1] Analyses of false positives/negatives reveal where an embedding may fail, guiding threshold and model selection [878c1538-1].
- Dimensionality and speed: If you need smaller vectors, MiniLM or compressed variants trade some accuracy for reduced size; evaluate on your tasks using MTEB or bespoke benchmarks before deployment MiniLM-based representations with a trainable projection layer perform reasonably on clustering and semantic benchmarks, enabling smaller vectors [65af70c1-4].

snippets:
Note that the DBSCAN algorithm typically calculates distances between points using Euclidean distance by default. However, in this task, cosine similarity was used as the measure to capture the semantic relationships in word embeddings, where the direction of the vectors holds more meaning than their magnitude. Hence, a cosine distance matrix was computed and provided as input to the DBSCAN algorithm. The cosine similarity between two label embeddings e ij and e kl was defined as: 

where e ij , e kl ∈ R d are the embeddings of labels l ij and l kl respectively. The cosine distance, based on this similarity, is defined as: 

A cosine distance of 0 indicates perfect similarity, while values closer to 1 suggest greater dissimilarity. Given the pairwise cosine distance matrix D, where each entry D ij represents the cosine distance between the label embeddings e ij and e kl , the DBSCAN algorithm was applied using D. By setting appropriate values for ε and the minimum number of samples, DBSCAN identified clusters of labels that were semantically similar, while outliers or noise labels that did not fit into any dense cluster were left unclustered. After clustering the labels, the frequency of each label's occurrence across the entire dataset was calculated. Within each cluster, the label with the highest frequency in the dataset was selected as the cluster's representative label. This approach ensures that the representative label is both semantically relevant and statistically dominant within the dataset. Once the representative labels were determined, all labels in the dataset that belonged to the same cluster were replaced with their respective cluster representative. 

Note that, among all the clusters, there were some with a low number of labels, which are considered noise or outliers. Clusters containing very few labels pose challenges for downstream tasks, as they do not provide sufficient examples for a classifier to learn meaningful patterns. To address this, a threshold-based merging strategy was implemented. This process involved identifying clusters with label counts below a predefined threshold and merging them into the closest neighboring cluster based on the cosine distance between their cluster representative label.

As the first evaluation suite to assess the sentence representation quality, we used the Massive Text Embedding Benchmark (MTEB) (Muennighoff et al., 2023). It comprises older benchmarks, such as BEIR (Thakur et al., 2021) or STS (Agirre et al., 2012); as well as a wide range of downstream tasks from different modalities, such as clustering, classification, or retrieval. 

We fine-tuned a base transformer (i.e., a model primarily pre-trained with a token-level loss) using the SSL training setup outlined in the previous section and compared two augmentation strategies: cropping and dropouts. We chose MPNet (Song et al., 2020;mpnet-base) as base model, following SBERT (Reimers & Gurevych, 2019; model all-mpnet-base-v2 on HuggingFace). This model has bert-base architecture with 110 M parameters and uses 768 embedding dimensions. We used mean pooling over all tokens to obtain a single 768-dimensional output vector for each input text, but also compared other pooling strategies (Supplementary Figure S1). 

For fine-tuning the base model we used the ICLR dataset (González-Márquez & Kobak, 2024), which consists of 24,347 scientific abstracts of all papers submitted to the ICLR conference within the years 2017-2024. This recently assembled dataset is well-suited for our purposes because it is not part of the MTEB benchmark. 

Fine-tuning on this dataset therefore enables a fair model comparison and avoids evaluation data leakage, which can potentially lead to inflated performance estimates. 

For simplicity, we did not use all MTEB tasks for evaluation, but focused on a subset of tasks from four different modalities: clustering, reranking, retrieval, and STS. Clustering tasks assess the K-means clustering results in the embedding space; retrieval and reranking tasks assess the quality of the nearest neighbors in the embedding space; STS tasks measure how well the embedding represents not only small but also large ground-truth pairwise distances (see Section A.2 for details).

sections.title: # Alternatives and hybrids
sections.text: Lexical baselines (n-grams, Levenshtein edit distance, phonetic hashing like Soundex/Levenshtein) are fast and useful for exact or near-exact matches and can be combined with embeddings for semantic matches. In practice, TF-IDF or n-gram similarity can pre-filter candidates, and embeddings score the remaining pairs to capture paraphrases and translation variants A hybrid system used TF-IDF for deduplication (cosine-thresholded) to remove redundant segments and a semantic model (BGE-M3) for database storage and retrieval [878c1538-2]. Specialized robust embeddings (e.g., RETSim) outperform n-gram methods in adversarial near-duplicate detection, making them valuable when data contains noisy or stylized variants RETSim is more robust than n-gram-based algorithms and faster than prior neural embeddings, suitable for large-scale deduplication and adversarial settings [878c1538-1].

citations.title: FinSage: A Multi-aspect RAG System for Financial Filings Question Answering
snippets:
Two embedding models are used in this project, each serving a distinct purpose: TF-IDF for text deduplication and BGE-M3 for storing text in the database. 

For the deduplication task, we employ the TF-IDF tool to convert the text into vector representations. This approach helps to identify and remove redundant text segments by comparing their vector similarities. The model uses term frequency and inverse document frequency to generate vectors, which are then compared using cosine similarity to detect high similarity between text segments. Text with similarities above a predefined threshold is removed, reducing redundancy. 

For storing text in the Chroma database, we use the BGE-M3 embedding model. This model, trained on large-scale datasets, transforms text into high-dimensional vectors that capture the semantic meaning of the content. These vectors are then stored in the database, enabling efficient indexing and retrieval for future similarity searches and semantic analysis.

citations.title: RETSim: Resilient and Efficient Text Similarity
snippets: In this paper, we introduced RETSim, a novel, multilingual text embedding which achieves stateof-the-art performance on near-duplicate text detection, dataset deduplication, and syntactic text similarity benchmarks. RETSim is significantly faster than previous neural-based text embeddings and more robust than n-gram based algorithms, which makes it suitable for large-scale text retrieval and dataset deduplication, especially in adversarial settings such as spam detection. Furthermore, we introduced the W4NT3D benchmark, the first multilingual dataset designed to measure the adversarial robustness of near-duplicate text detection algorithms. We open-source both RETSim and the W4NT3D benchmark under the MIT License. In this section, we randomly selected a set of false positives and false negatives for RETSim on the NEWS-COPY deduplication dataset to provide further insight into the results.

sections.title: # Step-by-step recipe
sections.text:
1) Data preparation: Normalize case and punctuation; keep both raw name and full description; deduplicate obvious exact duplicates if possible Deduplication pipelines iteratively compare embeddings and prune near-duplicates below a threshold [d5cd09cc-1].
2) Model selection: Choose a high-quality sentence encoder (e.g., SBERT all-mpnet-base-v2 or MiniLM) and, if multilingual, a multilingual variant; validate with MTEB-style tasks relevant to your domain MTEB provides comprehensive evaluation of embedding quality across multiple task types [a4e070ca-0] SBERT demonstrates strong performance on STS-style relatedness tasks with cosine similarity [65af70c1-1].
3) Embed and normalize: Encode names and descriptions; compute L2-normalized cosine vectors; consider adding TF-IDF/n-gram features for lexical overlap Sentence transformers generate vector representations of longer texts; cosine similarity captures semantic nuances [d5cd09cc-4] TF-IDF can be used alongside semantic embeddings for deduplication and retrieval [878c1538-2].
4) Candidate generation: Build an ANN index (e.g., FAISS) and retrieve top-K neighbors per name for candidate grouping FAISS-based nearest neighbor search supports efficient candidate retrieval for deduplication [d5cd09cc-1].
5) Clustering/deduplication: 
  - If you know the number of expected companies, cluster with mini-batch K-means and merge small clusters; 
  - If open-ended, use DBSCAN on cosine distance and merge small clusters; 
  - Always sample clusters and resolve conflicts with domain rules Mini-batch K-means with v-measure evaluation is standard for clustering tasks [a4e070ca-4] DBSCAN with cosine distance and threshold-based merging is effective for label/entry clustering [878c1538-3].
6) Thresholding and validation: 
  - Set pairwise cosine thresholds for deduplication and for linkage in clustering; 
  - Evaluate with task-specific metrics (Spearman for STS, V-measure for clustering, nDCG@k for retrieval); 
  - Inspect false positives/negatives and adjust thresholds and models accordingly Spearman correlation aligns with cosine-based STS evaluation [65af70c1-1] A threshold of 0.8 worked well in a large-scale deduplication setting [d5cd09cc-1] Inspection of false positives/negatives reveals model weaknesses and guides tuning [878c1538-1].
7) Multilingual support: Use multilingual encoders and evaluate on multilingual tasks; when translations exist, embeddings capture cross-language similarity better than lexical methods alone MTEB includes multilingual tasks to evaluate embeddings across languages [a4e070ca-0] Embedding plus ANN pipelines handle multilingual and translation-variant duplicates [d5cd09cc-4].
8) Robustness hardening: For adversarial or noisy data, consider specialized robust embeddings (e.g., RETSim) and add pre/post-processing for expansion/abbreviation normalization; stress-test on adversarial-like samples RETSim targets adversarial near-duplicate detection and achieves robust performance on deduplication and spam clustering [878c1538-0] RETSim is faster than prior neural embeddings and more robust than n-gram methods [878c1538-1].

snippets:
Note that the DBSCAN algorithm typically calculates distances between points using Euclidean distance by default. However, in this task, cosine similarity was used as the measure to capture the semantic relationships in word embeddings, where the direction of the vectors holds more meaning than their magnitude. Hence, a cosine distance matrix was computed and provided as input to the DBSCAN algorithm. The cosine similarity between two label embeddings e ij and e kl was defined as: 

where e ij , e kl ∈ R d are the embeddings of labels l ij and l kl respectively. The cosine distance, based on this similarity, is defined as: 

A cosine distance of 0 indicates perfect similarity, while values closer to 1 suggest greater dissimilarity. Given the pairwise cosine distance matrix D, where each entry D ij represents the cosine distance between the label embeddings e ij and e kl , the DBSCAN algorithm was applied using D. By setting appropriate values for ε and the minimum number of samples, DBSCAN identified clusters of labels that were semantically similar, while outliers or noise labels that did not fit into any dense cluster were left unclustered. After clustering the labels, the frequency of each label's occurrence across the entire dataset was calculated. Within each cluster, the label with the highest frequency in the dataset was selected as the cluster's representative label. This approach ensures that the representative label is both semantically relevant and statistically dominant within the dataset. Once the representative labels were determined, all labels in the dataset that belonged to the same cluster were replaced with their respective cluster representative. 

Note that, among all the clusters, there were some with a low number of labels, which are considered noise or outliers. Clusters containing very few labels pose challenges for downstream tasks, as they do not provide sufficient examples for a classifier to learn meaningful patterns. To address this, a threshold-based merging strategy was implemented. This process involved identifying clusters with label counts below a predefined threshold and merging them into the closest neighboring cluster based on the cosine distance between their cluster representative label.

We evaluate the performance of SBERT for STS without using any STS specific training data. We use the STS tasks 2012 -2016 (Agirre et al., 2012(Agirre et al., , 2013(Agirre et al., , 2014(Agirre et al., , 2015(Agirre et al., , 2016, the STS benchmark (Cer et al., 2017), and the SICK-Relatedness dataset (Marelli et al., 2014). These datasets provide labels between 0 and 5 on the semantic relatedness of sentence pairs. We showed in (Reimers et al., 2016) that Pearson correlation is badly suited for STS. Instead, we compute the Spearman's rank correlation between the cosine-similarity of the sentence embeddings and the gold labels. The setup for the other sentence embedding methods is equivalent, the similarity is computed by cosinesimilarity. The results are depicted in Table 1.

The results shows that directly using the output of BERT leads to rather poor performances. Averaging the BERT embeddings achieves an average correlation of only 54.81, and using the CLStoken output only achieves an average correlation of 29.19. Both are worse than computing average GloVe embeddings.

Using the described siamese network structure and fine-tuning mechanism substantially improves the correlation, outperforming both InferSent and Universal Sentence Encoder substantially. The only dataset where SBERT performs worse than Universal Sentence Encoder is SICK-R. Universal Sentence Encoder was trained on various datasets, including news, question-answer pages and discussion forums, which appears to be more suitable to the data of SICK-R. In contrast, SBERT was pre-trained only on Wikipedia (via BERT) and on NLI data.

While RoBERTa was able to improve the performance for several supervised tasks, we only observe minor difference between SBERT and SRoBERTa for generating sentence embeddings.

citations.title: X-ray Made Simple: Lay Radiology Report Generation and Robust Evaluation
snippets:
We first use NLTK to segment each report into individual sentences. Through analyzing large volumes of reports, we found that many repetitive sentences share similar semantics. To simplify the final dataset and reduce the burden of pairwise similarity computation, we apply extensive deduplication to the sentence-level inputs. To this end, we use GritLM (Muennighoff et al., 2024), a decoder-based embedding model that achieves state-of-the-art performance on the Massive Text Embedding Benchmark (MTEB) and the Reasoning as Retrieval Benchmark (RAR-b), to encode sentences and obtain their vector representations. 

We then iteratively compute pairwise cosine similarities between sentences, retaining those that do not exceed a similarity threshold of 0.8 with previously selected sentences and discarding the rest. Through this deduplication procedure, the number of sentences is reduced from approximately 490,000 to 50,000, substantially lowering computational cost and improving the efficiency of subsequent processing.

citations.title: RETSim: Resilient and Efficient Text Similarity
snippets: This paper introduces RETSim (Resilient and Efficient Text Similarity), a lightweight, multilingual deep learning model trained to produce robust metric embeddings for near-duplicate text retrieval, clustering, and dataset deduplication tasks. We demonstrate that RETSim is significantly more robust and accurate than MinHash and neural text embeddings, achieving new state-of-the-art performance on dataset deduplication, adversarial text retrieval benchmarks, and spam clustering tasks. sections.title: # Key takeaways
sections.text:
- Embedding-based similarity is the most reliable way to match company names under variations in wording, formatting, and language, especially when scaled with ANN search and clustering Neural sentence embeddings capture semantic information beyond shallow features and are essential for robust similarity [d5cd09cc-0] Modern encoders with cosine-thresholded deduplication and ANN scale to large corpora [d5cd09cc-1].
- Favor well-vetted models (SBERT/MiniLM/GritLM) and evaluate with MTEB-style metrics; for company-specific use, validate on domain data and adjust thresholds and clustering parameters to business requirements MTEB provides a broad suite for comparing embedding quality [a4e070ca-0] SBERT substantially improves STS over raw BERT and outperforms prior semantic encoders [65af70c1-1].
- Hybridize with TF-IDF/n-gram for lexical overlap and consider robust, adversarially trained embeddings (e.g., RETSim) when dealing with noisy or stylized variants TF-IDF plus semantic embeddings yields strong deduplication and retrieval [878c1538-2] RETSim improves robustness to adversarial near-duplicates and spam clustering [878c1538-0].
- For multilingual company data, use multilingual encoders and validate on multilingual tasks; embeddings outperform pure lexical baselines for translations and paraphrases Multilingual benchmarks in MTEB allow fair evaluation across languages [a4e070ca-0] Embedding-based ANN search handles multilingual, near-duplicate detection efficiently [d5cd09cc-4].

citations.title: Sentence-Embedding and Similarity via Hybrid Bidirectional-LSTM and CNN Utilizing Weighted-Pooling Attention
snippets:
In the present era, text understanding and information retrieval research have generated great interest among researchers for analyzing the sentence similarity in natural language processing (NLP). Although computing similarity facilitates many tasks such as plagiarism detection [1], query rank [2], and question answering [3], yet it is still a challenging issue, largely due to the intrinsic ambiguity of various linguistic sequences and the inadequate number of labeled training corpora available. On the other hand, conventional NLP methodologies utilized to operate similarity systems strongly depend on hand-crafted features [4]. Because a word is embedded in a multi-dimensional space with high-dimensional vectors, these features suffer from sparsity, unavoidably resulting in unacceptable complexity and inefficiency. 

Recent advancements in deep neural network (DNN) models have already brought outstanding performance improvements in various artificial intelligence operations related to computer vision, speech recognition, robotics, and NLP. In the last decade, many researchers have presented the effective modeling of words referred to as 'distributed word embedding', which are competent to explicitly encode both the semantic and syntactic information [5]. In this method, a word is embedded in the multi-dimensional vector space, where similar semantics contexts lie close to each other, e.g., the vector (("Madrid" − "Spain") + ("France")) is closer to vector ("Paris") than any other word vector. 

Today, word embedding has become extremely effective and is applied to various applications such as part-ofspeech (POS) tagging [6] and name entity recognition [7]. It has also demonstrated the potential for neural word representations for analogies tasks. 

Moreover, the increasing number of applications of DNNs has diverted the attention from word-level to larger texts, such as sentences embedding. Earlier approaches applied to look for sentence similarity are only able to capture the brief dependencies and similarities among characters, which is indeed not appropriate for finding similarity accurately. Therefore, these traditional approaches have limitations in capturing rich input sequence patterns between their correlations. In short, sentence embedding plays a vital role and is an emerging fundamental parameter in computing similarity.

question: What is Graph RAG?

sections.title: # What is Graph RAG?
sections.text:
Graph RAG (Graph Retrieval-Augmented Generation) is an extension of the Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG) paradigm that replaces or augments text-only retrieval with graph-structured memory or knowledge bases, enabling relational, path-based, and subgraph-level retrieval to improve reasoning and contextuality in large language models (LLMs). Graph-RAG augments the retrieval process by leveraging graph-based structures (e.g., knowledge graphs) to model relationships among entities and concepts, improving the relevance and contextuality of retrieved information compared to traditional RAG [e930c544-0] Graph Retrieval-Augmented Generation retrieves structured graph elements such as nodes, triples, paths, or subgraphs rather than unstructured text, enhancing relational knowledge and contextual understanding [e930c544-3] GraphRAG can be viewed as a branch of RAG that retrieves relevant relational knowledge from graph databases instead of text corpora, incorporating structural information beyond text [f39bd622-2].

At a high level, Graph RAG follows the same “retrieval then generation” loop as RAG, but the retrieval layer operates over graphs and the generation layer is conditioned on graph-derived context (e.g., nodes, edges, paths, or communities) plus textual descriptions, enabling relational reasoning that flat text retrieval alone may not support. In Graph RAG, the knowledge database is a graph G = (V, E) constructed from source documents, where nodes are entities and edges are relationships, and the retrieved context C is typically a subgraph with textual descriptions for entities and relations [e930c544-4] GraphRAG modifies indexing, retrieval, and generation into graph construction, graph-guided retrieval, and graph-augmented response generation, integrating structured knowledge via knowledge graphs [f39bd622-3].

citations.title: SemRAG: Semantic Knowledge-Augmented RAG for Improved Question-Answering
snippets: GraphRAG enhances traditional RAG by integrating structured knowledge through knowledge graphs, modifying indexing, retrieval, and generation into graph construction, graph-guided retrieval, and graph-augmented response generation [19]. In the indexing phase, GraphRAG builds a graph database from sources, public knowledge graphs or proprietary data, mapping nodes, edges, and relationships to facilitate structured retrieval. The retrieval process identifies relevant graph elements-entities, paths, or subgraphs-by aligning user queries with graph semantics, ensuring precise information extraction. During generation, retrieved graph elements augment prompts, enabling the model to generate more contextually accurate and informed responses [20]. Microsoft's advancements in GraphRAG introduce techniques such as iterative entity extraction and building hierarchical community detection via the Leiden algorithm, improving response retrieval efficiency and accuracy [21]. By leveraging structured knowledge, GraphRAG enhances retrieval efficiency and the contextual depth of generated responses compared to traditional RAG methods.

citations.title: CFT-RAG: An Entity Tree Based Retrieval Augmented Generation Algorithm With Cuckoo Filter
snippets:
Retrieval Augmented Generation Retrieval Augmented Generation(RAG) is a state-of-the-art method that combines information retrieval with large language models, with the aim of addressing the limitations of it in the absence of specific knowledge (Lewis et al., 2020). The core idea of RAG is to utilize an external knowledge base for retrieval and to incorporate relevant information into the generation process. Specifically, RAG first retrieves multiple relevant documents from the knowledge base on the basis of the input query, and then combines the retrieved knowledge with the input query to form the Figure 1. The workflow of CFT-RAG begins with a user query, which undergoes vector search to retrieve relevant documents. Key entities are then identified from entity trees by applying SpaCy and hierarchical tree searches. Context information related to these entities is retrieved and filtered efficiently by applying Cuckoo Filter. The retrieved context and hierarchical relationships are integrated into a comprehensive prompt, which is fed into an augmented large language model (LLM). The LLM processes this enriched prompt to generate a context-aware and accurate response to the user query. 

context and then generate the final answer through the generative model. This approach significantly improves the quality and relevance of the generated text (Karpukhin et al., 2020) and avoids the limitations of fixed model knowledge (Gupta et al., 2024). Compared to fine-tuning, RAG has a greater ability to update knowledge and also reduces the dependence on large-scale data. 

Graph-RAG Graph Retrieval-Augmented Generation (Graph-RAG) is an extension of RAG, where the information retrieval process is augmented by leveraging graph-based structures to organize and retrieve information (Lewis et al., 2020). The key difference between traditional RAG and Graph-RAG is the use of a graph, such as a knowledge graph, to model relationships between entities and concepts, which can improve the relevance and contextuality of the retrieved information (Hu et al., 2024). The algorithmic process of Graph-RAG enhances the understanding of relationships and provides more precise information retrieval than traditional RAG (Darrin et al., 2024). However, the complexity in graph construction and maintenance will be a trouble, the quality and completeness of the graph can also affect the accuracy of responses generated by the model.

citations.title: Graph Retrieval-Augmented Generation: A Survey
snippets:
RAG combines external knowledge with LLMs for improved task performance, integrating domainspecific information to ensure factuality and credibility. In the past two years, researchers have written many comprehensive surveys about RAG [34,45,59,62,178,195,202]. For example, Fan et al. [34] and Gao et al. [45] categorize RAG methods from the perspectives of retrieval, generation, and augmentation. Zhao et al. [202] review RAG methods for databases with different modalities. Yu et al. [195] systematically summarize the evaluation of RAG methods. These works J. ACM, Vol. 37, No. 4, Article 111. Publication date: September 2024. 

Graph Retrieval-Augmented Generation: A Survey 111:5 provide a structured synthesis of current RAG methodologies, fostering a deeper understanding and suggesting future directions of the area. 

From a broad perspective, GraphRAG can be seen as a branch of RAG, which retrieves relevant relational knowledge from graph databases instead of text corpus. However, compared to textbased RAG, GraphRAG takes into account the relationships between texts and incorporates the structural information as additional knowledge beyond text. Furthermore, during the construction of graph data, raw text data may undergo filtering and summarization processes, enhancing the refinement of information within the graph data. Although previous surveys on RAG have touched upon GraphRAG, they predominantly center on textual data integration. This paper diverges by placing a primary emphasis on the indexing, retrieval, and utilization of structured graph data, which represents a substantial departure from handling purely textual information and spurs the emergence of many new techniques.

snippets:
Despite their advanced language comprehension and text generation capabilities, Large Language Models (LLMs) face limitations due to gaps in domain-specific knowledge, real-time updates, and proprietary information beyond their pre-training corpus. These gaps often lead to ''hallucination", where inaccurate or fabricated content is generated. Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG), is an information retrieval technique that was initially introduced by Meta AI (Lewis et al., 2020) to improve the LLMs performance to retrieve correct answers from textual data. By utilising an external knowledge base, RAG has proven highly effective in enhancing LLM outputs as it addresses problems such as ''hallucination" caused by outdated information or insufficient domain-specific knowledge not included in the LLMs' pre-training data (Siriwardhana et al., 2023;Peng et al., 2024;Fan et al., 2024). sections.title: # How Graph RAG Differs from Traditional RAG
sections.text: Traditional RAG retrieves and conditions generation on text chunks matched to the query, often via dense vector similarity. Graph RAG shifts emphasis from lexical similarity to structural and relational similarity, retrieving graph elements (entities, relations, paths, communities) and optionally aligning them back to text for grounding. In standard RAG, retrieval returns top-K chunks ranked by sim(q, c) and the LLM produces the final response [e930c544-1] Unlike traditional RAG, Graph-RAG retrieves structured graph elements (nodes, triples, paths, or subgraphs) to enhance relational context [e930c544-3] The retrieved context in Graph RAG is typically a subgraph (entities and relations) whose nodes/edges carry textual descriptions for grounding [e930c544-4]. This shift lets Graph RAG exploit entity relationships, paths, and communities for tasks like multi-hop reasoning, entity-centric QA, and schema-aware generation. The key difference is modeling relationships via a graph (e.g., a knowledge graph) to improve relevance and contextuality [e930c544-0] Compared to text-based RAG, GraphRAG incorporates graph structure as additional knowledge and may refine information via filtering and summarization during graph construction [f39bd622-2].

sections.title: # Core Components and Architectures
sections.text:
- Graph construction. Systems build a graph from documents, public knowledge graphs, or proprietary data, defining nodes (entities, events, concepts), edges (relations), and mappings to supporting text. Indexing constructs a graph database from sources, knowledge graphs, or proprietary data, mapping nodes, edges, and relationships for structured retrieval [f39bd622-3] Raw text may be filtered and summarized during graph construction, refining information within the graph [f39bd622-4] DyG-RAG follows a general Graph RAG pipeline: a constructor transforms text data into a graph-structured source G [b4313e7a-3].

- Retrieval over graphs. Retrievers can return entities, relations, paths, or subgraphs aligned with the query semantics, sometimes organized into communities or hierarchical layers. Graph-RAG retrieves nodes, triples, paths, or subgraphs to enhance relational reasoning [e930c544-3] Retrieval is guided by graph semantics to identify relevant graph elements (entities, paths, subgraphs) [f39bd622-3] Workflows may include community detection (e.g., Leiden) and summaries to improve retrieval, though this adds overhead and token costs [b4313e7a-0] Hierarchical index graphs with document-level links can be efficient but are too coarse for nuanced reasoning, highlighting a granularity trade-off [b4313e7a-1].

- Generation conditioning. The LLM is conditioned on retrieved graph elements plus their textual descriptions (and sometimes on the graph path structure), to produce answers that are grounded in relational evidence. Each entity and relationship in the retrieved subgraph is associated with a textual description, which the LLM uses to generate the response [e930c544-4] During generation, retrieved graph elements augment prompts to enable more contextually accurate and informed responses [f39bd622-3] A query processor feeds Q to the retriever to obtain C, and the LLM generates the final answer using C′ as triggers [b4313e7a-3].

- Document-text alignment. Many Graph RAG systems retain links to original text chunks for grounding and citation, so graph nodes/edges often reference or summarize underlying documents. Nodes and edges are derived from D and associated with textual descriptions; context C is a subgraph selected to answer the query [e930c544-4] During graph construction, raw text can be filtered and summarized, enhancing refinement before mapping to graph elements [f39bd622-4].

citations.title: Query-Centric Graph Retrieval Augmented Generation
snippets: Document Expansion with Doc2Query & Doc2Query--. Doc2Query (Nogueira et al., 2019) is a document expansion technique that trains sequence-to-sequence models (e.g., T5 (Raffel et al., 2020)) to generate queries likely associated with a given document, thereby improving retrieval by appending the generated queries to the document chunks. Doc2Query-- (Gospodinov et al., 2023) refines this approach by filtering out irrelevant or hallucinated queries based on their similarity to the original chunks, which improves retrieval quality while reducing index overhead. The queries produced by these methods naturally operate at an intermediate granularity: richer and more interpretable than fine-grained entity triples, yet more precise than coarse-grained document chunks. This property makes them well suited for integration with graph-based RAG, where query nodes enable controllable, query-centric graph (QCG) construction that balances granularity and enhances both the accuracy and interpretability of multi-hop retrieval.

citations.title: SemRAG: Semantic Knowledge-Augmented RAG for Improved Question-Answering
snippets: GraphRAG enhances traditional RAG by integrating structured knowledge through knowledge graphs, modifying indexing, retrieval, and generation into graph construction, graph-guided retrieval, and graph-augmented response generation [19]. In the indexing phase, GraphRAG builds a graph database from sources, public knowledge graphs or proprietary data, mapping nodes, edges, and relationships to facilitate structured retrieval. The retrieval process identifies relevant graph elements-entities, paths, or subgraphs-by aligning user queries with graph semantics, ensuring precise information extraction. During generation, retrieved graph elements augment prompts, enabling the model to generate more contextually accurate and informed responses [20]. Microsoft's advancements in GraphRAG introduce techniques such as iterative entity extraction and building hierarchical community detection via the Leiden algorithm, improving response retrieval efficiency and accuracy [21]. By leveraging structured knowledge, GraphRAG enhances retrieval efficiency and the contextual depth of generated responses compared to traditional RAG methods.

citations.title: Query-Centric Graph Retrieval Augmented Generation
snippets: For instance, GraphRAG imposes considerable computational overhead: constructing fine-grained entity-level graphs and producing community summaries inflate token budgets and inference cost, and can erode contextual coherence (Min et al., 2025;Zhang et al., 2025a). Recent work simplifies graph construction by skipping community detection and summarization, and instead using lightweight information extractors (e.g., SpaCy (Honnibal et al., 2020)) or fine-tuned small LLMs (e.g., Phi-3-3.8B (Abdin et al., 2024), but at the cost of lower graph quality. Other efforts adopt hierarchical index graphs with document-level links (Chen et al., 2024), which are efficient but too coarse to support nuanced reasoning. These limitations highlight the need for strategies that balance granularity and effectiveness in graph-based RAG. Document expansion techniques, such as Doc2Query (Nogueira et al., 2019) for generating queries from documents and Doc2Query-- (Gospodinov et al., 2023) for filtering irrelevant queries, pro-Figure 1: Illustration of (a) coarse-grained document-level graphs, (b) fine-grained entity-level graphs, and (c) controllable-grained query-centric graphs for RAG. vide a query-centric expansion paradigm. We argue that integrating Doc2Query-generated queries with graphs enables the construction of a controllable query-centric graph that lies between finegrained entity-level and coarse-grained document-level representations. To overcome the above mentioned granularity dilemma, we propose Query-Centric Graph Retrieval-Augmented Generation (QCG-RAG), a framework that tailors graph construction and retrieval to the granularity of queries. QCG-RAG introduces a query-centric graph (QCG), constructed with Doc2Query and Doc2Query-techniques to generate query-guided nodes and edges, yielding indexing graphs with controllable granularity.

sections.title: # Typical Construction Patterns
sections.text:
- Entity- and relation-centric graphs. Nodes represent entities and relations; edges encode typed relationships; paths capture chains of relations for multi-hop reasoning. Graph-RAG retrieves entities, triples, paths, or subgraphs rather than unstructured text [e930c544-3] Fine-grained entity-level graphs and community summaries can inflate token budgets and reduce coherence, motivating trade-offs in granularity [b4313e7a-0].

- Community/hierarchical graphs. Graphs may include community structures (e.g., via Leiden) or hierarchical layers (documents linked to sections/paragraphs/entities) to balance coverage and efficiency. Microsoft-style GraphRAG has introduced hierarchical community detection via the Leiden algorithm to improve retrieval efficiency and accuracy [b4313e7a-0] Hierarchical index graphs with document-level links are efficient but too coarse for nuanced reasoning [b4313e7a-1].

- Semantic expansion with Doc2Query. Query-centric Graph RAG integrates Doc2Query to generate query-associated nodes and edges, enabling controllable granularity between entity triples and document chunks and improving multi-hop retrieval accuracy and interpretability. QCG-RAG constructs a query-centric graph (QCG) using Doc2Query and Doc2Query-- to generate query-guided nodes and edges, yielding indexing graphs with controllable granularity [b4313e7a-2] Doc2Query expands documents into associated queries (e.g., T5-based), and Doc2Query-- filters hallucinated/irrelevant queries, producing richer, intermediate-granularity queries well-suited for graph-based RAG [b4313e7a-1].

- Event-centric dynamic graphs. Event-centric Graph RAGs build time-ordered or temporal graphs for reasoning over sequences and changes. DyG-RAG frames Graph RAG with an event-centric pipeline: a constructor builds G from event data, a retriever finds relevant content C given Q, and LLMs generate answers using C′ as triggers [b4313e7a-3].

snippets:

Figure 1 illustrates (a) coarse-grained document-level graphs, (b) fine-grained entity-level graphs, and (c) controllable-grained query-centric graphs for RAG. The main contributions of this paper are threefold: 

• Query-Centric Graph Construction. We present the first query-driven, granularity-controllable graph construction framework for RAG, which improves graph quality and preserves interpretability via generated queries. 

• Query-Centric Retrieval & Generation Mechanism. We develop an effective multi-hop retrieval process on QCG, which enables accurate retrieval of relevant text chunks for complex queries. 

• Comprehensive Evaluation. We conduct experiments demonstrating that QCG-RAG consistently outperforms prior chunk-based and graph-based RAG methods in question answering accuracy.

sections.title: # Empirical Evidence and Benchmarks
sections.text: Comparative evaluations indicate that well-designed Graph RAG systems can outperform chunk-based and even prior graph-based RAG methods on question-answering tasks, particularly when retrieval is guided by graph semantics and community structures. Experiments on QCG-RAG show it consistently outperforms prior chunk-based and graph-based RAG methods in question-answering accuracy [b4313e7a-2]. Industry-aligned methods report efficiency and accuracy gains from hierarchical/community-aware indexing and iterative entity extraction, while noting that simplifications (e.g., skipping community summarization for lighter graphs) trade quality for cost. snippets: GraphRAG enhances traditional RAG by integrating structured knowledge through knowledge graphs, modifying indexing, retrieval, and generation into graph construction, graph-guided retrieval, and graph-augmented response generation [19]. During generation, retrieved graph elements augment prompts, enabling the model to generate more contextually accurate and informed responses [20]. citations.title: Query-Centric Graph Retrieval Augmented Generation
snippets: Document Expansion with Doc2Query & Doc2Query--. Doc2Query (Nogueira et al., 2019) is a document expansion technique that trains sequence-to-sequence models (e.g., T5 (Raffel et al., 2020)) to generate queries likely associated with a given document, thereby improving retrieval by appending the generated queries to the document chunks. Doc2Query-- (Gospodinov et al., 2023) refines this approach by filtering out irrelevant or hallucinated queries based on their similarity to the original chunks, which improves retrieval quality while reducing index overhead. The queries produced by these methods naturally operate at an intermediate granularity: richer and more interpretable than fine-grained entity triples, yet more precise than coarse-grained document chunks. This property makes them well suited for integration with graph-based RAG, where query nodes enable controllable, query-centric graph (QCG) construction that balances granularity and enhances both the accuracy and interpretability of multi-hop retrieval.

sections.title: # Limitations and Open Challenges
sections.text:
- Construction and maintenance complexity. Building high-quality graphs from raw text and heterogeneous sources, including schema design, entity linking, filtering, and summarization, is nontrivial and can become a bottleneck. Complexity in graph construction and maintenance is a trouble, and graph quality/completeness affects model accuracy [e930c544-0] Graph construction involves filtering and summarization to refine information, adding steps and potential error sources [f39bd622-4].

- Granularity trade-offs. Overly fine-grained graphs with detailed summaries and communities can inflate token budgets and reduce coherence; overly coarse graphs miss nuance. Fine-grained graphs and community summaries inflate token budgets and can erode contextual coherence [b4313e7a-0] Hierarchical document-level graphs are efficient but too coarse for nuanced reasoning [b4313e7a-1].

- Privacy and data leakage risks. If graphs expose sensitive relations or merged entities, retrieval can leak confidential information; careful access control and graph design are needed. A formal setup shows Graph RAG’s notations and motivates privacy risk analysis, where C (subgraph context) and textual descriptions can raise confidentiality concerns [f39bd622-4].

- Coherence and grounding. Aligning multi-hop graph paths and communities back to grounded text is essential to avoid drifting; retrieval must jointly respect graph structure and textual evidence. Community-based and fine-grained retrieval can reduce contextual coherence, indicating the need to balance structure with faithful grounding [b4313e7a-0] Retrieved subgraphs are accompanied by textual descriptions of entities/relations to support grounding [e930c544-4].

snippets:
Retrieval Augmented Generation Retrieval Augmented Generation(RAG) is a state-of-the-art method that combines information retrieval with large language models, with the aim of addressing the limitations of it in the absence of specific knowledge (Lewis et al., 2020). The core idea of RAG is to utilize an external knowledge base for retrieval and to incorporate relevant information into the generation process. Specifically, RAG first retrieves multiple relevant documents from the knowledge base on the basis of the input query, and then combines the retrieved knowledge with the input query to form the Figure 1. The workflow of CFT-RAG begins with a user query, which undergoes vector search to retrieve relevant documents. Key entities are then identified from entity trees by applying SpaCy and hierarchical tree searches. Context information related to these entities is retrieved and filtered efficiently by applying Cuckoo Filter. The retrieved context and hierarchical relationships are integrated into a comprehensive prompt, which is fed into an augmented large language model (LLM). The LLM processes this enriched prompt to generate a context-aware and accurate response to the user query. 

context and then generate the final answer through the generative model. This approach significantly improves the quality and relevance of the generated text (Karpukhin et al., 2020) and avoids the limitations of fixed model knowledge (Gupta et al., 2024). Compared to fine-tuning, RAG has a greater ability to update knowledge and also reduces the dependence on large-scale data. 

Graph-RAG Graph Retrieval-Augmented Generation (Graph-RAG) is an extension of RAG, where the information retrieval process is augmented by leveraging graph-based structures to organize and retrieve information (Lewis et al., 2020). The key difference between traditional RAG and Graph-RAG is the use of a graph, such as a knowledge graph, to model relationships between entities and concepts, which can improve the relevance and contextuality of the retrieved information (Hu et al., 2024). The algorithmic process of Graph-RAG enhances the understanding of relationships and provides more precise information retrieval than traditional RAG (Darrin et al., 2024). However, the complexity in graph construction and maintenance will be a trouble, the quality and completeness of the graph can also affect the accuracy of responses generated by the model.

sections.title: # Summary
sections.text:
- Definition and motivation: Graph RAG extends RAG by retrieving and reasoning over graph-structured knowledge, capturing entity relations, paths, and communities to improve contextuality and reasoning. Graph-RAG leverages graph-based structures (e.g., knowledge graphs) to model relationships and improve retrieval relevance [e930c544-0] It retrieves nodes, triples, paths, or subgraphs rather than unstructured text [e930c544-3].

- Pipeline: constructor → query processor/retriever over G → LLM generator conditioned on subgraph context and textual descriptions. A general Graph RAG pipeline constructs G from text sources, retrieves relevant content C given Q, and uses C′ to trigger LLM generation [b4313e7a-3] The graph G=(V,E) is built from D with nodes/edges and textual descriptions; context C is a subgraph [e930c544-4].

- Techniques: Doc2Query-based query-centric graphs, hierarchical/community-aware indexing (e.g., Leiden), and dynamic/event-centric graphs. QCG-RAG integrates Doc2Query and Doc2Query-- to build query-centric graphs and show improved QA accuracy [b4313e7a-2] Community detection and summarization improve retrieval but add overhead; hierarchical graphs are efficient but coarse [b4313e7a-0] DyG-RAG exemplifies event-centric Graph RAG for temporal reasoning [b4313e7a-3].

- Evidence: Well-designed Graph RAG systems outperform chunk-based and prior graph-based methods on QA, with trade-offs in granularity, cost, and privacy. QCG-RAG consistently outperforms prior RAG variants in QA accuracy [b4313e7a-2] Balancing granularity and structure is key to maintaining coherence and efficiency [b4313e7a-0] Privacy risks arise from subgraph context and entity/relationship descriptions, requiring careful design [f39bd622-4].

In short, Graph RAG is a principled way to bring relational, structured knowledge into retrieval-augmented generation, improving reasoning when queries depend on entity relations and multi-hop evidence, at the cost of more complex graph construction, maintenance, and privacy considerations. GraphRAG’s emphasis on graph indexing/retrieval and structured knowledge represents a departure from text-only RAG and motivates new techniques [f39bd622-2] The benefits come with added complexity in graph construction and dependence on graph quality [e930c544-0].

RAG combines external knowledge with LLMs for improved task performance, integrating domainspecific information to ensure factuality and credibility. In the past two years, researchers have written many comprehensive surveys about RAG [34,45,59,62,178,195,202]. For example, Fan et al. [34] and Gao et al. [45] categorize RAG methods from the perspectives of retrieval, generation, and augmentation. Zhao et al. [202] review RAG methods for databases with different modalities. Yu et al. [195] systematically summarize the evaluation of RAG methods. These works J. ACM, Vol. 37, No. 4, Article 111. Publication date: September 2024. 

Graph Retrieval-Augmented Generation: A Survey 111:5 provide a structured synthesis of current RAG methodologies, fostering a deeper understanding and suggesting future directions of the area. 

From a broad perspective, GraphRAG can be seen as a branch of RAG, which retrieves relevant relational knowledge from graph databases instead of text corpus. However, compared to textbased RAG, GraphRAG takes into account the relationships between texts and incorporates the structural information as additional knowledge beyond text. Furthermore, during the construction of graph data, raw text data may undergo filtering and summarization processes, enhancing the refinement of information within the graph data. Although previous surveys on RAG have touched upon GraphRAG, they predominantly center on textual data integration. This paper diverges by placing a primary emphasis on the indexing, retrieval, and utilization of structured graph data, which represents a substantial departure from handling purely textual information and spurs the emergence of many new techniques.

citations.title: CFT-RAG: An Entity Tree Based Retrieval Augmented Generation Algorithm With Cuckoo Filter
snippets:
Retrieval Augmented Generation Retrieval Augmented Generation(RAG) is a state-of-the-art method that combines information retrieval with large language models, with the aim of addressing the limitations of it in the absence of specific knowledge (Lewis et al., 2020). The core idea of RAG is to utilize an external knowledge base for retrieval and to incorporate relevant information into the generation process. Specifically, RAG first retrieves multiple relevant documents from the knowledge base on the basis of the input query, and then combines the retrieved knowledge with the input query to form the Figure 1. The workflow of CFT-RAG begins with a user query, which undergoes vector search to retrieve relevant documents. Key entities are then identified from entity trees by applying SpaCy and hierarchical tree searches. Context information related to these entities is retrieved and filtered efficiently by applying Cuckoo Filter. The retrieved context and hierarchical relationships are integrated into a comprehensive prompt, which is fed into an augmented large language model (LLM). The LLM processes this enriched prompt to generate a context-aware and accurate response to the user query. 

context and then generate the final answer through the generative model. This approach significantly improves the quality and relevance of the generated text (Karpukhin et al., 2020) and avoids the limitations of fixed model knowledge (Gupta et al., 2024). Compared to fine-tuning, RAG has a greater ability to update knowledge and also reduces the dependence on large-scale data. 

Graph-RAG Graph Retrieval-Augmented Generation (Graph-RAG) is an extension of RAG, where the information retrieval process is augmented by leveraging graph-based structures to organize and retrieve information (Lewis et al., 2020). The key difference between traditional RAG and Graph-RAG is the use of a graph, such as a knowledge graph, to model relationships between entities and concepts, which can improve the relevance and contextuality of the retrieved information (Hu et al., 2024). The algorithmic process of Graph-RAG enhances the understanding of relationships and provides more precise information retrieval than traditional RAG (Darrin et al., 2024). However, the complexity in graph construction and maintenance will be a trouble, the quality and completeness of the graph can also affect the accuracy of responses generated by the model.
