citations.title: TerEffic: Highly Efficient Ternary LLM Inference on FPGA
snippets:
Quantization has been a key strategy to accelerate inference as neural networks grow rapidly in parameter count. Among the various quantization methods, binary and ternary quantizations feature extremely compressed weights that require little memory capacity and bandwidth. They were initially validated in CNN models such as BNN [13], XNOR-Net [14], and TWN [15], achieving high efficiency with minimal accuracy loss. 

Entering the era of LLMs, larger model sizes and limited hardware resources further necessitate low-bit quantization, especially in the context of edge devices. LLMs utilizing binary or ternary quantization are also referred to as '1-bit' LLMs, as each weight theoretically takes less than 2 bits for storage. As a pioneer of 1-bit LLM, BitNet [8] employed binary quantization and introduced the BitLinear layer as a replacement for linear projections. As its variant and improvement, BitNet 1.58b [9] utilized ternary quantization to match the performance of fullprecision (fp16 or bf16) Transformers. Later, TernaryLLM [16] leveraged knowledge distillation in its training and surpassed previous low-bit quantization methods. However, as the Q, K, V matrices in the self-attention mechanism remain in high precision, the high-precision matrix multiplications were not eliminated. To address this issue and realize a fully 'MatMul-free' model, [17] used an RNN variant to replace the traditional self-attention in their ternary model and achieved excellent performance. Furthermore, this 1-bit quantization trend was extended to the Vision Transformer (ViT) domain [18] and a scaling law [19] was established, providing a theoretical basis for the impressive performance of these 1-bit models. Advances in post-training reparameterization [20] also paved the way for low-cost training of 1-bit LLMs. More recently, Microsoft released an official CPU inference framework for BitNet, bitnet.cpp [21]. However, this framework focused on the software level, while ternary models still have significant potential for improvements from custom hardware.

citations.title: PTQTP: Post-Training Quantization to Trit-Planes for Large Language Models
snippets:
PTQ for LLMs. PTQ has emerged as a promising approach for compressing LLMs without the computational overhead of retraining. GPTQ (Frantar et al., 2022) pioneered efficient quantization through layer-wise optimization, achieving 4-bit quantization while maintaining model performance. AWQ (Lin et al., 2024) further improved this by incorporating activation-aware scaling, demonstrating that the consideration of activations during quantization leads to better performance. Recent work has pushed towards even lower bit-width quantization. PBLLM (Shang et al., 2023) and BiLLM (Huang et al., 2024) achieved 1-bit quantization by identifying and preserving structurally salient weights while applying different quantization strategies to different weight groups. ARB-LLM (Li et al., 2025) further refined this approach through alternating optimization of binary weight groups. 

However, these methods rely on complex, unstructured weight categorizations that complicate hardware implementation. 

Ternary Quantization The transition from binary to ternary quantization represents a leap of model expressiveness while still preserving multiplier-less arithmetic. BitNet's (Wang et al., 2023) extension to 1.58-bit (ternary) weights (Ma et al., 2024) demonstrated superior performance compared to binary models, suggesting the value of the additional state in the ternary representation. There are also some other trit-plane-based works on image-compression domain (Lee et al., 2022;Jeon et al., 2023). 

Hardware Efficiency. A key advantage of binary and ternary quantization lies in their suitability for FPGA or ASIC deployment (e.g., FlightLLM (Zeng et al., 2024), DFX (Hong et al., 2023)), where multiplier-less feature-weight products can be efficiently implemented in hardware. Specifically, binary operations can be realized with XNOR gates and bit-counting, while ternary operations leverage simple adders, preserving computational efficiency while offering greater expressivity.

sections.title: # How the parameters are represented and computed
sections.text: At a linear layer, a full‑precision weight W∈R^{m×n} is quantized into a low‑bit representation W_q∈{-1,0,1}^{m×n} (binary or ternary) and used to compute y = W_q^T x via dot products. A ternary weight matrix allows only values {-1, 0, 1}, so the usual Wx is replaced by a sum of scaled sign activations, enabling adder‑based hardware pipelines [7f09eafa-2]. OneBit proposes a model structure and initialization tailored to 1‑bit weight quantization, showing that carefully designed parameterization can achieve a favorable size–performance trade‑off [7f09eafa-4]. Sigma‑Delta Quantization (SDQ‑LLM) generalizes low‑bit weight encoding by upsampling and dithering to control precision/compression jointly via an over‑sampling ratio (OSR), with Hadamard smoothing to reduce quantization noise [7f09eafa-1].

citations.title: OneBit: Towards Extremely Low-bit Large Language Models
snippets: We propose a novel model structure for 1-bit weight quantization and a corresponding parameter initialization method to address the difficulty in 1-bit quantization. Extensive experiments on LLMs of various sizes and series demonstrate that OneBit has clear advantages over representative strong baselines and achieves a good tradeoff between model size and performance. We further analyze the capabilities of such extremely low-bit quantized models and provide guidance for future research.

citations.title: SDQ-LLM: Sigma-Delta Quantization for 1-bit LLMs of any size
snippets:
In binarization, parameters are typically represented as binary values (e.g., -1 and +1) using the sign function. Representative methods include PB-LLM [23], BiLLM [10], and OneBit [22], which apply binary quantization to large language models to minimize memory and computation. In contrast, ternarization extends this approach by allowing an additional zero state (e.g., -1, 0, +1), offering a better trade-off between accuracy and efficiency. A representative ternarization-based approach is BitNet b1.58 [13], which achieves improved performance under extremely low-bit quantization settings. Extremely low-bit quantization of model parameters is significant for hardware deployment, as techniques like binarizing or ternarizing parameters can convert multiplication operations in linear transformations to addition operations, greatly reducing hardware computation costs. However, extremely low-bit quantization often leads to considerable accuracy loss, making it difficult to apply in practice. 

In the face of the formidable challenges posed by extremely lowbit quantization in large language models, we introduce the SDQ-LLM, Sigma-Delta Quantization for 1-bit LLMs of any size. By ingeniously repurposing the upsampling quantization principle rooted in sigma-delta analog-to-digital converters, SDQ-LLM pioneers a novel paradigm for parameter quantization in LLMs. Our research culminates in four key contributions that significantly advance the field: 

• We propose SDQ-LLM, an upsampling-based Sigma-Delta quantization scheme designed for LLM parameters. This method enables extremely low-bit quantization while maintaining continuous control over both precision and model size. By adjusting the Over-Sampling Ratio (OSR), SDQ-LLM achieves a flexible balance between accuracy and compression, making it adaptable to a wide range of requirements and ensuring optimal performance across different use cases. • To boost SDQ-LLM's quantization precision, we introduce the Hadamard matrix for weight smoothing. This technique reduces quantization errors and noise, ensuring more stable and reliable weight representations and improving the quantized model's overall quality.

sections.title: # Training and post‑training quantization: clipping, scaling, and STE
sections.text:
Because quantization is non‑differentiable, training uses approximations like the Straight‑Through Estimator (STE) to backpropagate gradients through the quantizer, along with clipping and scaling to keep weights within the low‑bit dynamic range. Quantization‑aware training (QAT) commonly applies STE during backprop to approximate gradients through non‑differentiable quantize‑op, while adding a regularization/distillation term can reduce quantization error and speed convergence [2da7a966-1]. For weights with b>2 bits, a typical QAT quantization function clips weights and rounds to a narrow range; for 1‑bit, DoReFa‑style schemes are used, and for 2‑bit, trained/ternary schemes are applied, with STE used across all cases [2da7a966-2]. In BitNet‑style LLMs, weights are mapped to ternary {-1,0,1} via per‑tensor clipping (e.g., absmean) and rounding, and activations are often quantized to 8 bits; non‑differentiable ops are handled with STE [26a371de-0]. Loss‑aware post‑training quantization (LAPQ) optimizes clipping parameters to directly minimize the loss, addressing the non‑convex, non‑separable nature of low‑precision quantized losses and improving accuracy over layer‑wise heuristics [2da7a966-0].

There are also fully 1‑bit or binary‑weight/activation approaches trained via QAT or PTQ. Several 1‑bit Transformer architectures (BitNet b1.58, OneBit, FBI‑LLM) replace linear layers with quantized equivalents to push weights to 1‑bit; other PTQ methods (BiLLM, STBLLM) achieve 1‑bit binary weights without fine‑tuning by exploiting residual structure and group partitioning, though activation quantization may remain a bottleneck for full speed‑ups [26a371de-3]. Fully binarized models target both weights and activations, but they are more challenging and often require specialized techniques for non‑linearities. Recent work explores fully binary weight and activation LLMs, motivated by the difficulty of going below 4 bits with earlier methods [26a371de-3].

citations.title: Loss aware post-training quantization
snippets:
In this paper we analyzed loss function of quantized neural networks. We show that for low precision quantization loss function is non-convex and non-separable. In such conditions existing methods that minimize some local metric can not perform well.

We introduce Loss Aware Post-training quantization (LAPQ), which optimizes clipping parameters of the quantization function by directly minimizing loss function. Our method outperforms most previously suggested methods for post-training quantization. Our method does not assume special hardware support like channel-wise or filter-wise quantization. To the best of our knowledge LAPQ is a first that achieve near FP32 accuracy at 4 bit layer-wise quantization in post-training regime.

citations.title: Achieving binary weight and activation for LLMs using Post-Training Quantization
snippets:
Considerable research efforts have been devoted to the low-resource computation of LLMs (Dettmers et al., 2024;Chen et al., 2024). Existing works have achieved near-lossless quantization at W4A4 through methods such as mixed-precision quantization (Zhao et al., 2024) and outlier smoothing using rotation factors (Ashkboos et al., 2024;Liu et al., 2024b). However, these methods encounter difficulties when attempting to push towards even lower-bit quantization below 4 bits. Recently, researchers start to seek binarization methods (Courbariaux and Bengio, 2016;Qin et al., 2022) for LLMs. One line of works are based on Quantization-Aware Training (QAT) method. For example, BitNet b1.58 (Wang et al., 2023), BitNet a4.8 (Wang et al., 2024), OneBit (Xu et al., 2024), and FBI-LLM (Ma et al., 2024) have designed 1-bit Transformer architectures specifically for LLMs, replacing original linear layers with specific quantized version. These methods can reduce the quantization bit-width of weights to 1 bit and demonstrate significant advantages over baseline models. However, these QAT methods require substantial computational resources, making it impractical for the quantization of LLMs. 

Another line of works explored the possibility of binarizing LLMs within the PTQ framework. BiLLM (Huang et al., 2024a) and STBLLM (Dong et al., 2024), inspired by the distribution characteristics of weight values and the Hessian matrix, adopt binary residual approximations for significant weights and optimal partitioning for group binarization of non-significant weights, which pushes the quantization boundary of LLM weights down to 1 bit. However, these works neglect the quantization of activation values, which obstructs the computational acceleration of the quantized model and ultimately results in relatively slow inference speed. 

Most recently, people start to explore fully binarized models for both weight and activation.

sections.title: # Activation quantization and stability
sections.text: Quantizing activations to very low bits can cause outliers and instability unless carefully controlled. In BitNet distillation, LLM inputs are often quantized at 8 bits (per‑token clipping), and 1.58‑bit weight quantization uses STE to handle non‑differentiable rounds/clip; additional normalization layers (SubLN) are inserted before quantized projections to stabilize hidden representation scales and improve training stability and downstream performance [26a371de-0]. For activation quantization, common pipelines clamp to [0,1], multiply by a scale (2^n−1), and round, with STE used for gradients; for binary activations, weights are often approximated as W≈α·sign(W) with α* being the mean/absolute mean of weights [26a371de-1]. However, integer‑only PTQ for LLMs faces challenges due to large activation fluctuations across tokens and channels, even in non‑linear blocks (e.g., SwiGLU, RMSNorm), which harms accuracy compared to CNNs/ViT; specialized smoothing (e.g., FSBR) is proposed to harmonize activation variance for low‑bit integer inference [26a371de-2].

sections.title: # Inference kernels and hardware efficiency
sections.text: The low‑bit representations enable multiplier‑less or near‑multiplier‑less matrix multiplications that map to fast bit‑wise operations and adders on CPU/GPU/accelerators. Hardware‑oriented analyses distinguish bit‑wise vs. element‑wise edge mpGEMM: bit‑wise methods operate at the bit level (e.g., LUT/XNOR‑based), while element‑wise methods handle elements with properties that allow non‑integer bits per weight; both exploit the fact that ternary/binary products can be implemented with adders and bit ops instead of general multipliers [7f09eafa-2]. Binary operations can be realized with XNOR gates and bit counting, while ternary operations use adders, enabling efficient FPGA/ASIC deployment; this is a key advantage for edge inference [7f09eafa-3]. Frameworks like llama.cpp and specialized bit‑wise LUT methods (T‑MAC) have been adapted for low‑bit LLMs, though bit‑wise LUTs can suffer spatial inefficiencies under bandwidth limits, and element‑wise K‑quants introduces dequantization steps and latency [7f09eafa-2].

citations.title: PTQTP: Post-Training Quantization to Trit-Planes for Large Language Models
snippets:
PTQ for LLMs. PTQ has emerged as a promising approach for compressing LLMs without the computational overhead of retraining. GPTQ (Frantar et al., 2022) pioneered efficient quantization through layer-wise optimization, achieving 4-bit quantization while maintaining model performance. AWQ (Lin et al., 2024) further improved this by incorporating activation-aware scaling, demonstrating that the consideration of activations during quantization leads to better performance. Recent work has pushed towards even lower bit-width quantization. PBLLM (Shang et al., 2023) and BiLLM (Huang et al., 2024) achieved 1-bit quantization by identifying and preserving structurally salient weights while applying different quantization strategies to different weight groups. ARB-LLM (Li et al., 2025) further refined this approach through alternating optimization of binary weight groups. 

However, these methods rely on complex, unstructured weight categorizations that complicate hardware implementation. 

Ternary Quantization The transition from binary to ternary quantization represents a leap of model expressiveness while still preserving multiplier-less arithmetic. BitNet's (Wang et al., 2023) extension to 1.58-bit (ternary) weights (Ma et al., 2024) demonstrated superior performance compared to binary models, suggesting the value of the additional state in the ternary representation. There are also some other trit-plane-based works on image-compression domain (Lee et al., 2022;Jeon et al., 2023). 

Hardware Efficiency. A key advantage of binary and ternary quantization lies in their suitability for FPGA or ASIC deployment (e.g., FlightLLM (Zeng et al., 2024), DFX (Hong et al., 2023)), where multiplier-less feature-weight products can be efficiently implemented in hardware. Specifically, binary operations can be realized with XNOR gates and bit-counting, while ternary operations leverage simple adders, preserving computational efficiency while offering greater expressivity.

sections.title: # How attention (Q/K/V) is handled
sections.text: Many 1‑bit LLM approaches quantize linear projections (in/outputs, FFN, MHSA outputs) but keep attention Q/K/V in higher precision to preserve quality, since exact inner products are critical for attention. State‑of‑the‑art ternary LLMs still retain high‑precision Q, K, V matrices, so the high‑precision matrix multiplications in self‑attention remain, preventing fully “MatMul‑free” inference; some works therefore replace attention with alternative mechanisms (e.g., RNN variants) to achieve MatMul‑free transformers [7f09eafa-0]. In practice, quantization is applied to linear layers (e.g., input/output embeddings often left unquantized; MHSA and FFN projections quantized), and QAT with STE is used to propagate gradients through on‑the‑fly quantization during forward passes [26a371de-4].

citations.title: TerEffic: Highly Efficient Ternary LLM Inference on FPGA
snippets:
Quantization has been a key strategy to accelerate inference as neural networks grow rapidly in parameter count. Among the various quantization methods, binary and ternary quantizations feature extremely compressed weights that require little memory capacity and bandwidth. They were initially validated in CNN models such as BNN [13], XNOR-Net [14], and TWN [15], achieving high efficiency with minimal accuracy loss. 

Entering the era of LLMs, larger model sizes and limited hardware resources further necessitate low-bit quantization, especially in the context of edge devices. LLMs utilizing binary or ternary quantization are also referred to as '1-bit' LLMs, as each weight theoretically takes less than 2 bits for storage. As a pioneer of 1-bit LLM, BitNet [8] employed binary quantization and introduced the BitLinear layer as a replacement for linear projections. As its variant and improvement, BitNet 1.58b [9] utilized ternary quantization to match the performance of fullprecision (fp16 or bf16) Transformers. Later, TernaryLLM [16] leveraged knowledge distillation in its training and surpassed previous low-bit quantization methods. However, as the Q, K, V matrices in the self-attention mechanism remain in high precision, the high-precision matrix multiplications were not eliminated. To address this issue and realize a fully 'MatMul-free' model, [17] used an RNN variant to replace the traditional self-attention in their ternary model and achieved excellent performance. Furthermore, this 1-bit quantization trend was extended to the Vision Transformer (ViT) domain [18] and a scaling law [19] was established, providing a theoretical basis for the impressive performance of these 1-bit models. Advances in post-training reparameterization [20] also paved the way for low-cost training of 1-bit LLMs. More recently, Microsoft released an official CPU inference framework for BitNet, bitnet.cpp [21]. However, this framework focused on the software level, while ternary models still have significant potential for improvements from custom hardware.

sections.title: # Putting it all together: a typical 1‑bit LLM pipeline
sections.text:
- Parameterization: Linear layers are replaced with “BitLinear/TernaryLinear,” where weights are clipped to a narrow range and mapped to {-1,1} (binary) or {-1,0,1} (ternary), sometimes with learned scale factors and per‑group quantization to capture outliers. BitNet’s BitLinear and its b1.58 ternary variant compress weights to 1–1.58 bits and match or surpass full‑precision Transformers on certain settings [7f09eafa-0]. SDQ‑LLM uses upsampling sigma‑delta quantization to flexibly trade precision for compression, aided by Hadamard smoothing [7f09eafa-1].
- Training: QAT or PTQ is used. QAT applies STE through quantize‑round‑clip operations, with clipping levels chosen by statistics (e.g., absmean) and sometimes optimized by loss‑aware methods to minimize the true loss. STE is standard for non‑differentiable quantization; regularization/distillation terms help mitigate quantization error [2da7a966-1]. LAPQ directly optimizes clipping parameters to reduce loss, outperforming layer‑wise heuristics [2da7a966-0]. Normalization adjustments (SubLN) before quantized projections improve stability and downstream accuracy [26a371de-0].
- Activation handling: Activations may be quantized to low bits (often 8‑bit in early BitNet work), or left higher‑precision to avoid instability; fully binary/1‑bit activation methods exist but are more sensitive and often require smoothing and specialized blocks. 8‑bit activations and STE are common in 1.58‑bit BitNet distillation [26a371de-0]. Integer‑only low‑bit LLMs need activation/channel smoothing to handle outliers in SwiGLU/RMSNorm [26a371de-2]. PTQ binarization methods often leave activation quantization aside or are still emerging, as activation outliers limit speed/accuracy gains [26a371de-3].
- Inference: Dot products are computed with adder/bit‑logic kernels, sometimes using element‑wise dequantization for grouped low‑bit weights or bit‑wise LUTs; attention projections and embeddings may remain higher‑precision. Bit‑wise vs element‑wise GEMM tradeoffs govern latency and memory bandwidth on edge hardware [7f09eafa-2]. Multiplier‑less arithmetic is a key driver for FPGA/ASIC acceleration [7f09eafa-3]. Some works aim for MatMul‑free transformers by replacing attention with ternary convolutions/RNNs [7f09eafa-0].

citations.title: PTQTP: Post-Training Quantization to Trit-Planes for Large Language Models
snippets:
PTQ for LLMs. PTQ has emerged as a promising approach for compressing LLMs without the computational overhead of retraining. GPTQ (Frantar et al., 2022) pioneered efficient quantization through layer-wise optimization, achieving 4-bit quantization while maintaining model performance. AWQ (Lin et al., 2024) further improved this by incorporating activation-aware scaling, demonstrating that the consideration of activations during quantization leads to better performance. Recent work has pushed towards even lower bit-width quantization. PBLLM (Shang et al., 2023) and BiLLM (Huang et al., 2024) achieved 1-bit quantization by identifying and preserving structurally salient weights while applying different quantization strategies to different weight groups. ARB-LLM (Li et al., 2025) further refined this approach through alternating optimization of binary weight groups. 

However, these methods rely on complex, unstructured weight categorizations that complicate hardware implementation. 

Ternary Quantization The transition from binary to ternary quantization represents a leap of model expressiveness while still preserving multiplier-less arithmetic. BitNet's (Wang et al., 2023) extension to 1.58-bit (ternary) weights (Ma et al., 2024) demonstrated superior performance compared to binary models, suggesting the value of the additional state in the ternary representation. There are also some other trit-plane-based works on image-compression domain (Lee et al., 2022;Jeon et al., 2023). 

Hardware Efficiency. A key advantage of binary and ternary quantization lies in their suitability for FPGA or ASIC deployment (e.g., FlightLLM (Zeng et al., 2024), DFX (Hong et al., 2023)), where multiplier-less feature-weight products can be efficiently implemented in hardware. Specifically, binary operations can be realized with XNOR gates and bit-counting, while ternary operations leverage simple adders, preserving computational efficiency while offering greater expressivity.

citations.title: SDQ-LLM: Sigma-Delta Quantization for 1-bit LLMs of any size
snippets:
In binarization, parameters are typically represented as binary values (e.g., -1 and +1) using the sign function. Representative methods include PB-LLM [23], BiLLM [10], and OneBit [22], which apply binary quantization to large language models to minimize memory and computation. In contrast, ternarization extends this approach by allowing an additional zero state (e.g., -1, 0, +1), offering a better trade-off between accuracy and efficiency. A representative ternarization-based approach is BitNet b1.58 [13], which achieves improved performance under extremely low-bit quantization settings. Extremely low-bit quantization of model parameters is significant for hardware deployment, as techniques like binarizing or ternarizing parameters can convert multiplication operations in linear transformations to addition operations, greatly reducing hardware computation costs. However, extremely low-bit quantization often leads to considerable accuracy loss, making it difficult to apply in practice. 

In the face of the formidable challenges posed by extremely lowbit quantization in large language models, we introduce the SDQ-LLM, Sigma-Delta Quantization for 1-bit LLMs of any size. By ingeniously repurposing the upsampling quantization principle rooted in sigma-delta analog-to-digital converters, SDQ-LLM pioneers a novel paradigm for parameter quantization in LLMs. Our research culminates in four key contributions that significantly advance the field: 

• We propose SDQ-LLM, an upsampling-based Sigma-Delta quantization scheme designed for LLM parameters. This method enables extremely low-bit quantization while maintaining continuous control over both precision and model size. By adjusting the Over-Sampling Ratio (OSR), SDQ-LLM achieves a flexible balance between accuracy and compression, making it adaptable to a wide range of requirements and ensuring optimal performance across different use cases. • To boost SDQ-LLM's quantization precision, we introduce the Hadamard matrix for weight smoothing. This technique reduces quantization errors and noise, ensuring more stable and reliable weight representations and improving the quantized model's overall quality.

citations.title: Achieving binary weight and activation for LLMs using Post-Training Quantization
snippets:
Considerable research efforts have been devoted to the low-resource computation of LLMs (Dettmers et al., 2024;Chen et al., 2024). Existing works have achieved near-lossless quantization at W4A4 through methods such as mixed-precision quantization (Zhao et al., 2024) and outlier smoothing using rotation factors (Ashkboos et al., 2024;Liu et al., 2024b). However, these methods encounter difficulties when attempting to push towards even lower-bit quantization below 4 bits. Recently, researchers start to seek binarization methods (Courbariaux and Bengio, 2016;Qin et al., 2022) for LLMs. One line of works are based on Quantization-Aware Training (QAT) method. For example, BitNet b1.58 (Wang et al., 2023), BitNet a4.8 (Wang et al., 2024), OneBit (Xu et al., 2024), and FBI-LLM (Ma et al., 2024) have designed 1-bit Transformer architectures specifically for LLMs, replacing original linear layers with specific quantized version. These methods can reduce the quantization bit-width of weights to 1 bit and demonstrate significant advantages over baseline models. However, these QAT methods require substantial computational resources, making it impractical for the quantization of LLMs. 

Another line of works explored the possibility of binarizing LLMs within the PTQ framework. BiLLM (Huang et al., 2024a) and STBLLM (Dong et al., 2024), inspired by the distribution characteristics of weight values and the Hessian matrix, adopt binary residual approximations for significant weights and optimal partitioning for group binarization of non-significant weights, which pushes the quantization boundary of LLM weights down to 1 bit. However, these works neglect the quantization of activation values, which obstructs the computational acceleration of the quantized model and ultimately results in relatively slow inference speed. 

Most recently, people start to explore fully binarized models for both weight and activation.

sections.title: # Accuracy and deployment trade‑offs
sections.text: Extremely low‑bit quantization can significantly reduce memory, bandwidth, and energy, but risks accuracy loss unless mitigations are applied. Binary/ternary parameterization reduces memory and compute substantially, yet naive low‑bit can incur large accuracy drops, motivating advanced schemes like SDQ‑LLM to balance precision and compression [7f09eafa-1]. Ternary weights generally offer a better accuracy‑efficiency trade‑off than binary, as shown by BitNet b1.58 and follow‑ups; hardware platforms (FPGA/ASIC) benefit from adder‑centric implementations [7f09eafa-3]. OneBit demonstrates that with proper architecture and initialization for 1‑bit weights, LLMs can achieve competitive size‑performance trade‑offs [7f09eafa-4]. However, pushing to fully integer or 1‑bit across all operators (including non‑linear blocks) remains challenging due to activation variance and operator support, requiring smoothing and specialized kernels [26a371de-2].

sections.title: # Practical takeaways
sections.text:
- “1‑bit LLMs” replace standard linear layers with quantized BitLinear/TernaryLinear modules whose weights live in {-1,0,1} or {-1,1}, enabling multiplier‑less inference kernels. This terminology arises because each weight needs less than 2 bits (1 bit for binary, 1.58 for ternary) [7f09eafa-0]. Ternary LLMs’ {-1,0,1} weights support adder‑based matmul replacements [7f09eafa-2].
- Training uses quantization‑aware methods (QAT/PTQ) with clipping/scale and STE to approximate gradients through quantizers, often augmented with loss‑aware clipping and extra normalization to stabilize training and improve downstream performance. QAT with STE is standard; regularization/distillation reduces quant error [2da7a966-1]. LAPQ optimizes clipping to the loss; SubLN helps stabilize quantized projections [2da7a966-0].
- Activation quantization to very low bits is optional and risky; many strong systems keep activations higher‑precision or use 8‑bit quantization, while fully binary/1‑bit activation methods require careful smoothing and non‑linear handling. 8‑bit activations are common in 1.58‑bit BitNet variants [26a371de-0]. Integer‑only LLMs need activation/channel smoothing to handle outliers [26a371de-2]. PTQ binarization often neglects activation quantization due to inference bottlenecks [26a371de-3].
- On the inference side, bit‑wise and element‑wise GEMM implementations leverage adders/XNOR logic for speed and efficiency on edge hardware, while attention Q/K/V are frequently left in higher precision to preserve inner‑product quality, with some works exploring MatMul‑free alternatives. Bit‑wise vs element‑wise kernels trade latency/bandwidth [7f09eafa-2]. Adder‑centric hardware is well‑suited to binary/ternary LLMs [7f09eafa-3]. High‑precision Q/K/V limit MatMul‑free claims; some models replace attention to achieve them [7f09eafa-0].

In short, a “1‑bit LLM” works by quantizing model parameters to extreme low precision (binary/ternary), training with quantization‑aware methods that approximate gradients via STE and optimize clipping/scale to preserve accuracy, and deploying with multiplier‑less GEMM kernels; attention sublayers are often kept higher‑precision, and fully 1‑bit activation schemes remain an active area due to stability and outlier challenges. These methods have achieved strong efficiency gains and, with ternary variants and knowledge distillation, competitive accuracy on Transformers [7f09eafa-0]. Newer techniques like SDQ‑LLM provide knobs to trade precision for compression [7f09eafa-1]. Stability improvements such as SubLN and carefully chosen activation quantization levels are crucial for downstream task performance [26a371de-0]. The main open challenges are achieving fully 1‑bit end‑to‑end models without sacrificing accuracy and optimizing hardware‑aware inference for non‑linear blocks [26a371de-3].

citations.title: Loss aware post-training quantization
snippets:
In this paper we analyzed loss function of quantized neural networks. We show that for low precision quantization loss function is non-convex and non-separable. In such conditions existing methods that minimize some local metric can not perform well.

We introduce Loss Aware Post-training quantization (LAPQ), which optimizes clipping parameters of the quantization function by directly minimizing loss function. Our method outperforms most previously suggested methods for post-training quantization. Our method does not assume special hardware support like channel-wise or filter-wise quantization. To the best of our knowledge LAPQ is a first that achieve near FP32 accuracy at 4 bit layer-wise quantization in post-training regime.

citations.title: Achieving binary weight and activation for LLMs using Post-Training Quantization
snippets:
Considerable research efforts have been devoted to the low-resource computation of LLMs (Dettmers et al., 2024;Chen et al., 2024). Existing works have achieved near-lossless quantization at W4A4 through methods such as mixed-precision quantization (Zhao et al., 2024) and outlier smoothing using rotation factors (Ashkboos et al., 2024;Liu et al., 2024b). However, these methods encounter difficulties when attempting to push towards even lower-bit quantization below 4 bits. Recently, researchers start to seek binarization methods (Courbariaux and Bengio, 2016;Qin et al., 2022) for LLMs. One line of works are based on Quantization-Aware Training (QAT) method. For example, BitNet b1.58 (Wang et al., 2023), BitNet a4.8 (Wang et al., 2024), OneBit (Xu et al., 2024), and FBI-LLM (Ma et al., 2024) have designed 1-bit Transformer architectures specifically for LLMs, replacing original linear layers with specific quantized version. These methods can reduce the quantization bit-width of weights to 1 bit and demonstrate significant advantages over baseline models. However, these QAT methods require substantial computational resources, making it impractical for the quantization of LLMs. 

Another line of works explored the possibility of binarizing LLMs within the PTQ framework. BiLLM (Huang et al., 2024a) and STBLLM (Dong et al., 2024), inspired by the distribution characteristics of weight values and the Hessian matrix, adopt binary residual approximations for significant weights and optimal partitioning for group binarization of non-significant weights, which pushes the quantization boundary of LLM weights down to 1 bit. However, these works neglect the quantization of activation values, which obstructs the computational acceleration of the quantized model and ultimately results in relatively slow inference speed. 

Most recently, people start to explore fully binarized models for both weight and activation.

However, the aforementioned integer-only methods are designed specifically for CNNs or small Transformer networks (e.g., Bert [12] and ViT [7]), which renders them inadequate for LLMs.First, they are incapable of straightforwardly supporting the non-linear operators inherent in LLMs, such as SwiGLU and RMSNorm.Furthermore, their accuracy on LLMs deteriorates significantly (as depicted in Table 4), even when those non-supported operators are executed in full-precision mode.This is because as the model size increasing, the presence of activation outliers in both linear and non-linear layers becomes prominent.As illustrated in Fig 1, Llama2-7B exhibits substantial variations in activation magnitude at both the token and channel levels, making previous approaches ineffective.Last but not least, these methods are limited to 8-bit quantization, whereas LLMs would benefit from lower bit-width quantization (e.g., 4-bit) to address the extensive computational requirements and storage demands.Consequently, how to accurately perform LLMs with efficient integer-only arithmetic remains an unresolved issue that requires further investigation.

question: What benchmarks are there for language models reasoning and what is the state of the art

sections.title: # Overview: Benchmarks for Language-Model Reasoning
sections.text: Reasoning benchmarks for large language models (LLMs) are typically organized into families: math/logic and multi-step arithmetic; science and physics; commonsense and implicit reasoning; program synthesis, code execution, and software engineering; multi-step textual reasoning; multi-agent/tool-use reasoning; and robustness/adversarial and contamination-robust evaluations. Recent surveys emphasize that reasoning behavior should be assessed beyond task-accuracy endpoints, cataloging evaluation methods that probe intermediate reasoning dynamics and error modes, not just final correctness.<cite id="c76c99a3-4">Complementary surveys and benchmark overviews identify canonical math (GSM8K, MATH), commonsense (HellaSwag, ARC), and broader capability suites (MMLU, BIG-bench, HELM), alongside newer hard problems like GPQA and domain-specific evaluations such as Humanity’s Last Exam [c76c99a3-0].

citations.title: Beyond Accuracy: Evaluating the Reasoning Behavior of Large Language Models - A Survey
snippets:
Specifically, we address the following research questions: 

RQ1: How do current LLMs behave across diverse reasoning tasks? RQ2: What are the prevalent evaluation methods employed to assess the reasoning behavior of large language models? 

Other Surveys. While various surveys on reasoning within large language models have emerged in recent years (Huang & Chang, 2023;Yu et al., 2024;Sun et al., 2024;Yang et al., 2023;Qiao et al., 2023;Chu et al., 2023;Mialon et al., 2023;Liu et al., 2024;Ahn et al., 2024), these studies predominantly focus on techniques that seek to enhance or benchmark the performance of LLMs on downstream reasoning tasks. However, there seems to exist no review of work yet that assesses the reasoning behavior of LLMs, rather than their final task performance. Hence, the contributions of this survey are as follows: (i) To the best of our knowledge, we present the first comprehensive review of literature that evaluates LLMbased reasoning beyond task accuracy, offering deeper insights into the models' reasoning behavior, and (ii) we suggest a taxonomy that categorizes prevalent evaluation methods designed to analyze the reasoning dynamics of LLMs.

sections.title: # Math and Logic Reasoning Benchmarks
sections.text:
GSM8K evaluates multi-step arithmetic reasoning over 8,500 grade-school word problems; its test set (1,319 examples) is widely used to probe math reasoning in LLMs. GSM8K is designed to measure multi-step reasoning via linguistically diverse problems and has become a standard testbed for LLM math ability [98b976a5-1]. Recent work reports that proprietary models like GPT‑4 exceed 90% accuracy on GSM8K, while strong open-source models reach roughly the 80% range, though robustness concerns persist about superficial pattern matching or training-data leakage. Analyses note accuracy above 90% for GPT‑4 and above 80% for cutting-edge open-source models on GSM8K, while highlighting ongoing debates about whether high scores reflect genuine understanding or artifacts like leakage [98b976a5-3]. GSM-Plus proposes more adversarial settings and finds gaps of up to 20 percentage points between reported and robust accuracies, underscoring the need for more rigorous evaluation [98b976a5-4]. 

MATH targets high-school-level math with challenging problems, and o1 achieved 94.8% accuracy on MATH, previously considered very difficult; this has spurred new, harder benchmarks (e.g., CollegeMath, UGMathBench) to keep pace with rapidly improving models. MATH and GSM8K are representative of elementary and high-school math; o1 reaches 94.8% on MATH, motivating harder variants and new benchmarks like UGMathBench to challenge current LLMs [3e9551dd-1]. Contemporary evaluations routinely include GSM8K, MATH-500 (a curated 500-problem subset used in step-by-step verification studies), and competition-level sets like AIME and AMC to probe advanced numeric reasoning [3e9551dd-0]. MATH‑500 is frequently used as a curated subset for step-by-step verification studies, and appears alongside GSM8K and AIME in recent multi-benchmark suites. MATH‑500 is selected by OpenAI for step-by-step studies and is commonly grouped with GSM8K and AIME when assessing mathematical reasoning [3e9551dd-2]. 

AIME and other competition-style sets probe precise numeric reasoning and problem-solving under competition constraints; they are increasingly used to separate frontier systems. Evaluations include AIME 2024 and AMC 2023 to assess competition-level mathematical reasoning in LLMs [3e9551dd-0]. Beyond school-level math, Sudoku‑Extreme and other logic puzzles test abstract rule induction and constraint satisfaction, often used to probe general reasoning and test-time computation efficiency. Sudoku‑Extreme and related logic puzzles serve as benchmarks for evaluating logical reasoning and efficient generalization to novel rules [555d32fa-2]. 

ARC/ARC‑AGI focuses on abstract reasoning with novel, minimal‑prior tasks presented as small input–output grid pairs, requiring generalization to new functions; ARC‑AGI has been called the “best known” abstraction benchmark and remains unbeaten as of 2024–2025, though ARC Prize increased private‑set scores from 33% to 55.5% and ARC‑AGI‑2 raises the difficulty bar further. ARC‑AGI remains unbeaten as of December 2024 and is viewed as the most important unsolved AI benchmark because it measures generalization to novel tasks; during ARC Prize, state-of-the-art rose from 33% to 55.5% via techniques like deep-learning‑guided program synthesis and test‑time training [555d32fa-1]. ARC‑AGI‑2 expands and refines tasks to emphasize compositional reasoning and symbolic abstraction, providing a more granular signal at higher fluid‑intelligence levels [555d32fa-2]. ARC‑AGI‑2 introduces a new, harder set while preserving the original task format, with human baselines indicating accessibility for people but difficulty for current AI systems [555d32fa-3]. Progress for frontier models has varied across ARC releases, with some entries achieving low‑double‑digit scores on ARC‑AGI‑2 by late 2025, reflecting the benchmark’s rising difficulty. In 2025, ARC‑AGI‑2’s tasks were substantially harder than ARC‑AGI‑1; leading LLMs struggled beyond a few percent initially, and by late 2025, reasoning LLMs reached low‑double‑digit scores [555d32fa-4].

citations.title: Hierarchical Reasoning Model
snippets:
ARC-AGI Challenge The ARC-AGI benchmark evaluates general fluid intelligence through IQtest-like puzzles that require inductive reasoning 27 . The initial version, ARC-AGI-1, presents challenges as input-label grid pairs that force AI systems to extract and generalize abstract rules from just a few examples. Each task provides a few input-output demonstration pairs (usually 2-3) and a test input. An AI model has two attempts to produce the correct output grid. Although some believe that mastering ARC-AGI would signal true artificial general intelligence, its primary purpose is to expose the current roadblocks in AGI progress. In fact, both conventional deep learning methods and CoT techniques have faced significant challenges with ARC-AGI-1, primarily because it requires the ability to generalize to entirely new tasks 28 . 

Addressing the limitations identified in ARC-AGI-1, ARC-AGI-2 significantly expands the benchmark by providing a more comprehensive and carefully refined collection of tasks. These new tasks emphasize deeper compositional reasoning, multi-step logic, contextual rule application, and symbolic abstraction. Human calibration studies show these tasks are challenging but doable for people, while being much harder for current AI systems, offering a clearer measure of general reasoning abilities 29 . 

Sudoku-Extreme Sudoku is a 9×9 logic puzzle, requiring each row, column, and 3×3 block to contain the digits 1-9 exactly once. A prediction is considered correct if it exactly matches the puzzle's unique solution. Sudoku's complex logical structure makes it a popular benchmark for evaluating logical reasoning in machine learning 62,63,64 . 

The most frequently used Sudoku dataset in research, namely the Kaggle dataset 65 , can be fully solved using elementary single-digit techniques 66 . The minimal 17-clue puzzles 62 , another widelyused collection, might seem more challenging due to its small number of clues. However, this perception is misleading-since 17 represents the minimum number of clues required to guarantee a unique Sudoku solution, these hints need to be highly orthogonal to each other. This orthogonal arrangement leads to many direct, easily-resolved solution paths 67 .

citations.title: ARC-AGI-2: A New Challenge for Frontier AI Reasoning Systems
snippets: The Abstraction and Reasoning Corpus for Artificial General Intelligence (ARC-AGI), introduced in 2019, established a challenging benchmark for evaluating the general fluid intelligence of artificial systems via a set of unique, novel tasks only requiring minimal prior knowledge. While ARC-AGI has spurred significant research activity over the past five years, recent AI progress calls for benchmarks capable of finer-grained evaluation at higher levels of cognitive complexity. We introduce ARC-AGI-2, an upgraded version of the benchmark. ARC-AGI-2 preserves the input-output pair task format of its predecessor, ensuring continuity for researchers. It incorporates a newly curated and expanded set of tasks specifically designed to provide a more granular signal to assess abstract reasoning and problem-solving abilities at higher levels of fluid intelligence. To contextualize the difficulty and characteristics of ARC-AGI-2, we present extensive results from human testing, providing a robust baseline that highlights the benchmark's accessibility to human intelligence, yet difficulty for current AI systems. ARC-AGI-2 aims to serve as a next-generation tool for rigorously measuring progress towards more general and human-like AI capabilities.

citations.title: ARC Prize 2024: Technical Report
snippets: As of December 2024, the ARC-AGI benchmark is five years old and remains unbeaten. We believe it is currently the most important unsolved AI benchmark in the world because it seeks to measure generalization on novel tasks -- the essence of intelligence -- as opposed to skill at tasks that can be prepared for in advance. This year, we launched ARC Prize, a global competition to inspire new ideas and drive open progress towards AGI by reaching a target benchmark score of 85\%. As a result, the state-of-the-art score on the ARC-AGI private evaluation set increased from 33\% to 55.5\%, propelled by several frontier AGI reasoning techniques including deep learning-guided program synthesis and test-time training. In this paper, we survey top approaches, review new open-source implementations, discuss the limitations of the ARC-AGI-1 dataset, and share key insights gained from the competition.

citations.title: Test-time Adaptation of Tiny Recursive Models
snippets:
The ARC (Abstract Reasoning Challenge) Prize is a competition to efficiently solve unseen abstract tasks using computers. ARC tasks are designed to be solvable by humans but challenging for programmable approaches. The competition imposes a limit on the amount of compute that may be used to solve tasks, which is why approaches must not just generalise to unseen tasks but also solve them efficiently. Historically, the leading approach to solving the first series of ARC tasks (ARC AGI I) was a brute force search -with heuristics -through a library of operations (e.g. flip, rotate, repattern) [1]. This was outperformed by a number of entries in the 2024 competition that involved pre-training a deep transformer model in the single billion parameter range. Such approaches involved pre-training on ARC training tasks prior to the competition, followed by post-training on test-time tasks within sandboxed competition environment with limited compute. These approaches lifted scores on ARC AGI I from roughly 20-30% up into the 40%+ range. 

In 2025, ARC AGI II tasks were released of significantly higher difficulty than those in ARC AGI I. At the time of release, previous year's competition approaches scored in the low single digits, and leading large language models -including those far exceeding the compute limits of the competition -struggled to score beyond a few percent on the updated benchmark. Although, by late 2025, reasoning language models were scoring in the low double digits.

sections.title: # Commonsense and Implicit Reasoning Benchmarks
sections.text: HellaSwag tests commonsense via multiple endings to a sentence and asks models to choose the most logical continuation, probing everyday causal and contextual reasoning. HellaSwag evaluates common sense reasoning by presenting sentences with multiple possible endings and requiring a choice of the most logical continuation [c76c99a3-3]. StrategyQA tests implicit reasoning about everyday strategies and plans, often requiring models to reason about optimal actions in short scenarios. Recent multi-benchmark studies include StrategyQA alongside math sets to cover commonsense and implicit reasoning tasks [3e9551dd-3]. ARC‑AGI also serves as a general abstraction and reasoning benchmark that requires minimal priors and tests the ability to extract and generalize abstract rules from few examples. ARC‑AGI is constructed to require a small number of priors and emphasizes reasoning and abstraction, contrasting with benchmarks that demand extensive general knowledge [555d32fa-0].

citations.title: Evaluating Large Language Models with Grid-Based Game Competitions: An Extensible LLM Benchmark and Leaderboard
snippets:
The HellaSwag benchmark tests common sense reasoning by presenting models with sentences and multiple possible endings, requiring them to choose the most logical continuation [25]. LiveBench addresses the test set contamination issue in LLM evaluation by offering a benchmark immune to such contamination and biases from human or LLM judging [26]. It features frequently updated questions from recent sources, automatic scoring against objective ground-truth values, and diverse tasks spanning math, coding, reasoning, language, instruction following, and data analysis [26]. 

The recent survey papers have provided comprehensive frameworks and methodologies that are invaluable for developing robust benchmarks. One such paper, "A Survey on Evaluation of Large Language Models," presents a detailed review focusing on three key dimensions: what to evaluate, where to evaluate, and how to evaluate [27]. It encompasses a broad spectrum of tasks, including general natural language processing, reasoning, medical applications, ethics, education, and more. This survey emphasizes the critical role of evaluation methods and benchmarks in assessing LLM performance, summarizing both successes and failures across different tasks, and highlighting future challenges in the field [27]. Similarly, "Evaluating Large Language Models: A Comprehensive Survey" categorizes LLM evaluation into knowledge and capability, alignment, and safety [28]. This survey underscores the importance of rigorous assessment and the development of comprehensive evaluation platforms to ensure the safe and beneficial development of LLMs. It aims to guide responsible LLM advancement, ensuring that their evolution maximizes societal benefits while minimizing potential risks [28]. Both surveys stress the necessity of treating evaluation as an essential discipline to aid the development of more proficient and ethically sound LLMs [29].

Gulati et al. (2024) show a benchmark of problems sourced from the William Lowell Putnam Mathematical Competition, also featuring variable name and constant variants. Although o1-preview achieves a precision of 41.95% on their benchmarks, its accuracy is around 30% lower on the altered problems. Such issues may be caused by data contamination and the tendency of all models so far to exhibit token bias (Jiang et al., 2024). While math benchmarks are invaluable in discovering the capabilities and limitations of logical reasoning in state-ofthe-art models, the problems in such benchmarks inevitably require a strong mathematical background for a reader to appreciate, follow along, or catch errors in the models' reasoning. 

Benchmarks That Do Not Require World Knowledge ARC-AGI (Chollet, 2019) is perhaps the best known benchmark of reasoning and abstraction benchmark for AI. ARC-AGI is carefully constructed to require a small number of priors, whereas our benchmark tests both a model's reasoning ability and its ability to recall extensive general knowledge. The ARC-AGI tests can be challenging for people, but "Each task included in ARC has been successfully solved by at least one member of a group of three high-IQ humans." In contrast, a few hundred people submit correct solutions to the Puzzle Challenges every week.

sections.title: # Code and Software Engineering Reasoning Benchmarks
sections.text:
HumanEval and MBPP are foundational for code generation; HumanEval comprises 164 Python problems validated by tests, while MBPP includes 500 programming problems in a few‑shot setting, and both are widely used to evaluate code LLMs in zero/few‑shot conditions. HumanEval (164 Python problems) and MBPP (500 problems) are standard evaluations for code LLMs, with HumanEval in zero-shot and MBPP in few-shot settings [a517d63b-0]. Multilingual extensions have been used to test cross‑language code generation, and recent open-source models show strong gains, sometimes surpassing smaller closed‑source systems. Evaluations expand HumanEval to seven additional languages and report that DeepSeek‑Coder‑Base achieves 50.3% on HumanEval and 66.0% on MBPP, exceeding similarly sized open-source baselines and surpassing GPT‑3.5‑Turbo in HumanEval after instruction tuning [a517d63b-0]. 

LiveCodeBench aggregates diverse coding tasks and execution-based evaluation, and recent methods report state-of-the-art Pass@K on HumanEval and MBPP (including “HumanEval+” and “MBPP+” with expanded test suites), with some approaches reaching or surpassing early GPT‑4 and even Claude‑3.5‑Opus on certain variants. DeepSeek‑Coder‑V2‑Instruct leads open-source results on multilingual HumanEval/MBPP+, averaging 75.3% (second to GPT‑4o at 76.4%), highlighting strong cross‑language coding performance [a517d63b-1]. ReflectionCoder shows on‑par or surpassing performance on HumanEval+ and MBPP+, reaching 82.9/76.8 and 84.1/72.0 respectively and being on‑par with Claude‑3‑Opus and above early GPT‑4 [a517d63b-2]. Newer evaluations emphasize self‑invoking code generation (HumanEval Pro, MBPP Pro), where models must handle functions that call themselves or evaluate dynamically, revealing ~10–15% drops in pass@1 for many LLMs and showing that large open-source models now match proprietary systems on these harder variants. On HumanEval Pro and MBPP Pro, most LLMs see a 10–15% absolute drop in pass@1, yet large open-source models are comparable to proprietary systems on self‑invoking benchmarks [a517d63b-4]. AutoCoder‑33B reports pass@1 of 90.9% on HumanEval and 82.5% on MBPP, ranking below GPT‑4 Turbo and Claude‑3‑Opus, with strong smaller variants as well [a517d63b-3]. 

Software engineering–focused evaluations such as SWE‑bench assess repairing real bugs/PRs and end‑to‑end repo‑level changes; they are increasingly used to measure tool‑use and iterative reasoning in code agents, though specific leaderboard numbers vary and are actively evolving. Benchmarks like LiveBench emphasize diverse tasks spanning coding and reasoning, while domain-specific suites (e.g., code and software engineering) probe realistic multi-file, tool-augmented workflows [c76c99a3-3].

citations.title: DeepSeek-Coder: When the Large Language Model Meets Programming - The Rise of Code Intelligence
snippets: HumanEval and MBPP Benchmarks The HumanEval (Chen et al., 2021) and MBPP (Austin et al., 2021) benchmarks are widely used for evaluating code LLMs. HumanEval consists of 164 hand-written Python problems that are validated using test cases to assess the code generated by a Code LLM in a zero-shot setting, while the MBPP benchmark includes 500 problems in a few-shot setting. To evaluate the model's multilingual capabilities, we expanded the Python problems of Humaneval Benchmark to seven additional commonly used programming languages, namely C++, Java, PHP, TypeScript (TS), C#, Bash, and JavaScript (JS) (Cassano et al., 2023). For both benchmarks, We adopted a greedy search approach and re-implemented the baseline results using the same script and environment for fair comparison. The results are presented in Table 3. As we can see, DeepSeek-Coder-Base achieves stateof-the-art performance with an average accuracy of 50.3% on HumanEval and 66.0% on MBPP. In comparison to the similarly sized open-source model CodeLlama-Base 34B, our model has demonstrated a notable improvement of 9% and 11% in accuracy, respectively. It's worth noting that even our smaller model, DeepSeek-Coder-Base 6.7B, surpasses the performance of CodeLlama-Base 34B. After instruction fine-tuning, our model surpasses the closed-source GPT-3.5-Turbo model in HumanEval benchmark, significantly reducing the performance gap between OpenAI GPT-4 and open-source models.

The HellaSwag benchmark tests common sense reasoning by presenting models with sentences and multiple possible endings, requiring them to choose the most logical continuation [25]. LiveBench addresses the test set contamination issue in LLM evaluation by offering a benchmark immune to such contamination and biases from human or LLM judging [26]. It features frequently updated questions from recent sources, automatic scoring against objective ground-truth values, and diverse tasks spanning math, coding, reasoning, language, instruction following, and data analysis [26]. 

The recent survey papers have provided comprehensive frameworks and methodologies that are invaluable for developing robust benchmarks. One such paper, "A Survey on Evaluation of Large Language Models," presents a detailed review focusing on three key dimensions: what to evaluate, where to evaluate, and how to evaluate [27]. It encompasses a broad spectrum of tasks, including general natural language processing, reasoning, medical applications, ethics, education, and more. This survey emphasizes the critical role of evaluation methods and benchmarks in assessing LLM performance, summarizing both successes and failures across different tasks, and highlighting future challenges in the field [27]. Similarly, "Evaluating Large Language Models: A Comprehensive Survey" categorizes LLM evaluation into knowledge and capability, alignment, and safety [28]. This survey underscores the importance of rigorous assessment and the development of comprehensive evaluation platforms to ensure the safe and beneficial development of LLMs. It aims to guide responsible LLM advancement, ensuring that their evolution maximizes societal benefits while minimizing potential risks [28]. Both surveys stress the necessity of treating evaluation as an essential discipline to aid the development of more proficient and ethically sound LLMs [29].

sections.title: # Multi-step Textual Reasoning and Variants
sections.text: Math and QA variants such as SVAMP, TabMWP, MultiArith, and ASDiv test multi‑step, structured reasoning; these datasets appear in recent multi-benchmark studies to cover arithmetic, tabular, and structured‑equation reasoning alongside open‑ended math. Multi-benchmark evaluations include GSM8K, SVAMP, and MATH‑500 to cover diverse mathematical reasoning scopes [3e9551dd-3]. GSM‑Plus and related works discuss GSM8K, SVAMP, and MetaMathQA as components of math reasoning evaluation and highlight robustness gaps compared to reported accuracies [98b976a5-3]. Variants like “GSM‑Plus” are designed to stress adversarial robustness and reveal overfitting or leakage, showing up to 20‑point drops versus nominal accuracies and emphasizing the need for harder, more adaptive evaluations. GSM‑Plus finds gaps of up to 20% between reported and robust accuracies, motivating more adversarial math evaluations [98b976a5-3].

sections.title: # Multi-agent and Tool-use Reasoning Benchmarks
sections.text: Contemporary benchmarks also evaluate multi‑agent and tool‑use reasoning, often through agent frameworks that orchestrate retrieval, planning, and tool/function calling; these are reflected in broader suites and in emerging leaderboards that compare agent systems on multi‑step, external‑tool tasks. Evaluations increasingly span diverse tasks including reasoning, coding, and data analysis, and recent surveys emphasize developing comprehensive platforms to assess capabilities and safety in multi-step settings [c76c99a3-3]. Multi‑benchmark studies grouping math, commonsense, and scientific reasoning with code further motivate agent‑style evaluations that coordinate planning and tool execution to achieve higher‑level goals. Benchmarks covering math and commonsense are frequently paired to probe multi-domain reasoning, a setup that motivates multi-agent and tool-augmented evaluations [3e9551dd-3].

sections.title: # Robustness, Adversarial, and Contamination-robust Evaluation
sections.text: Robustness-focused evaluations like GSM‑Plus probe whether high scores on standard benchmarks persist under adversarial perturbations, revealing large drops and highlighting fragility of current reasoning systems. GSM‑Plus shows robustness gaps up to 20% and argues for more rigorous, adversarial math evaluations to separate true understanding from artifacts [98b976a5-3]. To mitigate dataset contamination and judging biases, LiveBench introduces frequently updated questions, objective ground-truth scoring, and design choices aimed at being “benchmark immune,” covering math, coding, reasoning, and instruction following. LiveBench addresses contamination and bias with updated questions, automatic scoring, and diverse tasks, aiming for robust evaluation across math, coding, reasoning, language, instruction following, and data analysis [c76c99a3-3].

sections.title: # State of the Art: What Models Lead and What Benchmarks Say
sections.text:
- Math/logic: Frontier models show very high accuracy on school‑level math (GSM8K: GPT‑4 >90%; open‑source ~80%), while high‑school/competition‑level problems (MATH, MATH‑500, AIME) reveal more discriminative gaps; o1 achieved 94.8% on MATH and spurred new harder math suites (UGMathBench, CollegeMath). GPT‑4 and top open-source models exceed 90% and 80% accuracy on GSM8K, respectively [98b976a5-3]. o1 reaches 94.8% on MATH, motivating new undergraduate‑level math benchmarks like UGMathBench [3e9551dd-1]. Recent evaluations incorporate AIME/AMC to probe competition-level reasoning [3e9551dd-0]. ARC‑AGI remains a hard, unbeaten generalization benchmark, with ARC‑AGI‑2 raising the bar; ARC Prize improved private‑set scores to 55.5%, but ARC‑AGI‑2 remains challenging for frontier systems. ARC‑AGI state‑of‑the‑art increased to 55.5% during ARC Prize, driven by techniques like deep‑learning‑guided program synthesis and test‑time training [555d32fa-1]. ARC‑AGI‑2 is significantly harder and aims to provide finer‑grained assessment of abstract reasoning [555d32fa-3]. By late 2025, reasoning LLMs achieved low‑double‑digit scores on ARC‑AGI‑2, underscoring its difficulty [555d32fa-4]. 

- Science reasoning: GPQA is designed to stay challenging; even strong models struggle without multiple‑choice scaffolding, and recent work evaluates it with options removed to purify reasoning demands. GPQA‑Diamond is used without answer options in some evaluations to isolate pure reasoning ability [3e9551dd-2]. 

- Commonsense/implicit reasoning: HellaSwag and StrategyQA remain core; ARC‑AGI also serves as a general abstraction test requiring minimal priors and generalization from few examples. HellaSwag tests commonsense continuation; StrategyQA targets implicit planning and strategy [c76c99a3-3]. ARC‑AGI emphasizes abstraction and generalization with minimal priors [555d32fa-0]. 

- Code and software engineering: Open‑source code LLMs have rapidly closed gaps on HumanEval/MBPP and some variants, with multilingual and self‑invoking evaluations showing both progress and vulnerabilities; recent models (e.g., DeepSeek‑Coder‑V2‑Instruct, ReflectionCoder, AutoCoder) report top‑tier pass@1 or near‑top results on HumanEval/MBPP/+, sometimes matching or surpassing early GPT‑4 and Claude‑3.5‑Opus on certain variants, though self‑invoking settings expose ~10–15% drops across the board. DeepSeek‑Coder‑Base achieved 50.3% (HumanEval) and 66.0% (MBPP), surpassing CodeLlama‑34B and GPT‑3.5‑Turbo on HumanEval after instruction tuning [a517d63b-0]. DeepSeek‑Coder‑V2‑Instruct leads open-source on multilingual HumanEval/MBPP+, averaging 75.3% (second to GPT‑4o at 76.4%) [a517d63b-1]. ReflectionCoder reports 82.9/76.8 (HumanEval+/MBPP+) and on‑par performance with Claude‑3‑Opus and above early GPT‑4 [a517d63b-2]. AutoCoder‑33B reaches 90.9% on HumanEval and 82.5% on MBPP, ranking below GPT‑4 Turbo and Claude‑3‑Opus; strong small variants are also reported [a517d63b-3]. On HumanEval Pro and MBPP Pro, models exhibit ~10–15% pass@1 drops, with large open-source models now matching proprietary systems on self‑invoking code [a517d63b-4]. 

- Multi‑step textual reasoning: Standardized variants (SVAMP, TabMWP, MultiArith, ASDiv) continue to serve as component benchmarks in broader suites and are used to probe structured reasoning and equation‑form tasks; adversarial math suites like GSM‑Plus reveal robustness issues relative to nominal accuracies. GSM‑Plus and related works catalog GSM8K, SVAMP, and MetaMathQA and report robustness gaps up to 20% [98b976a5-3]. Recent suites include SVAMP and MATH‑500 alongside GSM8K to cover diverse reasoning demands [3e9551dd-3]. 

- Multi‑agent/tool‑use: Broader benchmark overviews and multi‑domain suites motivate agent and tool‑augmented evaluations, reflecting a trend toward complex, multi‑step, external‑tool reasoning rather than single‑turn QA. Surveys emphasize comprehensive platforms for multi-step and tool-augmented reasoning beyond single-task accuracy [c76c99a3-3]. 

- Robustness and contamination‑resistance: Adversarial math evaluations (GSM‑Plus) and contamination‑resistant designs (LiveBench) are increasingly critical to separate genuine reasoning gains from artifacts like leakage, prompting more rigorous, dynamic, and objective evaluation pipelines. GSM‑Plus documents robustness gaps and advocates adversarial evaluation [98b976a5-3]. LiveBench introduces frequent updates, objective ground-truth scoring, and contamination mitigation to improve benchmark reliability [c76c99a3-3].

citations.title: ARC-AGI-2: A New Challenge for Frontier AI Reasoning Systems
snippets: The Abstraction and Reasoning Corpus for Artificial General Intelligence (ARC-AGI), introduced in 2019, established a challenging benchmark for evaluating the general fluid intelligence of artificial systems via a set of unique, novel tasks only requiring minimal prior knowledge. While ARC-AGI has spurred significant research activity over the past five years, recent AI progress calls for benchmarks capable of finer-grained evaluation at higher levels of cognitive complexity. We introduce ARC-AGI-2, an upgraded version of the benchmark. ARC-AGI-2 preserves the input-output pair task format of its predecessor, ensuring continuity for researchers. It incorporates a newly curated and expanded set of tasks specifically designed to provide a more granular signal to assess abstract reasoning and problem-solving abilities at higher levels of fluid intelligence. To contextualize the difficulty and characteristics of ARC-AGI-2, we present extensive results from human testing, providing a robust baseline that highlights the benchmark's accessibility to human intelligence, yet difficulty for current AI systems. ARC-AGI-2 aims to serve as a next-generation tool for rigorously measuring progress towards more general and human-like AI capabilities.

citations.title: ARC Prize 2024: Technical Report
snippets: As of December 2024, the ARC-AGI benchmark is five years old and remains unbeaten. We believe it is currently the most important unsolved AI benchmark in the world because it seeks to measure generalization on novel tasks -- the essence of intelligence -- as opposed to skill at tasks that can be prepared for in advance. This year, we launched ARC Prize, a global competition to inspire new ideas and drive open progress towards AGI by reaching a target benchmark score of 85\%. As a result, the state-of-the-art score on the ARC-AGI private evaluation set increased from 33\% to 55.5\%, propelled by several frontier AGI reasoning techniques including deep learning-guided program synthesis and test-time training. In this paper, we survey top approaches, review new open-source implementations, discuss the limitations of the ARC-AGI-1 dataset, and share key insights gained from the competition.

citations.title: Test-time Adaptation of Tiny Recursive Models
snippets:
The ARC (Abstract Reasoning Challenge) Prize is a competition to efficiently solve unseen abstract tasks using computers. ARC tasks are designed to be solvable by humans but challenging for programmable approaches. The competition imposes a limit on the amount of compute that may be used to solve tasks, which is why approaches must not just generalise to unseen tasks but also solve them efficiently. Historically, the leading approach to solving the first series of ARC tasks (ARC AGI I) was a brute force search -with heuristics -through a library of operations (e.g. flip, rotate, repattern) [1]. This was outperformed by a number of entries in the 2024 competition that involved pre-training a deep transformer model in the single billion parameter range. Such approaches involved pre-training on ARC training tasks prior to the competition, followed by post-training on test-time tasks within sandboxed competition environment with limited compute. These approaches lifted scores on ARC AGI I from roughly 20-30% up into the 40%+ range. 

In 2025, ARC AGI II tasks were released of significantly higher difficulty than those in ARC AGI I. At the time of release, previous year's competition approaches scored in the low single digits, and leading large language models -including those far exceeding the compute limits of the competition -struggled to score beyond a few percent on the updated benchmark. Although, by late 2025, reasoning language models were scoring in the low double digits.

sections.title: # Practical Guidance: Choosing Benchmarks by Goal
sections.text:
- Measuring math/logic reasoning: Use GSM8K for multi‑step arithmetic; MATH/MATH‑500 for high‑school difficulty; AIME/AMC for competition‑level numeric precision; and ARC‑AGI‑2 for generalization to novel functions with few examples. GSM8K provides a standard multi-step arithmetic testbed [98b976a5-1]. MATH‑500 and AIME are used to probe advanced numeric and competition-level reasoning [3e9551dd-0]. ARC‑AGI‑2 stresses compositional and symbolic abstraction with increased difficulty [555d32fa-3]. 

- Probing science reasoning: Use GPQA (with or without options) and TheoremQA to assess graduate‑level physics and theorem‑linked math reasoning under challenging assumptions. GPQA‑Diamond (no options) isolates pure reasoning ability in physics [3e9551dd-2]. TheoremQA is included among high-level math/science reasoning resources used to evaluate robustness [98b976a5-3]. 

- Evaluating commonsense/implicit reasoning: Combine HellaSwag and StrategyQA with ARC‑AGI to capture both everyday causal knowledge and abstract rule induction from few examples. HellaSwag and StrategyQA target commonsense and implicit planning, while ARC‑AGI probes abstract reasoning [c76c99a3-3]. 

- Assessing code reasoning: Start with HumanEval/MBPP (and +/Pro variants) for generation; add LiveCodeBench for execution‑centric tasks; evaluate multilingual settings; and include self‑invoking tests to stress environment and tool understanding. HumanEval and MBPP are standard starting points for code generation evaluation [a517d63b-0]. HumanEval Pro/MBPP Pro reveal ~10–15% drops compared to original versions, reflecting more realistic code constraints [a517d63b-4]. 

- Measuring multi‑agent/tool‑use reasoning: Use multi‑domain suites and agent frameworks that require planning, retrieval, and function/tool calling to reflect real‑world workflows rather than single‑turn QA. Surveys highlight the need for comprehensive platforms that assess multi-step, tool-augmented reasoning [c76c99a3-3].

snippets: HumanEval and MBPP Benchmarks The HumanEval (Chen et al., 2021) and MBPP (Austin et al., 2021) benchmarks are widely used for evaluating code LLMs. HumanEval consists of 164 hand-written Python problems that are validated using test cases to assess the code generated by a Code LLM in a zero-shot setting, while the MBPP benchmark includes 500 problems in a few-shot setting. To evaluate the model's multilingual capabilities, we expanded the Python problems of Humaneval Benchmark to seven additional commonly used programming languages, namely C++, Java, PHP, TypeScript (TS), C#, Bash, and JavaScript (JS) (Cassano et al., 2023). snippets:
The HellaSwag benchmark tests common sense reasoning by presenting models with sentences and multiple possible endings, requiring them to choose the most logical continuation [25]. LiveBench addresses the test set contamination issue in LLM evaluation by offering a benchmark immune to such contamination and biases from human or LLM judging [26]. It features frequently updated questions from recent sources, automatic scoring against objective ground-truth values, and diverse tasks spanning math, coding, reasoning, language, instruction following, and data analysis [26]. 

The recent survey papers have provided comprehensive frameworks and methodologies that are invaluable for developing robust benchmarks. One such paper, "A Survey on Evaluation of Large Language Models," presents a detailed review focusing on three key dimensions: what to evaluate, where to evaluate, and how to evaluate [27]. It encompasses a broad spectrum of tasks, including general natural language processing, reasoning, medical applications, ethics, education, and more. This survey emphasizes the critical role of evaluation methods and benchmarks in assessing LLM performance, summarizing both successes and failures across different tasks, and highlighting future challenges in the field [27]. Similarly, "Evaluating Large Language Models: A Comprehensive Survey" categorizes LLM evaluation into knowledge and capability, alignment, and safety [28]. This survey underscores the importance of rigorous assessment and the development of comprehensive evaluation platforms to ensure the safe and beneficial development of LLMs. It aims to guide responsible LLM advancement, ensuring that their evolution maximizes societal benefits while minimizing potential risks [28]. Both surveys stress the necessity of treating evaluation as an essential discipline to aid the development of more proficient and ethically sound LLMs [29].

citations.title: ARC-AGI-2: A New Challenge for Frontier AI Reasoning Systems
snippets: The Abstraction and Reasoning Corpus for Artificial General Intelligence (ARC-AGI), introduced in 2019, established a challenging benchmark for evaluating the general fluid intelligence of artificial systems via a set of unique, novel tasks only requiring minimal prior knowledge. While ARC-AGI has spurred significant research activity over the past five years, recent AI progress calls for benchmarks capable of finer-grained evaluation at higher levels of cognitive complexity. We introduce ARC-AGI-2, an upgraded version of the benchmark. ARC-AGI-2 preserves the input-output pair task format of its predecessor, ensuring continuity for researchers. It incorporates a newly curated and expanded set of tasks specifically designed to provide a more granular signal to assess abstract reasoning and problem-solving abilities at higher levels of fluid intelligence. To contextualize the difficulty and characteristics of ARC-AGI-2, we present extensive results from human testing, providing a robust baseline that highlights the benchmark's accessibility to human intelligence, yet difficulty for current AI systems. ARC-AGI-2 aims to serve as a next-generation tool for rigorously measuring progress towards more general and human-like AI capabilities.
