sections.title: # Key Takeaways on SOTA
sections.text:
- Frontier models dominate school‑level math (GSM8K) and high‑school math (MATH), with o1 setting a new 94.8% MATH benchmark and ARC‑AGI‑2 pushing generalization limits; however, robustness and contamination concerns require adversarial and dynamic evaluation to confirm genuine gains. o1’s 94.8% on MATH illustrates progress on challenging math benchmarks [3e9551dd-1]. ARC‑AGI progress rose to 55.5% via ARC Prize, but the benchmark remains unbeaten and emphasizes novel task generalization [555d32fa-1]. GSM‑Plus shows robustness gaps up to 20% compared to nominal accuracies on GSM8K, indicating fragility [98b976a5-3]. 

- In code generation, strong open‑source models (e.g., DeepSeek‑Coder‑V2‑Instruct, ReflectionCoder, AutoCoder) now match or exceed many proprietary systems on core HumanEval/MBPP and multilingual variants, but self‑invoking and execution‑centric tests expose meaningful drops and highlight the need for tool‑use reasoning benchmarks. DeepSeek‑Coder‑V2‑Instruct averages 75.3% on multilingual HumanEval/MBPP+ (second to GPT‑4o at 76.4%) [a517d63b-1]. ReflectionCoder reaches 82.9/76.8 on HumanEval+/MBPP+ and is on‑par with Claude‑3‑Opus and above early GPT‑4 [a517d63b-2]. Self‑invoking variants (Pro) impose ~10–15% pass@1 drops and reveal that large open-source models can match proprietary systems under these constraints [a517d63b-4]. 

- Science and commonsense benchmarks (GPQA, HellaSwag, StrategyQA) remain discriminative; many frontier models still struggle on GPQA without multiple‑choice scaffolding, and ARC‑AGI‑2 continues to separate techniques like test‑time training and program synthesis from superficial pattern matching. GPQA without options emphasizes pure reasoning and remains challenging [3e9551dd-2]. ARC‑AGI progress reflects the impact of test‑time training and program synthesis guidance on abstract reasoning tasks [555d32fa-1]. 

- Emerging trends emphasize contamination‑resistant, frequently updated, objective‑scored suites (e.g., LiveBench) and adversarial robustness (e.g., GSM‑Plus) to provide a more trustworthy view of SOTA across reasoning tasks. LiveBench introduces frequent updates, objective scoring, and contamination mitigation to improve benchmark reliability [c76c99a3-3]. GSM‑Plus advocates adversarial evaluation to expose robustness gaps and reduce overfitting [98b976a5-3].

citations.title: ARC Prize 2024: Technical Report
snippets: As of December 2024, the ARC-AGI benchmark is five years old and remains unbeaten. We believe it is currently the most important unsolved AI benchmark in the world because it seeks to measure generalization on novel tasks -- the essence of intelligence -- as opposed to skill at tasks that can be prepared for in advance. This year, we launched ARC Prize, a global competition to inspire new ideas and drive open progress towards AGI by reaching a target benchmark score of 85\%. As a result, the state-of-the-art score on the ARC-AGI private evaluation set increased from 33\% to 55.5\%, propelled by several frontier AGI reasoning techniques including deep learning-guided program synthesis and test-time training. In this paper, we survey top approaches, review new open-source implementations, discuss the limitations of the ARC-AGI-1 dataset, and share key insights gained from the competition.

sections.title: # Limitations and What Would Improve the Evidence
sections.text: Some benchmark leaderboards (e.g., GPQA, SWE‑bench) vary by evaluation setup and tool configuration, and contamination/leakage can inflate results; recent adversarial and contamination‑resistant designs help but remain unevenly adopted. Debates persist about whether high math scores reflect genuine understanding or artifacts like leakage or superficial patterns, motivating adversarial evaluations such as GSM‑Plus [98b976a5-3]. LiveBench and similar efforts aim to mitigate contamination and judging biases through objective, updated tests and ground-truth scoring [c76c99a3-3]. Additional, dynamic, cross‑benchmark comparisons with standardized tool/tool‑call protocols and automated scoring would further clarify SOTA across domains.

snippets:
The HellaSwag benchmark tests common sense reasoning by presenting models with sentences and multiple possible endings, requiring them to choose the most logical continuation [25]. LiveBench addresses the test set contamination issue in LLM evaluation by offering a benchmark immune to such contamination and biases from human or LLM judging [26]. It features frequently updated questions from recent sources, automatic scoring against objective ground-truth values, and diverse tasks spanning math, coding, reasoning, language, instruction following, and data analysis [26]. 

The recent survey papers have provided comprehensive frameworks and methodologies that are invaluable for developing robust benchmarks. One such paper, "A Survey on Evaluation of Large Language Models," presents a detailed review focusing on three key dimensions: what to evaluate, where to evaluate, and how to evaluate [27]. It encompasses a broad spectrum of tasks, including general natural language processing, reasoning, medical applications, ethics, education, and more. This survey emphasizes the critical role of evaluation methods and benchmarks in assessing LLM performance, summarizing both successes and failures across different tasks, and highlighting future challenges in the field [27]. Similarly, "Evaluating Large Language Models: A Comprehensive Survey" categorizes LLM evaluation into knowledge and capability, alignment, and safety [28]. This survey underscores the importance of rigorous assessment and the development of comprehensive evaluation platforms to ensure the safe and beneficial development of LLMs. It aims to guide responsible LLM advancement, ensuring that their evolution maximizes societal benefits while minimizing potential risks [28]. Both surveys stress the necessity of treating evaluation as an essential discipline to aid the development of more proficient and ethically sound LLMs [29].

question: How the variant effect prediction happen in proteomics and genomics domain ? What are the LLM are there in this direction?

sections.title: # Overview
sections.text: Variant effect prediction aims to estimate whether a genetic variant (e.g., SNV, indel) alters biological function and disease risk. In genomics, this spans coding and noncoding variants, often using population allele frequency, conservation, predicted protein impact (splicing, missense), and disease annotations; in proteomics, it focuses on how the variant manifests in the protein product—changes to structure, stability, interactions, posttranslational modifications (PTMs), localization, and downstream proteome-level phenotypes detectable by mass spectrometry or functional assays. Computational models range from rule-based and feature aggregation tools to deep learning and large language models (LLMs)/protein language models (PLMs) that leverage sequence/structure and, increasingly, functional assays for training and benchmarking. High-throughput functional assays such as deep mutational scanning (DMS) have become central for benchmarking computational variant effect predictors and reducing circularity in evaluation [03de37d2-0]. DMS-based benchmarks show a strong correspondence with clinical classification performance for variant effect predictors, even for methods not trained directly on clinical data [03de37d2-3].

citations.title: Variant effect predictor correlation with functional assays is reflective of clinical classification performance
snippets:
As DMS and other functional assays are increasingly used to assess performance, VEP developers will inevitably target these benchmarks and optimize for performance against them. However, currently there is little indication that DMS inclusion in VEP training or optimization has had an impact on this benchmark, and the few methods trained directly with DMS data have proven to be relatively resistant to bias. We hope that this methodology can continue to be used to benchmark future predictors in a bias-free manner. 

Other recent studies have also attempted to assess the performance of state-of-the-art VEPs using alternate strategies. Tabet et al. tested the ability of 24 different VEPs to infer human traits from the UK Biobank and All of Us cohorts [60]. While this task is distinct from predicting pathogenicity, it should be largely free of any circularity concerns. Interestingly, their overall rankings are broadly similar to what we observe here. While many of our top-ranking VEPs were not included in their study, the three top methods they identified based on UK Biobank data, AlphaMissense, ESM-1v, and VARITY, all ranked higher in our DMS benchmark than any other methods they included, and overall, there is a strong correlation (r = 0.93) between our DMS win rate and their number of traits identified (Additional file 1: Fig. S6). 

The CAGI Annotate-All-Missense challenge presents an extremely valuable study, testing the performance of 60 VEPs in discriminating between 10,456 pathogenic and benign missense variants [46]. They avoid the issue of variant-level (type 1) circularity by only used variants deposited in ClinVar or HGMD after a specific cutoff date, and only considering predictions submitted before this date, or from methods that are not trained on clinical variants. They also explore the fact that methods that directly use allele frequency essentially have an unfair advantage when classifying benign variants, showing that the performance of these VEPs is much worse when considering rarer variants. While their main analysis does not account for gene-level circularity, they also present a gene-label balanced analysis, where they only consider equal numbers of pathogenic and benign variants from each gene.

citations.title: Variant effect predictor correlation with functional assays is reflective of clinical classification performance
snippets: Background Understanding the relationship between protein sequence and function is crucial for accurate genetic variant classification. Variant effect predictors (VEPs) play a vital role in deciphering this complex relationship, yet evaluating their performance remains challenging for several reasons including data circularity, where the same or related data is used for training and assessment. High-throughput experimental strategies like deep mutational scanning (DMS) offer a promising solution. Results In this study, we extend upon our previous benchmarking approach, assessing the performance of 97 different VEPs using DMS experiments from 36 different human proteins. In addition, a new pairwise, VEP-centric ranking method reduces the impact of missing predictions on the overall ranking. We observe a remarkably high correspondence between VEP performance in DMS-based benchmarks and clinical variant classification, especially for predictors that have not been directly trained on human clinical variants. Conclusions Our results suggest that comparing VEP performance against diverse functional assays represents a reliable strategy for assessing their relative performance in clinical variant classification. However, major challenges in clinical interpretation of VEP scores persist, highlighting the need for further research to fully leverage computational predictors for genetic diagnosis. We also address practical considerations for end users in terms of choice of methodology.

sections.title: # How variant effect prediction works in genomics
sections.text:
Genomic variant effect prediction typically concatenates multiple lines of evidence: conservation/safety, predicted functional consequence (coding vs. noncoding), splicing impact, population frequency, predicted pathogenicity from curated models, and, when available, functional assay data or clinical annotations. In clinical pipelines, variants are first filtered by allele frequency (e.g., gnomAD), then stratified by clinical significance (ClinVar/HGMD), and further prioritized using pathogenicity predictors such as REVEL, CADD, ClinPred, M-CAP, VEST4, BayesDel, MetaSVM, SpliceAI, and LoFTEE [03de37d2-4]. Tools like Ensembl’s VEP annotate functional consequences of variants (e.g., protein change, splice site impact), and composite scorers such as CADD produce a PHRED-like deleteriousness score used to triage variants [03de37d2-1]. 

Evaluation has moved beyond ClinVar circularity to emphasize independent functional assays and curated challenges. DMS measures functional scores for large variant libraries and mitigates type-1 circularity by using variants unseen in training; it also mitigates type-2 circularity because performance depends on relative ranking rather than class assignment [03de37d2-2]. Benchmarking with DMS and cross-study comparisons (e.g., UK Biobank/All of Us trait inference) show that modern predictors like AlphaMissense, ESM-1v, and VARITY rank highly, and DMS-based win rates correlate strongly with trait-prediction ability [03de37d2-0]. Large-scale challenges such as CAGI Annotate-All-Missense evaluate predictors on blinded clinical variants, revealing that frequency-dependent methods gain unfair advantages and that gene-level circularity remains a concern [03de37d2-3]. 

Modern transformer-based models integrate diverse genomic signals to predict variant impact. AlphaMissense (a deep learning model trained on missense variants and functional labels) is among top-performing predictors, and ESM-1v (a protein sequence LLM) has been used as a protein-function feature for variant effect tasks [03de37d2-0]. VARITY is a transformer-based model combining evolutionary and functional features to predict variant clinical impact and has shown competitive performance on benchmarked sets [03de37d2-0].

citations.title: Detection of germline variants with pathogenic potential in 48 patients with familial colorectal cancer by using whole exome sequencing
snippets:
Prioritization steps were performed on the initial set of 125.686 variants detected from variant calling on 48 samples, using the command-line based tool filter_vep from the VEP toolkit. This was performed in three stages. In stage one, variants were selected based on their frequency in the population database gnomAD (v2.1) [14]. Variants that were not present in the database were assigned a frequency of zero and were also included in the selection process. In the second stage, variants were classified and prioritized based on their clinical significance assigned in the ClinVar database [31]. In the third and final stage, variants passing through the previous two stages were filtered based on pathogenicity estimation scores of selected tools. This included REVEL [32], CADD [33], ClinPred [34], M-CAP [35], VEST4 [36], MetaSVM [37], BayesDel [38] for missense, nonsense and start-loss prediction; SpliceAI [39] for splicing alteration prediction; and Loftee [14] for loss of function prediction. 

Selection of in silico prediction tools was based on ranking generated by our benchmarking study comparing the performance of 45 different pathogenicity prediction tools (see Supplementary file 1). We also took into consideration other benchmarking studies with similar goals [40][41][42]. Figure 1 shows workflow for these filtering steps and the outcome of each step. For detailed information about the various filtering steps, please see Supplementary file 2.

snippets:
by using data from deep mutational scanning (DMS) studies as the "gold standard" to perform a benchmark of VEP performance against single amino acid variants (Livesey & Marsh, 2020). DMS encompasses a wide variety of high-throughput experimental techniques, whereby functional scores for large numbers of amino acid variants are measured (Fowler & Fields, 2014). Because most DMSderived functional scores are for variants never observed in the human population, using them to assess VEP performance can address the issues of limited benchmarking data availability that sometimes lead to type 1 circularity. Significant progress has been made in both VEP development and DMS methodologies since our previous study with multiple predictors based on cutting-edge machine learning techniques and many new DMS studies being published (preprint: Meier et al, 2021;Wu et al, 2021). sections.title: # How variant effect prediction works in proteomics
sections.text:
Proteomics variant effect prediction focuses on how mutations change protein sequence/structure, stability, and functional properties, often projecting these effects to proteome-wide outcomes (e.g., expression, PTMs, localization, identifiability) and downstream phenotypes. Sequence- and structure-informed models have advanced rapidly with protein language models (PLMs) and inverse folding. Protein language models (e.g., ESM variants) can recover conservation and functional/structural patterns and have been shown to accurately predict variant effects approaching alignment-based methods, enabling proteome-wide analysis [2778dda3-0]. FunC-ESMs combines ESM-1b for “conservation” with ESM-IF (Inverse Folding) to assess variant impact on protein stability, and was validated across scenarios and applied to characterize all human missense variants, including >70,000 clinically annotated ones across >10k proteins [2778dda3-0]. On these datasets, FunC-ESMs separates benign and pathogenic variants with high AUC, classifying ~78% of annotated pathogenic variants as deleterious, with a large share affecting stability and others affecting function via alternative mechanisms [2778dda3-1]. Proteome-scale predictions can label each variant as wildtype-like, stable-but-inactive, or total-loss, and annotate residues as tolerant, structurally critical, functionally relevant, or mixed, providing mechanistic hypotheses for disease variants [2778dda3-2]. 

Training and fine-tuning with functional labels improves accuracy and generalization. DMS assays provide comprehensive fitness landscapes for benchmarking and training, with repositories like MaveDB and ProteinGym standardizing data; rescaling across assays is needed due to experimental protocol differences [2778dda3-3]. Fine-tuning PLMs (e.g., ESM families) on DMS-labeled proteins improves zero-shot variant effect prediction and performance on held-out proteins and clinical benchmarks, while maintaining generalization at low sequence similarity [2778dda3-3]. 

Proteomics pipelines often integrate multiple functional annotations to refine variant impact. In applied analyses, variant effect predictions can be coupled with structure stability models (I-Mutant2.0, MUpro) to estimate free-energy changes (ΔΔG), surface exposure and burial (e.g., via residue environment descriptors), functional site exposure (e.g., ConSurf), PTM disruption/creation (e.g., MuSiTe), and binding site perturbation predictions to infer downstream proteomic consequences [2778dda3-4]. These multi-annotation integrations contextualize predicted stability effects with disorder propensity and residue exposure, supporting residue-level mechanistic interpretation across folded and disordered regions [2778dda3-2].

citations.title: Decoding molecular mechanisms for loss-of-function variants in the human proteome
snippets:
Having assessed the accuracy of the FunC-ESMs to identify the mechanism behind lossof-function variants, we proceeded to predict variant effects and assign residue labels for the proteins in the human genome and the mechanism behind disease variants (Fig. 1). 

We generated ESM-1b and ESM-IF scores, using as reference one protein sequence per human gene from the UniProt human reference proteome. We collected the predicted structures from the AlphaFold2 protein database (Jumper et al., 2021;Varadi et al., 2022a) and used these as input for ESM-IF. Similarly, we used the sequence for all human proteins as input to ESM-1b to assess variant effects. To analyse and interpret the output from FunC-ESMs, we also collected predictions of protein disorder (Hanson et al., 2017;Alderson et al., 2023), and calculated descriptors of the biochemical environment and residue exposure. In total, we collected data for 20,144 human proteins and to make predictions with 780,218 variants,distributed over 10,304,222 residues. 

The model predictions were used to designate each individual variant as either wildtype-like (WT-like), total-loss (TL), or stable-but-inactive (SBI). We found that 60% of the predicted substitutions were classified as WT-like, 19% as total-loss and 21% as stablebut-inactive (Fig. S4A). At the residue level, we also assigned a label based on the role of the residue in the protein: we designated residues where most variants were WT-like as 'tolerant'; and refer to positions critical for maintaining protein stability (with a dominance of total-loss variants) as 'structurally critical'. Residues with many variants predicted to be stable-but-inactive were labelled as 'functionally relevant'; residues without any dominant effect were designated as 'mixed'. Our results show that 57% of all residues were labelled as tolerant, 17% as structurally critical, 19% as functionally relevant, and 7% as mixed (Fig. S4D).

citations.title: Decoding molecular mechanisms for loss-of-function variants in the human proteome
snippets:
We also showed that residues that are conserved in evolution, but not due to a role for protein stability, are highly enriched in verified functionally relevant residues, and validated the results using prospective experiments in HPRT1 (Cagiada et al., 2023). Our approach thereby provided proof of principle for the ability to simultaneously predict disease variants and the molecular mechanisms underlying variants effects, and to discover functionally important positions in proteins (Cagiada et al., 2021(Cagiada et al., , 2023)). 

While this approach was accurate it relied on relatively slow computational methods for assessing variant effects, including the construction of high-quality multiple sequence alignments, limiting proteome-wide applications. Further, our approach was based on training a machine-learning model on a small set of proteins that have been studied experimentally by multi-modal MAVEs. To address these issues and enable accurate proteome-wide analyses we here present an approach that leverages accurate and fast pre-trained machine-learning models. In recent years, protein language models have been shown to enable accurate predictions of variant effects that approach the accu-racy of alignment-based methods (Meier et al., 2021;Outeiral and Deane, 2022;Brandes et al., 2023) and for assessing the impact of variants on protein stability (Notin et al., 2023). Specifically, we here combine the ESM-1b model (Rives et al., 2021) for protein 'conservation' with the ESM-IF ('Inverse Folding') model (Hsu et al., 2022) to assess the impact of variants on protein stability via a model that we call FunC-ESMs (Functional Characterisation via Evolutionary Scale Models). We validate FunC-ESMs across a range of scenarios and apply it to characterise all possible missense variants in the human proteome including seventy thousand clinically annotated variants distributed across more than ten thousand proteins.

citations.title: In-silico analysis predicts disruption of normal angiogenesis as a causative factor in osteoporosis pathogenesis
snippets:
SNVs associated with the hub genes were identified via the DisGeNET, PubMed and Google Scholar databases. 

Missense variations were shortlisted by checking the rsIDs in NCBI-SNP. The rsIDs are unique labels used to identify an SNP. Loss-of-function effect of the variant was predicted via the tool gnomAD. The variants were given as inputs one by one in the gnomAD v4.1.0 browser. Only those missense SNPs that passed all variant filters in gnomAD were subjected to structure stability prediction via I-Mutant2.0 and MUpro. I-Mutant2.0 (https:// foldi ng. biofo ld. org/i-mutant/) predicts protein stability changes when there is a single nucleotide mutation. The protein sequence, position and the new residue were given as inputs. The prediction is displayed as the free energy change value (DDG). If the value is less than 0, the substitution decreases stability and vice versa. The same method is also followed in MUpro too (https:// mupro. prote omics. ics. uci. edu/). MUpro also predicts changes in protein stability for single-nucleotide variants (SNVs) via amino acid sequences. The sequence without headers, the position of mutation, the original amino acid and the substitute amino acid were given as inputs. The result is obtained as a DDG value and is predicted as decreased or increased stability. The ConSurf webserver (https:// consu rf. tau. ac. il/ consu rf_ index. php) was used to identify whether the variation was in the functional region of the protein products of the hub genes. The FASTA sequence was used as input for the prediction. Musit-eDeep (https:// www. musite. net/) was used for the prediction of posttranslational modifications (PTMs) at the site of variation. The FASTA sequence was submitted to this server and a prediction model was selected to identify the PTMs. Protein ligand binding site prediction was performed via the COACH server.

citations.title: Fine-tuning Protein Language Models with Deep Mutational Scanning improves Variant Effect Prediction
snippets:
We finally evaluate the performance improvements of our approach on held-out test proteins and independent DMS and clinical annotation benchmarks, while ensuring low sequence similarity between training and evaluation proteins to assess model generalisation.

Deep Mutational Scanning (DMS) is an experimental technique that leverages high-throughput DNA sequencing and fitness selection assays to exhaustively measure the effect of variants in a protein region (Fowler & Fields, 2014), providing comprehensive maps of protein variant effects that can be used to understand the clinical relevance of human genetic variants (Findlay et al., 2018;Radford et al., 2023).Recognising the rapidly expanding volume of DMS data and the challenges with data compilation and reproducibility, the Atlas of Variant Effects (AVE) alliance (Fowler et al., 2021) developed MaveDB, an open-source repository of DMS assays (Esposito et al., 2019;Rubin et al., 2021).More recently, ProteinGym has emerged as an independent collection of manually curated DMS assays, providing a standardised framework for benchmarking protein fitness prediction and design (Notin et al., 2023).Despite the wide adoption of DMS datasets for benchmarking variant effect prediction models (Livesey & Marsh, 2023), one of the remaining challenges in combining DMS scores across assays and proteins is that their scale is highly dependent on experimental methods and selection assays, requiring rescaling and normalisation (Dunham & Beltrao, 2021).

Protein Language Models (PLMs) are pre-trained on large corpora of naturally evolved protein sequences using self-supervision and have shown great promise predicting the impact of missense variants without additional supervision (i.e.zero-shot) (Meier et al., 2021).The Evolutionary Scale Modelling (ESM) family of PLMs (Rives et al., 2021;Meier et al., 2021;Lin et al., 2023b) pre-trained with masked language modelling on the UniRef database (UniProt Consortium, 2023) demonstrated the ability to encode functional and structural patterns crucial for variant effect and structural predictions.

sections.title: # Regulatory and noncoding variant effect prediction
sections.text: A large fraction of disease-associated variants lie in noncoding regions, motivating specialized models that predict effects on gene regulation. RegVar is a DNN framework that predicts tissue-specific impacts of noncoding regulatory variants on target genes and outperforms existing prioritization methods across tissues, linking variants to putative regulators [0c3f0c09-0]. Benchmarking studies curate MPRA, raQTL, and eQTL datasets to evaluate models for predicting enhancer activity changes, classifying regulatory impact, and identifying causal variants within LD blocks [0c3f0c09-1]. CNN-based models (e.g., DeepSEA, SEI, TREDNet) often excel at local motif-aware regulatory effect prediction, while hybrid CNN–transformer models (e.g., Borzoi) better identify causal SNPs within LD blocks; fine-tuning boosts transformer performance and can close gaps under optimized conditions [0c3f0c09-2]. Transformer-based architectures (DNABERT, Nucleotide Transformer, Enformer) leverage large-scale pretraining and cell-type–aware contexts to model long-range regulatory effects and interpret noncoding variation [0c3f0c09-3]. However, standardized evaluations (e.g., DART-Eval) show that state-of-the-art DNA language models can perform poorly at predicting the direction and magnitude of allele-specific effects measured by MPRA, underscoring challenges in capturing subtle functional differences and the need for consistent benchmarks [0c3f0c09-4].

citations.title: Comparative Analysis of Deep Learning Models for Predicting Causative Regulatory Variants
snippets:
By integrating contextual information across broader genomic regions, Transformer models offer enhanced resolution for interpreting noncoding variation in a cell-type-aware manner. 

Selecting the most suitable model for detecting the regulatory effects of genetic variants remains a significant challenge despite several surveys offering detailed overviews of the deep learning ecosystem in this domain [26][27][28][29]. These surveys have highlighted the unique strengths and limitations of various models. However, they lack a unified framework for assessment. Specifically, existing reviews often fail to benchmark models on a standardized dataset, train or fine-tune them under consistent conditions, and evaluate their performance using uniform criteria. Furthermore, a fundamental difference between benchmarking models on regulatory regions versus regulatory variants is rarely addressed. While regulatory region analyses focus on identifying broader functional elements, regulatory variant assessments require evaluating the impact of specific sequence alterations within these regions, presenting distinct challenges and opportunities for model evaluation. Recent efforts such as DART-Eval [30] have taken necessary steps toward standardizing the evaluation of DNA language models by introducing a comprehensive benchmark that spans multiple regulatory genomics tasks, including variant effect prediction. Their results revealed that state-of-the-art Transformer-based models-including DNABERT-2 and Nucleotide Transformer-often performed poorly at predicting the direction and magnitude of allele-specific effects measured by MPRA. These findings highlight the limitations of current architectures in capturing subtle, functionally meaningful sequence differences introduced by single-nucleotide variants. Motivated by this, we expand the scope of our evaluation to include a broader set of models, incorporating CNN-based approaches such as SEI and TREDNet, which are known for their robustness in modeling local sequence motifs and regulatory element activity. 

In this study, we evaluate state-of-the-art deep learning models to predict the effects of genetic variants on enhancer activity in the human genome. Our approach involved curating and integrating nine datasets derived from diverse experimental methodologies, including massively parallel reporter assay (MPRA), reporter assay quantitative trait loci (raQTL), and expression quantitative trait loci (eQTL) studies. These datasets encompass 54,859 single-nucleotide polymorphisms (SNPs) in enhancer regions across four human cell lines.

citations.title: RegVar: Tissue-specific Prioritization of Non-coding Regulatory Variants
snippets: Noncoding genomic variants constitute the majority of trait-associated genome variations; however, identification of functional noncoding variants is still a challenge in human genetics, and a method systematically assessing the impact of regulatory variants on gene expression and linking them to potential target genes is still lacking. Here we introduce a deep neural network (DNN)-based computational framework, RegVar, that can accurately predict the tissue-specific impact of noncoding regulatory variants on target genes. We show that, by robustly learning the genomic characteristics of massive variant-gene expression associations in a variety of human tissues, RegVar vastly surpasses all current noncoding variants prioritization methods in predicting regulatory variants under different circumstances. The unique features of RegVar make it an excellent framework for assessing the regulatory impact of any variant on its putative target genes in a variety of tissues. RegVar is available as a webserver at http://regvar.cbportal.org/.

citations.title: Comparative Analysis of Deep Learning Models for Predicting Causative Regulatory Variants
snippets:
Genome-wide association studies (GWAS) have revealed that around 95% of diseaseassociated genetic variants occur in non-coding regions of the human genome, with causative variants commonly affecting regulatory elements that modulate gene expression [1,2,3]. These regulatory variants can profoundly affect phenotypes and alter disease susceptibility by dysregulating their target genes [4]. 

Deep learning has emerged as a transformative approach for predicting the regulatory effects of genetic variants, particularly within enhancer regions. These models harness large-scale genomic and epigenomic datasets to learn complex sequence-to-function relationships, identifying DNA sequence features that influence regulatory activity. 

Convolutional neural networks (CNNs), for example, have been successfully applied to detect variants that disrupt transcription factor binding sites or alter chromatin accessibility, offering mechanistic insights into their potential phenotypic consequences. Notable CNN-based models include DeepSEA [5], SEI [6], and TREDNet [7]. More recently, transformer-based architectures have demonstrated strong performance in capturing long-range dependencies and modeling cell-typespecific regulatory effects. These models-such as the DNABERT series [8,9], the Nucleotide Transformer family [10,11], and Enformer [12]-were pre-trained on large-scale genomic sequences using self-supervised objectives and subsequently finetuned for specialized tasks, including predicting DNA methylation patterns, enhancer activity, and the functional impact of disease-associated variants. By integrating contextual information across broader genomic regions, transformer models offer enhanced resolution for interpreting non-coding variation in a cell-type-aware manner. 

Selecting the most suitable model for detecting the regulatory effects of genetic variants remains a significant challenge despite several surveys offering detailed overviews of the deep learning ecosystem in this domain [13,14,15]. These surveys have highlighted the unique strengths and limitations of various models. However, they lack a unified framework for assessment. Specifically, existing reviews often fail to benchmark models on a standardized dataset, train or fine-tune them under consistent conditions, and evaluate their performance using uniform criteria.

citations.title: Comparative Analysis of Deep Learning Models for Predicting Causative Regulatory Variants
snippets: Motivation Genome-wide association studies (GWAS) have identified numerous noncoding variants associated with complex human diseases, disorders, and traits. However, resolving the uncertainty between GWAS association and causality remains a significant challenge. The small subset of noncoding GWAS variants with causative effects on gene regulatory elements can only be detected through accurate methods that assess the impact of DNA sequence variation on gene regulatory activity. Deep learning models, such as those based on Convolutional Neural Networks (CNNs) and transformers, have gained prominence in predicting the regulatory effects of genetic variants, particularly in enhancers, by learning patterns from genomic and epigenomic data. Despite their potential, selecting the most suitable model is hindered by the lack of standardized benchmarks, consistent training conditions, and performance evaluation criteria in existing reviews. Results This study evaluates state-of-the-art deep learning models for predicting the effects of genetic variants on enhancer activity using nine datasets stemming from MPRA, raQTL, and eQTL experiments, profiling the regulatory impact of 54,859 SNPs across four human cell lines. The results reveal that CNN models, such as TREDNet and SEI, consistently outperform other architectures in predicting the regulatory impact of single-nucleotide polymorphisms (SNPs). However, hybrid CNN-transformer models, such as Borzoi, display superior performance in identifying causal SNPs within a linkage disequilibrium block. While fine-tuning enhances the performance of transformer-based models, it remains insufficient to surpass CNN and hybrid models when evaluated under optimized conditions.

citations.title: Comparative Analysis of Deep Learning Models for Predicting Causative Regulatory Variants
snippets:
Specifically, existing reviews often fail to benchmark models on a standardized dataset, train or fine-tune them under consistent conditions, and evaluate their performance using uniform criteria. Furthermore, there is a fundamental difference between benchmarking models on regulatory regions versus regulatory variants, which is rarely addressed. While regulatory region analyses focus on identifying broader functional elements, regulatory variant assessments require evaluating the impact of specific sequence alterations within these regions, presenting distinct challenges and opportunities for model evaluation. 

In this study, we evaluate state-of-the-art deep learning models to predict the effects of genetic variants on enhancer activity in the human genome. Our approach involved curating and integrating nine datasets derived from diverse experimental methodologies, including massively parallel reporter assay (MPRA), reporter assay quantitative trait loci (raQTL), and expression quantitative trait loci (eQTL) studies. 

These datasets encompass 54,859 single-nucleotide polymorphisms (SNPs) in enhancer regions across four human cell lines. 

We tackle three tasks: predicting log2-fold changes in enhancer activity, classifying SNPs based on their regulatory impact, and identifying causal SNPs within linkage disequilibrium (LD) blocks. We also assess how data variability affects model performance, emphasizing the importance of data quality. Finally, we illustrate how enhancer detection models can be effectively leveraged for variant effect assessment, highlighting their practical utility in interpreting genomic data and prioritizing candidate regulatory variants. 

To ensure a robust and thorough assessment, we fine-tuned 22 deep learning models for each cell line, systematically exploring a broad spectrum of architectural designs and parameter configurations. Our results indicate that CNN models outperform more "advanced" architectures, such as transformers, on causative regulatory variant detection. However, fine-tuning significantly boosts the performance of transformerbased architectures, revealing their potential to surpass CNNs under optimized conditions.

sections.title: # What are the LLMs/models in this direction?
sections.text:
- Genomics/variant pathogenicity and mechanism:
 - AlphaMissense: deep learning model trained on missense variation and functional/clinical labels to predict deleteriousness and mechanisms, ranking among top predictors in DMS and trait-inference benchmarks. AlphaMissense ranks highly in DMS-based benchmarks and correlates with trait prediction from population-scale datasets [03de37d2-0]. 
 - ESM-1v: a protein sequence LLM that encodes functional and structural information and is used as a protein-function feature for variant effect prediction. ESM-1v contributes to variant effect modeling and has been integrated into clinical/trait prediction comparisons [03de37d2-0]. 
 - VARITY: a transformer-based model combining evolutionary and functional features to predict clinical impact of variants; performs competitively in large-scale evaluations. VARITY is identified among top predictors in cross-validation and external challenges [03de37d2-0]. 
 - Traditional VEPs and composite scorers widely used in pipelines (VEP, CADD, REVEL, ClinPred, M-CAP, VEST4, BayesDel, MetaSVM, SpliceAI, LoFTEE). These tools are routinely integrated in variant prioritization workflows based on frequency, functional prediction, and disease annotations [03de37d2-4]. CADD PHRED scores are used to triage variants in clinical and research settings [03de37d2-1]. 

- Proteomics/protein-level variant impact:
 - ESM-1b and ESM-IF (Inverse Folding): PLMs used to derive conservation and stability features; combined in FunC-ESMs to classify variant effects (WT-like, stable-but-inactive, total-loss) across the human proteome and annotate mechanisms. ESM-1b/ESM-IF enable rapid, proteome-wide variant effect assessment with accuracy approaching alignment-based methods [2778dda3-0]. FunC-ESMs shows strong separation of benign vs. pathogenic variants and quantifies the fraction attributable to stability versus other mechanisms [2778dda3-1]. Residue-level labels (tolerant, structurally critical, functionally relevant, mixed) provide mechanistic hypotheses for disease-associated variants [2778dda3-2]. 
 - DMS-informed training and benchmarking: large-scale mutational datasets (ProteinGym, MaveDB) and AVE alliance efforts provide standardized functional labels to train and validate models and address rescaling across assays. DMS resources and standardization efforts support benchmarking and improve cross-assay comparability [2778dda3-3]. 
 - Stability and PTM/localization integration: combining PLM outputs with stability (ΔΔG), surface exposure, functional site conservation, PTM prediction, and binding-site analysis to infer proteomic consequences. Tools like I-Mutant2.0, MUpro, ConSurf, and MuSiTe are commonly integrated to interpret structural and PTM effects of variants [2778dda3-4]. 

- Regulatory/noncoding:
 - CNN-based enhancer variant effect models (e.g., DeepSEA, SEI, TREDNet) and hybrid CNN–transformer models (e.g., Borzoi) trained to predict regulatory impact, causal variants, and enhancer activity changes; transformers (DNABERT, Nucleotide Transformer, Enformer) for cell-type–aware regulatory effect prediction. CNNs often dominate in SNP effect classification within enhancers, while hybrid architectures aid causal variant identification [0c3f0c09-2]. Transformers leverage long-range context and cell-type specificity to interpret noncoding variation [0c3f0c09-3]. Standardized evaluations reveal limitations in predicting allele-specific effects, motivating careful benchmarking and model selection [0c3f0c09-4]. 
 - Tissue-specific regulatory variant prioritization frameworks like RegVar link variants to target genes and regulatory mechanisms across tissues. RegVar outperforms existing methods in predicting tissue-specific regulatory impact and connecting variants to target genes [0c3f0c09-0].

citations.title: Decoding molecular mechanisms for loss-of-function variants in the human proteome
snippets:
Having assessed the accuracy of the FunC-ESMs to identify the mechanism behind lossof-function variants, we proceeded to predict variant effects and assign residue labels for the proteins in the human genome and the mechanism behind disease variants (Fig. 1). 

We generated ESM-1b and ESM-IF scores, using as reference one protein sequence per human gene from the UniProt human reference proteome. We collected the predicted structures from the AlphaFold2 protein database (Jumper et al., 2021;Varadi et al., 2022a) and used these as input for ESM-IF. Similarly, we used the sequence for all human proteins as input to ESM-1b to assess variant effects. To analyse and interpret the output from FunC-ESMs, we also collected predictions of protein disorder (Hanson et al., 2017;Alderson et al., 2023), and calculated descriptors of the biochemical environment and residue exposure. In total, we collected data for 20,144 human proteins and to make predictions with 780,218 variants,distributed over 10,304,222 residues. 

The model predictions were used to designate each individual variant as either wildtype-like (WT-like), total-loss (TL), or stable-but-inactive (SBI). We found that 60% of the predicted substitutions were classified as WT-like, 19% as total-loss and 21% as stablebut-inactive (Fig. S4A). At the residue level, we also assigned a label based on the role of the residue in the protein: we designated residues where most variants were WT-like as 'tolerant'; and refer to positions critical for maintaining protein stability (with a dominance of total-loss variants) as 'structurally critical'. Residues with many variants predicted to be stable-but-inactive were labelled as 'functionally relevant'; residues without any dominant effect were designated as 'mixed'. Our results show that 57% of all residues were labelled as tolerant, 17% as structurally critical, 19% as functionally relevant, and 7% as mixed (Fig. S4D).

citations.title: Detection of germline variants with pathogenic potential in 48 patients with familial colorectal cancer by using whole exome sequencing
snippets:
Prioritization steps were performed on the initial set of 125.686 variants detected from variant calling on 48 samples, using the command-line based tool filter_vep from the VEP toolkit. This was performed in three stages. In stage one, variants were selected based on their frequency in the population database gnomAD (v2.1) [14]. Variants that were not present in the database were assigned a frequency of zero and were also included in the selection process. In the second stage, variants were classified and prioritized based on their clinical significance assigned in the ClinVar database [31]. In the third and final stage, variants passing through the previous two stages were filtered based on pathogenicity estimation scores of selected tools. This included REVEL [32], CADD [33], ClinPred [34], M-CAP [35], VEST4 [36], MetaSVM [37], BayesDel [38] for missense, nonsense and start-loss prediction; SpliceAI [39] for splicing alteration prediction; and Loftee [14] for loss of function prediction. 

Selection of in silico prediction tools was based on ranking generated by our benchmarking study comparing the performance of 45 different pathogenicity prediction tools (see Supplementary file 1). We also took into consideration other benchmarking studies with similar goals [40][41][42]. Figure 1 shows workflow for these filtering steps and the outcome of each step. For detailed information about the various filtering steps, please see Supplementary file 2.

citations.title: Variant effect predictor correlation with functional assays is reflective of clinical classification performance
snippets:
As DMS and other functional assays are increasingly used to assess performance, VEP developers will inevitably target these benchmarks and optimize for performance against them. However, currently there is little indication that DMS inclusion in VEP training or optimization has had an impact on this benchmark, and the few methods trained directly with DMS data have proven to be relatively resistant to bias. Other recent studies have also attempted to assess the performance of state-of-the-art VEPs using alternate strategies. They also explore the fact that methods that directly use allele frequency essentially have an unfair advantage when classifying benign variants, showing that the performance of these VEPs is much worse when considering rarer variants. citations.title: Comparative Analysis of Deep Learning Models for Predicting Causative Regulatory Variants
snippets: Motivation Genome-wide association studies (GWAS) have identified numerous noncoding variants associated with complex human diseases, disorders, and traits. However, resolving the uncertainty between GWAS association and causality remains a significant challenge. The small subset of noncoding GWAS variants with causative effects on gene regulatory elements can only be detected through accurate methods that assess the impact of DNA sequence variation on gene regulatory activity. Deep learning models, such as those based on Convolutional Neural Networks (CNNs) and transformers, have gained prominence in predicting the regulatory effects of genetic variants, particularly in enhancers, by learning patterns from genomic and epigenomic data. Despite their potential, selecting the most suitable model is hindered by the lack of standardized benchmarks, consistent training conditions, and performance evaluation criteria in existing reviews. Results This study evaluates state-of-the-art deep learning models for predicting the effects of genetic variants on enhancer activity using nine datasets stemming from MPRA, raQTL, and eQTL experiments, profiling the regulatory impact of 54,859 SNPs across four human cell lines. The results reveal that CNN models, such as TREDNet and SEI, consistently outperform other architectures in predicting the regulatory impact of single-nucleotide polymorphisms (SNPs). However, hybrid CNN-transformer models, such as Borzoi, display superior performance in identifying causal SNPs within a linkage disequilibrium block. While fine-tuning enhances the performance of transformer-based models, it remains insufficient to surpass CNN and hybrid models when evaluated under optimized conditions.

sections.title: # Practical workflows and evaluation strategies
sections.text:
In genomics, end-to-end pipelines start from variant calling and use a combination of population filters, functional predictors, splicing/LoF models, regulatory annotations, and aggregate pathogenicity scores to prioritize variants for validation or clinical interpretation. Pipelines typically include gnomAD frequency filtering, ClinVar significance stratification, and multi-model scoring (REVEL, CADD, ClinPred, M-CAP, VEST4, BayesDel, MetaSVM, SpliceAI, LoFTEE) before downstream validation [03de37d2-4]. Rigorous evaluation increasingly relies on independent functional assays and challenges to mitigate circularity and compare methods fairly. DMS-based benchmarks provide continuous functional outcomes that reduce circularity and assess relative ranking [03de37d2-2]. Clinical challenges (e.g., CAGI) and trait-inference tasks provide external validity, while highlighting biases such as gene-level circularity and frequency-dependent advantages [03de37d2-3]. 

In proteomics, variant effect prediction integrates sequence/structure-based models, functional assays, and functional annotation layers to explain how mutations affect protein stability, function, PTMs, localization, and proteome-level phenotypes. PLMs and inverse folding enable rapid proteome-scale predictions of functional impact and stability, scalable to thousands of proteins and millions of variants [2778dda3-0]. Residue-level mechanistic labels and structural context help interpret disease mechanisms and guide functional follow-up [2778dda3-2]. Fine-tuning PLMs on DMS data improves accuracy and generalization, and standardized DMS repositories facilitate reproducible benchmarking [2778dda3-3]. Multi-omics integration with PTM and binding-site predictors provides an evidence-backed view of downstream proteomic consequences. Stability (ΔΔG), surface exposure, functional site conservation, PTM predictions (e.g., MuSiTe), and binding-site perturbation analysis are combined to interpret variant effects [2778dda3-4].

snippets:
Having assessed the accuracy of the FunC-ESMs to identify the mechanism behind lossof-function variants, we proceeded to predict variant effects and assign residue labels for the proteins in the human genome and the mechanism behind disease variants (Fig. 1). 

We generated ESM-1b and ESM-IF scores, using as reference one protein sequence per human gene from the UniProt human reference proteome. We collected the predicted structures from the AlphaFold2 protein database (Jumper et al., 2021;Varadi et al., 2022a) and used these as input for ESM-IF. Similarly, we used the sequence for all human proteins as input to ESM-1b to assess variant effects. To analyse and interpret the output from FunC-ESMs, we also collected predictions of protein disorder (Hanson et al., 2017;Alderson et al., 2023), and calculated descriptors of the biochemical environment and residue exposure. In total, we collected data for 20,144 human proteins and to make predictions with 780,218 variants,distributed over 10,304,222 residues. 

The model predictions were used to designate each individual variant as either wildtype-like (WT-like), total-loss (TL), or stable-but-inactive (SBI). We found that 60% of the predicted substitutions were classified as WT-like, 19% as total-loss and 21% as stablebut-inactive (Fig. S4A). At the residue level, we also assigned a label based on the role of the residue in the protein: we designated residues where most variants were WT-like as 'tolerant'; and refer to positions critical for maintaining protein stability (with a dominance of total-loss variants) as 'structurally critical'. Residues with many variants predicted to be stable-but-inactive were labelled as 'functionally relevant'; residues without any dominant effect were designated as 'mixed'. Our results show that 57% of all residues were labelled as tolerant, 17% as structurally critical, 19% as functionally relevant, and 7% as mixed (Fig. S4D).

citations.title: Variant effect predictor correlation with functional assays is reflective of clinical classification performance
snippets: Background Understanding the relationship between protein sequence and function is crucial for accurate genetic variant classification. Variant effect predictors (VEPs) play a vital role in deciphering this complex relationship, yet evaluating their performance remains challenging for several reasons including data circularity, where the same or related data is used for training and assessment. High-throughput experimental strategies like deep mutational scanning (DMS) offer a promising solution. Results In this study, we extend upon our previous benchmarking approach, assessing the performance of 97 different VEPs using DMS experiments from 36 different human proteins. In addition, a new pairwise, VEP-centric ranking method reduces the impact of missing predictions on the overall ranking. We observe a remarkably high correspondence between VEP performance in DMS-based benchmarks and clinical variant classification, especially for predictors that have not been directly trained on human clinical variants. Conclusions Our results suggest that comparing VEP performance against diverse functional assays represents a reliable strategy for assessing their relative performance in clinical variant classification. However, major challenges in clinical interpretation of VEP scores persist, highlighting the need for further research to fully leverage computational predictors for genetic diagnosis. We also address practical considerations for end users in terms of choice of methodology.

For detailed information about the various filtering steps, please see Supplementary file 2.

To address these issues and enable accurate proteome-wide analyses we here present an approach that leverages accurate and fast pre-trained machine-learning models. sections.title: # Key challenges and open problems
sections.text:
- Benchmarking and circularity: both genomics and proteomics face circularity issues when training and testing use related data; DMS and curated clinical challenges help, but gene-level circularity and dataset heterogeneity remain concerns. Gene-label-balanced analyses and non-circular datasets are needed to fairly compare predictors [03de37d2-3]. DMS mitigates circularity but may have relevance gaps for complex mechanisms like dominant-negative effects [03de37d2-2]. 
- Noncoding regulatory prediction: while CNNs and transformers make progress, standardized evaluations show difficulty in precisely predicting direction/magnitude of allele-specific effects; improving sensitivity for subtle regulatory changes and causal variant identification is an active area. State-of-the-art DNA language models can underperform on MPRA-based variant effect prediction, indicating room to enhance feature sensitivity and training protocols [0c3f0c09-4]. 
- Proteomics breadth: modern PLM-based methods excel at protein-level functional impact and stability but need more integration with proteome-wide experimental outputs (abundance, identifiability, PTM profiles, localization shifts) and multi-experiment harmonization. Rescaling across DMS assays and generalization across proteins are ongoing challenges [2778dda3-3]. Comprehensive pipelines that couple sequence models with PTM, binding-site, and structural stability predictors help bridge from protein-level effects to proteome-level phenotypes [2778dda3-4].

citations.title: Comparative Analysis of Deep Learning Models for Predicting Causative Regulatory Variants
snippets:
By integrating contextual information across broader genomic regions, Transformer models offer enhanced resolution for interpreting noncoding variation in a cell-type-aware manner. 

Selecting the most suitable model for detecting the regulatory effects of genetic variants remains a significant challenge despite several surveys offering detailed overviews of the deep learning ecosystem in this domain [26][27][28][29]. These surveys have highlighted the unique strengths and limitations of various models. However, they lack a unified framework for assessment. Specifically, existing reviews often fail to benchmark models on a standardized dataset, train or fine-tune them under consistent conditions, and evaluate their performance using uniform criteria. Furthermore, a fundamental difference between benchmarking models on regulatory regions versus regulatory variants is rarely addressed. While regulatory region analyses focus on identifying broader functional elements, regulatory variant assessments require evaluating the impact of specific sequence alterations within these regions, presenting distinct challenges and opportunities for model evaluation. Recent efforts such as DART-Eval [30] have taken necessary steps toward standardizing the evaluation of DNA language models by introducing a comprehensive benchmark that spans multiple regulatory genomics tasks, including variant effect prediction. Their results revealed that state-of-the-art Transformer-based models-including DNABERT-2 and Nucleotide Transformer-often performed poorly at predicting the direction and magnitude of allele-specific effects measured by MPRA. These findings highlight the limitations of current architectures in capturing subtle, functionally meaningful sequence differences introduced by single-nucleotide variants. Motivated by this, we expand the scope of our evaluation to include a broader set of models, incorporating CNN-based approaches such as SEI and TREDNet, which are known for their robustness in modeling local sequence motifs and regulatory element activity. 

In this study, we evaluate state-of-the-art deep learning models to predict the effects of genetic variants on enhancer activity in the human genome. Our approach involved curating and integrating nine datasets derived from diverse experimental methodologies, including massively parallel reporter assay (MPRA), reporter assay quantitative trait loci (raQTL), and expression quantitative trait loci (eQTL) studies. These datasets encompass 54,859 single-nucleotide polymorphisms (SNPs) in enhancer regions across four human cell lines.

sections.title: # Summary
sections.text:
- In genomics, variant effect prediction combines population, conservation, and model-based annotations (VEP/CADD/REVEL, splicing/LoF tools) and is increasingly guided by functional assays and clinical benchmarks; modern transformer-based models (AlphaMissense, ESM-1v, VARITY) achieve strong performance and mechanistic insights. ESM-derived models support rapid, large-scale variant effect characterization and clinical variant coverage [2778dda3-0]. Residue-level mechanistic labeling provides hypotheses for functional follow-up [2778dda3-2]. Standardized DMS resources and fine-tuning improve accuracy and generalization [2778dda3-3]. 
- In noncoding regulatory genomics, CNNs and transformer-based models predict enhancer activity and regulatory impact, with active work on standardized, variant-focused benchmarks and tissue-specific prioritization frameworks. RegVar demonstrates tissue-specific regulatory impact prediction across genes and variants [0c3f0c09-0]. Standardized evaluations reveal current limitations and guide model selection for variant effect tasks [0c3f0c09-4]. 

Collectively, these approaches reflect a shift from isolated, feature-based scoring to integrated, mechanism-aware models and functional benchmarks that connect DNA-to-protein effects to clinical and proteomic phenotypes, with LLM/PLM-based methods playing an increasingly central role. Comparisons across DMS and clinical tasks show that modern predictors’ relative rankings are consistent, supporting their use in both research and clinical interpretation [03de37d2-3]. Proteome-scale PLM analyses reveal that a majority of annotated pathogenic missense variants impact function via stability loss or other mechanisms, aligning computational predictions with experimentally informed expectations [2778dda3-1].

citations.title: Comparative Analysis of Deep Learning Models for Predicting Causative Regulatory Variants
snippets:
By integrating contextual information across broader genomic regions, Transformer models offer enhanced resolution for interpreting noncoding variation in a cell-type-aware manner. 

Selecting the most suitable model for detecting the regulatory effects of genetic variants remains a significant challenge despite several surveys offering detailed overviews of the deep learning ecosystem in this domain [26][27][28][29]. These surveys have highlighted the unique strengths and limitations of various models. However, they lack a unified framework for assessment. Specifically, existing reviews often fail to benchmark models on a standardized dataset, train or fine-tune them under consistent conditions, and evaluate their performance using uniform criteria. Furthermore, a fundamental difference between benchmarking models on regulatory regions versus regulatory variants is rarely addressed. While regulatory region analyses focus on identifying broader functional elements, regulatory variant assessments require evaluating the impact of specific sequence alterations within these regions, presenting distinct challenges and opportunities for model evaluation. Recent efforts such as DART-Eval [30] have taken necessary steps toward standardizing the evaluation of DNA language models by introducing a comprehensive benchmark that spans multiple regulatory genomics tasks, including variant effect prediction. Their results revealed that state-of-the-art Transformer-based models-including DNABERT-2 and Nucleotide Transformer-often performed poorly at predicting the direction and magnitude of allele-specific effects measured by MPRA. These findings highlight the limitations of current architectures in capturing subtle, functionally meaningful sequence differences introduced by single-nucleotide variants. Motivated by this, we expand the scope of our evaluation to include a broader set of models, incorporating CNN-based approaches such as SEI and TREDNet, which are known for their robustness in modeling local sequence motifs and regulatory element activity. 

In this study, we evaluate state-of-the-art deep learning models to predict the effects of genetic variants on enhancer activity in the human genome. Our approach involved curating and integrating nine datasets derived from diverse experimental methodologies, including massively parallel reporter assay (MPRA), reporter assay quantitative trait loci (raQTL), and expression quantitative trait loci (eQTL) studies. These datasets encompass 54,859 single-nucleotide polymorphisms (SNPs) in enhancer regions across four human cell lines.

citations.title: RegVar: Tissue-specific Prioritization of Non-coding Regulatory Variants
snippets: Noncoding genomic variants constitute the majority of trait-associated genome variations; however, identification of functional noncoding variants is still a challenge in human genetics, and a method systematically assessing the impact of regulatory variants on gene expression and linking them to potential target genes is still lacking. Here we introduce a deep neural network (DNN)-based computational framework, RegVar, that can accurately predict the tissue-specific impact of noncoding regulatory variants on target genes. We show that, by robustly learning the genomic characteristics of massive variant-gene expression associations in a variety of human tissues, RegVar vastly surpasses all current noncoding variants prioritization methods in predicting regulatory variants under different circumstances. The unique features of RegVar make it an excellent framework for assessing the regulatory impact of any variant on its putative target genes in a variety of tissues. RegVar is available as a webserver at http://regvar.cbportal.org/.

citations.title: Variant effect predictor correlation with functional assays is reflective of clinical classification performance
snippets: Background Understanding the relationship between protein sequence and function is crucial for accurate genetic variant classification. Variant effect predictors (VEPs) play a vital role in deciphering this complex relationship, yet evaluating their performance remains challenging for several reasons including data circularity, where the same or related data is used for training and assessment. High-throughput experimental strategies like deep mutational scanning (DMS) offer a promising solution. Results In this study, we extend upon our previous benchmarking approach, assessing the performance of 97 different VEPs using DMS experiments from 36 different human proteins. In addition, a new pairwise, VEP-centric ranking method reduces the impact of missing predictions on the overall ranking. We observe a remarkably high correspondence between VEP performance in DMS-based benchmarks and clinical variant classification, especially for predictors that have not been directly trained on human clinical variants. Conclusions Our results suggest that comparing VEP performance against diverse functional assays represents a reliable strategy for assessing their relative performance in clinical variant classification. However, major challenges in clinical interpretation of VEP scores persist, highlighting the need for further research to fully leverage computational predictors for genetic diagnosis. We also address practical considerations for end users in terms of choice of methodology.

snippets:
As DMS and other functional assays are increasingly used to assess performance, VEP developers will inevitably target these benchmarks and optimize for performance against them. However, currently there is little indication that DMS inclusion in VEP training or optimization has had an impact on this benchmark, and the few methods trained directly with DMS data have proven to be relatively resistant to bias. We hope that this methodology can continue to be used to benchmark future predictors in a bias-free manner. 

Other recent studies have also attempted to assess the performance of state-of-the-art VEPs using alternate strategies. Tabet et al. tested the ability of 24 different VEPs to infer human traits from the UK Biobank and All of Us cohorts [60]. While this task is distinct from predicting pathogenicity, it should be largely free of any circularity concerns. Interestingly, their overall rankings are broadly similar to what we observe here. While many of our top-ranking VEPs were not included in their study, the three top methods they identified based on UK Biobank data, AlphaMissense, ESM-1v, and VARITY, all ranked higher in our DMS benchmark than any other methods they included, and overall, there is a strong correlation (r = 0.93) between our DMS win rate and their number of traits identified (Additional file 1: Fig. S6). 

The CAGI Annotate-All-Missense challenge presents an extremely valuable study, testing the performance of 60 VEPs in discriminating between 10,456 pathogenic and benign missense variants [46]. They avoid the issue of variant-level (type 1) circularity by only used variants deposited in ClinVar or HGMD after a specific cutoff date, and only considering predictions submitted before this date, or from methods that are not trained on clinical variants. They also explore the fact that methods that directly use allele frequency essentially have an unfair advantage when classifying benign variants, showing that the performance of these VEPs is much worse when considering rarer variants. While their main analysis does not account for gene-level circularity, they also present a gene-label balanced analysis, where they only consider equal numbers of pathogenic and benign variants from each gene.

Deep Mutational Scanning (DMS) is an experimental technique that leverages high-throughput DNA sequencing and fitness selection assays to exhaustively measure the effect of variants in a protein region (Fowler & Fields, 2014), providing comprehensive maps of protein variant effects that can be used to understand the clinical relevance of human genetic variants (Findlay et al., 2018;Radford et al., 2023).Recognising the rapidly expanding volume of DMS data and the challenges with data compilation and reproducibility, the Atlas of Variant Effects (AVE) alliance (Fowler et al., 2021) developed MaveDB, an open-source repository of DMS assays (Esposito et al., 2019;Rubin et al., 2021).More recently, ProteinGym has emerged as an independent collection of manually curated DMS assays, providing a standardised framework for benchmarking protein fitness prediction and design (Notin et al., 2023).Despite the wide adoption of DMS datasets for benchmarking variant effect prediction models (Livesey & Marsh, 2023), one of the remaining challenges in combining DMS scores across assays and proteins is that their scale is highly dependent on experimental methods and selection assays, requiring rescaling and normalisation (Dunham & Beltrao, 2021).

Protein Language Models (PLMs) are pre-trained on large corpora of naturally evolved protein sequences using self-supervision and have shown great promise predicting the impact of missense variants without additional supervision (i.e.zero-shot) (Meier et al., 2021).The Evolutionary Scale Modelling (ESM) family of PLMs (Rives et al., 2021;Meier et al., 2021;Lin et al., 2023b) pre-trained with masked language modelling on the UniRef database (UniProt Consortium, 2023) demonstrated the ability to encode functional and structural patterns crucial for variant effect and structural predictions.

citations.title: Learning to Reason via Self-Iterative Process Feedback for Small Language Models
snippets: Small language models (SLMs) are more efficient, cost-effective, and customizable than large language models (LLMs), though they often underperform in specific areas like reasoning. Past methods for enhancing SLMs' reasoning, such as supervised fine-tuning and distillation, often depend on costly external signals, resulting in SLMs being overly confident with limited supervision signals, thus limiting their abilities. Therefore, this study enables SLMs to learn to reason from self-iterative feedback. By combining odds ratio preference optimization (ORPO), we fine-tune and align SLMs using positive and negative signals generated by themselves. Additionally, we introduce process supervision for rewards in preference alignment by sampling-based inference simulation and process reward models. Compared to Supervised Fine-Tuning (SFT), our method improves the performance of Gemma-2B by 12.43 (Acc) on GSM8K and 3.95 (Pass@1) on MBPP. Furthermore, the proposed method also demonstrated superior out-of-domain generalization capabilities on MMLU_Math and HumanEval.

Process Reward Model. Process supervision addresses a core limitation of outcome-only evaluation by giving rewards on intermediate reasoning steps, helping systems avoid trajectories that look correct but contain logical errors. 

The foundational approach involves collecting step-level human annotations for mathematical reasoning tasks and training process reward models on these dense supervision signals (Lightman et al., 2023;Xia et al., 2025). Followup work scales supervision with automated or weakly supervised labels, for example per-step Monte Carlo rollouts or self-generated labels (Wang et al., 2023a;Luo et al., 2024). Beyond standard PRMs, recent variants introduce progress or verifier signals that score both partial correctness and future success, improving search and ranking during decoding (Chen et al., 2025;Setlur et al., 2024). There are also training objectives that regularize PRMs to improve stability (Zhang et al., 2024). Practical studies discuss data generation, evaluation pitfalls, and how PRMs differ from value functions that predict eventual solvability from partial traces (Zhang et al., 2025). Process-level search with step-wise scoring has further been shown to beat outcome-level test-time compute baselines in several setups, including controlled decoding, tree-structured search, and value/verification-guided search (Mudgal et al., 2023;Liu et al., 2023;Yao et al., 2023;Snell et al., 2025;Setlur et al., 2024;Wang et al., 2025). 

Multi-Objective Alignment. Multi-objective alignment trains or steers language models for multiple, potentially conflicting objectives such as helpfulness, harmlessness, and honesty (Xie et al., 2025). Standard RLHF pipelines fit a scalar reward and fine-tune with PPO, or use scalarized preference optimization (Ouyang et al., 2022;Rafailov et al., 2023;Yuan et al., 2023;Xia et al., 2024;Dong et al.), but they collapse trade-offs into one score. snippets:
In contrast to Self-Consistency, there is a line of work which focuses on improving outputs from LLMs using iterative approaches. Self-Refine (Madaan et al., 2023) proposes a framework that aims to enhance the initial outputs of LLMs through iterative feedback and refinement. The key concept revolves around utilizing an LLM to generate an output, obtaining multi-aspect feedback from the same model regarding its own output, and subsequently refining the previously generated output based on this feedback. Notably, this iterative refinement framework does not require supervised training data or reinforcement learning, and it operates solely with a single LLM. Reflexion (Shinn et al., 2023) represents a significant advancement over previous approaches such as ReAct and DEPS. By employing a binary reward model, Reflexion equips agents with dynamic memory and selfreflection capabilities, effectively augmenting their reasoning trace and task-specific action selection abilities. Meanwhile, Iter-CoT adopts an iterative strategy to enhance reasoning steps and answers by utilizing the correct answer as supervisory information, ultimately generating exemplars through sampling from the boosted examples. Similarly, PHP employs iterative techniques by leveraging hints from previous loops to generate answers until no new answers are generated. 

In this paper, we conduct a comprehensive comparison of our proposed methods with Iter-CoT and PHP, both of which utilize additional supervisory information to guide and terminate the iteration process. In contrast, our method relies solely on the intrinsic capabilities of LLMs during the iteration, showcasing its distinctive approach and highlighting its potential advantages.

snippets:
Reasoning in Large Language Models. Recent research has extensively explored the reasoning capabilities of Large Language Models (LLMs). Previous studies have demonstrated that LLMs possess sophisticated reasoning abilities but exhibit distinct limitations in different reasoning domains [1,30]. Chain-of-Thought prompting has emerged as a pivotal advancement in enhancing LLMs' reasoning capabilities, enabling models to break down complex problems into intermediate steps [13,30]. Building upon this foundation, subsequent research has introduced various prompting techniques, including Tree-of-Thoughts [33] and Self-Consistency [29], which further improve reasoning performance through structured thinking processes. Recent works have also explored post-training approaches for LLMs using reinforcement learning and long Chain-of-Thoughts. These methods have been demonstrated to enhance LLMs' performance on mathematical reasoning tasks [6,21]. 

Self Improvement in Large Language Models. Recent studies in Large Language Models have demonstrated their potential for selfreflection and self-refinement, enabling them to iteratively improve their outputs. Researches such as those by Madaan et al. introduce frameworks like Self-Refine, where LLMs generate initial outputs, critique their own responses, and refine them based on iterative feedback [17]. Similarly, Renze & Guven investigate the effects of self-reflection in LLM agents on problem-solving tasks, showing that LLM agents can significantly improve their performance by reflecting on their mistakes and generating guidance for future attempts [23]. Their work highlights the importance of decomposing self-reflection into components such as explanations, instructions, and solutions, which contribute to performance gains across multiple LLMs and problem domains. Multi-Agent Debate. In recent years, the exploration of Multi-Agent Debate System systems leveraging Large Language Models (LLMs) has garnered significant attention in the field of artificial intelligence.
