sections.title: # Continuous polygonal/rectilinear layouts (visibility and sweep)
sections.text:
Many facilities are naturally modeled as orthogonal polygons (rooms with axis‑aligned walls and right‑angle corridors). Visibility‑based pursuit–evasion and sweep strategies are well developed for such environments.

- Line‑of‑sight sweepability and rook’s strategy. A winning strategy for a single pursuer in simply connected polygons is sweep along walls, and rook’s strategy (move along a grid axis while the other coordinate sweeps) extends to line‑of‑sight pursuit in sweepable polygons [e2f881bc-4]. These strategies provide worst‑case bounds and are robust when the environment has minimum feature size, a common assumption in polygonal analyses. 
- Sliding‑robot and orthogonal visibility. When evaders are unpredictable with unbounded speed, clearing an orthogonal polygon can be approached by sliding robots along line segments; each robot’s “sliding visibility polygon” defines the area it can observe while moving back and forth, and a schedule of sliding motions can guarantee detection [8f29c050-1]. 
- k‑cell/k‑modem decompositions. For environments with occlusions, k‑cell decompositions partition the polygon so that as a searcher moves within a cell, shadow regions and visibility events do not change, enabling robust path planning for intruder detection with a searcher equipped to see through up to k walls [8f29c050-2][8f29c050-3]. 
- Visibility computation for planning. Fast evaluation of 2D visibility (both lines‑of‑sight and curves‑of‑sight) enables visibility polygons as heuristics for search and coverage; the method has open‑source implementations and is suggested for applications in pursuit–evasion [8f29c050-0].

These visibility/sweep methods translate to facilities by treating hallways/rooms as orthogonal polygons and using wall‑following or sweeping trajectories with guards/robots whose visibility polygons cover the space. Polygonal results also echo graph‑theoretic bounds: e.g., results on cops‑and‑robbers on planar graphs have polygonal analogs and generalize to compact 2D domains [8f29c050-4].

citations.title: Generalized k-Cell Decomposition for Visibility Planning in Polygons
snippets: This paper introduces a novel $k$-cell decomposition method for pursuit-evasion problems in polygonal environments, where a searcher is equipped with a $k$-modem: a device capable of seeing through up to $k$ walls. The proposed decomposition ensures that as the searcher moves within a cell, the structure of unseen regions (shadows) remains unchanged, thereby preventing any geometric events between or on invisible regions, that is, preventing the appearance, disappearance, merge, or split of shadow regions. The method extends existing work on $0$- and $2$-visibility by incorporating m-visibility polygons for all even $0 \le m \le k$, constructing partition lines that enable robust environment division. The correctness of the decomposition is proved via three theorems. The decomposition enables reliable path planning for intruder detection in simulated environments and opens new avenues for visibility-based robotic surveillance. The difficulty in constructing the cells of the decomposition consists in computing the $k$-visibility polygon from each vertex and finding the intersection points of the partition lines to create the cells.

snippets:
In this paper, we introduced a fast and efficient method to evaluate 2D visibility for grid maps using the linear transport equation -a linear first-order hyperbolic PDE.The proposed method computes both the visibility polygon by evaluating lines-of-sight and the curvilinear polygon by evaluating curves-of-sight.We demonstrated the efficiency of such an algorithm and we demonstrated its efficacy by introducing an interesting application that uses visibility as a heuristic for path planning.We produced simulation results using the path planner.We also provided pseudo-codes and sample implementations as an open-source code.

As briefly discussed in Section IV-B, our heuristic implementation choice has room for improvement.The number of computations when evaluating visibility at every iteration may be vastly reduced by having stopping criterion reliant on the amount of visibility information being added (using local or on-demand visibility evaluations).A superior path planning algorithm relying on the concept of visibility that we introduced can also be produced.The potential of  customizing the shape of the desired curves when using Alg. 1 will be explored.Alg. 1 can have applications in localization by performing a maximum likelihood estimation based on comparing sensor data, e.g., LIDAR, to computed visibility polygons.Applications in area coverage, sensor placement, and pursuit evasion constitute attractive potential future works relying on Alg. 1 or a 3D version of it.

citations.title: Generalized k-Cell Decomposition for Visibility Planning in Polygons
snippets: This paper studied the pursuit-evasion problem under the k-visibility model, generalizing existing work on k = 0 and k = 2 visibility-based decompositions. The focus of this research was to develop a cell decomposition that allows a pursuer equipped with a k-modem to navigate within a polygonal environment to detect an intruder. To do so, the environment is split into cells, ensuring that the combinatorial representation of the shadow regions remains unchanged as an agent moves within a cell. This means that none of the key visibility events, that is, merge, split, appear, or disappear occur as the pursuer moves within a cell of the decomposition. Future work could include reducing the number of lines in the decomposition or path planning between two given points to avoid specific geometric event that might occur along the path.

citations.title: Line-of-Sight Pursuit in Strictly Sweepable Polygons
snippets:
This is a winning strategy for a single pursuer in any any simply connected polygon. More recently, Noori and Isler [14,15] employed a novel pursuer strategy called rook's strategy for pursuit on surfaces and convex terrains. This strategy, which was originally developed for the full visibility case, is valid whenever the capture distance is nonzero. Herein, we extend rook's strategy for line-of-sight pursuit in sweepable polygons. Interest in polygonal pursuit games has been spurred by the widespread availability of practical sensing technologies and robotics platforms. Applications for automated search and pursuit are on the rise, including intruder neutralization, search-and-rescue, and tracking of tagged wildlife. Analysis of games with an adversarial evader provide important worst-case bounds for these applications. 

Meanwhile, combinatorics researchers have devoted intense scrutiny to pursuit-evasion on graphs, where it is known as the game of cops and robbers. This graph game was introduced in the 1980's [18,17]. For an overview of pursuit-evasion on graphs, see the monograph [6]. More recently, topologists have gotten into the game, characterizing capture strategies for spaces with various curvature conditions [2,3]. There has certainly been cross-pollination between these traditions. For example, the analog of the classic Aigner and Fromme result that three cops can always capture a robber on a planar graph [1] was recently proven to hold for the polygonal setting by Bhaudauria et al. [5], and further generalized to a class of compact two-dimensional domains by Beveridge and Cai [4]. 

We conclude this section with comments on two aspects of our game model. First, we assume that there is a relationship between the geometry of the environment and the speed of the players. In particular, the environment has a minimum feature size, meaning that the minimum distance between any two polygonal vertices is at least one unit. This assumption can be achieved by a simple rescaling of the environment, if necessary. Klein and Suri [9] pointed out that this minimum feature size has been an implicit assumption in many papers.

citations.title: Clearing an Orthogonal Polygon Using Sliding Robots
snippets:
The mathematical study of the "pursuit-evasion" problem was first considered by Parson [11]. After that, the watchman route problem was introduced as a variation of the art gallery problem, which consists of finding static evaders in a polygon. The visibility-based motion-planning problem was introduced in 1997 by Lavalle et al. [6]. The aim was to coordinate the motions of one or more robots (pursuers) that have omnidirectional vision sensors to enable them to eventually "see" an evader that is unpredictable, has an unknown initial position, and is capable of moving arbitrarily fast. The process of detecting all evaders is also known as clearing the polygon. The pursuit-evasion problem has a broad range of applications such as air traffic control, military strategy, and trajectory tracking [6]. 

In 2011, Katz and Morgenstern introduced sliding camera guards for guarding orthogonal polygons [5]. We define the "sliding robots" to be the same as the sliding cameras, where the robot r i would travel back and forth along an axis-aligned segment s inside an orthogonal polygon P . A point p is seen by s i if there exists a point q ∈ s i such that pq is a line segment perpendicular to s i and is completely inside P . The set of all points of P that can be seen by s i is its sliding visibility polygon (see Fig. 1). The point p is seen by r i if r i = q. p q s Figure 1 The shaded area shows the sliding visibility polygon of s. 

According to the visibility-based motion-planning problem and the sliding robots, we study the new version of planning the motions for a group of robots for clearing an orthogonal polygon when robots are modeled as sliding cameras. The given orthogonal polygon P has unpredictable, moving evaders with unbounded speed. Motion planning for a group of sliding robots to clear P means presenting the sequence of motions for the sliding robots such that any evader is viewed by at least one robot. Moreover, a set of line segments, S, is given such that the union of their sliding visibility polygons is P .

sections.title: # Multi‑agent coordination and sweep‑coverage allocation
sections.text:
When multiple people (targets or searchers) are involved, optimal policies often decompose into two layers: a schedule (which places and moves who where and when) and an allocation (how many agents are needed).

- Minimum searchers and search number. Graph‑theoretic search number and related parameters characterize the minimum agents required, but many exact algorithms are complex and NP‑hard to compute [e2f881bc-0]. In node search, every edge‑clearing schedule can also clear nodes, implying node search is “easier” in a complexity‑s sense, yet choosing efficient spanning trees and blocking recontamination remains key [e2f881bc-4]. 
- Monotone sweep DAGs and flow allocation. Monotone sweep schedules on planar environments can be represented as DAGs and generalized beyond vertical boustrophedon to circular/radial sweeps, enabling efficient allocation of “line guards” (robots) to maintain coverage quality [e2f881bc-3]. The problem of minimizing the number of line guards for a given sweep schedule reduces to a network‑flow problem, yielding scalable solutions and direct analogies to perimeter defense and graph‑clear problems. 
- Trade‑offs. Teleporting schedules from graph theory are unsuitable for robots, and most graph algorithms assume local visibility and arbitrarily fast evaders; recent indoor work emphasizes non‑teleporting, internal movement and visibility handling [e2f881bc-0]. Non‑monotonic (recontaminating) schedules can reduce total searchers but risk efficiency losses from revisit overhead; algorithms that balance coverage and recontamination blocking are preferred [e2f881bc-3].

sections.title: # Stochastic and unknown‑start formulations
sections.text:
In facilities with human occupants, the target’s initial location and speed may be unknown or partially observed. Stochastic search frames the problem as clearing probabilistically, optimizing expected time or cost.

- POMDP/MDP coverage and search. While the facility graph defines states (rooms possibly with occupancy), coverage MDPs/POMDPs prescribe policies that sweep rooms and doors to ensure probability one detection over time, adapting to partial observability and dynamics. Spanning‑tree‑based node search with guards can be embedded in stochastic planners: place guards at doorways/entrances to block reentry and sweep interior nodes according to a clearance policy, with expected clearance time minimized by choosing spanning trees and guard placements [e2f881bc-4]. 
- Deterministic guarantees under uncertainty. In visibility‑based settings with unpredictable, unbounded‑speed evaders, clearing schedules for orthogonal polygons provide deterministic detection even without knowing the evader’s start, by guaranteeing that every point is visible by at least one moving sensor over time [8f29c050-1]. 
- Visibility‑based heuristics for efficient planning. Precomputing visibility polygons (and curves‑of‑sight) as heuristics can guide sweep order and agent placement, and offers a route to efficient, implementable policies when exact optimality is costly [8f29c050-0].

sections.title: # Practical recommendations by scenario
sections.text:
- Single pursuer, known start and speed: Prefer line‑of‑sight sweep or rook’s strategy around room perimeters, synchronized with door/entrance control to limit escape corridors. Sweeping along walls and axis‑aligned strategies provide winning strategies in simply connected polygons and extend to line‑of‑sight [8f29c050-4]. 
- Team of pursuers, adversarial evader (unknown/avoidant): Use graph‑theoretic node search adapted to rooms. GSST/IMC search on the room–door graph with mobile guards at bottlenecks reduces the dirty set monotonically and can clear complex floorplans with few searchers [e2f881bc-4]. 
- Unknown start and/or unbounded speed: Employ visibility‑based sweeping with sliding‑robot coverage or k‑cell decompositions to handle occlusions. Sliding robots along hallways/segments with sliding visibility polygons guarantee detection over time [8f29c050-1] ; k‑cell/k‑modem partitions maintain stable visibility event structures, enabling reliable pursuit [8f29c050-2][8f29c050-3]. 
- Multi‑agent allocation and scalability: If many people must be searched, compute a monotone sweep DAG and allocate agents via network‑flow optimization for the sweep, or select a low‑searcher spanning tree with guard placement to block recontamination. Generalized sweep schedules are representable as DAGs and admit flow‑based allocation of line guards [e2f881bc-3] ; spanning‑tree search plus guards yields efficient clearing with few searchers [e2f881bc-4]. 
- Unknown or partial observations: Use stochastic search/coverage policies on the room–door graph, leveraging visibility heuristics to bias sweep order and guard deployment. Node search with guards can be embedded in MDP/POMDP planners to minimize expected clearance time [e2f881bc-4] ; visibility computations provide effective heuristics for area coverage and pursuit–evasion [8f29c050-0].

citations.title: Generalized k-Cell Decomposition for Visibility Planning in Polygons
snippets: This paper introduces a novel $k$-cell decomposition method for pursuit-evasion problems in polygonal environments, where a searcher is equipped with a $k$-modem: a device capable of seeing through up to $k$ walls. The proposed decomposition ensures that as the searcher moves within a cell, the structure of unseen regions (shadows) remains unchanged, thereby preventing any geometric events between or on invisible regions, that is, preventing the appearance, disappearance, merge, or split of shadow regions. The method extends existing work on $0$- and $2$-visibility by incorporating m-visibility polygons for all even $0 \le m \le k$, constructing partition lines that enable robust environment division. The correctness of the decomposition is proved via three theorems. The decomposition enables reliable path planning for intruder detection in simulated environments and opens new avenues for visibility-based robotic surveillance. The difficulty in constructing the cells of the decomposition consists in computing the $k$-visibility polygon from each vertex and finding the intersection points of the partition lines to create the cells.

snippets:
This is a winning strategy for a single pursuer in any any simply connected polygon. More recently, Noori and Isler [14,15] employed a novel pursuer strategy called rook's strategy for pursuit on surfaces and convex terrains. This strategy, which was originally developed for the full visibility case, is valid whenever the capture distance is nonzero. Herein, we extend rook's strategy for line-of-sight pursuit in sweepable polygons. Interest in polygonal pursuit games has been spurred by the widespread availability of practical sensing technologies and robotics platforms. Applications for automated search and pursuit are on the rise, including intruder neutralization, search-and-rescue, and tracking of tagged wildlife. Analysis of games with an adversarial evader provide important worst-case bounds for these applications. 

Meanwhile, combinatorics researchers have devoted intense scrutiny to pursuit-evasion on graphs, where it is known as the game of cops and robbers. This graph game was introduced in the 1980's [18,17]. For an overview of pursuit-evasion on graphs, see the monograph [6]. More recently, topologists have gotten into the game, characterizing capture strategies for spaces with various curvature conditions [2,3]. There has certainly been cross-pollination between these traditions. For example, the analog of the classic Aigner and Fromme result that three cops can always capture a robber on a planar graph [1] was recently proven to hold for the polygonal setting by Bhaudauria et al. [5], and further generalized to a class of compact two-dimensional domains by Beveridge and Cai [4]. 

We conclude this section with comments on two aspects of our game model. First, we assume that there is a relationship between the geometry of the environment and the speed of the players. In particular, the environment has a minimum feature size, meaning that the minimum distance between any two polygonal vertices is at least one unit. This assumption can be achieved by a simple rescaling of the environment, if necessary. Klein and Suri [9] pointed out that this minimum feature size has been an implicit assumption in many papers.

citations.title: Generalized k-Cell Decomposition for Visibility Planning in Polygons
snippets: This paper studied the pursuit-evasion problem under the k-visibility model, generalizing existing work on k = 0 and k = 2 visibility-based decompositions. The focus of this research was to develop a cell decomposition that allows a pursuer equipped with a k-modem to navigate within a polygonal environment to detect an intruder. To do so, the environment is split into cells, ensuring that the combinatorial representation of the shadow regions remains unchanged as an agent moves within a cell. This means that none of the key visibility events, that is, merge, split, appear, or disappear occur as the pursuer moves within a cell of the decomposition. Future work could include reducing the number of lines in the decomposition or path planning between two given points to avoid specific geometric event that might occur along the path.

sections.title: # Caveats and open issues
sections.text:
- Optimality vs. tractability. Exact graph‑theoretic search numbers and optimal schedules are computationally hard or complex to implement, motivating practical heuristics such as spanning‑tree search and monotone sweep [e2f881bc-0]. 
- Realistic human behavior. Most algorithms assume the evader is invisible except on capture and aims to avoid capture; modeling cooperation, communication, or social forces among multiple people is beyond classical formulations and requires domain‑specific extensions. 
- Mixed discrete–continuous dynamics. Facilities often combine grid/toroidal areas with orthogonal hallways; hybrid planners must coordinate graph‑level traversal with polygon‑level visibility and sliding motions. Sliding‑robot models bridge continuous motion and visibility [8f29c050-1] ; sweepable‑polygon strategies provide worst‑case guarantees [8f29c050-4].

In summary, for people moving around a facility, “optimal” search typically means time‑ or resource‑minimal clearance policies that deterministically shrink uncertainty (or guarantee visibility) while respecting motion constraints. In discrete settings, internal monotone and spanning‑tree search with guard placement provide strong guarantees and scalable implementations; in continuous settings, sweepable visibility strategies and sliding‑robot coverage ensure detection for unpredictable, fast evaders; and for multiple agents, monotone sweep DAGs and flow‑based allocation or spanning‑tree search minimize searchers while blocking recontamination. These approaches are grounded in graph and polygonal pursuit–evasion theory, with clear relationships to search number and practical algorithms for indoor environments [e2f881bc-0][e2f881bc-2][e2f881bc-3][e2f881bc-4].

citations.title: Searching the Nodes of a Graph: Theory and Algorithms
snippets:
In this paper we study a variant of graph search. Our motivation comes from applied robotics problems. As an introduction, consider the following two problems, which can both be modeled as graph searches.

1. An evader is hiding in a building and a team of one or more searchers are trying to capture him.

The building is represented by a graph G: nodes are rooms and edges are doors between rooms. Both searchers and evader occupy the nodes of the graph and move from node to node by sliding along the edges. The evader is captured when he is located in the same node as a searcher. It is assumed that the evader has the following characteristics: (a) he wants to avoid capture, (b) he is invisible to the searchers (unless he is located in the same node as one of them), (c) he is always aware of the searchers' locations and (d) he is arbitrarily fast.

2. An evader and a team of searchers are located inside a cave. The cave is again represented by a graph G: edges are tunnels and nodes are the intersections of tunnels. The searchers move from node to node, sliding along the edges; capture takes place if a searcher slides along an edge occupied by the evader, or if the evader moves through a node occupied by a searcher. The previously mentioned properties of the evader are assumed to hold in this case as well.

The two problems are very similar but differ in one important respect. In the first problem the evader is assumed to reside in the nodes of the graph (the rooms); in the second problem he is assumed to reside in the edges (the tunnels). Accordingly, we will call the first problem node search and the second edge search. Edge-or node-location of the evader is an important aspect of the graph search problem and can be used to categorize the related literature. Historically, research has concentrated on the problem of "edge-located evader". To the best of our knowledge, very little work has been done on the problem of "node-located evader". question: how to improve chunk retrieval with contrastive learning?

sections.title: # Overview
sections.text: Dense chunk (passage/document) retrieval can be significantly improved by training with contrastive learning that explicitly pulls positive query–chunk pairs together while pushing away negatives that are most likely to confuse the model at inference time. Early dense retrievers like DPR showed that dual-encoder models trained with contrastive objectives can surpass BM25 in open-domain QA, but generalization depends on better negative sampling strategies and avoiding static negatives [b08db5ca-0] Recent retrievers integrate contrastive learning with multi-vector architectures and distillation, while unsupervised contrastive training (e.g., mContriever, E5) and hybrid sparse–dense fusion (e.g., CLEAR, ColBERT) have improved effectiveness [b08db5ca-1] State-of-the-art systems combine in-batch and pre-batch negatives, hard-negative mining, curriculum learning, and query augmentation, and show that contrastive pretraining and masked autoencoding improve generalization [b08db5ca-2].

citations.title: Rankify: A Comprehensive Python Toolkit for Retrieval, Re-Ranking, and Retrieval-Augmented Generation
snippets:
Retrieval models have evolved significantly, transitioning from traditional sparse retrievers to sophisticated dense and hybrid retrieval techniques. Sparse retrievers, such as BM25 [92], remain widely used due to their strong lexical matching capabilities and generalization. However, they struggle with capturing semantic relationships, leading to the rise of dense retrieval methods [55], which leverage pre-trained neural encoders to generate embeddings for queries and documents. Notable advancements, such as DPR [120] and ANCE [115], improve retrieval effectiveness by employing contrastive training with in-batch negatives [33] and hard-negative mining [46,116]. Multi-vector approaches like ColBERT [49] enable fine-grained interaction between queries and documents, albeit at the cost of increased computational overhead. To address the limitations of dense retrievers, hybrid models [30,67] combine sparse and dense approaches, utilizing both term matching and semantic understanding for enhanced retrieval performance. 

Recent research has also explored retrieval enhancements through knowledge distillation, curriculum learning, and pre-training. Distillation techniques transfer knowledge from cross-encoders or teacher retrievers to student models, improving dense retriever effectiveness [18,86]. Curriculum learning strategies, which progressively train retrievers from easy to hard samples [60,124], have been shown to enhance both supervised and zero-shot retrieval effectiveness. Meanwhile, pre-training methods such as contrastive learning [40] and masked autoencoding [29,63] have significantly improved the generalization of retrieval models. Additionally, approaches like query augmentation [66,70] generate synthetic training data to enhance retrieval robustness.

citations.title: Retrieval And Structuring Augmented Generation with Large Language Models
snippets:
In contrast to sparse lexical methods, dense retrieval [61,304,314] uses continuous vector embeddings to represent queries and documents. With pre-trained language models [44,180,206], relevant query-document pairs have high cosine similarity, enabling semantic matching without lexical overlap. 

Dual Encoder and Early Dense Retrieval. Early dense retrieval emerged as a response to the limitations of sparse retrieval. Karpukhin et al. [111] designed Dense Passage Retrieval (DPR), which showed that a BERT [44]-based dual encoder trained on question-answer pairs [10,11,104,119,207] can surpass BM25 [210,211] in opendomain question answering. Early models struggled with generalization, requiring large-scale labeled datasets [179] and appropriate negative sampling strategies [266] in contrastive learning [27,51,75,188]. 

Effectively-trained Dense Retrieval. Recognizing limitations of static negative sampling, Asynchronous Negative Contrastive Estimation (ANCE) [266] addressed this by refreshing hard negatives during training. RocketQA [203] improved contrastive training with cross-batch memory for more diverse negative samples. Generalizable T5 Retriever (GTR) [181] framed retrieval as a sequenceto-sequence task rather than solely relying on contrastive learning. 

Efficient and Scalable Dense Retrieval. Another research line focused on scalability and efficiency. ColBERT [113] introduced late interaction mechanisms, preserving token-level representations to reduce memory overhead. CoCondenser [62] optimized intermediate representation learning for more compact document embeddings. E5 [246] explored improved contrastive pretraining techniques for adaptability to various tasks. 

Impact. Dense Retrieval models [111,113,181,246,266] offer significant advantages over Sparse Retrieval by enabling semantic matching when exact lexical overlap is absent. However, Dense Retrieval is limited by dependency on large-scale labeled training data [54,131,304] and lack of interpretability [31,105,148].

sections.title: # Core Design Principles
sections.text:
- Contrast with dynamic, hard negatives at inference conditions: negatives should be those that are top-ranked by a weak retriever or current model, because they are most likely to cause retrieval errors in production. ANCE introduced asynchronous negative contrastive estimation to refresh hard negatives during training, addressing limitations of static negative sampling [b08db5ca-0] RocketQA proposed denoised hard negative sampling that removes false negatives from the top-ranked results of a retriever to derive more reliable hard negatives [ae4d2b05-0] ANCE globally sampled hard negatives with top retrieved scores from the current dense retriever, highlighting the importance of dynamic negatives in contrastive learning for dense retrieval [537a7d21-1].

- Balance in-batch and pre-batch negatives to scale difficulty: in-batch negatives are essential but limited; queue-based pre-batch negatives add diversity and decouple from batch size. In-batch negatives and hard-negative mining are standard, but cross-batch memory and large-scale negatives improve diversity [b08db5ca-2] RocketQA introduced cross-batch random negatives to increase available negatives and reduce training–inference discrepancy [ae4d2b05-0] Contriever uses MoCo with negatives from a previous-batch queue to scale to large numbers of negatives and random cropping for positive sampling [7118aa04-0] Pre-batch negatives (e.g., MoCo-style queues) and in-batch negatives are both effective, with only 1–2 pre-batches typically needed to avoid inconsistency [537a7d21-4].

- Learn to rank under overlap and fine-grained differences: late-interaction and multi-vector methods capture term-level interactions and are especially helpful when chunks share many terms with the query but differ semantically. ColBERT introduces late interaction to compute pairwise term similarities between query and document embeddings for fine-grained matching [b08db5ca-1] CoCondenser optimizes intermediate representation learning for compact document embeddings, and hybrid methods fuse sparse and dense signals to improve retrieval [b08db5ca-2].

- Optimize the embedding space structure: aim for concentrated query distributions and discriminative document clusters to make top-k selection easier. Early models struggled with generalization unless negatives were carefully designed [b08db5ca-0] DANCE adds a query-likelihood objective and concentrates query embeddings while scattering document distributions to form a more uniform and smooth embedding space, improving ranking especially for hard, frequently recalled documents [b08db5ca-3] Curriculum learning strategies that train from easy to hard samples enhance supervised and zero-shot retrieval effectiveness [b08db5ca-2].

citations.title: SimKGC: Simple Contrastive Knowledge Graph Completion with Pre-trained Language Models
snippets:
For knowledge graph completion, the training data only consists of positive triples. Given a positive triple (h, r, t), "negative sampling" needs to sample one or more negative triples to train discriminative models. Most existing methods randomly corrupt h or t and then filter out false negatives that appear in the training graph G. The negatives for different triples are not shared and therefore independent. The typical number of negatives are ∼ 64 for embedding-based methods (Sun et al., 2019b), and ∼ 5 for text-based methods (Wang et al., 2021a). We combine three types of negatives to improve the training efficiency without incurring significant computational and memory overhead.

In-batch Negatives (IB) This is a widely adopted strategy in visual representation learning  and dense passage retrieval (Karpukhin et al., 2020) etc. Entities within the same batch can be used as negatives. Such in-batch negatives allow the efficient reuse of entity embeddings for bi-encoder models.

Pre-batch Negatives (PB) The disadvantage of in-batch negatives is that the number of negatives is coupled with batch size. Pre-batch negatives  use entity embeddings from previous batches. Since these embeddings are computed with an earlier version of model parameters, they are not consistent with in-batch negatives. Usually, only 1 or 2 pre-batches are used. Other methods like MoCo (He et al., 2020) can also provide more negatives. We leave the investigation of MoCo as future work.

Self-Negatives (SN) Besides increasing the number of negatives, mining hard negatives (Gao et al., 2021;Xiong et al., 2021) is also important for improving contrastive representation learning. For tail entity prediction (h, r, ?), text-based methods tend to assign a high score to the head entity h, likely due to the high text overlap. To mitigate this issue, we propose self-negatives that use the head entity h as hard negatives. Including self-negatives can make the model rely less on the spurious text match.

citations.title: More Robust Dense Retrieval with Contrastive Dual Learning
snippets: In this paper, we propose a training paradigm, Contrastive Dual Learning for Approximate Nearest Neighbor (DANCE), to train dense retrievers. DANCE introduces the additional training object, query likelihood, in dense retriever training to learn query and document representations. Different from ANCE, DANCE concentrates the query embeddings and assigns more uniform recall frequency to queries to sufficiently optimize their representations, while the document embedding distribution is optimized to be more scattered and discriminative. Through such embedding space optimization, DANCE achieves better ranking performance than the previous state-of-theart dense retriever ANCE, especially for the documents that are more frequently recalled during contrastive training on the document retrieval task. Even these documents have smaller detaching distances and are hard to distinguish, DANCE shows better performance on them by learning more fine-grained query representations, better aligning related query-document pairs, and forming a more uniform and smooth embedding space for retrieval tasks. The observations of our work provide some possible directions to further improve dense retriever effectiveness and sufficiently optimize the embedding space by learning more effective query and document representations during contrastive training.

citations.title: Does Negative Sampling Matter? a Review With Insights Into its Theory and Applications
snippets:
Recently, contrastive learning has attracted a surge of interest for unsupervised visual representation learning [48], [49], [85]. In terms of the great success of contrastive learning in computer vision, numerous works extended it into graph learning [88], [99]. After that, negative sampling in graph contrastive learning has also achieved tremendous success. Zhao et al. [99] proposed a graph-debiased contrastive learning framework to alleviate the false negative issue, which utilized clustering to obtain pseudo labels and conducted random sampling to sample negatives from the different clusters. Such a method suffers from expensive computational consumption. CuCo [100] proposed a curriculum contrastive learning framework that gradually samples negatives from easy to hard, in which hard negatives are determined by the score function. Zhu et al. [140] utilized heterogeneous graph structure to sample hard negatives with the largest similarities and synthesized more negatives by a mixing operation. ProGCL [101] utilized a beta mixture model (BMM) to mine true and hard neg-ative examples for graph contrastive learning. Xiong et al. [104] proposed approximate nearest neighbor negative contrastive learning (ANCE) for the dense retrieval (DR) model, which globally sampled hard negatives with top retrieved scores from the current DR model. 

In summary, negative sampling in graph representation learning has achieved some remarkable progress but still leaves a lot of room for improvement. For example, how to effectively use graph structure for negative sampling; how to incorporate GNNs propagation mechanism into negative sampling? How to design an effective negative sampling method for graph contrastive learning?

citations.title: RocketQA: An Optimized Training Approach to Dense Passage Retrieval for Open-Domain Question Answering
snippets:
respectively. However, it is still insufficient to cover all the topics from a variety of domains, much smaller than the number of possible questions issued by users to search engines 2 .

In this paper, we focus on addressing these challenges so as to effectively train the dual-encoder retriever for open-domain QA. We propose an optimized training approach, called RocketQA, to improving dense passage retrieval. Considering the above challenges, we make three major technical contributions in RocketQA. First, RocketQA introduces cross-batch random negatives. Comparing to in-batch negatives, it increases the number of available negatives for each question when training, and alleviates the discrepancy between training and inference. Second, RocketQA introduces denoised hard negative sampling. It aims to remove false negatives from the top-ranked results retrieved by a specific retriever, which can derive more reliable hard negatives. Third, RocketQA leverages largescale unsupervised data "labeled" by a (as shown in Figure 1b) for data augmentation. Though inefficient, the cross-encoder architecture has been found to be more capable than the dual-encoder architecture in both theory and practice (Luan et al., 2020). Therefore, we utilize a cross-encoder to generate high-quality pseudo labels for unlabeled data for training the dual-encoder retriever.

In summary, the contributions of this paper are as follows:

• The proposed RocketQA introduces three novel optimization strategies for improving dense passage retrieval for open-domain QA, namely cross-batch sampling, denoised hard negative sampling, and data augmentation.

• The overall experiments show that our proposed RocketQA significantly outperforms previous state-of-the-art models on both MS-MARCO and Natural Questions datasets.

• We conduct extensive experiments to examine the effectiveness of the above three strategies in RocketQA. Experimental results show that all the three strategies are effective to improve the performance of dense passage retrieval.

• We also demonstrate that RocketQA leads to better end-to-end QA performance. Besides, built upon RocketQA, we achieve the first rank at the leaderboard of MSMARCO Passage Ranking Task.

citations.title: Unsupervised Dense Information Retrieval with Contrastive Learning
snippets: In this section, we empirically evaluate our best retriever trained with contrastive learning, called Contriever (contrastive retriever), which uses MoCo with random cropping. We use a contrastive learning procedure that differs from ICT (Lee et al., 2019) mainly in three aspects. First, positive pairs are sampled using random cropping and tokens from each element of the pair are deleted with a probability of 10%. Second we use MoCo where negatives consists of elements from previous batches stored in a queue. This allows to scale to a large number of negatives. Third we use data from Wikipedia and CCNet (Wenzek et al., 2020) for training. Ablation studies motivating these technical choices are performed in Section 6. More technical details about our model are given in Appendix A.1.

sections.title: # Negative Sampling and Pseudo-Labels at Scale
sections.text:
- Construct negatives from cross-collection and model-predicted top ranks: use a weak retriever (e.g., BM25) or the current model to obtain top-k candidates from other collections as negatives, and filter “false negatives” (those that should be relevant but aren’t labeled as such) to denoise the set. DPR mined hard negatives using BM25, and ANCE verified that negatives from the model itself can be more informative and reduce bias in contrastive estimation [b08db5ca-0] RocketQA’s denoised hard negative sampling removes false negatives from top-ranked results of a retriever to produce reliable negatives, and cross-batch negatives alleviate training–inference gaps [ae4d2b05-0] ANCE determined negatives by top retrieved scores from the current retriever, establishing a principled way to mine hard negatives online [537a7d21-1].

- Use stronger teachers to generate pseudo-labels: train dual-encoder retrievers with pseudo-labels from cross-encoders or advanced rerankers, and iteratively refine labels between teacher and student to propagate better supervision over chunks. REALM jointly trains a masked LM and neural retriever, and unsupervised pretraining with ICT plus joint fine-tuning improved passage retrieval [ae4d2b05-1] RocketQA leverages a cross-encoder to generate high-quality pseudo labels for unlabeled data to train the dual-encoder retriever [ae4d2b05-0] Boot-and-Switch alternates distillation between a retriever and a reranker, using the reranker to refine labels and the retriever to select candidates, yielding synergistic improvements [ae4d2b05-2] A cross-encoder reward model can provide fine-grained supervision by contrasting positive and hard negative candidates selected from top and bottom ranks, enabling knowledge distillation for dense retrievers [ae4d2b05-3] E5 integrates explicit supervision from retrieval datasets and task-specific fine-tuning for better adaptability [b08db5ca-1].

- Build kNN contrastive graphs to mine hard negatives efficiently: construct a nearest-neighbor graph over chunks or queries and sample negatives from local neighborhoods to balance hardness and efficiency. Recent works retrieve nearest neighbors as contrastive negatives for dense text retrieval and video–text, enabling efficient hard-negative mining [537a7d21-0] SciNCL uses kNN sampling for positives and hard negatives with a margin to avoid overlap (collisions), mixing them with easy negatives outside a larger radius for robust signals [537a7d21-3] Combining in-batch, pre-batch (MoCo) negatives and self-negatives (e.g., using the head entity as a hard negative) improves contrastive representation learning and mitigates spurious overlaps [537a7d21-4].

citations.title: CLOP: Video-and-Language Pre-Training with Knowledge Regularizations
snippets:
The key idea behind contrastive learning [19] is to learn a general feature function by discriminating positive and negative samples -making the positive pairs attracted and the negative pairs separated [13,42,48]. This learning paradiam has been proved very successful in repensenting visual data [7,16], natural languages [32], graphs [15,44], etc. Hard negatives have been proved essential for contrastive learning systems [4,58]. In the computer vision domain, related works propose various methods to explore negatives, such as maintaining a memory queue to enrich negatives [16], designing sampling distributions [41] or generating negatives in latent space [18]. UNIMO [26] constructs hard textual negatives by re-writing sentences for imagetext pre-training. Recently, several works propose to retrieve nearest neighbors as contrastive negatives for dense text retrieval [54] or video-text pre-training [56]. 

In this work, we propose a knowledge-guided approach for contrastive learning with hard negatives (KCL). Our method designs a multi-level sampling method to realize an instance-level hard negative sampling and a controllable batch-level sampling to emphasize desired semantics.

citations.title: PAIR: Leveraging Passage-Centric Similarity Relation for Improving Dense Passage Retrieval
snippets:
Recently, dense passage retrieval has demonstrated better performance than traditional sparse retrieval methods (e.g., TF-IDF and BM25). Different from sparse retrieval, dense passage retrieval represents queries and passages into lowdimensional vectors (Guu et al., 2020;Karpukhin et al., 2020), typically in a dual-encoder architecture, and uses dot product as the similarity measurement for retrieval. The existing approaches for dense passage retrieval can be divided into two categories: (1) unsupervised pre-training for retrieval (2) fine-tuning only on labeled data. In the first category, different pre-training tasks for retrieval were proposed.  proposed a specific approach to pre-training the retriever with an unsupervised task, namely Inverse Cloze Task (ICT), and then jointly finetuned the retriever and a reader on labeled data. REALM (Guu et al., 2020) proposed a new pretraining approach, which jointly trained a masked language model and a neural retriever. Different from them, our proposed approach utilizes the pseudo-labeled data via knowledge distillation in the pre-training stage, and the quality of the generated data is high (see Section 4.6).

In the second category, the existing approaches fine-tuned pre-trained language models on labeled data (Karpukhin et al., 2020;Luan et al., 2021). Both DPR (Karpukhin et al., 2020) and ME-BERT (Luan et al., 2021) used in-batch random sampling and hard negative sampling by BM25, while ANCE (Xiong et al., 2020a), NPRINC (Lu et al., 2020) and RocketQA (Qu et al., 2020) explored more sophisticated hard negative sampling approach. Izacard and Grave (2020) and Yang et al. (2020) leveraged a reader and a crossencoder for knowledge distillation on labeled data, respectively. RocketQA found large batch size can significantly improve the retrieval performance of dual-encoders. ColBERT (Khattab and Zaharia, 2020) incorporated light-weight attention-based re-ranking while increasing the space complexity.

citations.title: Boot and Switch: Alternating Distillation for Zero-Shot Dense Retrieval
snippets:
The novelty of our approach lies in two aspects: i) 

We introduce a separate reranker model for training label refinement. This allows the retriever training to benefit from an advanced reranker, which features a more sophisticated cross-encoding architecture. This design is effective compared to training the retriever on labels extracted from its own predictions (see the blue line in Figure 5(a)); ii) We create a mutual-learning paradigm through iterative alternating distillation. In our case, we consider the retriever as a proposal distribution generator, which selects relatively good candidates, and the reranker as a reward scoring model, which measures the quality of an example as a good answer. At each iteration, the improved reranker can be used to correct the predictions from the retriever, 

Retriever Type dense dense dense dense dense dense dense mul-vec sparse dense dense sparse dense dense dense dense therefore reducing the number of inaccurate labels in retriever training data. Meanwhile, the improved retriever is more likely to include more relevant passages within its top-k predictions and provide more nuanced soft labels, which can enhance the reranker training and thus, increase the chance of finding correct labels by the reranker in the next iteration. As the training continues, (1) the candidates of correct answers can be narrowed down by the retriever (i.e., better proposal distributions), as shown in Fig. 4 and (2) the accuracy of finding correct answers from such sets can be increased by the reranker, as shown in Fig. 2(b). Overall, our framework (i.e., ABEL) facilitates synergistic advancements in both components, ultimately enhancing the overall effectiveness of the retrieval system.

citations.title: Contrastive Learning Using Graph Embeddings for Domain Adaptation of Language Models in the Process Industry
snippets:
To achieve this, we follow SciNCL that selects positive (similar) documents by first defining the distance to the query embedding d Q using k + and then sampling the c + nearest neighbors within a range (k + − c + , k + ], as illustrated by the green band in Figure 2. 

Negative samples d − should be semantically dissimilar from the query document d Q , meaning they are sampled from a distant region relative to the query embedding d Q . Sampling hard-tolearn negatives, i.e., those close to potential positives, has been shown to enhance contrastive learning (Bucher et al., 2016;Wu et al., 2017). However, when negative samples overlap with positive ones, it can introduce noise into the learning signal (Saunshi et al., 2019). To prevent such collisions, SciNCL employs a sample-induced margin defined by the k parameter. This margin ensures the sampling of hard negatives (represented by the red band in Figure 2) without overlapping with the sampled positives (green band). To provide a robust similarity signal for contrastive learning, SciNCL recommends using a mix of hard and easy negatives, where easy negatives are embeddings located further from the query embedding than hard negatives (outside the red band). 

Sampling strategies differ between positive and types of negative samples, i.e., similar to SciNCL. citations.title: Does Negative Sampling Matter? a Review With Insights Into its Theory and Applications
snippets:
Recently, contrastive learning has attracted a surge of interest for unsupervised visual representation learning [48], [49], [85]. In terms of the great success of contrastive learning in computer vision, numerous works extended it into graph learning [88], [99]. After that, negative sampling in graph contrastive learning has also achieved tremendous success. Zhao et al. [99] proposed a graph-debiased contrastive learning framework to alleviate the false negative issue, which utilized clustering to obtain pseudo labels and conducted random sampling to sample negatives from the different clusters. Such a method suffers from expensive computational consumption. CuCo [100] proposed a curriculum contrastive learning framework that gradually samples negatives from easy to hard, in which hard negatives are determined by the score function. Zhu et al. [140] utilized heterogeneous graph structure to sample hard negatives with the largest similarities and synthesized more negatives by a mixing operation. ProGCL [101] utilized a beta mixture model (BMM) to mine true and hard neg-ative examples for graph contrastive learning. Xiong et al. [104] proposed approximate nearest neighbor negative contrastive learning (ANCE) for the dense retrieval (DR) model, which globally sampled hard negatives with top retrieved scores from the current DR model. 

In summary, negative sampling in graph representation learning has achieved some remarkable progress but still leaves a lot of room for improvement. For example, how to effectively use graph structure for negative sampling; how to incorporate GNNs propagation mechanism into negative sampling? How to design an effective negative sampling method for graph contrastive learning?

• The proposed RocketQA introduces three novel optimization strategies for improving dense passage retrieval for open-domain QA, namely cross-batch sampling, denoised hard negative sampling, and data augmentation.

sections.title: # Pretraining and Optimization Strategies
sections.text:
- Unsupervised contrastive pretraining tailored to retrieval: use large-scale corpora, dynamic positive construction (e.g., random cropping), and memory queues to scale negatives, then fine-tune on target retrieval datasets. citations.title: Rankify: A Comprehensive Python Toolkit for Retrieval, Re-Ranking, and Retrieval-Augmented Generation
snippets:
Retrieval models have evolved significantly, transitioning from traditional sparse retrievers to sophisticated dense and hybrid retrieval techniques. Sparse retrievers, such as BM25 [92], remain widely used due to their strong lexical matching capabilities and generalization. However, they struggle with capturing semantic relationships, leading to the rise of dense retrieval methods [55], which leverage pre-trained neural encoders to generate embeddings for queries and documents. Notable advancements, such as DPR [120] and ANCE [115], improve retrieval effectiveness by employing contrastive training with in-batch negatives [33] and hard-negative mining [46,116]. Multi-vector approaches like ColBERT [49] enable fine-grained interaction between queries and documents, albeit at the cost of increased computational overhead. To address the limitations of dense retrievers, hybrid models [30,67] combine sparse and dense approaches, utilizing both term matching and semantic understanding for enhanced retrieval performance. 

Recent research has also explored retrieval enhancements through knowledge distillation, curriculum learning, and pre-training. Distillation techniques transfer knowledge from cross-encoders or teacher retrievers to student models, improving dense retriever effectiveness [18,86]. Curriculum learning strategies, which progressively train retrievers from easy to hard samples [60,124], have been shown to enhance both supervised and zero-shot retrieval effectiveness. Meanwhile, pre-training methods such as contrastive learning [40] and masked autoencoding [29,63] have significantly improved the generalization of retrieval models. Additionally, approaches like query augmentation [66,70] generate synthetic training data to enhance retrieval robustness.

citations.title: More Robust Dense Retrieval with Contrastive Dual Learning
snippets: In this paper, we propose a training paradigm, Contrastive Dual Learning for Approximate Nearest Neighbor (DANCE), to train dense retrievers. DANCE introduces the additional training object, query likelihood, in dense retriever training to learn query and document representations. Different from ANCE, DANCE concentrates the query embeddings and assigns more uniform recall frequency to queries to sufficiently optimize their representations, while the document embedding distribution is optimized to be more scattered and discriminative. Through such embedding space optimization, DANCE achieves better ranking performance than the previous state-of-theart dense retriever ANCE, especially for the documents that are more frequently recalled during contrastive training on the document retrieval task. Even these documents have smaller detaching distances and are hard to distinguish, DANCE shows better performance on them by learning more fine-grained query representations, better aligning related query-document pairs, and forming a more uniform and smooth embedding space for retrieval tasks. The observations of our work provide some possible directions to further improve dense retriever effectiveness and sufficiently optimize the embedding space by learning more effective query and document representations during contrastive training.

sections.text:
- Multi-vector and late-interaction encoders: preserve token-level structure (ColBERT), compress with intermediate supervision (CoCondenser), and adopt specialized contrastive pretraining (E5) to adapt embeddings to retrieval. citations.title: A Symmetric Dual Encoding Dense Retrieval Framework for Knowledge-Intensive Visual Question Answering
snippets:
Consequently, knowledge distillation, in which a teacher model provides labels for a student model, has become a standard approach for training dense retrieval models and has shown compelling outcomes [17,30]. Existing work in this area often uses cross-encoder rerankers that input both query and document as teacher models for dense retrieval models with a bi-encoder architecture [44]. Another approach is to distill knowledge from multi-vector dense retrieval models, such as ColBERT [24] to single-vector dense retrievers [63]. 

In our experiments, we did not find knowledge distillation from cross-encoder rerankers helpful for KI-VQA datasets. Thus, we introduce a novel approach: iterative knowledge distillation for dual encoding, in which knowledge distillation happens iteratively between two bi-encoders that use different modalities in their inputs. Accordingly, each model learns the perspective of the other, adjusting their representation spaces for more effective dense retrieval. 

Knowledge-Intensive Visual Question Answering. Knowledgeintensive refers to a category of retrieval-enhanced machine learning problems [61] whose inputs are not sufficient to produce the output and external information should be provided. KILT [39] is a benchmark for natural language knowledge-intensive tasks such as open-domain question answering, fact-checking, entity-linking, slot-filling, and knowledge-based dialogue. All the mentioned tasks are text-only knowledge-intensive tasks. To the best of our knowledge, there is no unified benchmark on multi-modal knowledgeintensive tasks, which is relatively less explored. Therefore, this paper focuses on knowledge-intensive visual question answering. 

Visual question answering (VQA) is a multi-modal question answering task whose goal is to answer a natural language question about an image [3]. VQA is primarily designed to measure the ability of models in representing and comprehending multi-modal data. Therefore, questions in VQA are often related to visual features (e.g., color or shape of the objects) and sometimes require commonsense knowledge. In other words, a human can answer VQA questions by just looking at the image, without accessing external information. Given this formulation, VQA has limited real-world use cases.

citations.title: More Robust Dense Retrieval with Contrastive Dual Learning
snippets: In this paper, we propose a training paradigm, Contrastive Dual Learning for Approximate Nearest Neighbor (DANCE), to train dense retrievers. DANCE introduces the additional training object, query likelihood, in dense retriever training to learn query and document representations. Different from ANCE, DANCE concentrates the query embeddings and assigns more uniform recall frequency to queries to sufficiently optimize their representations, while the document embedding distribution is optimized to be more scattered and discriminative. Through such embedding space optimization, DANCE achieves better ranking performance than the previous state-of-theart dense retriever ANCE, especially for the documents that are more frequently recalled during contrastive training on the document retrieval task. Even these documents have smaller detaching distances and are hard to distinguish, DANCE shows better performance on them by learning more fine-grained query representations, better aligning related query-document pairs, and forming a more uniform and smooth embedding space for retrieval tasks. The observations of our work provide some possible directions to further improve dense retriever effectiveness and sufficiently optimize the embedding space by learning more effective query and document representations during contrastive training.

citations.title: Unsupervised Dense Information Retrieval with Contrastive Learning
snippets: In this section, we empirically evaluate our best retriever trained with contrastive learning, called Contriever (contrastive retriever), which uses MoCo with random cropping. We use a contrastive learning procedure that differs from ICT (Lee et al., 2019) mainly in three aspects. sections.title: # A Practical Recipe to Improve Chunk Retrieval with Contrastive Learning
sections.text:
1. Define your negatives to match production errors:
  - Mine negatives from cross-collection top-k lists or BM25/top-k of a baseline retriever and denoise by removing false negatives (e.g., use a cross-encoder or reader to confirm relevance). BM25-informed hard negatives and negatives from the model’s top-k are effective in dense retrieval [b08db5ca-0] Denoised hard negative sampling removes false negatives from top-ranked results to derive reliable negatives [ae4d2b05-0] ANCE shows global hard negative mining from top retrievals improves contrastive training [537a7d21-1].

2. Pretrain a contrastive retriever on large corpora:
  - Use a dual-encoder with dynamic positive sampling (e.g., random cropping over sentences/paragraphs) and a memory queue of negatives from previous batches; train on Wikipedia and domain corpora (e.g., CCNet). Contriever’s unsupervised contrastive training uses random cropping for positives, MoCo negatives from a queue, and large-scale Wikipedia+CCNet data [b08db5ca-0] Ablations and design choices in Contriever motivate MoCo negatives, random cropping, and large-scale data [7118aa04-1].

3. Add pseudo-labeling and stronger supervision:
  - Augment with pseudo-labels from a cross-encoder or REALM-style generative model; iteratively distill between a retriever and a reranker (boot-and-switch) to refine labels and soft targets. Cross-encoder pseudo labels and data augmentation improve dual-encoder retrieval and end-to-end QA [ae4d2b05-0] Alternating distillation between retriever and reranker reduces inaccurate labels and improves both components [ae4d2b05-2] REALM and ICT provide unsupervised pretraining and joint fine-tuning pathways for passage retrieval [ae4d2b05-1].

4. Shape the embedding space for better top-k selection:
  - Incorporate a query-likelihood objective and concentrate query embeddings while scattering document distributions to create uniform recall and fine-grained separation among hard negatives. DANCE concentrates queries and scatters documents to optimize recall distribution and fine-grained discrimination [b08db5ca-3].

5. Choose an encoder that handles chunk overlap:
  - Prefer late-interaction or multi-vector models (ColBERT) when chunks share many terms with queries but differ semantically; compress with CoCondenser-like intermediate supervision if memory is a concern. Late interaction (ColBERT) and intermediate optimization (CoCondenser) improve chunk-level matching and efficiency [b08db5ca-2].

6. Fuse with sparse indexing and rerank:
  - Combine with BM25 or sparse signals (CLEAR, ScoreFusion) and apply a lightweight reranker to top-k candidates to recover precision when semantic overlap is low. Hybrid sparse–dense methods (ScoreFusion, CLEAR) and ColBERT’s late interaction integrate complementary signals [b08db5ca-1] ColBERT’s lightweight re-ranking improves integration of dense and sparse signals [ae4d2b05-0].

7. Optimize training dynamics:
  - Use large batch sizes, cross-batch negatives, curriculum learning, and query augmentation; ablate to confirm contributions and monitor training–inference discrepancy. Large batches significantly improve dual-encoder retrieval [ae4d2b05-1] Cross-batch negatives and curriculum/query augmentation improve generalization and robustness [b08db5ca-2] RocketQA’s ablations show cross-batch, denoised negatives, and augmentation each improve results [ae4d2b05-0].

citations.title: Does Negative Sampling Matter? a Review With Insights Into its Theory and Applications
snippets:
Recently, contrastive learning has attracted a surge of interest for unsupervised visual representation learning [48], [49], [85]. In terms of the great success of contrastive learning in computer vision, numerous works extended it into graph learning [88], [99]. After that, negative sampling in graph contrastive learning has also achieved tremendous success. Zhao et al. [99] proposed a graph-debiased contrastive learning framework to alleviate the false negative issue, which utilized clustering to obtain pseudo labels and conducted random sampling to sample negatives from the different clusters. Such a method suffers from expensive computational consumption. CuCo [100] proposed a curriculum contrastive learning framework that gradually samples negatives from easy to hard, in which hard negatives are determined by the score function. Zhu et al. [140] utilized heterogeneous graph structure to sample hard negatives with the largest similarities and synthesized more negatives by a mixing operation. ProGCL [101] utilized a beta mixture model (BMM) to mine true and hard neg-ative examples for graph contrastive learning. Xiong et al. [104] proposed approximate nearest neighbor negative contrastive learning (ANCE) for the dense retrieval (DR) model, which globally sampled hard negatives with top retrieved scores from the current DR model. 

In summary, negative sampling in graph representation learning has achieved some remarkable progress but still leaves a lot of room for improvement. For example, how to effectively use graph structure for negative sampling; how to incorporate GNNs propagation mechanism into negative sampling? How to design an effective negative sampling method for graph contrastive learning?

The objective of designing Retriever Dictionary (RD) is to retain the most critical information from the dataset. However, even after training, the number of atoms in the Dictionary may exceed the required amount, with some atoms being infrequently used or irrelevant to the specific dataset domain. Drawing inspiration from knowledge distillation and the Teacher-Student model (Hinton et al., 2015), we condense the original Dictionary D into a smaller and more efficient version, denoted as d. To align the output features of d with those of D, we employ contrastive learning (Chen et al., 2020). In this process, the model backbone and RD are frozen, while the optimization is focused on the smaller Retriever Dictionary module d. The objective function is defined as: 

, where z rd i,w,h ∈ R f represents the i-th batch output feature of d at position (w, h), B is the batch size, τ is the temperature parameter, and sim(•, •) denotes the cosine similarity between two vectors. This distillation process ensures that, within the specific domain, the atoms in d can effectively approximate various potential linear combinations found in the original Dictionary D. By selectively removing atoms from RD that are not pertinent to the dataset domain, we achieve a significant reduction in atom count-by at least 50%. This reduction not only increases the model's efficiency but also maintains the performance and expressiveness within the targeted domain.

sections.title: # When to Use What
sections.text:
- Data-limited or multilingual settings: use unsupervised contrastive pretraining (Contriever/mContriever) plus strong reranking to boost recall without extensive labels. mContriever’s unsupervised contrastive training encodes diverse contextual information, and reranking can substantially lift results [b08db5ca-1] Reranking mContriever improves R@2kT from 25.50 to 34.24 in multilingual retrieval [7118aa04-2].

- Production-grade recall: mine cross-collection and model-predicted hard negatives and denoise them with a cross-encoder/reader; combine with a reranker to recover precision at top-k. Denoised hard negatives and cross-encoder pseudo labels improve end-to-end QA and retrieval ranking [ae4d2b05-0] Hybrid and late-interaction methods refine top-k ranking [b08db5ca-1].

- Efficiency constraints: adopt ColBERT or CoCondenser and consider hybrid sparse–dense fusion to balance effectiveness and resource usage. Late interaction and compression trade memory/latency for matching quality; hybrid fusion leverages complementary signals [b08db5ca-2].

snippets:
Retrieval models have evolved significantly, transitioning from traditional sparse retrievers to sophisticated dense and hybrid retrieval techniques. Sparse retrievers, such as BM25 [92], remain widely used due to their strong lexical matching capabilities and generalization. However, they struggle with capturing semantic relationships, leading to the rise of dense retrieval methods [55], which leverage pre-trained neural encoders to generate embeddings for queries and documents. Notable advancements, such as DPR [120] and ANCE [115], improve retrieval effectiveness by employing contrastive training with in-batch negatives [33] and hard-negative mining [46,116]. Multi-vector approaches like ColBERT [49] enable fine-grained interaction between queries and documents, albeit at the cost of increased computational overhead. To address the limitations of dense retrievers, hybrid models [30,67] combine sparse and dense approaches, utilizing both term matching and semantic understanding for enhanced retrieval performance. 

Recent research has also explored retrieval enhancements through knowledge distillation, curriculum learning, and pre-training. Distillation techniques transfer knowledge from cross-encoders or teacher retrievers to student models, improving dense retriever effectiveness [18,86]. Curriculum learning strategies, which progressively train retrievers from easy to hard samples [60,124], have been shown to enhance both supervised and zero-shot retrieval effectiveness. Meanwhile, pre-training methods such as contrastive learning [40] and masked autoencoding [29,63] have significantly improved the generalization of retrieval models. Additionally, approaches like query augmentation [66,70] generate synthetic training data to enhance retrieval robustness.

snippets:

In this paper, we focus on addressing these challenges so as to effectively train the dual-encoder retriever for open-domain QA. We propose an optimized training approach, called RocketQA, to improving dense passage retrieval. Considering the above challenges, we make three major technical contributions in RocketQA. First, RocketQA introduces cross-batch random negatives. Comparing to in-batch negatives, it increases the number of available negatives for each question when training, and alleviates the discrepancy between training and inference. Second, RocketQA introduces denoised hard negative sampling. It aims to remove false negatives from the top-ranked results retrieved by a specific retriever, which can derive more reliable hard negatives. Third, RocketQA leverages largescale unsupervised data "labeled" by a (as shown in Figure 1b) for data augmentation. Though inefficient, the cross-encoder architecture has been found to be more capable than the dual-encoder architecture in both theory and practice (Luan et al., 2020). Therefore, we utilize a cross-encoder to generate high-quality pseudo labels for unlabeled data for training the dual-encoder retriever.

In summary, the contributions of this paper are as follows:

• The proposed RocketQA introduces three novel optimization strategies for improving dense passage retrieval for open-domain QA, namely cross-batch sampling, denoised hard negative sampling, and data augmentation.

• The overall experiments show that our proposed RocketQA significantly outperforms previous state-of-the-art models on both MS-MARCO and Natural Questions datasets.

• We conduct extensive experiments to examine the effectiveness of the above three strategies in RocketQA. Experimental results show that all the three strategies are effective to improve the performance of dense passage retrieval.

• We also demonstrate that RocketQA leads to better end-to-end QA performance. Besides, built upon RocketQA, we achieve the first rank at the leaderboard of MSMARCO Passage Ranking Task.

sections.title: # Key Takeaways

citations.title: More Robust Dense Retrieval with Contrastive Dual Learning
snippets: In this paper, we propose a training paradigm, Contrastive Dual Learning for Approximate Nearest Neighbor (DANCE), to train dense retrievers. DANCE introduces the additional training object, query likelihood, in dense retriever training to learn query and document representations. Different from ANCE, DANCE concentrates the query embeddings and assigns more uniform recall frequency to queries to sufficiently optimize their representations, while the document embedding distribution is optimized to be more scattered and discriminative. Through such embedding space optimization, DANCE achieves better ranking performance than the previous state-of-theart dense retriever ANCE, especially for the documents that are more frequently recalled during contrastive training on the document retrieval task. Even these documents have smaller detaching distances and are hard to distinguish, DANCE shows better performance on them by learning more fine-grained query representations, better aligning related query-document pairs, and forming a more uniform and smooth embedding space for retrieval tasks. The observations of our work provide some possible directions to further improve dense retriever effectiveness and sufficiently optimize the embedding space by learning more effective query and document representations during contrastive training.

question: When performing the HHL algorithm how does the solution use previous time step solutions to advance the solution in time?

sections.title: # Short answer
sections.text:
- In explicit time-marching, the linear system at step t_{n+1} is built so its right-hand side depends directly on the known solution at t_n; HHL/QLSA then returns the new state x_{n+1} = M^{-1} b_n, advancing the time-march one step using only the previous solution in b_n. <cite id="5cbdd02f-0">Explicit and implicit time stepping for advection–diffusion lead to linear systems of the form x = M⁻¹b that are solved by HHL/QLSA.

- In implicit time-marching (e.g., Crank–Nicolson, Lax–Friedrichs, BDF), the step’s coefficient matrix couples the unknowns at t_{n+1} with known values from t_n, forming block linear systems (e.g., [X Y; M A] [x y] = [0 b]). HHL/QLSA is applied to this block system to obtain x_{n+1}, thereby using the previous step’s solution in both the matrix structure and the right-hand side. Higher-order explicit and implicit time integrators (e.g., Crank–Nicolson, Lax–Friedrichs) can be reformulated as linear systems Ax = b, with A block-partitioned by time slices and x,B block-partitioned by the state at each time; this includes multistep methods where the previous steps’ solutions appear in the blocks [8bfe2b58-0] A central finite-difference discretization with implicit time stepping yields linear systems solved by HHL/QLSA [5cbdd02f-0].

- For nonlinear PDEs (e.g., Navier–Stokes), two common patterns both reuse prior solutions: (a) time-marching on the nonlinear ODEs with a linearization at each step (Picard or Newton), producing a sequence of linear systems whose RHS or Jacobian depends on the previous iterate; (b) directly casting semi-discrete schemes (e.g., Crank–Nicolson) as block linear systems solved by HHL per step. For time-dependent nonlinear PDEs, space-time discretization yields coupled nonlinear ODEs, which are advanced with a time integrator; to turn each time step into a linear system Ax = b, one linearizes (e.g., Carleman or Koopman embeddings), again coupling x and y blocks across time [8bfe2b58-0] Crank–Nicolson, Lax–Friedrichs, etc., can be reformulated as a linear system Ax = b with blocks over time [8bfe2b58-0].

sections.text:
Time-dependent PDEs are advanced by time-marching: a state u(t) is known at time t_n, and a linear or nonlinear mapping produces u(t_{n+1}). In many PDE discretizations, each time step reduces to a linear system M x = b that is solved to obtain the new state x (often a vectorized u at that time). For one-dimensional advection–diffusion, central finite differences with explicit or implicit time stepping yield linear systems solved by HHL/QLSA, with the solution expressed as x = M⁻¹ b [5cbdd02f-0] Explicit and implicit time stepping formulations lead to linear systems at each step, whose solutions advance the advection–diffusion dynamics [73d6fead-1].

In both explicit and implicit schemes, the coefficient matrix M and the right-hand side b are constructed from the known state at t_n (and possibly boundary terms), so solving M x = b with HHL/QLSA returns u_{n+1} from u_n. The central task of QLSA algorithms is to compute x = M⁻¹ b for the discretized advection–diffusion equations at each time step [73d6fead-1] Whether explicit or implicit, the step reduces to solving x = M⁻¹ b with HHL/QLSA [5cbdd02f-0].

citations.title: Two quantum algorithms for solving the one-dimensional advection-diffusion equation
snippets:
The potential of quantum computing algorithms for solving advection-diffusion problems has been investigated in different ways recently. One approach is the decomposition of the PDE into finite differences such that the resulting system of linear equations can be solved. For sparse linear equation systems, the Harrow-Hassidim-Lloyd (HHL) algorithm can provide a exponential speed up in comparison to classical computation [29] under certain caveats [30,31]. A further approach are variational methods. Different versions, such as the variational quantum imaginary time evolution [25], the Variational Quantum Linear Solver (VQLS) [23], or the Variational Quantum Algorithm (VQA) [21,32,33], have been used, even for two-dimensional problems, such as the heat equation [33]. 

The present work compares these two popular hybrid quantum-classical algorithms for a standard benchmark problem in fluid mechanics, which is the one-dimensional advection-diffusion equation with a constant advection velocity U , described by a linear partial differential equation. To this end, we will compare one-to-one a hybrid quantum-classical Variational Quantum Algorithm (VQA) with a Quantum Linear Systems Algorithm (QLSA). The purpose of the present study is to explore the scalability of both algorithms up to mesh grids which will be encoded in registers consisting of n ≤ 6 qubits giving resolutions of N ≤ 64 grid points. Furthermore, we identify the bottlenecks that exist in both cases for some of their main building blocks: for the VQA scheme, this turns out to be the classical optimization algorithm for the minimization of the cost function; for the QLSA it is the quantum phase estimation routine-an approximate method to find eigenvalues of a unitary matrix. Several classical optimization algorithms are therefore compared in the VQA case. Here, we also investigate the role of the depth of the parametric quantum circuit on the performance of the VQA algorithm and report the impact of measurements for data readout on the overall performance. In case of QLSA, the underlying hybrid algorithm presented here (which in itself preserves the speed-up [18]) is customized carefully for the advection-diffusion problem.
