sections.title: # Summary
sections.text:
- Diffusion-first pipelines (e.g., One‑2‑3‑45, Wonder3D, Unique3D, InstantMesh) synthesize consistent multi-view signals and then reconstruct meshes, directly targeting multi-view mesh generation from images. They explicitly address multi-view inconsistency [692c2a10-0] and leverage modern view synthesis and transformers to produce textured meshes [49bca79f-0].
- Neural surfaces and 3D Gaussian splatting (NeuS/SDF, 3DGS) with mesh extraction or binding (SuGaR, MeshGS/BakedSDF, RaDe‑GS, MILo) provide high-quality, efficient reconstructions and practical mesh outputs for animation and simulation. In-the-loop methods reduce vertex counts while preserving detail [44993946-4].
- Classical MVS/SfM plus learning-based completion (MeshMVS, Pixel2Mesh/Mesh R‑CNN, COLMAP) remain strong baselines for many scenarios, with higher fidelity but heavier runtime and view requirements. They are valuable when accuracy outweighs speed [49bca79f-2].
- For humans, multi-view template methods (SMPL, HybrIK, VHA) with visibility and cross-view aggregation deliver robust meshes under occlusion and viewpoint changes. They exploit articulation and per-vertex reasoning [5b164ebf-1].
- Sparse-view settings benefit from adaptive view planning and consistency-aware view synthesis to bridge limited input with high-quality meshes. Progressive planning and neural regularization are key [49bca79f-4].

Overall, the current SOTA combines multi-view diffusion for rich and consistent view synthesis with fast feed-forward mesh extraction or mesh-in-the-loop Gaussian splatting, while classical pipelines and human-centric templates remain essential for robustness, especially under occlusion and sparse views. Empirical results show that enforcing view consistency and integrating strong mesh stages improves volume IoU and robustness to occlusion [692c2a10-2]. However, runtime and generalization remain open challenges, and benchmarks continue to highlight gaps between learning-based speed and NeRF-like fidelity [49bca79f-2].

citations.title: PVP-Recon: Progressive View Planning via Warping Consistency for Sparse-View Surface Reconstruction
snippets:
3D mesh surface reconstruction from multi-view RGB images has always been an important issue in computer vision and graphics. Classic multi-view stereo (MVS) algorithms [Schönberger et al. 2016;Yao et al. 2018] are well established in the field of 3D reconstruction, but struggle to handle areas with homogeneous textures. Recently, neural implicit methods [Wang et al. 2021;Yariv et al. 2021] propose to represent the scene as a signed distance field (SDF) and optimize mesh surfaces directly from 2D image supervision through differentiable rendering. Although neural implicit methods surpass previous works in achieving high-fidelity mesh reconstruction, they typically rely on densely captured images as inputs, whose acquisition process can be time-consuming. To alleviate this reliance, some methods attempt to reconstruct 3D mesh from a predefined set of sparse views, based on geometric priors [Yu et al. 2022] or generalizable priors [Long et al. 2022]. Evidently, the surface reconstruction quality will depend on the input sparse views. However, it remains unknown how to determine a suitable set of sparse input views to achieve good surface reconstruction of a given object. 

In this paper, we observe that two key factors contribute to good surface reconstruction under sparse views: (1) an effective view planning strategy to provide the most informative input images; and (2) a suitable neural representation with well-designed regularization techniques to encode the geometry. Thus, we propose PVP-Recon, a new sparse-view surface reconstruction system that contains two modules: (1) a view planning module for identifying most informative viewpoints for additional image capturing on the fly during surface optimization; and (2) a neural surface reconstruction module utilizing supplemented additional views to gradually improve reconstruction quality. The modules are easy to use and highly flexible, and they can be switched out in a modular manner against other existing approaches. 

Different from existing sparse-view reconstruction methods, our method does not use a predefined set of sparse images as input. Instead, we use our view planning module to progressively identify the most informative viewpoints for capturing additional images during the reconstruction process until a high-quality surface is obtained.

citations.title: Advances in Feed-Forward 3D Reconstruction and View Synthesis: A Survey
snippets:
Meshes are compatible with various graphics pipelines and have gained significant attention in feed-forward 3D reconstruction in recent years. For example, Pixel2Mesh [117] is proposed to produce a 3D mesh from a single input image, which leverages a 2D CNN to extract image features for progressive mesh deformation. Mesh R-CNN [118] extends Mask R-CNN [119] by incorporating 3D shape inference. It introduces a voxel branch that predicts a coarse cubified mesh for each detected object, which is subsequently refined through a mesh refinement branch. 

Recently, one-2-3-45 [120] leverages the diffusion-based model Zero-1-to-3 [121] to produce multiview images and feeds these images to an SDF-based generalizable neural surface reconstruction module [122] for feed-forward mesh reconstruction. One-2-3-45++ [123] enhances the consistency of synthesized multiview images and utilizes a 3D diffusion-based module conditioned on multiple views to generate a textured mesh in a coarse-to-fine manner. However, they often suffer from low reconstruction quality with compromised geometry. To address this issue, Won-der3D [88] introduces a cross-domain diffusion model to generate multiview-consistent normal maps and RGB images. By leveraging these consistent outputs, it reconstructs high-quality 3D meshes through a geometry fusion process. Unique3D [124] first employs a multiview diffusion model alongside a normal diffusion model to generate multiviewconsistent images and normal maps. It then introduces a fast and consistent mesh reconstruction algorithm that effectively integrates these outputs to produce high-quality 3D meshes with accurate geometry. 

In addition, several methods are proposed to utilize the strong capability of the large reconstruction model [10] to achieve high-quality mesh reconstruction. For example, MeshLRM [125] integrates differentiable surface extraction and rendering into a large reconstruction model, enabling the direct generation of high-fidelity 3D meshes from input images. InstantMesh [126] employs a multiview diffusion model to synthesize novel views and utilizes a transformerbased large reconstruction model to generate a high-quality 3D mesh from the multiview images.

sections.title: # Overview: Inspection games with one inspector and several inspectees
sections.text:
An inspection game pits an inspector with limited resources against multiple inspectees who may violate rules and benefit from noncompliance, with the inspector seeking to uncover violations through costly inspections that reveal them. An inspection game is a non-cooperative game whose players are often called an inspector and an inspectee, where the inspectee is obliged to follow regulations but has an incentive to violate, and the inspector tries to minimize the impact of such violations by means of inspections [f3d45112-0] In its simplest form, an inspection game is a two-player game between an individual inspected and an inspector; the individual chooses whether to violate or comply, and the inspector chooses whether to inspect, without observing each other’s choice [f3d45112-3]. These games typically admit mixed-strategy equilibria, in which the inspector randomizes when and how to inspect and inspectees randomize violations, and the classic models have been extended from two players to one inspector facing many inspectees and to sequential settings with limited inspection opportunities. Typically an inspection game has a mixed equilibrium [f3d45112-0] Analytically, early work focused on two-person zero-sum settings, but attention has shifted to n-person, non-zero-sum formulations where the inspector must distribute inspections over many periods or across many targets [f3d45112-1].

Two themes recur across the literature and are directly actionable for a single inspector facing many inspectees. First, the shape of detection (probability of finding a violation) as a function of effort determines whether to concentrate inspections on a single target or spread effort across targets at random or deterministically. When detection functions (probability of detecting) are convex in effort, inspection effort should be concentrated on one inspectee chosen at random, but when detection functions are concave it should be spread deterministically over the inspectees [aee5fac3-2]. Second, with budgets and multiple targets, optimal policies can be decomposed into (i) an assignment of inspectors or effort to inspectees and (ii) an optimal division of the budget across assigned inspectees, yielding explicit equilibrium allocations and procedures for a single inspector allocating a limited number of inspections or inspection time across many firms or units. Hohzaki extended a one-inspector–n inspectees non-zero-sum inspection game to include a budget constraint and decomposed it into an optimal assignment of inspection staff and an optimal division of the budget, obtaining a Nash equilibrium by first minimizing non-detection probability over feasible assignment plans and then dividing the budget to minimize remaining non-detection [aee5fac3-0] Deutsch, Golany, and Rothblum provided closed-form expressions of Nash equilibria in a similar single-inspector, multiple-inspectee game [aee5fac3-0].

Below, we synthesize the modeling, equilibrium, and mechanism-design insights into a practical playbook for a single inspector.

citations.title: Inspection and crime prevention: an evolutionary perspective
snippets:
An inspection game is a non-cooperative game whose players are often called an inspector and an inspectee. It models a situation where the inspectee, which may be an individual, an organisation, a state or a country, is obliged to follow certain regulations but has an incentive to violate them. The inspector tries to minimise the impact of such violations by means of inspections that uncover them. Typically an inspection game has a mixed equilibrium. 

Inspection games have a wide variety of applications including arms control [12,10,11,39], auditing of accounts [41,19,20], tax inspection [58,54,37,51,50,1], environmental protection [56,67,38,6], quality control in supply chains [52,61,40], stockkeeping [27] and communication infrastructures [34,23]. Some of these are surveyed in e.g. [15,7,12,16]. The research on inspection games can contribute to the construction of an effective inspection plan for the inspector when an illegal action is executed strategically. 

This subject has been investigated quite extensively during the last five decades. Still, it continues to draw attention. Throughout the 1960s and the three decades that ensured, the underlying motivation was the cold war between the US and the Soviet Union and the desire to monitor the various arms control agreements that were signed by the two superpowers. Analytically, these settings led quite naturally to two-person game formulations with various assumptions about the strategy sets that were feasible to each of the two parties. Since the early 1990s, attention has shifted to other directions and new circumstances require moving from two-person to n-person formulations, from zero-sum games to non-zero-sums. 

In the initial work done by Dresher [26] and Kuhn [43], they considered sequential inspection games for the treaty of arms reduction where one player wishes to violate the treaty in secret while the other player makes a plan for inspection. In a sequential inspection game, an inspector has to distribute a given number of inspections over a larger number of inspection periods in order to detect an illegal act that an inspectee, who can count the inspector's visits, performs in at most one of these periods. Maschler [46] generalized Dresher's modelling.

snippets:
Avenhaus, Von Stengel and Zamir [16] considered a one-inspector-one -inspectee non-zero-sum imperfect inspection game, where the inspector has a probability of a false alarm α and a probability of non-detection β, and the inspectee has a behavior strategy (q, ω), where q is the probability for acting illegally and ω is a probability distribution on violation procedure given the inspectee acts illegally. They decomposed this game into two games which are solved separately and the solution of one game is a parameter of the second game. First, assuming that the inspectee acts illegally, they formulated a zero-sum game where the inspector faces a hypothesis testing problem δ and the inspectee chooses an optimal violation mechanism ω. That is, for any test δ, the inspectee will choose a violation mechanism ω * to maximise the non-detection probability β(δ, ω). On the side of the inspector, first he chooses a fixed false alarm probability α and consider only those tests that result in this error probability. Then he will choose a test δ * that minimizes the worst-case non-detection probability β(δ * , ω * ). Namely, in equilibrium, the non-detection probability is represented by β(α) := min δ max ω β(δ, ω). Then they solved the original non-zero-sum game to get the optimal false alarm α * for the inspector and optimal probability q * for the inspectee acting illegally. 

Avenhaus and Kilgour [13] studied a one-inspector-two-inspectees nonzero-sum inspection game with imperfect inspections. They found a Nash equilibrium where the inspector divides his inspection effort among two inspectees. Further, they showed that when detection functions (probability of detecting), as functions of inspection effort, are convex, inspection effort should be concentrated on one inspectee chosen at random, but when detection functions are concave it should be spread deterministically over the inspectees.

sections.title: # 1) Model the setting and read equilibria
sections.text:
Begin by specifying payoffs and observability:
- Outcomes: compliance or violation by each inspectee; inspection can uncover violations (true positive) or miss them (false negative); inspections have costs and may generate false alarms (inspection costs, false positives).
- Inspectees’ incentives: gain from violating (e.g., hidden profit, reduced costs) vs. loss if detected (penalties, reputational damage).
- Inspector’s objective: maximize expected benefits from detections minus inspection costs, while accounting for false alarms.

In one-period, imperfect detection settings, equilibria often feature mixed strategies: the inspector chooses an inspection probability and false-alarm level, and inspectees randomize violation mechanisms to maximize the minimal detection risk; the inspector then minimizes the worst-case non-detection probability given false-alarm constraints. Avenhaus, Von Stengel, and Zamir decomposed a one-inspector–one-inspectee imperfect inspection game into a hypothesis-testing subgame (inspector fixes a false-alarm probability and chooses a test minimizing worst-case non-detection) and a non-zero-sum game to obtain equilibrium false-alarm and violation probabilities [aee5fac3-3]. In one-inspectee, multi-period sequential games with a fixed number of inspections, explicit recursive formulas for equilibrium payoffs and randomized schedules exist; moreover, if the inspector can credibly commit to a randomized schedule (“inspector leadership”), inspectees may remain compliant so long as inspections remain, simplifying the scheduling problem. In sequential inspection games with a limited number of inspections over many periods, the inspector’s optimal strategy can be described recursively and solved explicitly; under “inspector leadership,” the inspector commits to a randomized schedule and the inspectee acts legally while inspections remain [f3d45112-2] Explicit solutions in terms of sums of binomial coefficients are available for equilibrium payoffs and mixed strategy probabilities; the model extends naturally to nonzero-sum games and to settings where the inspector commits to a randomized schedule that deters illegal activity while inspections remain [f3d45112-4].

Key takeaway: Before choosing allocation rules, encode payoff parameters (gains from violation, detection/false-alarm costs) and solve or approximate the equilibrium to understand baseline detection risk and best-response inspection probabilities.

citations.title: Recursive Inspection Games
snippets:
Inspection games model situations where an inspector with limited resources verifies by means of inspections that an inspectee adheres to legal obligations, which the inspectee has an incentive to violate. Inspection games have been applied to arms control and disarmament, tax auditing, fare evasion, environmental pollution, and homeland security; for a survey see Avenhaus, von Stengel, and Zamir (2002), and more recent works such as Deutsch et al. (2013) or Delle Fave et al. (2014). This paper presents a generalization of a classical sequential inspection game by Dresher (1962). In Dresher's game, the inspector has to distribute a given number of inspections over a larger number of inspection periods in order to detect a violation that the inspectee, who can count the inspector's visits, performs in at most one of these periods. In our extension of this game, the inspectee may violate more than once, and collect a possibly different reward for each successful violation; for example, a violation may be the diversion of a certain amount of nuclear material in a time period, with the highest reward to the inspectee once he has diverted enough material to build a nuclear bomb. As in Dresher's game, the game ends if a violation is discovered by the inspector who inspects at the same time. This is in line with an application to arms control, and may also apply in other contexts where an identified violator of legal rules becomes subject to much tighter surveillance. 

A central aspect of our model and its analysis, and the reason for its choice of parameters, is that the inspector's mixed strategy in equilibrium does not depend on whether a successful violation took place during a time period without an inspection, about which the inspector is normally not informed. As we will explain in Section 3, the game can therefore, despite this lack of information, be described recursively by a sequence of 2 × 2 games for each stage. As long as there are remaining inspections (but fewer than the number of remaining time periods) and intended violations, the inspector and inspectee randomize at each stage whether to inspect and to violate. For the payoffs and mixed strategy probabilities in equilibrium we give explicit solutions in terms of the game parameters.

citations.title: Recursive Inspection Games
snippets: We consider a sequential inspection game where an inspector uses a limited number of inspections over a larger number of time periods to detect a violation (an illegal act) of an inspectee. Compared with earlier models, we allow varying rewards to the inspectee for successful violations. As one possible example, the most valuable reward may be the completion of a sequence of thefts of nuclear material needed to build a nuclear bomb. The inspectee can observe the inspector, but the inspector can only determine if a violation happens during a stage where he inspects, which terminates the game; otherwise the game continues. Under reasonable assumptions for the payoffs, the inspector’s strategy is independent of the number of successful violations. This allows to apply a recursive description of the game, even though this normally assumes fully informed players after each stage. The resulting recursive equation in three variables for the equilibrium payoff of the game, which generalizes several other known equations of this kind, is solved explicitly in terms of sums of binomial coefficients. We also extend this approach to nonzero-sum games and “inspector leadership” where the inspector commits to (the same) randomized inspection schedule, but the inspectee acts legally (rather than mixes as in the simultaneous game) as long as inspections remain.

This kind inspection game is referred to as an imperfect inspection game, see e.g. Rothenstein and Zamir [53], Canty, Rothenstein and Avenhaus [22]. Rothenstein and Zamir [53] extended Diamond's model [25] by including fixed errors of the first and second kind for a single inspection. Canty, Rothenstein and Avenhaus [22] solved a non-sequential inspection game with first and second kind errors based on a fixed detection time goal and obtained some special solutions for the sequential case. 

It is worth noting that the papers cited above study zero-sum inspection games. However under certain circumstances, one cannot justify the zerosum assumption and non-zero-sum formulations are presented, e.g. in Avenhaus and von Stengel [14], Avenhaus, Von Stengel and Zamir [16], Avenhaus [8], Avenhaus and Canty [9], Kolokoltsov and Malafeyev [42], Avenhaus and Kilgour [13], Hohzaki [39] and Deutsch, Golany and Rothblum [24]. 

Avenhaus [8], Kolokoltsov and Malafeyev [42] presented a one-inspectorone-inspectee non-zero-sum one-step imperfect inspection game, where the inspector has a non-detection probability β. Avenhaus and Canty [9] considered a similar model in a sequential setting, and subject to both kind errors. In these works, they gave an explicit form of the unique Nash equilibrium of this game, i.e. a mixed strategy profile (p * , q * ), where p * is the optimal probability with which the inspector inspects and q * is the optimal probability with which the inspectee acts illegally. 

Avenhaus, Von Stengel and Zamir [16] considered a one-inspector-one -inspectee non-zero-sum imperfect inspection game, where the inspector has a probability of a false alarm α and a probability of non-detection β, and the inspectee has a behavior strategy (q, ω), where q is the probability for acting illegally and ω is a probability distribution on violation procedure given the inspectee acts illegally.

sections.title: # 2) Allocate effort across many inspectees: concentration vs. spreading
sections.text:
A core design question is whether to audit/target a few units intensively or to spread inspections thinly across all. The allocation rule hinges on the curvature of detection as a function of effort:

- Convex detection: If the marginal reduction in non-detection probability from additional effort decreases (diminishing returns), it is optimal to concentrate inspections on a single inspectee chosen at random. This exploits the fact that effort “spends more time where it does good,” maximizing the chance of at least one successful detection per unit of effort. When detection functions are convex in effort, inspection effort should be concentrated on one inspectee chosen at random [aee5fac3-2].

- Concave detection: If returns to effort are diminishing at an increasing rate (or increasing at a decreasing rate depending on normalization), spread effort deterministically across inspectees so each receives a fixed share of the total effort, minimizing the maximum possible non-detection probability across targets. When detection functions are concave, inspection effort should be spread deterministically over the inspectees [aee5fac3-2].

These principles extend to settings with heterogeneous inspectees and budgets. A practical decomposition is to (i) assign the inspector’s time or visits to the most risky inspectees (based on prior violations, size, or exposure) and (ii) within each assignment, allocate visits to minimize aggregate non-detection risk, yielding a joint allocation that balances targeting and within-target intensity. Hohzaki’s decomposition separates an optimal assignment of inspection resources to inspectees from an optimal division of a budget across assigned inspectees, minimizing non-detection probability over feasible assignment plans and then dividing the budget to further minimize risk, producing a Nash equilibrium allocation [aee5fac3-0] Deutsch, Golany, and Rothblum provide closed-form equilibrium expressions for a similar one-inspector–multiple-inspectee game [aee5fac3-0].

Implementation tips:
- Estimate or calibrate detection functions for your domain (e.g., visit count vs. probability of finding a violation) and check curvature locally (convex vs concave) to pick concentration vs. spreading.
- If targeting is allowed, pre-select a “high-risk” cohort and either (a) concentrate visits within that cohort or (b) spread visits across the cohort while reserving spot checks for the highest-risk subset, depending on detected curvature and capacity constraints.

citations.title: Inspection and crime prevention: an evolutionary perspective
snippets:
Avenhaus, Von Stengel and Zamir [16] considered a one-inspector-one -inspectee non-zero-sum imperfect inspection game, where the inspector has a probability of a false alarm α and a probability of non-detection β, and the inspectee has a behavior strategy (q, ω), where q is the probability for acting illegally and ω is a probability distribution on violation procedure given the inspectee acts illegally. They decomposed this game into two games which are solved separately and the solution of one game is a parameter of the second game. First, assuming that the inspectee acts illegally, they formulated a zero-sum game where the inspector faces a hypothesis testing problem δ and the inspectee chooses an optimal violation mechanism ω. That is, for any test δ, the inspectee will choose a violation mechanism ω * to maximise the non-detection probability β(δ, ω). On the side of the inspector, first he chooses a fixed false alarm probability α and consider only those tests that result in this error probability. Then he will choose a test δ * that minimizes the worst-case non-detection probability β(δ * , ω * ). Namely, in equilibrium, the non-detection probability is represented by β(α) := min δ max ω β(δ, ω). Then they solved the original non-zero-sum game to get the optimal false alarm α * for the inspector and optimal probability q * for the inspectee acting illegally. 

Avenhaus and Kilgour [13] studied a one-inspector-two-inspectees nonzero-sum inspection game with imperfect inspections. They found a Nash equilibrium where the inspector divides his inspection effort among two inspectees. Further, they showed that when detection functions (probability of detecting), as functions of inspection effort, are convex, inspection effort should be concentrated on one inspectee chosen at random, but when detection functions are concave it should be spread deterministically over the inspectees.

sections.title: # 3) Sequential inspection with a limited number of inspections
sections.text:
If the inspector has a fixed budget of visits or a limited number of inspections over time, sequential scheduling becomes critical. Two useful structures emerge:

- Randomized schedules: The inspector can randomize which inspectee to visit at each step to keep inspectees indifferent or deterrence-maximizing, and explicit recursive formulas for equilibrium payoffs and inspection probabilities exist across periods under reasonable payoff assumptions. Sequential inspection with a limited number of inspections over many time periods admits a recursive description of equilibrium payoffs and can be solved explicitly; the optimal inspector strategy is independent of the number of successful violations under reasonable payoff assumptions [f3d45112-2] Equilibrium payoffs can be expressed as sums of binomial coefficients, and the model extends to nonzero-sum games and to “inspector leadership,” where the inspectee acts legally as long as inspections remain [f3d45112-4].

- Commitment/scheduling discipline: If the inspector can credibly commit to a randomized schedule (e.g., a publicly posted rotation with unpredictable selection), inspectees may remain compliant so long as inspections continue, which permits a simpler, less adversarial equilibrium and avoids the need to over-inspect high-risk targets to overcome their strategic mixing. Under “inspector leadership,” the inspector commits to a randomized inspection schedule and the inspectee acts legally as long as inspections remain [f3d45112-4]. In multi-inspector generalizations, uncoordinated inspectors can independently decide to inspect with some probability and target a randomly selected inspectee, yielding a tractable allocation when coordination is infeasible. In m-inspectors–n-inspectees one-step games, uncoordinated inspectors each inspect with probability p and, if they decide to inspect, target a single randomly chosen inspectee [aee5fac3-3].

Practical implications:
- When capacity is tight, use a randomized rotating schedule to maintain deterrence without inducing inspectees to “bury” violations just before inspections (a common response to deterministic cycles).
- If you can concentrate inspections on the most risky inspectees without undetectable pre-inspection leakage, targeted waves can be justified when detection exhibits convex returns to effort; otherwise, spread inspections more evenly across risk strata.

citations.title: Recursive Inspection Games
snippets: We consider a sequential inspection game where an inspector uses a limited number of inspections over a larger number of time periods to detect a violation (an illegal act) of an inspectee. Compared with earlier models, we allow varying rewards to the inspectee for successful violations. As one possible example, the most valuable reward may be the completion of a sequence of thefts of nuclear material needed to build a nuclear bomb. The inspectee can observe the inspector, but the inspector can only determine if a violation happens during a stage where he inspects, which terminates the game; otherwise the game continues. Under reasonable assumptions for the payoffs, the inspector’s strategy is independent of the number of successful violations. This allows to apply a recursive description of the game, even though this normally assumes fully informed players after each stage. The resulting recursive equation in three variables for the equilibrium payoff of the game, which generalizes several other known equations of this kind, is solved explicitly in terms of sums of binomial coefficients. We also extend this approach to nonzero-sum games and “inspector leadership” where the inspector commits to (the same) randomized inspection schedule, but the inspectee acts legally (rather than mixes as in the simultaneous game) as long as inspections remain.

citations.title: Recursive Inspection Games
snippets:
Inspection games model situations where an inspector with limited resources verifies by means of inspections that an inspectee adheres to legal obligations, which the inspectee has an incentive to violate. Inspection games have been applied to arms control and disarmament, tax auditing, fare evasion, environmental pollution, and homeland security; for a survey see Avenhaus, von Stengel, and Zamir (2002), and more recent works such as Deutsch et al. (2013) or Delle Fave et al. (2014). This paper presents a generalization of a classical sequential inspection game by Dresher (1962). In Dresher's game, the inspector has to distribute a given number of inspections over a larger number of inspection periods in order to detect a violation that the inspectee, who can count the inspector's visits, performs in at most one of these periods. In our extension of this game, the inspectee may violate more than once, and collect a possibly different reward for each successful violation; for example, a violation may be the diversion of a certain amount of nuclear material in a time period, with the highest reward to the inspectee once he has diverted enough material to build a nuclear bomb. As in Dresher's game, the game ends if a violation is discovered by the inspector who inspects at the same time. This is in line with an application to arms control, and may also apply in other contexts where an identified violator of legal rules becomes subject to much tighter surveillance. 

A central aspect of our model and its analysis, and the reason for its choice of parameters, is that the inspector's mixed strategy in equilibrium does not depend on whether a successful violation took place during a time period without an inspection, about which the inspector is normally not informed. As we will explain in Section 3, the game can therefore, despite this lack of information, be described recursively by a sequence of 2 × 2 games for each stage. As long as there are remaining inspections (but fewer than the number of remaining time periods) and intended violations, the inspector and inspectee randomize at each stage whether to inspect and to violate. For the payoffs and mixed strategy probabilities in equilibrium we give explicit solutions in terms of the game parameters.

sections.title: # 4) Mechanism design and audit policy levers
sections.text:
Mechanism design in oversight settings shows that a single inspector can amplify deterrence by choosing audit probabilities, penalties, and conditional policies that update inspection intensity based on history:

- Baseline audit probability and penalties: Higher detection probabilities (via deeper audits or higher penalties) reduce the net benefit of violating, and in multi-period conditional mechanisms, raising penalties increases the optimal audit probability after a noncompliance is found, while maintaining or reducing it when compliance is observed can control costs. The probability of detecting fraud is exogenously determined by criminal courts, structuring a multi-period model where only the manager and auditor actively choose strategies [cfb9436d-0] Under a conditional audit mechanism, if an under-declaration is found in one period, the audit probability is enhanced in the next period; the audit process has a quality r (probability the under-declaration is found), and penalties P and costs C are public parameters [cfb9436d-1] A Bayesian audit game specifies fraud prevalence h, detection probabilities under deep/shallow audits, and penalty sizes b and s, linking audit effort, fees, and penalties to payoffs and equilibrium behavior [cfb9436d-2] Empirical work indicates that increasing penalties for auditors and audit fees reduces the probability of financial fraud and that the number and effort of auditors are proportional to audit quality [cfb9436d-3].

- Conditional audit updating: After a violation is detected and sanctioned, increase inspection probability for the next period (or for the same inspectee if feasible) to deter recurrence; after a clean audit, optionally reduce inspection intensity to conserve resources, subject to maintaining credible deterrence. This is straightforward to implement with a single inspector and many firms by adjusting a firm-specific “risk score” or visit budget based on past outcomes and external risk signals. If under-declaration is found, the audit probability for the subsequent period is enhanced; the audit quality r and penalty P are exogenous parameters shaping the optimal policy [cfb9436d-1].

- Audit depth and fees: Choosing deep audits (higher r) and appropriate fees aligns auditor incentives and improves detection, but at higher costs; in private audit contexts, shallow auditing may be chosen absent sufficient litigation/reputation costs, so regulators should ensure sufficiently large penalties/reputation risks to elicit high audit effort. Deep auditing always detects fraud; shallow auditing never detects, and detection outcomes affect payoffs and deterrence [cfb9436d-2] If litigation and reputation costs are not sufficiently large, auditors have no incentive to exert high audit effort; optimal mechanisms must account for such constraints [cfb9436d-4].

Takeaway: Treat audit probability and penalty levels as policy knobs to set the equilibrium deterrence level. Use conditional policies to reallocate the inspector’s scarce time toward higher-moment risk (post-violation spikes, persistent noncompliance) while maintaining baseline coverage.

citations.title: The auditing game: the dark side of the private provision of a public good
snippets:
It is assumed here that each Auditor is of equally high ability, in contrast to Corona and Randhawa (2010). In their model, the type of auditor is defined ex ante and cannot change in the game; there, "nature" decides whether an auditor is of low or high ability. Instead, in our game, the Auditor chooses the level of auditing, i.e., whether the auditing will be deep or shallow, assuming that deep auditing is legally possible. Deep auditing means that auditors are completely independent and accurate up to the point of the minimum-profit constraint for the auditing firm. Such auditors might be called Kantian4 auditors. In contrast, shallow auditing implies that auditors either do not look actively to detect fraud or that they even collude tacitly with a fraudulent management. 

With honest accounting, it does not matter whether the Auditor chooses deep or shallow auditing. The game ends at this point, and the payoffs for the Manager and the Auditor are doled out. With fraudulent accounting, the Auditor may or may not detect fraud, depending on the chosen level of auditing. Deep auditing is assumed to always detect fraud, whereas shallow auditing will never. In the last step, the Courts decide on the level of fines (big or small), and payoffs are made. We note that the "external" losses of the Auditor from shallow accounting always encompass both the reputation loss and the fine imposed by the Courts. In this paper, we refer to reputation losses as the present value of market-imposed losses of sales on audit firms due to their shallow auditing. Since the probability of detecting accounting fraud is exogenously determined by criminal courts, a multiperiod model seems not to be required. 

The point that the probability of detecting fraud is exogenously determined leads to important implications. Structurally, in this three-player game, only two are active players in the sense that they make strategic choices. The Manager can choose to be honest or fraudulent, and the Auditor can decide to audit deeply or shallowly. The Courts, however, do not actively choose their fraud detection probability. This is rather given by an ex ante determined rate of control, as in other areas of state control, for instance, tax audits.

sections.title: # 5) Safety inspection practices: signals, tools, and empirical effects
sections.text:
Safety regulators (e.g., OSHA) provide concrete practices that map onto inspection game design:

- Signals for targeting: Larger firms have more employees and more opportunities for incidents and violations; employee complaints are a major driver of inspections, so firms with higher worker complaints or larger workforces warrant higher inspection probabilities. A larger number of employees significantly predicts more violations (coefficient = 0.548, z = 40.11, p < 0.001), and worker complaints are the most common cause of OSHA inspections [db5730b3-0].

- Enforcement toolkit: Inspectors use risk evaluation, guidance, awareness campaigns, and sanctions to secure compliance; penalties are calibrated to deter high-risk behavior, and evidence shows inspections and penalties can reduce injury rates, though results are mixed and depend on enforcement quality. Regulators detect misconduct through inspections and issue violation notices; employee complaints are the most common cause of OSHA inspections [db5730b3-1] OSHA inspections are reported to have reduced lost workday injuries by 19% by 1979–1985, though other studies find mixed effectiveness and highlight incomplete enforcement as a key factor [db5730b3-3].

- Internal information and interjurisdictional issues: When information flows within regulators are frictions, firms may shift violations to less-informed jurisdictions; inspections and penalties in one state reduce subsequent violations within that state but not others, and lighter cross-border penalties can embolden shifting—motivating coordination and shared databases. Firms caught violating in one state subsequently violate less in that state but more in others; information frictions prevent proactive cross-state inspection; cross-state violations face lower penalties; firms shift behavior into states with greater information frictions [db5730b3-2].

These insights suggest two design moves for a single inspector: (i) leverage local information (size, complaints, past violations) to set risk scores and targeting, and (ii) invest in information-sharing and documentation to reduce frictions that blunt targeting.

snippets:
First, a larger number of employees increases the likelihood of safety incidents. To verify this assumption, we regressed the number of violations (in year t) against the number of employees (natural logarithm transformed, year t-1) through a negative binomial regression. The results show that number of employees is a significant predictor (coefficient = 0.548, z = 40.11, p < 0.001). Large firms with number of employees one standard deviation above the mean have 1.322 more violations per year than average-size firms. Given that violation is rare (1.133 per firm per year), the effect magnitude of 1.322 is considerable. Second, the inclusion of the number of employees can also mitigate selection bias in safety violation. Employee complaint (whistle blowing) is the most common cause of OSHA inspection (OSHA, 2016). 22.13% of OSHA inspections in 2019 were prompted by worker complaints (OSHA 2021). A larger number of employees increases the number of watchful eyes over a firm's safety practices, which increases the chances of having whistle blowers and consequently OSHA inspections. 

In H1 and H2, we hypothesized a relationship between past safety violation experiences and subsequent safety violation incidents. The variable, violation experience, was measured as the total number of violations committed by a firm in all years before a certain year (year t). This measure is consistent with that used in studies on organizational learning from failure (e.g., Haunschild & Rhee 2004;Yiu et al. 2014). It captures total past experiences in all years before a safety violation incident in year t. In our sensitivity analysis, we replaced this variable with the number of safety violations committed by a firm in 1 year (instead of all years) before year t (i.e., in year t-1; see Section 4.2). 

In H3 and H4, we hypothesized moderating effects for penalty and OHSAS 18001 certification. 

The average penalty for a firm's past violations should reflect the cost of having violation in the firm's economic evaluation.

citations.title: The Impact of Information Frictions Within Regulators: Evidence from Workplace Safety Violations
snippets: The Occupational Safety and Health Administration (OSHA) is decentralized, wherein field offices coordinated at the state level undertake inspections. We study whether this structure can lead to interstate frictions in sharing information and how this impacts firms’ compliance with workplace safety laws. We find that firms caught violating in one state subsequently violate less in that state but violate more in other states. Despite this pattern, and in keeping with information frictions, violations in one state do not trigger proactive OSHA inspections in other states. Moreover, firms face lower monetary penalties when subsequent violations occur across state lines, likely due to the lack of documentation necessary to assess severe penalties. Finally, firms are more likely to shift violating behavior into states with greater information frictions. Our findings suggest that internal information within regulators impacts the likelihood and location of corporate misconduct.

citations.title: Safety regulation enforcement and production safety: The role of penalties and voluntary safety management systems
snippets:
Research has explored various factors that account for OHS performance improvement, including managers' attitudes (Pagell & Gobeli 2009), leadership (de Koster et al. 2011;de Vries et al. 2016), culture (Power et al. 2015), and capital structure (Pagell et al. 2019). Among these factors, the OHS management system is considered a vital antecedent to a firm's OHS performance (Lo et al. 2014;Robson et al. 2007;Wiengarten et al. 2017). The operation of a mandatory OHS management system requires substantial interaction between government agencies and firms. The government first establishes the legal standards that firms' safety practices must meet; firms then operate with compliance to these legal safety standards (Fan et al. 2014). However, operations under a mandatory OHS management system may encounter difficulties caused by goal divergence between regulators and firms. Regulators aim to motivate firms to improve safety performance and thus overall social welfare, while firms need to evaluate the balance between safety practice costs and safety performance in production (Pagell et al. 2020). These divergent goals resulting from a safety-productivity tradeoff may cause violation behavior by firms with regard to safety regulations. 

Government enforcement, including via inspections and penalties, is thus vital to ensure that mandated OHS management systems are running well in industries. There are two processes involved in safety violations in the US. The first is companies engaging in misconduct in safety practices and the second is the government detecting such misconduct and issuing violation notices. Corporate fraud is generally difficult to detect by outside stakeholders such as media, governments, and customers (Shi et al. 2017). However, inspections help overcome information asymmetry between regulators and firms and can spot any opportunistic (i.e., non-compliance) behavior of firms. In OSHA's policy, workers are motivated to report such misconduct because their health and lives are at stake. The misconduct in regard to safety practices is easier to observe by operational workers who daily interact in the operational system than by the external parties. Employee complaints are the most common cause of OSHA inspections (OSHA 2016). 

Inspections are conducted by well-trained and experienced safety and health compliance officers (OSHA 2018).

sections.title: # 6) A practical playbook for a single inspector with many inspectees
sections.text:
1) Calibrate detection and costs. Estimate detection probability as a function of effort per inspectee (e.g., visit count, time-on-site) and include false-alarm costs. Check curvature (convex vs. concave) to decide concentration vs. spreading of effort. When detection is convex in effort, concentrate inspections on a single inspectee chosen at random; when concave, spread effort deterministically across inspectees [aee5fac3-2].

2) Prioritize targets. Build a risk score from exogenous signals (prior violations, size, number of employees, complaints, sector hazards) and allocate a higher baseline visit budget to high-risk inspectees; if resources permit, run iterative waves focusing on the top risk strata. Larger firms have significantly more violations, and worker complaints are a major driver of inspections [db5730b3-0] Inspection and enforcement help overcome information asymmetry and spot noncompliance, with employee complaints being a primary trigger [db5730b3-1].

3) Choose audit depth and penalties strategically. Prefer deep audits where feasible to maximize detection and deterrence, but recognize higher costs; set penalties high enough to induce high audit effort from inspectors/auditors and to credibly deter violations. Deep auditing always detects fraud; shallow auditing never does, and penalties (b, s) shape deterrence [cfb9436d-2] If litigation and reputation costs are insufficient, auditors will not exert high effort; mechanisms must ensure binding participation and incentive compatibility [cfb9436d-4].

4) Implement randomized scheduling to sustain deterrence. Use a rotating, unpredictable schedule to maintain mixed-strategy equilibria and avoid enabling inspectees to time-shift violations; when capacity is tight, randomization across targets is often superior to deterministic cycles. Explicit randomized schedules can sustain equilibria where inspectees act legally as long as inspections remain [f3d45112-4] In multi-inspector settings, uncoordinated inspectors can each inspect with probability p and target a randomly chosen inspectee, a structure that generalizes to single-inspector orchestration [aee5fac3-3].

5) Adopt conditional policies to reallocate scarce inspections. After detecting a violation and imposing a penalty, increase inspection probability for the next period (or for the same inspectee if feasible) to deter recurrence; after clean audits, optionally reduce intensity to conserve capacity, maintaining an overall risk-based rhythm. If an under-declaration is found, enhance the audit probability in the subsequent period; audit quality r and penalty P are key parameters shaping the optimal conditional policy [cfb9436d-1].

6) Combine inspection with compliance tools. Use risk evaluation, guidance, and awareness campaigns alongside sanctions to improve long-term compliance and reduce repeat violations; document findings and share information to mitigate cross-domain shirting caused by internal information frictions. Inspectors use risk evaluation, promotion of best practices, information campaigns, guidance, and sanctions during inspections to secure compliance [db5730b3-1] Information frictions within regulators can lead firms to shift violations across jurisdictions and face lighter penalties, suggesting the value of information sharing [db5730b3-2].

7) Monitor outcomes and adjust. Track detection rates, false alarms, and injury/violation rates; if returns to effort are diminishing faster than expected, favor concentration on a random high-risk cohort; if detection shows better concave returns, spread effort more evenly. Periodically re-evaluate penalties and audit fees to maintain deterrence without excessive costs. Increasing penalties and audit fees reduces fraud; the number and effort of auditors are proportional to audit quality, indicating sensitivity of deterrence to fee/penalty settings [cfb9436d-3] Empirical evidence shows inspections and penalties can reduce injury rates, but effectiveness varies with enforcement quality [db5730b3-3].

citations.title: Safety regulation enforcement and production safety: The role of penalties and voluntary safety management systems
snippets:
Research has explored various factors that account for OHS performance improvement, including managers' attitudes (Pagell & Gobeli 2009), leadership (de Koster et al. 2011;de Vries et al. 2016), culture (Power et al. 2015), and capital structure (Pagell et al. 2019). Among these factors, the OHS management system is considered a vital antecedent to a firm's OHS performance (Lo et al. 2014;Robson et al. 2007;Wiengarten et al. 2017). The operation of a mandatory OHS management system requires substantial interaction between government agencies and firms. The government first establishes the legal standards that firms' safety practices must meet; firms then operate with compliance to these legal safety standards (Fan et al. 2014). However, operations under a mandatory OHS management system may encounter difficulties caused by goal divergence between regulators and firms. Regulators aim to motivate firms to improve safety performance and thus overall social welfare, while firms need to evaluate the balance between safety practice costs and safety performance in production (Pagell et al. 2020). These divergent goals resulting from a safety-productivity tradeoff may cause violation behavior by firms with regard to safety regulations. 

Government enforcement, including via inspections and penalties, is thus vital to ensure that mandated OHS management systems are running well in industries. There are two processes involved in safety violations in the US. The first is companies engaging in misconduct in safety practices and the second is the government detecting such misconduct and issuing violation notices. Corporate fraud is generally difficult to detect by outside stakeholders such as media, governments, and customers (Shi et al. 2017). However, inspections help overcome information asymmetry between regulators and firms and can spot any opportunistic (i.e., non-compliance) behavior of firms. In OSHA's policy, workers are motivated to report such misconduct because their health and lives are at stake. The misconduct in regard to safety practices is easier to observe by operational workers who daily interact in the operational system than by the external parties. Employee complaints are the most common cause of OSHA inspections (OSHA 2016). 

Inspections are conducted by well-trained and experienced safety and health compliance officers (OSHA 2018).

citations.title: Recursive Inspection Games
snippets:
Inspection games model situations where an inspector with limited resources verifies by means of inspections that an inspectee adheres to legal obligations, which the inspectee has an incentive to violate. Inspection games have been applied to arms control and disarmament, tax auditing, fare evasion, environmental pollution, and homeland security; for a survey see Avenhaus, von Stengel, and Zamir (2002), and more recent works such as Deutsch et al. (2013) or Delle Fave et al. (2014). This paper presents a generalization of a classical sequential inspection game by Dresher (1962). In Dresher's game, the inspector has to distribute a given number of inspections over a larger number of inspection periods in order to detect a violation that the inspectee, who can count the inspector's visits, performs in at most one of these periods. In our extension of this game, the inspectee may violate more than once, and collect a possibly different reward for each successful violation; for example, a violation may be the diversion of a certain amount of nuclear material in a time period, with the highest reward to the inspectee once he has diverted enough material to build a nuclear bomb. As in Dresher's game, the game ends if a violation is discovered by the inspector who inspects at the same time. This is in line with an application to arms control, and may also apply in other contexts where an identified violator of legal rules becomes subject to much tighter surveillance. 

A central aspect of our model and its analysis, and the reason for its choice of parameters, is that the inspector's mixed strategy in equilibrium does not depend on whether a successful violation took place during a time period without an inspection, about which the inspector is normally not informed. As we will explain in Section 3, the game can therefore, despite this lack of information, be described recursively by a sequence of 2 × 2 games for each stage. As long as there are remaining inspections (but fewer than the number of remaining time periods) and intended violations, the inspector and inspectee randomize at each stage whether to inspect and to violate. For the payoffs and mixed strategy probabilities in equilibrium we give explicit solutions in terms of the game parameters.

citations.title: Inspection and crime prevention: an evolutionary perspective
snippets:
Avenhaus, Von Stengel and Zamir [16] considered a one-inspector-one -inspectee non-zero-sum imperfect inspection game, where the inspector has a probability of a false alarm α and a probability of non-detection β, and the inspectee has a behavior strategy (q, ω), where q is the probability for acting illegally and ω is a probability distribution on violation procedure given the inspectee acts illegally. They decomposed this game into two games which are solved separately and the solution of one game is a parameter of the second game. First, assuming that the inspectee acts illegally, they formulated a zero-sum game where the inspector faces a hypothesis testing problem δ and the inspectee chooses an optimal violation mechanism ω. That is, for any test δ, the inspectee will choose a violation mechanism ω * to maximise the non-detection probability β(δ, ω). On the side of the inspector, first he chooses a fixed false alarm probability α and consider only those tests that result in this error probability. Then he will choose a test δ * that minimizes the worst-case non-detection probability β(δ * , ω * ). Namely, in equilibrium, the non-detection probability is represented by β(α) := min δ max ω β(δ, ω). Then they solved the original non-zero-sum game to get the optimal false alarm α * for the inspector and optimal probability q * for the inspectee acting illegally. 

Avenhaus and Kilgour [13] studied a one-inspector-two-inspectees nonzero-sum inspection game with imperfect inspections. They found a Nash equilibrium where the inspector divides his inspection effort among two inspectees. Further, they showed that when detection functions (probability of detecting), as functions of inspection effort, are convex, inspection effort should be concentrated on one inspectee chosen at random, but when detection functions are concave it should be spread deterministically over the inspectees.

citations.title: The Impact of Information Frictions Within Regulators: Evidence from Workplace Safety Violations
snippets: The Occupational Safety and Health Administration (OSHA) is decentralized, wherein field offices coordinated at the state level undertake inspections. We study whether this structure can lead to interstate frictions in sharing information and how this impacts firms’ compliance with workplace safety laws. We find that firms caught violating in one state subsequently violate less in that state but violate more in other states. Despite this pattern, and in keeping with information frictions, violations in one state do not trigger proactive OSHA inspections in other states. Moreover, firms face lower monetary penalties when subsequent violations occur across state lines, likely due to the lack of documentation necessary to assess severe penalties. Finally, firms are more likely to shift violating behavior into states with greater information frictions. Our findings suggest that internal information within regulators impacts the likelihood and location of corporate misconduct.

sections.title: # 8) Summary of key results to use in practice
sections.text:
- Mixed equilibria are typical; model your domain to understand baseline inspection and violation probabilities and to justify randomized schedules. Typically an inspection game has a mixed equilibrium [f3d45112-0].
- Concentrate effort if detection is convex in effort; spread effort if detection is concave; use risk signals to select which cohort to concentrate on at any time. When detection functions are convex, concentrate effort on a randomly chosen inspectee; when concave, spread effort deterministically [aee5fac3-2].
- With budgets and multiple inspectees, decompose into assignment and budget-division subproblems to obtain equilibrium allocations and implementable policies; explicit solutions exist in related models. Hohzaki’s decomposition yields a Nash equilibrium by first optimizing assignment plans and then dividing the budget to minimize non-detection probability [aee5fac3-0] Deutsch, Golany, and Rothblum provide closed-form Nash equilibria for similar single-inspector, multiple-inspectee games [aee5fac3-0].
- Sequential scheduling with a limited number of inspections can be handled by randomized rotations and explicit recursive formulas; credible “inspector leadership” can keep inspectees compliant while inspections remain. Sequential inspection games admit recursive equilibrium solutions and explicit formulas [f3d45112-2] Under inspector leadership, the inspectee acts legally as long as inspections remain [f3d45112-4].
- Mechanism design levers—audit probabilities, penalties, and conditional updating—significantly affect deterrence and resource use; higher penalties and audit fees reduce fraud, and conditional policies increase follow-up audits after violations. Conditional audit mechanisms enhance audit probability after a violation is found, with audit quality r and penalty P as key parameters [cfb9436d-1] Increasing penalties and audit fees reduces fraud; auditor effort scales with audit quality [cfb9436d-3].
- Safety inspection evidence supports targeting by size/complaints, combining inspection with risk tools and sanctions, and recognizing that information frictions and uneven penalties can induce cross-jurisdictional shifting of violations. Firms with more employees have more violations and are more likely to trigger inspections via worker complaints [db5730b3-0] Inspections help overcome information asymmetry and are a primary tool for detecting noncompliance [db5730b3-1] Firms shift violations into states with greater information frictions and receive lighter penalties across state lines [db5730b3-2] Inspections coupled with penalties have reduced injury rates, though effectiveness varies with enforcement quality [db5730b3-3].

By combining these theoretical results with empirical insights, a single inspector can design a risk-based, randomized, and dynamically updated inspection plan that maximizes expected detections and minimizes compliance costs while sustaining credible deterrence across many inspectees.

snippets:
Research has explored various factors that account for OHS performance improvement, including managers' attitudes (Pagell & Gobeli 2009), leadership (de Koster et al. 2011;de Vries et al. 2016), culture (Power et al. 2015), and capital structure (Pagell et al. 2019). Among these factors, the OHS management system is considered a vital antecedent to a firm's OHS performance (Lo et al. 2014;Robson et al. 2007;Wiengarten et al. 2017). The operation of a mandatory OHS management system requires substantial interaction between government agencies and firms. The government first establishes the legal standards that firms' safety practices must meet; firms then operate with compliance to these legal safety standards (Fan et al. 2014). However, operations under a mandatory OHS management system may encounter difficulties caused by goal divergence between regulators and firms. Regulators aim to motivate firms to improve safety performance and thus overall social welfare, while firms need to evaluate the balance between safety practice costs and safety performance in production (Pagell et al. 2020). These divergent goals resulting from a safety-productivity tradeoff may cause violation behavior by firms with regard to safety regulations. 

Government enforcement, including via inspections and penalties, is thus vital to ensure that mandated OHS management systems are running well in industries. There are two processes involved in safety violations in the US. The first is companies engaging in misconduct in safety practices and the second is the government detecting such misconduct and issuing violation notices. Corporate fraud is generally difficult to detect by outside stakeholders such as media, governments, and customers (Shi et al. 2017). However, inspections help overcome information asymmetry between regulators and firms and can spot any opportunistic (i.e., non-compliance) behavior of firms. In OSHA's policy, workers are motivated to report such misconduct because their health and lives are at stake. The misconduct in regard to safety practices is easier to observe by operational workers who daily interact in the operational system than by the external parties. Employee complaints are the most common cause of OSHA inspections (OSHA 2016). 

Inspections are conducted by well-trained and experienced safety and health compliance officers (OSHA 2018).

citations.title: Recursive Inspection Games
snippets:
Inspection games model situations where an inspector with limited resources verifies by means of inspections that an inspectee adheres to legal obligations, which the inspectee has an incentive to violate. Inspection games have been applied to arms control and disarmament, tax auditing, fare evasion, environmental pollution, and homeland security; for a survey see Avenhaus, von Stengel, and Zamir (2002), and more recent works such as Deutsch et al. (2013) or Delle Fave et al. (2014). This paper presents a generalization of a classical sequential inspection game by Dresher (1962). In Dresher's game, the inspector has to distribute a given number of inspections over a larger number of inspection periods in order to detect a violation that the inspectee, who can count the inspector's visits, performs in at most one of these periods. In our extension of this game, the inspectee may violate more than once, and collect a possibly different reward for each successful violation; for example, a violation may be the diversion of a certain amount of nuclear material in a time period, with the highest reward to the inspectee once he has diverted enough material to build a nuclear bomb. As in Dresher's game, the game ends if a violation is discovered by the inspector who inspects at the same time. This is in line with an application to arms control, and may also apply in other contexts where an identified violator of legal rules becomes subject to much tighter surveillance. 

A central aspect of our model and its analysis, and the reason for its choice of parameters, is that the inspector's mixed strategy in equilibrium does not depend on whether a successful violation took place during a time period without an inspection, about which the inspector is normally not informed. As we will explain in Section 3, the game can therefore, despite this lack of information, be described recursively by a sequence of 2 × 2 games for each stage. As long as there are remaining inspections (but fewer than the number of remaining time periods) and intended violations, the inspector and inspectee randomize at each stage whether to inspect and to violate. For the payoffs and mixed strategy probabilities in equilibrium we give explicit solutions in terms of the game parameters.

An inspection game is a non-cooperative game whose players are often called an inspector and an inspectee. It models a situation where the inspectee, which may be an individual, an organisation, a state or a country, is obliged to follow certain regulations but has an incentive to violate them. The inspector tries to minimise the impact of such violations by means of inspections that uncover them. 

A simple example of an inspection game can be described by the following 2x2 normal form game in Table 1, where the inspectee is the row player and the inspector is the column player, and the left (resp. right) entry of each cell corresponds to the payoffs for the individual (resp. inspector). citations.title: Inspection and crime prevention: an evolutionary perspective
snippets:
Avenhaus, Von Stengel and Zamir [16] considered a one-inspector-one -inspectee non-zero-sum imperfect inspection game, where the inspector has a probability of a false alarm α and a probability of non-detection β, and the inspectee has a behavior strategy (q, ω), where q is the probability for acting illegally and ω is a probability distribution on violation procedure given the inspectee acts illegally. They decomposed this game into two games which are solved separately and the solution of one game is a parameter of the second game. First, assuming that the inspectee acts illegally, they formulated a zero-sum game where the inspector faces a hypothesis testing problem δ and the inspectee chooses an optimal violation mechanism ω. That is, for any test δ, the inspectee will choose a violation mechanism ω * to maximise the non-detection probability β(δ, ω). On the side of the inspector, first he chooses a fixed false alarm probability α and consider only those tests that result in this error probability. Then he will choose a test δ * that minimizes the worst-case non-detection probability β(δ * , ω * ). Namely, in equilibrium, the non-detection probability is represented by β(α) := min δ max ω β(δ, ω). Then they solved the original non-zero-sum game to get the optimal false alarm α * for the inspector and optimal probability q * for the inspectee acting illegally. 

Avenhaus and Kilgour [13] studied a one-inspector-two-inspectees nonzero-sum inspection game with imperfect inspections. They found a Nash equilibrium where the inspector divides his inspection effort among two inspectees. Further, they showed that when detection functions (probability of detecting), as functions of inspection effort, are convex, inspection effort should be concentrated on one inspectee chosen at random, but when detection functions are concave it should be spread deterministically over the inspectees.

citations.title: The Impact of Information Frictions Within Regulators: Evidence from Workplace Safety Violations
snippets: The Occupational Safety and Health Administration (OSHA) is decentralized, wherein field offices coordinated at the state level undertake inspections. We study whether this structure can lead to interstate frictions in sharing information and how this impacts firms’ compliance with workplace safety laws. We find that firms caught violating in one state subsequently violate less in that state but violate more in other states. Despite this pattern, and in keeping with information frictions, violations in one state do not trigger proactive OSHA inspections in other states. Moreover, firms face lower monetary penalties when subsequent violations occur across state lines, likely due to the lack of documentation necessary to assess severe penalties. Finally, firms are more likely to shift violating behavior into states with greater information frictions. Our findings suggest that internal information within regulators impacts the likelihood and location of corporate misconduct.

citations.title: Recursive Inspection Games
snippets: We consider a sequential inspection game where an inspector uses a limited number of inspections over a larger number of time periods to detect a violation (an illegal act) of an inspectee. Compared with earlier models, we allow varying rewards to the inspectee for successful violations. As one possible example, the most valuable reward may be the completion of a sequence of thefts of nuclear material needed to build a nuclear bomb. The inspectee can observe the inspector, but the inspector can only determine if a violation happens during a stage where he inspects, which terminates the game; otherwise the game continues. Under reasonable assumptions for the payoffs, the inspector’s strategy is independent of the number of successful violations. This allows to apply a recursive description of the game, even though this normally assumes fully informed players after each stage. The resulting recursive equation in three variables for the equilibrium payoff of the game, which generalizes several other known equations of this kind, is solved explicitly in terms of sums of binomial coefficients. We also extend this approach to nonzero-sum games and “inspector leadership” where the inspector commits to (the same) randomized inspection schedule, but the inspectee acts legally (rather than mixes as in the simultaneous game) as long as inspections remain.

sections.title: # Overview
sections.text: Artificial intelligence in academic advising spans conversational agents, predictive analytics and early-warning systems, dashboards for advisors, knowledge/expert systems for degree planning, and natural language processing (NLP) to analyze student experiences, with the shared goal of improving access, personalization, and early intervention in students’ academic journeys. Artificial intelligence (AI) chatbots have proven complementary tools to address the accessibility limitations in traditional advising, offering 24/7 availability, reduced social barriers, and standardized information delivery [e1f8fb30-0] An early warning system using machine learning (e.g., logistic models, SVM, random forest) can identify at-risk students and notify advisors to prevent dropout [e1f8fb30-2] Conversational agents can serve as academic advisors by suggesting courses based on student data, flagging likely failure, and answering policy/program questions, sometimes in multiple languages [e1f8fb30-4] Learning analytics dashboards help educators and advisors identify behavioral and study patterns to optimize the learning environment and support personalized feedback [5d38afad-0] NLP methods can quantitatively analyze student reviews of advisors to understand interactions and inform service improvement [fbef8d17-0].

citations.title: Elevating Academic Advising: Natural Language Processing of Student Reviews
snippets:
Academic advising is a program or initiative employed within educational systems to offer students guidance and counsel [1]. It is widely respected and extensively employed to support students in educational institutions around the world [2]. The field of academic advising, as a student support service, has undergone significant transformation in recent years, paralleling the broader evolution within the educational landscape. In the realm of higher education, universities have made significant strides in implementing comprehensive evaluation processes for various educational aspects. These include the evaluation of teachers' performance, assessment of academic programs of study, appraisal of administrative services, and even the scrutiny of extracurricular activities and student support services. However, this progress rarely extends to academic advising [3]. Unlike the robust evaluation mechanisms in place for many academic processes, the assessment of academic advising performance remains relatively unexplored. 

In this paper, we utilize natural language processing methods for a quantitative examination of student feedback in an effective and streamlined approach to develop a more profound comprehension of students' interactions with academic advisors. The core purpose of this study is to evaluate assessments of advisors within the academic advising sphere and explore the demographic influences on students' sentiments and their evaluations. We employ sentiment analysis, a powerful artificial intelligence technique, to systematically assess the linguistic content of these reviews, thereby offering an impartial and practical evaluation of the academic advising process. By using statistical analyses, we performed word frequency analyses for both positive and negative expressions to provide valuable context to the language used in describing academic advisors. This comprehensive approach offered a nuanced understanding of the dynamics between students and their academic advisors, contributing to the ongoing development of academic advising services. 

The research presented in this paper was conducted within the INVEST European University (INnoVations of REgional Sustainability: European UniversiTy Alliance https://www.invest-alliance.eu/, accessed on 1 December 2023), which is an alliance that consists of five universities spread across Europe. This alliance allowed us to collect feedback and insights from students hailing from various European countries and academic backgrounds. By transcending the boundaries of a single institution, our research can offer a more comprehensive understanding of academic advising experiences, incorporating the multifaceted factors that shape students' perceptions and expectations.

citations.title: Learning Analytics Dashboards for Advisors - A Systematic Literature Review
snippets:
Learning analytics (LA) is an intelligent use of data that helps educators and advisors identify behavioural and study patterns in learners by processing, reporting, and working on their data to optimize the learning environment [1]. By exploiting the already available data extracted from the activity of the students at the distance learning platforms, Learning Analytics Dashboards (LAD) significantly impact the learning and teaching processes for different stakeholders [2]. Learning analytics offers new opportunities to enrich feedback practices in higher education [3], which influences student motivation. Advisor dashboards provide feedback to students by looking at their progress to improve their self-regulated learning [4]. 

Academic advising is a decision-making process that assists students in the clarification of their career and life goals and the development of an educational plan for the realization of these goals through communication and information exchanges with an advisor [5]. The key features and functionalities required for an advisor-focused LAD are centred around the early identification of at-risk students, personalized support strategies, integration with various data sources, predictive analytics capabilities, clear data visualization, and adherence to privacy and ethical guidelines [6]. The field of learning analytics is continuing to progress from initial scenarios of using data to predict which students are at risk of withdrawal or academic failure to more generic scenarios in which data are used to decide how best to improve the learning experience and academic outcomes of all students. The phrase closing the loop has been used to describe the need to connect actions (or interventions) back to the learners. Yet, this connection has not been sufficiently explored [7]. The rationale for this paper in the context of existing knowledge tries to explore that connection and fill the gap from the perspective of the advisors, as there is not so much data and work available on the dashboard for advisors. 

Considering this context, we conducted a literature review to understand the current state of the art in LAD for three different stakeholders: students, instructors, and advisors. As our interest relies on advisors, we then focused on analysing LAD for that specific kind of stakeholder. In this sense, our paper aims to answer the following research questions: RQ-1: What is the current state of the art related to LAD considering different stakeholders, such as students, instructors, and advisors?

The transition from secondary to higher education requires students to make crucial decisions regarding their areas of studies. Specifically, students matriculating into the A.
