citations.title: Investigating the Support Provided by Chatbots to Educational Institutions and Their Students: A Systematic Literature Review
snippets:
Apart from helping students gain specific knowledge, conversational agents can assist them in a variety of roles by supporting and helping them make decisions relevant to their academic future and responsibilities. In this section, 12 papers are being analyzed in order to examine these roles in further detail. 

The first important supportive role an educational chatbot can assume is that of an academic advisor. In this context, Wei et al. [79] implemented a CA that could support students in selecting the necessary optional academic subjects that would best fit their learning capabilities and liking, functioning as a course suggestion tool. Additionally, according to Bilquise and Shaalan [15], a chatbot could be used to support and provide academic advising services. In further detail, a CA could utilize students' data relevant to their academic progress and construct a suggestion for which courses a student should take. This suggestion could be handed to the academic advisor who supervises the specific student and who helps students organize their choices of academic courses. Moreover, a conversational bot can analyze a student's learning progress and conclude whether they are likely to fail some of their courses. Based on this function, the agent could update an academic advisor to reach the student or if that is not possible, inform the student directly, so the possibility of a student failing a course could be diminished, or even prevented from an early stage. Finally, the third capability of a conversational academic advisor, mentioned by the authors, is that it can respond to students' general questions relevant to the available studying programs and the provided curriculums. In a similar approach, Bilquise et al. [80] also implemented a conversational academic advisor. Specifically, their CA was able to express itself in English and in the local language and could answer students' questions relevant to the regulations and educational policies of the educational institution as well. Sweidan et al. [14] implemented a conversational system with many capabilities to support the students. The constructed CA was capable of tracking students' learning progress and helping them organize their course selection plan based on the courses they owed and their learning performance. Kuhail et al. [81] implemented a CA that could function also as an academic advisor. The proposed chatbot was capable of responding to students' questions relevant to the regulations and educational policies of the educational institution.

These adaptive systems offer distinct advantages including continuous availability, minimizing social barriers, and standardized information delivery [Hasal et al., 2021]. Implementing a chatbot alternative suggests a potential for enhanced accessibility to academic advising services, particularly for students who may be reluctant to engage with traditional advising.

sections.title: # Predictive Analytics and Early Warning
sections.text: Institutions use student data—LMS activity, course performance, placement and demographic attributes—to model risk of failure or attrition and to guide proactive advising on major and pathway decisions. Machine learning has been investigated to identify students at risk early during course progression; models based on course performance and academic history can predict risk as early as week six to enable early interventions [5d38afad-2] Reasonable machine learning performance for predicting course attrition has been shown by week 5–6 in prior work, motivating systems that integrate LMS and institutional data [5d38afad-2] Predictive analytics can create evidence-based profiles of student performance so advisors can proactively guide major and course pathway decisions to improve degree attainment and field-specific success [5d38afad-1]. Reviews synthesize that early warning and risk prediction are now common, but emphasize the need to connect interventions back to outcomes (“closing the loop”). The field is progressing from predicting risk to using data to decide how to improve learning and academic outcomes, yet the connection between actions/interventions and learner outcomes (closing the loop) has been insufficiently explored [5d38afad-0].

citations.title: AI-based Academic Advising Framework: A Knowledge Management Perspective
snippets:
Machine learning algorithms have been investigated in numerous studies to identify students at risk at an early stage during course progression. Some studies relied on LMS click patterns to predict low-performing students [26]- [28]. LMS interaction requires interacting with the course content online, which in turn generates a click pattern that can be analyzed for student engagement within the course. This model is not appropriate for the institution of the study, as most of the courses are face-to-face. Students mainly use the online environment to download course resources, attend online sessions, or submit assessments. Click patterns would not be an ideal indicator of student engagement especially when the student is using the course resources offline. To this effect, this study proposes the use of course performance data and student academic history to predict the risk of failing a course. The proposed system will be used to low performing students as early as week six so early intervention strategies can be engaged. Howard et al. (2018) showed that reasonable machine learning performance can be achieved at week 5-6 to predict course attrition. Fig. 5 shows the architecture of the proposed advising system. 

The system integrates LMS data and institutional data to build a machine learning model. The main elements of the system are explained in three stages: 

1) Build and deploy the machine learning model: In this stage data historical is extracted from the institutional database and the LMS at the beginning of the academic year. The institutional database contains the following data: 

 Students enrollment records that include the high school score, IELTS score, placement test scores, gender and status (working or not), and other profiling information  Academic data such as program of study, credit hours completed, credit hours registered, courses completed, overall GPA, and attendance record. 

LMS Data contains the coursework assessment data. Coursework assessments are usually conducted at regular intervalsweek 6, week 12, week 15. The final assessment is scheduled on week 16. www.ijacsa.thesai.org 

In stage 1, the machine learning model is developed using historical data of the last 4-5 years. The data will be preprocessed and used for training and testing multiple machine learning algorithms. Several machine learning algorithms will be used and evaluated to determine the best performing algorithm suited for the data provided.

citations.title: The Use of Predictive Analytics to Shift the Culture of Academic Advising Toward a Focus on Student Success
snippets: This paper explores the use of data through a predictive analytical approach to shift the current culture of academic advising from one of compliance to one that focuses on student learning and success in all areas of an educational experience.As educational institutions demonstrate an ever-increasing reliance on the use of data to make evidence-based decisions, the use of much of the same data can be used to develop an evidence-based profile of student performance. Advisors using analytics can predict future outcomes and proactively guide students to make betterdecisions regarding their selection of an academic major or coursework pathways, improving a student’s likelihood of attaining a degree and consequent success in a given field. Due to the technological advances in the areas of educational data mining and the use of analytics, the capacity to guide students using rational, evidence-based information is now a possibility. This paper sets the stage for the use of predictive analytics that can influence a cultural shift in academic advising while offering caution that educational institutions must assess the quality of the data decisions that are being made.

citations.title: Learning Analytics Dashboards for Advisors - A Systematic Literature Review
snippets:
Learning analytics (LA) is an intelligent use of data that helps educators and advisors identify behavioural and study patterns in learners by processing, reporting, and working on their data to optimize the learning environment [1]. By exploiting the already available data extracted from the activity of the students at the distance learning platforms, Learning Analytics Dashboards (LAD) significantly impact the learning and teaching processes for different stakeholders [2]. Learning analytics offers new opportunities to enrich feedback practices in higher education [3], which influences student motivation. Advisor dashboards provide feedback to students by looking at their progress to improve their self-regulated learning [4]. 

Academic advising is a decision-making process that assists students in the clarification of their career and life goals and the development of an educational plan for the realization of these goals through communication and information exchanges with an advisor [5]. The key features and functionalities required for an advisor-focused LAD are centred around the early identification of at-risk students, personalized support strategies, integration with various data sources, predictive analytics capabilities, clear data visualization, and adherence to privacy and ethical guidelines [6]. The field of learning analytics is continuing to progress from initial scenarios of using data to predict which students are at risk of withdrawal or academic failure to more generic scenarios in which data are used to decide how best to improve the learning experience and academic outcomes of all students. The phrase closing the loop has been used to describe the need to connect actions (or interventions) back to the learners. Yet, this connection has not been sufficiently explored [7]. The rationale for this paper in the context of existing knowledge tries to explore that connection and fill the gap from the perspective of the advisors, as there is not so much data and work available on the dashboard for advisors. 

Considering this context, we conducted a literature review to understand the current state of the art in LAD for three different stakeholders: students, instructors, and advisors. As our interest relies on advisors, we then focused on analysing LAD for that specific kind of stakeholder. In this sense, our paper aims to answer the following research questions: RQ-1: What is the current state of the art related to LAD considering different stakeholders, such as students, instructors, and advisors?

sections.title: # Dashboards and Data Integration for Advisors
sections.text: Learning analytics dashboards tailored to advisors surface at-risk indicators, student profiles, and intervention suggestions, often integrating LMS and institutional data with visualization and personalization features to support decision-making and communication. Advisor-focused dashboards highlight early identification of at-risk students, personalized strategies, integration with multiple data sources, predictive analytics, clear visualization, and adherence to privacy and ethical guidelines [5d38afad-0] Predictive analytics in advisor dashboards identify at-risk students, provide comprehensive student profiles and intervention recommendations, and include communication tools to foster interactions; explainability and interactive features are emphasized to build trust and address legal and ethical concerns [5d38afad-3] Examples include LISSA to promote data-driven advisor–student discussions and models inspired by Early Warning Systems and GPS advising in Latin American universities [5d38afad-3]. Practical guidance notes technological, institutional, and individual adoption barriers alongside promising practices for using analytics in teaching and advising. Learning and advising management systems based on educational big data can generate insights and feedback for data-informed decision making, but adoption is hindered by challenges that require practical strategies and considerations [5d38afad-4].

citations.title: Learning Analytics Dashboards for Advisors - A Systematic Literature Review
snippets:
What key features and functionalities were identified in a learning analytics dashboard for advisors to provide better advising options to students? 

In our current exploration, we delve into the key features and functionalities identified in Learning Analytics Dashboards (LADs) designed to empower advisors in providing effective support and data-informed decisions to students. These dedicated dashboards, tailored for advisors, significantly enhance the academic advising process through a range of essential features. Notably, predictive analytics take centre stage, enabling the identification of at-risk students and the timely initiation of interventions. These dashboards provide comprehensive student profiles, offer valuable intervention recommendations, and equip advisors with communication tools to foster meaningful interactions. Usability, characterized by a user-friendly design, and transparency in predictive algorithms are considered fundamental aspects of these tools. Personalization features empower advisors to tailor guidance to the unique needs of individual students, while feedback mechanisms facilitate seamless interaction. Furthermore, integration with Learning Management Systems ensures the synchronization of data, and scalability is a key consideration to accommodate growing student populations. Beyond these general features, specific research papers highlight innovative approaches in the field. For instance, LISSA promotes data-driven discussions between advisors and students [19], while Latin American universities draw inspiration from models such as the Early Warning System (EWS) and GPS advising to explore academic advising dashboards that employ descriptive and predictive analytics. Additionally, research underscores the importance of interactive and explainable dashboards to enhance user trust and address the legal and ethical concerns associated with predictive models in higher education. Collectively, these findings shape the evolving landscape of Learning Analytics Dashboards for advisors.

citations.title: Using Predictive Analytics in Teaching and Advising: Promising Practices and Practical Considerations
snippets: Higher education institutions are facing increasing pressure to provide evidence of student learning; teaching pedagogical best practices are moving to an increasingly individualized and student-focused learning model; and innovative technologies are allowing for greater mining of student data. Within this environment, learning and advising management systems, based on educational big data, or learning analytics, are being developed to better measure, analyze, report and predict data related to student learning, retention and completion. These learning analytics-informed systems have the potential to generate new insight into courses and student learning by creating responsive feedback mechanisms that can shape data-informed decision making as it relates to teaching, learning and advising. Despite the benefits of using learning analytics-informed learning and advising management systems, there are barriers and challenges related to broad adoption and use of innovations like these systems in higher education.In the summer of 2015, we conducted an instrumental case study to learn more about the technological, institutional, and individual factors related to adoption and use of learning analytics-informed educational technology tools on campus.AÂ  In this short lightning talk, we will present the findings from the studyA¢â¬â¢s focus group interviews and observations.AÂ  Further, we will share promising practices and practical considerations related to use of learning analytics tools to measure and predict academic performance.

sections.title: # Degree Planning and Expert Systems
sections.text: Rule-based engines and expert systems support long-term academic planning, course selection recommendations, and scholarship eligibility, sometimes embedded in web-based advising kits where students construct plans while systems resolve conflicts and suggest feasible schedules. A planning engine (Tarot) develops long-term academic plans and answers questions about maximum course load, GPA, optimal course timing, and resource constraints [e1f8fb30-2] Web-based systems select “next course to take” using student inputs, preferences, requirements, and availability; knowledge bases encode program rules, and clustering can classify student profiles to speed advisor comparisons [e1f8fb30-3] A knowledge-based advising kit (KRAK) enables student-driven degree planning and semester scheduling, collecting program requirements and course/faculty information, and resolving schedule conflicts without a hidden decision algorithm [e1f8fb30-3] Expert systems have also been implemented for course and scholarship recommendations based on eligibility [e1f8fb30-2].

citations.title: From Traditional to Intelligent Academic Advising: A Systematic Literature Review of e-Academic Advising
snippets:
Also, it facilitates decision making about the next courses' enrolment process. Author in [11] proposed an intelligent automated advising system using the bot framework. The system is implemented using both agent and object-oriented approaches. It supports students and assists the advising process by making fast and easy access to useful information and helps in considering some academic issues that usually take considerable time. The system splits into database as a backend, AdvisorBot as a front agent, Knowledge Base, and Cognitive module. The designed chatbot is able to answer students' questions about academic performance, courses, and future career. Author in [12] also proposed a chatbot for Hong Kong Open University students. It provides the student with courses information, it collects students' opinions, and provides a recommendation. The chatbot is applied on the telegram as a communication medium. The designed chatbot provides a description of the courses by suggesting the course website or booklet to the student. 

Authors in [13] proposed an early warning system that is used to identify at-risk students and notify advisors about them to prevent student dropout. The system also accurately predicts student dropout risk and delivers it with student performance information and some background to the advisor on a weekly basis. In this way, the system increases the meeting quality between student and advisor. The system is implemented by using machine learning techniques (Logistic Model (LM), the Additive Logistic Model (ALM), the Support Vector Machines (SVM) model, and the Random Forest (RF) Algorithm.). 

Author in [14] represented two educational expert systems used to recommend the courses and scholarships based on the student's eligibility. The scholarship recommendation system is the first proposed system of this type. Both expert systems are implemented and tested by the Oracle Policy Automation (OPA) software. 

Author in [15] proposed a new system called Tarot. The system consists of a planning engine designed for course advising. The system is able to develop a long-term academic plan, it also handles a variety of questions about some present and future matters such as: maximum course load, student GBA, the best time to take a certain course and the minimum number of teachers needed to cover possible registered courses. The system was implemented using Prolog with complex constraints and rules.

snippets:
The advisory session is recorded in order to identify the main phrases and information used during that process and then encoded using Artificial Intelligence Markup Language along with the dialog system (implemented in Python). The usage of natural language, for the purpose, is also suggested, by Latorre-Navarro and Harris [21], to facilitate students to get advice and interact with the system. A crucial component of this intelligent advising system is the knowledge base that encompasses the electrical and the computer engineering program requirements of Florida University. Under the context of intelligent advising platforms, Gavriushenko et al. [22] advocated the use of a clustering technique to classify students' profiles and to identify similar cases that may be compared by academic advisors to speed-up this advising process. 

Machine learning techniques are helpful to develop intelligent prototype academic advising systems as pointed out in reference [12]. Hsu et al. [23] proposed a Web-based academic advising system for undergraduate programs (computer science and civil engineering) at Florida Atlantic University. They focused on the selection of the "next course to take" option which allows a student to input information related to all courses already taken in order to get a list of courses for selection in the following semester. The selection is based on students' preferences, course requirements and their availability. The system relies on students' inputs which can be improved by just inputting their university ID and, thus, minimizing errors. 

Ozturan and Ayan [24] recommended a simple advising framework for management information system students at Bo gaziçi University, where the system generates a list of suggested courses, considering the status of students. sections.title: # NLP to Understand and Improve Advising Quality
sections.text: NLP and sentiment analysis are being applied to student reviews of advisors to extract patterns, quantify satisfaction, and relate perceptions to demographic factors, informing professional development and service improvement. NLP sentiment analysis provides an impartial, scalable evaluation of student feedback on advising, offering insights into student–advisor dynamics across multiple universities [fbef8d17-0] Across 1,151 reviews, advisor age and traits (empathy, approachability, effectiveness) were associated with review sentiment; younger advisors received more favorable evaluations, and positive reviews emphasized support for academic goals [fbef8d17-2] This first-known NLP study of advisor reviews highlights the importance of managing expectations and enhancing advisor skills to foster positive interactions and academic success [fbef8d17-3]. Beyond reviews, conversational systems use NLP to assist with multiple advising tasks, continuously learning to improve responses and planning support. An intelligent conversational advising system combines NLP, a knowledge base, expert planning, and a web platform, demonstrating viability in a real-world deployment and initiating a corpus for advising research [e1f8fb30-4].

citations.title: Investigating the Support Provided by Chatbots to Educational Institutions and Their Students: A Systematic Literature Review
snippets:
Apart from helping students gain specific knowledge, conversational agents can assist them in a variety of roles by supporting and helping them make decisions relevant to their academic future and responsibilities. In this section, 12 papers are being analyzed in order to examine these roles in further detail. 

The first important supportive role an educational chatbot can assume is that of an academic advisor. In this context, Wei et al. [79] implemented a CA that could support students in selecting the necessary optional academic subjects that would best fit their learning capabilities and liking, functioning as a course suggestion tool. Additionally, according to Bilquise and Shaalan [15], a chatbot could be used to support and provide academic advising services. In further detail, a CA could utilize students' data relevant to their academic progress and construct a suggestion for which courses a student should take. This suggestion could be handed to the academic advisor who supervises the specific student and who helps students organize their choices of academic courses. Moreover, a conversational bot can analyze a student's learning progress and conclude whether they are likely to fail some of their courses. Based on this function, the agent could update an academic advisor to reach the student or if that is not possible, inform the student directly, so the possibility of a student failing a course could be diminished, or even prevented from an early stage. Finally, the third capability of a conversational academic advisor, mentioned by the authors, is that it can respond to students' general questions relevant to the available studying programs and the provided curriculums. In a similar approach, Bilquise et al. [80] also implemented a conversational academic advisor. Specifically, their CA was able to express itself in English and in the local language and could answer students' questions relevant to the regulations and educational policies of the educational institution as well. Sweidan et al. [14] implemented a conversational system with many capabilities to support the students. The constructed CA was capable of tracking students' learning progress and helping them organize their course selection plan based on the courses they owed and their learning performance. Kuhail et al. [81] implemented a CA that could function also as an academic advisor. The proposed chatbot was capable of responding to students' questions relevant to the regulations and educational policies of the educational institution.

citations.title: Elevating Academic Advising: Natural Language Processing of Student Reviews
snippets:
Academic advising is a program or initiative employed within educational systems to offer students guidance and counsel [1]. It is widely respected and extensively employed to support students in educational institutions around the world [2]. The field of academic advising, as a student support service, has undergone significant transformation in recent years, paralleling the broader evolution within the educational landscape. In the realm of higher education, universities have made significant strides in implementing comprehensive evaluation processes for various educational aspects. These include the evaluation of teachers' performance, assessment of academic programs of study, appraisal of administrative services, and even the scrutiny of extracurricular activities and student support services. However, this progress rarely extends to academic advising [3]. Unlike the robust evaluation mechanisms in place for many academic processes, the assessment of academic advising performance remains relatively unexplored. 

In this paper, we utilize natural language processing methods for a quantitative examination of student feedback in an effective and streamlined approach to develop a more profound comprehension of students' interactions with academic advisors. The core purpose of this study is to evaluate assessments of advisors within the academic advising sphere and explore the demographic influences on students' sentiments and their evaluations. We employ sentiment analysis, a powerful artificial intelligence technique, to systematically assess the linguistic content of these reviews, thereby offering an impartial and practical evaluation of the academic advising process. By using statistical analyses, we performed word frequency analyses for both positive and negative expressions to provide valuable context to the language used in describing academic advisors. This comprehensive approach offered a nuanced understanding of the dynamics between students and their academic advisors, contributing to the ongoing development of academic advising services. 

The research presented in this paper was conducted within the INVEST European University (INnoVations of REgional Sustainability: European UniversiTy Alliance https://www.invest-alliance.eu/, accessed on 1 December 2023), which is an alliance that consists of five universities spread across Europe. This alliance allowed us to collect feedback and insights from students hailing from various European countries and academic backgrounds. By transcending the boundaries of a single institution, our research can offer a more comprehensive understanding of academic advising experiences, incorporating the multifaceted factors that shape students' perceptions and expectations.

citations.title: Elevating Academic Advising: Natural Language Processing of Student Reviews
snippets: Academic advising is often pivotal in shaping students’ educational experiences and choices. This study leverages natural language processing to quantitatively evaluate reviews of academic advisors, aiming to provide actionable insights on key feedback phrases and demographic factors for enhancing advising services. This analysis encompassed a comprehensive evaluation of 1151 reviews of undergraduate students for academic advisors, which were collected within a European University alliance consisting of five universities, offering a diverse pool of feedback from a wide range of academic interactions. Employing sentiment analysis powered by artificial intelligence, we computed compound sentiment scores for each academic advisor’s reviews. Subsequently, statistical analyses were conducted to provide insights into how demographic factors may or may not influence students’ sentiment and evaluations of academic advisory services. The results indicated that advisor’s gender had no substantial influence on the sentiment of the reviews. On the contrary, the academic advisors’ age showed a notable impact, with younger advisors surprisingly receiving more favorable evaluations. Word frequency analyses, both for positive and negative expressions, were also performed to contextualize the language used in describing academic advisors. The prevalent word combinations in reviews of highly rated academic advisors emphasized attributes like empathy, approachability, and effectiveness in guiding students towards achieving their academic goals. Conversely, advisors with less favorable reviews were often perceived as inadequate in addressing students’ concerns related to their academic journey, revealing persistent challenges in the student–advisor interaction that impacted their evaluation. This analysis of academic advisor reviews contributes to the body of literature by highlighting the significance of managing student expectations and enhancing advisor skills and qualities to foster positive interactions and academic success.

citations.title: Elevating Academic Advising: Natural Language Processing of Student Reviews
snippets:
In this study, we utilized sentiment analysis to quantitatively evaluate reviews of academic advisors, aiming to provide actionable insights for enhancing academic advising services. This study primarily focused on academic advisors within the context of a European University alliance, thus aiming to attain a more extensive dataset that encompasses a broader spectrum of student experiences. Our analysis revealed that advisor characteristics, particularly age and specific traits like empathy, knowledgeability, approachability, and the ability to provide academic support toward academic goals, significantly influence the positivity or negativity of student ratings and reviews. This study is, to our knowledge, the first to employ natural language processing to gain insights into how academic advisors are portrayed by their students. 

This work underscores the importance of evaluating academic advising processes in higher education. It not only identifies key elements that influence student perceptions but also offers a concrete AI method for assessing and improving academic advising services. By shedding light on the dynamics between academic advisors and students, this study contributes to the ongoing development of academic advising and highlights the path to more effective and student-centered educational experiences. 

Institutional Review Board Statement: The INVEST project, supported by ERASMUS+ and H2020, has developed the "INVEST4EXCELLENCE Open Science Code", which serves as a comprehensive framework for ethical research practices, transparency, and collaboration. Our research is aligned with these principles. 

Informed Consent Statement: Informed consent was obtained from all subjects involved in the study.

sections.title: # Implementation and Integration

citations.title: AI-based Academic Advising Framework: A Knowledge Management Perspective
snippets:
Machine learning algorithms have been investigated in numerous studies to identify students at risk at an early stage during course progression. Some studies relied on LMS click patterns to predict low-performing students [26]- [28]. LMS interaction requires interacting with the course content online, which in turn generates a click pattern that can be analyzed for student engagement within the course. This model is not appropriate for the institution of the study, as most of the courses are face-to-face. Students mainly use the online environment to download course resources, attend online sessions, or submit assessments. Click patterns would not be an ideal indicator of student engagement especially when the student is using the course resources offline. To this effect, this study proposes the use of course performance data and student academic history to predict the risk of failing a course. The proposed system will be used to low performing students as early as week six so early intervention strategies can be engaged. Howard et al. (2018) showed that reasonable machine learning performance can be achieved at week 5-6 to predict course attrition. Fig. 5 shows the architecture of the proposed advising system.

LMS Data contains the coursework assessment data. Coursework assessments are usually conducted at regular intervalsweek 6, week 12, week 15. The final assessment is scheduled on week 16. www.ijacsa.thesai.org

citations.title: Learning Analytics Dashboards for Advisors - A Systematic Literature Review
snippets:
What key features and functionalities were identified in a learning analytics dashboard for advisors to provide better advising options to students? 

In our current exploration, we delve into the key features and functionalities identified in Learning Analytics Dashboards (LADs) designed to empower advisors in providing effective support and data-informed decisions to students. These dedicated dashboards, tailored for advisors, significantly enhance the academic advising process through a range of essential features. Notably, predictive analytics take centre stage, enabling the identification of at-risk students and the timely initiation of interventions. These dashboards provide comprehensive student profiles, offer valuable intervention recommendations, and equip advisors with communication tools to foster meaningful interactions. Usability, characterized by a user-friendly design, and transparency in predictive algorithms are considered fundamental aspects of these tools. Personalization features empower advisors to tailor guidance to the unique needs of individual students, while feedback mechanisms facilitate seamless interaction. Furthermore, integration with Learning Management Systems ensures the synchronization of data, and scalability is a key consideration to accommodate growing student populations. Beyond these general features, specific research papers highlight innovative approaches in the field. For instance, LISSA promotes data-driven discussions between advisors and students [19], while Latin American universities draw inspiration from models such as the Early Warning System (EWS) and GPS advising to explore academic advising dashboards that employ descriptive and predictive analytics. Additionally, research underscores the importance of interactive and explainable dashboards to enhance user trust and address the legal and ethical concerns associated with predictive models in higher education. Collectively, these findings shape the evolving landscape of Learning Analytics Dashboards for advisors.

citations.title: Learning Analytics Dashboards for Advisors - A Systematic Literature Review
snippets:
Learning analytics (LA) is an intelligent use of data that helps educators and advisors identify behavioural and study patterns in learners by processing, reporting, and working on their data to optimize the learning environment [1]. By exploiting the already available data extracted from the activity of the students at the distance learning platforms, Learning Analytics Dashboards (LAD) significantly impact the learning and teaching processes for different stakeholders [2]. Learning analytics offers new opportunities to enrich feedback practices in higher education [3], which influences student motivation. Advisor dashboards provide feedback to students by looking at their progress to improve their self-regulated learning [4]. 

Academic advising is a decision-making process that assists students in the clarification of their career and life goals and the development of an educational plan for the realization of these goals through communication and information exchanges with an advisor [5]. The key features and functionalities required for an advisor-focused LAD are centred around the early identification of at-risk students, personalized support strategies, integration with various data sources, predictive analytics capabilities, clear data visualization, and adherence to privacy and ethical guidelines [6]. The field of learning analytics is continuing to progress from initial scenarios of using data to predict which students are at risk of withdrawal or academic failure to more generic scenarios in which data are used to decide how best to improve the learning experience and academic outcomes of all students. The phrase closing the loop has been used to describe the need to connect actions (or interventions) back to the learners. Yet, this connection has not been sufficiently explored [7]. The rationale for this paper in the context of existing knowledge tries to explore that connection and fill the gap from the perspective of the advisors, as there is not so much data and work available on the dashboard for advisors. 

Considering this context, we conducted a literature review to understand the current state of the art in LAD for three different stakeholders: students, instructors, and advisors. As our interest relies on advisors, we then focused on analysing LAD for that specific kind of stakeholder. In this sense, our paper aims to answer the following research questions: RQ-1: What is the current state of the art related to LAD considering different stakeholders, such as students, instructors, and advisors?

sections.title: # Challenges and Cautions
sections.text: Reviews and frameworks emphasize fairness, privacy, transparency, and the need to “close the loop” by linking analytics to outcomes and maintaining human oversight in advising decisions. Learning analytics advances move from predicting risk to deciding best practices for improving outcomes, but the field still needs to better connect interventions to learner outcomes (closing the loop) [5d38afad-0] Advisor dashboards must adhere to privacy and ethical guidelines, with clear visualization and responsible data use [5d38afad-0] Institutions should assess the quality of data and decisions when adopting predictive analytics to avoid shifting from compliance-focused to harmful practices [5d38afad-1]. Practical deployment faces technological and institutional barriers, including data integration complexity, adoption by staff and students, and ensuring that automation complements rather than replaces essential human advising relationships. Despite potential benefits, barriers to broad adoption exist, requiring promising practices and practical considerations for learning analytics tools to measure and predict academic performance [5d38afad-4].

sections.title: # What’s Emerging and Open Questions
sections.text: Recent work explores advisor-specific dashboards inspired by early warning and GPS advising models, and NLP methods tailored to advising evaluation and support, but more rigorous outcome evaluations and standardized ethics-by-design practices are needed. citations.title: Elevating Academic Advising: Natural Language Processing of Student Reviews
snippets:
Academic advising is a program or initiative employed within educational systems to offer students guidance and counsel [1]. It is widely respected and extensively employed to support students in educational institutions around the world [2]. The field of academic advising, as a student support service, has undergone significant transformation in recent years, paralleling the broader evolution within the educational landscape. In the realm of higher education, universities have made significant strides in implementing comprehensive evaluation processes for various educational aspects. These include the evaluation of teachers' performance, assessment of academic programs of study, appraisal of administrative services, and even the scrutiny of extracurricular activities and student support services. However, this progress rarely extends to academic advising [3]. Unlike the robust evaluation mechanisms in place for many academic processes, the assessment of academic advising performance remains relatively unexplored. 

In this paper, we utilize natural language processing methods for a quantitative examination of student feedback in an effective and streamlined approach to develop a more profound comprehension of students' interactions with academic advisors. The core purpose of this study is to evaluate assessments of advisors within the academic advising sphere and explore the demographic influences on students' sentiments and their evaluations. We employ sentiment analysis, a powerful artificial intelligence technique, to systematically assess the linguistic content of these reviews, thereby offering an impartial and practical evaluation of the academic advising process. By using statistical analyses, we performed word frequency analyses for both positive and negative expressions to provide valuable context to the language used in describing academic advisors. This comprehensive approach offered a nuanced understanding of the dynamics between students and their academic advisors, contributing to the ongoing development of academic advising services. 

The research presented in this paper was conducted within the INVEST European University (INnoVations of REgional Sustainability: European UniversiTy Alliance https://www.invest-alliance.eu/, accessed on 1 December 2023), which is an alliance that consists of five universities spread across Europe. This alliance allowed us to collect feedback and insights from students hailing from various European countries and academic backgrounds. By transcending the boundaries of a single institution, our research can offer a more comprehensive understanding of academic advising experiences, incorporating the multifaceted factors that shape students' perceptions and expectations.

sections.title: # Practical Takeaways for Adoption
sections.text:
- Start with clear goals: extend access via chatbots, reduce advising load via automation, and proactively identify risk via early warning, ensuring analytics directly inform advisor actions and are evaluated for impact. Chatbots extend access by offering 24/7 availability and reducing intimidation [e1f8fb30-0] Dashboards and early warning systems enable timely, personalized interventions when integrated with advisor workflows [5d38afad-3] Closing the loop and evaluating outcomes remains a key gap to address [5d38afad-0].
- Invest in data quality and governance, explainable models, and privacy protections; co-design tools with advisors and students to ensure usability and trust. Privacy and ethical guidelines must be embedded in advisor dashboards and analytics practices [5d38afad-0] Explainable and interactive dashboards enhance user trust and address legal and ethical concerns [5d38afad-3].
- Combine rule-based planning and expert systems with learning analytics to provide accurate, constraint-aware degree plans and eligibility guidance while surfacing equity considerations in recommendations. Planning engines and expert systems operationalize constraints for long-term plans and eligibility recommendations [e1f8fb30-2] Risk models should be validated in context and aligned with program-specific data and LMS signals [5d38afad-2].

In sum, AI is being used in academic advising to broaden access through conversational agents, to detect and mitigate risk via predictive analytics, to streamline planning and scholarship guidance through expert systems, and to understand and improve advising quality with NLP; institutions are encouraged to integrate these tools within ethical, explainable, and human-centered workflows and to rigorously evaluate whether analytics translate into improved student outcomes. Chatbots enhance accessibility and standardize information delivery [e1f8fb30-0] Predictive models using institutional and LMS data can support early intervention and personalized guidance [5d38afad-2] Expert planning and scholarship recommendation systems operationalize complex rules [e1f8fb30-2] NLP analyses reveal advisor traits and practices associated with higher satisfaction and can guide professional development [fbef8d17-2] Adopting analytics responsibly requires privacy, ethics, and closing the loop on interventions [5d38afad-0].

citations.title: Bias-Aware AI Chatbot for Engineering Advising at the University of Maryland A. James Clark School of Engineering
snippets:
The transition from secondary to higher education requires students to make crucial decisions regarding their areas of studies. Specifically, students matriculating into the A. James Clark School of Engineering must choose from 22 programs. UMD's traditional college advising system provides necessary guidance to students during these decisions. Yet the current system exhibits notable limitations: appointment wait times, intimidating formal environments, and reduced information retention, all of which create barriers to academic guidance [Fox, 2022]. 

Artificial intelligence (AI) chatbots have proven complementary tools to address the accessibility limitations in traditional advising, academic or otherwise. These adaptive systems offer distinct advantages including continuous availability, minimizing social barriers, and standardized information delivery [Hasal et al., 2021]. Implementing a chatbot alternative suggests a potential for enhanced accessibility to academic advising services, particularly for students who may be reluctant to engage with traditional advising.

snippets:
Also, it facilitates decision making about the next courses' enrolment process. Author in [11] proposed an intelligent automated advising system using the bot framework. The system is implemented using both agent and object-oriented approaches. It supports students and assists the advising process by making fast and easy access to useful information and helps in considering some academic issues that usually take considerable time. The system splits into database as a backend, AdvisorBot as a front agent, Knowledge Base, and Cognitive module. In this way, the system increases the meeting quality between student and advisor. The system is implemented by using machine learning techniques (Logistic Model (LM), the Additive Logistic Model (ALM), the Support Vector Machines (SVM) model, and the Random Forest (RF) Algorithm.). 

Author in [14] represented two educational expert systems used to recommend the courses and scholarships based on the student's eligibility. The scholarship recommendation system is the first proposed system of this type. Both expert systems are implemented and tested by the Oracle Policy Automation (OPA) software.

citations.title: Elevating Academic Advising: Natural Language Processing of Student Reviews
snippets: Academic advising is often pivotal in shaping students’ educational experiences and choices. This study leverages natural language processing to quantitatively evaluate reviews of academic advisors, aiming to provide actionable insights on key feedback phrases and demographic factors for enhancing advising services. This analysis encompassed a comprehensive evaluation of 1151 reviews of undergraduate students for academic advisors, which were collected within a European University alliance consisting of five universities, offering a diverse pool of feedback from a wide range of academic interactions. Employing sentiment analysis powered by artificial intelligence, we computed compound sentiment scores for each academic advisor’s reviews. Subsequently, statistical analyses were conducted to provide insights into how demographic factors may or may not influence students’ sentiment and evaluations of academic advisory services. The results indicated that advisor’s gender had no substantial influence on the sentiment of the reviews. On the contrary, the academic advisors’ age showed a notable impact, with younger advisors surprisingly receiving more favorable evaluations. Word frequency analyses, both for positive and negative expressions, were also performed to contextualize the language used in describing academic advisors. The prevalent word combinations in reviews of highly rated academic advisors emphasized attributes like empathy, approachability, and effectiveness in guiding students towards achieving their academic goals. Conversely, advisors with less favorable reviews were often perceived as inadequate in addressing students’ concerns related to their academic journey, revealing persistent challenges in the student–advisor interaction that impacted their evaluation. This analysis of academic advisor reviews contributes to the body of literature by highlighting the significance of managing student expectations and enhancing advisor skills and qualities to foster positive interactions and academic success.

question: Are there any articles focusing on the use of attention mechanisms in ranking? Where the weights generated by the attention mechanism are fused as weights for the base ranking?

sections.text: Yes. There is a substantial body of work in information retrieval and ranking that uses attention mechanisms and explicitly fuses the attention weights with base ranking components (e.g., embeddings, features, or signals) to compute the final relevance scores or rankings. Below are representative lines of work and how they fuse attention weights with base ranking mechanisms.

sections.title: # What “attention in ranking” looks like and why it’s used
sections.text:
- Surveys of neural ranking explicitly categorize models “by attention,” i.e., models that introduce attention mechanisms to interact with or fuse latent/semantic representations, preserve token order, or share weights across query and document encoders; this confirms attention is a first-class design pattern in modern ranking systems rather than a niche gimmick Attention is one of the core dimensions used to characterize neural ranking models [c6f917c0-2]. 
- In many ranking settings, attention is used as a listwise or feature-level fusion operator: compute attention weights over a set of inputs (e.g., items, tokens, modalities), then combine those weights with base representations or scores (e.g., via weighted sums or element-wise interactions) to produce a unified ranking signal Attention mechanism, as a listwise approach, is designed for explicitly capturing inter-item relationships [aebd24d8-2].

In other words, for a given query and document, there are no special computations that are applied only to the query or document. 2. snippets: Learning to Rank (LTR) has been extensively studied in search and recommendation systems, and existing methods generally fall into three paradigms: pointwise, pairwise, and listwise. Pointwise approaches [7] treat ranking as a regression or classification task, predicting each item's relevance independently. Pairwise methods [3,16] optimize relative preferences by training on positive-negative item pairs, improving discriminative capability. Listwise approaches further consider the entire ranking list, optimizing list-level metrics and modeling item dependencies more effectively. Attention mechanism, as a listwise approach, is designed for explicitly capturing inter-item relationships. Pobrotyn et al. [14] introduced a context-aware listwise model using self-attention to model pairwise interactions within a candidate list. To address this, we propose Cross-Attention-Rank, which incorporates the user features via cross-attention, aligning user embeddings with item features for personalized ranking.

sections.title: # Representative models where attention weights are fused with base ranking components
sections.text:
1) Attention over embeddings with listwise decoding (end-to-end ranking)
- An attention-based deep neural network for learning to rank models learn embeddings for queries and items (from CNNs or word2vec), then apply an attention-based mechanism to incorporate different embeddings, followed by a decoder to learn ranks in a listwise fashion; this is a direct example of using attention weights to combine base embedding signals for ranking An attention-based deep neural network incorporates different embeddings of queries and search results with an attention-based mechanism and applies a decoder to learn ranks listwise [d88723cb-4]. 
- Broader surveys describe two common patterns: (a) symmetric architectures where separate Q and D encoders attend to compute a relevance feature, and (b) ordered-tokens designs where pairwise token interactions are aggregated into a global representation—both rely on attention weights fusing per-element signals into a relevance score Neural ranking architectures are categorized by whether they use attention, whether they preserve token order, and whether they share weights between query and document [c6f917c0-2].

2) Token/field/passage-level attention to form global importance weights
- In document or passage ranking, attention can be applied hierarchically: compute local attention over tokens relative to a query term, and then attention over query terms to obtain a global passage-level importance weight by fusing the local attentions (e.g., via a product), which is then used to rank passages An attention-based deep neural network incorporates different embeddings of queries and search results with an attention-based mechanism and applies a decoder to learn ranks listwise [d88723cb-4] In joint attention, similarity scores between modalities are combined with a weighted attention mechanism to achieve effective fusion of information [d88723cb-0]. 
- A concrete passage ranking/QA example uses two attention mechanisms: local passage attention per query term and term-level attention; the global attention weight for each passage is obtained by the product of these two attention weights, which directly fuses attention coefficients to determine the passage’s contribution to the final ranking signal A global attention weight for each passage can be obtained from the product of local passage attention and term importance, a g (k,i)=a u k ×a pi [d88723cb-0].

3) Multi-signal or multimodal fusion with attention weights
- In joint semantic and relevance matching, attention can fuse heterogeneous signals (e.g., semantic similarity and relevance features) into a unified ranking feature; the attention weights learn how to blend these components per query-document pair A joint model overview shows how semantic and relevance matching features can be integrated; attention is one dimension that characterizes such designs [c6f917c0-2]. 
- Multimodal transformer rankers use joint attention to compute similarity between features across modalities and then combine these with a weighted attention mechanism to achieve effective cross-modal fusion; the learned feature-level attention weights control how strongly each modality contributes to the fused representation used for ranking In joint attention, similarity scores between features of each modality are combined with a weighted attention mechanism to achieve effective fusion of information from different modalities; feature weights of each modality are learned [d88723cb-0]. 
- More generally, scaled-dot product attention defines attention weights A over queries and keys, and the output features are the weighted summation of values; this pattern is directly applicable to ranking by fusing attention weights with base latent representations to form a unified relevance vector or score Scaled dot-product attention computes attention weights and outputs features as weighted summations of values [aebd24d8-2].

4) Attention to personalize or gate base ranking signals
- In personalized ranking, cross-attention between user and item spaces can be used to align user embeddings with item features; the attention weights from this cross-attention then modulate how base item representations contribute to the final prediction, effectively fusing user-specific importance with the base ranking signal Cross-attention aligns user embeddings with item features for personalized ranking [aebd24d8-2]. 
- In listwise attention variants, self-attention over a candidate list is used to model pairwise interactions and inter-item dependencies; these attention weights can be used to fuse base scores (e.g., pointwise relevance or embeddings) into a listwise ranking that respects item interactions A context-aware listwise model using self-attention captures pairwise interactions within a candidate list [aebd24d8-2].

5) Attention weights as coefficients to reweight distances or scores
- Beyond fusion of latent representations, attention weights can be used to scale or weight base similarity/distance components. For example, in multimodal attentive metric learning for ranking, the model computes an attention vector and then element-wise multiplies the attention weights with a base distance; the authors note that naive softmax normalization yields very small weights, which can overly suppress differences, so they scale the normalized weights to avoid degenerate fusion of base signals Joint attention combines modality similarities with weighted attention for fusion [d88723cb-0] In practice, attention weights are normalized with softmax; however, when used to element-wise multiply a small base distance, the small weights can weaken distinguishing power, so the normalized weights are enlarged by a factor α to better fuse the signals [d88723cb-1].

citations.title: An Attention-Based Deep Net for Learning to Rank
snippets: In information retrieval, learning to rank constructs a machine-based ranking model which given a query, sorts the search results by their degree of relevance or importance to the query. Neural networks have been successfully applied to this problem, and in this paper, we propose an attention-based deep neural network which better incorporates different embeddings of the queries and search results with an attention-based mechanism. This model also applies a decoder mechanism to learn the ranks of the search results in a listwise fashion. The embeddings are trained with convolutional neural networks or the word2vec model. We demonstrate the performance of this model with image retrieval and text querying data sets.

citations.title: 3D attention mechanism for fine-grained classification of table tennis strokes using a Twin Spatio-Temporal Convolutional Neural Networks
snippets:
One of the pioneering works introducing the use of an attention model in neural networks for image classification is presented in [22]. The authors are interested in the contribution of feature channels along convolutional layers into decision making. The attention model here is "global": a channel weighting mechanism is introduced by "attention blocks". The processing consists of three steps: i) synthesis (squeeze), ii) excitation (excitation) and iii) feature scaling (scale). Thus, for each channel, a block is a small network of neurons that learns a weighting coefficient. The next layers of the network ingest the characteristic channels thus weighted. This global weighting has been used as a basis for the authors of [23] who propose "double attention" blocks, i.e. ensuring a global and spatial weighting of the characteristics in convolution network layers. The authors of [12], [24] use the principles of residual neural networks to propose "residual" learning of the attention masks incorporated in the convolution layers. Their experiments on CIFAR data bases show that on CIFAR 10 the residual attention network with depth of 452 has the best error rate compared to all the basic residual networks (3.90%). The authors propose the incorporation of attention mechanisms in both forward (forward) and backward (backward) runs. This is also the approach we had in [11], but by selecting important characteristics and not by weighting features and channels. Note that when minimizing the objective function by gradient descent, the attention mechanisms are implicitly introduced via the derivative calculation where the weighted characteristics are used. The authors of [12] report that this use in back propagation makes the training data robust to noise. This is also our approach in this work.

Other works such as [25] propose "Teacher-student" networks where the "Teacher" network is the one that learns attention and guides the student network for the image classification task. In our approach we also use a kind of attention transfer as in our architecture the attention branch and trunck brunch will join together for selection of important features. Also, in [26], attention mechanism is coupled with LSTM to learn the correlation between different data modalities such as text and image and therefore leads to better embedding.

sections.title: # How attention weights are typically fused
sections.text:
- Weighted summation of values/representations: In scaled-dot attention, the output is a weighted sum of values where the attention map A provides the coefficients; this is commonly used to fuse base encodings (e.g., Q and D embeddings) into a unified relevance feature The output features are the weighted summation of the values determined by the attention weights [aebd24d8-2]. 
- Product/fusion across multiple attention layers: Hierarchical attention can fuse local and global attentions via products to produce a global importance weight for longer documents or passages, which is then used to rank at the item level Global attention weights are obtained by multiplying local passage attention and term importance [d88723cb-0]. 
- Listwise aggregation: Attention over a candidate list can fuse base pairwise or pointwise signals into a list-level score that respects inter-item dependencies, often followed by a decoder to optimize NDCG/LM loss Self-attention models pairwise interactions within a candidate list and can be followed by a decoder for listwise ranking [aebd24d8-2]. 
- Cross-attention gating: In personalized ranking, cross-attention produces user- and item-specific weights that gate or reweight base item features/embeddings before prediction, aligning user preferences with the base ranking signal Cross-attention aligns user embeddings with item features for personalized ranking [aebd24d8-2].

sections.title: # Practical considerations
sections.text:
- Normalization and scale: When attention weights are used to modulate relatively small base distances or scores (as in metric learning or similarity scoring), naive softmax weights can become too small, effectively damping differences; scaling or clamping the attention coefficients is often necessary to ensure effective fusion Softmax-normalized attention weights can be very small and overly suppress base distances; enlarging normalized weights by a factor α improves model discriminative power [d88723cb-1]. 
- Interpretability and stability: While attention provides interpretability via importance weights, naive ranking by attention alone can be brittle; combining attention with gradients or using listwise decoders can lead to more robust and interpretable feature selection or ranking Ranking by descending attention weights can be informative but is not a gold standard; combining attention weights with gradients can produce more reliable importance sets [aebd24d8-1]. 
- Architectural choices: Surveys highlight design choices such as symmetric vs. asymmetric encoders, ordered tokens, and weight sharing that interact with attention-based fusion; selecting these based on the task (e.g., symmetric for pair-wise relevance extraction, ordered tokens for tensor interaction) can improve performance Neural ranking models are characterized by attention presence, symmetric vs. asymmetric designs, ordered tokens, and weight sharing strategies [c6f917c0-2].

citations.title: Is Attention Interpretable?
snippets:
Exhaustively searching the space of component subsets would be far too time-consuming in practice, so we introduce three other ranking schemes. 

The first is to randomly rank importance. We expect that this ranking will perform quite poorly, but it provides a point of comparison by which to validate that ranking by descending attention weights is at least somewhat informative. 

The second ranking scheme, inspired by Li et al. (2015) and Feng et al. (2018), is to order the attention weights by the gradient of the decision function with respect to each calculated attention weight, in descending order. Since each of the datasets on which we evaluate has either five or ten output classes, we take the decision function given a real-valued model output vector to be 

Unlike the last two proposed rankings, our third ranking scheme uses attention weights, but supplements them with information about the gradient. For this ranking, we multiply each of our calculated gradients from our previous proposed ranking scheme by their corresponding attention weight magnitude. Under this ordering, attended items that have both a high attention weight and a high calculated gradient with respect to their attention weight will be ranked most important. 

We introduce these last two rankings as an attempt to discover smaller sets not produced by the attention weight ranking. Note, however, that we still do not take either as a gold-standard indicator of importance to the model, as with the gradient in Ross et al. ( 2017) and Melis and Jaakkola (2018), but merely as an alternative ordering method. The "gold standard" in our case would be the minimal set of attention weights to zero out for the decision to change, which none of our ordering methods will necessarily find for a particular instance.

sections.title: # Pointers to start reading (and where attention weights are fused)
sections.text:
- Surveys and taxonomy: A survey on neural ranking models provides a taxonomy that includes attention-based models and explains how attention interacts with other design choices (ordered tokens, representation, weight sharing), serving as a roadmap to find specific fusions in the literature A neural ranking survey categorizes models by attention and other architectural properties [c6f917c0-2].

- Multimodal/joint fusion: Transformer-based joint attention models learn feature-level attention weights to fuse multiple signals for ranking, showing how attention controls the contribution of each modality or feature group Joint attention combines modality similarities with weighted attention for effective fusion [d88723cb-0]. 
- Personalized ranking via cross-attention: Cross-attention aligns user and item spaces so that attention weights act as personalized gates over base item representations, improving personalization without manual feature engineering Cross-attention aligns user embeddings with item features for personalized ranking [aebd24d8-2].

citations.title: An Attention-Based Deep Net for Learning to Rank
snippets: In information retrieval, learning to rank constructs a machine-based ranking model which given a query, sorts the search results by their degree of relevance or importance to the query. Neural networks have been successfully applied to this problem, and in this paper, we propose an attention-based deep neural network which better incorporates different embeddings of the queries and search results with an attention-based mechanism. This model also applies a decoder mechanism to learn the ranks of the search results in a listwise fashion. The embeddings are trained with convolutional neural networks or the word2vec model. We demonstrate the performance of this model with image retrieval and text querying data sets.

citations.title: 3D attention mechanism for fine-grained classification of table tennis strokes using a Twin Spatio-Temporal Convolutional Neural Networks
snippets:
One of the pioneering works introducing the use of an attention model in neural networks for image classification is presented in [22]. The authors are interested in the contribution of feature channels along convolutional layers into decision making. The attention model here is "global": a channel weighting mechanism is introduced by "attention blocks". The processing consists of three steps: i) synthesis (squeeze), ii) excitation (excitation) and iii) feature scaling (scale). Thus, for each channel, a block is a small network of neurons that learns a weighting coefficient. The next layers of the network ingest the characteristic channels thus weighted. This global weighting has been used as a basis for the authors of [23] who propose "double attention" blocks, i.e. ensuring a global and spatial weighting of the characteristics in convolution network layers. The authors of [12], [24] use the principles of residual neural networks to propose "residual" learning of the attention masks incorporated in the convolution layers. Their experiments on CIFAR data bases show that on CIFAR 10 the residual attention network with depth of 452 has the best error rate compared to all the basic residual networks (3.90%). The authors propose the incorporation of attention mechanisms in both forward (forward) and backward (backward) runs. This is also the approach we had in [11], but by selecting important characteristics and not by weighting features and channels. Note that when minimizing the objective function by gradient descent, the attention mechanisms are implicitly introduced via the derivative calculation where the weighted characteristics are used. The authors of [12] report that this use in back propagation makes the training data robust to noise. This is also our approach in this work.

Other works such as [25] propose "Teacher-student" networks where the "Teacher" network is the one that learns attention and guides the student network for the image classification task. In our approach we also use a kind of attention transfer as in our architecture the attention branch and trunck brunch will join together for selection of important features. Also, in [26], attention mechanism is coupled with LSTM to learn the correlation between different data modalities such as text and image and therefore leads to better embedding.

sections.title: # Generative AI Competences Framework: Individual, Team, and Organizational Capabilities
sections.text: This framework synthesizes competencies needed to design, deploy, and govern generative AI (GenAI) responsibly, spanning individual skills, team capabilities, and organizational governance. It draws on education and workforce initiatives (UNESCO), ethics and assessment tools (EU HLEG Trustworthy AI and ALTAI), global principles (OECD AI Principles), sector-neutral risk/process guidance (NIST AI RMF, ISO standards), and practitioner-oriented risk and evaluation frameworks (OWASP, EU AI Act, governance indices). The goal is a coherent, actionable map of knowledge, skills, and processes for trustworthy GenAI across contexts.

sections.title: # 1) Individual Competencies: From Literacy to Specialized Expertise
sections.text:
Foundational GenAI literacy. Individuals should develop baseline understanding of what GenAI is, its capabilities and limitations, and how to interact with it critically and responsibly. A competency-based model proposes twelve defining competencies spanning foundational AI literacy, prompt engineering and programming skills, data literacy, evaluation, and ethical/legal awareness, with a progression suitable for education and professional training and aligned to policymakers and educators who need to design responsible use cases and governance guidelines A competency-based model for generative AI literacy covering foundational skills, prompt engineering, programming, and ethical/legal considerations is proposed and positioned for policymakers, educators, and practitioners [6cb39474-2]. Similar work frames generative AI literacy as a set of guidelines to empower effective, responsible, and critical interaction, offering a starting point for curricula and organizational training Generative AI literacy is defined as a set of guidelines enabling effective, responsible, and critical interaction, intended to support educators, companies, and organizations in building competency frameworks [6cb39474-3].

Ethical, legal, and human-centered thinking. Education and research guidance from UNESCO emphasizes a human-centered approach, data privacy, ethical standards, and enhanced teacher training, reflecting a broader competency need in institutional governance, consent, and responsible innovation across domains UNESCO guidance emphasizes a human-centered approach, data privacy, ethical standards, and enhanced training for responsible integration of generative AI in education and research [6cb39474-0]. UNESCO’s AI Competency Framework for Students articulates four areas—human-centered thinking, AI ethics, technical applications, and system design—providing an explicit structure for individual skill development from conceptual understanding to system-level design UNESCO’s AI Competency Framework for Students focuses on human-centered thinking, AI ethics, technical applications, and system design [6cb39474-0].

Practitioner and domain-specific skills. Competency models note that GenAI spans multiple domains and requires domain-specific sub-skills and ethical tailoring; thus, foundational competencies should be complemented by specialized training in areas like healthcare, finance, or creative industries GenAI applications span domains and require specialized sub-skills and ethical considerations, motivating domain-specific competency refinements [6cb39474-1]. For example, in public health, capacity-building and trustworthiness are critical, with barriers like inadequate data governance and low trust requiring targeted training and governance competencies to enable responsible adoption Public health surveillance emphasizes responsible AI adoption, highlighting the need to address data governance and trust barriers through capacity building and trustworthy practices [a8bed75b-4].

citations.title: Generative AI Literacy: A Comprehensive Framework for Literacy and Responsible Use
snippets:
Generative AI-broadly referring to large-scale, pretrained generative models, such as foundational and large language models (LLMs)-has gained unparalleled worldwide popularity over the past several years. This interest surged into a global phenomenon following the launch of ChatGPT-3.5 in November 2022 [80]. After the release of the "Five Big Ideas in AI" from the AI4K12 organization in 2019 [119], followed by AI literacy competency frameworks proposed by Long & Magerko in 2020 [69] and Ng et al. in 2021 [86], the field of artificial intelligence (AI) has undergone a significant transformation with the rise of generative AI 1 , especially since the worldwide boom of ChatGPT in early 2023 2 , followed by other large language generative AI applications like Copilot 3 , Gemini 4 and Deepseek 5 . Unlike 

We conducted an exploratory review of existing literature to inform our generative AI literacy guidelines. Given the rapidly evolving nature of generative AI, we anticipate that future researchers will subsequently expand upon this work to develop more refined and up-to-date guidelines (e.g. generative AI could soon be embodied or embedded in classrooms). This framework serves as an initial step toward developing more comprehensive resources for educators, policymakers, and researchers to design learning interventions-such as curricula, workshops, and other tools-aimed at improving the public's understanding of generative AI. We define generative AI literacy as: 

A set of guidelines for designing learning interventions aimed at enhancing users' understanding of generative AI, enabling them to interact with it effectively, responsibly, and critically. These guidelines are intended to assist educators, schools, companies, and organizations in developing frameworks that empower their members, such as students, employees, and stakeholders, to use generative AI in ethical and informed ways. 

The most widely used generative AI is the generative language model-commonly referred to as large language models (LLMs) or large, pre-trained language models (PLMs) [77].
