citations.title: A shape completion model for corrective osteotomy of distal radius malunion
snippets:
Once the SSM was created, it was extended into a shape completion model using an isotropic Gaussian process model [14]. Specifically, Gaussian process regression was used, which utilizes the statistical correlations captured by the SSM to predict the missing portion of the bone from known partial shape data. This shape completion model was designed to predict the distal 12% of the radius, based on the proximal 88%. The 12% cutoff value was chosen to include most commonly seen metaphyseal extra-articular radius fracture locations [17]. The location of the cutoff height is depicted in Fig. 2. 

A key step in creating the shape completion model was determining optimal hyperparameter values for the Gaussian process. These hyperparameters influence how well the model predicts missing shapes and must be manually tuned. They include noise, which represents the level of noise in the data; sigma, which controls the amount of correlation between neighboring points; and scale, which defines the size of the Gaussian kernel [14]. This hyperparameter tuning was performed systematically by evaluating noise levels of 5, 10, 15, and 20; sigma values of 50, 100, 150, 200, 250, and 300; and scale values of 5, 10, and 15. The optimal hyperparameter combination was identified as the one minimizing the mean prediction error. 

To determine the values for the hyperparameters, the validation set was used. First, the distal 12% of each 3D bone model from the validation set was discarded. Next, each remaining proximal 88% of these 3D bone models was registered to the SSM's mean shape to establish correspondence. Then, the shape completion model predicted the missing distal portion. The predicted complete 3D bone model including the 12% distal part was compared to its actual reference 3D model. The error between predicted and reference was quantified by calculating the mean difference as a Euclidean distance between both 3D models. This procedure was repeated for all ten 3D models of the validation set. Once the optimal hyperparameter values were identified, the test set 3D models were used to evaluate the shape completion model. The test set was processed in the same manner as the validation set, but only with the optimal hyperparameter settings.

sections.title: # Articulated 3D Gaussian Representations Driven by Bones
sections.text:
Recent 3D Gaussian splatting work connects skeletal motion to Gaussian-based geometry via skinning. One approach uses linear blend skinning (LBS) to transform each 3D Gaussian’s center and rotation according to bone transformations, with skinning weights computed from Mahalanobis distances between Gaussians and bones at rest, plus learned delta skinning weights via a weight MLP conditioned on joint angles. Each 3D Gaussian’s pose can be transformed by LBS using bone transformations, with skinning weights w_im determined by Mahalanobis distance between a Gaussian i and bone m based on Gaussian radii, and forward/inverse transformations computed from rest and target poses [ffb6a8b2-2]. Delta skinning weights w_Δ_im can be predicted by a weight MLP that takes joint angles and Gaussian center position as input, enabling fine geometry deformation beyond linear blend weights [ffb6a8b2-2]. Collision-avoidance can be enforced by penalizing 3D overlap (via 1σ isosurface similarity) and anatomical plausibility by adding bone-length priors aligned with a PCA-based normal distribution, which constrain predicted bone lengths to high-probability regions [ffb6a8b2-2].

These techniques reflect a broader trend: 3D Gaussian splatting and related Gaussian radiance/field representations are increasingly used for articulated self-modeling and scene representations. While the above robotics study does not focus on clinical bones, it provides a blueprint for representing bone-like structures as collections of 3D Gaussians that deform coherently with skeletal motion, which is directly transferable to musculoskeletal simulations and reconstructions. Articulated Gaussian splatting with bone-driven skinning provides a coherent way to deform 3D Gaussians with joint motion, constrain overlap to avoid self-penetration, and regularize predictions using bone-length priors [ffb6a8b2-2].

sections.title: # Medical Imaging and Morphology: Gaussian-Based Features and Models for Bone Structures
sections.text:
A direct line of work models bone tissue classes using Gaussian mixture models (GMMs) in CT. For example, vertebral bone density distributions have been fit as a two-Gaussian mixture separating cortical and trabecular components, with mixing proportions, means, and variances estimated via maximum-likelihood (e.g., EM), enabling probabilistic tissue classification. Bone density in vertebrae can be modeled as a two-Gaussian mixture, one component for cortical bone and one for trabecular bone, with mixing weights, means, and variances estimated by maximizing the log-likelihood over sample intensities [c975bab6-0]. Preprocessing may include Gaussian filtering (e.g., σ=1) and thresholding to isolate bone, and the GMM likelihood provides a statistically principled way to separate tissue classes [c975bab6-0].

Surface curvature features extracted from trabecular bone meshes—especially Gaussian curvature—serve as intrinsic descriptors related to mechanical properties. Studies compute principal, mean, and Gaussian curvatures at mesh vertices and show strong correlations between curvature distributions and histomorphometric parameters, with Gaussian curvature particularly predictive of trabecular thickness and topology. Trabecular bone surface curvature features (principal, mean, and Gaussian curvatures) computed from STL meshes capture fundamental shape details and have been linked to bone failure prediction [aa8a7ca1-0]. Curvature-based descriptors correlate strongly with plate area (R^2≈0.80), plate thickness (R^2≈0.63), and rod length (R^2≈0.70), while Gaussian curvature–based models predict trabecular thickness more accurately than mean-principal curvature models [aa8a7ca1-1]. Gaussian curvature’s sign classifies surface types (negative for saddle-shaped, zero for flat, positive for spherical), and trabecular architectures often exhibit hyperbolic (negative) Gaussian curvature consistent with high topological complexity [aa8a7ca1-2]. In practice, these curvatures are computed per vertex using finite-difference approximations on triangle meshes [aa8a7ca1-3].

Orientation analysis of trabecular networks also leverages Gaussian-based modeling. One approach fits two Gaussian curves to the histogram of oriented projections, estimating principal and secondary trabecular directions and their angular variability, which characterizes anisotropy relevant to mechanical loading. Local Hessian-based orientation computed across Gaussian-smoothed images (σ from 1–5) is used to estimate trabecular orientation, and two Gaussian curve fits recover principal (Tb.OrP) and secondary (Tb.OrS) directions with an associated spread (Tb.Int) that reflects anisotropy [aa8a7ca1-4].

The mean curvature describes how much a surface is locally convex or concave. The Gaussian curvature quantifies the type of the surface: < 0 signifies a saddleshaped region (hyperbolic), = 0 implies an intrinsically flat region (such as a plane, cylinder or cone), and > 0 describes a sphere-shaped region ( Figure 1). The Gaussian curvature distributions clearly showed that the geometry of trabecular bone is, on average, hyperbolic in nature ( < 0). This has been reported before for a few bone biopsies [25]. sections.title: # Orthopedic Workflows and Applications
sections.text:
These Gaussian-based methods integrate into practical orthopedic pipelines. For planning and comparative modeling, CT- and MRI-derived bone models are registered and compared to assess osseous anatomy, with Gaussian filters and thresholds used to segment bone from soft tissue before downstream analyses. In proximal femur studies, semi-automatic segmentation uses thresholding (e.g., HU>190) and Gaussian filtering to delineate osseous anatomy across 3D-CT and Dixon-based MRI [c975bab6-1]. Global registration aligns MRI-based femur models to CT, after which differences in mean, standard deviation, and maximum error across patients are quantified [c975bab6-1]. Gaussian filtering and global thresholds (e.g., 273/1000 for hydroxyapatite concentration) are used to binarize 3D images and separate cortical and trabecular regions in tibial specimens for volumetric analysis [c975bab6-3]. Clinical MRI workflows generate 3D bone models (femur, tibia, bone bruises) and use point-based registration to align pre- and post-operative states, enabling distance and intersection metrics between bone tunnels and bruised regions [c975bab6-4].

In biomechanics-focused pipelines, curvature-derived features and Gaussian curvature–based descriptors can be combined with FE analysis to predict microarchitectural parameters or failure risk, while GP-based shape completion fills missing regions for more complete FE meshes. Models based on curvature distributions show strong predictive power for trabecular plate metrics and plate number, suggesting utility for predicting failure and onset of osteoporotic changes [aa8a7ca1-1]. Isotropic GP regression for distal radius completion enables downstream meshing and analysis when only partial acquisitions are available, with hyperparameters selected to minimize prediction error [ffb6a8b2-3].

Segmentation of the osseous anatomy of the proximal femur on 3D-CT was performed using a semi-automated method with a high-pass filter and a threshold value of 190 Hounsfield units. MRI segmentation was performed manually by a radiologist cooperating with a segmentation specialist. A low pass filter was applied to the fat suppressed image to extract the low signal areas that encompassed the bone, fatty tissues, tendons, and ligaments (Fig 2A). For the Dixon-VIBE images, the outlining boundary of the cortex or subchondral bone plate was extracted by applying a low pass filter to the fat-only or in-phase images (Fig 2B). The extracted boundary of the cortex or subchondral bone plate served as a guideline between the osseous anatomy and overlying subcutaneous fat (Fig 2C). In certain areas where tendon attached, such as the greater trochanter, the boundary between the tendon and bone was determined by visual assessment by the radiologist. In the WE fat suppression method, the boundary between the osseous structures and overlying subcutaneous fat or tendon was judged by the radiologist without a guideline, unlike in the Dixon technique. A 2-week interval was maintained between the Dixonbased 3D-MRI and WE-based 3D-MRI bone segmentations, to avoid recall bias. The Materialise Mimics program (Materialise, Leuven, Belgium) was used for the segmentation process. 

The stereolithography (STL) file of the 3D-CT semi-automatically segmented proximal femur model served as a reference for the 3D-MRI segmentation models of the proximal femur. A global registration method was used to register the Dixon-based 3D-MRI segmented bone model and the WE-based 3D-MRI segmented proximal femur model to the 3D-CT bone model. Global registration was applied over multiple iterations until the average distance error of the registrations between the CT and MRI-based 3D femur models reached a nadir. snippets:
Once the SSM was created, it was extended into a shape completion model using an isotropic Gaussian process model [14]. Specifically, Gaussian process regression was used, which utilizes the statistical correlations captured by the SSM to predict the missing portion of the bone from known partial shape data. This shape completion model was designed to predict the distal 12% of the radius, based on the proximal 88%. The 12% cutoff value was chosen to include most commonly seen metaphyseal extra-articular radius fracture locations [17]. The location of the cutoff height is depicted in Fig. 2. 

A key step in creating the shape completion model was determining optimal hyperparameter values for the Gaussian process. This hyperparameter tuning was performed systematically by evaluating noise levels of 5, 10, 15, and 20; sigma values of 50, 100, 150, 200, 250, and 300; and scale values of 5, 10, and 15. The optimal hyperparameter combination was identified as the one minimizing the mean prediction error. 

To determine the values for the hyperparameters, the validation set was used. First, the distal 12% of each 3D bone model from the validation set was discarded. Next, each remaining proximal 88% of these 3D bone models was registered to the SSM's mean shape to establish correspondence. Then, the shape completion model predicted the missing distal portion. The predicted complete 3D bone model including the 12% distal part was compared to its actual reference 3D model. The error between predicted and reference was quantified by calculating the mean difference as a Euclidean distance between both 3D models. This procedure was repeated for all ten 3D models of the validation set. Once the optimal hyperparameter values were identified, the test set 3D models were used to evaluate the shape completion model. The test set was processed in the same manner as the validation set, but only with the optimal hyperparameter settings.

sections.title: # From Gaussian Descriptors to 3D Gaussian Splatting and Beyond
sections.text: While classical FE and imaging pipelines rely on polygonal meshes or implicit surfaces, modern 3D Gaussian representations offer compact, probabilistic geometry that can be deformed with skeletal motion and overlapped with collision penalties. In articulated models, per-Gaussian skinning weights based on Mahalanobis distance to bones and learned delta weights provide a data-driven way to simulate plausible bone-driven deformations, with explicit constraints on overlap and bone length to enforce anatomical plausibility. Skinning weights computed from Mahalanobis distance between Gaussians and bones, combined with delta weights via a weight MLP, yield realistic deformations under joint motion [ffb6a8b2-2]. Collision avoidance and bone-length priors provide regularization by penalizing Gaussian 3D overlap and constraining predicted lengths to lie within high-probability PCA regions [ffb6a8b2-2]. These ideas align conceptually with GPMMs’ anisotropic priors for bones and with Gaussian curvature descriptors in trabecular mechanics, suggesting a unified pathway from statistical shape priors and curvature features to 3D Gaussian splatting for musculoskeletal reconstructions.

sections.title: # Limitations and Open Problems
sections.text: Several gaps remain. First, while GPMMs and curvature/Gaussian descriptors are well established for bones, there is limited direct evidence of end-to-end Gaussian Splatting applied to clinical bone datasets for diagnosis or FE prediction; most splatting demonstrations are in robotics or general 3D reconstruction rather than orthopedic decision support. Articulated Gaussian splatting with bone-driven skinning has been demonstrated for robot self-modeling, but is not yet widely reported on clinical bone datasets [ffb6a8b2-2]. Second, coupling GP priors with explicit biomechanical solvers (FE) remains largely conceptual or model-driven; more work is needed to validate predictive accuracy of Gaussian-based descriptors for stress, fracture risk, or remodeling in vivo. Curvature-based models correlate with histomorphometric metrics and suggest potential for failure prediction, but broader validation and integration with FE is needed [aa8a7ca1-1]. Third, multi-scale GPMMs that integrate bone-level and ligament-attachment details are promising but require standardized datasets and cross-study validation to ensure robustness across populations and imaging protocols. Multi-scale GP setups combining bone-level and landmark kernels offer rich priors, but evaluation across diverse musculoskeletal datasets is essential [ffb6a8b2-4].

sections.title: # Practical Recommendations and Research Directions
sections.text:
- Build bridges between Gaussian descriptors and FE: Use curvature/Gaussian-based features as inputs to surrogate models that predict FE-derived outcomes (stress hotspots, von Mises failure) from CT-derived surfaces, with uncertainty quantification from GP priors. Gaussian curvature–based descriptors’ strong correlations with trabecular thickness and plate metrics motivate their use as inputs to predictive models [aa8a7ca1-1].
- Standardize GPMM pipelines for bones: Adopt anisotropic, bone-axis–aligned kernels and include joint/segment constraints as priors; evaluate generalization and specificity across cohorts and devices. Anisotropic GPMMs emphasize length-axis variation and can be evaluated with standard generalization/specificity/compactness criteria [ffb6a8b2-1].
- Explore 3D Gaussian splatting for orthopedic reconstructions: Translate bone-driven skinning and collision regularization from robotics to clinical workflows, starting with cadaveric or retrospective CT/MRI datasets to assess registration accuracy and mesh fidelity. Bone-driven Gaussian skinning with collision and length priors provides a template for anatomically plausible reconstructions [ffb6a8b2-2].
- Integrate GMM tissue classification into FE surrogates: Combine cortical/trabecular GMM-derived tissue masks with curvature/anisotropy features to create material-property fields for FE, enabling probabilistic predictions of strength and fracture risk. Two-Gaussian cortical/trabecular density models provide a probabilistic tissue segmentation that can be mapped to material properties [c975bab6-0].

sections.title: # Summary
sections.text: In summary, “bones” and “3D Gaussians” intersect in three complementary ways: (1) Gaussian processes and anisotropic kernels as shape priors and completion tools for bones, including joint/bone-length constraints; (2) Gaussian-based imaging descriptors from CT/MRI—GMM tissue modeling, Gaussian filtering, curvature features, and Gaussian-curve orientation fitting—that capture morphology and mechanics at micro- and macro- scales; and (3) articulated, bone-driven 3D Gaussian splatting and skinning that deform Gaussians coherently with skeletal motion and enforce anatomical constraints. Anisotropic GPMMs and evaluation metrics provide a principled way to model and compare bone shape variation [ffb6a8b2-1] Isotropic GP regression can complete partial bone models with hyperparameter tuning and quantitative validation [ffb6a8b2-3] Multi-scale GP priors per bone and landmarks can couple bone-level and attachment-scale shape variation [ffb6a8b2-4] Two-Gaussian mixtures separate cortical and trabecular density in vertebrae for probabilistic tissue classification [c975bab6-0] Gaussian curvature features computed from trabecular meshes correlate with histomorphometric and mechanical metrics [aa8a7ca1-0] Gaussian-curve fitting of oriented histograms quantifies trabecular anisotropy and principal directions [aa8a7ca1-4] Bone-driven Gaussian splatting with Mahalanobis-based skinning and delta weights enables anatomically plausible articulated deformations with collision and length priors [ffb6a8b2-2]. Together, these lines of work chart a path from imaging and statistics to geometric representations that respect skeletal structure and mechanics.

citations.title: A shape completion model for corrective osteotomy of distal radius malunion
snippets:
Once the SSM was created, it was extended into a shape completion model using an isotropic Gaussian process model [14]. Specifically, Gaussian process regression was used, which utilizes the statistical correlations captured by the SSM to predict the missing portion of the bone from known partial shape data. This shape completion model was designed to predict the distal 12% of the radius, based on the proximal 88%. The 12% cutoff value was chosen to include most commonly seen metaphyseal extra-articular radius fracture locations [17]. The location of the cutoff height is depicted in Fig. 2. 

A key step in creating the shape completion model was determining optimal hyperparameter values for the Gaussian process. These hyperparameters influence how well the model predicts missing shapes and must be manually tuned. They include noise, which represents the level of noise in the data; sigma, which controls the amount of correlation between neighboring points; and scale, which defines the size of the Gaussian kernel [14]. This hyperparameter tuning was performed systematically by evaluating noise levels of 5, 10, 15, and 20; sigma values of 50, 100, 150, 200, 250, and 300; and scale values of 5, 10, and 15. The optimal hyperparameter combination was identified as the one minimizing the mean prediction error. 

To determine the values for the hyperparameters, the validation set was used. First, the distal 12% of each 3D bone model from the validation set was discarded. Next, each remaining proximal 88% of these 3D bone models was registered to the SSM's mean shape to establish correspondence. Then, the shape completion model predicted the missing distal portion. The predicted complete 3D bone model including the 12% distal part was compared to its actual reference 3D model. The error between predicted and reference was quantified by calculating the mean difference as a Euclidean distance between both 3D models. This procedure was repeated for all ten 3D models of the validation set. Once the optimal hyperparameter values were identified, the test set 3D models were used to evaluate the shape completion model. The test set was processed in the same manner as the validation set, but only with the optimal hyperparameter settings.

sections.text: Below is a curated set of papers and evidence on ambiguity in LLM-based agents, grouped by theme. Each item includes concrete mechanisms, datasets, or findings relevant to ambiguity detection, clarification, and mitigation in agent workflows.

sections.title: # Why Ambiguity Matters for LLM Agents
sections.text: LLM agents operate with high-level, under-specified goals and dynamically interpret tasks by planning and invoking tools, which makes them particularly susceptible to errors when instructions are ambiguous or underspecified. LLM agents dynamically interpret high-level, under-specified goals and integrate tools and knowledge, but this openness leads to unpredictable, inconsistent, or unsafe behaviors when navigating ambiguous instructions [d6dbc7a4-0]. In real-world agent applications, task descriptions vary in quality; detecting ambiguity requires recognizing unclear expectations or missing key information, while over-interacting wastes user time [d6dbc7a4-4]. Ambiguity can be a latent safety risk because benign instructions may encode multiple interpretations that diverge from intended outcomes. ToolEmu frames a realistic threat model where benign user instructions contain ambiguities that can lead to failures [d6dbc7a4-3].

citations.title: Check Yourself Before You Wreck Yourself: Selectively Quitting Improves LLM Agent Safety
snippets: Our evaluation leverages the ToolEmu benchmark, an LM-emulated sandbox designed for identifying risks in LLM agents. The framework is ideal for our study as it focuses on the realistic threat model of instruction underspecification, where benign user instructions contain ambiguities that can lead to failures. Its use of an adversarial emulator creates challenging scenarios to robustly test agent safety.

citations.title: Evaluation-Driven Development and Operations of LLM Agents: A Process Model and Reference Architecture
snippets:
Large language models (LLMs) are large-scale, pretrained language models with tens of billions of parameters, adaptable to a wide range of downstream tasks, including question answering, summarization, and reasoning [1]. Recent advancements in LLMs have led to the emergence of LLM-based agents, commonly known as LLM agents, which autonomously perform complex tasks (e.g., the AI Scientist [2]). Unlike traditional AI/LLM systems that rely on predefined inputs and structured task execution, LLM agents dynamically interpret high-level, under-specified goals. They perceive context, reason, plan, and execute workflows, often integrating external tools, knowledge bases, and other agents to extend their capabilities [3]. 

Despite their transformative potential, LLM agents introduce significant concerns regarding performance and safety [4]. Their open-ended reasoning, planning and execution processes can produce unpredictable, inconsistent, or even unsafe behaviors, particularly when navigating ambiguous instructions or novel scenarios. Moreover, their autonomy-such as selecting tools, adjusting workflows, and adapting responses-raises governance challenges, as these agents may take actions misaligned with human intent or regulatory constraints. Thus, rigorous, continuous evaluation is essential to ensure that LLM agents operate as expected and evolve safely over time. 

While increasing research attention has been devoted to benchmarking and testing frameworks for LLMs and LLM agents (e.g., [5,6]), existing approaches largely fail to address the full scope of LLM agent evaluation. Classical software engineering methods-such as Test-Driven Development (TDD) and Behavior-Driven Development (BDD)-have proven effective for deterministic systems with clear, predefined specifications. However, these methods are not inherently suited to LLM agents, which operate in open-ended, adaptive contexts and continuously adjust their behavior based on real-world interactions. The effective evaluation of LLM agents requires the following considerations: 

• Evaluating LLM Agents at the System Level. Current evaluation frameworks predominantly assess LLMs at the model level, focusing on such as prompt-response correctness or benchmark-based scores.

citations.title: Interactive Agents to Overcome Ambiguity in Software Engineering
snippets: In real-world LLM and agent applications, task descriptions and prompts can vary in quality (Chowdhury et al., 2024). To detect ambiguity, a model must recognize unclear expectations or identify missing key information in its planned approach. However, interacting unnecessarily when sufficient information is already available can introduce inefficiencies and place an undue burden on the user. Here, we examine the capabilities of LLMs to detect ambiguous instructions in software engineering contexts.

sections.title: # Evidence That LLMs Struggle With Ambiguity and How Multi-Agent Debate Helps
sections.text:
LLMs tend to favor one interpretation among multiple plausible ones and often fail to enumerate or detect ambiguity, limiting their utility in agent settings that need to choose clarifications or tools. LLMs often bias toward one interpretation among many for an ambiguous utterance; prompting for multiple interpretations does not reliably help ambiguity detection [b261daba-0]. A multi-agent protocol evaluates whether an instruction is sufficiently clear; if ambiguous, agents propose a single optimal clarifying question within constrained reasoning [b261daba-1]. Experiments use a programmatically generated ambiguity dataset and structured debate to assess single vs. multi-agent configurations at identifying ambiguities and proposing clarifying questions [b261daba-4].

Debate-style multi-agent frameworks leverage “cognitive diversity” to surface alternative interpretations, critique them, and converge on clarifications or plans that better match user intent. Multi-agent debate frameworks have agents independently generate responses and iteratively review/revise via peer critique, with variants like MAD using affirmative/negative agents and a judge to decide when to stop [9a1244de-2]. Integrating third-party LLMs into multi-agent systems can diversify perspectives, adjust attention weights based on uncertainty, and reach broader consensus, mitigating single-model blind spots [9a1244de-3]. Leader–follower debate protocols are used to pre-execution analyze commands, generate actionable clarification questions, and leverage cognitive diversity to consider multiple interpretations [9a1244de-4]. Surveys in conversational QA and compound AI highlight that agentic orchestration brings explicit disambiguation capabilities, often via agent specifications, policies for when to clarify, and mechanisms like memory and verification to keep trajectories aligned. Agentic orchestration makes disambiguation a first-class capability, with agent cards/specs encoding policies for clarification, memory to reduce context drift, and LLM verification as checkpoints [9a1244de-1]. Multi-agent collaborative and debate frameworks are core to organizing LLM agents and have been shown to enhance factuality and reasoning through iterative critique and revision [9a1244de-2].

citations.title: Enhancing Multi-Agent Consensus Through Third-Party LLM Integration: Analyzing Uncertainty and Mitigating Hallucinations in Large Language Models
snippets:
Large Language Models (LLMs) have exhibited robust reasoning and creative capabilities. In order to manage more intricate tasks, AutoGen amalgamates the functionalities of LLMs, human inputs, and various tools by constructing agents with distinct roles, thereby offering a tailored multi-agent dialogue setting [1]. This has catalyzed the evolution of multiagent debate systems. In these systems, multiple agents articulate their arguments, while a neutral moderator oversees the debate process to facilitate the attainment of a final resolution [2].By employing multiple instances of language models and engaging in several rounds of proposal and debate regarding their respective answers and reasoning processes, a consensus final answer is ultimately achieved [3]. 

In the process of multi-agent debate, it is common to deploy the same Large Language Model (LLM) for each agent and assign them the same role. This approach has proven effective in multi-agent debates, but it also has limitations, especially when the model's knowledge scope is restricted and lacks external feedback from different models. The use of a single model can lead to a monolithic viewpoint in the debate process, limiting the depth and breadth of the debate. 1(a), we introduce third-party LLMs to enrich the knowledge of multi-agent system, which can provide agents with different perspectives. Agents can adjust their answers based on more information and deeper thinking. The uncertainty and confidence weighting mechanism allows each agent to dynamically adjust its attention weights in the second and third rounds of debate, so that it can self-adjust according to other agents' feedback and approach the correct answer more accurately. As shown in Figure 1(b), all agents in traditional methods depend on a single LLM, which makes the answers have consistent bias and lack of diversity and depth of thinking. 

Therefore, this paper raises a question: Can a third-party model be introduced to complete tasks through the collaboration of multiple Large Language Models? It explores combinations of different LLMs to estimate the confidence levels of each agent and seeks to achieve a broader consensus. 

Our research motivation is to explore how the introduction of third-party Large Language Models (LLMs) and strategies for combining different LLMs can enhance the decisionmaking capabilities and problem-solving depth of multi-agent systems.

citations.title: Ambiguity in LLMs is a concept missing problem
snippets:
LLMs often bias towards generating one interpretation among many for an ambiguous utterance [Saparina and Lapata, 2025]. Prompting LLMs to produce multiple interpretations and directly comparing their semantics do not help ambiguity detection. To show LLMs do not produce different interpretations for an ambiguous utterance, we extract a sentence from the AMBROSIA dataset [Saparina and Lapata, 2024] and prompt Llama-3.3-70B-Instruct [Meta AI, 2024] to generate two interpretations for this sentence. 

Ambiguous Question (): 

Interpretation 1: Show all gate agents who speak Spanish and all pilots who speak Spanish. 

Interpretation 2: Show all gate agents and pilots who speak Spanish. 

Show all Spanish-speaking gate agents and pilots.

citations.title: Beyond Single Models: Enhancing LLM Detection of Ambiguity in Requests through Debate
snippets:
Zhang [12]. Vision-Language Models (VLMs) like FreeGrasp resolve object ambiguities in cluttered scenes [13] and enhance spatial reasoning [14]. Although LLMs allow for broader understanding, challenges such as grounding and hallucinations persist [10,15], making clarifications generated by LLM vital. Our study's use of smaller, locally deployable LLMs targets efficient, low-latency inference for real-time robotics. 

To address single LLM limitations such as biases or presupposing one interpretation [16,17], multi-LLM collaboration and debate are emerging [18]. These frameworks improve reasoning and ambiguity resolution by allowing agents to critique and refine interpretations [16]. Lakara et al. proposed the LLM-Consensus, where agents assess contextual consistency, identify ambiguities, and refine reasoning, potentially using external information [16]. Koupaee et al.'s Madisse framework assigns initial stances to LLM agents for multi-round debates on summary faithfulness, uncovering errors and identifying "ambiguity" from multiple correct interpretations [17]. Such debates show potential for detecting subtle numerical, attribute, and spatial ambiguities. Hierarchical structures, such as leader-follower models, are also explored; ReMA uses a high-level metathinking agent for oversight and a low-level agent for execution [19]. 

The principles of multi-agent debate influence our leader-follower methodology by facilitating structured debate. This helps in considering multiple interpretations and evaluating clarifications for optimal questions, leveraging 'cognitive diversity' for effective ambiguity resolution. While frameworks like Madisse [17] demonstrate debate for evaluating summary faithfulness, our work specifically applies and assesses a debate protocol for the pre-execution analysis of commands in a human-robot in-teraction context, focusing on generating actionable clarification questions.

citations.title: Disambiguation in Conversational Question Answering in the Era of LLMs and Agents: A Survey
snippets:
The next wave of disambiguation in Conversational QA is being shaped by three emerging trends: agentic orchestration, simulation-and reward-driven policy optimization, and evaluation with LLM-asa-judge. 

Agentic orchestration for disambiguation. Recent generations of LLMs (Meta AI, 2024;OpenAI, 2025b,a) offer longer context windows, more reliable tool use, and reasoning-centric architectures. These advances make it increasingly feasible to deploy multi-agent CQA systems (Dibia et al., 2024;Fourney et al., 2024). Within such frameworks, disambiguation becomes a first-class capability for every agent, but especially for the orchestrator or coordinator agent, which explicitly handles user requests and is responsible for carrying forward the task with the help of other agents. 

To operationalize this capability, the orchestrator can leverage agent cards or specifications in tandem with other agents to agree on common nomenclature or establish a constitution. By standardizing specification languages, these can systematically encode explicit policies for query handling and clarification, with Agents.md offering a promising step toward such standardization. For instance, an agent card may include a disambiguation extension that determines when to issue clarification prompts (e.g, which tools to use). Moreover, agentic orchestration can incorporate auxiliary mechanisms, such as memory and verification, to safeguard trajectory alignment. Memory management preserves relevant conversational history (Anthropic, 2025) while filtering out noise, thereby reducing the risk of context drift. LLM verification (discussed separately later) serves as an additional checkpoint, validating whether the system's chosen path aligns with the intended query resolution. 

Conversational engines can further enhance this process by engaging users in real-time clarification. Inspired by Bayesian Experimental Design (BED) (Rainforth et al., 2024), a promising direction in this space, as explored in Kobalczyk et al. (2025), is to actively select questions that maximize expected information gain, shifting from implicit reasoning about the best question to explicit evaluation via sampling from the solution space.

sections.title: # Benchmarks and Evaluations for Ambiguous/Under-Specified Instructions
sections.text: Several benchmarks and evaluation frameworks target instruction following and robustness in agentic scenarios, explicitly capturing long, complex, and underspecified instructions that are common in real applications. AgentBench, Agent-Board, ToolQA, and T-Eval collectively assess multi-turn, partially observable, tool-using tasks, but most focus on general domains and miss vertical domains [d6dbc7a4-1]. AGENTIF collects 50 industrial and open-source agentic tasks, combining each with user queries and system prompts to form long, complex instructions with constraint types (e.g., condition, example, tool specs), and annotates instruction constraints to benchmark instruction following beyond short prompts [d6dbc7a4-2]. A process model and reference architecture emphasize evaluation-driven development/operations for agents due to risks from open-ended planning and execution under ambiguity [d6dbc7a4-0]. Domain-specific evaluations further demonstrate the need for robust handling of ambiguity: in nuclear plant data retrieval, strict schemas and constrained decoding are used to ensure function-call correctness and prevent crashes from format errors. Strict schemas enforced via JSON and Pydantic models, with constrained decoding (e.g., OpenAI’s structured-output mode) that uses grammar-based masking and selective generation to guarantee format compliance and handle complex/nested structures [4e1d334f-2].

citations.title: AGENTIF: Benchmarking Instruction Following of Large Language Models in Agentic Scenarios
snippets:
Large language models (LLMs) have demonstrated strong capabilities in real-world agentic applications [19]. Growing studies focus on developing LLM-based agents to address practical demands, such as Web Agents [7,8], Education Agents [4], GUI Agents [31,32], and PPT Agents [34]. While these agentic scenarios expand the application scope of LLMs, they also pose a new challenge: agentic tasks usually involve long and complex instructions, such as extended system prompts and detailed tool specifications. Correctly following such instructions is a prerequisite for solving these tasks and reflects a fundamental capability of LLMs. However, whether LLMs can effectively follow instructions in real-world agentic scenarios remains underexplored. Previous work on benchmarking instruction following of LLMs has mainly focused on relatively short instructions, which are usually synthetically generated. For example, the widely used benchmark IFEval [36] is synthetically constructed with various constraint types, such as formatting, and has an average instruction length of only 45 words. Subsequent studies have expanded the instruction scope to include more constraint types [14,23,33,29], system prompts [22], multi-turn conversations [10], and action constraints [16]. Nonetheless, the instructions in these benchmarks are typically short and usually synthetically generated, resulting in a gap from real-world agentic applications. Figure 2 illustrates an instruction from a real-world agentic scenario. We can observe that the instruction is long with complex structures and constraint types, such as condition constraints, example constraints, and tool specifications, posing novel and significant challenges for LLMs. As existing instruction-following benchmarks typically lack coverage of such agentic instructions, it is necessary to systematically evaluate LLMs' ability to handle them. 

Considering the above concerns, we propose AGENTIF, the first benchmark to evaluate instruction following of LLMs in real-world agentic scenarios. Specifically, we first collect 50 agentic tasks from industrial applications and open-source agentic systems. For each task, we manually annotate around 20 user queries, each combined with the corresponding agentic system prompt to form an instruction. We then extract all the constraints from each instruction and investigate their types.

citations.title: Evaluation-Driven Development and Operations of LLM Agents: A Process Model and Reference Architecture
snippets:
Large language models (LLMs) are large-scale, pretrained language models with tens of billions of parameters, adaptable to a wide range of downstream tasks, including question answering, summarization, and reasoning [1]. Recent advancements in LLMs have led to the emergence of LLM-based agents, commonly known as LLM agents, which autonomously perform complex tasks (e.g., the AI Scientist [2]). Unlike traditional AI/LLM systems that rely on predefined inputs and structured task execution, LLM agents dynamically interpret high-level, under-specified goals. They perceive context, reason, plan, and execute workflows, often integrating external tools, knowledge bases, and other agents to extend their capabilities [3]. 

Despite their transformative potential, LLM agents introduce significant concerns regarding performance and safety [4]. Their open-ended reasoning, planning and execution processes can produce unpredictable, inconsistent, or even unsafe behaviors, particularly when navigating ambiguous instructions or novel scenarios. Moreover, their autonomy-such as selecting tools, adjusting workflows, and adapting responses-raises governance challenges, as these agents may take actions misaligned with human intent or regulatory constraints. Thus, rigorous, continuous evaluation is essential to ensure that LLM agents operate as expected and evolve safely over time. 

While increasing research attention has been devoted to benchmarking and testing frameworks for LLMs and LLM agents (e.g., [5,6]), existing approaches largely fail to address the full scope of LLM agent evaluation. Classical software engineering methods-such as Test-Driven Development (TDD) and Behavior-Driven Development (BDD)-have proven effective for deterministic systems with clear, predefined specifications. However, these methods are not inherently suited to LLM agents, which operate in open-ended, adaptive contexts and continuously adjust their behavior based on real-world interactions. The effective evaluation of LLM agents requires the following considerations: 

• Evaluating LLM Agents at the System Level. Current evaluation frameworks predominantly assess LLMs at the model level, focusing on such as prompt-response correctness or benchmark-based scores.

citations.title: Enhancing Accuracy and Maintainability in Nuclear Plant Data Retrieval: A Function-Calling LLM Approach Over NL-to-SQL
snippets:
One challenge with agentic LLM systems is ensuring that every piece of data exchanged fits a strict schema or structure. We chose JSON as our preferred format because the data has to be structured, and JSON offers a standard, human-readable way to do so. Whether it's parameters for function calls or data fetched from a database, even slight deviations from the expected structure can lead to crashes or unpredictable behavior. This risk is compounded by issues with data types-for example, the LLM might output a date in a non-standard format or return a string where an integer is expected. To address this, we rely on Pydantic models to enforce precise data types (dtypes) and validate every parameter. If the output doesn't conform to the schema, the system automatically retries the operation, often correcting the issue on subsequent attempts. 

OpenAI's structured output mode further enhances reliability through a technique called constrained decoding. Constrained decoding manipulates the token generation process to ensure that outputs strictly adhere to a predefined schema. It begins by defining a schema-such as a JSON Schema-that outlines the desired structure, which is then converted into a context-free grammar (CFG) that encapsulates the rules of the output language [2]. During token generation, the model dynamically constrains its choices by considering previously generated tokens, the CFG rules, and the current position in the output structure [2]. This process includes token masking, where the list of valid tokens is used to lower the probability of invalid tokens to zero [2]. Additionally, selective generation allows the model to produce tokens only for parts of the output that require active generation-skipping boilerplate or deterministic elements [1][3]-while optimizations during preprocessing help speed up generation and reduce latency [1][3]. This constrained decoding approach ensures 100% consistency with the specified output format and is particularly effective for handling complex, nested, or recursive data structures [3].

citations.title: LegalAgentBench: Evaluating LLM Agents in Legal Domain
snippets:
With the rapid advancement of LLM agents, the demand for evaluating their reasoning and decisionmaking capabilities in complex tasks has grown significantly. Numerous benchmarks have been developed, providing essential references for the systematic study of LLM agents (Liu et al., 2023b;Zhuang et al., 2023;Ye et al., 2024;Yao et al., 2024;Huang et al., 2023;Xie et al., 2023). 

AgentBench (Liu et al., 2023b) is a multidimensional benchmark platform that spans eight distinct environments, including operating systems, databases, and knowledge graphs. It systematically evaluates the performance of LLM agents in multi-turn open-ended generation settings. Agent-Board (Ma et al., 2024) focuses on the systematic evaluation of LLMs in multi-turn interactions. 

It introduces fine-grained progress rate metrics and multidimensional analysis tools to comprehensively assess LLMs' multitasking capabilities in partially observable environments, offering a scientific framework for evaluating interactive LLM performance. ToolQA (Zhuang et al., 2023) covers eight domains and 13 tools, with tasks specifically designed to require external tools and reference materials for problem-solving. This avoids reliance solely on the model's internal knowledge, establishing a new benchmark for assessing LLMs' tool-using abilities. T-Eval (Chen et al., 2024) decomposes the tool utilization abilities of LLMs into six dimensions: planning, reasoning, retrieval, understanding, instruction execution, and result evaluation. This framework comprehensively measures LLMs' performance in using external tools across multiple levels. 

These benchmarks provide diverse tools for exploring the capability boundaries of LLM agents. However, they primarily focus on evaluating LLMs in general domains, lacking systematic guidance and targeted frameworks for vertical domains such as law and medicine. To address this gap, this paper introduces a dataset specifically designed to evaluate LLM agents in the legal domain, offering valuable insights and support for research and practice.

sections.title: # Mitigating Ambiguity With Structured Outputs and Schema Enforcement
sections.text: Structured outputs reduce free-form misinterpretations by constraining LLMs to predefined schemas, providing hard guarantees for downstream tools and agent workflows. Structured output means model-generated content conforms to a predefined machine-readable format (especially JSON Schema), enabling function calling, structured extraction, and multi-step agent workflows; direct prompting alone often underperforms [4e1d334f-0]. Schema-constrained generation validates JSON against a schema and can encode custom rules (e.g., patterns for phone numbers, proper escaping), with failure defined by strict adherence checks via jsonschema [4e1d334f-1]. Constrained generation methods (e.g., Outlines, SGLang, XGrammar) improve adherence but can degrade output quality on complex schemas, and tool-call re-parsing adds post-processing overhead and inconsistencies [4e1d334f-3]. Hybrid approaches that embed schema knowledge and use iterative re-checks or control tokens achieve reliable adherence; schema-first methods guide models to fill required slots and avoid malformed outputs, with trade-offs across fine-tuning, prompt engineering, and constraint-based decoding [4e1d334f-4]. In practice, schema-first pipelines enforce data types and retry on failure, which directly addresses ambiguity-induced type/format errors that propagate into tool calls and database operations. Pydantic models enforce precise data types and validate every parameter; constrained decoding ensures 100% consistency with the specified output format, including handling escape sequences and nested structures [4e1d334f-2].

citations.title: Think Inside the JSON: Reinforcement Strategy for Strict LLM Schema Adherence
snippets:
By embedding knowledge of the schema at the prompt level and using a specialized procedure to keep the generation on track (via tagging, iterative re-checks, or extra control tokens), hybrid systems achieve schema adherence more reliably than a vanilla LLM approach [BTW23]. This structured, schema-first method is key to guaranteeing the outputs are valid, parseable, and aligned with downstream consumption requirements. Schema acts as a blueprint for how the final text must be organized while controllable generation mechanism conditions the model's decoding process on these schema constraints. Instead of free-form text generation, the model is guided to fill in required slots, adhere to the correct format, and avoid extraneous or malformed outputs [BTW23]. 

Each of these approaches comes with effectiveness trade-offs, especially under the stringent demands of regulated industries. Fine-tuning and RLHF can deeply instill format compliance into a model but at high development cost and with less transparency. Prompt engineering is more flexible and avoid retraining, but it relies on the base model's capacity to follow instructions. Constraint-based decoding offers hard guarantees on structure, appealing for compliance, though it requires integrating external constraint logic with the model's output stream. The choice often depends on the specific use case and constraints -for instance, biomanufacturers must consider not only technical accuracy but also validation, auditing, and data governance. Ensuring that LLM-generated records are both accurate in content and precise in format is vital to meet quality and regulatory standards. Recent work underlines that reliable structured generation remains an open challenge, calling for continued research into methods that can robustly align LLM outputs with predefined schemas [ea24a].

citations.title: Learning to Generate Structured Output with Schema Reinforcement Learning
snippets:
Complex Schema. This task requires LLMs to generate a valid JSON string under the constraint of a given schema, which is a fundamental ability in schema-constrained generation scenarios. In this task, LLMs will be provided with a schema and asked to generate a valid JSON string for it. During validation, we first check whether the output string is a valid JSON. If the string is valid, we then use the Python jsonschema library to verify if the generated JSON string strictly adheres to the provided schema constraints. 

Custom Formats. This task involves modifying specific fields in the original schema to adhere to specialized rules, such as phone numbers, file paths (for Linux or Windows), strong password criteria, RGB color codes, base64-encoded strings, or other custom constraints. These rules, expressed as flexible, non-strict guidelines in the field descriptions, go beyond typical JSON Schema specifications. The process first checks the JSON syntax and compliance with the schema, then validates field values based on their unique instructions. We insert const or pattern in the schema for validating those fields. If all checks pass, the response is considered correct. 

Escape Translation. This sub-task tests the LLM's ability to properly handle and escape special characters in strings. The LLM is given a string with special characters that must be escaped correctly and then inserted into a randomly selected field within a nested schema. The evaluation focuses on whether the LLM generates a valid JSON string, as improper escaping can break its validity. It also verifies that the special string is correctly inserted into the designated field. This task highlights the challenge of managing escape sequences in JSON, where specific characters (e.g.,\", \\, \n) must be escaped to maintain correct syntax. Mismanagement of these sequences can result in parsing errors, invalidating the entire output.

citations.title: Learning to Generate Structured Output with Schema Reinforcement Learning
snippets:
The advancement of large language models (LLMs) has significantly expanded their applications across domains such as coding [18], writing [19], and automation [20]. A key aspect of these tasks is generating content in predefined formats, with JSON being one of the most widely used formats for structured data exchange, configuration, and API interaction. 

One approach for structured JSON generation involves direct prompting with a JSON schema [9], where the model is asked to generate valid JSON. While effective for models with native JSON support, those without it often struggle to capture complex schema relationships, resulting in broken or incomplete JSON. To address these limitations, constrained generation methods have been proposed. For example, Outlines [21] restrict the model's predictions to a set of valid tokens, improving schema adherence. Techniques like SGLang [22] and XGrammar [23] further enhance this by improving decoding efficiency. However, these methods can degrade output quality, particularly with complex schemas [24,10]. Additionally, tool call re-parsing [11,25,12,26] can help generate valid JSON by converting tool outputs, but this often requires significant post-processing and struggles to align with standard schemas, leading to inconsistencies. 

While there are benchmarks [27,28,29,30,31] for evaluating structured generation, they typically focus on simpler schemas and lack a detailed analysis of how LLMs perform with complex JSON structures. This work aims to fill this gap by rigorously testing LLMs' ability to adhere to complex, nuanced JSON schemas.

citations.title: SLOT: Structuring the Output of Large Language Models
snippets:
Structured Output and JSON Schema. In the context of LLM, the term structured output means that model-generated content conforms to a predefined, machine readable format rather than freeform natural language (Dong et al., 2024;Jiang et al., 2023b;OpenAI, 2024). Generating structured data from unstructured inputs enables the ability of LLM-based applications to answer questions via function calling, extract structured data and build multi-step agent workflows that allow LLMs to take actions. One of the most widelyused structure format is JSON Schema, which is a declarative language to define structure and constraints for JSON data. JSON schema maintains a consistent pattern, making it easier to ensure data validity and exchange structured data between applications. In this paper, we focus specifically on JSON schema due to its wide adoption. 

Existing Approaches. To enable the model generation to conform to a target JSON schema, existing works mainly opted for three approaches, which have their strengths and weaknesses. Direct prompting, although straightforward, often yields lower performance (Tam et al., 2024). Constrained decoding methods, exemplified by works like (Dong et al., 2024;OpenAI, 2024) Problem Formulation. We focus on the postprocessing setting (Fig. 1), where we assume access to an LLM's unstructured output. We define our task as a text-to-structure problem, i.e., to transform an existing LLM's free-form text output into a structured format according to a specified JSON schema. A more detailed comparison between SLOT and existing mechanisms is presented in Appx (Fig. 4). Given x as an input text and f as the formatting specification, let M θ be a generative model parameterized by θ: M θ (x, f ) → y ′ , and we seek to optimize the probability distribution P y|x, f ; θ) where y is the groundtruth structured output and y ′ the model's structured output. Note that the input text x typically represents a response from an LLM rather than a user query.

sections.title: # Integrated Orchestration: Memory, Verification, and Clarification Policies
sections.text: Agentic orchestration frameworks encode policies for when to ask clarifying questions, use tools, or escalate to users, while memory and verification help maintain alignment under ambiguity. Orchestrator agents can include disambiguation extensions that determine when to issue clarification prompts and which tools to use; memory reduces context drift and LLM verification serves as a checkpoint for trajectory alignment [9a1244de-1]. Conversational engines can select clarifying questions with high expected information gain (e.g., Bayesian Experimental Design-inspired selection), shifting from implicit to explicit evaluation of optimal questions [9a1244de-1]. Safety-oriented testing platforms like ToolEmu expose underspecified tasks to stress agent decision-making and guardrails before real-world execution. ToolEmu, an LM-emulated sandbox, targets the realistic risk of instruction underspecification by adversarially emulating challenging scenarios to test agent safety [d6dbc7a4-3].

citations.title: Check Yourself Before You Wreck Yourself: Selectively Quitting Improves LLM Agent Safety
snippets: Our evaluation leverages the ToolEmu benchmark, an LM-emulated sandbox designed for identifying risks in LLM agents. The framework is ideal for our study as it focuses on the realistic threat model of instruction underspecification, where benign user instructions contain ambiguities that can lead to failures. Its use of an adversarial emulator creates challenging scenarios to robustly test agent safety.

To address this gap, this paper introduces a dataset specifically designed to evaluate LLM agents in the legal domain, offering valuable insights and support for research and practice.

sections.text: Surveys and systematizations of multi-agent methods and debate provide broader context for how agentic orchestration can operationalize ambiguity detection and resolution, including clarifying question generation and policy encoding. snippets:
The next wave of disambiguation in Conversational QA is being shaped by three emerging trends: agentic orchestration, simulation-and reward-driven policy optimization, and evaluation with LLM-asa-judge. 

Agentic orchestration for disambiguation. Recent generations of LLMs (Meta AI, 2024;OpenAI, 2025b,a) offer longer context windows, more reliable tool use, and reasoning-centric architectures. These advances make it increasingly feasible to deploy multi-agent CQA systems (Dibia et al., 2024;Fourney et al., 2024). Within such frameworks, disambiguation becomes a first-class capability for every agent, but especially for the orchestrator or coordinator agent, which explicitly handles user requests and is responsible for carrying forward the task with the help of other agents. 

To operationalize this capability, the orchestrator can leverage agent cards or specifications in tandem with other agents to agree on common nomenclature or establish a constitution. By standardizing specification languages, these can systematically encode explicit policies for query handling and clarification, with Agents.md offering a promising step toward such standardization. For instance, an agent card may include a disambiguation extension that determines when to issue clarification prompts (e.g, which tools to use). Moreover, agentic orchestration can incorporate auxiliary mechanisms, such as memory and verification, to safeguard trajectory alignment. Memory management preserves relevant conversational history (Anthropic, 2025) while filtering out noise, thereby reducing the risk of context drift. LLM verification (discussed separately later) serves as an additional checkpoint, validating whether the system's chosen path aligns with the intended query resolution. 

Conversational engines can further enhance this process by engaging users in real-time clarification. Inspired by Bayesian Experimental Design (BED) (Rainforth et al., 2024), a promising direction in this space, as explored in Kobalczyk et al. (2025), is to actively select questions that maximize expected information gain, shifting from implicit reasoning about the best question to explicit evaluation via sampling from the solution space.

sections.title: # Practical Takeaways for Building Agents That Handle Ambiguity
sections.text:
- Detect ambiguity early: Train or prompt models to enumerate plausible interpretations and highlight missing information, but beware that naive multi-interpretation prompting may not reliably surface ambiguity. LLMs often default to a single interpretation; prompting for multiple interpretations does not reliably help ambiguity detection [b261daba-0]. Agents can be tasked to decide if a command is sufficiently clear or propose a single optimal clarifying question [b261daba-1].
- Use schema-first design: Enforce JSON Schema with constrained decoding and data validation (e.g., Pydantic), and retry/recover on format/type errors; this provides hard guarantees and reduces downstream failures from ambiguous outputs. Structured outputs via JSON Schema enable reliable downstream actions [4e1d334f-0]. Constrained decoding and Pydantic validation ensure format compliance and recoverability [4e1d334f-2].
- Orchestrate with memory and verification: Encode disambiguation policies in agent specs, use memory to avoid context drift, and add verification checkpoints to align trajectories with user intent; select clarifications with information-theoretic guidance when engaging users. Agent cards/specs can encode disambiguation policies; memory and LLM verification help safeguard trajectory alignment; active question selection maximizes information gain [9a1244de-1].
- Leverage multi-agent debate: Use leader–follower or third-party model integration to diversify reasoning and identify edge cases; iterative critique and consensus can improve detection of numerical, attribute, and spatial ambiguities before execution. Introducing third-party LLMs diversifies perspectives and improves consensus under uncertainty [9a1244de-3]. Debate protocols can generate actionable clarification questions and evaluate interpretations in pre-execution analysis [9a1244de-4].
- Evaluate under real-world ambiguity: Use agentic benchmarks that capture long, complex, and underspecified instructions (e.g., AGENTIF) and safety-oriented sandboxes like ToolEmu to stress-test ambiguity handling and guardrails. AGENTIF benchmarks instruction following for long, complex agentic instructions with annotated constraint types [d6dbc7a4-2]. ToolEmu focuses on instruction underspecification as a realistic threat for agent safety [d6dbc7a4-3].

citations.title: Enhancing Multi-Agent Consensus Through Third-Party LLM Integration: Analyzing Uncertainty and Mitigating Hallucinations in Large Language Models
snippets:
Large Language Models (LLMs) have exhibited robust reasoning and creative capabilities. In order to manage more intricate tasks, AutoGen amalgamates the functionalities of LLMs, human inputs, and various tools by constructing agents with distinct roles, thereby offering a tailored multi-agent dialogue setting [1]. This has catalyzed the evolution of multiagent debate systems. In these systems, multiple agents articulate their arguments, while a neutral moderator oversees the debate process to facilitate the attainment of a final resolution [2].By employing multiple instances of language models and engaging in several rounds of proposal and debate regarding their respective answers and reasoning processes, a consensus final answer is ultimately achieved [3]. 

In the process of multi-agent debate, it is common to deploy the same Large Language Model (LLM) for each agent and assign them the same role. This approach has proven effective in multi-agent debates, but it also has limitations, especially when the model's knowledge scope is restricted and lacks external feedback from different models. The use of a single model can lead to a monolithic viewpoint in the debate process, limiting the depth and breadth of the debate. 1(a), we introduce third-party LLMs to enrich the knowledge of multi-agent system, which can provide agents with different perspectives. Agents can adjust their answers based on more information and deeper thinking. The uncertainty and confidence weighting mechanism allows each agent to dynamically adjust its attention weights in the second and third rounds of debate, so that it can self-adjust according to other agents' feedback and approach the correct answer more accurately. As shown in Figure 1(b), all agents in traditional methods depend on a single LLM, which makes the answers have consistent bias and lack of diversity and depth of thinking. 

Therefore, this paper raises a question: Can a third-party model be introduced to complete tasks through the collaboration of multiple Large Language Models? It explores combinations of different LLMs to estimate the confidence levels of each agent and seeks to achieve a broader consensus. 

Our research motivation is to explore how the introduction of third-party Large Language Models (LLMs) and strategies for combining different LLMs can enhance the decisionmaking capabilities and problem-solving depth of multi-agent systems.

Ambiguous Question (): 

Interpretation 1: Show all gate agents who speak Spanish and all pilots who speak Spanish. 

Interpretation 2: Show all gate agents and pilots who speak Spanish. 

Show all Spanish-speaking gate agents and pilots.

citations.title: AGENTIF: Benchmarking Instruction Following of Large Language Models in Agentic Scenarios
snippets:
Large language models (LLMs) have demonstrated strong capabilities in real-world agentic applications [19]. Growing studies focus on developing LLM-based agents to address practical demands, such as Web Agents [7,8], Education Agents [4], GUI Agents [31,32], and PPT Agents [34]. While these agentic scenarios expand the application scope of LLMs, they also pose a new challenge: agentic tasks usually involve long and complex instructions, such as extended system prompts and detailed tool specifications. Correctly following such instructions is a prerequisite for solving these tasks and reflects a fundamental capability of LLMs. However, whether LLMs can effectively follow instructions in real-world agentic scenarios remains underexplored. Previous work on benchmarking instruction following of LLMs has mainly focused on relatively short instructions, which are usually synthetically generated. For example, the widely used benchmark IFEval [36] is synthetically constructed with various constraint types, such as formatting, and has an average instruction length of only 45 words. Subsequent studies have expanded the instruction scope to include more constraint types [14,23,33,29], system prompts [22], multi-turn conversations [10], and action constraints [16]. Nonetheless, the instructions in these benchmarks are typically short and usually synthetically generated, resulting in a gap from real-world agentic applications. Figure 2 illustrates an instruction from a real-world agentic scenario. We can observe that the instruction is long with complex structures and constraint types, such as condition constraints, example constraints, and tool specifications, posing novel and significant challenges for LLMs. As existing instruction-following benchmarks typically lack coverage of such agentic instructions, it is necessary to systematically evaluate LLMs' ability to handle them. 

Considering the above concerns, we propose AGENTIF, the first benchmark to evaluate instruction following of LLMs in real-world agentic scenarios. Specifically, we first collect 50 agentic tasks from industrial applications and open-source agentic systems. For each task, we manually annotate around 20 user queries, each combined with the corresponding agentic system prompt to form an instruction. We then extract all the constraints from each instruction and investigate their types.

citations.title: SLOT: Structuring the Output of Large Language Models
snippets:
Structured Output and JSON Schema. In the context of LLM, the term structured output means that model-generated content conforms to a predefined, machine readable format rather than freeform natural language (Dong et al., 2024;Jiang et al., 2023b;OpenAI, 2024). Generating structured data from unstructured inputs enables the ability of LLM-based applications to answer questions via function calling, extract structured data and build multi-step agent workflows that allow LLMs to take actions. One of the most widelyused structure format is JSON Schema, which is a declarative language to define structure and constraints for JSON data. JSON schema maintains a consistent pattern, making it easier to ensure data validity and exchange structured data between applications. In this paper, we focus specifically on JSON schema due to its wide adoption. 

Existing Approaches. To enable the model generation to conform to a target JSON schema, existing works mainly opted for three approaches, which have their strengths and weaknesses. Direct prompting, although straightforward, often yields lower performance (Tam et al., 2024). Constrained decoding methods, exemplified by works like (Dong et al., 2024;OpenAI, 2024) Problem Formulation. We focus on the postprocessing setting (Fig. 1), where we assume access to an LLM's unstructured output. We define our task as a text-to-structure problem, i.e., to transform an existing LLM's free-form text output into a structured format according to a specified JSON schema. A more detailed comparison between SLOT and existing mechanisms is presented in Appx (Fig. 4). Given x as an input text and f as the formatting specification, let M θ be a generative model parameterized by θ: M θ (x, f ) → y ′ , and we seek to optimize the probability distribution P y|x, f ; θ) where y is the groundtruth structured output and y ′ the model's structured output. Note that the input text x typically represents a response from an LLM rather than a user query.

citations.title: Enhancing Accuracy and Maintainability in Nuclear Plant Data Retrieval: A Function-Calling LLM Approach Over NL-to-SQL
snippets:
One challenge with agentic LLM systems is ensuring that every piece of data exchanged fits a strict schema or structure. We chose JSON as our preferred format because the data has to be structured, and JSON offers a standard, human-readable way to do so. Whether it's parameters for function calls or data fetched from a database, even slight deviations from the expected structure can lead to crashes or unpredictable behavior. This risk is compounded by issues with data types-for example, the LLM might output a date in a non-standard format or return a string where an integer is expected. To address this, we rely on Pydantic models to enforce precise data types (dtypes) and validate every parameter. If the output doesn't conform to the schema, the system automatically retries the operation, often correcting the issue on subsequent attempts. 

OpenAI's structured output mode further enhances reliability through a technique called constrained decoding. Constrained decoding manipulates the token generation process to ensure that outputs strictly adhere to a predefined schema. It begins by defining a schema-such as a JSON Schema-that outlines the desired structure, which is then converted into a context-free grammar (CFG) that encapsulates the rules of the output language [2]. During token generation, the model dynamically constrains its choices by considering previously generated tokens, the CFG rules, and the current position in the output structure [2]. This process includes token masking, where the list of valid tokens is used to lower the probability of invalid tokens to zero [2]. Additionally, selective generation allows the model to produce tokens only for parts of the output that require active generation-skipping boilerplate or deterministic elements [1][3]-while optimizations during preprocessing help speed up generation and reduce latency [1][3]. This constrained decoding approach ensures 100% consistency with the specified output format and is particularly effective for handling complex, nested, or recursive data structures [3].

citations.title: Evaluation-Driven Development and Operations of LLM Agents: A Process Model and Reference Architecture
snippets:
Large language models (LLMs) are large-scale, pretrained language models with tens of billions of parameters, adaptable to a wide range of downstream tasks, including question answering, summarization, and reasoning [1]. Recent advancements in LLMs have led to the emergence of LLM-based agents, commonly known as LLM agents, which autonomously perform complex tasks (e.g., the AI Scientist [2]). Unlike traditional AI/LLM systems that rely on predefined inputs and structured task execution, LLM agents dynamically interpret high-level, under-specified goals. They perceive context, reason, plan, and execute workflows, often integrating external tools, knowledge bases, and other agents to extend their capabilities [3]. 

Despite their transformative potential, LLM agents introduce significant concerns regarding performance and safety [4]. Their open-ended reasoning, planning and execution processes can produce unpredictable, inconsistent, or even unsafe behaviors, particularly when navigating ambiguous instructions or novel scenarios. Moreover, their autonomy-such as selecting tools, adjusting workflows, and adapting responses-raises governance challenges, as these agents may take actions misaligned with human intent or regulatory constraints. Thus, rigorous, continuous evaluation is essential to ensure that LLM agents operate as expected and evolve safely over time. 

While increasing research attention has been devoted to benchmarking and testing frameworks for LLMs and LLM agents (e.g., [5,6]), existing approaches largely fail to address the full scope of LLM agent evaluation. Classical software engineering methods-such as Test-Driven Development (TDD) and Behavior-Driven Development (BDD)-have proven effective for deterministic systems with clear, predefined specifications. However, these methods are not inherently suited to LLM agents, which operate in open-ended, adaptive contexts and continuously adjust their behavior based on real-world interactions. The effective evaluation of LLM agents requires the following considerations: 

• Evaluating LLM Agents at the System Level. Current evaluation frameworks predominantly assess LLMs at the model level, focusing on such as prompt-response correctness or benchmark-based scores.

citations.title: Think Inside the JSON: Reinforcement Strategy for Strict LLM Schema Adherence
snippets:
By embedding knowledge of the schema at the prompt level and using a specialized procedure to keep the generation on track (via tagging, iterative re-checks, or extra control tokens), hybrid systems achieve schema adherence more reliably than a vanilla LLM approach [BTW23]. This structured, schema-first method is key to guaranteeing the outputs are valid, parseable, and aligned with downstream consumption requirements. Schema acts as a blueprint for how the final text must be organized while controllable generation mechanism conditions the model's decoding process on these schema constraints. Instead of free-form text generation, the model is guided to fill in required slots, adhere to the correct format, and avoid extraneous or malformed outputs [BTW23]. 

Each of these approaches comes with effectiveness trade-offs, especially under the stringent demands of regulated industries. Fine-tuning and RLHF can deeply instill format compliance into a model but at high development cost and with less transparency. Prompt engineering is more flexible and avoid retraining, but it relies on the base model's capacity to follow instructions. Constraint-based decoding offers hard guarantees on structure, appealing for compliance, though it requires integrating external constraint logic with the model's output stream. The choice often depends on the specific use case and constraints -for instance, biomanufacturers must consider not only technical accuracy but also validation, auditing, and data governance. Ensuring that LLM-generated records are both accurate in content and precise in format is vital to meet quality and regulatory standards. Recent work underlines that reliable structured generation remains an open challenge, calling for continued research into methods that can robustly align LLM outputs with predefined schemas [ea24a].

citations.title: LegalAgentBench: Evaluating LLM Agents in Legal Domain
snippets:
With the rapid advancement of LLM agents, the demand for evaluating their reasoning and decisionmaking capabilities in complex tasks has grown significantly. Numerous benchmarks have been developed, providing essential references for the systematic study of LLM agents (Liu et al., 2023b;Zhuang et al., 2023;Ye et al., 2024;Yao et al., 2024;Huang et al., 2023;Xie et al., 2023). 

AgentBench (Liu et al., 2023b) is a multidimensional benchmark platform that spans eight distinct environments, including operating systems, databases, and knowledge graphs. It systematically evaluates the performance of LLM agents in multi-turn open-ended generation settings. Agent-Board (Ma et al., 2024) focuses on the systematic evaluation of LLMs in multi-turn interactions. 

It introduces fine-grained progress rate metrics and multidimensional analysis tools to comprehensively assess LLMs' multitasking capabilities in partially observable environments, offering a scientific framework for evaluating interactive LLM performance. ToolQA (Zhuang et al., 2023) covers eight domains and 13 tools, with tasks specifically designed to require external tools and reference materials for problem-solving. This avoids reliance solely on the model's internal knowledge, establishing a new benchmark for assessing LLMs' tool-using abilities. T-Eval (Chen et al., 2024) decomposes the tool utilization abilities of LLMs into six dimensions: planning, reasoning, retrieval, understanding, instruction execution, and result evaluation. This framework comprehensively measures LLMs' performance in using external tools across multiple levels. 

These benchmarks provide diverse tools for exploring the capability boundaries of LLM agents. However, they primarily focus on evaluating LLMs in general domains, lacking systematic guidance and targeted frameworks for vertical domains such as law and medicine. To address this gap, this paper introduces a dataset specifically designed to evaluate LLM agents in the legal domain, offering valuable insights and support for research and practice.
