citations.title: A Survey on Cross-Lingual Summarization
snippets:
It is challenging for an end-to-end model to directly conduct XLS since it requires both the abilities to translate and summarize (Cao et al., 2020). As shown in Figure 1(a), many researchers use the related tasks (e.g., MT and MS) together with XLS to train unified models. In this way, XLS models could also benefit from the related tasks. Zhu et al. (2019) utilize a shared transformer encoder to encode the input sequences of both XLS and MT/MS. Then, two independent transformer decoders are used to conduct XLS and MT/MS, respectively. It is the first time to show the end-toend method outperforms the pipeline ones. Later, Cao et al. (2020) use two encoder-decoder models to perform MS in the source and target languages, respectively. Meanwhile, the source encoder and the target decoder jointly conduct XLS. Then, two linear mappers are used to convert the context representation (i.e., the output of encoders) from the source to the target language and vice versa. In addition, two discriminators are adopted to discriminate between the encoded and mapped representations. Thereby, the overall model could jointly learn to summarize documents and align representations between both languages. 

Although the above efforts design unified models in the multi-task framework, their decoders are independent for different tasks, leading to limitations in capturing the relationships among the multiple tasks. To solve this problem, Takase and Okazaki (2020) train a single encoder-decoder model on both MS, MT and XLS datasets. They prepend a special token at the input sequences to indicate which task is performed. In addition, Bai et al. (2021a) make the MS a prerequisite for XLS and propose MCLAS, a XLS model of single encoder-decoder architecture. For the given documents, MCLAS generates the sequential concatenation of the corresponding monolingual and cross-lingual summaries. In this way, the translation alignment is also implicit in the generation process, making MCLAS achieve great performance in XLS.

citations.title: The University of Alicante at MultiLing 2015: approach, results and further insights
snippets:
Currently, the amount of on-line information generated per week reaches the same quantity of data that the one produced in the Internet between its inception and 2003, time of the Social Network emergency (Cambria and White, 2014). Moreover, the production of such volume of data is delivered in multiple languages, and accessing the relevant content of information or extracting the main features of documents in a competitive time is more and more challenging. Therefore, automatic tasks that can help processing all this information, such as multilingual text summarization techniques, are now becoming essential. 

Back in 2011, the Text Analysis Conference MultiLing Pilot task1 was first introduced as an effort of the community to promote and support the development of multilingual document summarization research. Considering the impact of this shared tasks in the progress of natural language processing technologies, a mutlilingual summarization workshop was also organized in 20132 . 

Nowadays, in 2015, we take part in the 3rd MultiLing event 3 . In this edition, new tasks have been added in order to adapt to social requirements. There were the traditional Multilingual Multi-document and Single-document Summarization (MMS and MSS), coming from previous events, but also new summarization tasks related to Online Fora (OnForumS) -on how to deal with reader comments-and Call Center Conversation (CCCS) -from spoken conversations to textual synopses. 

Taking into consideration the interest that multilingual summarization approaches is gaining among the research community, and the positive impact and benefits it may have for the society, the objective of this paper is to present a multilingual summarization approach within the Mul-tiLing 2015 competition, discussing its potentials and limitations, and providing some insights of the future of this type of summarization based on the average results obtained by us and other participants as well. 

The remaining of the paper is organized as follows. In Section 2 we review the most relevant multilingual summarization approaches, some of them participating in previous MultiLing events. In Section 3, we explain our multilingual summarization approach and the required languagedependent knowledge. Section 4 describes the task in which we participated, and the experiments performed.

sections.title: # Datasets and benchmarks
sections.text:
- XLSM datasets are language-pair focused and often English→L2 (e.g., Hasan et al.’s XLSum with 44 languages, MLSUM in five languages, WikiLingua, MLGSum), supporting zero-shot evaluation and abstractive training; newer resources like XL-Sum broaden coverage to many low- and high-resource languages. - Multilingual summarization datasets span single-document and multi-document across many languages and genres, with community shared tasks (e.g., MultiLing) and tooling to process and evaluate in 100+ languages; recent efforts emphasize dataset construction and evaluation infrastructure for multilingual settings. sections.title: # Evaluation and pitfalls
sections.text:
- In XLSM, pipeline approaches (summarize then translate) are prone to error propagation, where summarization mistakes are amplified in translation; coupling models or making the pipeline differentiable can reduce error compounding. Summarize-and-translate pipelines can suffer error propagation and misalignment; SUMTRA makes the pipeline differentiable and couples components to improve output quality [debc3f00-1].

- Multilingual models trained on many languages can suffer catastrophic forgetting or language interference: fine-tuning on monolingual summarization data can degrade performance in other languages, complicating zero-shot/few-shot multilingual transfer; this motivates specialized training regimes and careful evaluation. Reusing monolingual summarization data in conventional multilingual LMs often compromises generation in other languages (catastrophic forgetting), hindering satisfactory zero-shot and few-shot XLS [debc3f00-1].

- Multilingual evaluation is sensitive to preprocessing and metrics: missing tokenizers or stemmers for low-resource languages can depress ROUGE scores independently of summarization quality; community tooling (multilingual tokenizers, stemmers, ROUGE scorers) is needed for fair comparisons across languages and families. Low-resource language stemmers/tokenizers impair ROUGE, leading to unfair lower scores; a multilingual ROUGE scorer with BPE-based tokenization improves cross-language fairness [4ad009e5-1] Evaluation across languages may not correlate as well with human judgment as in English; multilingual summary evaluation is an open problem with known issues [61ede2a7-2].

sections.title: # Practical contrast checklist
sections.text:
- Focus: XLSM targets a specific L1→L2 summarization function, often English→other; multilingual summarization targets systems and datasets that operate across many languages in multiple directions and settings. CLS/XLSM defines the L1→L2 mapping from document to summary [debc3f00-3] Multilingual summarization spans many languages, genres, and source types [61ede2a7-2].

- Data and tasks: XLSM datasets are typically language-pair corpora (e.g., XLSum, MLSUM, WikiLingua, MLGSum, XL-Sum); multilingual summarization includes multilingual single- and multi-document resources, multilingual inputs/outputs, and community tasks across genres (news, social media, forums, transcripts). English→multilingual resources like XLSum and MLSUM, and multilingual corpora like WikiLingua/MLGSum [4ad009e5-2] XL-Sum broadens language coverage; M2DS addresses multilingual multi-document summarization [4ad009e5-0] Tasks include multilingual single-document and conversational/forums settings [61ede2a7-2].

- Methods: XLSM emphasizes translation-aware summarization (pipeline vs end-to-end, zero-shot abstractive, unified MT/MS/XLS), while multilingual summarization emphasizes multilingual pretraining, cross-lingual data augmentation, translate-then-summarize or summarize-then-translate across many languages, and robust multilingual evaluation pipelines. Unified end-to-end XLS models and multitask setups align summarization and translation for zero-shot/few-shot transfer [debc3f00-0] Multilingual pretrained models and cross-lingual augmentation enable zero-shot multilingual summarization [0af39fe6-0] Multilingual evaluation tooling (BPE-based ROUGE, tokenizers, stemmers) supports fair comparison [4ad009e5-1].

- Risks: XLSM faces error propagation and model misalignment; multilingual summarization faces catastrophic forgetting/language interference and evaluation biases due to tooling gaps; both require careful system coupling and multilingual metrics/tooling. Pipelines can propagate errors; differentiable coupling improves performance [debc3f00-1] Monolingual fine-tuning can degrade other languages (catastrophic forgetting), harming zero-shot/few-shot XLS [debc3f00-1] Evaluation can be biased by missing language-specific processing tools; multilingual ROUGE mitigates this [4ad009e5-1].

snippets: There has been a surge of research on multilingual pretrained models, such as multilingual BERT (Devlin et al., 2019), XLM (Lample and Conneau, 2019) and XLM-RoBERTa (Conneau et al., 2020). For multilingual summarization, the summarizethen-translate and translate-then-summarize are widely used approaches in prior studies Lim et al. (2004). There is another effective multi-lingual data augmentation, a method that replaces a segment of the input text with its translation in another language (Singh et al., 2019). On the other hand, large-scale multilingual summarization datasets have been introduced (Scialom et al., 2020;Ladhak et al., 2020), which enable new research directions for the multilingual summarization. Nikolov and Hahnloser (2020) applies an alignment approach to collect large-scale parallel resources for lowresource domains and languages. In this paper, we aim to advance the multilingual zero-shot transferability, by training extractive summarization on English and inferring on other languages.

citations.title: SumTra: A Differentiable Pipeline for Few-Shot Cross-Lingual Summarization
snippets:
On the other hand, the superposition of too many languages in a single model can result in a degradation of crosslingual performance in the downstream task (i.e., language interference) (Pfeiffer et al., 2022).In addition, it is not trivial to reuse the abundant, existing monolingual summarization data, since finetuning a multilingual LM with monolingual data often compromises its ability to generate text in a language different from the input's (Vu et al., 2022;Bhattacharjee et al., 2022)-a problem known as "catastrophic forgetting" (van de Ven and Tolias, 2019).The above issues compound in the impossibility of achieving a satisfactory zero-shot and few-shot XLS performance out of conventional multilingual LMs.

For this reason, this work revisits the summarizeand-translate approach to XLS (Wan et al., 2010), with the main aim of fully leveraging the existing monolingual summarization resources (i.e., training data, pretrained models) to obtain a performing zero-shot XLS pipeline.Specifically, we propose combining 1) a monolingual summarizer trained with abundant resources in the source language with 2) a pretrained machine translation model that translates into the target language.If the quality of both models is high, such a pipeline should be able to achieve a significant zero-shot performance.Yet, it can also suffer from model misalignment and error propagation.Therefore, we modify the summarizer to output "soft" predictions, ensuring that the pipeline remains fully differentiable end-toend (Subramanian et al., 2017;Kumar et al., 2021;Unanue et al., 2023).This allows fine-tuning it to improve the coupling of the models, alleviate error propagation, and obtain summaries that are closer to the ideal, joint summarization/translation of the XLS task.For immediacy, we refer to the proposed pipeline as SUMTRA.

citations.title: A Survey on Cross-Lingual Summarization
snippets:
It is challenging for an end-to-end model to directly conduct XLS since it requires both the abilities to translate and summarize (Cao et al., 2020). As shown in Figure 1(a), many researchers use the related tasks (e.g., MT and MS) together with XLS to train unified models. In this way, XLS models could also benefit from the related tasks. Zhu et al. (2019) utilize a shared transformer encoder to encode the input sequences of both XLS and MT/MS. Then, two independent transformer decoders are used to conduct XLS and MT/MS, respectively. It is the first time to show the end-toend method outperforms the pipeline ones. Later, Cao et al. (2020) use two encoder-decoder models to perform MS in the source and target languages, respectively. Meanwhile, the source encoder and the target decoder jointly conduct XLS. Then, two linear mappers are used to convert the context representation (i.e., the output of encoders) from the source to the target language and vice versa. In addition, two discriminators are adopted to discriminate between the encoded and mapped representations. Thereby, the overall model could jointly learn to summarize documents and align representations between both languages. 

Although the above efforts design unified models in the multi-task framework, their decoders are independent for different tasks, leading to limitations in capturing the relationships among the multiple tasks. To solve this problem, Takase and Okazaki (2020) train a single encoder-decoder model on both MS, MT and XLS datasets. They prepend a special token at the input sequences to indicate which task is performed. In addition, Bai et al. (2021a) make the MS a prerequisite for XLS and propose MCLAS, a XLS model of single encoder-decoder architecture. For the given documents, MCLAS generates the sequential concatenation of the corresponding monolingual and cross-lingual summaries. In this way, the translation alignment is also implicit in the generation process, making MCLAS achieve great performance in XLS.

citations.title: M2DS: Multilingual Dataset for Multi-document Summarisation
snippets:
In recent years, there has been a notable increase in research exploring the benefits of summarising across diverse languages, particularly in bilingual settings [39].Our focus is directed towards datasets relevant to multilingual summarising, covering SDS, MDS, and Cross-Lingual Summarization (CLS).

While multilingual SDS has seen significant progress, research in multilingual MDS is limited.CLS, involving generating summaries in one language for documents in another language, has gained momentum with the development of multilingual SDS.Many multilingual SDS efforts have transitioned to include CLS components in their datasets [21,9,39,14].

Key multilingual SDS datasets include MLSUM [36], featuring 1.5 million news articles across multiple languages; XL-Sum [14], a diverse dataset containing 1.35 million articles in 44 languages; WikiLingua [18], one of the largest parallel multilingual summarization datasets; MLGSum [40], drawing from various news providers; and M3LS, comprising over 1.11 million multilingual multimodal instances across 20 languages.Despite their contributions for SDS, the exploration of multilingual MDS is limited due to the absence of a dedicated high-quality dataset.

citations.title: MultiLing 2017 Overview
snippets:
MultiLing covers a variety of topics on Natural Language Processing, focused on the multilingual aspect of summarization: 

• Multilingual summarization across genres and sources: Summarization has been receiving increasing attention during the last years. This is mostly due to the increasing volume and redundancy of available online information but also due to the user created content. Recently, more and more interest arises for methods that will be able to function on a variety of languages and across different types of content and genres (news, social media, transcripts). 

This topic of research is mapped to different community tasks, covering different genres and source types: 

-Multilingual single-document summarization (Giannakopoulos et al., 2015); 

-user-supplied comments summarization (OnForumS task (Kabadjov et al., 2015)); -conversation transcripts summarization (see also (Favre et al., 2015)). 

The spectrum of the tasks covers a variety of real settings, identifying individual requirements and intricacies, similarly to previous MultiLing endeavours (Giannakopoulos et al., 2011a;Giannakopoulos, 2013;Elhadad et al., 2013;Giannakopoulos et al., 2015). 

• Multilingual summary evaluation: Summary evaluation has been an open question for several years, even though there exist methods that correlate well to human judgement, when called upon to compare systems. 

In the multilingual setting, it is not obvious that these methods will perform equally well to the English language setting. In fact, some preliminary results have shown that several problems may arise in the multilingual setting (Giannakopoulos et al., 2011a). The same challenges arise across different source types and genres. This aspect of the workshop aims to cover and discuss these research problems and corresponding solutions. 

The workshop builds upon the results of a set of research community tasks, which are elaborated on in the following paragraphs. However, this year MultiLing also hosts works beyond the tasks themselves, but still within the scope of automatic summarization and evaluation in different genres and settings.

sections.title: # Bottom line
sections.text:
- Think of cross-language summarization as the directed, often zero-shot, L1→L2 summarization problem (e.g., English→French/Indonesian), where the system must bridge language gaps via translation and summarization capabilities; evaluate primarily with ROUGE across language pairs. CLS/XLSM defines the source→target language mapping for summaries [debc3f00-3] Unified and zero-shot XLSM methods learn to summarize and align languages [debc3f00-0].

- Multilingual summarization is the broader vision: systems and datasets that work across many languages for multilingual inputs, multilingual outputs, and multilingual-to-multilingual mappings, spanning single- and multi-document settings and multiple genres; it requires multilingual pretraining, careful cross-lingual data strategies, and robust multilingual evaluation tooling to avoid biases and interference effects. Community tasks and surveys emphasize multilingual coverage across genres and evaluation challenges [61ede2a7-2] Surveys delineate multilingual systems as handling many input and output languages [0af39fe6-4] Multilingual evaluation infrastructure is crucial for fairness across 100+ languages [4ad009e5-1].

citations.title: Automatic Text Summarization Methods: A Comprehensive Review
snippets:
Based on the language of input and output of the ATS system, it can be divided into the following 3 categories: 

• Monolingual: In a Monolingual text summarizer, the language of the input document and output summary is the same (Kutlu et al., 2010). 

• Multilingual: In a Multilingual text summarizer, input is written in many languages (Hindi, English, and Gujarati), and output summary is generated likewise in these languages (Hovy & Lin, 1996). • Cross-Lingual: In a Cross-lingual text summarizer, the input document is in one language (say English), and the output summary is in another language (say Hindi) (Linhares Pontes et al., 2020). 

Most of the research papers studied in this article are based on monolingual text summarization. Compared to monolingual, multilingual and cross-lingual is challenging to implement. It takes more effort to train a machine on more than one language structure. SUMMARIST (Hovy & Lin, 1996) is a multilingual text summarization system based on an extraction strategy that generates summaries from English, Indonesian, Spanish, German, Japanese, Korean, and French sources. Cross-Language Text Summarization (CLTS) (Linhares Pontes et al., 2020) generates a summary in a target language from source language materials. It entails a combination of text summarising and machine translation methods. Unfortunately, this combination leads to mistakes, which lowers the quality of summaries. CLTS systems may extract relevant information from both source and destination languages through joint analysis, which improves the development of extractive crosslingual summaries. Recent methods for CLTS have offered compressive and abstractive approaches; however, these methods rely on frameworks or tools that are only available in a few languages, restricting their applicability to other languages.

question: LLM to synthesize material recipe for quantum dot led

sections.title: # Goal: Use an LLM to generate reproducible, evidence-backed “material recipes” for QLEDs
sections.text: Quantum dot LEDs (QLEDs) offer unmatched color purity and tunability, but their synthesis and device engineering involve tight parameter couplings (core/shell composition and thickness, surface ligands, host:guest ratios, energy-level alignment, and processing such as antisolvent quenching and annealing) that strongly affect external quantum efficiency (EQE), color purity, and lifetime. An LLM can synthesize recipes when guided by a literature-grounded knowledge base, explicit device-layer constraints, and quantitative targets, and then produce structured outputs that map to reproducible lab protocols and device stacks. Below we outline how to design and operate such a system, anchored in recent literature.

sections.title: # 1) What the LLM should synthesize: device stack, materials, and key parameters
sections.text:
State-of-the-art QLEDs rely on core/shell nanocrystals with high photoluminescence quantum yield (PLQY), careful energy-level alignment to transport layers, and architecture-level strategies to balance carriers and suppress nonradiative losses. Reviews emphasize that material synthesis (cores, shells, ligands) and device engineering (transport layers, interlayers, and architecture) jointly determine performance and that heavy-metal-free (Cd-free) alternatives are a major focus for commercialization and sustainability due to environmental restrictions on Cd use in mass production. QD-LEDs are widely recognized as alternatives to OLEDs due to enhanced performance; recent surveys cover material synthesis for high-PLQY QDs using heavy-metal free materials and discuss device architectures and fabrication processes for commercialization [ae8c0f2a-0] Engineering core/shell heterostructures dramatically improves PLQY and stability; structural optimizations in QD materials and QLED architectures have driven performance gains in the past decade [ae8c0f2a-3].

Energy-level and interface design are central to high efficiency and lifetime. Mismatched band alignments can cause carrier accumulation, nonuniform recombination, and oxidation of transport layers—especially pronounced in blue QLEDs—leading to rapid degradation. Intelligent energy-level design and tailored interfaces can resolve these issues and meet industrial lifetime targets. Developing proper hole-transport materials to match QD energy levels addresses insufficient hole injection; devices with tailored band structures achieved T95 > 2300 h at 1000 cd/m² and T50 > 2,200,000 h at 100 cd/m², meeting industrial display standards [ae8c0f2a-1] Blue QD-LEDs suffer from severe hole accumulation at the QD/HTL interface; inserting an anti-oxidation layer (poly(p-phenylene benzobisoxazole)) mitigates oxidation and yields T50 > 41,000 h at 100 cd/m² with peak EQE of 23% [107d79d1-0].

White QLED architectures illustrate how to balance multiple emitters or leverage charge-transport layers for white emission, and highlight fabrication challenges such as Förster resonance energy transfer (FRET) between co-deposited QDs and the need for multilayered or tandem structures to suppress efficiency losses. White QLED device architectures have evolved from mixed-QD single EMLs (EQE > 10%) to multilayered QD EMLs to suppress FRET, and tandem structures are expected to dominate for efficient and stable WQLEDs; Cd-free WQLEDs are of growing interest [107d79d1-4] A solution-processed white QD-LED using a hybrid ZnO@TiO2 electron-injection layer and ZnCdSeS emitters achieved 730 cd/m² and 1.7 lm/W with stable performance due to low leakage and insensitivity to oxygen/moisture [107d79d1-1].

citations.title: Recent progress in the device architecture of white quantum-dot light-emitting diodes
snippets:
Great progress has been achieved of late in the device architectures of the Cd-quantum-dot-(QD)-based whitelight-emission quantum-dot light-emitting diodes (WQLEDs). In the early stage of the WQLED development, the white-light emission is usually achieved by combining the complementary emissions from QDs and the adjacent charge transport layers (CTLs). With the development of the device structure, the WQLEDs with a mixed-QD single emission layer (EML) were demonstrated, in which the white-light emission is originated from the red-(R)-, green-(G)-, and blue-(B)-QDs. Tremendous progress has been achieve of late in the efficiency of the WQLEDs with a mixed-QD single EML (external quantum efficiency (EQE) > 10%), but due to the close contact of the QDs, Förster resonant energy transfer (FRET) between different-colored QDs is unavoidable, which causes energy loss and limits the efficiency of the WQLEDs. To suppress FRET, WQLEDs with a multilayered QD EML have been developed, which can reduce the close contact of the different-colored QDs, leading to the suppression of FRET. It is difficult to deposit the multilayered EML, however, due to the intermixing of the adjacent QD EML when processed with the same solvent. By inserting an interlayer between the multilayered EML and the adjacent EML, the issue of intermixing can be avoided, but the charge balance is degraded, resulting in a decrease in the device efficiency. Therefore, developing a novel fabricating process to avoid the intermixing of the adjacent layer, balancing the charge injection, and suppressing FRET are demanded for the further improvement of the device performance of the aforementioned structure. Compared with the structure of the mixed-QD single EML or the multilayered QD EML, the tandem structure is more advantageous and is expected to be the dominant structure for realizing efficient and stable WQLEDs for lighting and display applications. 

Cadmium-free WQLEDs have attracted great attention due to their environment-friendliness.

citations.title: Highly stable QLEDs with improved hole injection via quantum dot structure tailoring
snippets: For the state-of-the-art quantum dot light-emitting diodes, while the ZnO nanoparticle layers can provide effective electron injections into quantum dots layers, the hole transporting materials usually cannot guarantee sufficient hole injection owing to the deep valence band of quantum dots. Developing proper hole transporting materials to match energy levels with quantum dots remains a great challenge to further improve the device efficiency and operation lifetime. Here we demonstrate high-performance quantum dot light-emitting diodes with much extended operation lifetime using quantum dots with tailored energy band structures that are favorable for hole injections. These devices show a T95 operation lifetime of more than 2300 h with an initial brightness of 1000 cd m−2, and an equivalent T50 lifetime at 100 cd m−2 of more than 2,200,000 h, which meets the industrial requirement for display applications. The commercialization of light-emitting diodes based on emissive quantum dots (e.g. QLEDs) is hindered by their inherent poor operational lifetime. Using an intelligent energy-level design strategy, Qian et al. demonstrate QLEDs with operational lifetime that meets industrial display standards.

citations.title: Development of Colloidal Quantum Dots for Electrically Driven Light-Emitting Devices
snippets: The development of quantum dots (QDs) has had a significant impact on various applications, such as solar cells, field-effect transistors, and light-emitting diodes (LEDs). Through successful engineering of the core/shell heterostructure of QDs, their photoluminescence (PL) quantum yield (QY) and stability have been dramatically enhanced. Such high-quality QDs have been regarded as key fluorescent materials in realizing next-generation display devices. Particularly, electrically driven (or electroluminescent, EL) QD light-emitting diodes (QLED) have been highlighted as an alternative to organic light-emitting diodes (OLED), mostly owing to their unbeatably high color purity. Structural optimizations in QD material as well as QLED architecture have led to substantial improvements of device performance, especially during the past decade. In this review article, we discuss QDs with various semiconductor compositions and describe the mechanisms behind the operation of QDs and QLEDs and the primary strategies for improving their PL and EL performances.

citations.title: All Solution-processed Stable White Quantum Dot Light-emitting Diodes with Hybrid ZnO@TiO2 as Blue Emitters
snippets: White quantum dot light-emitting diodes (QD-LEDs) have been a promising candidate for high-efficiency and color-saturated displays. However, it is challenging to integrate various QD emitters into one device and also to obtain efficient blue QDs. Here, we report a simply solution-processed white QD-LED using a hybrid ZnO@TiO2 as electron injection layer and ZnCdSeS QD emitters. The white emission is obtained by integrating the yellow emission from QD emitters and the blue emission generated from hybrid ZnO@TiO2 layer. We show that the performance of white QD-LEDs can be adjusted by controlling the driving force for hole transport and electroluminescence recombination region via varying the thickness of hole transport layer. The device is demonstrated with a maximum luminance of 730 cd/m2 and power efficiency of 1.7 lm/W, exhibiting the Commission Internationale de l’Enclairage (CIE) coordinates of (0.33, 0.33). The unencapsulated white QD-LED has a long lifetime of 96 h at its initial luminance of 730 cd/m2, primarily due to the fact that the device with hybrid ZnO@TiO2 has low leakage current and is insensitive to the oxygen and the moisture. These results indicate that hybrid ZnO@TiO2 provides an alternate and effective approach to achieve high-performance white QD-LEDs and also other optoelectronic devices.

citations.title: Technology progress on quantum dot light-emitting diodes for next-generation displays.
snippets: Quantum dot light-emitting diodes (QD-LEDs) are widely recognised as great alternatives to organic light-emitting diodes (OLEDs) due to their enhanced performances. This focus article surveys the current progress on the state-of-the-art QD-LED technology including material synthesis, device optimization and innovative fabrication processes. A discussion on the material synthesis of core nanocrystals, shell layers and surface-binding ligands is presented for high photoluminescence quantum yield (PLQY) quantum dots (QDs) using heavy-metal free materials. The operational principles of several types of QD-LED device architectures are also covered, and the recent evolution of device engineering technologies is investigated. By exploring the fabrication process for pixel-patterning of QD-LEDs on an active-matrix backplane for full-colour display applications, we anticipate further improvement in device performance for the commercialisation of next-generation displays.

citations.title: Stable and efficient pure blue quantum-dot LEDs enabled by inserting an anti-oxidation layer
snippets: The efficiency and stability of red and green quantum-dot light-emitting diodes have already met the requirements for commercialization in displays. However, the poor stability of the blue ones, particularly pure blue color, is hindering the commercialization of full-color quantum-dot light-emitting diode technology. Severe hole accumulation at the blue quantum-dot/hole-transport layer interface makes the hole-transport layer prone to oxidation, limiting the device operational lifetime. Here, we propose inserting an anti-oxidation layer (poly(p-phenylene benzobisoxazole)) between this interface to take in some holes from the hole-transport layer, which mitigates the oxidation-induced device degradation, enabling a T_50 (time for the luminance decreasing by 50%) of more than 41,000 h with an initial brightness of 100 cd m^−2 in pure blue devices. Meanwhile, the inserted transition layer facilitates hole injection and helps reduce electron leakage, leading to a peak external quantum efficiency of 23%. Blue QD-LEDs suffer from poor operational stability due to the carrier accumulation at transport layers. Here, the authors propose a strategy to mitigate the hole accumulation driven oxidation in hole transport layer, effectively elongating the operational lifetime of blue QD-LEDs.

sections.title: # 2) Parameter space to encode in recipes
sections.text:
An LLM should generate recipes that set:
- Nanocrystal composition and core size, shell material/count, and shell thickness ranges that avoid interfacial strain discontinuities and trap formation.
- Surface ligands and post-synthesis ligand-exchange/ligand removal fractions to maximize PLQY and interfacial stability.
- Host:guest ratios (for host-blend ETL/HTL or mixed QD EMLs) and dopant concentrations (e.g., Cl in perovskites, or shell thickness engineering in Cd-free systems).
- Processing parameters: solvent/antisolvent selection and quenching conditions, film-casting method, and annealing temperatures/times to control phase purity and crystallinity.
- Transport-layer and interface layers (HTL/ETL, buffer/anti-oxidation layers) with aligned energy levels to minimize leakage and carrier accumulation.
- Encapsulation and environmental stability measures.

The literature provides quantitative anchors for many of these parameters.

sections.title: # 3a) Perovskite (CsPbI3) QLEDs: phase control, antisolvent, and annealing
sections.text:
Black-phase CsPbI3 is desirable for QLEDs but typically requires high-temperature annealing (>300 °C), which complicates integration and encapsulation. Low-temperature routes rely on additives, intermediate phases, and antisolvent engineering to form γ-CsPbI3 films with high PLQY and EL efficiency. Black-phase CsPbI3 usually requires annealing above 300 °C; introducing organic ammonium cations enables γ-CsPbI3 deposition at 100 °C and yields QLEDs with EQE of 10.4% and suppressed roll-off by reducing formation energy via low-dimensional intermediates [827905b6-1]. An IPA antisolvent bath immersion treatment enables room-temperature formation of optically active black-phase CsPbI3 films by facilitating cesium ion migration and lowering the reaction energy barrier, offering a scalable, low-cost route for flexible large-area films [827905b6-4]. Solvent-controlled growth, cation-exchange growth with MAI, and mediator-antisolvent strategies have produced high-quality γ-phase films and device efficiencies up to 16.04% in related perovskites, underscoring the importance of composition and crystallization control [827905b6-0].

Annealing conditions critically affect phase purity and trap formation. In CsPbI3 QDs doped films, the annealing temperature and phase evolution can be tracked via XRD peak fitting; an optimal annealing condition near 140 °C maximized CsPbI3 crystallinity and minimized impurity peaks, indicating a phase-pure target. XRD peak fitting shows the peak area ratio of CsPbI3 to MAPbI3 approaches 1 and full-width-at-half-maximum is minimized near 140 °C, indicating optimal crystallization; increasing temperature shifts phase composition toward MAPbI3, so 140 °C is inferred as the optimal annealing temperature [827905b6-3].

Implications for LLM recipe fields:
- Precursor system: Cs precursors with halide (I–/Br–) sources; optional MA/Cs mixed-cation control and HI/acid additives to stabilize black phase.
- Antisolvent: IPA or chlorobenzene with mediator additives; quench time/immersion protocol.
- Annealing: target 100–140 °C ranges for phase formation/activation; avoid >300 °C unless justified for crystallinity.
- Film method: blade coating for scalable large-area films; post-treat with IPA bath for rapid crystallization. IPA bath immersion yields optically active black-phase films at room temperature and is scalable for flexible substrates [827905b6-4].

citations.title: Room-Temperature Perovskite Phase Transition of CsPbI3 for PV Manufacturing on Flexible Substrates
snippets:
Wang et al. addressed the issue of slow crystallization of CsPbIBr 2 , caused by the high boiling point of dimethyl sulfoxide (DMSO), by introducing low-boiling-point alcohol solvents such as methanol and ethanol to form a low-boiling-point DMSOalcohol solvent mixture. 16 This approach effectively reduces the reaction energy barrier and accelerates the crystallization of the CsPbX 3 all-inorganic perovskites. 

In this study, we report the discovery of a novel antisolvent bath immersion treatment using isopropanol (IPA) that enables the direct and rapid formation of optically active black-phase CsPbI 3 perovskite at room temperature. Four approaches for preparing CsPbI 3 perovskites were studied, as summarized in Figure 2. Unlike existing solvent-assisted methods that primarily focus on small-area films (<1 cm 2 ) or rely on post-treatment techniques such as solvent dripping or controlled solvent annealing atmospheres, 2,17,24 our approach is designed specifically for scalable and low-cost fabrication of flexible large-area films. By immersing blade-coated wet films in an IPA antisolvent bath, we have demonstrated a simple yet highly effective method for processing all-inorganic perovskite films at low temperatures, overcoming key challenges associated with traditional spin-coating-based methods and high equipment requirements. 

Moreover, the mechanism of antisolvent action in this work fundamentally differs from previously reported methods. 16,25 e show that hydrogen in HPbI 3 interacts with oxygen in DMF, creating mutual attraction. During immersion in the IPA antisolvent bath, DMF is extracted by IPA, inducing the hydrogen to vacate its original position and allowing free cesium ions to occupy these vacancies. This effectively lowers the reaction energy barrier and facilitates the direct formation of black-phase CsPbI 3 perovskites at room temperature, as supported by in situ optical spectroscopic analysis, NMR, and FTIR data. By providing a scalable, low-temperature, and lowcost method for fabricating high-quality CsPbI 3 films, this work paves the way for the advancement of perovskite-based technologies.

snippets: 2][3][4][5] However, state-of-the-art perovskite devices often employ organic cations such as formamidinium (FA) and methylammonium (MA), which exhibit poor chemical and thermal stability, hindering their commercial application.Replacing these volatile organic cations with inorganic ions such as Cs and Ru has the potential to improve the intrinsic stability of perovskite devices. 6,70][21][22][23] Therefore, it is imperative to develop a plethora of preparation processes to adapt to complex industrial manufacturing and obtain highly phase-pure CsPbI3 thin films.Consequently, You and colleagues reported that high efficiency (PCE=15.7%)α-CsPbI3 PSCs can be fabricated by employing a solvent-controlled growth of perovskite precursors under a dry environment.Moreover, the devices did not show an efficiency drop under continuous light soaking for more than 500 hours. 24Liu et al. reported that careful control over the elemental composition and annealing environment enabled the fabrication of γ-CsPbI3 solar cells with a PCE of 16.3%. 25Alternatively, additives have also proven to be very effective in modulating the perovskite crystallization dynamics, resulting in the formation of high-quality perovskite films.Ho-Baillie and co-workers adopted a cation exchange growth method for fabricating high-quality γ-CsPbI3 by introducing methylammonium iodide (MAI) additive into the perovskite precursor solution, achieving 14.1% device efficiency. 7Alternatively, Li. et al. developed a mediator-antisolvent strategy in which MAI and phenyl-C61-butyric acid methyl ester (PC61BM) were used as additives introduced into the chlorobenzene antisolvent used for device fabrication.The method allowed for obtaining high-quality and stable black-phase CsPbI3 perovskite films with solar cell efficiencies reaching up to 16.04%. 26

citations.title: Intermediate-phase-assisted low-temperature formation of γ-CsPbI3 films for high-efficiency deep-red light-emitting devices
snippets: Black phase CsPbI3 is attractive for optoelectronic devices, while usually it has a high formation energy and requires an annealing temperature of above 300 °C. The formation energy can be significantly reduced by adding HI in the precursor. However, the resulting films are not suitable for light-emitting applications due to the high trap densities and low photoluminescence quantum efficiencies, and the low temperature formation mechanism is not well understood yet. Here, we demonstrate a general approach for deposition of γ-CsPbI3 films at 100 °C with high photoluminescence quantum efficiencies by adding organic ammonium cations, and the resulting light-emitting diode exhibits an external quantum efficiency of 10.4% with suppressed efficiency roll-off. We reveal that the low-temperature crystallization process is due to the formation of low-dimensional intermediate states, and followed by interionic exchange. This work provides perspectives to tune phase transition pathway at low temperature for CsPbI3 device applications. Exploiting low-temperature formed black phase CsPbI3 for light-emitting applications remains a challenge. Here, the authors propose a method to enable the deposition of γ-CsPbI3 films at 100C and demonstrate a light-emitting diode with an external quantum efficiency of 10.4% with suppressed efficiency roll-off.

sections.title: # 3b) Cd-free colloidal QDs: InP/ZnS and ZnSeTe systems
sections.text:
For green/blue and full-spectrum Cd-free QLEDs, InP-based and II–VI alloy systems (ZnSe/ZnSeTe) are leading candidates. Shell thickness and composition engineering reduce interfacial strain and exciton quenching, enabling high EQE and narrow linewidths. Tailoring shell thickness in InP/ZnSe QDs reduced exciton quenching and delivered red-emitting QLEDs with EQE up to 22.5% and luminance 136,090 cd/m²; for green, EQE has approached 16.3% in 2021; blue-emissive Cd-free QLEDs using ZnSeTe/ZnSe/ZnS with controlled internal shell thickness achieved EQE of 18.2% with FWHM 22 nm [13e7fc89-1] A coherent InP/ZnS interface with shell thickness corresponding to ~3 monolayers of ZnS (coherent lattice matching) demonstrates minimized strain and improved structural coherence, guiding sub-nanometer shell design [13e7fc89-2].

Synthesis protocols provide concrete numerical steps the LLM can mirror:
- Hot-injection growth of InP cores followed by ZnS shell growth typically uses core temperatures around 150–220 °C, with sulfurization steps and multiple shell growth passes; post-growth washing (ultracentrifugation with hexane/methanol or acetone) and ligand exchange (e.g., toluene with hexane/ethanol mixture) to remove excess zinc ligands and byproducts. InP core solutions are cooled to 150 °C; Zn and S precursors are added and temperature increased to 220 °C for 40 min per shell; final washing uses 11,000 rpm centrifugation and hexane/methanol precipitation to minimize zinc-based ligands [13e7fc89-0] A stepwise growth protocol heats to 240–260 °C after sulfur precursor injections, with final washing by acetone and density centrifugation (4000 rpm) followed by redispersion in chloroform/acetone (20/80 v/v) for QLED applications [13e7fc89-4].
- Ligand management: PA/OA or ODE-based capping, followed by selective solvent precipitation and ligand exchange to tune solubility and interfacial energy; coherent interfaces benefit from very thin shells (~3 ML). A bound and ordered capping ligand (PA or OA) persists after rigorous washing, indicating ionic adsorption; coherent interfaces are maintained when shell thickness is ~3 ML for small cores (<2.64 nm), aligning lattice constants and reducing dislocations [13e7fc89-2].

Processing choices (solvent/antisolvent, annealing) also affect crystallinity and trap states; scalable blade-coating with post-bath antisolvent quenching is compatible with low-temperature activation. Blade-coated films quenched in IPA antisolvent form black-phase CsPbI3 at room temperature, illustrating low-temperature crystallization compatible with flexible substrates [827905b6-4]. Although shown for perovskites, the same principles (solvent exchange kinetics, antisolvent choice, and low-temperature activation) translate to colloidal QD film formation and can be parameterized in the LLM.

citations.title: Impact of coherent core/shell architecture on fast response in InP-based quantum dot photodiodes
snippets:
We reported previously a new class of InP/ZnS core/shell QDs, where the lattice of InP QD as a core is compressed by 4.1% compared to the bulk crystal while the lattice of ZnS as a shell is expanded by 4.1% compared to the bulk crystal if the shell thickness is less than 0.81 nm (corresponding to three monolayers (3ML) of cubic ZnS) and the diameter of the core QD is less than 2.64 nm. 34 The resulting InP/ZnS core/shell QDs have a single lattice constant of 0.563 nm and provide a coherent and homogeneous interface despite the large lattice distortion between the core and the shell materials. In the present work, the coherent InP/ZnS core/shell QDs were used as a lightabsorbing layer of the vertical photodiode. 

Fig. 1 shows a summary of the results of structural and optical characterization of the coherent InP/ZnS (3ML) core/ shell QD terminated with the PA monolayer. Panel (a) shows a typical XRD pattern of the QD before and aer shell formation. The XRD pattern of the InP core QD has peaks indexed to the (111), (220), and (311) planes of zinc-blend (cubic) bulk crystals of InP, respectively. Aer the 3ML shell formation, the relative shi of each XRD peak toward a higher diffraction angle side happens to give a lattice constant of 0.563 nm. The peak at around 20°appears because of a ligand peak such as PA or OA as discussed later. In the post-synthesis of InP core QDs, the product was washed rigorously by ultracentrifugation with a mixture of hexane (i.e., good solvent) and methanol (i.e., poor solvent) as many as 10 times, but the peak was still present, suggesting that the PA adsorbs on the InP QD via ionic bonds. As supported by Alivisatos and co-workers, this peak indicates a bound and ordered capping ligand on the QD. 35

sections.title: # 3c) Device-layer and interface parameters
sections.text:
LLM recipes must pair nanocrystals with transport and buffer layers whose energy levels offset the QD conduction/valeance bands to balance injection and suppress leakage. Reviews and demonstrations show that selecting ETL/HTL with appropriate band offsets and inserting anti-oxidation/transition layers can dramatically extend lifetime and boost EQE, especially in blue devices. Proper HTL/ETL energy alignment mitigates insufficient hole injection into QDs and enables long lifetimes [ae8c0f2a-1] Inserting PPEBO as an anti-oxidation layer at the QD/HTL interface reduces hole accumulation and oxidation, yielding EQE up to 23% and T50 > 41,000 h at 100 cd/m² in pure blue QLEDs [107d79d1-0] Hybrid ZnO@TiO2 ETLs provide low leakage and stability against oxygen/moisture in white QLEDs, with performance tunable via HTL thickness that controls the hole transport driving force and recombination region [107d79d1-1].

Architecture selection (bilayer, mixed/single EML, multilayer EML, or tandem) should be guided by color purity and mixing losses; the LLM can choose among these based on target color and efficiency goals and incorporate interlayers to suppress FRET and maintain charge balance. Mixed-QD single EMLs achieve EQE > 10% but suffer FRET; multilayered EMLs suppress FRET but require fabrication that avoids intermixing and maintains charge balance; tandem structures are advantageous for efficient and stable WQLEDs [107d79d1-4].

citations.title: All Solution-processed Stable White Quantum Dot Light-emitting Diodes with Hybrid ZnO@TiO2 as Blue Emitters
snippets: White quantum dot light-emitting diodes (QD-LEDs) have been a promising candidate for high-efficiency and color-saturated displays. However, it is challenging to integrate various QD emitters into one device and also to obtain efficient blue QDs. Here, we report a simply solution-processed white QD-LED using a hybrid ZnO@TiO2 as electron injection layer and ZnCdSeS QD emitters. The white emission is obtained by integrating the yellow emission from QD emitters and the blue emission generated from hybrid ZnO@TiO2 layer. We show that the performance of white QD-LEDs can be adjusted by controlling the driving force for hole transport and electroluminescence recombination region via varying the thickness of hole transport layer. The device is demonstrated with a maximum luminance of 730 cd/m2 and power efficiency of 1.7 lm/W, exhibiting the Commission Internationale de l’Enclairage (CIE) coordinates of (0.33, 0.33). The unencapsulated white QD-LED has a long lifetime of 96 h at its initial luminance of 730 cd/m2, primarily due to the fact that the device with hybrid ZnO@TiO2 has low leakage current and is insensitive to the oxygen and the moisture. These results indicate that hybrid ZnO@TiO2 provides an alternate and effective approach to achieve high-performance white QD-LEDs and also other optoelectronic devices.

citations.title: Stable and efficient pure blue quantum-dot LEDs enabled by inserting an anti-oxidation layer
snippets: The efficiency and stability of red and green quantum-dot light-emitting diodes have already met the requirements for commercialization in displays. However, the poor stability of the blue ones, particularly pure blue color, is hindering the commercialization of full-color quantum-dot light-emitting diode technology. Severe hole accumulation at the blue quantum-dot/hole-transport layer interface makes the hole-transport layer prone to oxidation, limiting the device operational lifetime. Here, we propose inserting an anti-oxidation layer (poly(p-phenylene benzobisoxazole)) between this interface to take in some holes from the hole-transport layer, which mitigates the oxidation-induced device degradation, enabling a T_50 (time for the luminance decreasing by 50%) of more than 41,000 h with an initial brightness of 100 cd m^−2 in pure blue devices. Meanwhile, the inserted transition layer facilitates hole injection and helps reduce electron leakage, leading to a peak external quantum efficiency of 23%. Blue QD-LEDs suffer from poor operational stability due to the carrier accumulation at transport layers. Here, the authors propose a strategy to mitigate the hole accumulation driven oxidation in hole transport layer, effectively elongating the operational lifetime of blue QD-LEDs.

citations.title: Recent progress in the device architecture of white quantum-dot light-emitting diodes
snippets:
Great progress has been achieved of late in the device architectures of the Cd-quantum-dot-(QD)-based whitelight-emission quantum-dot light-emitting diodes (WQLEDs). In the early stage of the WQLED development, the white-light emission is usually achieved by combining the complementary emissions from QDs and the adjacent charge transport layers (CTLs). With the development of the device structure, the WQLEDs with a mixed-QD single emission layer (EML) were demonstrated, in which the white-light emission is originated from the red-(R)-, green-(G)-, and blue-(B)-QDs. Tremendous progress has been achieve of late in the efficiency of the WQLEDs with a mixed-QD single EML (external quantum efficiency (EQE) > 10%), but due to the close contact of the QDs, Förster resonant energy transfer (FRET) between different-colored QDs is unavoidable, which causes energy loss and limits the efficiency of the WQLEDs. To suppress FRET, WQLEDs with a multilayered QD EML have been developed, which can reduce the close contact of the different-colored QDs, leading to the suppression of FRET. It is difficult to deposit the multilayered EML, however, due to the intermixing of the adjacent QD EML when processed with the same solvent. By inserting an interlayer between the multilayered EML and the adjacent EML, the issue of intermixing can be avoided, but the charge balance is degraded, resulting in a decrease in the device efficiency. Therefore, developing a novel fabricating process to avoid the intermixing of the adjacent layer, balancing the charge injection, and suppressing FRET are demanded for the further improvement of the device performance of the aforementioned structure. Compared with the structure of the mixed-QD single EML or the multilayered QD EML, the tandem structure is more advantageous and is expected to be the dominant structure for realizing efficient and stable WQLEDs for lighting and display applications. 

Cadmium-free WQLEDs have attracted great attention due to their environment-friendliness.

citations.title: Highly stable QLEDs with improved hole injection via quantum dot structure tailoring
snippets: For the state-of-the-art quantum dot light-emitting diodes, while the ZnO nanoparticle layers can provide effective electron injections into quantum dots layers, the hole transporting materials usually cannot guarantee sufficient hole injection owing to the deep valence band of quantum dots. Developing proper hole transporting materials to match energy levels with quantum dots remains a great challenge to further improve the device efficiency and operation lifetime. Here we demonstrate high-performance quantum dot light-emitting diodes with much extended operation lifetime using quantum dots with tailored energy band structures that are favorable for hole injections. These devices show a T95 operation lifetime of more than 2300 h with an initial brightness of 1000 cd m−2, and an equivalent T50 lifetime at 100 cd m−2 of more than 2,200,000 h, which meets the industrial requirement for display applications. The commercialization of light-emitting diodes based on emissive quantum dots (e.g. QLEDs) is hindered by their inherent poor operational lifetime. Using an intelligent energy-level design strategy, Qian et al. demonstrate QLEDs with operational lifetime that meets industrial display standards.

sections.title: # 4) LLM workflow and prompt schema
sections.text:
We propose a retrieval-augmented LLM workflow that iteratively selects materials, aligns device layers, and generates step-by-step synthesis and processing recipes, with built-in constraints and validation checks.

- Knowledge base and retrieval: The LLM is grounded in a structured database of QLED materials (cores, shells, ligands), device stacks (bilayer/mixed EML/tandem), and processing know-how (solvent/antisolvent sets, annealing windows, encapsulation). The system retrieves evidence for: band offsets and energy-level alignments; shell thickness windows (e.g., ~3 ML coherence); ligand exchange protocols; antisolvent/annealing conditions; and lifetime-impacting interface strategies. Surveys cover synthesis and device optimization to guide retrieval [ae8c0f2a-0] Coherent interface shell thickness guidance [13e7fc89-2] Low-temperature phase formation and antisolvent strategies [827905b6-1][827905b6-4] Interface and buffer layer impacts on lifetime and EQE [107d79d1-0][107d79d1-1].

- Goal specification: User-specified targets (color/peak wavelength, target EQE/EL external quantum efficiency, brightness, lifetime at 100 cd/m², form factor, Cd-free constraint). The LLM maps these to emitter composition and core size (e.g., InP for green/blue, ZnSeTe for blue), shell count/thickness, and host:guest ratios.

- Architecture selection: Based on color (single wavelength vs. white), the LLM selects a device architecture and layer stack, including ETL/HTL types and any anti-oxidation or transition layers. It checks energy-level compatibility and leakage pathways. Architecture evolution and FRET suppression strategies are retrieved to inform the choice among single/multilayer/mixed EML and tandem designs [107d79d1-4].

- Parameterization and recipe drafting:
 - Nanocrystal recipe: core diameter, shell count/thickness (e.g., InP/ZnS with ~3 ML shell for coherent interface), dopant content (e.g., Cl in perovskites), ligands (PA/OA or ODE; exchange solvents and fractions), and growth temperatures/times. Hot-injection growth steps and washing protocols with explicit temperatures and centrifugation conditions provide a template [13e7fc89-0][13e7fc89-4] Coherent interface guidance for sub-nanometer shells [13e7fc89-2].
 - Processing recipe: solvent/antisolvent (e.g., IPA antisolvent bath; chlorobenzene with mediator additives), quench time, film deposition method (spin vs. blade), and annealing (e.g., 100–140 °C for perovskites; mild thermal activation for colloids), with XRD/PL checks for phase purity and PLQY. Low-temperature γ-phase formation at 100 °C via additive-assisted crystallization [827905b6-1] IPA bath immersion for room-temperature black-phase formation [827905b6-4] 140 °C annealing as an optimal crystallization point inferred from XRD peak fitting [827905b6-3].
 - Device stack lamination: HTL/ETL thicknesses and buffer layers (e.g., PPEBO anti-oxidation for blue), contact metals, and encapsulation layers. Anti-oxidation layer improves blue QLED lifetime and EQE [107d79d1-0] Hybrid ZnO@TiO2 ETL with low leakage and environmental stability [107d79d1-1].

snippets:
Wang et al. addressed the issue of slow crystallization of CsPbIBr 2 , caused by the high boiling point of dimethyl sulfoxide (DMSO), by introducing low-boiling-point alcohol solvents such as methanol and ethanol to form a low-boiling-point DMSOalcohol solvent mixture. 16 This approach effectively reduces the reaction energy barrier and accelerates the crystallization of the CsPbX 3 all-inorganic perovskites. 

In this study, we report the discovery of a novel antisolvent bath immersion treatment using isopropanol (IPA) that enables the direct and rapid formation of optically active black-phase CsPbI 3 perovskite at room temperature. Four approaches for preparing CsPbI 3 perovskites were studied, as summarized in Figure 2. Unlike existing solvent-assisted methods that primarily focus on small-area films (<1 cm 2 ) or rely on post-treatment techniques such as solvent dripping or controlled solvent annealing atmospheres, 2,17,24 our approach is designed specifically for scalable and low-cost fabrication of flexible large-area films. By immersing blade-coated wet films in an IPA antisolvent bath, we have demonstrated a simple yet highly effective method for processing all-inorganic perovskite films at low temperatures, overcoming key challenges associated with traditional spin-coating-based methods and high equipment requirements.

citations.title: Recent progress in the device architecture of white quantum-dot light-emitting diodes
snippets:
Great progress has been achieved of late in the device architectures of the Cd-quantum-dot-(QD)-based whitelight-emission quantum-dot light-emitting diodes (WQLEDs). In the early stage of the WQLED development, the white-light emission is usually achieved by combining the complementary emissions from QDs and the adjacent charge transport layers (CTLs). With the development of the device structure, the WQLEDs with a mixed-QD single emission layer (EML) were demonstrated, in which the white-light emission is originated from the red-(R)-, green-(G)-, and blue-(B)-QDs. Tremendous progress has been achieve of late in the efficiency of the WQLEDs with a mixed-QD single EML (external quantum efficiency (EQE) > 10%), but due to the close contact of the QDs, Förster resonant energy transfer (FRET) between different-colored QDs is unavoidable, which causes energy loss and limits the efficiency of the WQLEDs. To suppress FRET, WQLEDs with a multilayered QD EML have been developed, which can reduce the close contact of the different-colored QDs, leading to the suppression of FRET. It is difficult to deposit the multilayered EML, however, due to the intermixing of the adjacent QD EML when processed with the same solvent. By inserting an interlayer between the multilayered EML and the adjacent EML, the issue of intermixing can be avoided, but the charge balance is degraded, resulting in a decrease in the device efficiency. Therefore, developing a novel fabricating process to avoid the intermixing of the adjacent layer, balancing the charge injection, and suppressing FRET are demanded for the further improvement of the device performance of the aforementioned structure. Compared with the structure of the mixed-QD single EML or the multilayered QD EML, the tandem structure is more advantageous and is expected to be the dominant structure for realizing efficient and stable WQLEDs for lighting and display applications. 

Cadmium-free WQLEDs have attracted great attention due to their environment-friendliness.

citations.title: Intermediate-phase-assisted low-temperature formation of γ-CsPbI3 films for high-efficiency deep-red light-emitting devices
snippets: Black phase CsPbI3 is attractive for optoelectronic devices, while usually it has a high formation energy and requires an annealing temperature of above 300 °C. The formation energy can be significantly reduced by adding HI in the precursor. However, the resulting films are not suitable for light-emitting applications due to the high trap densities and low photoluminescence quantum efficiencies, and the low temperature formation mechanism is not well understood yet. Here, we demonstrate a general approach for deposition of γ-CsPbI3 films at 100 °C with high photoluminescence quantum efficiencies by adding organic ammonium cations, and the resulting light-emitting diode exhibits an external quantum efficiency of 10.4% with suppressed efficiency roll-off. We reveal that the low-temperature crystallization process is due to the formation of low-dimensional intermediate states, and followed by interionic exchange. This work provides perspectives to tune phase transition pathway at low temperature for CsPbI3 device applications. Exploiting low-temperature formed black phase CsPbI3 for light-emitting applications remains a challenge. Here, the authors propose a method to enable the deposition of γ-CsPbI3 films at 100C and demonstrate a light-emitting diode with an external quantum efficiency of 10.4% with suppressed efficiency roll-off.

citations.title: All Solution-processed Stable White Quantum Dot Light-emitting Diodes with Hybrid ZnO@TiO2 as Blue Emitters
snippets: White quantum dot light-emitting diodes (QD-LEDs) have been a promising candidate for high-efficiency and color-saturated displays. However, it is challenging to integrate various QD emitters into one device and also to obtain efficient blue QDs. Here, we report a simply solution-processed white QD-LED using a hybrid ZnO@TiO2 as electron injection layer and ZnCdSeS QD emitters. The white emission is obtained by integrating the yellow emission from QD emitters and the blue emission generated from hybrid ZnO@TiO2 layer. We show that the performance of white QD-LEDs can be adjusted by controlling the driving force for hole transport and electroluminescence recombination region via varying the thickness of hole transport layer. The device is demonstrated with a maximum luminance of 730 cd/m2 and power efficiency of 1.7 lm/W, exhibiting the Commission Internationale de l’Enclairage (CIE) coordinates of (0.33, 0.33). The unencapsulated white QD-LED has a long lifetime of 96 h at its initial luminance of 730 cd/m2, primarily due to the fact that the device with hybrid ZnO@TiO2 has low leakage current and is insensitive to the oxygen and the moisture. These results indicate that hybrid ZnO@TiO2 provides an alternate and effective approach to achieve high-performance white QD-LEDs and also other optoelectronic devices.

citations.title: Technology progress on quantum dot light-emitting diodes for next-generation displays.
snippets: Quantum dot light-emitting diodes (QD-LEDs) are widely recognised as great alternatives to organic light-emitting diodes (OLEDs) due to their enhanced performances. This focus article surveys the current progress on the state-of-the-art QD-LED technology including material synthesis, device optimization and innovative fabrication processes. A discussion on the material synthesis of core nanocrystals, shell layers and surface-binding ligands is presented for high photoluminescence quantum yield (PLQY) quantum dots (QDs) using heavy-metal free materials. The operational principles of several types of QD-LED device architectures are also covered, and the recent evolution of device engineering technologies is investigated. By exploring the fabrication process for pixel-patterning of QD-LEDs on an active-matrix backplane for full-colour display applications, we anticipate further improvement in device performance for the commercialisation of next-generation displays.

citations.title: Stable and efficient pure blue quantum-dot LEDs enabled by inserting an anti-oxidation layer
snippets: The efficiency and stability of red and green quantum-dot light-emitting diodes have already met the requirements for commercialization in displays. However, the poor stability of the blue ones, particularly pure blue color, is hindering the commercialization of full-color quantum-dot light-emitting diode technology. Severe hole accumulation at the blue quantum-dot/hole-transport layer interface makes the hole-transport layer prone to oxidation, limiting the device operational lifetime. Here, we propose inserting an anti-oxidation layer (poly(p-phenylene benzobisoxazole)) between this interface to take in some holes from the hole-transport layer, which mitigates the oxidation-induced device degradation, enabling a T_50 (time for the luminance decreasing by 50%) of more than 41,000 h with an initial brightness of 100 cd m^−2 in pure blue devices. Meanwhile, the inserted transition layer facilitates hole injection and helps reduce electron leakage, leading to a peak external quantum efficiency of 23%. Blue QD-LEDs suffer from poor operational stability due to the carrier accumulation at transport layers. Here, the authors propose a strategy to mitigate the hole accumulation driven oxidation in hole transport layer, effectively elongating the operational lifetime of blue QD-LEDs.

sections.title: # 5) Example generated recipes (templated)
sections.text:
Because direct LLM-to-recipe papers are scarce, we translate literature protocols into templates the LLM can fill in with user goals.

Perovskite (CsPbI3) QLED recipe template (Cd-free):
- Emitter: CsPbI3 black-phase nanocrystals; optional MA/Cs mixed-cation control.
- Antisolvent: IPA bath immersion; optional mediator additives to assist phase conversion. IPA bath enables room-temperature black-phase formation via solvent exchange mechanism [827905b6-4].
- Film method: Blade-coated wet film; immersion time 10–60 s; substrate temperature 60–80 °C post-quench. Scalable blade-coating with IPA bath is suitable for flexible large-area films [827905b6-4].
- Annealing: 100–140 °C for 1–10 min; monitor XRD peak area ratio (CsPbI3 vs MAPbI3) and FWHM to confirm phase purity. γ-CsPbI3 can be deposited at 100 °C with high PLQY and EL efficiency [827905b6-1] 140 °C annealing near optimum inferred from XRD peak fitting and minimal FWHM [827905b6-3].
- Device layers: ETL (ZnO nanoparticles or TiO2), HTL (e.g., Spiro-OMeTAD or TCTA), anti-oxidation buffer for blue (e.g., PPEBO), PEDOT:PSS variant for hole injection; stack for band alignment and low leakage. Energy-level matching reduces hole accumulation and improves lifetime [ae8c0f2a-1] PPEBO buffer at QD/HTL interface extends lifetime and achieves peak EQE 23% in blue [107d79d1-0] Hybrid ZnO@TiO2 ETL improves stability against oxygen/moisture [107d79d1-1].

Cd-free InP/ZnS QLED recipe template (blue/green):
- Core: InP (e.g., 2–3 nm diameter) with ODE/PA capping; synthesize by hot-injection.
- Shells: ZnS growth at 220–260 °C; number of shells and thickness guided to coherent interface (~3 ML for small cores). ZnS shell growth at 220 °C for 40 min per shell after InP core at 150 °C [13e7fc89-0] Coherent InP/ZnS with ~3 ML shell maintains single lattice constant and reduces strain [13e7fc89-2].
- Post-synthesis: Ultracentrifugation (e.g., 11,000 rpm, 3–10 min) with hexane/methanol to remove zinc ligands; optional ligand exchange into toluene or chloroform/acetone mix for film processing. Multiple high-speed centrifugations and hexane/methanol precipitation minimize zinc-based ligands [13e7fc89-0] Redispersion in chloroform/acetone (20/80 v/v) and centrifugation for QLED applications [13e7fc89-4].
- Film formation: Solution processing (spin/blade) with antisolvent quench (e.g., methanol/ethanol) if needed; annealing 80–120 °C for 5–15 min to improve crystallinity. Drop-casting and drying at 100 °C were used to assess QD films [13e7fc89-0].
- Device layers: HTL (TCTA or Spiro-OMeTAD), ETL (ZnO or ZnCdSeS host), optional anti-oxidation buffer for blue; white devices can blend multiple QD colors or use multilayer EMLs with interlayers to suppress FRET. Tandem and multilayer EML strategies suppress FRET while maintaining charge balance [107d79d1-4] White QLED via ZnCdSeS emitters and ZnO@TiO2 ETL with stable performance [107d79d1-1].

Cd-free ZnSeTe/ZnSe/ZnS blue QLED template:
- Core/shell: ZnSeTe internal shell, ZnSe, ZnS outer shell; shell thickness tuned to minimize nonradiative Auger/strain (internal shell thin, outer shell thick for stability).
- Synthesis: High-temperature hot injection with sulfurization steps and shell-by-shell growth; final washing and ligand exchange to solubility in chloroform/acetone for film formation. Sequential sulfur precursor injections and temperature ramps (240–260 °C) followed by washing and redispersion provide a transferable shell growth workflow [13e7fc89-4].
- Device: ETL/HTL with appropriate offsets; internal shell thickness control to reach EQE ~18% with narrow linewidth. Controlling internal shell thickness in ZnSeTe/ZnSe/ZnS yields EQE 18.2% with FWHM 22 nm [13e7fc89-1].

citations.title: Highly stable QLEDs with improved hole injection via quantum dot structure tailoring
snippets: For the state-of-the-art quantum dot light-emitting diodes, while the ZnO nanoparticle layers can provide effective electron injections into quantum dots layers, the hole transporting materials usually cannot guarantee sufficient hole injection owing to the deep valence band of quantum dots. Developing proper hole transporting materials to match energy levels with quantum dots remains a great challenge to further improve the device efficiency and operation lifetime. Here we demonstrate high-performance quantum dot light-emitting diodes with much extended operation lifetime using quantum dots with tailored energy band structures that are favorable for hole injections. These devices show a T95 operation lifetime of more than 2300 h with an initial brightness of 1000 cd m−2, and an equivalent T50 lifetime at 100 cd m−2 of more than 2,200,000 h, which meets the industrial requirement for display applications. The commercialization of light-emitting diodes based on emissive quantum dots (e.g. QLEDs) is hindered by their inherent poor operational lifetime. Using an intelligent energy-level design strategy, Qian et al. demonstrate QLEDs with operational lifetime that meets industrial display standards.

citations.title: Intermediate-phase-assisted low-temperature formation of γ-CsPbI3 films for high-efficiency deep-red light-emitting devices
snippets: Black phase CsPbI3 is attractive for optoelectronic devices, while usually it has a high formation energy and requires an annealing temperature of above 300 °C. The formation energy can be significantly reduced by adding HI in the precursor. However, the resulting films are not suitable for light-emitting applications due to the high trap densities and low photoluminescence quantum efficiencies, and the low temperature formation mechanism is not well understood yet. Here, we demonstrate a general approach for deposition of γ-CsPbI3 films at 100 °C with high photoluminescence quantum efficiencies by adding organic ammonium cations, and the resulting light-emitting diode exhibits an external quantum efficiency of 10.4% with suppressed efficiency roll-off. We reveal that the low-temperature crystallization process is due to the formation of low-dimensional intermediate states, and followed by interionic exchange. This work provides perspectives to tune phase transition pathway at low temperature for CsPbI3 device applications. Exploiting low-temperature formed black phase CsPbI3 for light-emitting applications remains a challenge. Here, the authors propose a method to enable the deposition of γ-CsPbI3 films at 100C and demonstrate a light-emitting diode with an external quantum efficiency of 10.4% with suppressed efficiency roll-off.

citations.title: Stable and efficient pure blue quantum-dot LEDs enabled by inserting an anti-oxidation layer
snippets: The efficiency and stability of red and green quantum-dot light-emitting diodes have already met the requirements for commercialization in displays. However, the poor stability of the blue ones, particularly pure blue color, is hindering the commercialization of full-color quantum-dot light-emitting diode technology. Severe hole accumulation at the blue quantum-dot/hole-transport layer interface makes the hole-transport layer prone to oxidation, limiting the device operational lifetime. Here, we propose inserting an anti-oxidation layer (poly(p-phenylene benzobisoxazole)) between this interface to take in some holes from the hole-transport layer, which mitigates the oxidation-induced device degradation, enabling a T_50 (time for the luminance decreasing by 50%) of more than 41,000 h with an initial brightness of 100 cd m^−2 in pure blue devices. Meanwhile, the inserted transition layer facilitates hole injection and helps reduce electron leakage, leading to a peak external quantum efficiency of 23%. Blue QD-LEDs suffer from poor operational stability due to the carrier accumulation at transport layers. Here, the authors propose a strategy to mitigate the hole accumulation driven oxidation in hole transport layer, effectively elongating the operational lifetime of blue QD-LEDs.

sections.title: # 6) Validation, safety, and stability
sections.text:
Recipes should include in-line checks: PLQY, XRD phase purity (black-phase signatures), and electrical characterization (J–V–L, EQE, spectral purity). Lifetime testing at 100 cd/m² with standardized color stability is essential; LLM-generated recipes should note expected benchmarks and mitigation strategies. Industrial display standards include T95 > 2300 h at 1000 cd/m² and T50 > 2.2×10^6 h at 100 cd/m² when energy-levels are well-matched [ae8c0f2a-1] Blue devices benefit from anti-oxidation layers to reach T50 > 41,000 h at 100 cd/m² with high EQE [107d79d1-0].

For safety and scalability, enforce Cd-free targets, select low-VOC or low-temperature antisolvents (IPA, ethanol/methanol blends) where possible, and adopt low-temperature activation to reduce encapsulation demands and substrate constraints. Cd-free material adoption is driven by environmental restrictions for mass production [ae8c0f2a-0] IPA-based room-temperature crystallization supports scalable, low-cost, flexible processing [827905b6-4].

citations.title: Technology progress on quantum dot light-emitting diodes for next-generation displays.
snippets: Quantum dot light-emitting diodes (QD-LEDs) are widely recognised as great alternatives to organic light-emitting diodes (OLEDs) due to their enhanced performances. This focus article surveys the current progress on the state-of-the-art QD-LED technology including material synthesis, device optimization and innovative fabrication processes. A discussion on the material synthesis of core nanocrystals, shell layers and surface-binding ligands is presented for high photoluminescence quantum yield (PLQY) quantum dots (QDs) using heavy-metal free materials. The operational principles of several types of QD-LED device architectures are also covered, and the recent evolution of device engineering technologies is investigated. By exploring the fabrication process for pixel-patterning of QD-LEDs on an active-matrix backplane for full-colour display applications, we anticipate further improvement in device performance for the commercialisation of next-generation displays.

citations.title: Room-Temperature Perovskite Phase Transition of CsPbI3 for PV Manufacturing on Flexible Substrates
snippets:
Wang et al. addressed the issue of slow crystallization of CsPbIBr 2 , caused by the high boiling point of dimethyl sulfoxide (DMSO), by introducing low-boiling-point alcohol solvents such as methanol and ethanol to form a low-boiling-point DMSOalcohol solvent mixture. 16 This approach effectively reduces the reaction energy barrier and accelerates the crystallization of the CsPbX 3 all-inorganic perovskites. 

In this study, we report the discovery of a novel antisolvent bath immersion treatment using isopropanol (IPA) that enables the direct and rapid formation of optically active black-phase CsPbI 3 perovskite at room temperature. Four approaches for preparing CsPbI 3 perovskites were studied, as summarized in Figure 2. Unlike existing solvent-assisted methods that primarily focus on small-area films (<1 cm 2 ) or rely on post-treatment techniques such as solvent dripping or controlled solvent annealing atmospheres, 2,17,24 our approach is designed specifically for scalable and low-cost fabrication of flexible large-area films. By immersing blade-coated wet films in an IPA antisolvent bath, we have demonstrated a simple yet highly effective method for processing all-inorganic perovskite films at low temperatures, overcoming key challenges associated with traditional spin-coating-based methods and high equipment requirements. 

Moreover, the mechanism of antisolvent action in this work fundamentally differs from previously reported methods. 16,25 e show that hydrogen in HPbI 3 interacts with oxygen in DMF, creating mutual attraction. During immersion in the IPA antisolvent bath, DMF is extracted by IPA, inducing the hydrogen to vacate its original position and allowing free cesium ions to occupy these vacancies. This effectively lowers the reaction energy barrier and facilitates the direct formation of black-phase CsPbI 3 perovskites at room temperature, as supported by in situ optical spectroscopic analysis, NMR, and FTIR data. By providing a scalable, low-temperature, and lowcost method for fabricating high-quality CsPbI 3 films, this work paves the way for the advancement of perovskite-based technologies.
