citations.title: Highly stable QLEDs with improved hole injection via quantum dot structure tailoring
snippets: For the state-of-the-art quantum dot light-emitting diodes, while the ZnO nanoparticle layers can provide effective electron injections into quantum dots layers, the hole transporting materials usually cannot guarantee sufficient hole injection owing to the deep valence band of quantum dots. Developing proper hole transporting materials to match energy levels with quantum dots remains a great challenge to further improve the device efficiency and operation lifetime. Here we demonstrate high-performance quantum dot light-emitting diodes with much extended operation lifetime using quantum dots with tailored energy band structures that are favorable for hole injections. These devices show a T95 operation lifetime of more than 2300 h with an initial brightness of 1000 cd m−2, and an equivalent T50 lifetime at 100 cd m−2 of more than 2,200,000 h, which meets the industrial requirement for display applications. The commercialization of light-emitting diodes based on emissive quantum dots (e.g. QLEDs) is hindered by their inherent poor operational lifetime. Using an intelligent energy-level design strategy, Qian et al. demonstrate QLEDs with operational lifetime that meets industrial display standards.

sections.title: # 7) Limitations and next steps
sections.text:
Direct demonstrations of LLMs autonomously generating reproducible QLED recipes with validated performance are limited; current practice relies on human experts and semi-automated tools. However, the literature provides explicit, numerically grounded parameters for nanocrystal growth, shell thickness regimes, antisolvent/annealing windows, and interface design that an LLM can retrieve and structure into recipes. Future work should incorporate: (i) a curated, versioned database of QLED materials and processes with units and tolerances; (ii) retrieval and unit consistency checks; (iii) safety and compliance filters for solvents and emissions; and (iv) closed-loop validation via simulation (device physics) and small-batch fabrication feedback to refine parameters.

In summary, an LLM can synthesize material recipes for QLEDs by combining literature-backed nanocrystal synthesis parameters (shell thickness, ligand exchange, antisolvent/annealing) with device-layer energy-level alignment and interface strategies, producing structured, reproducible protocols and highlighting lifetime and safety considerations for Cd-free deployments. Recent QLED surveys and fabrication advances define the synthesis and device engineering parameter space [ae8c0f2a-0] Cd-free QD engineering shows how shell thickness and composition control unlock high EQE and narrow linewidths [13e7fc89-1][13e7fc89-2] Perovskite processing demonstrates low-temperature phase formation, optimal annealing windows, and scalable antisolvent quenching [827905b6-1][827905b6-3][827905b6-4] Interface and buffer layer choices are pivotal for blue QLED stability and white QLED performance [107d79d1-0][107d79d1-1].

citations.title: All Solution-processed Stable White Quantum Dot Light-emitting Diodes with Hybrid ZnO@TiO2 as Blue Emitters
snippets: White quantum dot light-emitting diodes (QD-LEDs) have been a promising candidate for high-efficiency and color-saturated displays. However, it is challenging to integrate various QD emitters into one device and also to obtain efficient blue QDs. Here, we report a simply solution-processed white QD-LED using a hybrid ZnO@TiO2 as electron injection layer and ZnCdSeS QD emitters. The white emission is obtained by integrating the yellow emission from QD emitters and the blue emission generated from hybrid ZnO@TiO2 layer. We show that the performance of white QD-LEDs can be adjusted by controlling the driving force for hole transport and electroluminescence recombination region via varying the thickness of hole transport layer. The device is demonstrated with a maximum luminance of 730 cd/m2 and power efficiency of 1.7 lm/W, exhibiting the Commission Internationale de l’Enclairage (CIE) coordinates of (0.33, 0.33). The unencapsulated white QD-LED has a long lifetime of 96 h at its initial luminance of 730 cd/m2, primarily due to the fact that the device with hybrid ZnO@TiO2 has low leakage current and is insensitive to the oxygen and the moisture. These results indicate that hybrid ZnO@TiO2 provides an alternate and effective approach to achieve high-performance white QD-LEDs and also other optoelectronic devices.

snippets:
We reported previously a new class of InP/ZnS core/shell QDs, where the lattice of InP QD as a core is compressed by 4.1% compared to the bulk crystal while the lattice of ZnS as a shell is expanded by 4.1% compared to the bulk crystal if the shell thickness is less than 0.81 nm (corresponding to three monolayers (3ML) of cubic ZnS) and the diameter of the core QD is less than 2.64 nm. 34 The resulting InP/ZnS core/shell QDs have a single lattice constant of 0.563 nm and provide a coherent and homogeneous interface despite the large lattice distortion between the core and the shell materials. In the present work, the coherent InP/ZnS core/shell QDs were used as a lightabsorbing layer of the vertical photodiode. 

Fig. 1 shows a summary of the results of structural and optical characterization of the coherent InP/ZnS (3ML) core/ shell QD terminated with the PA monolayer. Panel (a) shows a typical XRD pattern of the QD before and aer shell formation. The XRD pattern of the InP core QD has peaks indexed to the (111), (220), and (311) planes of zinc-blend (cubic) bulk crystals of InP, respectively. Aer the 3ML shell formation, the relative shi of each XRD peak toward a higher diffraction angle side happens to give a lattice constant of 0.563 nm. The peak at around 20°appears because of a ligand peak such as PA or OA as discussed later. In the post-synthesis of InP core QDs, the product was washed rigorously by ultracentrifugation with a mixture of hexane (i.e., good solvent) and methanol (i.e., poor solvent) as many as 10 times, but the peak was still present, suggesting that the PA adsorbs on the InP QD via ionic bonds. sections.title: # Executive summary: a practical workflow for project-description similarity
sections.text: A robust approach is to represent each project description as dense embeddings that capture semantic meaning, handle long documents via chunking/aggregation, and rank candidates by cosine similarity; then optionally rerank top candidates with a cross-encoder or NLI-style reranker to improve precision for nuanced matches. This pipeline is widely used for semantic search and has proven effective on long or hybrid documents, including enterprise and legal text, and it scales well with modern open-source encoders while offering measurable improvements when adding a reranking stage. Sentence transformers (e.g., MPNet, MiniLM, RoBERTa variants) are widely used for semantic search; long documents are chunked (e.g., 256 tokens) and represented by averaging embeddings, with cosine similarity used to rank matches [203e2885-0] Embedding-based retrieval can select relevant segments from hybrid long documents by computing per-segment similarities and picking top-ranked slices; Sentence-Transformer is commonly used due to its sequence-length practicality [203e2885-1] A two-stage strategy combining sentence-level bi-encoders for initial retrieval and a cross-encoder for sentence-pair relevance can align on methods/lead content and re-rank candidates effectively [203e2885-2] Comparative evaluations of dense retrievers on BEIR and MTEB typically use nDCG@10 as the main metric, with top open-source models including sentence/miniLM-scale bi-encoders and larger instruction-tuned retrievers [55d4e41d-0].

citations.title: Long-Form Information Retrieval for Enterprise Matchmaking
snippets:
Sentence transformers have been widely used for text embedding for text classification and semantic search tasks. As the transformer is trained to capture the relationship between two pieces of text (text_1 and text_2) using attention-based architecture, it suits our need in not only identifying similar documents to query but also finding documents that relevant to the query from the problemsolving perspective. 

We tested three sentence transformers, namely, mpnet [19], MiniLM [20], and roberta [21], chosen for their performance on various semantic search tasks. All three models are trained on over 1 billion text pairs. We use such transformers to compute the representations of query documents and product documents. Notably, many of the query documents and product descriptions are long documents that exceed the token limit imposed by sentence transformers. We addressed the limitation by segmenting the documents in chunks of max 256 tokens each and using the average embedding for final document representation. We then calculated the similarities between a query document and candidate documents using cosine similarity.

citations.title: LeiBi@COLIEE 2022: Aggregating Tuned Lexical Models with a Cluster-driven BERT-based Model for Case Law Retrieval
snippets: Transformer-based models are limited in taking into account long documents, so we split the queries and documents at the sentence-level and embed the document in sentence-level using Sentence-BERT (SBERT [21]). We develop a method that exploits clusters of sentences extracted from a query and a document. The proposed method, utilizes three different pre-fine-tuned SBERT's models to obtain appropriate embeddings for each part of the proposed method. Given a query Q d , we first identify the three most important sentences and use them as query representation, inspired by the Lead-3 model [18]. Lead-3 proposes that the first three sentences of the document are good representatives for extractive summarization. To this aim, we apply K-means (k=3) as our clustering method to find three clusters of query sentences; each cluster contains semantically similar sentences. Then, we compute the centroid of the cluster and select a sentence of cluster that is most close to its centroid as the representation of the cluster. To do that, we use a bi-encoder model that is pre-fine-tuned for computing cosine similarity between two separately embedded sentences. To compute the overall relevance score between the Q d and each d we sum the similarity scores of 3S q and 3S d using a cross-encoder model that is pre-fine-tuned to compute probability of relevance between two sentences. citations.title: Enabling and Analyzing How to Efficiently Extract Information from Hybrid Long Documents with LLMs
snippets:
Long documents contain many tokens, leading to a large number of document segments. Processing all segments would significantly increase LLMs invocations and introduce irrelevant information, potentially affecting extraction accuracy. Therefore, we adopt an embedding-based retrieval strategy (Li et al., 2021) to select the most relevant segments. We calculate the similarity between each document segment and the keyword based on their embeddings and retrieve the top-ranked segments with the highest similarity scores. 

To obtain embeddings, we use the Sentence-Transformer model (Reimers and Gurevych, 2019) in this module. Due to its sequence length limita-tions smaller than LLMs, document segments are divided into multiple slices. The similarity between each slice and the keyword is calculated, and the maximum similarity value among the slices within a segment is considered as the similarity between the segment and the keyword.

sections.title: # 1) Representations: what to embed and how to handle long texts
sections.text:
For project descriptions, prefer sentence or passage encoders that produce dense, semantically meaningful vectors and support long inputs via chunking/aggregation. If your descriptions exceed model context limits, split into overlapping or hierarchical chunks and aggregate embeddings (e.g., mean pooling) before similarity computation; cosine similarity is the standard choice for normalized vectors. Long documents exceeding token limits are handled by segmenting into chunks (e.g., 256 tokens) and averaging embeddings; cosine similarity is used to compute document–document similarity [203e2885-0] Due to sequence limits, document segments are divided into slices; per-slice similarities are aggregated (e.g., maximum within a segment) to represent the segment’s similarity to a keyword [203e2885-1].

Small, fast, multilingual-capable encoders are a good starting point because they balance speed, quality, and coverage:
- English baseline: all-MiniLM-L6-v2 or Sentence-BERT variants for zero-shot embedding and ranking via cosine similarity. all-MiniLM-L6-v2 is a strong small model evaluated across MTEB tasks and is commonly chosen for speed and transferability [55d4e41d-1] Sentence-BERT produces dense sentence embeddings and computes semantic similarities via cosine similarity for efficient ranking and top-k selection [203e2885-4].
- Multilingual baseline: BGE-small (bge-small-en, bge-small-zh, etc.) or gte-base for cross-language coverage. bge-small-en-v1.5 and gte-base are smaller models that achieve competitive results on MTEB, making them practical choices when multilinguality or speed is prioritized [55d4e41d-1] MMTEB covers 250+ languages across multiple task types, including retrieval and clustering (primarily English), and can be used to assess multilingual embedding quality [d84b65d1-2].
- If you need better retrieval quality at moderate cost, consider mid-sized models frequently topping open-source leaderboards (e.g., gte-Qwen1.5, GritLM), evaluated on MTEB/BEIR and nDCG@10. Open-source dense retrievers like GritLM and gte-Qwen1.5 are evaluated on MTEB, CMTEB, MMTEB, and long-context benchmarks using nDCG@10 [d84b65d1-0] Evaluations on BEIR and MTEB commonly report nDCG@10 and include a range of open-source dense retrievers alongside BM25 baselines [55d4e41d-0].

For truly long-context project sets (multi-thousand tokens), evaluate long-context retrieval benchmarks and techniques (e.g., pruning LLM context, specialized long-document encoders) to understand trade-offs in recall and latency. MLDR assesses long-context multilingual retrieval across 13 languages; NeedleRetrieval/PasskeyRetrieval provide synthetic long-context tests; nDCG@10 is used across evaluations [d84b65d1-0].

citations.title: Long-Form Information Retrieval for Enterprise Matchmaking
snippets:
Sentence transformers have been widely used for text embedding for text classification and semantic search tasks. As the transformer is trained to capture the relationship between two pieces of text (text_1 and text_2) using attention-based architecture, it suits our need in not only identifying similar documents to query but also finding documents that relevant to the query from the problemsolving perspective. 

We tested three sentence transformers, namely, mpnet [19], MiniLM [20], and roberta [21], chosen for their performance on various semantic search tasks. All three models are trained on over 1 billion text pairs. We use such transformers to compute the representations of query documents and product documents. Notably, many of the query documents and product descriptions are long documents that exceed the token limit imposed by sentence transformers. We addressed the limitation by segmenting the documents in chunks of max 256 tokens each and using the average embedding for final document representation. We then calculated the similarities between a query document and candidate documents using cosine similarity.

sections.title: # 2) Similarity metrics and evaluation: what to measure and when
sections.text:
Choose metrics that match your use case:
- For retrieval/ranking: use nDCG@k and Recall@k across a held-out test set; these are standard in open-source benchmark reports and reflect graded relevance and top-N precision. nDCG@10 is the main metric in comparative retrieval evaluations on BEIR and related datasets [55d4e41d-0] Long-context and multilingual evaluations also report nDCG@10, with top-k selection used for Recall-oriented assessments [d84b65d1-0].
- For semantic/lexical overlap within pairs or summaries: combine cosine similarity (distributional/TF-IDF baselines), BERTScore (token-level semantic similarity), and ROUGE (n-gram/LCS overlap). ROUGE and cosine similarity have been used to assess similarity between synthetic and reference texts; ROUGE emphasizes n-gram overlap and F1, while cosine similarity measures vector angle for semantic proximity [9740adec-0] Cosine similarity is efficient and length-insensitive but ignores word order and semantics; BLEU and ROUGE add n-gram and LCS sensitivity, with BLEU penalizing common n-grams and ROUGE capturing content overlap [9740adec-1] A comprehensive evaluation combining lexical (ROUGE, BLEU), semantic (BERTScore) and embedding cosine similarity provides a multi-dimensional view of text similarity [9740adec-4].
- If order and fluency matter, include sentence-level metrics like METEOR to capture precision/recall and fragmentation penalties. METEOR combines precision and recall with a fragmentation penalty and correlates better with human judgments at the sentence level than BLEU [9740adec-3].

Practical guidance:
- Start with nDCG@k/Recall@k on a held-out set of labeled pairs to compare retrievers. Retrieval evaluations typically prioritize nDCG@k with BM25 as a lexical baseline [55d4e41d-0].
- Add pairwise similarity checks for matched vs. unmatched pairs using BERTScore, ROUGE, and cosine to ensure your signal correlates with human judgments. Combining ROUGE, BERTScore, and embedding cosine similarity yields a more robust evaluation than any single metric [9740adec-4].

citations.title: MaLAware: Automating the Comprehension of Malicious Software Behaviours using Large Language Models (LLMs)
snippets:
Comparing generated text with ground truth requires a multi-dimensional evaluation to ensure MaLAware's effectiveness. The evaluation metric selection spans lexical metrics (ROUGE [16], BLEU [17]), semantic similarity metrics (BERTScore [18], Semantic Similarity), structural and readability metrics (Flesch-Kincaid Readability [19], Distinct-N [20]), and content focus metrics (Keyphrase Matching [21]). 

Lexical metrics assess word and sequence overlap between generated and reference text, with ROUGE evaluating n-gram overlap and focusing on recall to capture key information and maintain alignment. BERTScore measures contextual similarity using pre-trained models like BERT, computing cosine similarity of token embeddings for precision, recall, and F1, ensuring robustness to paraphrasing. Structural and readability metrics evaluate coherence, fluency, and uniqueness, with Distinct-N highlighting n-gram diversity to ensure engaging and meaningful summaries. The content focus metrics verify accurate capture and retention of key information. 

In total, we use 11 performance metrics for comprehensive evaluation, detailed below: 

1) ROUGE-1: It measures unigram (single word) overlap, providing a basic assessment of word-level content relevance. 

2) ROUGE-2: It measures bigram (two consecutive words) overlap, capturing the contextual and sequential alignment between the summaries. 

3) ROUGE-L: It evaluates the longest common subsequence (LCS), focusing on the structural similarity and fluency of the text. 

4) Semantic similarity: It evaluates the semantic closeness between generated and reference summaries by computing cosine similarity between sentence embeddings generated by models like sentence transformers. 

5) BERTScore-Precision: It measures how much of the generated content is relevant to the reference. 

6) BERTScore-Recall: It measures how well the generated content captures all key points from the reference. 

7) BERTScore-F1-Score: It provides a balanced view of BERTScore-precision and BERTScore-recall. 

8) Flesch-Kincaid Readability Score: This metric assesses the readability of a text based on its sentence length and syllable count.

snippets: • BLEU (Bilingual Evaluation Understudy) is a precision-based metric that evaluates text similarity by comparing n-grams between generated and reference texts [32]. • ROUGE (Recall-Oriented Understudy for Gisting Evaluation) is a recall-based metric that computes overlapping n-grams, word sequences, and the longest common subsequences [31]. The ROUGE family includes ROUGE-1, ROUGE-2, and ROUGE-L, each providing measures for precision, recall, and the F1-score. • TF-IDF (Term Frequency-Inverse Document Frequency) is a statistical measure that evaluates word importance in a document relative to a corpus by balancing term frequency and inverse document frequency [63]. • METEOR (Metric for Evaluation of Translation with Explicit ORdering) is a metric that evaluates text similarity by aligning unigrams between generated and reference texts using exact, stem, synonym, and paraphrase matches. Unlike BLEU, METEOR incorporates both precision and recall, along with a fragmentation penalty to account for word order, resulting in higher correlation with human judgments at the sentence level [33]. • Embedding Similarity which use embedding models to embed the sentences first and calculates the cosine similarity between two embedding vectors. citations.title: Beyond Lexical Boundaries: LLM-Generated Text Detection for Romanian Digital Libraries
snippets:
For a better understanding of the similarity between human-written and artificially generated texts, a series of statistical similarity metrics were computed, such as cosine similarity [63], BLEU scores [33], and ROUGE scores [34], followed by non-parametric statistical tests to determine the differences or patterns in the similarity scores, while also extracting and comparing various textual complexity indices between human and machine-generated sets of documents. 

Cosine similarity measures the relatedness of documents using a bag-of-words representation that considers term frequency. The main advantages of this approach are its efficiency for high-dimensional data, such as text, and its insensitivity to document length, while as for disadvantages, it ignores semantic meaning and word order. BLEU is a standard machine translation metric that measures the precision of n-grams (word sequences) in the generated text. The main benefit is the penalization of overusing common words, while the shortcoming is represented by its sensitivity to the reference length, as well as its disregard for recall and semantic meaning. The ROUGE scores are a set of metrics used for evaluating text quality by comparing it to a reference text by measuring n-gram overlap (ROUGE-N) and the longest common subsequence (ROUGE-L). As an advantage, ROUGE is sensitive to content overlap and partial matches, while as a disadvantage, it may not capture the semantic meaning well due to its limitation to the recall and precision of n-grams. Therefore, analyzing the three scores together provides a more grounded view of text similarity, covering different aspects, such as incorporating structural and distributional aspects of the text (cosine), adding a layer of specificity via analyzing the presence of key phrases and content overlap (ROUGE), and offering a view on how well machine-generated texts align with human references in terms of specific word sequences (BLEU). 

The previous three similarity scores (i.e., cosine similarity, BLEU score, and ROUGE score) were computed between human-written documents and artificially generated texts.

sections.title: # 3) Section-aware and citation-heavy comparisons
sections.text:
Project descriptions often have structured sections (title, objectives, methods, results, publications/citations). To improve precision:
- Focus methods comparison: extract or cluster sentences from the methods section and compute similarity among clusters; lead sentences (e.g., Lead-3) can serve as compact representatives. Selecting leading sentences and clustering query and document sentences (e.g., k=3) then computing cosine between cluster representatives yields strong initial retrieval; a cross-encoder reranker then scores overall relevance [203e2885-2].
- Hybrid lexical + semantic: use BM25/keyword overlap to identify candidate sections (e.g., “methods” or “results”), then apply dense embeddings for ranking within those sections to cut noise from citations or abstracts. Embedding-based retrieval first selects relevant segments using embeddings, while keyword-driven similarity aggregation handles sequence-length constraints [203e2885-1].
- For citation-heavy documents, separate citations and compare the body text (abstract, objectives, methods, results) specifically; if needed, use sentence embeddings to detect duplicated methods or approaches across projects. Sentence-level embedding and clustering ensure coverage of all sentences while enabling targeted similarity computation and cross-encoder reranking for relevance [203e2885-2].

sections.title: # 4) Putting it together: a production-ready pipeline
sections.text:
- Preprocess and chunk: split each project description into overlapping or hierarchical chunks (e.g., by section then tokens), deduplicate/overlap to avoid losing key boundary information. Chunking long documents into 256-token windows with average embeddings is a common strategy for long texts [203e2885-0] Slicing documents into manageable chunks and aggregating per-slice similarities is effective when sequence limits constrain model input [203e2885-1].
- Embed: compute dense embeddings for queries and passages using a fast baseline (e.g., all-MiniLM-L6-v2, BGE-small, gte-base) and normalize vectors for cosine similarity. all-MiniLM-L6-v2 and BGE-small/gte-base are strong small models on MTEB and suitable when speed and coverage are priorities [55d4e41d-1] Sentence-BERT embeddings support cosine similarity ranking and top-k selection for efficient retrieval [203e2885-4].
- Rank: use cosine similarity to rank candidates, then apply a reranker:
 - Cross-encoder or NLI-style sentence-pair models for higher-precision top-N selection. A bi-encoder for initial sentence retrieval and a cross-encoder for sentence-pair relevance can re-rank candidates effectively [203e2885-2].
 - MCQA-style or multiple-choice rerankers as lightweight alternatives when latency must be minimal. Cross-encoder and MCQA-based rerankers can improve retrieval accuracy in RAG; implementations exist via sentence-transformers and Hugging Face transformers [55d4e41d-2].
- Evaluate: 
 - Retrieval: nDCG@k and Recall@k on labeled queries (e.g., expert-curated pairs/triples). nDCG@10 is the standard metric in BEIR/MTEB-style evaluations [55d4e41d-0] Long-context and multilingual evaluations also use nDCG@10 and top-k selection [d84b65d1-0].
 - Pairwise similarity: BERTScore (precision/recall/F1), ROUGE (N/L), cosine similarity; optionally METEOR for fluency. Combining cosine, BLEU, and ROUGE provides complementary views of similarity (distributional, n-gram precision, and content recall) [9740adec-1] BERTScore and embedding cosine complement lexical ROUGE/BLEU for semantic robustness to paraphrasing [9740adec-4].
- Scale: index embeddings with approximate nearest-neighbor structures and warm the top-N with the reranker to keep latency low while maintaining quality. After computing embeddings for queries and documents, cosine similarity ranking at scale is practical; chunking/aggregation enables handling long texts [203e2885-0] Embedding-based retrieval with per-segment similarity scoring and top-k selection is efficient for hybrid long documents [203e2885-1].

Therefore, we adopt an embedding-based retrieval strategy (Li et al., 2021) to select the most relevant segments. We calculate the similarity between each document segment and the keyword based on their embeddings and retrieve the top-ranked segments with the highest similarity scores. 

To obtain embeddings, we use the Sentence-Transformer model (Reimers and Gurevych, 2019) in this module. Due to its sequence length limita-tions smaller than LLMs, document segments are divided into multiple slices. The similarity between each slice and the keyword is calculated, and the maximum similarity value among the slices within a segment is considered as the similarity between the segment and the keyword.

The similarity between the embeddings of the query and each passage is calculated using cosine similarity. The retrieval framework employs a top-k selection mechanism, where the cosine similarity scores are used to rank all passages, and the top-k most similar passages are selected as relevant. citations.title: Long-Form Information Retrieval for Enterprise Matchmaking
snippets:
Sentence transformers have been widely used for text embedding for text classification and semantic search tasks. As the transformer is trained to capture the relationship between two pieces of text (text_1 and text_2) using attention-based architecture, it suits our need in not only identifying similar documents to query but also finding documents that relevant to the query from the problemsolving perspective. 

We tested three sentence transformers, namely, mpnet [19], MiniLM [20], and roberta [21], chosen for their performance on various semantic search tasks. All three models are trained on over 1 billion text pairs. We use such transformers to compute the representations of query documents and product documents. Notably, many of the query documents and product descriptions are long documents that exceed the token limit imposed by sentence transformers. We addressed the limitation by segmenting the documents in chunks of max 256 tokens each and using the average embedding for final document representation. We then calculated the similarities between a query document and candidate documents using cosine similarity.

citations.title: Beyond Lexical Boundaries: LLM-Generated Text Detection for Romanian Digital Libraries
snippets:
For a better understanding of the similarity between human-written and artificially generated texts, a series of statistical similarity metrics were computed, such as cosine similarity [63], BLEU scores [33], and ROUGE scores [34], followed by non-parametric statistical tests to determine the differences or patterns in the similarity scores, while also extracting and comparing various textual complexity indices between human and machine-generated sets of documents. 

Cosine similarity measures the relatedness of documents using a bag-of-words representation that considers term frequency. The main advantages of this approach are its efficiency for high-dimensional data, such as text, and its insensitivity to document length, while as for disadvantages, it ignores semantic meaning and word order. BLEU is a standard machine translation metric that measures the precision of n-grams (word sequences) in the generated text. The main benefit is the penalization of overusing common words, while the shortcoming is represented by its sensitivity to the reference length, as well as its disregard for recall and semantic meaning. The ROUGE scores are a set of metrics used for evaluating text quality by comparing it to a reference text by measuring n-gram overlap (ROUGE-N) and the longest common subsequence (ROUGE-L). As an advantage, ROUGE is sensitive to content overlap and partial matches, while as a disadvantage, it may not capture the semantic meaning well due to its limitation to the recall and precision of n-grams. Therefore, analyzing the three scores together provides a more grounded view of text similarity, covering different aspects, such as incorporating structural and distributional aspects of the text (cosine), adding a layer of specificity via analyzing the presence of key phrases and content overlap (ROUGE), and offering a view on how well machine-generated texts align with human references in terms of specific word sequences (BLEU). 

The previous three similarity scores (i.e., cosine similarity, BLEU score, and ROUGE score) were computed between human-written documents and artificially generated texts.

citations.title: LeiBi@COLIEE 2022: Aggregating Tuned Lexical Models with a Cluster-driven BERT-based Model for Case Law Retrieval
snippets: Transformer-based models are limited in taking into account long documents, so we split the queries and documents at the sentence-level and embed the document in sentence-level using Sentence-BERT (SBERT [21]). We develop a method that exploits clusters of sentences extracted from a query and a document. The proposed method, utilizes three different pre-fine-tuned SBERT's models to obtain appropriate embeddings for each part of the proposed method. Given a query Q d , we first identify the three most important sentences and use them as query representation, inspired by the Lead-3 model [18]. Lead-3 proposes that the first three sentences of the document are good representatives for extractive summarization. To this aim, we apply K-means (k=3) as our clustering method to find three clusters of query sentences; each cluster contains semantically similar sentences. Then, we compute the centroid of the cluster and select a sentence of cluster that is most close to its centroid as the representation of the cluster. The three representative sentences are denoted as 3S Qd . Then, given a candidate document d, we find the most similar sentences (3S d ) of that document to 3S Q d , by computing cosine similarity. To do that, we use a bi-encoder model that is pre-fine-tuned for computing cosine similarity between two separately embedded sentences. To compute the overall relevance score between the Q d and each d we sum the similarity scores of 3S q and 3S d using a cross-encoder model that is pre-fine-tuned to compute probability of relevance between two sentences. We re-rank candidate documents based on this relevance score. We miss no part of candidate query and document into our methodology due to the sentence-level embedding and considering all of sentence embeddings into our methodology for computing relevance score.

sections.title: # 5) Choosing models: what to test and why
sections.text:
Use public leaderboards and benchmarks to select models that generalize to your domain:
- General English: MTEB and CMTEB cover retrieval, clustering, classification, STS, and multilingual tasks; report nDCG@k and retrieval task scores. MMTEB includes 250+ languages and 10 task types, with MTEB(Eng, v2) and MTEB(Multilingual) providing broad coverage [d84b65d1-2] Evaluations on BEIR, MIRACL, MTEB language subsets, MLDR, and synthetic long-context benchmarks use nDCG@10 [d84b65d1-0].
- Multilingual project sets: include BGE family (en, zh, de, fr) and gte-base; assess cross-lingual retrieval if mixing languages. MMTEB includes cross-lingual retrieval evaluations (XOR-Retrieve, XTREME-UP) pairing English passages with queries in many languages [d84b65d1-2] MTEB-FR, MTEB-ZH, and MTEB-DE subsets help assess multilingual retrievers [d84b65d1-0].
- Long-context: test long-context retrieval on MLDR and synthetic Needle/Passkey; compare pruning LLMs vs specialized dense retrievers. MLDR provides long-context multilingual retrieval across 13 languages; NeedleRetrieval/PasskeyRetrieval serve as synthetic stress tests [d84b65d1-0].

Practical small-model short list to compare on your data:
- all-MiniLM-L6-v2 (English baseline).
- BGE-small (your target language).
- gte-base (balanced quality/speed).
- One mid-sized open-source retriever (e.g., gte-Qwen1.5 or GritLM) for a quality upper-bound. These models are reported as competitive on MTEB and suitable for speed-sensitive production [55d4e41d-1] gated mid-sized models like GritLM and gte-Qwen1.5 are evaluated on diverse benchmarks, including long-context settings [d84b65d1-0].

sections.title: # 6) When to add reranking and hybrid strategies
sections.text:
If many projects produce noisy or partial matches, add a reranker:
- Cross-encoder/NLI-style sentence or passage pair rerankers improve top-N precision while keeping latency manageable if you only rerank top-K candidates. A cross-encoder can score overall relevance between representative sentences and re-rank candidate documents effectively [203e2885-2] Cross-encoder and MCQA-based rerankers have been shown to improve retrieval accuracy in RAG pipelines [55d4e41d-2].
- Consider hybrid lexical+semantic retrieval: use BM25 to pre-filter by key terms (e.g., grant program terms, methodologies, diseases) and then apply dense reranking to the top candidates. BM25 remains competitive on BEIR and serves as a strong lexical baseline against which dense retrievers are compared [55d4e41d-0].

sections.title: # 7) Multilingual and domain-specific notes
sections.text: If project descriptions span multiple languages, select multilingual encoders and validate on cross-lingual retrieval subsets; otherwise, ensure consistent language tagging and pretraining data overlap with your domain. MMTEB includes cross-lingual retrieval evaluations and multilingual coverage across many languages [d84b65d1-2] MTEB language subsets (FR, ZH, DE) allow targeted multilingual retriever assessment [d84b65d1-0]. For scientific domains, evaluate on biomedical or code retrieval tasks if available, and consider domain-adapted fine-tuning when domain specificity is critical. Biomedical retrieval workbench (BMRetriever) compares dense retrievers and notes trade-offs; concurrent strong models like BGE and E5 variants are referenced for their hybrid or graph-based training [55d4e41d-3].

citations.title: BMRetriever: Tuning Large Language Models as Better Biomedical Text Retrievers
snippets:
Due to the knowledge distillation from a teacher model, which involves additional supervised training signals, we consider E5-Large-v2 (335M) as an unfair comparison. 

• BGE-Large (Chen et al., 2024) is a dense retrieval model (335M) that uses graph-based embedding techniques and a multi-stage training paradigm similar to E5 (Wang et al., 2022b). However, since BGE employs a hybrid retrieval strategy incorporating additional lexical and multi-vector retrieval, we consider it an unfair comparison for our focus on dense retrieval only. 

We acknowledge BGE as a concurrent work and provide its performance for reference purposes. 

• LLaRA (Li et al., 2023a) uses LLM-generated text embeddings to reconstruct input sentence tokens and predict next sentence tokens. 

• RepLLaMA (Ma et al., 2023) is a dense retriever (7B) that fine-tunes the LLaMA model for effective representation learning in passage and document retrieval using the MS MARCO datasets (Bajaj et al., 2016). 

• LLM2Vec (BehnamGhader et al., 2024) is an unsupervised approach that transforms LLMs into text encoders by enabling bidirectional attention via masked next token prediction and adopts unsupervised contrastive learning for sequence representation learning. 

• E5-Mistral (Wang et al., 2024) is an enhanced version of the E5 (Wang et al., 2022b) that incorporates synthetic data generated by LLMs for a diverse range of text embedding tasks. 

• CPT-text (Neelakantan et al., 2022) is a dense retrieval model pre-trained on web-scale data using a contrastive objective with neighboring text passages as positive pairs. We only consider its performance as a reference rather than a fair comparison due to its large size (175B parameters).

sections.title: # 8) Handling citations and section-specific comparisons
sections.text:
To avoid spurious matches driven by citation lists:
- Explicitly separate the citation section and compare the body text (abstract, objectives, methods, results) for similarity. Sentence-level embedding and clustering ensure that all content is considered while enabling targeted similarity and cross-encoder re-ranking based on content relevance rather than citation volume [203e2885-2].
- If you need to detect reused methods or tools, focus retrieval on methods sections using Lead-3 or sentence clusters and compute similarity among clusters before reranking with a cross-encoder. Lead-3 representative sentences plus cross-encoder reranking provide a strong, section-aware strategy for methods-focused comparison [203e2885-2].

sections.title: # 9) Validation and ablation best practices
sections.text:
- Build a labeled test set: include expert-annotated positive pairs (near-duplicate or strongly overlapping projects) and hard negatives with similar titles/keywords but different content; report nDCG@k, Recall@k, and pairwise F1/ROUGE-LS. Comparative retrieval studies report nDCG@k and include BM25 baselines to contextualize gains [55d4e41d-0] Pairwise evaluation combining ROUGE, BERTScore, and embedding cosine provides complementary, more reliable signals than any single metric [9740adec-4].
- Ablate components: compare chunking vs. full-document embedding, cosine vs. dot/Euclidean, and zero-shot encoders vs. fine-tuned models; measure impact on top-10 and Recall@5/10. Chunking and averaging enable long-document comparison with cosine similarity [203e2885-0] Per-slice similarity aggregation and top-k selection provide a principled way to handle sequence limits [203e2885-1].
- Evaluate multilingual and long-context coverage if relevant; use MLDR and synthetic long-context benchmarks to anticipate latency-quality trade-offs. MLDR and synthetic long-context benchmarks help assess long-context retrieval across languages and identify effective strategies [d84b65d1-0].

citations.title: MaLAware: Automating the Comprehension of Malicious Software Behaviours using Large Language Models (LLMs)
snippets:
Comparing generated text with ground truth requires a multi-dimensional evaluation to ensure MaLAware's effectiveness. The evaluation metric selection spans lexical metrics (ROUGE [16], BLEU [17]), semantic similarity metrics (BERTScore [18], Semantic Similarity), structural and readability metrics (Flesch-Kincaid Readability [19], Distinct-N [20]), and content focus metrics (Keyphrase Matching [21]). 

Lexical metrics assess word and sequence overlap between generated and reference text, with ROUGE evaluating n-gram overlap and focusing on recall to capture key information and maintain alignment. BERTScore measures contextual similarity using pre-trained models like BERT, computing cosine similarity of token embeddings for precision, recall, and F1, ensuring robustness to paraphrasing. Structural and readability metrics evaluate coherence, fluency, and uniqueness, with Distinct-N highlighting n-gram diversity to ensure engaging and meaningful summaries. The content focus metrics verify accurate capture and retention of key information. 

In total, we use 11 performance metrics for comprehensive evaluation, detailed below: 

1) ROUGE-1: It measures unigram (single word) overlap, providing a basic assessment of word-level content relevance. 

2) ROUGE-2: It measures bigram (two consecutive words) overlap, capturing the contextual and sequential alignment between the summaries. 

3) ROUGE-L: It evaluates the longest common subsequence (LCS), focusing on the structural similarity and fluency of the text. 

4) Semantic similarity: It evaluates the semantic closeness between generated and reference summaries by computing cosine similarity between sentence embeddings generated by models like sentence transformers. 

5) BERTScore-Precision: It measures how much of the generated content is relevant to the reference. 

6) BERTScore-Recall: It measures how well the generated content captures all key points from the reference.

snippets:
Long documents contain many tokens, leading to a large number of document segments. Processing all segments would significantly increase LLMs invocations and introduce irrelevant information, potentially affecting extraction accuracy. Therefore, we adopt an embedding-based retrieval strategy (Li et al., 2021) to select the most relevant segments. We calculate the similarity between each document segment and the keyword based on their embeddings and retrieve the top-ranked segments with the highest similarity scores.

Due to its sequence length limita-tions smaller than LLMs, document segments are divided into multiple slices. snippets:
Comparing generated text with ground truth requires a multi-dimensional evaluation to ensure MaLAware's effectiveness. The evaluation metric selection spans lexical metrics (ROUGE [16], BLEU [17]), semantic similarity metrics (BERTScore [18], Semantic Similarity), structural and readability metrics (Flesch-Kincaid Readability [19], Distinct-N [20]), and content focus metrics (Keyphrase Matching [21]). 

Lexical metrics assess word and sequence overlap between generated and reference text, with ROUGE evaluating n-gram overlap and focusing on recall to capture key information and maintain alignment. BERTScore measures contextual similarity using pre-trained models like BERT, computing cosine similarity of token embeddings for precision, recall, and F1, ensuring robustness to paraphrasing. Structural and readability metrics evaluate coherence, fluency, and uniqueness, with Distinct-N highlighting n-gram diversity to ensure engaging and meaningful summaries. The content focus metrics verify accurate capture and retention of key information. 

In total, we use 11 performance metrics for comprehensive evaluation, detailed below: 

1) ROUGE-1: It measures unigram (single word) overlap, providing a basic assessment of word-level content relevance. 

2) ROUGE-2: It measures bigram (two consecutive words) overlap, capturing the contextual and sequential alignment between the summaries. 

3) ROUGE-L: It evaluates the longest common subsequence (LCS), focusing on the structural similarity and fluency of the text. 

4) Semantic similarity: It evaluates the semantic closeness between generated and reference summaries by computing cosine similarity between sentence embeddings generated by models like sentence transformers. 

5) BERTScore-Precision: It measures how much of the generated content is relevant to the reference. 

6) BERTScore-Recall: It measures how well the generated content captures all key points from the reference. 

7) BERTScore-F1-Score: It provides a balanced view of BERTScore-precision and BERTScore-recall. 

8) Flesch-Kincaid Readability Score: This metric assesses the readability of a text based on its sentence length and syllable count.

citations.title: Beyond Lexical Boundaries: LLM-Generated Text Detection for Romanian Digital Libraries
snippets:
For a better understanding of the similarity between human-written and artificially generated texts, a series of statistical similarity metrics were computed, such as cosine similarity [63], BLEU scores [33], and ROUGE scores [34], followed by non-parametric statistical tests to determine the differences or patterns in the similarity scores, while also extracting and comparing various textual complexity indices between human and machine-generated sets of documents. 

Cosine similarity measures the relatedness of documents using a bag-of-words representation that considers term frequency. The main advantages of this approach are its efficiency for high-dimensional data, such as text, and its insensitivity to document length, while as for disadvantages, it ignores semantic meaning and word order. BLEU is a standard machine translation metric that measures the precision of n-grams (word sequences) in the generated text. The main benefit is the penalization of overusing common words, while the shortcoming is represented by its sensitivity to the reference length, as well as its disregard for recall and semantic meaning. The ROUGE scores are a set of metrics used for evaluating text quality by comparing it to a reference text by measuring n-gram overlap (ROUGE-N) and the longest common subsequence (ROUGE-L). As an advantage, ROUGE is sensitive to content overlap and partial matches, while as a disadvantage, it may not capture the semantic meaning well due to its limitation to the recall and precision of n-grams. Therefore, analyzing the three scores together provides a more grounded view of text similarity, covering different aspects, such as incorporating structural and distributional aspects of the text (cosine), adding a layer of specificity via analyzing the presence of key phrases and content overlap (ROUGE), and offering a view on how well machine-generated texts align with human references in terms of specific word sequences (BLEU). 

The previous three similarity scores (i.e., cosine similarity, BLEU score, and ROUGE score) were computed between human-written documents and artificially generated texts.

snippets: Selecting ranking model Our task can be formulated as a text retrieval task: we have a model (DMR) that encodes a query P DMR (s t ) and compare it with a document c t,i , resulting in a score that can be used to rank candidates. We also use bge-small-en-v1.5 (Xiao et al., 2023a) and gte-base (Li et al., 2023b), which are two smaller models that achieve competitive results on the MTEB benchmark (Muennighoff et al., 2023). citations.title: LeiBi@COLIEE 2022: Aggregating Tuned Lexical Models with a Cluster-driven BERT-based Model for Case Law Retrieval
snippets: Transformer-based models are limited in taking into account long documents, so we split the queries and documents at the sentence-level and embed the document in sentence-level using Sentence-BERT (SBERT [21]). We develop a method that exploits clusters of sentences extracted from a query and a document. The proposed method, utilizes three different pre-fine-tuned SBERT's models to obtain appropriate embeddings for each part of the proposed method. Given a query Q d , we first identify the three most important sentences and use them as query representation, inspired by the Lead-3 model [18]. Lead-3 proposes that the first three sentences of the document are good representatives for extractive summarization. To this aim, we apply K-means (k=3) as our clustering method to find three clusters of query sentences; each cluster contains semantically similar sentences. Then, we compute the centroid of the cluster and select a sentence of cluster that is most close to its centroid as the representation of the cluster. The three representative sentences are denoted as 3S Qd . Then, given a candidate document d, we find the most similar sentences (3S d ) of that document to 3S Q d , by computing cosine similarity. To do that, we use a bi-encoder model that is pre-fine-tuned for computing cosine similarity between two separately embedded sentences. To compute the overall relevance score between the Q d and each d we sum the similarity scores of 3S q and 3S d using a cross-encoder model that is pre-fine-tuned to compute probability of relevance between two sentences. We re-rank candidate documents based on this relevance score. We miss no part of candidate query and document into our methodology due to the sentence-level embedding and considering all of sentence embeddings into our methodology for computing relevance score.

sections.title: # Limitations and where to go next
sections.text:
Public benchmarks provide generalizable signals but may not perfectly match niche scientific project descriptions; consider building a domain-specific test set. Long-document handling via chunking can fragment context; overlapping windows and hierarchical chunking mitigate this. Multilingual retrieval quality varies by language; assess on language-specific subsets. For citation-heavy corpora, ensure explicit exclusion or isolation of citation sections during similarity scoring. MTEB notes gaps for very long documents and task imbalance across categories, highlighting the need for domain-specific datasets [d84b65d1-4] Chunking and averaging are pragmatic for long documents but require tuning to balance coverage and noise [203e2885-0].

In summary, start with a fast sentence/passage encoder (MiniLM/BGE/gte), chunk and normalize long project descriptions, rank by cosine, and add a cross-encoder reranker for top-N; evaluate with nDCG@k/Recall@k for retrieval and BERTScore/ROUGE/cosine for pairwise similarity; for citation-heavy or section-specific needs, focus comparisons on methods via Lead-3 or sentence clustering and pre-filter with lexical search. Sentence transformers with chunking and cosine similarity provide a solid zero-shot baseline for long project descriptions [203e2885-0] Embedding-based retrieval over segmented documents is efficient and effective when sequence limits constrain models [203e2885-1] Sentence clustering and cross-encoder reranking improve precision for targeted comparisons [203e2885-2] nDCG@k and BM25 baselines are standard for retrieval evaluation [55d4e41d-0] Combining lexical, semantic, and embedding-based metrics yields a robust validation of project-description similarity [9740adec-4].

citations.title: MTEB: Massive Text Embedding Benchmark
snippets:
While MTEB aims to be a diverse benchmark to provide holistic performance reviews, the benchmark has its limitations. We list them here:

1. Long document datasets MTEB covers multiple text lengths (S2S, P2P, S2P), but very long documents are still missing. The longest datasets in MTEB have a few hundred words, and longer text sizes could be relevant for use cases like retrieval.

2. Task imbalance Tasks in MTEB have a different amount of datasets with summarization consisting of only a single dataset. This means MTEB average scores, which are computed over all datasets, are biased towards tasks with many datasets, notably retrieval, classification and clustering. As MTEB grows, we hope to add more datasets to currently underrepresented tasks like summarization or pair classification.

3. Multinguality MTEB contains multilingual classification, STS and bitext mining datasets. However, retrieval and clustering are English-only. SGPT-BLOOM-7B1-msmarco is geared towards multilingual retrieval datasets and due to the lack thereof cannot be comprehensively benchmarked in MTEB. Further, MTEB does not contain any code datasets that could be used to benchmark code models (Neelakantan et al., 2022;Allal et al., 2023). It should be easy to extend MTEB with datasets, such as CodeSearchNet

sections.title: # What is 3D Gaussian Splatting and how does it relate to diffusion?
sections.text:
3D Gaussian Splatting (GS) represents a scene as a collection of 3D Gaussian primitives (splats) with per-primitive color, opacity, and covariance; during rendering, only Gaussians that will be visible contribute to each screen tile, enabling fast rendering by avoiding ray traversal of empty space. 3D Gaussian Splatting has emerged as a faster alternative to NeRF due to lower optimization and rendering costs, though depth maps produced by naively replacing color with position during rendering can exhibit floaters and artifacts, motivating depth-supervised variants [59b2d60b-0] The 3D Gaussian representation uses splats as image primitives mixed by Gaussian densities at different locations in space and renders by tiling the screen with GPU-accelerated visibility sorting, avoiding volumetric sampling through a large neural network [59b2d60b-1]. Compared to NeRF, GS typically trains and renders much faster while achieving high visual quality, making it attractive for view synthesis and content creation. GS is rapidly displacing NeRF in popularity due to much lower time for optimization and rendering while advancing photorealism [59b2d60b-0] 3D Gaussian Splatting has become a mainstream representation, achieving NeRF-like results with significantly less training time and enabling intuitive geometry and editing [59b2d60b-4].

GS has also been extended to dynamic scenes via 4D Gaussian Splatting, which splits the representation into a time-dependent 3D scene encoding and a deformation field, supporting motion while retaining high quality and faster training/rendering than Dynamic NeRF. 4D Gaussian Splatting uses time-dependent 3D Gaussian representations with a differential splatting process and reports high-quality dynamic scenes with faster training and rendering than D-NeRF [59b2d60b-1]. Beyond static and dynamic radiance, GS primitives are increasingly used in AI-driven generation and editing workflows, where they are either conditioned on, denoised by, or grown by diffusion models. For AI-based content generation, diffusion models have been used to guide the generation of 3D Gaussian splatting models, and for editing; GS has also been integrated into 4D reconstruction with tri-plane approaches [488e5247-0].

citations.title: ScalingGaussian: Enhancing 3D Content Creation with Generative Gaussian Splatting
snippets:
Representations of 3D assets can be categorized into implicit representations and explicit representations. The former defines 3D shapes through implicit functions without directly storing 3D geometric information. Implicit representations are typically more compact and capable of representing complex topological structures [12,13,14,15,16]. Neural Radiance Fields (NeRF) [16] are a typical method of implicit representation, enabling the generation of highquality 3D content with known camera parameters. NeRF employs a multi-layer perceptron (MLP) to map 3D coordinates and viewing directions to color and density, and generates new views through volume rendering. NeRF has limitations in handling high-frequency details, often leading to aliasing artifacts. Mip-NeRF (Multiscale Representation) [13] addresses this issue by introducing a multiscale feature, i.e., replacing the rendering rays with anti-aliased conical frustums to effectively mitigate the blurring problem when dealing with high-frequency details. DSNeRF [17] incorporates depth supervision alongside color supervision, allowing scene reconstruction with fewer input views and faster training speeds compared to NeRF. Although NeRF-based methods can generate high-quality and highly realistic 3D content, they are computationally intensive, resulting in very time-consuming training and rendering processes [4,13,16]. 

Recently, 3D Gaussian Splatting [18] has emerged as the mainstream 3D representation method, replacing NeRF. As an explicit representation, 3D Gaussian Splatting can achieve results comparable to NeRF. It has demonstrated impressive speed in image-to-3D tasks and does not require the extensive training time that NeRF does. Furthermore, 3D Gaussian Splatting provides a more intuitive representation of geometric shapes, making the generated 3D content easier to edit. SparseGS [19] enhances 3D Gaussian Splatting by incorporating depth supervision from rendered images. This approach enables scene reconstruction with fewer images and improves rendering accuracy and efficiency. Due to the superior performance of 3D Gaussian Splatting, our method also employs 3D Gaussians as the representation technique, which enables us to generate detailed 3D assets from singleview images in a significantly short amount of time.

citations.title: Self-Evolving Depth-Supervised 3D Gaussian Splatting from Rendered Stereo Pairs
snippets:
In recent years, NeRF [40] has deeply revolutionized several aspects of computer vision, introducing innovative paradigms and redefining our understanding of the field. First and foremost, NeRF has represented a turning point for image rendering and novel view synthesis [37,40,78], casting these tasks as the optimization of a continuous 3D representation of the scene encoded in multi-layer perceptrons (MLPs), queried with (x, y, z) coordinates in space and (θ , φ ) view angles to predict color and opacity for any generic 3D point. Rendering is achieved by casting rays and accumulating colors and opacities along them into pixels. 

However, the recent advent of 3D Gaussian Splatting (GS) [29] is rapidly conquering the main stage at the expense of NeRF, due to the much lower time required for both optimization and rendering. While GS has certainly advanced the state-of-the-art in terms of photorealism and rendering speed, the underlying geometry modeled by the Gaussians does not reflect the same quality as the rendering. This is evident in the depth maps generated by GS itselfby replacing the color components of the Gaussians with their position during the rendering process -as we can notice in Fig. 1, where examples from BlendedMVS and ETH3D are affected by several floaters and artifacts. Some works from the literature [2,13,51,63,68] show evidence that using depth priors as a form of additional supervision when optimizing a NeRF can improve the quality of the rendered images, especially when very few images are available for training. Intuitively, this strategy also has the potential to improve the underlying geometry encoded by the NeRF itself, although no attention has been paid to this by prior works, nor to the different, possible approaches for retrieving depth priors from the very same images used to train NeRF -and to the intrinsic limitation each choice brings. 

In this paper, we first delve into a study of Depth-Supervised 3D Gaussian Splatting (DS-GS) variants by examining and measuring the impact that different depth-from-image solutions have on the optimization of both the appearance and geometry modeled by GS.

citations.title: Characterizing Satellite Geometry via Accelerated 3D Gaussian Splatting
snippets:
Replacing NeRF representation with a point-based representation reduces training times since there is no huge neural network to optimize. In addition, the point-based scene representation avoids NeRF's reliance on a full volumetric representation of the scene. Hence, 3D Splatting avoids NeRF's expensive sampling of points on the paths traced by each ray and passing them through a large neural network. 

The 3D Gaussian representation instead uses "splats" or layers of simple textures ("image primitives") to be mixed by the Gaussian densities at different locations in space. Novel views are rendered using separate tiles of the whole screen. GPU-accelerated sorting algorithms allow extremely fast mixing for generating tiles by only considering splats that will be visible. 

Dynamic Scenes. Dynamic NeRF (D-NeRF) [31] reconstructs and render novel images of objects under rigid and non-rigid motions from a single camera moving around the scene. It considers time as an additional input and splits the learning process of the fully connected network into two parts: one encodes the scene into a canonical space and one maps this canonical representation into the deformed scene at a particular time. The canonical network is trained to take in 3D coordinates and the viewing directions to yield a radiance field. Then, the deformation network outputs the displacement that takes the point to its position in the canonical space. D-NeRF can render dynamic scenes and retains high-quality image details. While D-NeRF performs better with dynamic scenes, it still faces slow training and rendering difficulties. 

4D Gaussian Splatting [35] propose a representation that uses the 3D Gaussian Splatting point-based representation and 4D neural voxels. Similar to D-NeRF, the framework is split into a 3D scene representation and a deformation field parts. However, the two pieces are time-dependent 3D Gaussian representations that can be rendered using a differential splatting process. 4D Gaussian Splatting is reported to produce high-quality dynamic scenes with the faster training and rendering than D-NeRF.

sections.title: # How diffusion models interface with 3D Gaussian Splatting
sections.text:
Diffusion can act as a prior, a denoising guide, or a generative engine for GS primitives in three main ways:

- Diffusion priors for generalization and geometry improvement: VEGS aligns Gaussians using pre-extracted normals and leverages diffusion priors to generate augmented camera views and enforce geometry consistency, which mitigates floaters and fragmentation and improves overall 3D coherence without additional human supervision. Chen et al. utilized diffusion models to guide the generation of 3D Gaussian splatting models [488e5247-0] VEGS employs diffusion priors for denoising loss guidance and to supervise augmented camera generation, reducing floating artifacts and fragmented geometries for more accurate, coherent representations [488e5247-1].

- Bridging 2D and 3D diffusion to initialize and optimize GS: GaussianDreamer reviews both 2D and 3D diffusion, and proposes initializing 3D Gaussians with 3D diffusion models, then further optimizing them with 2D diffusion to refine appearance and geometry efficiently. GaussianDreamer reviews 2D/3D diffusion and 3D Gaussian Splatting, and describes initializing 3D Gaussians with 3D diffusion models, followed by 2D diffusion optimization of the Gaussians [488e5247-2].

- End-to-end diffusion over functional GS representations: DiffGS formulates GS with disentangled Gaussian Splatting Functions and trains a Gaussian variational auto-encoder plus a latent diffusion model to generate and scale Gaussian distributions; a discretization algorithm extracts Gaussians at arbitrary numbers via octree-guided sampling and optimization, enabling controllable primitive counts and quality. DiffGS introduces a diffusion-based generative model for 3D Gaussian Splatting, representing GS with three disentangled Gaussian Splatting Functions, compressing/generating via a Gaussian VAE and latent diffusion, and sampling optimized Gaussians at arbitrary numbers through octree-guided discretization [488e5247-4].

These approaches reflect a broader trend: diffusion provides flexible, data-driven priors for GS geometry/appearance, while GS supplies an explicit, render-ready structure that supports fast iteration and downstream pipelines. As an explicit representation, GS is convenient to obtain from images and more suitable for real-time rendering; its adoption spans SLAM, monocular vision, 4D reconstruction, and content generation/editing with diffusion [488e5247-0].

sections.title: # Performance, speed, and quality trade-offs
sections.text:
GS methods typically deliver high-quality novel view synthesis at real-time or near–real-time frame rates due to explicit, sparse primitives and tile-based rendering that avoids sampling empty space, though results can vary by dataset and method. Tile-based rendering and GPU-accelerated sorting enable extremely fast mixing by considering only visible splats, yielding faster rendering than NeRF-style sampling [59b2d60b-1] RayGauss reports 25 FPS on Blender and outperforms GS on many indoor Mip-NeRF360 scenes (e.g., +0.56 dB PSNR over 3DGS), while GS-based methods can add more Gaussians to compensate for splatting artifacts [59b2d60b-3] 3D Gaussian Splatting achieves results comparable to NeRF with much faster training and intuitive geometry/editing, and methods like Micro-splatting report higher SSIM/PSNR and lower LPIPS with competitive training time [59b2d60b-4]. Dynamic extensions can preserve detail while improving throughput relative to Dynamic NeRF. 4D Gaussian Splatting reports high-quality dynamic scenes with faster training and rendering than D-NeRF [59b2d60b-1].

However, GS is not without limitations. Without strong geometric supervision, GS reconstructions can exhibit depth/geometry artifacts (e.g., floaters) and poor far-view generalization; depth-supervised variants and diffusion-based priors can alleviate these issues at inference or training time. Replacing color with position in GS reveals depth floaters and artifacts on BlendedMVS and ETH3D, and depth priors have been shown to improve quality when few images are available [59b2d60b-0] VEGS uses diffusion priors to mitigate floating artifacts and fragmented geometries, improving coherence of GS reconstructions [488e5247-1]. Some GS methods add post-processing or regularization to address aliasing and fidelity: for example, Micro-splatting and related techniques improve anti-aliasing and consistency, while comparative analyses show GS can trade geometric fidelity for speed depending on scene type and setup. RayGauss notes GS likely adds more Gaussians to compensate for splatting artifacts and performs better on indoor than outdoor Mip-NeRF360 scenes, suggesting sensitivity to scene characteristics [59b2d60b-3] Micro-splatting introduces isotropy-informed covariance regularization and reports higher SSIM/PSNR and lower LPIPS than original 3DGS on Mip-NeRF scenes, with training time and FPS indicating computational benefits [e9cfa79f-2].

citations.title: RayGauss: Volumetric Gaussian-Based Ray Casting for Photorealistic Novel View Synthesis
snippets:
NeuRBF [6] performs well, similar to our method, but has an infer-ence time of a few seconds per image-about 100x longer than ours (25 FPS on Blender dataset, see Tab. 3)-and does not support the Mip-NeRF360 dataset. Results on the Mip-NeRF 360 Dataset: Regarding Mip-NeRF 360, we provide quantitative results in Tab. 2 and qualitative comparisons in Fig. 2. A general trend is that our approach performs better on most indoor scenes than state-of-the-art methods like Mip-Splatting [2], and slightly worse on outdoor scenes. This may be due to the adaptive control of gaussians strategy, which adapts well in Gaussian Splatting [12] but may perform worse with our approach. Nevertheless, we achieved better overall results than Mip-Splatting and 3D Gaussian Splatting, with an average PSNR of 29.71 dB, +0.56 dB higher than 3D Gaussian Splatting. Zip-NeRF performs slightly better on Mip-NeRF 360 but requires over 7 hours of training per scene and about 1.5 seconds per image for inference, which is significantly higher than our approach (see Tab. 3). 

Performance Analysis: We discuss here results in Tab. 3, which show the performance of our approach compared to Gaussian Splatting. These metrics were obtained using an RTX 4090 GPU with 24GB of RAM on 800x800 pixel images. Our approach has slower training and infer- ence times compared to Gaussian Splatting due to the computational cost of ray casting. Generally, our computation times depend mainly on the number of rays, while Gaussian Splatting's times are influenced by the number of projected primitives. However, our training times remain reasonable (30 minutes per scene on Blender) and real-time inference is achieved on Blender, although slower on Mip-NeRF 360. We also note that our method generates fewer primitives for better visual quality. Thus, Gaussian Splatting likely adds more Gaussians to compensate for splatting artifacts.

citations.title: ScalingGaussian: Enhancing 3D Content Creation with Generative Gaussian Splatting
snippets:
Representations of 3D assets can be categorized into implicit representations and explicit representations. The former defines 3D shapes through implicit functions without directly storing 3D geometric information. Implicit representations are typically more compact and capable of representing complex topological structures [12,13,14,15,16]. Neural Radiance Fields (NeRF) [16] are a typical method of implicit representation, enabling the generation of highquality 3D content with known camera parameters. NeRF employs a multi-layer perceptron (MLP) to map 3D coordinates and viewing directions to color and density, and generates new views through volume rendering. NeRF has limitations in handling high-frequency details, often leading to aliasing artifacts. Mip-NeRF (Multiscale Representation) [13] addresses this issue by introducing a multiscale feature, i.e., replacing the rendering rays with anti-aliased conical frustums to effectively mitigate the blurring problem when dealing with high-frequency details. DSNeRF [17] incorporates depth supervision alongside color supervision, allowing scene reconstruction with fewer input views and faster training speeds compared to NeRF. Although NeRF-based methods can generate high-quality and highly realistic 3D content, they are computationally intensive, resulting in very time-consuming training and rendering processes [4,13,16]. 

Recently, 3D Gaussian Splatting [18] has emerged as the mainstream 3D representation method, replacing NeRF. As an explicit representation, 3D Gaussian Splatting can achieve results comparable to NeRF. It has demonstrated impressive speed in image-to-3D tasks and does not require the extensive training time that NeRF does. Furthermore, 3D Gaussian Splatting provides a more intuitive representation of geometric shapes, making the generated 3D content easier to edit. SparseGS [19] enhances 3D Gaussian Splatting by incorporating depth supervision from rendered images. This approach enables scene reconstruction with fewer images and improves rendering accuracy and efficiency. Due to the superior performance of 3D Gaussian Splatting, our method also employs 3D Gaussians as the representation technique, which enables us to generate detailed 3D assets from singleview images in a significantly short amount of time.

citations.title: Self-Evolving Depth-Supervised 3D Gaussian Splatting from Rendered Stereo Pairs
snippets:
In recent years, NeRF [40] has deeply revolutionized several aspects of computer vision, introducing innovative paradigms and redefining our understanding of the field. First and foremost, NeRF has represented a turning point for image rendering and novel view synthesis [37,40,78], casting these tasks as the optimization of a continuous 3D representation of the scene encoded in multi-layer perceptrons (MLPs), queried with (x, y, z) coordinates in space and (θ , φ ) view angles to predict color and opacity for any generic 3D point. Rendering is achieved by casting rays and accumulating colors and opacities along them into pixels. 

However, the recent advent of 3D Gaussian Splatting (GS) [29] is rapidly conquering the main stage at the expense of NeRF, due to the much lower time required for both optimization and rendering. While GS has certainly advanced the state-of-the-art in terms of photorealism and rendering speed, the underlying geometry modeled by the Gaussians does not reflect the same quality as the rendering. This is evident in the depth maps generated by GS itselfby replacing the color components of the Gaussians with their position during the rendering process -as we can notice in Fig. 1, where examples from BlendedMVS and ETH3D are affected by several floaters and artifacts. Some works from the literature [2,13,51,63,68] show evidence that using depth priors as a form of additional supervision when optimizing a NeRF can improve the quality of the rendered images, especially when very few images are available for training. Intuitively, this strategy also has the potential to improve the underlying geometry encoded by the NeRF itself, although no attention has been paid to this by prior works, nor to the different, possible approaches for retrieving depth priors from the very same images used to train NeRF -and to the intrinsic limitation each choice brings. 

In this paper, we first delve into a study of Depth-Supervised 3D Gaussian Splatting (DS-GS) variants by examining and measuring the impact that different depth-from-image solutions have on the optimization of both the appearance and geometry modeled by GS.

sections.title: # When to use GS vs. diffusion, and how they complement each other
sections.text:
GS is attractive when you need fast training and real-time rendering from unstructured multiview images, especially for view synthesis, iterative editing, or pipelines requiring explicit geometry for downstream processing (e.g., SLAM, conversion to point clouds/meshes). GS offers much lower optimization and rendering time than NeRF while achieving high-quality rendering [59b2d60b-0] As an explicit representation, GS supports real-time rendering and integrates with geometry processing pipelines; it has been used in SLAM and content generation/editing [488e5247-0]. Diffusion models complement GS by supplying strong priors for geometry/appearance under view missingness, far-view generalization, or creative control. Examples include using diffusion to denoise/regularize GS training with augmented cameras (VEGS), to initialize and polish GS via 2D/3D diffusion (GaussianDreamer), or to directly generate functional GS distributions with controllable discretization (DiffGS). Diffusion priors can guide augmented camera views and regularize GS geometry, reducing floaters and fragmentation [488e5247-1] Bridging 2D and 3D diffusion enables GS initialization and further optimization for high-quality results [488e5247-2] DiffGS models GS as functional components and uses latent diffusion to generate and scale high-quality Gaussians with octree-guided discretization [488e5247-4].

Practical tips:
- Expect strong speedups vs. NeRF for reconstruction and view synthesis, but verify geometry quality on challenging viewpoints; consider adding depth supervision or diffusion priors if floaters/fragmentation appear. GS achieves speed and quality but can suffer depth floaters, with depth priors improving quality especially with few views [59b2d60b-0] Diffusion priors help mitigate GS artifacts and improve coherence [488e5247-1].
- For dynamic scenes, prefer 4D GS or similar time-decomposed representations to retain quality and efficiency over time. 4D GS supports dynamic scenes with faster training/rendering than D-NeRF [59b2d60b-1].
- If you need generative/editable 3D, GS paired with diffusion (e.g., GaussianDreamer, DiffGS, VEGS) offers a practical balance of explicit representation and probabilistic priors for creative control and robustness. Diffusion has been used to guide GS generation and editing [488e5247-0] GS initialization and optimization with 2D/3D diffusion improves quality [488e5247-2] DiffGS provides a diffusion-based generative model tailored to GS functions with controllable discretization [488e5247-4].

sections.title: # Summary
sections.text:
- 3D Gaussian Splatting is an explicit, sparse 3D representation that models scenes with 3D Gaussians and renders by aggregating visible splats, delivering high-quality view synthesis with significantly lower training and rendering costs than NeRF, though it can suffer geometry artifacts without additional supervision. GS trades some geometric fidelity for speed and can show floaters, but improves quality with depth supervision [59b2d60b-0] GS avoids volumetric sampling and supports fast rendering via tiled, GPU-accelerated mixing [59b2d60b-1].
- Diffusion models are increasingly used to guide GS: as priors for far-view generalization (VEGS), to initialize and refine GS via 2D/3D diffusion (GaussianDreamer), and to generate functional GS distributions with controllable discretization (DiffGS). Diffusion priors regularize GS geometry and improve coherence [488e5247-1] Bridging 2D and 3D diffusion supports efficient GS initialization and optimization [488e5247-2] DiffGS proposes a functional schema and latent diffusion pipeline tailored to GS [488e5247-4].
- In practice, GS is favored for speed and explicit geometry, while diffusion adds robustness, generalization, and creative control; combining them is a strong recipe for modern 3D view synthesis, reconstruction, and content creation. GS provides intuitive geometry and fast generation/editing, underpinning recent generative pipelines [59b2d60b-4] Diffusion-guided GS has been applied to 4D reconstruction and avatar generation [488e5247-0].
