citations.title: ScalingGaussian: Enhancing 3D Content Creation with Generative Gaussian Splatting
snippets:
Representations of 3D assets can be categorized into implicit representations and explicit representations. The former defines 3D shapes through implicit functions without directly storing 3D geometric information. Implicit representations are typically more compact and capable of representing complex topological structures [12,13,14,15,16]. Neural Radiance Fields (NeRF) [16] are a typical method of implicit representation, enabling the generation of highquality 3D content with known camera parameters. NeRF employs a multi-layer perceptron (MLP) to map 3D coordinates and viewing directions to color and density, and generates new views through volume rendering. NeRF has limitations in handling high-frequency details, often leading to aliasing artifacts. Mip-NeRF (Multiscale Representation) [13] addresses this issue by introducing a multiscale feature, i.e., replacing the rendering rays with anti-aliased conical frustums to effectively mitigate the blurring problem when dealing with high-frequency details. DSNeRF [17] incorporates depth supervision alongside color supervision, allowing scene reconstruction with fewer input views and faster training speeds compared to NeRF. Although NeRF-based methods can generate high-quality and highly realistic 3D content, they are computationally intensive, resulting in very time-consuming training and rendering processes [4,13,16]. 

Recently, 3D Gaussian Splatting [18] has emerged as the mainstream 3D representation method, replacing NeRF. As an explicit representation, 3D Gaussian Splatting can achieve results comparable to NeRF. It has demonstrated impressive speed in image-to-3D tasks and does not require the extensive training time that NeRF does. Furthermore, 3D Gaussian Splatting provides a more intuitive representation of geometric shapes, making the generated 3D content easier to edit. SparseGS [19] enhances 3D Gaussian Splatting by incorporating depth supervision from rendered images. This approach enables scene reconstruction with fewer images and improves rendering accuracy and efficiency. Due to the superior performance of 3D Gaussian Splatting, our method also employs 3D Gaussians as the representation technique, which enables us to generate detailed 3D assets from singleview images in a significantly short amount of time.

citations.title: Self-Evolving Depth-Supervised 3D Gaussian Splatting from Rendered Stereo Pairs
snippets:
In recent years, NeRF [40] has deeply revolutionized several aspects of computer vision, introducing innovative paradigms and redefining our understanding of the field. First and foremost, NeRF has represented a turning point for image rendering and novel view synthesis [37,40,78], casting these tasks as the optimization of a continuous 3D representation of the scene encoded in multi-layer perceptrons (MLPs), queried with (x, y, z) coordinates in space and (θ , φ ) view angles to predict color and opacity for any generic 3D point. Rendering is achieved by casting rays and accumulating colors and opacities along them into pixels. 

However, the recent advent of 3D Gaussian Splatting (GS) [29] is rapidly conquering the main stage at the expense of NeRF, due to the much lower time required for both optimization and rendering. While GS has certainly advanced the state-of-the-art in terms of photorealism and rendering speed, the underlying geometry modeled by the Gaussians does not reflect the same quality as the rendering. This is evident in the depth maps generated by GS itselfby replacing the color components of the Gaussians with their position during the rendering process -as we can notice in Fig. 1, where examples from BlendedMVS and ETH3D are affected by several floaters and artifacts. Some works from the literature [2,13,51,63,68] show evidence that using depth priors as a form of additional supervision when optimizing a NeRF can improve the quality of the rendered images, especially when very few images are available for training. Intuitively, this strategy also has the potential to improve the underlying geometry encoded by the NeRF itself, although no attention has been paid to this by prior works, nor to the different, possible approaches for retrieving depth priors from the very same images used to train NeRF -and to the intrinsic limitation each choice brings. 

In this paper, we first delve into a study of Depth-Supervised 3D Gaussian Splatting (DS-GS) variants by examining and measuring the impact that different depth-from-image solutions have on the optimization of both the appearance and geometry modeled by GS.

The 3D Gaussian representation instead uses "splats" or layers of simple textures ("image primitives") to be mixed by the Gaussian densities at different locations in space. Dynamic Scenes. Dynamic NeRF (D-NeRF) [31] reconstructs and render novel images of objects under rigid and non-rigid motions from a single camera moving around the scene. The canonical network is trained to take in 3D coordinates and the viewing directions to yield a radiance field. Then, the deformation network outputs the displacement that takes the point to its position in the canonical space. D-NeRF can render dynamic scenes and retains high-quality image details. question: has anyone propose metric like to judge whether a coding LLM has some knowledge

sections.text: Yes. Researchers have proposed multiple families of metrics and benchmarks to assess whether a coding LLM possesses relevant knowledge, from code-generation correctness and unit-test pass rates to code understanding and reasoning in code, domain/knowledge tasks, and reliability/factuality under code contexts. Below is an overview of the main approaches and what they measure, with examples and the key metrics used.

What “knowledge” means in coding LLMs
- Factual/program knowledge: knowing APIs, libraries, language semantics, and distributed facts across codebases.
- Code-generation knowledge: producing functions that satisfy specifications and pass tests.
- Reasoning with code: applying math/physics/logic to code, and composing multi-step solutions.
- Reliability/knowledge use in context: not hallucinating, correctly invoking APIs, and producing testable code.
Metrics and benchmarks used to judge coding knowledge

1) Code-generation correctness and functional testing
- HumanEval and MBPP use unit tests and function execution to measure whether generated code satisfies specifications; extensions like EvalPlus increase test coverage and robustness, and report pass@k where at least one sample among k generations passes the tests. EvalPlus uses an LLMon-based mutation strategy to automatically generate large, diverse test cases and evaluate functional correctness at scale. EvalPlus is a code synthesis evaluation framework to benchmark the functional correctness of LLM-generated code; it uses an LLM-and mutation-based strategy to automatically generate large amounts of test cases and compare against ground-truth implementations [e4d7fe49-4] HumanEval and MBPP are commonly used coding benchmarks, with many extensions such as EvalPlus that extend HumanEval’s test cases and robustness checks [e4d7fe49-2] Codex introduces HumanEval, an evaluation set relying on manually constructed test cases to evaluate LLM solutions; many similar benchmarks (e.g., CoderEval) evaluate generated code via tests [e4d7fe49-4] For most benchmarks, pass@k is reported by generating k responses per question and counting the percentage for which at least one correct response is obtained [39dc7c63-4].
- SWE-bench and curated variants measure whether models can read issues, reason about code, and produce fixes with unit tests; well-defined, human-validated subsets remove poorly specified tasks and yield fairer comparisons, improving solve rates over naïve setups. A human-validated subset of SWE-bench removes poorly defined tasks, and models perform significantly better on this reduced subset, demonstrating the usefulness of well-defined tasks for fair evaluation [e4d7fe49-1].
- Multi-turn program evaluation and LiveCodeBench assess broader coding knowledge (e.g., algorithm selection, test prediction) and report pass@k across contamination-resistant, dynamically updated problems from LeetCode/AtCoder/CodeForces. More involved evaluations include multi-turn program evaluation and SWE-bench, which require resolving GitHub issues [e4d7fe49-2] LiveCodeBench (release v2) collects 511 problems from LeetCode, AtCoder, and CodeForces and evaluates code generation, execution, and test prediction using Pass@K in a contamination-free design [39dc7c63-0].

Moreover, the coding ability of an LLM can be informative of its reasoning abilities [Madaan et al., 2022]; thus, performance on coding benchmark is of broader interest. While HumanEval [Chen et al., 2021] and MBPP [Austin et al., 2021] are the most commonly used coding benchmarks, many extensions and further benchmarks have been proposed [Lu et al., 2021, Nijkamp et al., 2023, Zhu et al., 2022, Liu et al., 2023, Jimenez et al., 2023, Khan et al., 2023, Yang et al., 2024, Yan et al., 2023], we highlight a few: EvalPlus extends HumanEval's test cases [Liu et al., 2023], MultiPL-E [Cassano et al., 2023] to other languages, ReCode with robustness checks [Wang et al., 2023], HUMANEVALPACK [Muennighoff et al., 2023] with code repair and explanation tasks, and buggy-HumanEval [Dinh et al., 2023] with bugs in the reference code. Relatedly, the DS-1000 [Lai et al., 2023] benchmark evaluates models' abilities on data science problems that require using external libraries. More involved evaluations include the multi-turn program evaluation benchmark [Nijkamp et al., 2023] and SWE-bench [Jimenez et al., 2023], which requires the LLM to resolve GitHub issues. snippets:
The core principle of G-Pass@k lies in evaluating model performance under varying thresholds of correctness, providing a nuanced understanding of model behavior across different stringency levels. By integrating measures of both stability and potential, G-Pass@k delivers a comprehensive assessment of an LLM's capabilities, particularly valuable for complex reasoning tasks. 

To thoroughly study the reasoning stability of current LLMs using G-Pass@k, we conduct comprehensive experiments to evaluate various mod-arXiv:2412.13147v5 [cs.AI] 8 Aug 2025 els on multiple mathematical reasoning benchmarks, encompassing different categories of large language models. These include general LLMs, mathematics-specialized models, and Chain-of-Thought (CoT) enhanced reasoning models, which are known for their step-by-step reasoning capabilities in complex mathematical problem-solving. We also introduce LiveMathBench, a challenging bilingual mathematics benchmark assembled from multiple competitions and examinations to mitigate the impact of data leakage. 

Through systematic comparison between traditional metrics (Greedy Accuracy, Pass@k) and G-Pass@k, our findings reveal distinctive insights into model performance that conventional evaluation approaches may overlook and demonstrate significant limitations in traditional evaluation metrics regarding output stability assessment. We observe a substantial performance degradation across all models as the G-Pass@k threshold becomes more stringent, a pattern consistent across both established open-source benchmarks (MATH (Lightman et al., 2024) and AIME (AIME2024, 2024; AIME2025, 2025)) and our proposed LiveMath-Bench. Specifically, the key observations include: 

• Instability in LLM Reasoning (Section 3.2, Section 3.5): Both closed-source and open-source models exhibit significant instability when applied to challenging reasoning tasks. Performance drops exceed 50% in many cases, with the worst instances showing declines of up to 90%. snippets:
Moreover, the coding ability of an LLM can be informative of its reasoning abilities [Madaan et al., 2022]; thus, performance on coding benchmark is of broader interest. While HumanEval [Chen et al., 2021] and MBPP [Austin et al., 2021] are the most commonly used coding benchmarks, many extensions and further benchmarks have been proposed [Lu et al., 2021, Nijkamp et al., 2023, Zhu et al., 2022, Liu et al., 2023, Jimenez et al., 2023, Khan et al., 2023, Yang et al., 2024, Yan et al., 2023], we highlight a few: EvalPlus extends HumanEval's test cases [Liu et al., 2023], MultiPL-E [Cassano et al., 2023] to other languages, ReCode with robustness checks [Wang et al., 2023], HUMANEVALPACK [Muennighoff et al., 2023] with code repair and explanation tasks, and buggy-HumanEval [Dinh et al., 2023] with bugs in the reference code. More involved evaluations include the multi-turn program evaluation benchmark [Nijkamp et al., 2023] and SWE-bench [Jimenez et al., 2023], which requires the LLM to resolve GitHub issues. sections.text:
Practical guidance on choosing metrics
- To judge whether a coding LLM has factual/program knowledge of libraries and APIs, prefer datasets that require using external libraries or domain tools (e.g., DS-1000) and measure functional correctness via tests. DS-1000 evaluates abilities on data science problems requiring external libraries [e4d7fe49-2] EvalPlus and HumanEval-style test-based metrics quantify functional correctness of generated code [e4d7fe49-4].
- To judge reasoning/knowledge beyond codegen (e.g., math/CS reasoning embedded in code), use math/competition-style benchmarks (MATH/AIME/GPQA) and report stability-aware metrics like G-Pass@k in addition to pass@k. GPQA Diamond and competition-style sets provide accurate or contamination-resistant evaluations of deep reasoning [39dc7c63-0] G-Pass@k exposes instability and provides nuanced assessment across thresholds [39dc7c63-1].

CodeJudge-Eval measures the ability to judge others’ code correctness, distinct from generation [e4d7fe49-0] RepoQA evaluates retrieving specific functions from large codebases from natural language [e4d7fe49-4].

citations.title: Are Your LLMs Capable of Stable Reasoning?
snippets:
The core principle of G-Pass@k lies in evaluating model performance under varying thresholds of correctness, providing a nuanced understanding of model behavior across different stringency levels. By integrating measures of both stability and potential, G-Pass@k delivers a comprehensive assessment of an LLM's capabilities, particularly valuable for complex reasoning tasks. 

To thoroughly study the reasoning stability of current LLMs using G-Pass@k, we conduct comprehensive experiments to evaluate various mod-arXiv:2412.13147v5 [cs.AI] 8 Aug 2025 els on multiple mathematical reasoning benchmarks, encompassing different categories of large language models. These include general LLMs, mathematics-specialized models, and Chain-of-Thought (CoT) enhanced reasoning models, which are known for their step-by-step reasoning capabilities in complex mathematical problem-solving. We also introduce LiveMathBench, a challenging bilingual mathematics benchmark assembled from multiple competitions and examinations to mitigate the impact of data leakage. 

Through systematic comparison between traditional metrics (Greedy Accuracy, Pass@k) and G-Pass@k, our findings reveal distinctive insights into model performance that conventional evaluation approaches may overlook and demonstrate significant limitations in traditional evaluation metrics regarding output stability assessment. We observe a substantial performance degradation across all models as the G-Pass@k threshold becomes more stringent, a pattern consistent across both established open-source benchmarks (MATH (Lightman et al., 2024) and AIME (AIME2024, 2024; AIME2025, 2025)) and our proposed LiveMath-Bench. Specifically, the key observations include: 

• Instability in LLM Reasoning (Section 3.2, Section 3.5): Both closed-source and open-source models exhibit significant instability when applied to challenging reasoning tasks. Performance drops exceed 50% in many cases, with the worst instances showing declines of up to 90%. This issue is particularly significant in highdifficulty questions, underscoring the necessity for further enhancement of current LLMs' ability to address complex questions. 

• Inconsistency Between Expanded Model Scale and Enhanced Reasoning Ability (Section 3.2): Merely scaling up model size does not necessarily enhance stable reasoning capabilities. The expected improvements in performance and stability are not consistently observed.

More involved evaluations include the multi-turn program evaluation benchmark [Nijkamp et al., 2023] and SWE-bench [Jimenez et al., 2023], which requires the LLM to resolve GitHub issues. While existing benchmarks evaluate a diverse set of LLM behaviors across models, these benchmarks do not, however, include a programmer-in-the-loop, as there would be in a real-world setup. Our evaluation complements this existing line of work by conducting a user study, where programmers put these behaviors to the test in realistic scenarios.

citations.title: CodeJudge-Eval: Can Large Language Models be Good Judges in Code Understanding?
snippets: In this work, we present CodeJudge-Eval, a novel benchmark designed to evaluate LLMs' code understanding capabilities by assessing their performance as code judges. We tested 12 popular LLMs, both proprietary and open-source, on our benchmark. The results demonstrate the benchmark's difficulty, with open-source models often performing worse than random guessing. Moreover, our analysis shows that a model's ability to generate correct code does not necessarily imply it can accurately evaluate other solutions for the same task.

question: planning with Large Language Models

sections.title: # What “planning with Large Language Models” entails
sections.text: Planning with LLMs refers to using LLMs to generate sequences of actions that achieve goals, either directly as text-based plans or by translating natural language into formal planning languages that can be executed by classical solvers or tools, and then iterating with feedback from the environment, execution outcomes, or evaluators to improve plans over time. LLM-based agents have achieved success in embodied decision-making by grounding actions with value functions and enhancing planning via thinking modules or world abstractions [dbc1af94-2] LLMs can generate structured outputs like executable code and are being explored to build neuro-symbolic planning frameworks, with recent surveys covering LLM-augmented planning agents and PDDL-LLM research [dbc1af94-3]. A central tension is that while LLMs excel at high-level reasoning, their plans can be infeasible or hallucinated; thus, hybrid pipelines that validate, translate, or hand off to classical planners are often more reliable for correctness and efficiency. LLM-generated plans often contain mistaken or hallucinated actions and are unreliable as standalone planners [1b51f93d-1] Translating to PDDL and planning with classical solvers offers advantages: PDDL can be scrutinized, execution is faster than querying an LLM per step, programs can scale to larger tasks, and PDDL avoids context-window limits [3fe83b46-0].

citations.title: Learn as Individuals, Evolve as a Team: Multi-agent LLMs Adaptation in Embodied Environments
snippets: LLM-based Single-agent Planning Recent advancements in large language models (LLMs) have led to the development of highly capable models, including LLaMA 3 [34,9], GPT-4 [1,16], and DeepSeek-R1 [10]. By leveraging their extensive general knowledge and exceptional reasoning capabilities, LLM-based agents have achieved remarkable success in embodied decision-making tasks that integrate perception, action, and interaction with physical or simulated environments [31]. Seminal works such as SayCan [2], grounded decoding [14] and Text2Motion [21] ground agent actions by using value functions to bridge language with real-world tasks. Follow-up studies have enhanced LLM planning capabilities by introducing thinking modules [15,20] or world abstractions [25]. Others have leveraged in-context learning [30] when expert demonstrations are available. Another research direction focuses on aligning visual perception with language objectives, resulting in algorithms such as VLMaps [13], TaPA [35], mobility VLA [36], and NavGPT [40,39]. These methods refine LLMs' ability to plan and act in environments requiring seamless integration of language and vision.

citations.title: MORPHeus: a Multimodal One-armed Robot-assisted Peeling System with Human Users In-the-loop
snippets: Language serves as a natural interface to incorporate human preferences into long-horizon planning [27,28].In recent years, there has been significant progress in large language models [29][30][31][32][33][34][35][36].Given their extensive pre-training on diverse text data, LLMs exhibit impressive zero-shot generalization capabilities, making them suitable for use in robot planning [37][38][39].Therefore, we use LLM to perform long-horizon planning with human-in-the-loop, taking their preferences into consideration.However, compared to directly generating task plans using LLMs, converting natural language to Planning Domain Definition Language (PDDL), and planning with a classical planner has the following advantages: (1) the PDDL generated by LLM can be quickly scrutinized; (2) executing a synthesized program is often quicker than repeatedly querying the LLM for each new job; (3) synthesized programs can be customized for tasks of any size; (4) using PDDL circumvents the context window size limitations inherent to LLMs [40].We therefore use LLM integrated with PDDL for long-horizon planning.Previously, research has already focused on fine-tuning Large Language Models (LLMs) for the PDDL domain [41], as well as on translating natural language into PDDL [42][43][44][45].These capabilities make LLMs well-suited for human-in-the-loop planning scenarios.

citations.title: How Far Are LLMs from Symbolic Planners? An NLP-Based Perspective
snippets: The reasoning and planning abilities of Large Language Models (LLMs) have been a frequent topic of discussion in recent years. Their ability to take unstructured planning problems as input has made LLMs'integration into AI planning an area of interest. Nevertheless, LLMs are still not reliable as planners, with the generated plans often containing mistaken or hallucinated actions. Existing benchmarking and evaluation methods investigate planning with LLMs, focusing primarily on success rate as a quality indicator in various planning tasks, such as validating plans or planning in relaxed conditions. In this paper, we approach planning with LLMs as a natural language processing (NLP) task, given that LLMs are NLP models themselves. We propose a recovery pipeline consisting of an NLP-based evaluation of the generated plans, along with three stages to recover the plans through NLP manipulation of the LLM-generated plans, and eventually complete the plan using a symbolic planner. This pipeline provides a holistic analysis of LLM capabilities in the context of AI task planning, enabling a broader understanding of the quality of invalid plans. Our findings reveal no clear evidence of underlying reasoning during plan generation, and that a pipeline comprising an NLP-based analysis of the plans, followed by a recovery mechanism, still falls short of the quality and reliability of classical planners. On average, only the first 2.65 actions of the plan are executable, with the average length of symbolically generated plans being 8.4 actions. The pipeline still improves action quality and increases the overall success rate from 21.9% to 27.5%.

citations.title: LLMs as Planning Formalizers: A Survey for Leveraging Large Language Models to Construct Automated Planning Models
snippets: The advancements of Large Language Models (LLMs) have shown promise in generating highly structured outputs, such as executable code, from NL descriptions (Li et al., 2023;Wang et al., 2024;Nijkamp et al., 2023). PDDL-LLM research is recent, with initial studies in (Miglani and Yorke-Smith, 2020;Feng et al., 2018;Simon and Muise, 2021;Chalvatzaki et al., 2023). Currently, researchers are further exploring the nuances of varying pipelines to balance the effectiveness and limitations of LLMs in building such neuro-symbolic frameworks. Huang et al. (2024c) survey a limited amount of papers to compose their high-level abstraction of LLM-augmented planning agents. Pallagani et al. (2024) go beyond the scope of traditional AP, encapsulating broader constructs, whereas Zhao et al. (2024) provide an extensive overview of LLM-TAMP applications. The work most akin to our paper is (Li et al., 2024a), which reviews studies using LLMs in planning with PDDL; however, their survey mainly consists of works comprising LLMs-as-Planners (cf. Figure 1).

sections.title: # 1) LLMs as planners (text-to-plan)
sections.text: Directly prompting LLMs to plan can yield interpretable, natural-language plans but suffers from low validity and success, particularly as tasks grow in complexity and length. Fine-tuning on planning corpora does not yield robust planning; however, chain-of-thought style prompting improves the probability that a plan is executable [1b51f93d-0] On average, only the first 2.65 actions of LLM-generated plans are executable, and symbolic pipelines that recover and hand off to planners improve success from 21.9% to 27.5% [1b51f93d-1]. Even advanced models show substantial gaps versus classical planners on simple problems, motivating structured-translation or hybrid methods. GPT-4 achieves only 35% accuracy on simple planning problems when planned directly [1b51f93d-4].

citations.title: Chasing Progress, Not Perfection: Revisiting Strategies for End-to-End LLM Plan Generation
snippets: The capability of Large Language Models (LLMs) to plan remains a topic of debate. Some critics argue that strategies to boost LLMs' reasoning skills are ineffective in planning tasks, while others report strong outcomes merely from training models on a planning corpus. This study reassesses recent strategies by developing an end-to-end LLM planner and employing diverse metrics for a thorough evaluation. We find that merely fine-tuning LLMs on a corpus of planning instances does not lead to robust planning skills, as indicated by poor performance on out-of-distribution test sets. At the same time, we find that various strategies, including Chain-of-Thought, do enhance the probability of a plan being executable. This indicates progress towards better plan quality, despite not directly enhancing the final validity rate. Among the strategies we evaluated, reinforcement learning with our novel `Longest Contiguous Common Subsequence' reward emerged as the most effective, contributing to both plan validity and executability. Overall, our research addresses key misconceptions in the LLM-planning literature; we validate incremental progress in plan executability, although plan validity remains a challenge. Hence, future strategies should focus on both these aspects, drawing insights from our findings.

citations.title: Planetarium: A Rigorous Benchmark for Translating Text to Structured Planning Languages
snippets:
Recently, there has been growing interest in using large language models (LLMs) to solve planning problems. Some research has focused on generating plans directly with LLMs (Valmeekam et al., 2023a(Valmeekam et al., , 2022(Valmeekam et al., , 2023b;;Silver et al., 2022Silver et al., , 2023)). However, this approach has shown limited success; GPT-4 only achieves 35% accuracy on simple planning problems (Valmeekam et al., 2023a). Another line of research uses LLMs to convert natural language prompts into structured planning languages, such as the planning domain definition language (Liu et al., 2023;Xie et al., 2023;Guan et al., 2023;Chalvatzaki et al., 2023;Yang et al., 2023b). Early evidence suggests this method performs better than : An example of one planning goal corresponding to many correct PDDL goals. All PDDL goals in the top row represent the displayed goal correctly. The bottom row illustrates PDDL goals with different error types, showing instances that are solvable (a planner can generate a plan, but for a different planning problem), parseable (the PDDL syntax is correct but will not produce any plan from a planner), and not parseable (it is not valid PDDL). Translating natural language to PDDL enables a hybrid, best-of-both-worlds approach. The LLM is responsible for interpreting natural language, and the resulting PDDL can be given to traditional, symbolic planners that have been developed over decades (Fikes and Nilsson, 1971;McDermott et al., 1998;Helmert, 2006;Baier et al., 2009;Vidal and Geffner, 2006). These traditional planners are efficient and ensure the correctness of their so-lutions. In contrast, leaving the planning to LLMs does not guarantee correctness, making them unreliable for critical applications.

sections.title: # 2) Translating to structured planning languages (PDDL/code) + classical planners
sections.text:
A common pattern is to use LLMs to interpret natural language and produce formal specifications or code that planners can solve, combining linguistic understanding with verified symbolic reasoning. LLM-empowered planning includes structured language planning (LLM as planner), natural language planning, and programming language planning [3fe83b46-4] Converting natural language to PDDL and planning with a classical solver leverages PDDL’s scrutability, faster execution, scalability, and avoidance of context-window limits [3fe83b46-0]. Several frameworks instantiate this:
- LLM+P: LLM creates domain/problem PDDL, a classical planner computes plans, and the LLM translates the plan back to natural language, improving decomposition and avoiding dead loops. LLM+P uses PDDL as an intermediary: problem-to-PDDL translation, classical planner to generate a PDDL plan, and translation back to language [3fe83b46-1].
- PDDL-WM and LLV: Iteratively construct/refine PDDL domain models with LLMs and validate via parsers or simulators, using feedback to correct logical errors and improve feasibility. PDDL-WM uses LLM to iteratively construct and refine PDDL domain models, validated by parsers and user feedback; LLV introduces external validators (parser or simulator) to check and iteratively refine LLM plans via error feedback; FSP-LLM aligns plans with logical constraints via prompt optimization [3fe83b46-4].
- TwoStep and related work: LLMs decompose goals into subtasks while classical planners handle formal planning, or generate PDDL goals to avoid open-loop state tracking; this “use each tool for what it does best” division improves correctness. TwoStep uses LLM to infer commonsense decompositions while a PDDL system ensures plan correctness; LLMs can generate PDDL goals to eliminate the need for open-/closed-loop state tracking; LLMs have also been used for multi-agent planning via code and task allocation [3fe83b46-3].

Empirically, translation-to-PDDL outperforms direct LLM planning in reliability and enables efficient search in mature planners. Recovery pipelines that translate to PDDL and then use a symbolic planner improve action quality and overall success relative to raw LLM plans [1b51f93d-1] Translating to PDDL enables a hybrid approach where LLMs interpret language and planners provide efficient, correct solutions [1b51f93d-4].

citations.title: Large Model Empowered Embodied AI: A Survey on Decision-Making and Embodied Learning
snippets: High-level planning produces reasonable plans according to task instructions and perceived information. Traditional high-level planning relies on rule-based methods [59,75,126]. Given initial states and goals specified in Planning Domain Definition Language (PDDL), heuristic search planner verifies action preconditions for feasibility and employs search trees to select optimal action sequences, thereby generating an efficient and cost-effective plan [90]. Although effective in structured environments, rule-based methods struggle with adaptability in unstructured or dynamic scenarios. Large models, leveraging their zero-shot and few-shot generalization capabilities, have driven breakthroughs in addressing these challenges. According to the form of planning, LLMempowered high-level planning can be categorized into structured language planning, natural language planning, and programming language planning, as illustrated in Fig. 6. 3.1.1 Structured Language Planning with LLM. LLM can enhance structured language planning through two key strategies, as shown in Fig. 6(a). (1) The first strategy employs LLM as the planner, utilizing its zero/few-shot generalization capability to produce plans. However, Valmeekam et al. [185] demonstrated that LLM often generated infeasible plans due to strict PDDL syntax and semantics, leading to logical errors. To mitigate this problem, LLV [9] introduced an external validator, a PDDL parser or an environment simulator, to check and iteratively refine LLM-generated plans through error feedback. FSP-LLM [175] optimized prompt engineering to align plans with logical constraints, ensuring feasibility of tasks. (2) The second strategy leverages LLM to automate PDDL generation, reducing manual effort in domain modeling. In LLM+P [116], LLM created PDDL domain files and problem descriptions, which were then solved by traditional planners, combining linguistic understanding with symbolic reasoning. PDDL-WM [64] used LLM to iteratively construct and refine PDDL domain models, which were validated by parsers and user feedback to ensure correctness and executability.

snippets: PDDL can also be used as a translation target for natural language, with LLMs used to generate either a PDDL plan or goal [14], [15]. snippets: LLM+P utilizes planning domain definition language (PDDL) as an intermediary interface for describing planning problems. sections.title: # 3) Tool-use and API orchestration
sections.text: Modern benchmarks emphasize multi-step tasks that require calling external tools/APIs, demanding retrieval, parameterization, and multi-hop execution planning. MCP-Bench evaluates LLM agents on realistic, multi-step tasks requiring tool use, cross-tool coordination, precise parameter control, and planning/reasoning, with 28 MCP servers across 250 tools; agents must retrieve relevant tools from fuzzy instructions, plan multi-hop trajectories, ground responses in intermediate outputs, and orchestrate cross-domain workflows [83cb50c1-0]. Tool-augmented LLMs show measurable gains but persistent deficits: planning competence correlates with model strength, yet retrieval, argument construction, and correct API selection remain challenging. API-Bank introduces a runnable evaluation with 73 tools and 314 annotated dialogues, showing GPT-3.5 improves over GPT-3 in tool use and GPT-4 excels in planning, but substantial headroom remains; a trained tool-augmented model (Lynx) exceeds Alpaca by over 26 points and approaches GPT-3.5 [83cb50c1-4]. Surveys and benchmarks note that many prior tool-use evaluations isolate tool-use from planning or assume explicit tool names, whereas realistic settings require fuzzy retrieval and multi-turn adaptation. Recent benchmarks often evaluate tool-use or planning in isolation; MCP-Bench and new multi-turn planning benchmarks (e.g., COMPASS) combine tool-calling, planning, and preference optimization with incremental requirement revelation [83cb50c1-1].

citations.title: MCP-Bench: Benchmarking Tool-Using LLM Agents with Complex Real-World Tasks via MCP Servers
snippets: We introduce MCP-Bench, a benchmark for evaluating large language models (LLMs) on realistic, multi-step tasks that demand tool use, cross-tool coordination, precise parameter control, and planning/reasoning for solving tasks. Built on the Model Context Protocol (MCP), MCP-Bench connects LLMs to 28 representative live MCP servers spanning 250 tools across domains such as finance, traveling, scientific computing, and academic search. Unlike prior API-based benchmarks, each MCP server provides a set of complementary tools designed to work together, enabling the construction of authentic, multi-step tasks with rich input-output coupling. Tasks in MCP-Bench test agents'ability to retrieve relevant tools from fuzzy instructions without explicit tool names, plan multi-hop execution trajectories for complex objectives, ground responses in intermediate tool outputs, and orchestrate cross-domain workflows - capabilities not adequately evaluated by existing benchmarks that rely on explicit tool specifications, shallow few-step workflows, and isolated domain operations. We propose a multi-faceted evaluation framework covering tool-level schema understanding and usage, trajectory-level planning, and task completion. Experiments on 20 advanced LLMs reveal persistent challenges in MCP-Bench. Code and data: https://github.com/Accenture/mcp-bench.

citations.title: API-Bank: A Comprehensive Benchmark for Tool-Augmented LLMs
snippets: Recent research has demonstrated that Large Language Models (LLMs) can enhance their capabilities by utilizing external tools. However, three pivotal questions remain unanswered: (1) How effective are current LLMs in utilizing tools? (2) How can we enhance LLMs' ability to utilize tools? (3) What obstacles need to be overcome to leverage tools? To address these questions, we introduce API-Bank, a groundbreaking benchmark, specifically designed for tool-augmented LLMs. For the first question, we develop a runnable evaluation system consisting of 73 API tools. We annotate 314 tool-use dialogues with 753 API calls to assess the existing LLMs' capabilities in planning, retrieving, and calling APIs. For the second question, we construct a comprehensive training set containing 1,888 tool-use dialogues from 2,138 APIs spanning 1,000 distinct domains. Using this dataset, we train Lynx, a tool-augmented LLM initialized from Alpaca. Experimental results demonstrate that GPT-3.5 exhibits improved tool utilization compared to GPT-3, while GPT-4 excels in planning. However, there is still significant potential for further improvement. Moreover, Lynx surpasses Alpaca's tool utilization performance by more than 26 pts and approaches the effectiveness of GPT-3.5. Through error analysis, we highlight the key challenges for future research in this field to answer the third question.

citations.title: COMPASS: A Multi-Turn Benchmark for Tool-Mediated Planning & Preference Optimization
snippets:
Tool-Use and Planning Benchmarks Recent benchmarks have evaluated language model agents across tool-use and planning capabilities, though typically in isolation. Tool-use benchmarks like Tau-Bench (Yao et al., 2024;Barres et al., 2025) provide comprehensive API libraries but focus primarily on instruction-following in a online customer service setting. Patil et al. ( 2025) includes a wider tool library but user multi-turn is based on predetermined conversation trajectories, while others (Wang et al., 2023) evaluate coding scenarios with oracle-like users. Planning benchmarks have emerged to assess constraint satisfaction and optimization: Zheng et al. ( 2024) evaluates natural language planning tasks while eliminating tool-use complexity, and Kohli et al. (2024) presents flight booking scenarios in multiple-choice format without interactive tool integration. More comprehensive planning evaluation includes multi-day travel planning with hard constraints (Xie et al., 2024), though without the multi-turn preference revelation that characterizes real user interactions. Our work is the first to combine tool-calling, planning, and preference optimization in a multi-turn setting-a combination essential for agents deployed in real-world scenarios where users progressively reveal constraints while agents must dynamically adapt their search and optimization strategies. Concurrent work Qian et al. ( 2025) also explores user preference optimization in a planning setting but with a stronger focus on preference elicitation. 

Multi-Turn Interactions and Task-Oriented Dialogue Assessing agent capabilities in multi-turn settings is crucial for real-world deployment, as users naturally reveal requirements incrementally rather than specifying complete constraints upfront (Laban et al., 2025). Traditional task-oriented dialogue systems (Budzianowski et al., 2018;Rastogi et al., 2019) provide foundational insights: multi-turn interactions occur because users reveal new requirements, request information, and adapt goals when constraints cannot be satisfied. However, these systems typically lack the tool integration and utility optimization challenges present in modern agent evaluation.

sections.title: # 4) Multi-agent, hierarchical, and human-in-the-loop planning
sections.text: Multi-agent and hierarchical decompositions can improve scalability and robustness by separating high-level decomposition from low-level execution and enabling feedback and coordination. LLMs have been used for multi-agent planning via code generation and task allocation, and TwoStep uses LLM decomposition with classical planning for correctness [3fe83b46-3] LLM-empowered high-level planning can be categorized as structured language, natural language, or programming language planning, with LLMs supporting structured planning via two strategies: LLM-as-planner and automating PDDL generation [3fe83b46-4]. Human-in-the-loop preferences and corrections are natural fits for LLMs’ zero-shot generalization in long-horizon tasks, especially when combined with structured outputs for tractable validation and iteration. LLMs support long-horizon human-in-the-loop planning, but converting to PDDL and planning with a classical solver offers advantages for scrutiny, speed, scalability, and avoiding context-window limits [3fe83b46-0].

citations.title: TwoStep: Multi-agent Task Planning using Classical Planners and Large Language Models
snippets: PDDL can also be used as a translation target for natural language, with LLMs used to generate either a PDDL plan or goal [14], [15]. Generating a PDDL goal eliminates the need to track or predict world state after each action, which is required when using LLMs for open-or closed-loop planning, respectively.. However, using a classical planner necessitates specification of all domain information. LLMs have also been used for multi-agent planning through code generation [16] and task allocation through dialogue and path planning [17]. In this paper, we use LLMs to infer commonsense ways to decompose a goal, but leave formal planning to a PDDL system to ensure plan correctness, using each tool for what it is better at.

citations.title: Large Model Empowered Embodied AI: A Survey on Decision-Making and Embodied Learning
snippets: High-level planning produces reasonable plans according to task instructions and perceived information. Traditional high-level planning relies on rule-based methods [59,75,126]. Given initial states and goals specified in Planning Domain Definition Language (PDDL), heuristic search planner verifies action preconditions for feasibility and employs search trees to select optimal action sequences, thereby generating an efficient and cost-effective plan [90]. Although effective in structured environments, rule-based methods struggle with adaptability in unstructured or dynamic scenarios. Large models, leveraging their zero-shot and few-shot generalization capabilities, have driven breakthroughs in addressing these challenges. According to the form of planning, LLMempowered high-level planning can be categorized into structured language planning, natural language planning, and programming language planning, as illustrated in Fig. 6. 3.1.1 Structured Language Planning with LLM. LLM can enhance structured language planning through two key strategies, as shown in Fig. 6(a). (1) The first strategy employs LLM as the planner, utilizing its zero/few-shot generalization capability to produce plans. However, Valmeekam et al. [185] demonstrated that LLM often generated infeasible plans due to strict PDDL syntax and semantics, leading to logical errors. To mitigate this problem, LLV [9] introduced an external validator, a PDDL parser or an environment simulator, to check and iteratively refine LLM-generated plans through error feedback. FSP-LLM [175] optimized prompt engineering to align plans with logical constraints, ensuring feasibility of tasks. (2) The second strategy leverages LLM to automate PDDL generation, reducing manual effort in domain modeling. In LLM+P [116], LLM created PDDL domain files and problem descriptions, which were then solved by traditional planners, combining linguistic understanding with symbolic reasoning. PDDL-WM [64] used LLM to iteratively construct and refine PDDL domain models, which were validated by parsers and user feedback to ensure correctness and executability.

sections.title: # 5) Retrieval, memory, and state tracking
sections.text: Grounding plans with external knowledge and maintaining state improves decision-making in dynamic or information-intensive settings. Feedback-driven frameworks like ReAct and Reflexion explicitly incorporate observations, environment feedback, and memory to revise plans and avoid error propagation. ReAct interleaves Thought, Action, and Observation steps so each step conditions on environment feedback and optionally human critiques or self-evaluation; Reflexion adds explicit Evaluator and Self-reflection LMs plus short- and long-term memory buffers, storing linguistic feedback in episodic memory to shape future decisions [1b51f93d-2]. These mechanisms help address LLMs’ susceptibility to hallucination by anchoring reasoning in current observations and past episodes. Chain-of-Thought improves the executability of plans, indicating progress toward mitigating invalid reasoning [1b51f93d-0] Replanning mechanisms such as CAPE and Text2Reaction adjust local plans after failures by comparing expected vs. actual feedback, though retrospective replanning is constrained by predefined strategies [1b51f93d-3].

citations.title: Chasing Progress, Not Perfection: Revisiting Strategies for End-to-End LLM Plan Generation
snippets: The capability of Large Language Models (LLMs) to plan remains a topic of debate. Some critics argue that strategies to boost LLMs' reasoning skills are ineffective in planning tasks, while others report strong outcomes merely from training models on a planning corpus. This study reassesses recent strategies by developing an end-to-end LLM planner and employing diverse metrics for a thorough evaluation. We find that merely fine-tuning LLMs on a corpus of planning instances does not lead to robust planning skills, as indicated by poor performance on out-of-distribution test sets. At the same time, we find that various strategies, including Chain-of-Thought, do enhance the probability of a plan being executable. This indicates progress towards better plan quality, despite not directly enhancing the final validity rate. Among the strategies we evaluated, reinforcement learning with our novel `Longest Contiguous Common Subsequence' reward emerged as the most effective, contributing to both plan validity and executability. Overall, our research addresses key misconceptions in the LLM-planning literature; we validate incremental progress in plan executability, although plan validity remains a challenge. Hence, future strategies should focus on both these aspects, drawing insights from our findings.

citations.title: LightPlanner: Unleashing the Reasoning Capabilities of Lightweight Large Language Models in Task Planning
snippets:
To improve task planning success rates, some studies have incorporated reasoning mechanisms into conventional planning processes [11], [22], [29]. Inner Monologue [22] uses LLMs and a self-questioning mechanism to enhance multistep planning success rates. ReAct [28] proposes a reasoningthen-action strategy to improve action decision accuracy. Reflexion [30] enhances language model agents through feedback, allowing them to reflect on task outcomes and make better decisions. However, these methods typically perform basic reasoning and do not fully exploit the capabilities of LLMs. Works like DeepSeek-R1 [31], [32] demonstrate that more comprehensive reasoning processes can significantly boost LLM performance in complex tasks. 

Other studies explore replanning mechanisms to enhance task success rates. CAPE [2] uses replanning to analyze failed actions and guide the LLM to regenerate affected subplans. Text2Reaction [33] adjusts local plans by comparing expected and actual feedback. These approaches focus on enabling LLMs to modify plans based on predefined error-handling strategies after failures. However, retrospective replanning is constrained by these predefined strategies and cannot inherently improve the initial task planning performance of LLMs. In contrast, LightPlanner employs hierarchical deep reasoning and dynamically parameterized skill function calls to maximize the inference capabilities of lightweight LLMs, thereby enhancing planning performance in complex scenarios.

citations.title: HADA: Human-AI Agent Decision Alignment Architecture
snippets:
The planning module decomposes a user's high-level goal into a sequence of smaller, tractable subtasks that the agent can address in turn. This explicit task-structure not only guides downstream execution but also gives the system a scaffold for more reliable reasoning. Planning without Feedback. When the plan is created in a single pass, task decomposition relies on internal chains of reasoning generated by an LLM. Two widely cited paradigms are Chain-of-Thought and Tree-of-Thoughts, representing single-path and multi-path reasoning, respectively (Wang et al., 2024b). 

Planning with Feedback. One-shot plans struggle with long-horizon or error-prone tasks because they lack a mechanism to correct earlier decisions. Feedback-driven approaches overcome this limitation by iteratively revising the plan in light of previous actions and observations. Among the most influential are ReAct (Yao et al., 2023b) and Reflexion (Shinn et al., 2023b). ReAct interleaves three repeated steps-Thought, Action, and Observation-so that each new reasoning step conditions on feedback from the environment, optional human critiques, or model-based self-evaluation (Yao et al., 2023b). In contrast, Reflexion augments an agent with explicit Evaluator and Self-reflection LMs plus short-and long-term memory buffers. After every episode, linguistic feedback is stored in an episodic memory that shapes future decisions, enabling continual improvement across coding, reasoning, and decision-making tasks (Shinn et al., 2023b).

sections.title: # Benchmarks and quantitative evidence
sections.text:
- Direct LLM planning: Even strong models struggle on simple problems without structured support, and large portions of generated plans are inexecutable without recovery and validation. GPT-4 achieves only 35% accuracy on simple planning problems when planned directly [1b51f93d-4] On average, only the first 2.65 actions are executable; recovery pipelines raise success from 21.9% to 27.5% [1b51f93d-1].
- Translation to PDDL: Benchmarks like Planetarium provide rigorous evaluation of NL-to-PDDL translation quality and demonstrate that translation-to-PDDL outperforms direct LLM planning under hybrid execution with classical planners. Early evidence suggests translation to PDDL performs better than direct LLM planning and enables reliable hybrid pipelines [1b51f93d-4].
- Tool-augmented planning: MCP-Bench and API-Bank quantify multi-step planning with tool retrieval and API execution, showing GPT-4’s relative strength in planning and substantial room to improve retrieval, argument construction, and API selection across models and training data. MCP-Bench evaluates multi-tool, multi-hop planning with live servers and proposes tool-, trajectory-, and task-level metrics [83cb50c1-0] API-Bank’s annotated runnable tasks show GPT-4 excels at planning while GPT-3.5 improves over GPT-3; training a tool-augmented LLM (Lynx) yields >26-point gains over Alpaca [83cb50c1-4].
- Planning-specific benchmarks: Collections like PlanBench, Natural Plan, TravelPlanner, ACPBench, and AutoPlan-Bench assess plan generation, optimization, verification, and NL-to-PDDL conversion, providing standardized tasks and metrics for the community. LLM+AP benchmarks include PlanBench (cost-optimal, plan verification), Natural Plan (realistic planning/scheduling with APIs), TravelPlanner (agent-based travel planning), ACPBench (actions, change, planning across 13 domains), and AutoPlan-Bench (LLMs convert PDDL to NL and back) [83cb50c1-2].
- Classical vs. LLM planning: Comparative analyses show classical planners remain more reliable for solving symbolically correct plans, while LLMs contribute to problem formalization, decomposition, and natural-language communication of plans. Symbolic pipelines still underperform classical planners, with only partial recovery of plan quality [1b51f93d-1] LLM-generated PDDL domain/problem files can be solved by traditional planners, combining linguistic understanding with symbolic reasoning [3fe83b46-4].

citations.title: MCP-Bench: Benchmarking Tool-Using LLM Agents with Complex Real-World Tasks via MCP Servers
snippets: We introduce MCP-Bench, a benchmark for evaluating large language models (LLMs) on realistic, multi-step tasks that demand tool use, cross-tool coordination, precise parameter control, and planning/reasoning for solving tasks. Built on the Model Context Protocol (MCP), MCP-Bench connects LLMs to 28 representative live MCP servers spanning 250 tools across domains such as finance, traveling, scientific computing, and academic search. Unlike prior API-based benchmarks, each MCP server provides a set of complementary tools designed to work together, enabling the construction of authentic, multi-step tasks with rich input-output coupling. Tasks in MCP-Bench test agents'ability to retrieve relevant tools from fuzzy instructions without explicit tool names, plan multi-hop execution trajectories for complex objectives, ground responses in intermediate tool outputs, and orchestrate cross-domain workflows - capabilities not adequately evaluated by existing benchmarks that rely on explicit tool specifications, shallow few-step workflows, and isolated domain operations. We propose a multi-faceted evaluation framework covering tool-level schema understanding and usage, trajectory-level planning, and task completion. Experiments on 20 advanced LLMs reveal persistent challenges in MCP-Bench. Code and data: https://github.com/Accenture/mcp-bench.

citations.title: How Far Are LLMs from Symbolic Planners? An NLP-Based Perspective
snippets: The reasoning and planning abilities of Large Language Models (LLMs) have been a frequent topic of discussion in recent years. Their ability to take unstructured planning problems as input has made LLMs'integration into AI planning an area of interest. Nevertheless, LLMs are still not reliable as planners, with the generated plans often containing mistaken or hallucinated actions. Existing benchmarking and evaluation methods investigate planning with LLMs, focusing primarily on success rate as a quality indicator in various planning tasks, such as validating plans or planning in relaxed conditions. In this paper, we approach planning with LLMs as a natural language processing (NLP) task, given that LLMs are NLP models themselves. We propose a recovery pipeline consisting of an NLP-based evaluation of the generated plans, along with three stages to recover the plans through NLP manipulation of the LLM-generated plans, and eventually complete the plan using a symbolic planner. This pipeline provides a holistic analysis of LLM capabilities in the context of AI task planning, enabling a broader understanding of the quality of invalid plans. Our findings reveal no clear evidence of underlying reasoning during plan generation, and that a pipeline comprising an NLP-based analysis of the plans, followed by a recovery mechanism, still falls short of the quality and reliability of classical planners. On average, only the first 2.65 actions of the plan are executable, with the average length of symbolically generated plans being 8.4 actions. The pipeline still improves action quality and increases the overall success rate from 21.9% to 27.5%.

citations.title: Planetarium: A Rigorous Benchmark for Translating Text to Structured Planning Languages
snippets:
Recently, there has been growing interest in using large language models (LLMs) to solve planning problems. Some research has focused on generating plans directly with LLMs (Valmeekam et al., 2023a(Valmeekam et al., , 2022(Valmeekam et al., , 2023b;;Silver et al., 2022Silver et al., , 2023)). However, this approach has shown limited success; GPT-4 only achieves 35% accuracy on simple planning problems (Valmeekam et al., 2023a). Another line of research uses LLMs to convert natural language prompts into structured planning languages, such as the planning domain definition language (Liu et al., 2023;Xie et al., 2023;Guan et al., 2023;Chalvatzaki et al., 2023;Yang et al., 2023b). Early evidence suggests this method performs better than : An example of one planning goal corresponding to many correct PDDL goals. All PDDL goals in the top row represent the displayed goal correctly. The bottom row illustrates PDDL goals with different error types, showing instances that are solvable (a planner can generate a plan, but for a different planning problem), parseable (the PDDL syntax is correct but will not produce any plan from a planner), and not parseable (it is not valid PDDL). See Section 5 for details. 

generating plans directly with LLMs (Liu et al., 2023). Despite its promise, there are no rigorous techniques or benchmarks for evaluating the translation of natural language planning descriptions to PDDL. 

Translating natural language to PDDL enables a hybrid, best-of-both-worlds approach. The LLM is responsible for interpreting natural language, and the resulting PDDL can be given to traditional, symbolic planners that have been developed over decades (Fikes and Nilsson, 1971;McDermott et al., 1998;Helmert, 2006;Baier et al., 2009;Vidal and Geffner, 2006). These traditional planners are efficient and ensure the correctness of their so-lutions. In contrast, leaving the planning to LLMs does not guarantee correctness, making them unreliable for critical applications.

citations.title: API-Bank: A Comprehensive Benchmark for Tool-Augmented LLMs
snippets: Recent research has demonstrated that Large Language Models (LLMs) can enhance their capabilities by utilizing external tools. However, three pivotal questions remain unanswered: (1) How effective are current LLMs in utilizing tools? (2) How can we enhance LLMs' ability to utilize tools? (3) What obstacles need to be overcome to leverage tools? To address these questions, we introduce API-Bank, a groundbreaking benchmark, specifically designed for tool-augmented LLMs. For the first question, we develop a runnable evaluation system consisting of 73 API tools. We annotate 314 tool-use dialogues with 753 API calls to assess the existing LLMs' capabilities in planning, retrieving, and calling APIs. For the second question, we construct a comprehensive training set containing 1,888 tool-use dialogues from 2,138 APIs spanning 1,000 distinct domains. Using this dataset, we train Lynx, a tool-augmented LLM initialized from Alpaca. Experimental results demonstrate that GPT-3.5 exhibits improved tool utilization compared to GPT-3, while GPT-4 excels in planning. However, there is still significant potential for further improvement. Moreover, Lynx surpasses Alpaca's tool utilization performance by more than 26 pts and approaches the effectiveness of GPT-3.5. Through error analysis, we highlight the key challenges for future research in this field to answer the third question.

citations.title: LLMs as Planning Formalizers: A Survey for Leveraging Large Language Models to Construct Automated Planning Models
snippets:
LLMs, with their non-deterministic output behaviors, make it challenging to assess the quality of frameworks used in planning benchmarks. This heightens the importance of robustness, especially for evaluating LLMs' ability to extract planning models (Behnke and Bercher, 2024). 

LLM+AP benchmarks typically fall into two categories: (1) evaluating LLMs' direct planning abilities; (2) assessing the quality of planning specifications produced by LLMs. While this survey focuses on the latter, we recognize that end-to-end planning benchmarks can also support research on LLMgenerated models for external planners. 

LLMs-as-Planner Benchmarks: To determine whether testing PDDL domains have been leaked to training data of LLMs, Mystery Blocksworld (Kambhampati et al., 2024) obfuscates the classic Blocksworld (Gupta et al., 2010) planning problem by altering the named types so they are semantically equivalent but syntactically nonsensical. ALFWorld (Shridhar et al., 2021) and Household Guan et al. (2023) tackles the complexities of real-world typical household environment that uses PDDL semantics to produce textual observations and high-level actions. TravelPlanner (Xie et al., 2024a) assesses language models' abilities in planning through agent-based interactions in a travel-planning environment. Zheng et al. (2024) extend this work with Natural Plan, which evaluates LLMs on realistic planning and scheduling benchmarks using APIs. PlanBench (Valmeekam et al., 2023a) aims to systematically evaluate LLM planning capabilities with an emphasis on costoptimal planning and plan verification. ACPBench (Kokel et al., 2024) standardizes evaluation tasks and metrics for assessing reasoning about actions, changes (transitions), and planning-across 13 domains, on 22 SOTA language models. AutoPlan-Bench (Stein and Koller, 2023) first converts PDDL planning benchmarks into NL via LLMs, and then tasks LLMs to produce a plan through various prompting techniques.

sections.title: # Strengths, limitations, and failure modes
sections.text:
Strengths:
- Interpretable, natural-language plans and flexible, zero-shot decomposition across domains and multimodal settings. LLM-based agents integrate perception, action, and interaction with modules for thinking and world abstractions [dbc1af94-2].
- Rapid prototyping and adaptability: LLMs can propose high-level strategies and revise plans with feedback, human preferences, or episodic memory. ReAct and Reflexion operationalize iterative feedback and memory to improve long-horizon planning and decision-making [1b51f93d-2].

Limitations and failure modes:
- Plan feasibility and hallucination: LLMs often produce infeasible or logically inconsistent plans that fail to execute or optimize cost/time. LLM plans often contain mistaken/hallucinated actions; only a small fraction of actions are executable without recovery [1b51f93d-1].
- brittleness and variance: Performance can degrade on out-of-distribution tasks; fine-tuning alone is insufficient; chain-of-thought helps executability but not final validity. Fine-tuning on planning corpora fails on OOD tests; chain-of-thought increases executability, but validity remains challenging [1b51f93d-0].
- Tool-use pitfalls: Retrieval errors, wrong API selection, poor argument construction, and brittle state grounding impede multi-step execution even for strong models. Despite GPT-4’s planning strengths, retrieval, argument construction, and API selection remain challenging; training data and methods can close part of the gap [83cb50c1-4].
- Safety and compliance: LLMs may hallucinate unsafe actions or fail to respect constraints; hybrid pipelines with validators, parsers, and simulators mitigate but do not eliminate risks. Validator components (parser/simulator) iteratively check and refine plans, addressing logical errors and improving feasibility [3fe83b46-4].

citations.title: Learn as Individuals, Evolve as a Team: Multi-agent LLMs Adaptation in Embodied Environments
snippets: LLM-based Single-agent Planning Recent advancements in large language models (LLMs) have led to the development of highly capable models, including LLaMA 3 [34,9], GPT-4 [1,16], and DeepSeek-R1 [10]. By leveraging their extensive general knowledge and exceptional reasoning capabilities, LLM-based agents have achieved remarkable success in embodied decision-making tasks that integrate perception, action, and interaction with physical or simulated environments [31]. Seminal works such as SayCan [2], grounded decoding [14] and Text2Motion [21] ground agent actions by using value functions to bridge language with real-world tasks. Follow-up studies have enhanced LLM planning capabilities by introducing thinking modules [15,20] or world abstractions [25]. Others have leveraged in-context learning [30] when expert demonstrations are available. Another research direction focuses on aligning visual perception with language objectives, resulting in algorithms such as VLMaps [13], TaPA [35], mobility VLA [36], and NavGPT [40,39]. These methods refine LLMs' ability to plan and act in environments requiring seamless integration of language and vision.

sections.title: # Design patterns and best practices
sections.text:
- Hybridize LLMs with classical planners: Use LLMs for interpretation and decomposition, and planners for correctness and efficiency; validate translations via parsers/simulators and iteratively refine. PDDL translation plus classical planning improves scrutiny, execution speed, scalability, and context-capacity [3fe83b46-0] LLV adds external validators; PDDL-WM iteratively refines domain models with feedback [3fe83b46-4].
- Embrace feedback and reflection: Incorporate ReAct-style Thought–Action–Observation loops and Reflexion-style evaluators and episodic memory to correct errors and adapt to user preferences over time. ReAct conditions steps on environment feedback and critiques; Reflexion adds explicit evaluators and memory buffers [1b51f93d-2].

[185] demonstrated that LLM often generated infeasible plans due to strict PDDL syntax and semantics, leading to logical errors. citations.title: Planetarium: A Rigorous Benchmark for Translating Text to Structured Planning Languages
snippets:
Recently, there has been growing interest in using large language models (LLMs) to solve planning problems. Some research has focused on generating plans directly with LLMs (Valmeekam et al., 2023a(Valmeekam et al., , 2022(Valmeekam et al., , 2023b;;Silver et al., 2022Silver et al., , 2023)). However, this approach has shown limited success; GPT-4 only achieves 35% accuracy on simple planning problems (Valmeekam et al., 2023a). Another line of research uses LLMs to convert natural language prompts into structured planning languages, such as the planning domain definition language (Liu et al., 2023;Xie et al., 2023;Guan et al., 2023;Chalvatzaki et al., 2023;Yang et al., 2023b). Early evidence suggests this method performs better than : An example of one planning goal corresponding to many correct PDDL goals. All PDDL goals in the top row represent the displayed goal correctly. The bottom row illustrates PDDL goals with different error types, showing instances that are solvable (a planner can generate a plan, but for a different planning problem), parseable (the PDDL syntax is correct but will not produce any plan from a planner), and not parseable (it is not valid PDDL). See Section 5 for details. 

generating plans directly with LLMs (Liu et al., 2023). Despite its promise, there are no rigorous techniques or benchmarks for evaluating the translation of natural language planning descriptions to PDDL. 

Translating natural language to PDDL enables a hybrid, best-of-both-worlds approach. The LLM is responsible for interpreting natural language, and the resulting PDDL can be given to traditional, symbolic planners that have been developed over decades (Fikes and Nilsson, 1971;McDermott et al., 1998;Helmert, 2006;Baier et al., 2009;Vidal and Geffner, 2006). These traditional planners are efficient and ensure the correctness of their so-lutions. In contrast, leaving the planning to LLMs does not guarantee correctness, making them unreliable for critical applications.

citations.title: COMPASS: A Multi-Turn Benchmark for Tool-Mediated Planning & Preference Optimization
snippets:
Tool-Use and Planning Benchmarks Recent benchmarks have evaluated language model agents across tool-use and planning capabilities, though typically in isolation. Tool-use benchmarks like Tau-Bench (Yao et al., 2024;Barres et al., 2025) provide comprehensive API libraries but focus primarily on instruction-following in a online customer service setting. Patil et al. ( 2025) includes a wider tool library but user multi-turn is based on predetermined conversation trajectories, while others (Wang et al., 2023) evaluate coding scenarios with oracle-like users. Planning benchmarks have emerged to assess constraint satisfaction and optimization: Zheng et al. ( 2024) evaluates natural language planning tasks while eliminating tool-use complexity, and Kohli et al. (2024) presents flight booking scenarios in multiple-choice format without interactive tool integration. More comprehensive planning evaluation includes multi-day travel planning with hard constraints (Xie et al., 2024), though without the multi-turn preference revelation that characterizes real user interactions. Our work is the first to combine tool-calling, planning, and preference optimization in a multi-turn setting-a combination essential for agents deployed in real-world scenarios where users progressively reveal constraints while agents must dynamically adapt their search and optimization strategies. Concurrent work Qian et al. ( 2025) also explores user preference optimization in a planning setting but with a stronger focus on preference elicitation. 

Multi-Turn Interactions and Task-Oriented Dialogue Assessing agent capabilities in multi-turn settings is crucial for real-world deployment, as users naturally reveal requirements incrementally rather than specifying complete constraints upfront (Laban et al., 2025). Traditional task-oriented dialogue systems (Budzianowski et al., 2018;Rastogi et al., 2019) provide foundational insights: multi-turn interactions occur because users reveal new requirements, request information, and adapt goals when constraints cannot be satisfied. However, these systems typically lack the tool integration and utility optimization challenges present in modern agent evaluation.

snippets:
The planning module decomposes a user's high-level goal into a sequence of smaller, tractable subtasks that the agent can address in turn. This explicit task-structure not only guides downstream execution but also gives the system a scaffold for more reliable reasoning. Planning without Feedback. When the plan is created in a single pass, task decomposition relies on internal chains of reasoning generated by an LLM. Two widely cited paradigms are Chain-of-Thought and Tree-of-Thoughts, representing single-path and multi-path reasoning, respectively (Wang et al., 2024b). 

Planning with Feedback. One-shot plans struggle with long-horizon or error-prone tasks because they lack a mechanism to correct earlier decisions. Feedback-driven approaches overcome this limitation by iteratively revising the plan in light of previous actions and observations. Among the most influential are ReAct (Yao et al., 2023b) and Reflexion (Shinn et al., 2023b). In contrast, Reflexion augments an agent with explicit Evaluator and Self-reflection LMs plus short-and long-term memory buffers. After every episode, linguistic feedback is stored in an episodic memory that shapes future decisions, enabling continual improvement across coding, reasoning, and decision-making tasks (Shinn et al., 2023b).

citations.title: MORPHeus: a Multimodal One-armed Robot-assisted Peeling System with Human Users In-the-loop
snippets: Language serves as a natural interface to incorporate human preferences into long-horizon planning [27,28].In recent years, there has been significant progress in large language models [29][30][31][32][33][34][35][36].Given their extensive pre-training on diverse text data, LLMs exhibit impressive zero-shot generalization capabilities, making them suitable for use in robot planning [37][38][39].Therefore, we use LLM to perform long-horizon planning with human-in-the-loop, taking their preferences into consideration.However, compared to directly generating task plans using LLMs, converting natural language to Planning Domain Definition Language (PDDL), and planning with a classical planner has the following advantages: (1) the PDDL generated by LLM can be quickly scrutinized; (2) executing a synthesized program is often quicker than repeatedly querying the LLM for each new job; (3) synthesized programs can be customized for tasks of any size; (4) using PDDL circumvents the context window size limitations inherent to LLMs [40].We therefore use LLM integrated with PDDL for long-horizon planning.Previously, research has already focused on fine-tuning Large Language Models (LLMs) for the PDDL domain [41], as well as on translating natural language into PDDL [42][43][44][45].These capabilities make LLMs well-suited for human-in-the-loop planning scenarios.

citations.title: API-Bank: A Comprehensive Benchmark for Tool-Augmented LLMs
snippets: Recent research has demonstrated that Large Language Models (LLMs) can enhance their capabilities by utilizing external tools. However, three pivotal questions remain unanswered: (1) How effective are current LLMs in utilizing tools? (2) How can we enhance LLMs' ability to utilize tools? (3) What obstacles need to be overcome to leverage tools? To address these questions, we introduce API-Bank, a groundbreaking benchmark, specifically designed for tool-augmented LLMs. For the first question, we develop a runnable evaluation system consisting of 73 API tools. We annotate 314 tool-use dialogues with 753 API calls to assess the existing LLMs' capabilities in planning, retrieving, and calling APIs. For the second question, we construct a comprehensive training set containing 1,888 tool-use dialogues from 2,138 APIs spanning 1,000 distinct domains. Using this dataset, we train Lynx, a tool-augmented LLM initialized from Alpaca. Experimental results demonstrate that GPT-3.5 exhibits improved tool utilization compared to GPT-3, while GPT-4 excels in planning. However, there is still significant potential for further improvement. Moreover, Lynx surpasses Alpaca's tool utilization performance by more than 26 pts and approaches the effectiveness of GPT-3.5. Through error analysis, we highlight the key challenges for future research in this field to answer the third question.

snippets:
LLMs, with their non-deterministic output behaviors, make it challenging to assess the quality of frameworks used in planning benchmarks. This heightens the importance of robustness, especially for evaluating LLMs' ability to extract planning models (Behnke and Bercher, 2024). 

LLM+AP benchmarks typically fall into two categories: (1) evaluating LLMs' direct planning abilities; (2) assessing the quality of planning specifications produced by LLMs. While this survey focuses on the latter, we recognize that end-to-end planning benchmarks can also support research on LLMgenerated models for external planners. 

LLMs-as-Planner Benchmarks: To determine whether testing PDDL domains have been leaked to training data of LLMs, Mystery Blocksworld (Kambhampati et al., 2024) obfuscates the classic Blocksworld (Gupta et al., 2010) planning problem by altering the named types so they are semantically equivalent but syntactically nonsensical. ALFWorld (Shridhar et al., 2021) and Household Guan et al. (2023) tackles the complexities of real-world typical household environment that uses PDDL semantics to produce textual observations and high-level actions. TravelPlanner (Xie et al., 2024a) assesses language models' abilities in planning through agent-based interactions in a travel-planning environment. Zheng et al. (2024) extend this work with Natural Plan, which evaluates LLMs on realistic planning and scheduling benchmarks using APIs. PlanBench (Valmeekam et al., 2023a) aims to systematically evaluate LLM planning capabilities with an emphasis on costoptimal planning and plan verification. ACPBench (Kokel et al., 2024) standardizes evaluation tasks and metrics for assessing reasoning about actions, changes (transitions), and planning-across 13 domains, on 22 SOTA language models. AutoPlan-Bench (Stein and Koller, 2023) first converts PDDL planning benchmarks into NL via LLMs, and then tasks LLMs to produce a plan through various prompting techniques.

sections.title: # Outlook and open problems
sections.text:
Despite progress, LLMs still trail classical planners in reliability and optimality on symbolically well-specified problems, and multi-step tool-mediated planning remains error-prone due to retrieval, grounding, and preference elicitation challenges. Recovery pipelines improve success but do not match classical planners; only a small portion of LLM plans are executable without correction [1b51f93d-1] Combining tool-calling, planning, and preference optimization in multi-turn settings remains underexplored and challenging [83cb50c1-1]. Research opportunities include robust retrieval and grounding under ambiguity, principled plan verification and repair mechanisms, RL or constrained decoding that improves plan validity and cost optimality, and standardized, leakage-controlled evaluations for NL-to-PDDL translation and LLM-plus-planner pipelines. Surveys emphasize leakage concerns and the need for robust evaluation of LLMs as planners and LLM-generated planning specifications [83cb50c1-2] Reinforcement learning with Longest Contiguous Common Subsequence reward improves plan validity and executability over chain-of-thought alone [1b51f93d-0].

In practice, the most dependable systems blend LLMs’ interpretive and decompositional strengths with classical planning and tool execution, augmented by retrieval, memory, and verification—yielding better safety, transparency, and performance on realistic, multi-step planning tasks. Hybrid pipelines that translate to PDDL and use classical planners combine linguistic understanding with symbolic reasoning for correctness [3fe83b46-4] Reflection and memory mechanisms improve decision quality in long-horizon, feedback-driven planning [1b51f93d-2].
