citations.title: How Far Are LLMs from Symbolic Planners? An NLP-Based Perspective
snippets: The reasoning and planning abilities of Large Language Models (LLMs) have been a frequent topic of discussion in recent years. Their ability to take unstructured planning problems as input has made LLMs'integration into AI planning an area of interest. Nevertheless, LLMs are still not reliable as planners, with the generated plans often containing mistaken or hallucinated actions. Existing benchmarking and evaluation methods investigate planning with LLMs, focusing primarily on success rate as a quality indicator in various planning tasks, such as validating plans or planning in relaxed conditions. In this paper, we approach planning with LLMs as a natural language processing (NLP) task, given that LLMs are NLP models themselves. We propose a recovery pipeline consisting of an NLP-based evaluation of the generated plans, along with three stages to recover the plans through NLP manipulation of the LLM-generated plans, and eventually complete the plan using a symbolic planner. This pipeline provides a holistic analysis of LLM capabilities in the context of AI task planning, enabling a broader understanding of the quality of invalid plans. Our findings reveal no clear evidence of underlying reasoning during plan generation, and that a pipeline comprising an NLP-based analysis of the plans, followed by a recovery mechanism, still falls short of the quality and reliability of classical planners. On average, only the first 2.65 actions of the plan are executable, with the average length of symbolically generated plans being 8.4 actions. The pipeline still improves action quality and increases the overall success rate from 21.9% to 27.5%.

citations.title: Chasing Progress, Not Perfection: Revisiting Strategies for End-to-End LLM Plan Generation
snippets: The capability of Large Language Models (LLMs) to plan remains a topic of debate. Some critics argue that strategies to boost LLMs' reasoning skills are ineffective in planning tasks, while others report strong outcomes merely from training models on a planning corpus. This study reassesses recent strategies by developing an end-to-end LLM planner and employing diverse metrics for a thorough evaluation. We find that merely fine-tuning LLMs on a corpus of planning instances does not lead to robust planning skills, as indicated by poor performance on out-of-distribution test sets. At the same time, we find that various strategies, including Chain-of-Thought, do enhance the probability of a plan being executable. This indicates progress towards better plan quality, despite not directly enhancing the final validity rate. Among the strategies we evaluated, reinforcement learning with our novel `Longest Contiguous Common Subsequence' reward emerged as the most effective, contributing to both plan validity and executability. Overall, our research addresses key misconceptions in the LLM-planning literature; we validate incremental progress in plan executability, although plan validity remains a challenge. Hence, future strategies should focus on both these aspects, drawing insights from our findings.

question: DRL for smart traffic management

sections.title: # Overview: Why DRL for Smart Traffic Management
sections.text: Deep reinforcement learning (DRL) has emerged as a promising approach for smart traffic management because it can learn adaptive policies in large, dynamic environments without hand-crafted rules, and it has been shown to outperform traditional fixed-time and heuristic controllers in simulation on key metrics such as delay, queue length, and travel time. DRL-based signal control studies report large reductions in waiting time and increases in speed compared to legacy fixed-time control under congestion, with reward design critically affecting performance [0e738d2c-0] Hybrid systems integrating model predictive control, graph learning, and DRL have also been proposed to better capture spatiotemporal traffic dynamics and adapt to real-time conditions [0e738d2c-0]. DRL is applied across multiple control tasks—signal optimization at intersections, coordination across networks, ramp metering on freeways, and adaptive variable speed limits—often using centralized training with decentralized execution to scale to citywide networks. DRL is increasingly used for smart traffic control/management (signals, ramp metering, congestion pricing, route guidance), with large-scale simulators serving as training/testbeds [195eb981-0] Recent surveys emphasize RL- and deep RL-based signal control methods as part of a broader evolution from classical approaches to data-driven learning [195eb981-1].

citations.title: Towards a Very Large Scale Traffic Simulator for Multi-Agent Reinforcement Learning Testbeds
snippets:
Traffic congestion becomes one of the most severe urban problems in recent years, and smart and effective control and management strategies (e.g., signal control, congestion pricing, ramp metering, route guidance, etc.) are in great need to alleviate the congestion issue. Traditionally, mathematical programming is employed to obtain the optimal policy on small-scale networks, while it may fail in city-wide networks due to the exponentially growing problem scale and complexity. To this end, Deep Reinforcement Learning (DRL) emerges as one of the tools for decision-making in a largescale and complex environment, and its application in smart traffic control and management attracts wide attentions in recent years.

The development of DRL for traffic management and control requires accurate and large-scale traffic simulators as training and testing environments. Table I presents a summary of traffic simulators for DRL tasks. Most simulators leverage car-following models and lane-change models in a microscopic level. However, due to the computational cost of microscopic model, it is difficult to operate a very large-scale scenario based on these simulators. Mesoscopic and Macroscopic traffic models were developed in the transportation community to improve the simulation efficiency. Mesoscopic simulation models the congestion dynamics on links. However, the gridlock effect, a special case of traffic congestion that vehicles are blocked in a circle queue, is prone to happen under large-scale scenarios due to the improper settings of link attributes; macroscopic models prevent the vehicle gridlock, but it sacrifices the simulation precision. Therefore, a model that incorporates advantages of both mesoscopic models and macroscopic models would be the optimal one to fulfill the very large-scale traffic simulation. In this paper,

citations.title: Implementation of a Real-Time Analysis Simulation System for Traffic Signal Control Algorithms to Reduce Vehicle Exhaust Emissions and Improve Traffic Flow
snippets:
To overcome the limitations of legacy traffic signal control methods, a signal control algorithm using deep reinforcement learning was studied [19]. This algorithm was evaluated by the waiting time of vehicles approaching the intersection, the average speed, and the number of stops as main performance indicators. Using various reward functions and state definitions, it showed excellent performance, such as a 42% reduction in waiting time and a 29% increase in vehicle speed compared to legacy fixed-time signal control in traffic congestion situations. In particular, it was confirmed that the design of the reward function had a great impact on performance and that a value-based reinforcement learning algorithm provided better results than a policy-based one. This study confirmed the possibility of a traffic signal control system that can dynamically adjust signals in real-time according to traffic volume and suggested a method that can contribute to solving urban traffic congestion problems. 

SUMO [3] is an open-source software for traffic simulation and is a tool that can precisely model individual vehicles, signal systems, and pedestrian movements on the road through microscopic simulation. When information on traffic volume is entered through an XML-formatted file, traffic flow simulation is possible with only SUMO's basic simulation engine. SUMO is an open platform that can be expanded through customization by 3rd party programmers. 

In particular, it can communicate with external programs through TraCI (Traffic Control Interface), so real-time traffic control is possible by applying signal control algorithms in languages such as Python. Through this, various traffic data can be collected from simulations, and CO2 emissions, vehicle waiting times, and signal control performance can be analyzed. However, SUMO has a somewhat high entry barrier because it requires complex settings and various file processing to provide various data formats and functions. In addition, since the visualization function is simple, additional linkage and integration work with various external tools is required to add additional advanced visualization functions. 

A system that effectively controls traffic signals in complex urban traffic situations by combining Model Predictive Control (MPC), Graph Convolutional Networks (GCNs), Gated Recurrent Units (GRUs), and Deep Reinforcement Learning (DRL) has been studied [20]. This system can effectively reflect spatiotemporal characteristics to predict traffic flow more accurately and can optimize signal control by adapting to real-time traffic situations through deep reinforcement learning.

citations.title: A Survey on Traffic Signal Control Methods
snippets: In this survey, we will cover many classical or widely accepted transportation approaches in traffic signal control. We refer readers interested in comprehensive transportation approaches to [Li et al. 2014;Papageorgiou et al. 2003;Roess et al. 2004]. The application of reinforcement learning methods in traffic signal control is relatively new. Recent advances in deep reinforcement learning also arouses new applications of RL in traffic signal control problem. While [Yau et al. 2017] and [Mannion et al. 2016] provide comprehensive surveys mainly on earlier studies before the popularity of deep reinforcement learning, in this survey, we will have comprehensive coverage in RL-based traffic signal control approaches, including the recent advances in deep RL-based traffic signal control methods.

sections.title: # Core Tasks and DRL Algorithms
sections.text:
At the intersection, DRL agents take as state features or raw images of queued vehicles and choose phase transitions or phase durations as actions, with rewards tied to aggregate performance (e.g., total delay, queue, stops). A common formulation uses lane-occupancy counts as states, discrete or softened traffic-light phases as actions, and negative aggregate delay as reward, with policy gradients or cross-entropy methods [0e738d2c-3]. Value-based methods like DQN and policy-based methods like A2C/actor-critic are both used; reward design and representation are key drivers of performance. One study found value-based DRL outperformed policy-based variants under congestion and that reward functions strongly impacted results [0e738d2c-0] A DQN-based controller with a discrete traffic state encoding achieved 82% delay, 66% queue, and 20% travel-time reductions versus a strong neural-network baseline in SUMO [0e738d2c-2] A SUMO-based DQN and a Grouping-DQN variant improved maximum queue length and queue time over A2C, with Weibull-based demand to increase realism [0e738d2c-4].

For multi-intersection networks, multi-agent DRL (MARL) is used to coordinate signals by sharing neighbor state and using centralized critics and decentralized actors. citations.title: Using a Deep Reinforcement Learning Agent for Traffic Signal Control
snippets: Ensuring transportation systems are efficient is a priority for modern society. Technological advances have made it possible for transportation systems to collect large volumes of varied data on an unprecedented scale. We propose a traffic signal control system which takes advantage of this new, high quality data, with minimal abstraction compared to other proposed systems. We apply modern deep reinforcement learning methods to build a truly adaptive traffic signal control agent in the traffic microsimulator SUMO. We propose a new state space, the discrete traffic state encoding, which is information dense. The discrete traffic state encoding is used as input to a deep convolutional neural network, trained using Q-learning with experience replay. Our agent was compared against a one hidden layer neural network traffic signal control agent and reduces average cumulative delay by 82%, average queue length by 66% and average travel time by 20%.

citations.title: Application of Traffic Light Control in Oversaturated Urban Network Using Multi-Agent Deep Reinforcement Learning
snippets:
The computational complexity of traffic signal control using a traditional reinforcement learning system increases exponentially with extended state space, complicated intersection features, and heterogeneous intersection structures.

Numerous types of research have been conducted by using deep reinforcement learning (DRL) to adapt traffic signal control [9] for a single intersection [10], [11], [12], and multiple intersections [13], [14], [15], [16], [17].Although reinforcement learning has succeeded in traffic light control in a single intersection, it is still challenging to apply in multiple traffic light controls because the dimensionality of the state and action space grows computationally intractable with the number of intersections.In practical applications, there are many situations where the environment is only partially observable, meaning that agents lack complete information about its state to engage with.This situation can be simulated by using a partially observable Markov decision process (POMDP).Due to multi-agent taxonomies such as the curse of dimensionality and multi-agent credit assignment, deep reinforcement learning for multi-agent environments is inherently more challenging than singleagent environments [18].The local information about intersections would ultimately lead to modeling complexities as the size of the traffic network grows.Furthermore, the observable region surrounding local intersections impacts traffic control.

Modeling and exploiting other agents' behaviors in a multiagent system (MAS) has received much attention in the past decade [19].A multi-agent RL (MARL) algorithm has been proposed as a possible solution to the abovementioned issues.However, the scalability of multi-agent deep reinforcement learning approaches is often limited and vulnerable to partial observability.Centralized learning with decentralized execution is an alternative and popular strategy in which agents are trained simultaneously by using a centralized mechanism via an open communication channel [18], [20].The centralized control mechanism teaches agents to control the traffic signals across the road network by using global information.On the other hand, using local knowledge, decentralized control techniques model signal light control at multiple intersections as a multi-agent system.Each agent is in charge of a specific intersection and only sees and senses certain aspects of the traffic situation.

citations.title: Implementation of a Real-Time Analysis Simulation System for Traffic Signal Control Algorithms to Reduce Vehicle Exhaust Emissions and Improve Traffic Flow
snippets:
To overcome the limitations of legacy traffic signal control methods, a signal control algorithm using deep reinforcement learning was studied [19]. This algorithm was evaluated by the waiting time of vehicles approaching the intersection, the average speed, and the number of stops as main performance indicators. Using various reward functions and state definitions, it showed excellent performance, such as a 42% reduction in waiting time and a 29% increase in vehicle speed compared to legacy fixed-time signal control in traffic congestion situations. In particular, it was confirmed that the design of the reward function had a great impact on performance and that a value-based reinforcement learning algorithm provided better results than a policy-based one. This study confirmed the possibility of a traffic signal control system that can dynamically adjust signals in real-time according to traffic volume and suggested a method that can contribute to solving urban traffic congestion problems. 

SUMO [3] is an open-source software for traffic simulation and is a tool that can precisely model individual vehicles, signal systems, and pedestrian movements on the road through microscopic simulation. When information on traffic volume is entered through an XML-formatted file, traffic flow simulation is possible with only SUMO's basic simulation engine. SUMO is an open platform that can be expanded through customization by 3rd party programmers. 

In particular, it can communicate with external programs through TraCI (Traffic Control Interface), so real-time traffic control is possible by applying signal control algorithms in languages such as Python. Through this, various traffic data can be collected from simulations, and CO2 emissions, vehicle waiting times, and signal control performance can be analyzed. However, SUMO has a somewhat high entry barrier because it requires complex settings and various file processing to provide various data formats and functions. In addition, since the visualization function is simple, additional linkage and integration work with various external tools is required to add additional advanced visualization functions. 

A system that effectively controls traffic signals in complex urban traffic situations by combining Model Predictive Control (MPC), Graph Convolutional Networks (GCNs), Gated Recurrent Units (GRUs), and Deep Reinforcement Learning (DRL) has been studied [20]. This system can effectively reflect spatiotemporal characteristics to predict traffic flow more accurately and can optimize signal control by adapting to real-time traffic situations through deep reinforcement learning.

citations.title: Optimization Control of Adaptive Traffic Signal with Deep Reinforcement Learning
snippets: The optimization and control of traffic signals is very important for logistics transportation. It not only improves the operational efficiency and safety of road traffic, but also conforms to the direction of the intelligent, green, and sustainable development of modern cities. In order to improve the optimization effect of traffic signal control, this paper proposes a traffic signal optimization method based on deep reinforcement learning and Simulation of Urban Mobility (SUMO) software for urban traffic scenarios. The intersection training scenario was established using SUMO micro traffic simulation software, and the maximum vehicle queue length and vehicle queue time were selected as performance evaluation indicators. In order to be more relevant to the real environment, the experiment uses Weibull distribution to simulate vehicle generation. Since deep reinforcement learning takes into account both perceptual and decision-making capabilities, this study proposes a traffic signal optimization control model based on the deep reinforcement learning Deep Q Network (DQN) algorithm by considering the realism and complexity of traffic intersections, and first uses the DQN algorithm to train the model in a training scenario. After that, the G-DQN (Grouping-DQN) algorithm is proposed to address the problems that the definition of states in existing studies cannot accurately represent the traffic states and the slow convergence of neural networks. Finally, the performance of the G-DQN algorithm model was compared with the original DQN algorithm model and Advantage Actor-Critic (A2C) algorithm model. The experimental results show that the improved algorithm increased the main indicators in all aspects.

citations.title: A Deep Reinforcement Learning Approach for Traffic Signal Control Optimization
snippets: Inefficient traffic signal control methods may cause numerous problems, such as traffic congestion and waste of energy. Reinforcement learning (RL) is a trending data-driven approach for adaptive traffic signal control in complex urban traffic networks. Although the development of deep neural networks (DNN) further enhances its learning capability, there are still some challenges in applying deep RLs to transportation networks with multiple signalized intersections, including non-stationarity environment, exploration-exploitation dilemma, multi-agent training schemes, continuous action spaces, etc. In order to address these issues, this paper first proposes a multi-agent deep deterministic policy gradient (MADDPG) method by extending the actor-critic policy gradient algorithms. MADDPG has a centralized learning and decentralized execution paradigm in which critics use additional information to streamline the training process, while actors act on their own local observations. The model is evaluated via simulation on the Simulation of Urban MObility (SUMO) platform. Model comparison results show the efficiency of the proposed algorithm in controlling traffic lights.

citations.title: Hierarchical reinforcement learning-based traffic signal control
snippets:
In contrast to traditional approaches, deep reinforcement learning (DRL)-based traffic signal control does not require pre-defined traffic signal plans and can be learned directly from intersections in the real world 3,14 . DRLbased methods treat each intersection as an agent, use a quantitative representation of traffic conditions as state, and traffic signal choice as action. 

For instance, IntelliLight 4 optimizes signal light control for a single intersection using the feature representation of current crossroad traffic conditions as input and recommends a phase as output. Previous work 5 uses a graph convolution network (GCN) to represent the lane structure of an intersection, and work 15 refines the phase decision of each intersection using RL models with a continuous phase duration output. The recent work 16 introduce a safe reinforcement learning-based fully adaptive multimodal traffic signal controller to resolves public transport priority request conflicts and ensures traffic safety. However, all these methods focus on optimizing a single intersection without considering communication between intersections in the road network. 

Multi-agent-based TSCS Some studies have exploited multi-agent DRL (MADRL) to control traffic lights at multiple intersections within a region. For example, the previous works of 5,11,17,18 and 19 proposed TSCS that share real-time traffic information of intersections within a particular region. Traffic information refers to the traffic flow, waiting time, queue length, and signal color, etc. Because the agents in these systems are provided the traffic conditions of other intersections as part of the state input, they coordinate better with their counterparts at neighboring intersections. In order to be able to adapt to large-scale road networks, the work 20 controls traffic signals in a distributed manner and enhances collaboration among agents by introducing GCN and selfattention mechanisms. And for heterogeneous intersection, the work 21 introduce a value-decomposition-based spatiotemporal graph attention multi-agent DRL model that expressly accommodates intersection heterogeneity. However, these MARL methods lack sufficient coordination mechanisms among agents with flat learning, resulting in suboptimal performance.

sections.title: # Benchmarks and Simulators
sections.text: Most DRL traffic-control studies are conducted in microscopic simulators such as SUMO, often via the TraCI interface for real-time control and data exchange. SUMO provides detailed vehicle-level simulation of intersections and can interface with external controllers for real-time signal optimization and performance analysis [0e738d2c-0] Experiments commonly use SUMO with TraCI to obtain event data and manipulate signals in real time, implemented with Keras/TensorFlow [0e738d2c-1]. Broader testbeds and surveys emphasize the need for large-scale simulators and discuss trade-offs among microscopic, mesoscopic, and macroscopic models for efficiency and fidelity. Traffic simulators underpin DRL research; microscopic models are precise but computationally heavy, mesoscopic can suffer gridlock artifacts at scale, and macroscopic sacrifice precision—hybrid approaches are proposed to balance efficiency and realism [195eb981-0].

Traffic congestion becomes one of the most severe urban problems in recent years, and smart and effective control and management strategies (e.g., signal control, congestion pricing, ramp metering, route guidance, etc.) are in great need to alleviate the congestion issue. Traditionally, mathematical programming is employed to obtain the optimal policy on small-scale networks, while it may fail in city-wide networks due to the exponentially growing problem scale and complexity. To this end, Deep Reinforcement Learning (DRL) emerges as one of the tools for decision-making in a largescale and complex environment, and its application in smart traffic control and management attracts wide attentions in recent years.

The development of DRL for traffic management and control requires accurate and large-scale traffic simulators as training and testing environments. However, due to the computational cost of microscopic model, it is difficult to operate a very large-scale scenario based on these simulators. sections.title: # Empirical Performance vs. Baselines
sections.text:
Across tasks, DRL typically outperforms fixed-time signals and several heuristic or model-based controllers in simulation, though gains vary by task and reward design. At single intersections, DQN and policy-gradient methods have shown large improvements in delay and queue metrics compared to fixed-time or simple neural baselines. A DQN agent reduced average delay by 82%, average queue by 66%, and average travel time by 20% versus a one-hidden-layer neural controller in SUMO [0e738d2c-2] DQN and Grouping-DQN improved maximum queue length and queue time over A2C in SUMO scenarios with realistic demand [0e738d2c-4]. For ramp metering, multi-task DRL has been benchmarked against the widely used ALINEA controller and a no-control baseline, showing competitive performance and enabling nonparametric control policies tuned to freeway bottlenecks. On a 33 km freeway section with 29 ramps in BeATS, a multi-task DRL policy (trained with shared/ specialized last-layer weights) matched or exceeded ALINEA and a non-weight-regularized DRL baseline, improving total outflow-based rewards over the no-control baseline [eda2e1b4-2]. Reviews of DVSL control report average travel time (ATT) reductions versus no control and note trade-offs across reward formulations for emissions and safety. An actor-critic DVSL controller improved ATT by 5.8–8.1% (2.9–6.2% for DQN and Q-learning in some scenarios), with different reward signals yielding varied improvements and emission trade-offs [712708e7-3].

Network-level coordination with MARL has shown benefits over single-intersection control and local heuristics, although performance depends on effective credit assignment and representation of neighbor states via graph learning. Multi-agent approaches that incorporate neighbor information and advanced representations (GCN, self-attention) improve coordination, while flat learning mechanisms can lead to suboptimal performance [13a96dca-1]. Hybrid RL-MPC controllers have also been reported to enhance real-time adaptability and performance under spatiotemporal dynamics. Combining MPC, graph learning, and DRL supports accurate prediction and online adaptation for signal control [0e738d2c-0].

citations.title: Variable Speed Limit and Ramp Metering for Mixed Traffic Flows: A Review and Open Questions
snippets:
In [84], a DRL model was proposed for Differential Variable Speed Limit (DVSL) control where dynamic and distinct speed limits can be imposed among lanes. It is based on the Actor-Critic (AC) architecture to learn a large number of discrete speed limits in the continuous action space. Four reward scenarios were tested. The reward scenarios r 1 and r 4 are based on several factors such as on-ramp inflow and off-ramp outflow. The reward scenario r 2 was the average speed in the downstream bottleneck. The reward scenario r 3 was computed by the total number of emerging braking vehicles in the controlled section. DVSL-r 1 , DVSL-r 2 , and DVSL-r 4 methods showed Average Travel Time (ATT) reduction of 1.08%, 4.1%, and 2.94%, respectively, while DVSL-r 3 showed an increase in ATT of 6.2%. DVSL-r 2 had the best emission reduction in HC and No x , while DVSL-r 4 showed the best emission reduction in CO and PMx. The AC-based DVSL agent was compared to the baseline scenario with no control, and baseline scenarios with AC and Deep Q-Network (DQN)-based VSL controllers. The DVSL improved ATT by 8.1% in scenarios with incidents and 5.8% in scenarios without incidents, while the VSL-DQN improved ATT by 1.7% and 2.9%, respectively. The VSL-DQN and QL performed better than the VSL-AC by a very slight margin. 

In [90], a traffic flow control system was tested that includes AVs whose speeds are controlled by a centralized agent based on deep learning. The learning structure is based on Recurrent Neural Networks (RNNs), where the Gated Recurrent Unit (GRU) algorithm solves the vanishing gradient problem that occurs when learning a classical RNN network. Introducing 10% AVs into the traffic flow enables better control of the traffic flow in a structure where each AV is a mobile actuator of the control system. The state of the agent's environment is determined by the density and average speed of the HDVs and the AVs.

Numerous types of research have been conducted by using deep reinforcement learning (DRL) to adapt traffic signal control [9] for a single intersection [10], [11], [12], and multiple intersections [13], [14], [15], [16], [17].Although reinforcement learning has succeeded in traffic light control in a single intersection, it is still challenging to apply in multiple traffic light controls because the dimensionality of the state and action space grows computationally intractable with the number of intersections.In practical applications, there are many situations where the environment is only partially observable, meaning that agents lack complete information about its state to engage with.This situation can be simulated by using a partially observable Markov decision process (POMDP).Due to multi-agent taxonomies such as the curse of dimensionality and multi-agent credit assignment, deep reinforcement learning for multi-agent environments is inherently more challenging than singleagent environments [18].The local information about intersections would ultimately lead to modeling complexities as the size of the traffic network grows.Furthermore, the observable region surrounding local intersections impacts traffic control.

Modeling and exploiting other agents' behaviors in a multiagent system (MAS) has received much attention in the past decade [19].A multi-agent RL (MARL) algorithm has been proposed as a possible solution to the abovementioned issues.However, the scalability of multi-agent deep reinforcement learning approaches is often limited and vulnerable to partial observability.Centralized learning with decentralized execution is an alternative and popular strategy in which agents are trained simultaneously by using a centralized mechanism via an open communication channel [18], [20].The centralized control mechanism teaches agents to control the traffic signals across the road network by using global information.On the other hand, using local knowledge, decentralized control techniques model signal light control at multiple intersections as a multi-agent system.Each agent is in charge of a specific intersection and only sees and senses certain aspects of the traffic situation.

citations.title: Hierarchical reinforcement learning-based traffic signal control
snippets:
In contrast to traditional approaches, deep reinforcement learning (DRL)-based traffic signal control does not require pre-defined traffic signal plans and can be learned directly from intersections in the real world 3,14 . DRLbased methods treat each intersection as an agent, use a quantitative representation of traffic conditions as state, and traffic signal choice as action. 

For instance, IntelliLight 4 optimizes signal light control for a single intersection using the feature representation of current crossroad traffic conditions as input and recommends a phase as output. Previous work 5 uses a graph convolution network (GCN) to represent the lane structure of an intersection, and work 15 refines the phase decision of each intersection using RL models with a continuous phase duration output. The recent work 16 introduce a safe reinforcement learning-based fully adaptive multimodal traffic signal controller to resolves public transport priority request conflicts and ensures traffic safety. However, all these methods focus on optimizing a single intersection without considering communication between intersections in the road network. 

Multi-agent-based TSCS Some studies have exploited multi-agent DRL (MADRL) to control traffic lights at multiple intersections within a region. For example, the previous works of 5,11,17,18 and 19 proposed TSCS that share real-time traffic information of intersections within a particular region. Traffic information refers to the traffic flow, waiting time, queue length, and signal color, etc. Because the agents in these systems are provided the traffic conditions of other intersections as part of the state input, they coordinate better with their counterparts at neighboring intersections. In order to be able to adapt to large-scale road networks, the work 20 controls traffic signals in a distributed manner and enhances collaboration among agents by introducing GCN and selfattention mechanisms. And for heterogeneous intersection, the work 21 introduce a value-decomposition-based spatiotemporal graph attention multi-agent DRL model that expressly accommodates intersection heterogeneity. However, these MARL methods lack sufficient coordination mechanisms among agents with flat learning, resulting in suboptimal performance.

sections.title: # Ramp Metering with DRL
sections.text: DRL has been successfully applied to ramp metering, learning policies from video or detector inputs to regulate on-ramp inflows at bottlenecks. Multi-task DRL has been benchmarked against ALINEA on a realistic freeway corridor and achieved expert-level performance in simulation, with rewards tied to total outflow and training schedules aligned to peak demand periods. A 29-ramp corridor study compared no control, a standard DRL policy, and a multi-task weight-regularization approach, reporting improved performance over ALINEA and the no-control baseline in aggregated outflow metrics [eda2e1b4-2]. Alternative DRL designs use raw video as inputs, extracting vehicle positions to form state, enabling flexible control beyond fixed phase schemes and potentially reducing computation burden by focusing on key ramps or time steps. A DRL ramp-metering method uses traffic video frames to decide per-step metering (green/red or phase selection) and learns a Q-network from raw visual representations of vehicle locations [eda2e1b4-4].

snippets:
In order to demonstrate the applicability of this novel method to real world cases, we consider the Ramp-Metering problem in a 20 miles (33 km) long section of the 210 Eastbound freeway in southern California as illustrated in Figure 8. For this simulation, we use the BeATS simulator calibrated by traffic experts based on real-world data. Every simulation run lasts for 4 hours, after a 30 minutes warmup period to initialize the freeway. The simulation starts at 12pm and the traffic peak happens between 3pm and 4pm, as the demand curve reaches a maximum (Fig. 14). 

Two reinforcement learning algorithms and the ALINEA control scheme are benchmarked against the baseline scenario in which no control occurs at all: 

• NoRM, baseline: The baseline without any ramp metering. Cars instantly enter the freeway when they reach an onramp, and if the freeway has enough capacity • NoMWR, standard deep reinforcement learning: The Reinforcement Learning based policy we introduce, trained with shared weights for the last layer • MWR, novel approach to training: The same policy as NoMWR, but trained with MWR. • Alinea, parametric control: The state of the art reference algorithm, using with model and parameters the exact same values used in the simulator it is being benchmarked on. 1) Reinforcement Learning problem: In this scenario, the agent takes an action every 32 seconds. An action is a R 29 vector with the ramp-metering rates for the 29 on-ramps on the highway section, in vehicle per time unit. The reward we collect at every time step is the total outflow in the last 32 seconds (in number of vehicle per time unit). 

The highway is discretized in 167 cells of 200 meters each to generate an observation vector in R 167×3 . For every cell, the following 3 data values are provided to the network:  TABLE I: Aggregated scores of the different control strategies over the congested period. Reinforcement learning enables a non parametric control scheme whose performance is similar to that of the parametric ALINEA scheme and MWR, the new learning algorithm we introduce, for improves this performance.

sections.title: # Adaptive/Variable Speed Limits (VSL) with DRL
sections.text: DRL has also been used for adaptive and differential VSL, including lane-specific limits at recurrent bottlenecks. Actor-critic and DQN agents learn policies from rich state inputs (occupancy, speed, topology) to impose dynamic speed limits that improve efficiency and safety, with reward functions balancing throughput, bottleneck speed, braking, and emissions. A DRL model with actor-critic architecture learned many discrete lane-level limits in a continuous action space, improving efficiency, safety, and emissions on a freeway bottleneck in simulation [712708e7-0] The RL-VSL framework treats state as detector-derived traffic conditions, actions as limit changes sent to variable signs, and rewards from bottleneck performance, addressing state summarization and correlation learning challenges with DRL [712708e7-2]. Graph-based DRL (DVS-RG) that encodes road topology and traffic dynamics reports substantial gains over prior methods in SUMO tests, reducing waiting time and potential collisions. DVS-RG uses graph state representation and a normalized reward combining efficiency and safety, achieving 68.44% lower waiting time and 15.93% fewer potential collisions than state-of-the-art DRL baselines in SUMO [712708e7-1]. A recent review across VSL and ramp metering summarizes that DVSL with actor-critic rewards can reduce ATT by 1–4.1% depending on reward design, with notable emission trade-offs, and that DQN-based VSL can underperform in some scenarios; comparisons against centralized learning with AVs suggest higher control efficacy as AV penetration increases. Actor-critic DVSL variants reduced ATT by 1.08–4.1% depending on reward, with emission trade-offs, and improved ATT by 5.8–8.1% over no control in incident and non-incident conditions, while DQN-based VSL improved by 1.7–2.9%; a centralized DRL controller with 10% AVs showed improved traffic flow [712708e7-3].

citations.title: DVS-RG: Differential Variable Speed Limits Control using Deep Reinforcement Learning with Graph State Representation
snippets: Variable speed limit (VSL) control is an established yet challenging problem to improve freeway traffic mobility and alleviate bottlenecks by customizing speed limits at proper locations based on traffic conditions. Recent advances in deep reinforcement learning (DRL) have shown promising results in solving VSL control problems by interacting with sophisticated environments. However, the modeling of these methods ignores the inherent graph structure of the traffic state which can be a key factor for more efficient VSL control. Graph structure can not only capture the static spatial feature but also the dynamic temporal features of traffic. Therefore, we propose the DVS-RG: DRL-based differential variable speed limit controller with graph state representation. DVS-RG provides distinct speed limits per lane in different locations dynamically. The road network topology and traffic information(e.g., occupancy, speed) are integrated as the state space of DVS-RG so that the spatial features can be learned. The normalization reward which combines efficiency and safety is used to train the VSL controller to avoid excessive inefficiencies or low safety. The results obtained from the simulation study on SUMO show that DRL-RG achieves higher traffic efficiency (the average waiting time reduced to 68.44\%) and improves the safety measures (the number of potential collision reduced by 15.93\% ) compared to state-of-the-art DRL methods.

citations.title: Variable Speed Limit and Ramp Metering for Mixed Traffic Flows: A Review and Open Questions
snippets:
In [84], a DRL model was proposed for Differential Variable Speed Limit (DVSL) control where dynamic and distinct speed limits can be imposed among lanes. It is based on the Actor-Critic (AC) architecture to learn a large number of discrete speed limits in the continuous action space. Four reward scenarios were tested. The reward scenarios r 1 and r 4 are based on several factors such as on-ramp inflow and off-ramp outflow. The reward scenario r 2 was the average speed in the downstream bottleneck. The reward scenario r 3 was computed by the total number of emerging braking vehicles in the controlled section. DVSL-r 1 , DVSL-r 2 , and DVSL-r 4 methods showed Average Travel Time (ATT) reduction of 1.08%, 4.1%, and 2.94%, respectively, while DVSL-r 3 showed an increase in ATT of 6.2%. DVSL-r 2 had the best emission reduction in HC and No x , while DVSL-r 4 showed the best emission reduction in CO and PMx. The AC-based DVSL agent was compared to the baseline scenario with no control, and baseline scenarios with AC and Deep Q-Network (DQN)-based VSL controllers. The DVSL improved ATT by 8.1% in scenarios with incidents and 5.8% in scenarios without incidents, while the VSL-DQN improved ATT by 1.7% and 2.9%, respectively. The VSL-DQN and QL performed better than the VSL-AC by a very slight margin. 

In [90], a traffic flow control system was tested that includes AVs whose speeds are controlled by a centralized agent based on deep learning. The learning structure is based on Recurrent Neural Networks (RNNs), where the Gated Recurrent Unit (GRU) algorithm solves the vanishing gradient problem that occurs when learning a classical RNN network. Introducing 10% AVs into the traffic flow enables better control of the traffic flow in a structure where each AV is a mobile actuator of the control system. The state of the agent's environment is determined by the density and average speed of the HDVs and the AVs.

citations.title: Differential Variable Speed Limits Control for Freeway Recurrent Bottlenecks via Deep Reinforcement learning
snippets: Variable speed limits (VSL) control is a flexible way to improve traffic condition,increase safety and reduce emission. There is an emerging trend of using reinforcement learning technique for VSL control and recent studies have shown promising results. Currently, deep learning is enabling reinforcement learning to develope autonomous control agents for problems that were previously intractable. In this paper, we propose a more effective deep reinforcement learning (DRL) model for differential variable speed limits (DVSL) control, in which the dynamic and different speed limits among lanes can be imposed. The proposed DRL models use a novel actor-critic architecture which can learn a large number of discrete speed limits in a continues action space. Different reward signals, e.g. total travel time, bottleneck speed, emergency braking, and vehicular emission are used to train the DVSL controller, and comparison between these reward signals are conducted. We test proposed DRL baased DVSL controllers on a simulated freeway recurrent bottleneck. Results show that the efficiency, safety and emissions can be improved by the proposed method. We also show some interesting findings through the visulization of the control policies generated from DRL models.

citations.title: Differential Variable Speed Limits Control for Freeway Recurrent Bottlenecks via Deep Reinforcement learning
snippets:
The reinforcement learning (RL) studied how artificial agents take actions in an environment so as to maximize its longterm cumulative reward. As a result, a well-trained RL agent can theoretically achieve a proactive control scheme to optimize its benefits. The framework of RL based VSL control is given in Fig. 1. For RL based VSL control, environment is composed of a transportation networks with bottlenecks, traffic state detectors and the variable speed signs. State is a feature representation of the traffic state collected from detectors. Agent takes state as input and learns a model to change the speed limits. The speed limits are sent to the variable speed signs of enviroment and the reward (e.g., the traffic state of bottlenecks) is sent back to the agent. 

Two unique challenges arise in applying traditional RL to VSL control: (i) The difficulties in state summarization and representation. (ii) The limited capability for learning the correlation between enviroment and optimal speed limits. In related fields including ramp metering (Belletti et al., 2018) and traffic light control (Van der Pol and Oliehoek, 2016;Wei et al., 2018), recent studies have applied deep reinforcement learning (DRL) techniques to address these two challenges. In DRL framework, massive traffic information collected from a large amount of traffic detectors can be described as a vector or an image and is directly taken as an input for neural networks of DRL. By the powerful function approximation properties of neural networks, the DRL agent can learn optimal phase of traffic lights, succeeding controllers that used to be hand-engineered. Another motivation of this study is to handle the VSL control with the emergence of connected and autonomous vehicles (CAV) technologies (Roncoli et al., 2015). Though CAV has not been implemented in the real world transportation system yet, it is believed that the CAV technologies will improve the safety of traffic, alleviate congestion and reduce vehicular emission. In the authors' opinion, the CAV technologies will bring two major benefits to VSL control. (i) CAV facilitates vehicles to communicate with infrastructures such as traffic state detectors, traffic lights and variable speed signs.

sections.title: # Safety, Robustness, and Real-World Deployment
sections.text: Safety and robustness remain central concerns. DRL can face delayed rewards and sparse feedback (e.g., crashes or long-horizon travel time), making credit assignment and safety guarantees difficult; methods include reward engineering, adversarial robustness training, and hybrid control with fallbacks to MPC or fixed timers. VSL DRL training is sensitive and slow, with delayed rewards for travel time and total flow; adversarial perturbations have been explored to improve robustness, but require knowledge of perturbation generation [712708e7-4]. Hybrid RL-MPC controllers have been proposed to provide safety envelopes and stabilize learning in real time by leveraging predictive models for constraints and horizon effects. An MPC+GCN/GRU+DRL system aims to reflect spatiotemporal traffic features and optimize signals adaptively in real time [0e738d2c-0]. Some works incorporate public transport priority and safety-aware RL to resolve request conflicts and enforce modal precedence. A safe reinforcement learning-based fully adaptive multimodal signal controller has been introduced to handle public transport priority requests and ensure safety alongside RL optimization [13a96dca-1]. Real-world evaluations are emerging: some studies report trials on real rush-hour demand and intersection management for mixed traffic, comparing DRL controllers against static signs and prior DRL baselines, with performance competitive among traffic signal controllers. An approach evaluated on real-world rush-hour demand compared a reinforcement-learning-based intersection manager (CVTSC) against static-priority signs and a prior DRL traffic-light controller, finding the learned controller achieved state-of-the-art performance among tested signal schemes [eda2e1b4-4].

citations.title: Multi-Lane Differential Variable Speed Limit Control via Deep Neural Networks Optimized by an Adaptive Evolutionary Strategy
snippets:
In a control engineering context, RL can be viewed as a feedback control algorithm. Given the coherence between RL and VSL, researchers start to investigate reinforcement learning (RL) techniques for VSL control [14 -16]. Several studies have reported the superior performance of RL techniques over traditional control approaches. 

The success of modern RL systems is largely due to their combination with deep neural networks. With deep neural networks, RL agents are able to learn a meaningful state representation [17]. In general, deep reinforcement learning (DRL) is defined as the utilization of deep learning algorithms within RL. As DRL algorithms have performed amazing feats in recent years, there have been some attempts to apply DRL to VSL control [15,18]. Ke et al. [18] investigated using the transfer learning method to improve the transferability of deep reinforcement learning variable speed limits (VSL) control. For VSL control, DRL exhibit major difference from traditional RL methods. Their controllers are built upon deep neural networks which have the capacity to learn more complex representations of the environments. This expressive power allows for learning more optimal speed limits [15]. 

Despite the promising results of DRL, training the deep neural networks of DRL is still not an easy task. The algorithms for training DRL agents are highly sensitive and require a long learning process [19,20]. This issue mainly stems from the difficulties in defining a representative reward function for VSL agents. There are some recent works that use adversarial perturbed state observations to obtain the worst case reward in order to improve the robustness of the agent [21,22]. However, we need to know how the perturbations are generated. Essentially, the goal of traffic management is to reduce travel time and increase traffic flow capacity. However, in practice, the average travel time and total flow cannot be computed until all the vehicles have completed their routes, which causes the issue of delayed rewards. Handling delayed rewards is one of the most critical challenges in RL research [23,24]. The training through one-step agent-environment interaction is ineffective because the definition of which action induces rewards is ambiguous. This problem is often solved by reward engineering so that the reward is more related to the current action of the agent.

citations.title: Implementation of a Real-Time Analysis Simulation System for Traffic Signal Control Algorithms to Reduce Vehicle Exhaust Emissions and Improve Traffic Flow
snippets:
To overcome the limitations of legacy traffic signal control methods, a signal control algorithm using deep reinforcement learning was studied [19]. This algorithm was evaluated by the waiting time of vehicles approaching the intersection, the average speed, and the number of stops as main performance indicators. Using various reward functions and state definitions, it showed excellent performance, such as a 42% reduction in waiting time and a 29% increase in vehicle speed compared to legacy fixed-time signal control in traffic congestion situations. In particular, it was confirmed that the design of the reward function had a great impact on performance and that a value-based reinforcement learning algorithm provided better results than a policy-based one. This study confirmed the possibility of a traffic signal control system that can dynamically adjust signals in real-time according to traffic volume and suggested a method that can contribute to solving urban traffic congestion problems. 

SUMO [3] is an open-source software for traffic simulation and is a tool that can precisely model individual vehicles, signal systems, and pedestrian movements on the road through microscopic simulation. When information on traffic volume is entered through an XML-formatted file, traffic flow simulation is possible with only SUMO's basic simulation engine. SUMO is an open platform that can be expanded through customization by 3rd party programmers. 

In particular, it can communicate with external programs through TraCI (Traffic Control Interface), so real-time traffic control is possible by applying signal control algorithms in languages such as Python. Through this, various traffic data can be collected from simulations, and CO2 emissions, vehicle waiting times, and signal control performance can be analyzed. However, SUMO has a somewhat high entry barrier because it requires complex settings and various file processing to provide various data formats and functions. In addition, since the visualization function is simple, additional linkage and integration work with various external tools is required to add additional advanced visualization functions. 

A system that effectively controls traffic signals in complex urban traffic situations by combining Model Predictive Control (MPC), Graph Convolutional Networks (GCNs), Gated Recurrent Units (GRUs), and Deep Reinforcement Learning (DRL) has been studied [20]. This system can effectively reflect spatiotemporal characteristics to predict traffic flow more accurately and can optimize signal control by adapting to real-time traffic situations through deep reinforcement learning.

sections.title: # Practical Implementation and Trade-offs
sections.text: Practical DRL deployments hinge on simulator integration (e.g., SUMO via TraCI), compute/latency constraints for online control, and data quality. SUMO supports real-time control and rich metric collection (vehicles, emissions, delays), but has a steep setup curve and limited visualization out of the box, often motivating integration with external tools. SUMO enables precise microscopic simulation and real-time control via TraCI, but requires complex configuration and often integration for advanced visualization and analysis [0e738d2c-0] SUMO+TraCI allows manipulating signals and collecting event-based data in Python, with Keras/TensorFlow used for the DRL controller [0e738d2c-1]. Algorithmically, value-based (DQN) and policy-based (A2C/PPO-like) methods coexist; representation choices (discrete encodings, images, GCN/attention) affect sample efficiency, stability, and scalability. A discrete traffic state encoding fed into a CNN with Q-learning reduced delay and queue substantially relative to a neural fixed-time controller [0e738d2c-2] Graph-based and attention-based encodings help multi-agent coordination across heterogeneous intersections [13a96dca-1]. DRL can be sensitive to reward design, delayed feedback, and partial observability, and multi-agent settings face non-stationarity and credit assignment issues that require careful state sharing, centralized training, and sometimes value decomposition or attention-based credit assignment. Reward design had a “great impact” on DRL traffic signal performance [0e738d2c-0] Delayed rewards complicate training; robustness methods and careful reward engineering are needed [712708e7-4] MARL scalability and partial observability motivate CTDE and distributed mechanisms [13a96dca-2].

citations.title: Using a Deep Reinforcement Learning Agent for Traffic Signal Control
snippets: Ensuring transportation systems are efficient is a priority for modern society. Technological advances have made it possible for transportation systems to collect large volumes of varied data on an unprecedented scale. We propose a traffic signal control system which takes advantage of this new, high quality data, with minimal abstraction compared to other proposed systems. We apply modern deep reinforcement learning methods to build a truly adaptive traffic signal control agent in the traffic microsimulator SUMO. We propose a new state space, the discrete traffic state encoding, which is information dense. The discrete traffic state encoding is used as input to a deep convolutional neural network, trained using Q-learning with experience replay. Our agent was compared against a one hidden layer neural network traffic signal control agent and reduces average cumulative delay by 82%, average queue length by 66% and average travel time by 20%.

Modeling and exploiting other agents' behaviors in a multiagent system (MAS) has received much attention in the past decade [19].A multi-agent RL (MARL) algorithm has been proposed as a possible solution to the abovementioned issues.However, the scalability of multi-agent deep reinforcement learning approaches is often limited and vulnerable to partial observability.Centralized learning with decentralized execution is an alternative and popular strategy in which agents are trained simultaneously by using a centralized mechanism via an open communication channel [18], [20].The centralized control mechanism teaches agents to control the traffic signals across the road network by using global information.On the other hand, using local knowledge, decentralized control techniques model signal light control at multiple intersections as a multi-agent system.Each agent is in charge of a specific intersection and only sees and senses certain aspects of the traffic situation.

snippets:
To overcome the limitations of legacy traffic signal control methods, a signal control algorithm using deep reinforcement learning was studied [19]. This algorithm was evaluated by the waiting time of vehicles approaching the intersection, the average speed, and the number of stops as main performance indicators. SUMO is an open platform that can be expanded through customization by 3rd party programmers.

snippets:

DRLbased methods treat each intersection as an agent, use a quantitative representation of traffic conditions as state, and traffic signal choice as action. 

For instance, IntelliLight 4 optimizes signal light control for a single intersection using the feature representation of current crossroad traffic conditions as input and recommends a phase as output. Previous work 5 uses a graph convolution network (GCN) to represent the lane structure of an intersection, and work 15 refines the phase decision of each intersection using RL models with a continuous phase duration output. The recent work 16 introduce a safe reinforcement learning-based fully adaptive multimodal traffic signal controller to resolves public transport priority request conflicts and ensures traffic safety. However, all these methods focus on optimizing a single intersection without considering communication between intersections in the road network. 

Multi-agent-based TSCS Some studies have exploited multi-agent DRL (MADRL) to control traffic lights at multiple intersections within a region. For example, the previous works of 5,11,17,18 and 19 proposed TSCS that share real-time traffic information of intersections within a particular region. Traffic information refers to the traffic flow, waiting time, queue length, and signal color, etc. Because the agents in these systems are provided the traffic conditions of other intersections as part of the state input, they coordinate better with their counterparts at neighboring intersections. In order to be able to adapt to large-scale road networks, the work 20 controls traffic signals in a distributed manner and enhances collaboration among agents by introducing GCN and selfattention mechanisms. And for heterogeneous intersection, the work 21 introduce a value-decomposition-based spatiotemporal graph attention multi-agent DRL model that expressly accommodates intersection heterogeneity. However, these MARL methods lack sufficient coordination mechanisms among agents with flat learning, resulting in suboptimal performance.

sections.title: # Representative Case Studies and Quantitative Gains
sections.text:
- Single-intersection signal control: DQN-based agents have reduced average delay by 82%, average queue by 66%, and travel time by 20% relative to strong neural baselines in SUMO, with further improvements using improved state definitions and grouping-aware DQN over DQN and A2C baselines. A DQN agent reduced delay, queue, and travel time significantly versus a one-hidden-layer neural controller [0e738d2c-2] Grouping-DQN improved queue metrics over DQN and A2C in SUMO scenarios [0e738d2c-4] Another study reported 42% waiting-time reduction and 29% speed increase versus fixed-time control under congestion [0e738d2c-0].
- Multi-intersection coordination: MADDPG and graph/attention-based MARL in SUMO improved control quality over single-intersection baselines, with centralized critics and neighbor-state sharing mitigating non-stationarity and credit assignment issues. MADDPG improved traffic light control in multi-intersection SUMO scenarios [13a96dca-0] GCN/self-attention and value-decomposition-based methods address heterogeneity and coordination [13a96dca-1].
- Ramp metering: Multi-task DRL on a 33 km freeway outperformed ALINEA and a no-control baseline on total outflow-based rewards, demonstrating expert-level control under peak periods. Multi-task DRL matched or exceeded ALINEA and improved over no control in aggregated outflow metrics across scenarios [eda2e1b4-2]. Video-based DRL metering learned policies from raw traffic imagery, enabling flexible control beyond stop-and-go schemes. A DRL metering method used traffic video to decide per-step control, learning a Q-network from visual vehicle positions [eda2e1b4-4].
- VSL: Actor-critic and graph-based DRL controllers reduced waiting time and potential collisions (e.g., 68.44% and 15.93% improvements in SUMO), and DVSL improved ATT by 5.8–8.1% over no control, with reward formulations affecting emissions and safety. DVS-RG achieved 68.44% lower waiting time and 15.93% fewer potential collisions than prior DRL methods [712708e7-1] DVSL improved ATT by 5.8–8.1% in incident and non-incident scenarios over baselines [712708e7-3].

citations.title: Using a Deep Reinforcement Learning Agent for Traffic Signal Control
snippets: Ensuring transportation systems are efficient is a priority for modern society. Technological advances have made it possible for transportation systems to collect large volumes of varied data on an unprecedented scale. We propose a traffic signal control system which takes advantage of this new, high quality data, with minimal abstraction compared to other proposed systems. We apply modern deep reinforcement learning methods to build a truly adaptive traffic signal control agent in the traffic microsimulator SUMO. We propose a new state space, the discrete traffic state encoding, which is information dense. The discrete traffic state encoding is used as input to a deep convolutional neural network, trained using Q-learning with experience replay. Our agent was compared against a one hidden layer neural network traffic signal control agent and reduces average cumulative delay by 82%, average queue length by 66% and average travel time by 20%.

In order to demonstrate the applicability of this novel method to real world cases, we consider the Ramp-Metering problem in a 20 miles (33 km) long section of the 210 Eastbound freeway in southern California as illustrated in Figure 8. Every simulation run lasts for 4 hours, after a 30 minutes warmup period to initialize the freeway. citations.title: DVS-RG: Differential Variable Speed Limits Control using Deep Reinforcement Learning with Graph State Representation
snippets: Variable speed limit (VSL) control is an established yet challenging problem to improve freeway traffic mobility and alleviate bottlenecks by customizing speed limits at proper locations based on traffic conditions. Recent advances in deep reinforcement learning (DRL) have shown promising results in solving VSL control problems by interacting with sophisticated environments. However, the modeling of these methods ignores the inherent graph structure of the traffic state which can be a key factor for more efficient VSL control. Graph structure can not only capture the static spatial feature but also the dynamic temporal features of traffic. Therefore, we propose the DVS-RG: DRL-based differential variable speed limit controller with graph state representation. DVS-RG provides distinct speed limits per lane in different locations dynamically. The road network topology and traffic information(e.g., occupancy, speed) are integrated as the state space of DVS-RG so that the spatial features can be learned. The normalization reward which combines efficiency and safety is used to train the VSL controller to avoid excessive inefficiencies or low safety. The results obtained from the simulation study on SUMO show that DRL-RG achieves higher traffic efficiency (the average waiting time reduced to 68.44\%) and improves the safety measures (the number of potential collision reduced by 15.93\% ) compared to state-of-the-art DRL methods.

citations.title: Optimization Control of Adaptive Traffic Signal with Deep Reinforcement Learning
snippets: The optimization and control of traffic signals is very important for logistics transportation. It not only improves the operational efficiency and safety of road traffic, but also conforms to the direction of the intelligent, green, and sustainable development of modern cities. In order to improve the optimization effect of traffic signal control, this paper proposes a traffic signal optimization method based on deep reinforcement learning and Simulation of Urban Mobility (SUMO) software for urban traffic scenarios. The intersection training scenario was established using SUMO micro traffic simulation software, and the maximum vehicle queue length and vehicle queue time were selected as performance evaluation indicators. In order to be more relevant to the real environment, the experiment uses Weibull distribution to simulate vehicle generation. Since deep reinforcement learning takes into account both perceptual and decision-making capabilities, this study proposes a traffic signal optimization control model based on the deep reinforcement learning Deep Q Network (DQN) algorithm by considering the realism and complexity of traffic intersections, and first uses the DQN algorithm to train the model in a training scenario. After that, the G-DQN (Grouping-DQN) algorithm is proposed to address the problems that the definition of states in existing studies cannot accurately represent the traffic states and the slow convergence of neural networks. Finally, the performance of the G-DQN algorithm model was compared with the original DQN algorithm model and Advantage Actor-Critic (A2C) algorithm model. The experimental results show that the improved algorithm increased the main indicators in all aspects.

citations.title: Variable Speed Limit and Ramp Metering for Mixed Traffic Flows: A Review and Open Questions
snippets:
In [84], a DRL model was proposed for Differential Variable Speed Limit (DVSL) control where dynamic and distinct speed limits can be imposed among lanes. It is based on the Actor-Critic (AC) architecture to learn a large number of discrete speed limits in the continuous action space. Four reward scenarios were tested. The reward scenarios r 1 and r 4 are based on several factors such as on-ramp inflow and off-ramp outflow. The reward scenario r 2 was the average speed in the downstream bottleneck. The reward scenario r 3 was computed by the total number of emerging braking vehicles in the controlled section. DVSL-r 1 , DVSL-r 2 , and DVSL-r 4 methods showed Average Travel Time (ATT) reduction of 1.08%, 4.1%, and 2.94%, respectively, while DVSL-r 3 showed an increase in ATT of 6.2%. DVSL-r 2 had the best emission reduction in HC and No x , while DVSL-r 4 showed the best emission reduction in CO and PMx. The AC-based DVSL agent was compared to the baseline scenario with no control, and baseline scenarios with AC and Deep Q-Network (DQN)-based VSL controllers. The DVSL improved ATT by 8.1% in scenarios with incidents and 5.8% in scenarios without incidents, while the VSL-DQN improved ATT by 1.7% and 2.9%, respectively. The VSL-DQN and QL performed better than the VSL-AC by a very slight margin. 

In [90], a traffic flow control system was tested that includes AVs whose speeds are controlled by a centralized agent based on deep learning. The learning structure is based on Recurrent Neural Networks (RNNs), where the Gated Recurrent Unit (GRU) algorithm solves the vanishing gradient problem that occurs when learning a classical RNN network. Introducing 10% AVs into the traffic flow enables better control of the traffic flow in a structure where each AV is a mobile actuator of the control system. The state of the agent's environment is determined by the density and average speed of the HDVs and the AVs.

citations.title: A Deep Reinforcement Learning Approach for Traffic Signal Control Optimization
snippets: Inefficient traffic signal control methods may cause numerous problems, such as traffic congestion and waste of energy. Reinforcement learning (RL) is a trending data-driven approach for adaptive traffic signal control in complex urban traffic networks. Although the development of deep neural networks (DNN) further enhances its learning capability, there are still some challenges in applying deep RLs to transportation networks with multiple signalized intersections, including non-stationarity environment, exploration-exploitation dilemma, multi-agent training schemes, continuous action spaces, etc. In order to address these issues, this paper first proposes a multi-agent deep deterministic policy gradient (MADDPG) method by extending the actor-critic policy gradient algorithms. MADDPG has a centralized learning and decentralized execution paradigm in which critics use additional information to streamline the training process, while actors act on their own local observations. The model is evaluated via simulation on the Simulation of Urban MObility (SUMO) platform. Model comparison results show the efficiency of the proposed algorithm in controlling traffic lights.

sections.title: # Open Challenges and Research Directions
sections.text: Despite promising results, several challenges remain. Real-world field trials remain limited relative to simulation studies, and standardized, reproducible benchmarks across tasks and scales are still evolving. Work highlights the need for very large-scale simulators to test DRL at city scale while balancing efficiency and fidelity [195eb981-0]. Multi-agent credit assignment, scalability to hundreds of intersections, and robustness to model mismatch and adversarial perturbations are active areas, with CTDE, graph learning, and value decomposition as promising directions. MARL studies emphasize the need for better coordination mechanisms and handling heterogeneity [13a96dca-1] Robustness to delayed rewards and adversarial state perturbations is needed for VSL DRL [712708e7-4]. Hybrid RL with MPC and safety-aware RL can provide stability and guarantees, but integration complexity and computation/comms overhead for real-time control must be managed, often through careful simulator/controller co-design. Hybrid MPC+GCN/GRU+DRL systems aim to balance predictive accuracy and adaptive learning for real-time signal control [0e738d2c-0]. Finally, broader surveys point to the role of multi-agent DRL and intelligent routing in future AV-dominated networks, where learned controllers can dynamically manage routing, congestion, and even signal elimination through adaptive speed control. Advanced AI (multi-agent systems and DRL) has been shown to efficiently manage network-wide traffic flow, reduce delays and throughput, and support complex coordination [195eb981-4].

citations.title: Towards a Very Large Scale Traffic Simulator for Multi-Agent Reinforcement Learning Testbeds
snippets:
Traffic congestion becomes one of the most severe urban problems in recent years, and smart and effective control and management strategies (e.g., signal control, congestion pricing, ramp metering, route guidance, etc.) are in great need to alleviate the congestion issue. Traditionally, mathematical programming is employed to obtain the optimal policy on small-scale networks, while it may fail in city-wide networks due to the exponentially growing problem scale and complexity. To this end, Deep Reinforcement Learning (DRL) emerges as one of the tools for decision-making in a largescale and complex environment, and its application in smart traffic control and management attracts wide attentions in recent years.

The development of DRL for traffic management and control requires accurate and large-scale traffic simulators as training and testing environments. Table I presents a summary of traffic simulators for DRL tasks. Most simulators leverage car-following models and lane-change models in a microscopic level. However, due to the computational cost of microscopic model, it is difficult to operate a very large-scale scenario based on these simulators. Mesoscopic and Macroscopic traffic models were developed in the transportation community to improve the simulation efficiency. Mesoscopic simulation models the congestion dynamics on links. However, the gridlock effect, a special case of traffic congestion that vehicles are blocked in a circle queue, is prone to happen under large-scale scenarios due to the improper settings of link attributes; macroscopic models prevent the vehicle gridlock, but it sacrifices the simulation precision. citations.title: Multi-Lane Differential Variable Speed Limit Control via Deep Neural Networks Optimized by an Adaptive Evolutionary Strategy
snippets:
In a control engineering context, RL can be viewed as a feedback control algorithm. Given the coherence between RL and VSL, researchers start to investigate reinforcement learning (RL) techniques for VSL control [14 -16]. Several studies have reported the superior performance of RL techniques over traditional control approaches. 

The success of modern RL systems is largely due to their combination with deep neural networks. With deep neural networks, RL agents are able to learn a meaningful state representation [17]. In general, deep reinforcement learning (DRL) is defined as the utilization of deep learning algorithms within RL. As DRL algorithms have performed amazing feats in recent years, there have been some attempts to apply DRL to VSL control [15,18]. Ke et al. [18] investigated using the transfer learning method to improve the transferability of deep reinforcement learning variable speed limits (VSL) control. For VSL control, DRL exhibit major difference from traditional RL methods. Their controllers are built upon deep neural networks which have the capacity to learn more complex representations of the environments. This expressive power allows for learning more optimal speed limits [15]. 

Despite the promising results of DRL, training the deep neural networks of DRL is still not an easy task. The algorithms for training DRL agents are highly sensitive and require a long learning process [19,20]. This issue mainly stems from the difficulties in defining a representative reward function for VSL agents. There are some recent works that use adversarial perturbed state observations to obtain the worst case reward in order to improve the robustness of the agent [21,22]. However, we need to know how the perturbations are generated. Essentially, the goal of traffic management is to reduce travel time and increase traffic flow capacity. However, in practice, the average travel time and total flow cannot be computed until all the vehicles have completed their routes, which causes the issue of delayed rewards. Handling delayed rewards is one of the most critical challenges in RL research [23,24]. The training through one-step agent-environment interaction is ineffective because the definition of which action induces rewards is ambiguous. This problem is often solved by reward engineering so that the reward is more related to the current action of the agent.

Multi-agent-based TSCS Some studies have exploited multi-agent DRL (MADRL) to control traffic lights at multiple intersections within a region.
