sections.title: # Practical Guidance for Deploying DRL in Traffic
sections.text:
- Start with a realistic simulator interface: SUMO with TraCI supports real-time control and rich metrics but requires careful setup and integration for visualization and operations dashboards. SUMO’s TraCI enables real-time signal application and performance analysis, though setup complexity and visualization limitations necessitate integrations [0e738d2c-0] SUMO+TraCI with Keras/TensorFlow is a common stack for DRL controllers [0e738d2c-1].
- Choose algorithm and representation wisely: For intersections, CNN-based DQN or actor-critic with image or discrete state encodings can yield strong improvements; for multi-agent settings, MADDPG-like CTDE with neighbor state and graph/attention encodings can improve coordination; for safety-critical tasks, incorporate safety-aware RL and fallback controllers. Discrete state encodings with DQN reduced delay/queue/travel time substantially [0e738d2c-2] MADDPG with centralized critics and decentralized actors improved multi-intersection control [13a96dca-0] GCN/self-attention and value-decomposition-based methods enhance coordination and handle heterogeneity [13a96dca-1] Safe RL-based multimodal controllers address public transport priority and safety conflicts [13a96dca-1].
- Validate with diverse baselines and rewards: Compare against fixed-time signals, model-based controllers (e.g., ALINEA for ramp metering), and decentralized heuristics; design rewards to reduce delay/queue while penalizing unsafe or abrupt actions; include emission and safety metrics where relevant. Ramp metering compared DRL variants and ALINEA, using outflow-based rewards over multi-hour peak periods [eda2e1b4-2] DVSL reward formulations led to different ATT and emission outcomes, with comparative improvements versus no control and DQN/QL baselines [712708e7-3].
- Plan for scalability and safety: Use CTDE and graph-based state sharing to scale to networks; implement constraint handling and hybrid MPC/DRL for real-time stability; budget compute/latency for online control and plan for data collection and continual learning. CTDE with decentralized execution addresses partial observability and scalability in MARL [13a96dca-2] Hybrid MPC+learning systems can better handle spatiotemporal dynamics and real-time adaptation [0e738d2c-0].

citations.title: Using a Deep Reinforcement Learning Agent for Traffic Signal Control
snippets: Ensuring transportation systems are efficient is a priority for modern society. Technological advances have made it possible for transportation systems to collect large volumes of varied data on an unprecedented scale. We propose a traffic signal control system which takes advantage of this new, high quality data, with minimal abstraction compared to other proposed systems. We apply modern deep reinforcement learning methods to build a truly adaptive traffic signal control agent in the traffic microsimulator SUMO. We propose a new state space, the discrete traffic state encoding, which is information dense. The discrete traffic state encoding is used as input to a deep convolutional neural network, trained using Q-learning with experience replay. Our agent was compared against a one hidden layer neural network traffic signal control agent and reduces average cumulative delay by 82%, average queue length by 66% and average travel time by 20%.

citations.title: Application of Traffic Light Control in Oversaturated Urban Network Using Multi-Agent Deep Reinforcement Learning
snippets:
The computational complexity of traffic signal control using a traditional reinforcement learning system increases exponentially with extended state space, complicated intersection features, and heterogeneous intersection structures.

Numerous types of research have been conducted by using deep reinforcement learning (DRL) to adapt traffic signal control [9] for a single intersection [10], [11], [12], and multiple intersections [13], [14], [15], [16], [17].Although reinforcement learning has succeeded in traffic light control in a single intersection, it is still challenging to apply in multiple traffic light controls because the dimensionality of the state and action space grows computationally intractable with the number of intersections.In practical applications, there are many situations where the environment is only partially observable, meaning that agents lack complete information about its state to engage with.This situation can be simulated by using a partially observable Markov decision process (POMDP).Due to multi-agent taxonomies such as the curse of dimensionality and multi-agent credit assignment, deep reinforcement learning for multi-agent environments is inherently more challenging than singleagent environments [18].The local information about intersections would ultimately lead to modeling complexities as the size of the traffic network grows.Furthermore, the observable region surrounding local intersections impacts traffic control.

Modeling and exploiting other agents' behaviors in a multiagent system (MAS) has received much attention in the past decade [19].A multi-agent RL (MARL) algorithm has been proposed as a possible solution to the abovementioned issues.However, the scalability of multi-agent deep reinforcement learning approaches is often limited and vulnerable to partial observability.Centralized learning with decentralized execution is an alternative and popular strategy in which agents are trained simultaneously by using a centralized mechanism via an open communication channel [18], [20].The centralized control mechanism teaches agents to control the traffic signals across the road network by using global information.On the other hand, using local knowledge, decentralized control techniques model signal light control at multiple intersections as a multi-agent system.Each agent is in charge of a specific intersection and only sees and senses certain aspects of the traffic situation.

citations.title: Implementation of a Real-Time Analysis Simulation System for Traffic Signal Control Algorithms to Reduce Vehicle Exhaust Emissions and Improve Traffic Flow
snippets:
To overcome the limitations of legacy traffic signal control methods, a signal control algorithm using deep reinforcement learning was studied [19]. This algorithm was evaluated by the waiting time of vehicles approaching the intersection, the average speed, and the number of stops as main performance indicators. Using various reward functions and state definitions, it showed excellent performance, such as a 42% reduction in waiting time and a 29% increase in vehicle speed compared to legacy fixed-time signal control in traffic congestion situations. In particular, it was confirmed that the design of the reward function had a great impact on performance and that a value-based reinforcement learning algorithm provided better results than a policy-based one. This study confirmed the possibility of a traffic signal control system that can dynamically adjust signals in real-time according to traffic volume and suggested a method that can contribute to solving urban traffic congestion problems. 

SUMO [3] is an open-source software for traffic simulation and is a tool that can precisely model individual vehicles, signal systems, and pedestrian movements on the road through microscopic simulation. When information on traffic volume is entered through an XML-formatted file, traffic flow simulation is possible with only SUMO's basic simulation engine. SUMO is an open platform that can be expanded through customization by 3rd party programmers. 

In particular, it can communicate with external programs through TraCI (Traffic Control Interface), so real-time traffic control is possible by applying signal control algorithms in languages such as Python. Through this, various traffic data can be collected from simulations, and CO2 emissions, vehicle waiting times, and signal control performance can be analyzed. However, SUMO has a somewhat high entry barrier because it requires complex settings and various file processing to provide various data formats and functions. In addition, since the visualization function is simple, additional linkage and integration work with various external tools is required to add additional advanced visualization functions. 

A system that effectively controls traffic signals in complex urban traffic situations by combining Model Predictive Control (MPC), Graph Convolutional Networks (GCNs), Gated Recurrent Units (GRUs), and Deep Reinforcement Learning (DRL) has been studied [20]. This system can effectively reflect spatiotemporal characteristics to predict traffic flow more accurately and can optimize signal control by adapting to real-time traffic situations through deep reinforcement learning.

citations.title: Variable Speed Limit and Ramp Metering for Mixed Traffic Flows: A Review and Open Questions
snippets:
In [84], a DRL model was proposed for Differential Variable Speed Limit (DVSL) control where dynamic and distinct speed limits can be imposed among lanes. It is based on the Actor-Critic (AC) architecture to learn a large number of discrete speed limits in the continuous action space. Four reward scenarios were tested. The reward scenarios r 1 and r 4 are based on several factors such as on-ramp inflow and off-ramp outflow. The reward scenario r 2 was the average speed in the downstream bottleneck. In [90], a traffic flow control system was tested that includes AVs whose speeds are controlled by a centralized agent based on deep learning. The learning structure is based on Recurrent Neural Networks (RNNs), where the Gated Recurrent Unit (GRU) algorithm solves the vanishing gradient problem that occurs when learning a classical RNN network. Introducing 10% AVs into the traffic flow enables better control of the traffic flow in a structure where each AV is a mobile actuator of the control system. citations.title: A Deep Reinforcement Learning Approach for Traffic Signal Control Optimization
snippets: Inefficient traffic signal control methods may cause numerous problems, such as traffic congestion and waste of energy. Reinforcement learning (RL) is a trending data-driven approach for adaptive traffic signal control in complex urban traffic networks. Although the development of deep neural networks (DNN) further enhances its learning capability, there are still some challenges in applying deep RLs to transportation networks with multiple signalized intersections, including non-stationarity environment, exploration-exploitation dilemma, multi-agent training schemes, continuous action spaces, etc. In order to address these issues, this paper first proposes a multi-agent deep deterministic policy gradient (MADDPG) method by extending the actor-critic policy gradient algorithms. MADDPG has a centralized learning and decentralized execution paradigm in which critics use additional information to streamline the training process, while actors act on their own local observations. The model is evaluated via simulation on the Simulation of Urban MObility (SUMO) platform. Model comparison results show the efficiency of the proposed algorithm in controlling traffic lights.

sections.title: # Summary
sections.text: DRL has demonstrated substantial improvements over fixed-time and heuristic controllers across key smart traffic management tasks—intersection signal control, multi-agent coordination, ramp metering, and adaptive VSL—often outperforming or matching parametric baselines in simulation when paired with appropriate representations and reward design. Single-intersection DRL achieved large reductions in delay, queue, and travel time [0e738d2c-2] DRL for ramp metering matched or exceeded ALINEA and outperformed no control [eda2e1b4-2] Graph-based DRL for VSL reduced waiting time and potential collisions in SUMO [712708e7-1] DVSL improved ATT by several percent over baselines with careful reward design [712708e7-3]. While real-world deployments and standardized benchmarks remain active areas, hybrid RL-MPC approaches, safety-aware RL, and graph/MARL methods provide practical pathways to scalable, robust, and deployable DRL-based traffic management systems. Hybrid MPC+learning controllers support real-time adaptability [0e738d2c-0] MARL with GCN/attention and value decomposition addresses coordination and heterogeneity [13a96dca-1] Safe RL for multimodal priorities and conflicts [13a96dca-1] Very large-scale simulators are needed to test DRL at city scale [195eb981-0].

Traditionally, mathematical programming is employed to obtain the optimal policy on small-scale networks, while it may fail in city-wide networks due to the exponentially growing problem scale and complexity. citations.title: DVS-RG: Differential Variable Speed Limits Control using Deep Reinforcement Learning with Graph State Representation
snippets: Variable speed limit (VSL) control is an established yet challenging problem to improve freeway traffic mobility and alleviate bottlenecks by customizing speed limits at proper locations based on traffic conditions. Recent advances in deep reinforcement learning (DRL) have shown promising results in solving VSL control problems by interacting with sophisticated environments. However, the modeling of these methods ignores the inherent graph structure of the traffic state which can be a key factor for more efficient VSL control. Graph structure can not only capture the static spatial feature but also the dynamic temporal features of traffic. Therefore, we propose the DVS-RG: DRL-based differential variable speed limit controller with graph state representation. DVS-RG provides distinct speed limits per lane in different locations dynamically. The road network topology and traffic information(e.g., occupancy, speed) are integrated as the state space of DVS-RG so that the spatial features can be learned. The normalization reward which combines efficiency and safety is used to train the VSL controller to avoid excessive inefficiencies or low safety. The results obtained from the simulation study on SUMO show that DRL-RG achieves higher traffic efficiency (the average waiting time reduced to 68.44\%) and improves the safety measures (the number of potential collision reduced by 15.93\% ) compared to state-of-the-art DRL methods.

question: What is the state of the art in cross subject EEG emotion recognition?

sections.title: # Summary and Scope
sections.text: Cross-subject EEG emotion recognition aims to recognize emotions of unseen or different subjects by learning representations and models that are robust to inter-subject variability while leveraging data across users for generalization. A key challenge is the limited generalization of EEG emotion models trained for a single dataset or subject, motivating cross-corpus and cross-subject approaches that transfer without retraining [302a181a-0]. Inter-subject variability can dramatically drop accuracy from intra-subject (e.g., 96% on SEED with an MLP) to cross-subject settings (as low as 58%), underscoring the need for subject-invariant representations [302a181a-1]. Beyond cross-subject, cross-dataset generalization is even harder due to differences in recording settings and stimuli [302a181a-3].

citations.title: Towards Practical Emotion Recognition: An Unsupervised Source-Free Approach for EEG Domain Adaptation
snippets:
Emotion, a fundamental mental phenomenon, is deeply connected to human cognition and behavior, shaping daily life experiences. Recognizing emotions is a critical focus in psychology, medicine, and engineering. In psychology, it provides a quantitative foundation for understanding emotion-related behaviors. In medicine, it aids in the diagnosis and treatment of conditions such as autism spectrum disorder (ASD) and depression and helps track patient recovery [1,2]. In engineering, emotion recognition advances affective brain-computer interfaces (aBCIs), enabling better integration of emotional states into technology. 

Physiological signals, such as electroencephalogram (EEG), offer a more objective approach to emotion recognition than non-physiological signals like facial expressions, gestures, and voice, which can be influenced by environmental or social factors [3,4]. EEG measures brain activity through electrical signals, providing high reliability and precision, while also being portable and cost-effective. 

Advancements in deep learning have greatly improved EEG decoding performance through various neural network models [5][6][7]. However, these models generally perform well on test data with a distribution similar to the training data, but their performance significantly declines when applied to a new domain with a different data distribution, a phenomenon known as domain shift [8]. The considerable variations in EEG signals across individuals challenge the effectiveness of cross-domain emotion recognition models. Additionally, deep neural networks typically require a vast quantity of labeled data for training. Collecting and annotating EEG signals is often a labor-intensive and costly process. 

Unsupervised domain adaptation (UDA) is gaining attention to address these challenges, aiming to enhance model performance on the target domain by utilizing information from the source domain. Recent research on domain adaptation for classifying EEG emotions has largely focused on cross-subject and cross-session scenarios within the same dataset [9][10][11][12][13]. However, less attention has been given to the cross-dataset scenario, which presents even greater challenges due to variations in EEG signals not only from individual differences but also from differences in EEG recording settings and stimuli. 

Another limitation of traditional unsupervised domain adaptation methods is that they require access to the source domain data while adapting to the target domain.

citations.title: EEG-SCMM: Soft Contrastive Masked Modeling for Cross-Corpus EEG-Based Emotion Recognition
snippets:
Emotions are human attitudinal experiences and behavioral responses to objective things, closely related to an individual's health conditions and behavioral patterns [45]. Compared to speech [40], gestures [31], and facial expressions [2], electroencephalography (EEG) offers a more direct and objective measurement of human emotions by capturing brain activity across various scalp locations [16]. Therefore, researchers have increasingly emphasized EEGbased emotion recognition in recent years [50,51,53,56], aiming to advance the development of affective brain-computer interfaces (aBCIs). However, three critical challenges remain to be addressed in current approaches. 

(1) Insufficient Generalization Capability. Most existing EEGbased emotion recognition methods are typically designed for a single dataset, necessitating model retraining when the dataset changes. This requirement significantly limits the scalability and generalizability of the model, hindering its application on different datasets. To address this issue, the concept of cross-corpus has been proposed, which is designed to be generalized across multiple datasets. A cross-corpus model is trained on one dataset and can be directly applied to another without retraining from scratch. This concept, which originated in natural language processing [38,52], has been extended to various domains in recent years [5,35,37]. sections.title: # Benchmarks and Protocols
sections.text: Several public datasets underpin cross-subject evaluation. MAHNOB-HCI, SEED, SEED-IV, and DEAP are the most widely used; SEED and SEED-IV offer multiple sessions with 62-channel EEG and balanced designs, while DEAP has 32 channels and labeled valence/arousal dimensions but is harder to overfit and often underperforms SEED in cross-subject evaluation [dc83288e-1]. Cross-dataset protocols commonly align subsets across SEED, SEED-IV, and MPED to study transfer across channels, subjects, and stimuli; for example, 3-class tasks use neutral/sad/happy and 4-class tasks add fear [302a181a-2]. SEED/SEED-IV/DEAP differ in sessions, subjects, devices, and stimuli, which contributes to distribution shifts that challenge generalization [302a181a-3].

snippets:
Despite the large number of potential applications of emotion recognition from EEG signals, to the best of our knowledge, MAHNOB-HCI (Soleymani et al., 2012), SEED (Duan et al., 2013;Zheng and Lu, 2015), SEED IV (Zheng et al., 2019), and DEAP (Koelstra et al., 2012) are the only four publicly available emotional EEG datasets on the topic. From those four datasets, the most studied ones in cross-subject emotion classification are the DEAP and SEED datasets (e.g., Li et al., 2020;Cimtay and Ekmekcioglu, 2020, from which we decided to focus on the SEED dataset because of the following reasons. Firstly, the collected data is well-balanced between sessions and participants, which simplifies the assessment of the classification results. Secondly, as Li et al. (2018) mentioned in his study, the performance on DEAP is significantly inferior to that on SEED, which may be due to the relatively low quality of the data and the emotional ratings of trials. This led them to conduct further evaluation only in the SEED dataset. Thirdly, neural networks easily overfit with the DEAP dataset, which would increase the complexity of the neural network models since it would be necessary to include data augmentation, early stopping, higher dropout, and/or regularization for each model (e.g., Cimtay and Ekmekcioglu, 2020;Yang H. Y. et al., 2019). Lastly, the literature offers many reports on cross-subject emotion recognition models using the SEED dataset, which permits the comparison with other papers. 

The SEED dataset contains 62-channel EEG data collected from 15 participants, who carried out three sessions over the same 15 film clips. An emotional rating was previously assigned to each film clip and obtained by averaging the ratings of 20 participants who were asked to indicate one keyword (positive, neutral, or negative) after watching them. In the subsequent experiment with EEG recordings, the clips used across sessions and participants at each trial shared the same pseudo-random order of ratings to balance evoked emotions throughout the EEG recordings smoothly.

citations.title: Enhancing Cross-Dataset EEG Emotion Recognition: A Novel Approach With Emotional EEG Style Transfer Network
snippets: The objective of this paper is to investigate cross-dataset EEG emotion recognition tasks. In alignment with the principles of previous experiments, we establish groups of experiment protocols for cross-dataset EEG emotion recognition based on SEED [Zheng and Lu, 2015], SEED-IV [Zheng et al., 2018], and MPED [Song et al., 2019] datasets, with detailed information provided in Appendix B. Table I of Appendix B summarizes the setup details of the cross-dataset EEG emotion recognition experiments. In brief, to maintain category balance in the training samples, we choose neutral, sad, and happy (joy) emotions of SEED, SEED-IV, and MPED datasets for 3-category cross-dataset experiments. For 4-category cross-dataset experiments, we choose neutral, happy (joy), sad, and fear emotions from SEED-IV and MPED datasets. All subjects' samples from one dataset are considered as source domain data, while one subject's samples from another dataset are utilized as target domain data. This approach allows us to conduct experiments on two types of cross-dataset EEG emotion recognition tasks, involving three and four categories of emotions. For instance, we denote the 3-category cross-dataset EEG emotion recognition experiment using the MPED 3 dataset as the source domain and the SEED 3 dataset as the target domain as MPED 3 → SEED 3 in this paper.

citations.title: Towards Practical Emotion Recognition: An Unsupervised Source-Free Approach for EEG Domain Adaptation
snippets:
Emotion, a fundamental mental phenomenon, is deeply connected to human cognition and behavior, shaping daily life experiences. Recognizing emotions is a critical focus in psychology, medicine, and engineering. In psychology, it provides a quantitative foundation for understanding emotion-related behaviors. In medicine, it aids in the diagnosis and treatment of conditions such as autism spectrum disorder (ASD) and depression and helps track patient recovery [1,2]. In engineering, emotion recognition advances affective brain-computer interfaces (aBCIs), enabling better integration of emotional states into technology. 

Physiological signals, such as electroencephalogram (EEG), offer a more objective approach to emotion recognition than non-physiological signals like facial expressions, gestures, and voice, which can be influenced by environmental or social factors [3,4]. EEG measures brain activity through electrical signals, providing high reliability and precision, while also being portable and cost-effective. 

Advancements in deep learning have greatly improved EEG decoding performance through various neural network models [5][6][7]. However, these models generally perform well on test data with a distribution similar to the training data, but their performance significantly declines when applied to a new domain with a different data distribution, a phenomenon known as domain shift [8]. The considerable variations in EEG signals across individuals challenge the effectiveness of cross-domain emotion recognition models. Additionally, deep neural networks typically require a vast quantity of labeled data for training. Collecting and annotating EEG signals is often a labor-intensive and costly process. 

Unsupervised domain adaptation (UDA) is gaining attention to address these challenges, aiming to enhance model performance on the target domain by utilizing information from the source domain. Recent research on domain adaptation for classifying EEG emotions has largely focused on cross-subject and cross-session scenarios within the same dataset [9][10][11][12][13]. However, less attention has been given to the cross-dataset scenario, which presents even greater challenges due to variations in EEG signals not only from individual differences but also from differences in EEG recording settings and stimuli. 

Another limitation of traditional unsupervised domain adaptation methods is that they require access to the source domain data while adapting to the target domain.

sections.title: # Quantitative State of the Art and Trends
sections.text:
- Intra- vs cross-subject gap and baselines:
 - With an MLP on SEED, cross-subject accuracy can drop to 58% versus 96% intra-subject, highlighting the baseline gap that advanced methods aim to close [302a181a-1].
 - Within-dataset or cross-subject methods like BiDANN, TANN, and PR-PL often outperform on single datasets but degrade under cross-corpus shifts, emphasizing the distinct difficulty of cross-subject generalization [302a181a-0].

- Cross-dataset (source-free) results:
 - Cross-dataset setups (e.g., SEED ↔ SEED-IV/MPED) are used to quantify transfer across datasets and subjects [302a181a-2].
 - A recent source-free unsupervised domain adaptation method reports 58.99% accuracy for SEED → DEAP and 65.84% for DEAP → SEED, outperforming four strong baselines by 5.44% and 3.86% respectively, with statistical significance in most cases [dc83288e-2].

- Dataset-dependent performance:
 - Studies often find SEED yields more reliable and higher performance than DEAP due to data quality and annotation consistency, while DEAP tends to overfit unless augmented with regularization [dc83288e-1].

citations.title: Towards Practical Emotion Recognition: An Unsupervised Source-Free Approach for EEG Domain Adaptation
snippets:
To assess the model's performance, we conduct cross-dataset testing by training on one dataset (either DEAP or SEED) and testing on the other, considering both directions. As no SF-UDA methods currently exist for EEG emotion recognition, we evaluate our approach by comparing it with four general state-of-the-art methods [15,16,21,22], known for their strong performance. We reimplemented these open-source methods and evaluated them on the same datasets used in our experiments to ensure a fair comparison. 

Table 1 presents the overall accuracy comparisons across the datasets. Our method outperforms all other approaches, achieving the highest overall accuracy of 58.99% for SEED → DEAP (trained on SEED and tested on DEAP) and 65.84% for DEAP → SEED (trained on DEAP and tested on SEED). These results are 5.44% and 3.86% higher, respectively, than the second-best approach, by Ragab et al. for SEED → DEAP and Zhao et al. for DEAP → SEED. To further validate the significance of these performance differences, we conduct a paired-sample t-test using p-values. The test confirms that the accuracy differences for DEAP → SEED are highly significant (**) when compared to all other approaches. For SEED → DEAP, the difference is significant (*) when compared to the approaches by Ragab et al. and Zhao et al., while it remains highly significant compared to the other methods. Fig. 4 displays boxplots illustrating the accuracy distributions across subjects on the test dataset for our method and other SF-UDA approaches. Notably, our method achieves the highest median accuracy among all approaches. In the DEAP → SEED scenario, our method demonstrates superior performance, attaining the highest median accuracy of 65.02%, with minimal variation in accuracies compared to the alternatives. In the SEED → DEAP scenario, although the methods by Ragab et al. and Ahmed et al. show slightly lower variability, their overall accuracy remains low. In contrast, our proposed method achieves the highest median accuracy of 57.07%.

citations.title: EEG-SCMM: Soft Contrastive Masked Modeling for Cross-Corpus EEG-Based Emotion Recognition
snippets:
Emotions are human attitudinal experiences and behavioral responses to objective things, closely related to an individual's health conditions and behavioral patterns [45]. Compared to speech [40], gestures [31], and facial expressions [2], electroencephalography (EEG) offers a more direct and objective measurement of human emotions by capturing brain activity across various scalp locations [16]. Therefore, researchers have increasingly emphasized EEGbased emotion recognition in recent years [50,51,53,56], aiming to advance the development of affective brain-computer interfaces (aBCIs). However, three critical challenges remain to be addressed in current approaches. 

(1) Insufficient Generalization Capability. Most existing EEGbased emotion recognition methods are typically designed for a single dataset, necessitating model retraining when the dataset changes. This requirement significantly limits the scalability and generalizability of the model, hindering its application on different datasets. To address this issue, the concept of cross-corpus has been proposed, which is designed to be generalized across multiple datasets. A cross-corpus model is trained on one dataset and can be directly applied to another without retraining from scratch. This concept, which originated in natural language processing [38,52], has been extended to various domains in recent years [5,35,37]. Although existing EEG-based emotion recognition methods, such as BiDANN [28], TANN [26], and PR-PL [57], have demonstrated superior performance in within-subject or cross-subject tasks within a single dataset, their effectiveness significantly degrades in crosscorpus scenarios, where the differences in data distribution across datasets far exceed the intra-dataset variability [35]. 

(2) Modeling Strategy Limitation. Recently, researchers have explored domain adaptation techniques to address cross-corpus EEG-based emotion recognition [14,58]. This is motivated by their  efficacy to solve the problem of domain shift [10]. Despite initial success, such approaches often require prior access to all labeled source data and unlabeled target data for model training.

sections.title: # Methodological Landscape
sections.text:
1) Domain Adaptation and Domain Generalization
- Adversarial and discrepancy-minimizing approaches: Domain adaptation (DA) and domain generalization (DG) methods aim to minimize distribution shifts between source (training subject) and target (test subject) by aligning latent representations [302a181a-1]. Some DA methods (e.g., BiDANN, TANN, PR-PL) excel within or cross-subject within a single corpus but struggle under larger cross-corpus shifts [302a181a-0]. Hybrid transfer learning strategies combine domain adaptation with fine-tuning to balance domain-invariant learning and target-specific adaptation, though coordinating the two is challenging [302a181a-4].
- Graph-regularized and adaptive methods: Domain-invariant adaptive graph regularized label propagation leverages graph structure to enforce invariance and improve cross-subject performance on SEED/SEED-IV, and can be extended to cross-dataset with DEAP [26ce0344-3].
- Multi-source/multi-subject paradigms: Multi-subject learning aims to learn general attributes across participants and rapidly adapt to a target individual with limited labels [26ce0344-4].

2) Contrastive and Self-/Unsupervised Representation Learning
- Subject-invariant representations: Contrastive learning frameworks explicitly learn subject-invariant emotion features, motivated by evidence that subject-invariance exists at the representational level in neuroscience and psychology [302a181a-1].
- Cross-corpus masked modeling: Soft Contrastive Masked Modeling (EEG-SCMM) targets cross-corpus generalization by aligning representations across datasets, noting that cross-corpus shifts exceed intra-dataset variability and that many DA methods require labeled source and unlabeled target data [302a181a-0].

3) Transformers and Interpretable Architectures
- Transformer-based interpretable models (e.g., ERTNet) are evaluated on DEAP and SEED-V, leveraging multi-head attention and explainability; SEED-V is used to probe generalization and robustness across datasets [dc83288e-0].
- Interpretable transformer designs are increasingly adopted, with cross-dataset evaluations (DEAP/SEED-V) used to assess generalization [26ce0344-0].

4) Source-Free and Unsupervised Domain Adaptation
- Unsupervised source-free approaches address cross-subject and cross-session without target labels, and more recent work explores source-free domain adaptation (SF-UDA) specifically for EEG emotion recognition [302a181a-3].
- State-of-the-art source-free UDA methods report improved cross-dataset accuracies versus prior baselines (e.g., 58.99% SEED→DEAP; 65.84% DEAP→SEED), with statistical validation showing significant gains in many cases [dc83288e-2].

5) Few-shot Personalization and Cross-view Fusion
- FACE (Few-shot Adapter with Cross-view Fusion) tackles cross-subject with limited target labels by dynamically fusing global brain connectivity and localized patterns via subject-specific fusion weights, and uses meta-learning–enhanced adapters to reduce overfitting; it reports superior generalization over prior SOTA on multiple EEG benchmarks [302a181a-4].

6) Cross-dataset Protocols and Fusion with Peripheral Signals
- Cross-dataset protocols (SEED/SEED-IV/MPED) standardize training/test splits across datasets to quantify cross-setting generalization [302a181a-2].
- Emotional EEG style transfer networks operationalize cross-dataset training with category-balanced emotion subsets and subject-wise domain assignments to enable controlled transfer [302a181a-2].

citations.title: FACE: Few-shot Adapter with Cross-view Fusion for Cross-subject EEG Emotion Recognition
snippets: Cross-subject EEG emotion recognition is challenged by significant inter-subject variability and intricately entangled intra-subject variability. Existing works have primarily addressed these challenges through domain adaptation or generalization strategies. However, they typically require extensive target subject data or demonstrate limited generalization performance to unseen subjects. Recent few-shot learning paradigms attempt to address these limitations but often encounter catastrophic overfitting during subject-specific adaptation with limited samples. This article introduces the few-shot adapter with a cross-view fusion method called FACE for cross-subject EEG emotion recognition, which leverages dynamic multi-view fusion and effective subject-specific adaptation. Specifically, FACE incorporates a cross-view fusion module that dynamically integrates global brain connectivity with localized patterns via subject-specific fusion weights to provide complementary emotional information. Moreover, the few-shot adapter module is proposed to enable rapid adaptation for unseen subjects while reducing overfitting by enhancing adapter structures with meta-learning. Experimental results on three public EEG emotion recognition benchmarks demonstrate FACE's superior generalization performance over state-of-the-art methods. FACE provides a practical solution for cross-subject scenarios with limited labeled data.

snippets:
The SEED dataset consists of EEG emotion data gathered from 15 subjects. Each subject viewed 15 movie clips intended to evoke three emotional states: positive, negative, and neutral. In contrast, the SEED-IV dataset also includes EEG emotion data from 15 subjects but involves 24 movie clips aimed at inducing four emotions: happy, sad, neutral, and fear. For both SEED and SEED-IV datasets, participants participated in three sessions conducted on different days, with one week intervals between sessions. citations.title: EEG-SCMM: Soft Contrastive Masked Modeling for Cross-Corpus EEG-Based Emotion Recognition
snippets:
Emotions are human attitudinal experiences and behavioral responses to objective things, closely related to an individual's health conditions and behavioral patterns [45]. Compared to speech [40], gestures [31], and facial expressions [2], electroencephalography (EEG) offers a more direct and objective measurement of human emotions by capturing brain activity across various scalp locations [16]. Therefore, researchers have increasingly emphasized EEGbased emotion recognition in recent years [50,51,53,56], aiming to advance the development of affective brain-computer interfaces (aBCIs). However, three critical challenges remain to be addressed in current approaches. 

(1) Insufficient Generalization Capability. Most existing EEGbased emotion recognition methods are typically designed for a single dataset, necessitating model retraining when the dataset changes. This requirement significantly limits the scalability and generalizability of the model, hindering its application on different datasets. To address this issue, the concept of cross-corpus has been proposed, which is designed to be generalized across multiple datasets. A cross-corpus model is trained on one dataset and can be directly applied to another without retraining from scratch. This concept, which originated in natural language processing [38,52], has been extended to various domains in recent years [5,35,37]. Although existing EEG-based emotion recognition methods, such as BiDANN [28], TANN [26], and PR-PL [57], have demonstrated superior performance in within-subject or cross-subject tasks within a single dataset, their effectiveness significantly degrades in crosscorpus scenarios, where the differences in data distribution across datasets far exceed the intra-dataset variability [35]. 

(2) Modeling Strategy Limitation. Recently, researchers have explored domain adaptation techniques to address cross-corpus EEG-based emotion recognition [14,58]. This is motivated by their  efficacy to solve the problem of domain shift [10]. Despite initial success, such approaches often require prior access to all labeled source data and unlabeled target data for model training.

citations.title: Hybrid transfer learning strategy for cross-subject EEG emotion recognition
snippets: If the labeled data in the target domain is limited, utilizing fine-tuning may become challenging. Therefore, some researchers have begun exploring the application of domain adaptation for cross-subject eeg emotion recognition. For example, Jin et al. (2017) introduced the implementation of the Domain Adaptation Network (DAN) for knowledge migration in EEG-based sentiment identification to tackle the core issue of reducing disparities between the origin participant and destination participant in an attempt to eradicate subject variability. Li et al. (2019) introduced a domain adaptation technique for EEG emotion recognition, enhanced by reducing the classification error on the source domain while simultaneously harmonizing the latent representations of the source and target domains to enhance their similarity. Wang et al. (2021a) introduced a proficient domain adaptation approach using the multi-subject learning paradigm to address crosssubject emotion classification tasks with restricted EEG data. This technique empowers the model to grasp overarching attributes from diverse participants and swiftly adjust to the specific target individual (Wang et al., 2021a). However, only relying on domain adaptation methods may not effectively leverage the available label information in the target domain, which can result in performance degradation. Domain adaptation typically focuses on reducing the performance gap between different domains, especially between the source and target domains. Fine-tuning involves further training on target domain data to adapt to its specific characteristics, thus enhancing the performance of the model in the target domain. Therefore, combining these two techniques can lead to more significant performance improvements, allowing the model to better adapt to cross-subject EEG emotion recognition tasks. However, effectively coordinating both domain adaptation and fine-tuning techniques and harnessing their strengths to reduce inter-domain differences, enhance model adaptability, and ultimately improve emotion recognition accuracy is a challenging task. The challenge of this task lies in the need for careful balance between the two techniques, ensuring that the model can adapt well to the data characteristics of the target domain while preserving its generalization capability. Additionally, the selection of appropriate domain adaptation methods and fine-tuning strategies must also be considered.

citations.title: Cross-Subject EEG-Based Emotion Recognition Through Neural Networks With Stratified Normalization
snippets:
Despite the large number of potential applications of emotion recognition from EEG signals, to the best of our knowledge, MAHNOB-HCI (Soleymani et al., 2012), SEED (Duan et al., 2013;Zheng and Lu, 2015), SEED IV (Zheng et al., 2019), and DEAP (Koelstra et al., 2012) are the only four publicly available emotional EEG datasets on the topic. From those four datasets, the most studied ones in cross-subject emotion classification are the DEAP and SEED datasets (e.g., Li et al., 2020;Cimtay and Ekmekcioglu, 2020, from which we decided to focus on the SEED dataset because of the following reasons. Firstly, the collected data is well-balanced between sessions and participants, which simplifies the assessment of the classification results. Secondly, as Li et al. (2018) mentioned in his study, the performance on DEAP is significantly inferior to that on SEED, which may be due to the relatively low quality of the data and the emotional ratings of trials. This led them to conduct further evaluation only in the SEED dataset. Thirdly, neural networks easily overfit with the DEAP dataset, which would increase the complexity of the neural network models since it would be necessary to include data augmentation, early stopping, higher dropout, and/or regularization for each model (e.g., Cimtay and Ekmekcioglu, 2020;Yang H. Y. et al., 2019). Lastly, the literature offers many reports on cross-subject emotion recognition models using the SEED dataset, which permits the comparison with other papers. 

The SEED dataset contains 62-channel EEG data collected from 15 participants, who carried out three sessions over the same 15 film clips. An emotional rating was previously assigned to each film clip and obtained by averaging the ratings of 20 participants who were asked to indicate one keyword (positive, neutral, or negative) after watching them. In the subsequent experiment with EEG recordings, the clips used across sessions and participants at each trial shared the same pseudo-random order of ratings to balance evoked emotions throughout the EEG recordings smoothly.

citations.title: Towards Practical Emotion Recognition: An Unsupervised Source-Free Approach for EEG Domain Adaptation
snippets:
Emotion, a fundamental mental phenomenon, is deeply connected to human cognition and behavior, shaping daily life experiences. Recognizing emotions is a critical focus in psychology, medicine, and engineering. In psychology, it provides a quantitative foundation for understanding emotion-related behaviors. In medicine, it aids in the diagnosis and treatment of conditions such as autism spectrum disorder (ASD) and depression and helps track patient recovery [1,2]. In engineering, emotion recognition advances affective brain-computer interfaces (aBCIs), enabling better integration of emotional states into technology. 

Physiological signals, such as electroencephalogram (EEG), offer a more objective approach to emotion recognition than non-physiological signals like facial expressions, gestures, and voice, which can be influenced by environmental or social factors [3,4]. EEG measures brain activity through electrical signals, providing high reliability and precision, while also being portable and cost-effective. 

Advancements in deep learning have greatly improved EEG decoding performance through various neural network models [5][6][7]. However, these models generally perform well on test data with a distribution similar to the training data, but their performance significantly declines when applied to a new domain with a different data distribution, a phenomenon known as domain shift [8]. The considerable variations in EEG signals across individuals challenge the effectiveness of cross-domain emotion recognition models. Additionally, deep neural networks typically require a vast quantity of labeled data for training. Collecting and annotating EEG signals is often a labor-intensive and costly process. 

Unsupervised domain adaptation (UDA) is gaining attention to address these challenges, aiming to enhance model performance on the target domain by utilizing information from the source domain. Recent research on domain adaptation for classifying EEG emotions has largely focused on cross-subject and cross-session scenarios within the same dataset [9][10][11][12][13]. However, less attention has been given to the cross-dataset scenario, which presents even greater challenges due to variations in EEG signals not only from individual differences but also from differences in EEG recording settings and stimuli. 

Another limitation of traditional unsupervised domain adaptation methods is that they require access to the source domain data while adapting to the target domain.

sections.title: # Practical Considerations and Open Challenges
sections.text:
- Data quality, annotation, and overfitting: Poor data quality and inconsistent annotations in DEAP can depress performance, while SEED’s balanced design and higher data quality support better generalization; DEAP often requires augmentation, early stopping, and stronger regularization [dc83288e-1].
- Subject shift vs. other shifts: Cross-subject variability is only one source of shift; cross-dataset scenarios add channel, device, and stimulus differences, making cross-dataset a stricter test and often a better proxy for real-world deployment [302a181a-3].
- Label scarcity and target-domain access: Few-shot personalization and hybrid transfer learning address limited target labels, but balancing adaptation and fine-tuning remains an art, and many DA methods still require some target data or access to unlabeled target samples [302a181a-4]. Some DA approaches need labeled source and unlabeled target data, constraining deployment when only labeled source or labeled target is available [302a181a-0].
- Cross-corpus difficulty: Cross-corpus shifts are larger than intra-dataset or even cross-subject shifts, and many existing methods that work within a dataset degrade under cross-corpus conditions [302a181a-0].
- Evaluation protocols: Cross-subject and cross-dataset protocols should carefully balance classes and delineate source and target subjects/datasets to fairly assess generalization [302a181a-2].

citations.title: FACE: Few-shot Adapter with Cross-view Fusion for Cross-subject EEG Emotion Recognition
snippets: Cross-subject EEG emotion recognition is challenged by significant inter-subject variability and intricately entangled intra-subject variability. Existing works have primarily addressed these challenges through domain adaptation or generalization strategies. However, they typically require extensive target subject data or demonstrate limited generalization performance to unseen subjects. Recent few-shot learning paradigms attempt to address these limitations but often encounter catastrophic overfitting during subject-specific adaptation with limited samples. This article introduces the few-shot adapter with a cross-view fusion method called FACE for cross-subject EEG emotion recognition, which leverages dynamic multi-view fusion and effective subject-specific adaptation. Specifically, FACE incorporates a cross-view fusion module that dynamically integrates global brain connectivity with localized patterns via subject-specific fusion weights to provide complementary emotional information. Moreover, the few-shot adapter module is proposed to enable rapid adaptation for unseen subjects while reducing overfitting by enhancing adapter structures with meta-learning. Experimental results on three public EEG emotion recognition benchmarks demonstrate FACE's superior generalization performance over state-of-the-art methods. FACE provides a practical solution for cross-subject scenarios with limited labeled data.

citations.title: Enhancing Cross-Dataset EEG Emotion Recognition: A Novel Approach With Emotional EEG Style Transfer Network
snippets: The objective of this paper is to investigate cross-dataset EEG emotion recognition tasks. In alignment with the principles of previous experiments, we establish groups of experiment protocols for cross-dataset EEG emotion recognition based on SEED [Zheng and Lu, 2015], SEED-IV [Zheng et al., 2018], and MPED [Song et al., 2019] datasets, with detailed information provided in Appendix B. Table I of Appendix B summarizes the setup details of the cross-dataset EEG emotion recognition experiments. For instance, we denote the 3-category cross-dataset EEG emotion recognition experiment using the MPED 3 dataset as the source domain and the SEED 3 dataset as the target domain as MPED 3 → SEED 3 in this paper.

sections.title: # What Counts as “State of the Art” Today
sections.text:
- Cross-subject methods that close the intra→cross gap include: adversarial and discrepancy-based domain adaptation for subject-invariant features; contrastive/self-supervised learning that explicitly encourages subject-invariance; hybrid transfer (DA + fine-tuning); and recent source-free UDA and few-shot personalization with cross-view fusion. These address the large drop from intra-subject to cross-subject performance (e.g., from 96% to ~58% MLP baselines on SEED) [302a181a-1]. Few-shot adapters with meta-learning and dynamic multi-view fusion (FACE) report superior cross-subject generalization on public benchmarks under limited target labels [302a181a-4]. Style transfer and cross-dataset training protocols provide practical cross-setting transfer, with category-balanced designs to mitigate distribution shifts [302a181a-2].
- Cross-dataset state of the art emphasizes source-free and unsupervised adaptation. Recent source-free UDA methods achieve notable gains over strong baselines on SEED↔DEAP, suggesting progress toward practical cross-setting generalization without target labels [dc83288e-2].
- Architectures: Interpretable transformers and contrastive masked modeling are emerging for cross-corpus tasks [dc83288e-0] , while graph-regularized label propagation and multi-subject learning provide alternative routes to domain-invariant representations [26ce0344-3].

snippets:
However, most studies have mainly focused on intrasubject emotion recognition [5]. To reach satisfactory recognition performance, researchers needed to collect sufficient data (generally half an hour to more than one hour) within one subject to learn subject-dependent EEG representations for emotion recognition [14], [23], [24]. This laborious and time-consuming training procedure has become a major bottleneck for the practical use of EEG-based emotion recognition. Therefore, developing emotion recognition methods with good cross-subject generalizability is desirable for realistic applications, especially in the cases of new users [25], [26]. 

The substantial inter-subject variabilities of emotion-related EEG activities posed great challenge for cross-subject emotion recognition [27], [28]. For example, the cross-subject emotion recognition accuracy on the widely used SEED dataset [9], [14] could be as low as 58% with a generic multiple layer perceptron classifier. In comparison, the intra-subject emotion recognition could achieve high accuracy of 96% with the same classifier [29]. The substantial drop in the emotion recognition performance from the intra-subject to the cross-subject scenario could be explained by the well-acknowledged individual difference in EEGbased emotion representations due to factors such as individualized experience and dispositional characteristics [30], [31], [32], [33]. Nonetheless, subject-invariance of emotion representation has also been well documented in the field of psychology and neuroscience [15], [34], [35], [36], [37]. Previous fMRI and EEG studies have identified distinct and stable neural representations for different emotions across subjects [15], [34], [35], [36], [37], suggesting the possibility of developing cross-subject emotion recognition algorithms. 

To address the issue of inter-subject variability, researchers have applied domain adaptation (DA) and domain generalization (DG) methods to cross-subject emotion recognition [26], [38]. The DA methods aim to minimize the discrepancy between data distributions of the source domain (i.e., the training subject) and the target domain (i.e., the testing subject).

snippets:
To assess the model's performance, we conduct cross-dataset testing by training on one dataset (either DEAP or SEED) and testing on the other, considering both directions. As no SF-UDA methods currently exist for EEG emotion recognition, we evaluate our approach by comparing it with four general state-of-the-art methods [15,16,21,22], known for their strong performance. We reimplemented these open-source methods and evaluated them on the same datasets used in our experiments to ensure a fair comparison. 

Table 1 presents the overall accuracy comparisons across the datasets. Our method outperforms all other approaches, achieving the highest overall accuracy of 58.99% for SEED → DEAP (trained on SEED and tested on DEAP) and 65.84% for DEAP → SEED (trained on DEAP and tested on SEED). These results are 5.44% and 3.86% higher, respectively, than the second-best approach, by Ragab et al. for SEED → DEAP and Zhao et al. for DEAP → SEED. To further validate the significance of these performance differences, we conduct a paired-sample t-test using p-values. The test confirms that the accuracy differences for DEAP → SEED are highly significant (**) when compared to all other approaches. For SEED → DEAP, the difference is significant (*) when compared to the approaches by Ragab et al. and Zhao et al., while it remains highly significant compared to the other methods. Fig. 4 displays boxplots illustrating the accuracy distributions across subjects on the test dataset for our method and other SF-UDA approaches. Notably, our method achieves the highest median accuracy among all approaches. In the DEAP → SEED scenario, our method demonstrates superior performance, attaining the highest median accuracy of 65.02%, with minimal variation in accuracies compared to the alternatives. In the SEED → DEAP scenario, although the methods by Ragab et al. and Ahmed et al. show slightly lower variability, their overall accuracy remains low. In contrast, our proposed method achieves the highest median accuracy of 57.07%.

sections.title: # Recommendations and Outlook
sections.text:
- For cross-subject deployment, prefer methods combining: (i) subject-invariant representation learning (contrastive/adversarial), (ii) hybrid transfer (DA + targeted fine-tuning) to exploit scarce labels, and (iii) few-shot personalization with regularization and cross-view fusion to mitigate overfitting. These directly target inter-subject variability [302a181a-1] , and have shown improved generalization in recent benchmarks [302a181a-4].
- For cross-dataset generalization, adopt source-free UDA and cross-dataset protocols that mirror real deployment (different devices, stimuli). Style transfer and carefully balanced cross-dataset setups can operationalize this [302a181a-2] , and recent source-free methods report meaningful improvements [dc83288e-2].
- Benchmarking should standardize cross-subject/cross-dataset splits on SEED/SEED-IV/DEAP/MPED with clear subject and class balance, and report per-subject and overall accuracies with statistical tests. Accounting for dataset disparities in sessions, channels, and stimuli is critical [302a181a-3].
- Open challenges include robust generalization under severe cross-corpus shifts, personalization with very few labeled target samples, and scalable data-efficient pretraining without target labels. Cross-corpus remains a major bottleneck, and many DA methods still have restrictive data access assumptions [302a181a-0].

citations.title: Towards Practical Emotion Recognition: An Unsupervised Source-Free Approach for EEG Domain Adaptation
snippets:
Emotion, a fundamental mental phenomenon, is deeply connected to human cognition and behavior, shaping daily life experiences. Recognizing emotions is a critical focus in psychology, medicine, and engineering. In psychology, it provides a quantitative foundation for understanding emotion-related behaviors. In medicine, it aids in the diagnosis and treatment of conditions such as autism spectrum disorder (ASD) and depression and helps track patient recovery [1,2]. In engineering, emotion recognition advances affective brain-computer interfaces (aBCIs), enabling better integration of emotional states into technology. 

Physiological signals, such as electroencephalogram (EEG), offer a more objective approach to emotion recognition than non-physiological signals like facial expressions, gestures, and voice, which can be influenced by environmental or social factors [3,4]. EEG measures brain activity through electrical signals, providing high reliability and precision, while also being portable and cost-effective. 

Advancements in deep learning have greatly improved EEG decoding performance through various neural network models [5][6][7]. However, these models generally perform well on test data with a distribution similar to the training data, but their performance significantly declines when applied to a new domain with a different data distribution, a phenomenon known as domain shift [8]. The considerable variations in EEG signals across individuals challenge the effectiveness of cross-domain emotion recognition models. Additionally, deep neural networks typically require a vast quantity of labeled data for training. Collecting and annotating EEG signals is often a labor-intensive and costly process. 

Unsupervised domain adaptation (UDA) is gaining attention to address these challenges, aiming to enhance model performance on the target domain by utilizing information from the source domain. Recent research on domain adaptation for classifying EEG emotions has largely focused on cross-subject and cross-session scenarios within the same dataset [9][10][11][12][13]. However, less attention has been given to the cross-dataset scenario, which presents even greater challenges due to variations in EEG signals not only from individual differences but also from differences in EEG recording settings and stimuli. 

Another limitation of traditional unsupervised domain adaptation methods is that they require access to the source domain data while adapting to the target domain.

citations.title: EEG-SCMM: Soft Contrastive Masked Modeling for Cross-Corpus EEG-Based Emotion Recognition
snippets:
Emotions are human attitudinal experiences and behavioral responses to objective things, closely related to an individual's health conditions and behavioral patterns [45]. Compared to speech [40], gestures [31], and facial expressions [2], electroencephalography (EEG) offers a more direct and objective measurement of human emotions by capturing brain activity across various scalp locations [16]. Therefore, researchers have increasingly emphasized EEGbased emotion recognition in recent years [50,51,53,56], aiming to advance the development of affective brain-computer interfaces (aBCIs). However, three critical challenges remain to be addressed in current approaches. 

(1) Insufficient Generalization Capability. Most existing EEGbased emotion recognition methods are typically designed for a single dataset, necessitating model retraining when the dataset changes. This requirement significantly limits the scalability and generalizability of the model, hindering its application on different datasets. To address this issue, the concept of cross-corpus has been proposed, which is designed to be generalized across multiple datasets. A cross-corpus model is trained on one dataset and can be directly applied to another without retraining from scratch. This concept, which originated in natural language processing [38,52], has been extended to various domains in recent years [5,35,37]. Although existing EEG-based emotion recognition methods, such as BiDANN [28], TANN [26], and PR-PL [57], have demonstrated superior performance in within-subject or cross-subject tasks within a single dataset, their effectiveness significantly degrades in crosscorpus scenarios, where the differences in data distribution across datasets far exceed the intra-dataset variability [35]. 

(2) Modeling Strategy Limitation. Recently, researchers have explored domain adaptation techniques to address cross-corpus EEG-based emotion recognition [14,58]. This is motivated by their  efficacy to solve the problem of domain shift [10]. Despite initial success, such approaches often require prior access to all labeled source data and unlabeled target data for model training.

sections.title: # Key Takeaways
sections.text:
- The SOTA in cross-subject EEG emotion recognition is driven by domain adaptation and contrastive/self-supervised representation learning to learn subject-invariant features, hybrid transfer (DA + fine-tuning), and few-shot personalization with meta-learning and cross-view fusion, which collectively reduce the intra→cross-subject performance gap. This gap can be large (e.g., 96% intra vs ~58% cross-subject with MLP on SEED) [302a181a-1]. Recent few-shot adapters (e.g., FACE) show superior generalization under limited labels [302a181a-4].
- Cross-dataset generalization has advanced with source-free unsupervised domain adaptation, achieving notable gains over prior methods on SEED↔DEAP, and with cross-dataset protocols that balance classes and delineate source/target domains. State-of-the-art source-free UDA reports 58.99% (SEED→DEAP) and 65.84% (DEAP→SEED) with significant t-tests [dc83288e-2]. Emotional style transfer networks provide a practical framework for cross-setting transfer [302a181a-2].
- Dataset choice and quality strongly influence results; SEED/SEED-IV generally enable more reliable cross-subject evaluation than DEAP, which is more prone to overfitting without heavy regularization. These factors should be central to fair SOTA comparisons [dc83288e-1]. Cross-dataset disparities in recording and stimuli further complicate generalization [302a181a-3].

snippets:
Despite the large number of potential applications of emotion recognition from EEG signals, to the best of our knowledge, MAHNOB-HCI (Soleymani et al., 2012), SEED (Duan et al., 2013;Zheng and Lu, 2015), SEED IV (Zheng et al., 2019), and DEAP (Koelstra et al., 2012) are the only four publicly available emotional EEG datasets on the topic. From those four datasets, the most studied ones in cross-subject emotion classification are the DEAP and SEED datasets (e.g., Li et al., 2020;Cimtay and Ekmekcioglu, 2020, from which we decided to focus on the SEED dataset because of the following reasons. Firstly, the collected data is well-balanced between sessions and participants, which simplifies the assessment of the classification results. Secondly, as Li et al. (2018) mentioned in his study, the performance on DEAP is significantly inferior to that on SEED, which may be due to the relatively low quality of the data and the emotional ratings of trials. This led them to conduct further evaluation only in the SEED dataset. Thirdly, neural networks easily overfit with the DEAP dataset, which would increase the complexity of the neural network models since it would be necessary to include data augmentation, early stopping, higher dropout, and/or regularization for each model (e.g., Cimtay and Ekmekcioglu, 2020;Yang H. Y. et al., 2019). Lastly, the literature offers many reports on cross-subject emotion recognition models using the SEED dataset, which permits the comparison with other papers. 

The SEED dataset contains 62-channel EEG data collected from 15 participants, who carried out three sessions over the same 15 film clips. An emotional rating was previously assigned to each film clip and obtained by averaging the ratings of 20 participants who were asked to indicate one keyword (positive, neutral, or negative) after watching them. In the subsequent experiment with EEG recordings, the clips used across sessions and participants at each trial shared the same pseudo-random order of ratings to balance evoked emotions throughout the EEG recordings smoothly.

citations.title: FACE: Few-shot Adapter with Cross-view Fusion for Cross-subject EEG Emotion Recognition
snippets: Cross-subject EEG emotion recognition is challenged by significant inter-subject variability and intricately entangled intra-subject variability. Existing works have primarily addressed these challenges through domain adaptation or generalization strategies. However, they typically require extensive target subject data or demonstrate limited generalization performance to unseen subjects. Recent few-shot learning paradigms attempt to address these limitations but often encounter catastrophic overfitting during subject-specific adaptation with limited samples. This article introduces the few-shot adapter with a cross-view fusion method called FACE for cross-subject EEG emotion recognition, which leverages dynamic multi-view fusion and effective subject-specific adaptation. Specifically, FACE incorporates a cross-view fusion module that dynamically integrates global brain connectivity with localized patterns via subject-specific fusion weights to provide complementary emotional information. Moreover, the few-shot adapter module is proposed to enable rapid adaptation for unseen subjects while reducing overfitting by enhancing adapter structures with meta-learning. Experimental results on three public EEG emotion recognition benchmarks demonstrate FACE's superior generalization performance over state-of-the-art methods. FACE provides a practical solution for cross-subject scenarios with limited labeled data.

question: Teach me about all latest progress on diagnosis, such as counterfactual explanation, of VLM models like CLIP

sections.text:
Overview and why diagnosis matters for CLIP-like VLMs
- CLIP and successors learn powerful cross-modal representations but remain difficult to interpret; traditional attributions, perturbations, and concept-based methods often yield inconsistent or spurious explanations, limiting our ability to diagnose biases and failure modes in downstream applications. Despite CLIP's widespread adoption, understanding how it processes and represents information remains a challenge. The distributed nature of its learned representations and the complexity of the optimized loss function make it particularly difficult to interpret. Traditional explainability approaches have limited success in addressing this challenge: gradient-based feature attributions, perturbation-based approaches, and concept-based methods are constrained and yield inconsistent or confounded results, hindering identification and mitigation of potential biases or failure modes [f9237867-0]. 
- Diagnosing VLMs therefore requires mechanisms that expose internal reasoning under controlled “what-if” changes and quantify where models rely on memorized priors versus in-context perception. Visual counterfactuals can challenge world knowledge priors by presenting plausible contradictions, revealing how models integrate in-context pixels with memorized attributes and where predictions switch from priors to perception [f9237867-1].

snippets: Vision-language models, particularly contrastive languageimage pre-training (CLIP, Radford et al., 2021;Cherti et al., 2023), revolutionize multimodal understanding by Proceedings of the 42 nd International Conference on Machine Learning, Vancouver, Canada. Through contrastive learning on massive datasets, CLIP and its less adopted successor SigLIP (Zhai et al., 2023) demonstrate remarkable capabilities that extend far beyond their primary objective of cross-modal similarity search. Its representation is a foundational component in text-to-image generation models like Stable Diffusion (Podell et al., 2024) and serves as a powerful feature extractor for numerous downstream vision and language tasks (Shen et al., 2022), establishing CLIP as a crucial building block in modern VLMs (Liu et al., 2023;Wang et al., 2024). The distributed nature of its learned representations and the complexity of the optimized loss function make it particularly difficult to interpret. Traditional explainability approaches have limited success in addressing this challenge: gradient-based feature attributions (Simonyan, 2013;Shrikumar et al., 2017;Selvaraju et al., 2017;Sundararajan et al., 2017;Abnar & Zuidema, 2020) struggle to provide human-interpretable explanations, perturbation-based approaches (Zeiler & Fergus, 2014;Ribeiro et al., 2016;Lundberg & Lee, 2017;Adebayo et al., 2018;Baniecki et al., 2025) yield inconsistent results, and concept-based methods (Ramaswamy et al., 2023;Oikarinen et al., 2023) are constrained by their reliance on manually curated concept datasets. citations.title: Pixels Versus Priors: Controlling Knowledge Priors in Vision-Language Models through Visual Counterfacts
snippets:
In our framework, world knowledge priors refer to linguistic associations between visual attributes and objects that the model has memorized during pretraining. In contrast, visual perception is defined by the in-context visual input, which we manipulate to create counterfactual images. These counterfactuals are designed to challenge the model's world knowledge of visual attributes by presenting plausible but contradictory visual evidence. For example, we contrast the size-related knowledge prior "strawberries are bigger than flies" with the counterfactual "flies are bigger than strawberries," violating expected size relations (see Figure 2). 

Using Visual CounterFact, we find that MLLMs often ignore world knowledge when shown counterfactual images, favoring perceptual input even when prompted for general facts. We then trace where in the forward pass predictions shift from in-weight knowledge (e.g., strawberries are red) to in-context perception (this strawberry is blue), finding that this transition consistently emerges in mid-to-late layers. During this transition, models frequently flip between the two answers, revealing a competition between in-context pixel and inweights prior information, with pixels often overriding priors in the model's output. To control this behavior, we use our Pixels Versus Priors steering to control whether a vision-language model relies on knowledge priors or pixel information. PvP is a novel framework to construct steering vectors for vision-language models that control whether the model responds based on memorized knowledge or in-context visual input. Through this steering, we successfully shift an average of 99.3% of color predictions and 80.8% of size predictions from memorized priors to counterfactual answers. 

Together, these contributions provide a new visual counterfactual benchmark and a mechanism for interpreting and controlling the behavior of vision-language models. We present the necessary foundation for a mechanistic understanding of how MLLMs integrate image input with prior knowledge of visual attributes, bridging the gap between interpretability research in language models and the emerging needs of multimodal models.

sections.text:
Counterfactual explanation and diagnosis methods
- Visual counterfactuals to separate priors vs. perception: “Pixels Versus Priors” constructs counterfactual images that violate intuitive attribute relations (e.g., “flies are bigger than strawberries”) and shows models flip answers mid-architecture, indicating competition between priors and perception. The framework also derives steering vectors to shift predictions, achieving 99.3% average color and 80.8% size shifts from memorized priors to counterfactual answers, providing a mechanistic diagnostic and control knob for VLM behavior. Visual CounterFact reveals a competition between in-context pixel input and in-weight knowledge priors, with consistent transitions in mid-to-late layers and frequent flips between answers. Pixels Versus Priors steering vectors shift an average of 99.3% of color and 80.8% of size predictions from memorized priors to counterfactual answers, enabling interpretability and control over reliance on priors versus perception [f9237867-1]. 
- Joint image–text counterfactual training for causal reasoning: CF-VLM introduces joint image–text counterfactual samples with three objectives—cross-modal alignment, counterfactual scenario discrimination, and fine-grained causal discrimination—to target decision points. Empirically, it improves accuracy on ARO, ConMe, and VL-Checklist and reduces visual hallucinations, demonstrating diagnosis-to-mitigation value for failure modes like hallucination. CF-VLM integrates joint image-text counterfactuals and multi-level supervision to target causal decision points, achieving superior performance on ARO, ConMe, and VL-Checklist and reducing visual hallucinations, indicating enhanced robustness and applicability in high-stakes settings [f9237867-2]. 
- Region-level counterfactual supervision for evidence grounding: DeFacto enforces region-faithful reasoning via automatic counterfactual datasets that mask question-relevant regions, training models to abstain or reason correctly when evidence is removed. It improves both answer accuracy and visual grounding faithfulness over strong baselines and shows that counterfactual training and region-level rewards are necessary for interpretability and robustness. DeFacto introduces counterfactual supervision to enforce region-faithful reasoning and abstention when evidence is missing, building a 100k-image counterfactual dataset automatically. Experiments show consistent gains in answer accuracy and visual grounding faithfulness over strong baselines, and ablations confirm the necessity of counterfactual training and region-level rewards for interpretability and robustness [9af3f8c0-2]. 
- Counterfactual test sets for robustness of perception/understanding: RO-Bench evaluates MLLMs on counterfactual videos and shows that fine-tuning with reliable counterfactual perturbations can increase robustness metrics by 21.73% over a baseline and improve performance across 20 downstream video tasks by an average of 12.78%, underscoring the value of counterfactual-based diagnostics and data in improving generalization and robustness. RO-Bench constructs counterfactual video test sets for robustness evaluation; models trained with high-quality counterfactual data (LLaVA-Next Ro) improve robustness metrics by 21.73% over LLaVA-Next and gain 12.78% on average across 20 downstream tasks, highlighting the importance of reliable counterfactual test sets and fine-tuning with counterfactual perturbations [9af3f8c0-1].

snippets:
Recent advances in vision-language models (VLMs) [52][53][54], such as CLIP [6] and BLIP [1], have demonstrated remarkable performance in cross-modal tasks through large-scale image-text pretraining. However, these models often struggle with fine-grained discrimination and causal reasoning, relying on superficial statistical correlations rather than capturing deep causal relationships between visual and textual content [5,7]. Existing approaches employ contrastive learning to enhance embedding space discriminability, such as triplet loss [17], but primarily focus on binary matching, overlooking the impact of causal attribute changes on semantics [19]. 

Counterfactual learning has emerged as a promising approach to address the causal reasoning limitations of VLMs [18,55,56]. introduced counterfactual visual explanations by modifying key visual elements to analyze model decisions, while CPL [19] leveraged counterfactual prompts to improve cross-modal understanding. However, these methods typically focus on single-modality counterfactuals, lacking joint image-text counterfactual designs [57] and using singular objectives that fail to leverage counterfactual samples for multi-level semantic supervision. 

Our CF-VLM framework advances VLM causal reasoning by integrating joint image-text counterfactual samples with three complementary training objectives: cross-modal alignment, counterfactual scenario discrimination, and fine-grained causal discrimination. Unlike TripletCLIP [16], which optimizes coarse-grained similarity, CF-VLM targets causal decision points, achieving superior accuracy on benchmarks like ARO, ConMe, and VL-Checklist, while reducing visual hallucinations, demonstrating enhanced robustness and applicability in high-stakes scenarios.
