citations.title: One Task Vector is not Enough: A Large-Scale Study for In-Context Learning
snippets:
Transformer-based Large Language Models (LLMs) (Vaswani et al., 2017) excel at in-context learning (ICL), adapting to new tasks via a few prompt-based examples without weight updates (Brown et al., 2020) and have shown impressive empirical results (Liu et al., 2023;Dong et al., 2022). This capability enables rapid task adaptation; however, how LLMs internally represent and apply task information remains unclear. Recent work points to "task vectors" (Hendel et al., 2023) or "function vectors" (Todd et al., 2024) -specific hidden state activations -as the mechanism for encoding task rules. 

Prior studies, such as Hendel et al. (2023), suggest that ICL compresses demonstration sets into task vectors that guide query processing. Todd et al. (2024) used causal analysis to locate these vectors, showing they capture semantic task aspects. While techniques like sparse autoencoders (SAEs) have begun to shed light on the interpretable features within a given task vector (Kharlapenko et al.,  2024), the fundamental question of whether a single such vector suffices for complex, multi-faceted tasks remains largely unexplored. Luo et al. (2024) extended this to vision-language models, demonstrating that task vectors are cross-modal, clustering by task rather than input modality (e.g., text or image) and emerging at intermediate layers to summarize tasks before generation. On some tasks, task vectors achieve near-excellent performance, often over 90% accuracy. However, current stud-  ies mainly utilize toy, manually crafted datasets (see Tab. 1), which limits our understanding of task vector dynamics in diverse, large-scale settings. 

To address this gap, we introduce QUITEAFEW, a novel dataset comprising 3,096 diverse fewshot learning tasks, each with 30 unique inputoutput pairs derived from the Alpaca dataset (Taori et al., 2023). This dataset spans a broad spectrum of tasks, from algorithmic operations to openended generative challenges, enabling a comprehensive exploration of in-context learning (ICL).

sections.title: # Where to look next
sections.text: If you want to dive into optimization/steering frameworks specifically named (e.g., OTTV, DAVINCI, VECTORS) or head-to-head ablations with LoRA/adapter baselines, start from the surveys and fairness/transfer papers above and follow their references to recent method papers; many of these frameworks are being evaluated and compared within the activation-level and weight-difference task-vector ecosystems documented here. Recent surveys and fairness-oriented studies summarize task-vector methods and point to optimization and comparison directions, tying weight-difference vectors to interpretability and fairness constraints [2f37936b-1]. Mechanistic summaries and recent empirical directions enumerate where vectors are extracted from (hidden states, attention heads, MLPs), how they are constructed (PCA, optimization), and emerging theory on their emergence [4ced5249-4].

sections.title: # Overview
sections.text: Learning to Rank (LTR) models trained on historical click data face structural biases that distort learned preferences and degrade fairness and utility. The two dominant biases are position bias (top-rank items receive more attention/interaction) and popularity/presentation bias (well-known or prominently presented items get more clicks), which are amplified by feedback loops. Modern approaches correct these by reweighting clicks with propensities, modeling relevance conditional on exposure, and evaluating and mitigating exposure at both training and inference time. LTR trained on biased click data is vulnerable to position and popularity bias, which are amplified by feedback loops [0de572e4-0] Position bias arises because higher-ranked items receive more attention and clicks regardless of true relevance [0de572e4-1] Popularity bias occurs because more popular items are more likely to be posted, observed, and clicked [0de572e4-0].

snippets:
The phenomenon of position bias is commonly observed in many ranking and information retrieval systems, including digital advertising and recommender systems. Position bias is the tendency of users to pay greater attention to higher-ranked items, regardless of their actual relevance to the query. For example, the eye-tracking study [13] and [14] show that in web search, the highest-ranked items receive the most attention; the study of digital library recommendation system [5] discovers that items shown at the top positions are more often clicked regardless of their actual relevance.

However, due to inherited position bias, these models tend to exhibit lower predicted click-through rates (CTR) for lowerranked items. This bias in prediction can then affect subsequent training data collection, leading to a persistent and cyclical effect. 

The accumulative position bias of the training data will skew the MLR model, leading to increasingly unfair item rank prediction [6]. To address this position bias problem, various approaches have been proposed, including factorization models [4], inverse propensity scores [9,15,19], deep neural network-based CTR prediction models [8,17,21], and more. Pioneering approaches such as [4] proposed a factorization model that decouples CTR into positionnormalized CTR and position bias, which are then estimated by an Expectation-Maximization (EM) algorithm framework. To remove the position bias for learning to rank models, a propensity-weighted empirical risk minimization framework is proposed in [15]. In [10], an unbiased LambdaMART model is proposed, which jointly estimates the biases at click positions and unclick positions and learns an unbiased ranker. Several literatures dedicate to the propensity estimation, such as [1,2,18]. Recently, increasing research studies correcting position bias in the deep-ranking models. In [12], the authors propose to combine recurrent neural network and survival analysis techniques to model unbiased user behaviors.

sections.title: # Modeling and Measuring Bias in Click Data
sections.text:
Position and popularity biases create confounding between relevance and clicks, requiring causal or econometric treatment. Counterfactual LTR formalizes unbiased prediction as P(y=1 | do(x)=1, d), i.e., the probability a user would click if the item were exposed at the given position/context, rather than P(y=1 | x, d), which conflates exposure with relevance. Unbiased LTR changes the objective from P(y=1 | x, d) to P(y=1 | do(x)=1, d) to disentangle observation/exposure from relevance [0de572e4-0].

Popularity and presentation biases can be quantified via exposure and position distributions in logs, and fairness metrics that track group-wise exposure and diversity. Attention-Weighted Rank Fairness (AWRF) measures the divergence between a list’s cumulated exposure per group and a target exposure vector, combining it with nDCG to jointly optimize accuracy and exposure fairness [6417bea0-2] Exposure-aware reward models weight observed clicks more strongly at the bottom and unclicked items more strongly at the top, following exposure drop-off functions like logarithmic nDCG or Rank-Biased Precision [6417bea0-0].

Exposure bias can also be mitigated by modeling item exposure probabilities at inference, decoupling engagement from popularity effects. An exposure-aware retrieval approach that models P(exposed | item) increased unique item retrieval by 25% and reduced over-recommended content by 40% while maintaining engagement in production video recommendation [6417bea0-3] By reframing scoring to P(positive | item, exposed) instead of P(positive & exposed | item), inference-time exposure modeling controls popularity bias vs. engagement trade-offs and improves retrieval of niche content [6417bea0-4].

sections.title: # Families of Debiasing Methods
sections.text:
Debiasing strategies typically fall into three categories: propensity-based reweighting, econometrics/control-function approaches, and direct click-model-based disentangling. Each trades off assumptions, variance, and user experience cost.

- Propensity-based reweighting (IPS/WOPE): Estimate the probability of exposure/click under interventions and reweight logs so that clicks are representative of unbiased interactions. Inverse propensity scoring uses intervention data to estimate missing counterfactual clicks and debias LTR on the full dataset [0de572e4-1] Position-bias-aware learning methods, including factorization models that separate position-normalized CTR from position bias, and unbiased LambdaMART that jointly estimates biases at click and unclick positions, have been proposed to mitigate position bias [0de572e4-1]. Practical concerns include high-variance when propensities are estimated from sparse interventions and misspecification sensitivity. Model-based unbiased LTR can outperform propensity-only methods when propensities are misspecified, and IPW-based methods benefit from variance reduction strategies [0de572e4-2].

- Econometrics/control-function approaches: Use auxiliary signals or randomized experiments to control confounding and estimate causal effects of relevance on clicks. State-of-the-art position-bias correction includes click models, propensity-based approaches, and econometrics-based models; two-tower position-based click models disentangle relevance and bias but can fail under confounding, while randomized result rerandomization provides ground-truth propensities at the cost of user experience [c6bba5ea-2].

- Direct disentangling via click models and dual learning: Jointly estimate observation/exposure probabilities and relevance, or co-train a ranker with a debiaser. Position-based click models (e.g., PBM) and two-tower architectures estimate observation probability and relevance separately, but confounding can still bias estimates [0de572e4-1] Dual Learning Algorithm jointly trains a ranker and a debiasing module as deep networks, treating raw clicks as a lower bound and human labels as an upper bound for performance comparison [c6bba5ea-4].

When interventions are limited or context varies, advanced treatment-effect estimation can reduce variance. Heterogeneous treatment effect estimation enables debiasing with limited intervention traffic and is effective under long-tail queries and sparse clicks [c6bba5ea-3].

citations.title: Counterfactual Learning to Rank using Heterogeneous Treatment Effect Estimation
snippets: Learning-to-Rank (LTR) models trained from implicit feedback (e.g. clicks) suffer from inherent biases. A well-known one is the position bias -- documents in top positions are more likely to receive clicks due in part to their position advantages. To unbiasedly learn to rank, existing counterfactual frameworks first estimate the propensity (probability) of missing clicks with intervention data from a small portion of search traffic, and then use inverse propensity score (IPS) to debias LTR algorithms on the whole data set. These approaches often assume the propensity only depends on the position of the document, which may cause high estimation variance in applications where the search context (e.g. query, user) varies frequently. While context-dependent propensity models reduce variance, accurate estimations may require randomization or intervention on a large amount of traffic, which may not be realistic in real-world systems, especially for long tail queries. In this work, we employ heterogeneous treatment effect estimation techniques to estimate position bias when intervention click data is limited. We then use such estimations to debias the observed click distribution and re-draw a new de-biased data set, which can be used for any LTR algorithms. We conduct simulations with varying experiment conditions and show the effectiveness of the proposed method in regimes with long tail queries and sparse clicks.

citations.title: Correcting for Position Bias in Learning to Rank: A Control Function Approach
snippets:
Learning-to-rank (LTR) systems have become a core component in many online applications, from search engines to recommender systems. These systems typically use implicit feedback data, such as user clicks, as a proxy for user preferences due to its ease of collection compared to costly manual human annotations. While valuable, implicit feedback data is prone to biases [2,61], with position bias being particularly pervasive. Position bias is the tendency of users to interact more with higher-ranked documents, regardless of their true relevance [13,27]. This skews click data, causing LTR models to overestimate higher-ranked documents and underestimate lower ones. Training on such biased data degrades ranking performance and reinforces a feedback loop that negatively affects user experience. This is a preprint version. 

State-of-the-art methods that address position bias can be broadly categorized as click models, propensity-based approaches, and econometrics-based models. Click models [9,13,16,54] estimate true relevance of documents by hypothesizing how users browse and maximizing the likelihood of observed clicks. Click models rely on assumptions about complex user click behavior, which sometimes may not hold in practice. Two-tower models [20,59], following the position-based click model (PBM) [47], attempt to disentangle relevance and bias from clicks by modeling them separately, but may fail when confounding exists between the two. Propensity-based methods treat clicks as counterfactual events and re-weight them using inverse propensity weighting (IPW) to achieve relevance-equivalent training loss [28,55]. Propensity estimation often relies on result randomization [28,41,55], which can harm user experience [2,56]. Some methods [2,24,35,52,63] jointly learn propensities and rankers, but coupling the two raises concerns about the unbiasedness if either model is misspecified [1,18,51].

To answer RQ1, we compare MULTR with other unbiased learningto-rank algorithms in the simulation experiments. Table 1 summarizes the performance of different unbiased learning to rank algorithms under various click situations. We find that: 

• Our model-based unbiased learning to rank achieves the best performance among all the state-of-the-art methods in terms of nDCG and ERR, which indicates our model is robust when propensity cannot be accurately estimated. • Reducing variance can enhance performance on unbiased learning to rank. As MULTR shares the same method with DLA in estimating propensity, the improvements over DLA demonstrate the necessity of handling variance in IPW-based methods. • The naive method may achieve better performance than some unbiased learning to rank methods when clicks are generated by a cascade model. One explanation is that documents displayed at a lower rank have a higher opportunity to be examined; thus they receive more clicks, which alleviates the bias in click data. This observation confirms that a mismatch between propensity estimation and real bias could lead to performance even worse than raw click data. • The oracle model with human annotation consistently achieves the best performance. It implies that there is still room to improve in unbiased learning to rank methods.

snippets:
We made comprehensive comparisons between our method and the baselines. The baselines were created by combining the state-of-the-art debiasing methods and learningto-rank algorithms. There were six debiasing methods. To make fair comparison, the same click dataset was utilized for all debiasing methods. The number of positions was set to 10. 

Randomization: The method, proposed by Joachims et al. [14], uses randomization to infer the observation probabilities as position biases. We randomly shuffled the rank lists and then estimated the position biases as in [1]. 

Regression-EM: The method, proposed by Wang et al. [22], directly estimates the position biases using a regression-EM model. 

Dual Learning Algorithm: The method, proposed by Ai et al. [1], jointly learns a ranker and conducts debiasing of click data. The algorithm implements both the ranking model and the debiasing model as deep neural networks. 

Pairwise Debiasing: Our proposed debiasing method can conduct debiasing when combined with a pairwise learning-to-rank algorithm. In this experiment, we set the hyper-parameter p as 0. 

Click Data: In this method, the raw click data without debiasing is used to train a ranker, whose performance is considered as a lower bound. 

Labeled Data: In this method, human annotated relevance labels are used as data for training of ranker, whose performance is considered as an upper bound. 

There were three learning-to-rank algorithms. DNN: A deep neural network was implemented as a ranker, as in [1]. We directly used the code provided by Ai et al. ‡ . ‡ https://github.com/QingyaoAi/Dual-Learning-Algorithm-for-Unbiased-Learning-to-Rank LambdaMART: We implemented Unbiased LambdaMART by modifying the LambdaMART tool in LightGBM [15]. The total number of trees was 300, learning rate was 0.05, number of leaves for one tree was 31, feature fraction was 0.9, and bagging fraction was 0.9. 

In summary, there were 13 baselines to compare with our proposed Unbiased LambdaMART algorithm.

sections.title: # Addressing Popularity Bias
sections.text:
Popularity bias inflates clicks for already-popular items and is exacerbated by recommendation/ranking feedback loops. Methods include exposure-aware scoring and training-time demerit, as well as bias-aware modeling that decomposes total score into bias and preference components. Popularity bias arises because more popular items are more likely to be posted, observed, and clicked, leading to rich-get-richer dynamics [0de572e4-0] Bias-aware user modeling decomposes overall click score into a bias score and a bias-independent preference score to reduce position and popularity influences [0de572e4-3] Adversarial and bias-aware click models have been shown to outperform learning on biased data, with larger gains on unbiased test sets, indicating that modeling and removing position bias improves click prediction [0de572e4-4].

In retrieval pipelines, popularity bias can be mitigated without sacrificing engagement by modeling exposure and adjusting scores at inference. Exposure-aware retrieval scores adjust rankings at inference to decouple engagement from exposure bias, improving diversity while maintaining performance [6417bea0-4].

snippets: We compare DebiasGAN with many baseline news recommendation methods, including EBNR (Okura  et al., 2017), DKN (Wang et al., 2018a), NAML (Wu et al., 2019a), NPA (Wu et al., 2019b), LSTUR (An et al., 2019), and FIM (Wang et al., 2020). We also compare several methods for eliminating position biases, including (1) IPW (Joachims et al., 2017;Wu et al., 2021b), using inverse propensity weighting in model learning; (2) Reg-EM (Wang et al., 2018b), a regression based EM method to estimate the propensity weight; (3) PAL (Guo et al., 2019), a position bias-aware learning method for CTR prediction. (4) DPIN (Huang et al., 2021), a deep position interaction network for CTR prediction. For fair comparison, in these methods we use the same bias-aware click model with our approach. The results the two datasets are shown in Tables 2  and 3, respectively. We find that debiased methods outperform those directly learned on biased click data. This is because removing position biases can help learn more accurate click prediction model. In addition, our approach outperforms other debiasing methods, and the improvement on the Uniform dataset is greater. This is because our approach considers the user preference for position biases to better model and eliminate position biases. Moreover, our approach uses adversarial learning to help model unbiased user interests. Thus, our model yields larger performance gains when the test data is unbiased.

citations.title: Personalized News Recommendation: Methods and Challenges
snippets: User behavior data usually encodes various kinds of biases. Some kinds of biases are related to news. For example, click behaviors are influenced by the positions and sizes of news displayed on the webpages (i.e., presentation bias) [230]. In addition, popular news may have higher chances to be clicked than unpopular news (i.e., popularity bias) [157]. These types of bias information may affect the accuracy of user interest modeling and model training. A few works explore to eliminate the influence of certain kinds of bias information to improve personalized news recommendation. For instance, DebiasRec [230] aims to reduce the influence of position and size biases on news recommendation. It uses a bias-aware user modeling method to learn debiased user interest representations, and uses a bias-aware click prediction method that decomposes the overall click score into a bias score and a bias-independent user preference score. PP-Rec [157] uses a popularity-aware user modeling method to learn calibrated user interest representations, and it separately models the popularity of news and users' personal preference on news, which can help better model personalized user interest. These methods mainly aim to infer debiased user interest from biased user data. However, without any prior knowledge about unbiased data distribution, the bias information usually cannot be fully eliminated. In addition, many kinds of bias such as exposure and selection biases are rarely studied in the news recommendation field. Thus, it is important for future research to understand how different biases affect user behaviors and the recommendation model as well as how to eliminate their effect in model training and evaluation.

sections.title: # Learning to Rank Algorithms for Unbiased Ranking
sections.text:
Several LTR algorithms incorporate debiasing principles, from pairwise and listwise objectives to counterfactual and fairness-aware losses. Unbiased LambdaMART modifies gradient boosting decision tree ranking to jointly estimate ranker and debiasing components, and demonstrates competitive performance against state-of-the-art unbiased methods [c6bba5ea-4] CTR models with position-normalized signals and position-bias decoupling have been shown to reduce position bias in predictions [0de572e4-1]. Recent works also propose mutual-information minimization and model-based control to learn unbiased relevance. InfoRank formulates unbiased LTR via conditional mutual information minimization, explicitly targeting position and popularity biases [0de572e4-0] Model-based Unbiased LTR shows robustness to misspecified propensities and emphasizes variance reduction in IPW-based methods [0de572ea4-2].

Exposure-aware objectives can be integrated into bandit-style or gradient-based LTR with carefully designed reward weighting. Exposure-aware reward models weight observed clicks more strongly at lower ranks and penalize high-rank unclicks more heavily, aligning with exposure drop-off and RBP functions and improving cascading bandit ranking under exposure bias [6417bea0-0].

This bias in prediction can then affect subsequent training data collection, leading to a persistent and cyclical effect. 

The accumulative position bias of the training data will skew the MLR model, leading to increasingly unfair item rank prediction [6]. To address this position bias problem, various approaches have been proposed, including factorization models [4], inverse propensity scores [9,15,19], deep neural network-based CTR prediction models [8,17,21], and more. Pioneering approaches such as [4] proposed a factorization model that decouples CTR into positionnormalized CTR and position bias, which are then estimated by an Expectation-Maximization (EM) algorithm framework. To remove the position bias for learning to rank models, a propensity-weighted empirical risk minimization framework is proposed in [15]. In [10], an unbiased LambdaMART model is proposed, which jointly estimates the biases at click positions and unclick positions and learns an unbiased ranker. Several literatures dedicate to the propensity estimation, such as [1,2,18]. Recently, increasing research studies correcting position bias in the deep-ranking models. In [12], the authors propose to combine recurrent neural network and survival analysis techniques to model unbiased user behaviors.

sections.title: # Getting Unbiased Click Data and Fair Evaluation
sections.text: Unbiased data is essential for training and evaluation. In practice, unbiased or debiased test sets can be obtained via controlled surveys or randomized serving, while for training, propensity estimation or exposure modeling can create synthetic unbiased samples. uCTRL evaluates on synthetic debiased test data (uniform sampling across items) and true debiased test data (Yahoo! R3 via survey), and compares against methods that explicitly mitigate popularity bias [c6bba5ea-0]. Fair evaluation increasingly combines utility metrics with exposure fairness objectives. TREC Fair Ranking tracks combine nDCG with AWRF, requiring runs to be both accurate and fair by controlling group-wise exposure [6417bea0-2].

sections.title: # Practical Recommendations
sections.text:
- Diagnose bias first: Build exposure and position histograms from logs; compute group-wise exposure and diversity; and quantify feedback loop effects. Use exposure-aware metrics during evaluation and early-stage model selection. AWRF-based evaluation jointly measures exposure fairness and utility, guiding trade-off management [6417bea0-2] Exposure-aware reward shaping helps quantify how clicks decay with position and how unclicked items at the top indicate bias [6417bea0-0].

- Choose a debiasing strategy by constraints:
 - If you can run small-scale interventions or rerandomizations: use propensity estimation (IPS/WOPE) and control-function methods to reweight clicks; combine with variance reduction and robust rankers. Propensity-based IPW and randomized rerandomization provide ground-truth propensities but must balance user-experience costs [c6bba5ea-2] Robust model-based approaches and variance reduction improve performance under misspecification and sparse interventions [0de572e4-2].
 - If interventions are limited and context varies: use heterogeneous treatment effect estimation or exposure-modeling to estimate propensities with lower variance. Heterogeneous treatment effect estimation effectively debiases with limited intervention traffic [c6bba5ea-3].
 - If serving controls are possible: implement exposure-aware ranking or candidate generation that models P(exposed | item, context) to mitigate popularity bias and increase diversity online. Exposure modeling at inference increased unique item retrieval and reduced over-recommendation while maintaining engagement [6417bea0-3] Inference-time exposure-aware scoring decouples engagement from exposure bias and improves niche content discovery [6417bea0-4].

- Prefer unbiased or debiased training data where possible: combine unbiased logs (from randomized serving or surveys), synthetic unbiased samples (propensity-weighted or exposure-controlled), and bias-aware labeling. Synthetic unbiased test construction via uniform sampling and survey-based unbiased test sets enable fair comparisons across debiasing methods [c6bba5ea-0] Raw click-only training serves as a lower bound and human-labeled data as an upper bound for unbiased ranker evaluation [c6bba5ea-4].

- Use unbiased LTR algorithms: adopt counterfactual or model-based LTR (e.g., unbiased LambdaMART, InfoRank, model-based unbiased LTR) and integrate exposure-aware rewards; monitor performance under long-tail queries and popularity skew. Unbiased LTR objectives explicitly target position and popularity biases [0de572e4-0] Unbiased LambdaMART jointly estimates bias and relevance and is competitive with state-of-the-art unbiased methods [c6bba5ea-4] Exposure-aware rewards improve learning under cascading click models with position bias [6417bea0-0].

- Evaluate and iterate with fairness: combine traditional utility metrics (nDCG, ERR) with exposure fairness metrics (AWRF or group-wise exposure targets) and A/B tests that measure engagement and diversity outcomes. AWRF combined with nDCG yields a composite metric where both accuracy and exposure fairness are required to score well [6417bea0-2] Online A/B tests validating exposure-aware retrieval demonstrate improved diversity and reduced over-recommendation [6417bea0-3].

citations.title: Counterfactual Learning to Rank using Heterogeneous Treatment Effect Estimation
snippets: Learning-to-Rank (LTR) models trained from implicit feedback (e.g. clicks) suffer from inherent biases. A well-known one is the position bias -- documents in top positions are more likely to receive clicks due in part to their position advantages. To unbiasedly learn to rank, existing counterfactual frameworks first estimate the propensity (probability) of missing clicks with intervention data from a small portion of search traffic, and then use inverse propensity score (IPS) to debias LTR algorithms on the whole data set. These approaches often assume the propensity only depends on the position of the document, which may cause high estimation variance in applications where the search context (e.g. query, user) varies frequently. While context-dependent propensity models reduce variance, accurate estimations may require randomization or intervention on a large amount of traffic, which may not be realistic in real-world systems, especially for long tail queries. In this work, we employ heterogeneous treatment effect estimation techniques to estimate position bias when intervention click data is limited. We then use such estimations to debias the observed click distribution and re-draw a new de-biased data set, which can be used for any LTR algorithms. We conduct simulations with varying experiment conditions and show the effectiveness of the proposed method in regimes with long tail queries and sparse clicks.

citations.title: Correcting for Position Bias in Learning to Rank: A Control Function Approach
snippets:
Learning-to-rank (LTR) systems have become a core component in many online applications, from search engines to recommender systems. These systems typically use implicit feedback data, such as user clicks, as a proxy for user preferences due to its ease of collection compared to costly manual human annotations. While valuable, implicit feedback data is prone to biases [2,61], with position bias being particularly pervasive. Position bias is the tendency of users to interact more with higher-ranked documents, regardless of their true relevance [13,27]. This skews click data, causing LTR models to overestimate higher-ranked documents and underestimate lower ones. Training on such biased data degrades ranking performance and reinforces a feedback loop that negatively affects user experience. This is a preprint version. 

State-of-the-art methods that address position bias can be broadly categorized as click models, propensity-based approaches, and econometrics-based models. Click models [9,13,16,54] estimate true relevance of documents by hypothesizing how users browse and maximizing the likelihood of observed clicks. Click models rely on assumptions about complex user click behavior, which sometimes may not hold in practice. Two-tower models [20,59], following the position-based click model (PBM) [47], attempt to disentangle relevance and bias from clicks by modeling them separately, but may fail when confounding exists between the two. Propensity-based methods treat clicks as counterfactual events and re-weight them using inverse propensity weighting (IPW) to achieve relevance-equivalent training loss [28,55]. Propensity estimation often relies on result randomization [28,41,55], which can harm user experience [2,56]. Some methods [2,24,35,52,63] jointly learn propensities and rankers, but coupling the two raises concerns about the unbiasedness if either model is misspecified [1,18,51].

citations.title: Finding Interest Needle in Popularity Haystack: Improving Retrieval by Modeling Item Exposure
snippets:
We introduced an exposure-aware retrieval approach that models item exposure probability, mitigating popularity bias at inference time while preserving engagement. Unlike prior ranking-stage or training-time corrections, our method enables real-time control over exposure effects, balancing fairness and engagement. 

Large-scale online A/B tests in a production video recommendation system showed a 25% increase in unique item retrieval and a 40% reduction in over-recommended content, all while maintaining engagement. This demonstrates its effectiveness in enhancing niche content retrieval in large-scale industry-grade recommendation systems using GPU-accelerated inference.

citations.title: Model-based Unbiased Learning to Rank
snippets:
To answer RQ1, we compare MULTR with other unbiased learningto-rank algorithms in the simulation experiments. Table 1 summarizes the performance of different unbiased learning to rank algorithms under various click situations. We find that: 

• Our model-based unbiased learning to rank achieves the best performance among all the state-of-the-art methods in terms of nDCG and ERR, which indicates our model is robust when propensity cannot be accurately estimated. • Reducing variance can enhance performance on unbiased learning to rank. As MULTR shares the same method with DLA in estimating propensity, the improvements over DLA demonstrate the necessity of handling variance in IPW-based methods. • The naive method may achieve better performance than some unbiased learning to rank methods when clicks are generated by a cascade model. One explanation is that documents displayed at a lower rank have a higher opportunity to be examined; thus they receive more clicks, which alleviates the bias in click data. This observation confirms that a mismatch between propensity estimation and real bias could lead to performance even worse than raw click data. • The oracle model with human annotation consistently achieves the best performance. It implies that there is still room to improve in unbiased learning to rank methods.

citations.title: Finding Interest Needle in Popularity Haystack: Improving Retrieval by Modeling Item Exposure
snippets:
Prior approaches like Inverse Propensity Scoring (IPS) address popularity bias at the ranking stage [2,3,4,5] but fail in retrieval due to severe data sparsity [4,6]. While exposure modeling [5] and Off Policy Correction [7] have been explored in retrieval, they primarily focus on legacy collaborative filtering models and are limited to correcting bias during training. Other retrieval-stage solutions, such as negative sampling adjustments [3,11,12], still reinforce exposure bias by treating unseen items as irrelevant, skewing recommendations toward already-popular content. 

Our work explicitly models item exposure at the retrieval stage, a first in class industrial-scale retrieval model built on top of latest model architecture and GPU accelerators [8]. Instead of passively correcting for exposure in training, we introduce an exposure-aware retrieval score that adjusts item ranking at inference, providing real-time control over popularity bias vs. engagement trade-offs. By reframing candidate selection as P(positive label | item, exposed) rather than P(positive label & exposed | item), our approach decouples engagement likelihood from exposure bias, enabling fairer recommendations while maintaining engagement. A/B tests confirm a 25% increase in uniquely retrieved items and a 40% reduction in overrecommended popular items, making this a deployable, scalable solution for real-world recommender systems.

sections.title: # Limitations and Open Challenges
sections.text: Assumptions about exposure/click models can be wrong, and propensity misspecification or sparse interventions can inflate variance. A mismatch between propensity estimation and real bias can yield worse performance than using raw biased data, underscoring the need for robustness [0de572e4-2]. Some biases (e.g., presentation and exposure in complex UIs) are hard to fully eliminate without prior knowledge of unbiased exposure distributions. Without prior knowledge of unbiased exposure, biases like exposure and selection remain difficult to fully remove, and many bias types are under-studied [0de572e4-3]. Continued work on exposure modeling, heterogeneous treatment effects with limited interventions, and fairness-aware optimization under real-world constraints remains active. Debiasing with limited intervention data and long-tail sparsity remains challenging, motivating advanced treatment effect estimation [c6bba5ea-3].

citations.title: Personalized News Recommendation: Methods and Challenges
snippets: User behavior data usually encodes various kinds of biases. Some kinds of biases are related to news. For example, click behaviors are influenced by the positions and sizes of news displayed on the webpages (i.e., presentation bias) [230]. In addition, popular news may have higher chances to be clicked than unpopular news (i.e., popularity bias) [157]. These types of bias information may affect the accuracy of user interest modeling and model training. A few works explore to eliminate the influence of certain kinds of bias information to improve personalized news recommendation. For instance, DebiasRec [230] aims to reduce the influence of position and size biases on news recommendation. It uses a bias-aware user modeling method to learn debiased user interest representations, and uses a bias-aware click prediction method that decomposes the overall click score into a bias score and a bias-independent user preference score. PP-Rec [157] uses a popularity-aware user modeling method to learn calibrated user interest representations, and it separately models the popularity of news and users' personal preference on news, which can help better model personalized user interest. These methods mainly aim to infer debiased user interest from biased user data. However, without any prior knowledge about unbiased data distribution, the bias information usually cannot be fully eliminated. In addition, many kinds of bias such as exposure and selection biases are rarely studied in the news recommendation field. Thus, it is important for future research to understand how different biases affect user behaviors and the recommendation model as well as how to eliminate their effect in model training and evaluation.

sections.title: # Summary
sections.text:
- Position and popularity biases in click data fundamentally confound relevance estimation; unbiased LTR reframes objectives to counterfactual causal effects and disentangles exposure from relevance. Unbiased LTR changes the target from P(y=1|x,d) to P(y=1|do(x)=1,d) to remove position and popularity confounds [0de572e4-0].
- Effective debiasing mixes three ingredients: propensity estimation with variance control, econometrics/control functions for identifiability, and direct exposure modeling; the choice depends on intervention availability, model complexity, and user-experience trade-offs. Click models, propensity/IPW, and econometrics-based approaches each offer different trade-offs for correcting position bias [c6bba5ea-2] Model-based and variance-reduction techniques improve robustness [0de572e4-2].
- Popularity bias is best addressed with exposure-aware ranking at both training and inference, and with fairness metrics that control group-wise exposure while preserving utility. Inference-time exposure modeling improves diversity and reduces over-recommendation [6417bea0-3] AWRF combines exposure fairness with nDCG for joint evaluation [6417bea0-2].
- Practical pipelines should diagnose bias via exposure/position analysis, construct unbiased or debiased datasets, adopt unbiased LTR algorithms with exposure-aware rewards, and evaluate with composite metrics and A/B tests. Synthetic and survey-based unbiased datasets enable rigorous comparisons of debiasing methods [c6bba5ea-0] Unbiased LambdaMART and dual-learning demonstrate feasible algorithmic paths [c6bba5ea-4].

This skews click data, causing LTR models to overestimate higher-ranked documents and underestimate lower ones. Training on such biased data degrades ranking performance and reinforces a feedback loop that negatively affects user experience. This is a preprint version. 

State-of-the-art methods that address position bias can be broadly categorized as click models, propensity-based approaches, and econometrics-based models. Click models [9,13,16,54] estimate true relevance of documents by hypothesizing how users browse and maximizing the likelihood of observed clicks. Click models rely on assumptions about complex user click behavior, which sometimes may not hold in practice. Two-tower models [20,59], following the position-based click model (PBM) [47], attempt to disentangle relevance and bias from clicks by modeling them separately, but may fail when confounding exists between the two. Propensity-based methods treat clicks as counterfactual events and re-weight them using inverse propensity weighting (IPW) to achieve relevance-equivalent training loss [28,55]. Propensity estimation often relies on result randomization [28,41,55], which can harm user experience [2,56]. Some methods [2,24,35,52,63] jointly learn propensities and rankers, but coupling the two raises concerns about the unbiasedness if either model is misspecified [1,18,51].

sections.title: # Overview: How model size influences sentiment analysis
sections.text: Across widely used transformer models, increasing parameter scale and stronger pretraining/fine-tuning generally improve sentiment classification, though gains saturate and come with efficiency and overfitting trade-offs that depend on domain and data volume. Comparative evaluations on sentiment/emotion tasks show that RoBERTa and DeBERTa outperform BERT, with DeBERTa’s disentangled attention improving representation quality and helping on complex, multi-class sentiment problems. <cite id="04751abf-2">When data is limited, scaling up model size can still help, but pushing to very deep variants can plateau or even hurt performance, indicating limits to naive scaling [04751abf-0]. In domain-specific sentiment (e.g., hate/sentiment mixtures), larger base models (RoBERTa, DeBERTa, ELECTRA) substantially outperform smaller ones like DistilBERT, and domain adaptation further narrows but does not erase the advantage of larger architectures [04751abf-3].

sections.title: # Standard sentiment datasets (IMDB, SST, TweetEval/Social media)
sections.text: Larger-scale pretraining and stronger architectures yield consistent gains on standard sentiment benchmarks. On IMDB and SST-2, robust RoBERTa variants trained on large corpora and evaluated under noise settings achieve higher F1 than BERT baselines, illustrating the benefit of scale and robust pretraining for sentiment [33422564-2]. Twitter-RoBERTa (trained on ~58M tweets and fine-tuned on TweetEval) substantially outperforms SVM/FastText baselines (~72% vs ~63% accuracy), and an expanded-corpus variant with 123.86M tweets improved accuracy to 73.7%, directly linking larger pretraining data and model scale to better performance on short, noisy social media text [33422564-3]. Transformer-ensemble hybrid approaches that fuse multiple large models (BERT, GPT-2, RoBERTa, XLNet, DistilBERT) achieve state-of-the-art accuracy on IMDB (95.00%) and Sentiment140 (94.00%), surpassing RoBERTa-GRU and other baselines, indicating that combining larger models can further boost sentiment classification, especially on noisy social media [33422564-4]. Within the same family, optimized RoBERTa/DeBERTa variants tend to outperform BERT on sentiment/regression tasks, and model choice interacts with data size and task complexity [04751abf-0].

sections.title: # Finance-specific sentiment: model size, domain pretraining, and LLMs
sections.text: In finance, larger or domain-specialized models show clear gains over lexicons and smaller baselines. FinBERT, tailored to financial texts, achieves strong accuracy on finance sentiment tasks (reported ~94% on finance-related classification), and a controlled fine-tuning of a base RoBERTa on financial phrase datasets yields comparable results while offering greater experimental transparency [01d314b4-2]. RoBERTa-Large (24 layers, 1024 hidden units, 16 heads; ~355M parameters) fine-tuned on financial datasets such as Financial PhraseBank and SemEval-2017 Task 5 demonstrates strong specialization for financial sentiment [01d314b4-2]. Despite having fewer total parameters than RoBERTa (~417.8MB vs 1.32GB), FinBERT delivers competitive execution speed on GPU and outperforms lexicon-based baselines, highlighting that domain-tuned large models can be both efficient and accurate for finance sentiment [01d314b4-0]. On a large Refinitiv news corpus, modern LLMs (OPT, BERT, FinBERT, RoBERTa, LLaMA-3) consistently outperform the Loughran–McDonald lexicon for sentiment-driven stock-return prediction, with OPT and RoBERTa showing particularly strong F1 and directional accuracy, underscoring the value of scaled language models for complex financial news [01d314b4-3]. A practical multi-LLM integration (FinSentLLM) combines FinBERT (domain precision) with Twitter-RoBERTa-sentiment (broad linguistic coverage) and stacks expert signals and structured financial semantics without additional fine-tuning, improving robustness and efficiency for financial sentiment forecasting [01d314b4-1]. Comparative finance surveys emphasize that BERT-based models (RoBERTa, FinBERT) are optimized for structured financial sentiment classification, while GPT-based LLMs (GPT-4, OPT, LLaMA) excel at real-time interpretation and generation, suggesting complementary roles across model size and architecture [01d314b4-4].

Similarly to RoBERTa, the FinBERT model also underwent testing on a GPU, resulting in a nearly 12-fold improvement in execution speed compared to running it on a CPU. As expected, the XLex-based model outperforms the FinBERT model in terms of speed. 

The second important aspect of the lexicon-based model is the size. The model size is an important factor to consider when deciding which model to be used in production  17. The difference in size is considerable. As can be seen, the lexicon-based model is about three orders of magnitude smaller than the RoBERTa transformer model. The XLex-based model exhibits an identical size for each specific source dataset, with the XLex-based model registering sizes of 363KB, 202KB, and 233KB for the nasdaq, f inancial_phrase_bank (f pb), and f iqa_f pb_sentf in_neutral source datasets, respectively. Additionally, the RoBERTa-based model maintains a size of 1.32GB, regardless of the evaluation dataset used. The size of the FinBERT model is 417.8MB. Although there are approaches to make transformer-based models smaller [74], transformers are not suitable for certain use cases, such as environments with limited computational resources or embedded devices. On the other hand, Table 17 shows that lexicon-based models have a size that is suitable for such applications. 

Another important advantage of lexicon-based approaches is their interpretability. Lexicon-based sentiment models are generally more interpretable than transformer-based sentiment models because they rely on a pre-defined set of rules that are easy to understand and interpret. In a lexicon-based sentiment model, each word is assigned a sentiment score based on its associated sentiment value in the sentiment dictionary, and the overall sentiment of the text is calculated based on the sum or average of the sentiment scores of the words in the text. This makes it easy to understand why a particular text was classified as positive, negative, or neutral, as the sentiment scores assigned to each word in the text are transparent and interpretable.

In parallel, we inject structured financial semantics derived from text patterns (e.g., profit This design leverages diverse strengths while mitigating weaknesses: FinBERT offers domain precision but may inherit financespecific biases; RoBERTa-sentiment brings broader linguistic coverage. We used 20% of these articles as a test set. We measured the accuracy of each model in predicting the direction of stock returns based on news sentiment. This accuracy indicates how well the model links the sentiment in financial news with stock returns over a three-day period. We evaluated six models: OPT, BERT, FinBERT, LLAMA 3, RoBERTa and the Loughran-McDonald dictionary. Their performance in sentiment analysis is shown in FinBERT. The Loughran-McDonald dictionary, a traditional finance text analysis tool, had significantly lower accuracy. This indicates that language models like OPT, BERT, FinBert, LLAMA 3 and RoBERTa are better at understanding and analysing complex financial news. The precision and recall values further support the superiority of the OPT model; its F1 score, which combines precision and recall, also confirms its effectiveness in sentiment analysis. To develop an explainable lexicon, we begin by using a transformer-based model tailored for sentiment analysis. Specifically, FinBERT is a notable model in this domain, designed explicitly for analyzing financial texts [68]. However, FinBERT is fine-tuned on a closed dataset comprising 10,000 sentences from analyst reports sourced from Thompson Reuters's proprietary Investext database. To ensure a controlled environment over the fine-tuning process, we take charge of it by using a publicly available financial sentiment dataset and one of the available base transformer models, specifically RoBERTa. According to a survey [37], the RoBERTa model demonstrates exceptional performance in various finance-related sentiment classification tasks, achieving an accuracy of 94%. Therefore, we decided to use RoBERTa as our starting model. 

To provide a comprehensive analysis, we also included results obtained using the FinBERT model. While both models produce comparable results (as shown in Table 14), the key advantage of using the fine-tuned RoBERTa model lies in the customized approach and rigorous control we have over the data and fine-tuning process, thereby boosting our flexibility to perform experiments. 

The datasets utilized for learning the explainable dictionaries are presented in Table 12, where they are labeled as "Source" datasets. The results of the XLex model are then evaluated using the datasets labeled as "Evaluation". 

To construct the sentiment dictionaries, we use SHAP to interpret the output of the pre-trained transformer model. This approach aids us in identifying individual words and classifying them as either positive or negative in sentiment. This approach is discussed in detail in Subsection III-B. 

The RoBERTa-Large model is originally trained in a self-supervised manner on an extensive corpus of English text 4 . The RoBERTa-Large model comprises 24 layers, 1024 hidden units, 16 attention heads and is based on a total of 355 million parameters. Subsequently, we fine-tune the foundational RoBERTa model using the approach outlined in [37]. citations.title: Large language models in finance : what is financial sentiment?
snippets: Financial sentiment has become a crucial yet complex concept in finance, increasingly used in market forecasting and investment strategies. Despite its growing importance, there remains a need to define and understand what financial sentiment truly represents and how it can be effectively measured. We explore the nature of financial sentiment and investigate how large language models (LLMs) contribute to its estimation. We trace the evolution of sentiment measurement in finance, from market-based and lexicon-based methods to advanced natural language processing techniques. The emergence of LLMs has significantly enhanced sentiment analysis, providing deeper contextual understanding and greater accuracy in extracting sentiment from financial text. We examine how BERT-based models, such as RoBERTa and FinBERT, are optimized for structured sentiment classification, while GPT-based models, including GPT-4, OPT, and LLaMA, excel in financial text generation and real-time sentiment interpretation. A comparative analysis of bidirectional and autoregressive transformer architectures highlights their respective roles in investor sentiment analysis, algorithmic trading, and financial decision-making. By exploring what financial sentiment is and how it is estimated within LLMs, we provide insights into the growing role of AI-driven sentiment analysis in finance.

sections.title: # Architecture choices and scaling patterns
sections.text: Replacing BERT with RoBERTa and further enhancing with DeBERTa typically improves sentiment performance by strengthening masking strategies and position/context modeling. Across sentiment/emotion tasks, RoBERTa and DeBERTa outperform BERT, with DeBERTa’s disentangled attention capturing absolute and relative positions to improve fine-grained understanding [04751abf-0]. On a broad suite of NLP tasks, a DeBERTa trained on half the RoBERTa data outperforms RoBERTa-Large, achieving improvements such as +0.9% on MNLI and +2.3% on SQuAD v2.0, illustrating that targeted architectural enhancements and efficient pretraining can yield better quality per parameter [12a89f23-4]. RoBERTa-Large’s scale (24×1024×16; ~355M) is a common high-water mark for finance sentiment, and its fine-tuned variants consistently lead over smaller BERT-family models [01d314b4-2]. However, scaling does not always help without adequate data: in BabyLM experiments, switching from RoBERTa to DeBERTa accounted for performance differences, but moving to “large” improved behavioral benchmarks, yet further scaling to 48-layer DeBERTa-XL did not improve BLiMP tasks and was about 2% worse than the large model, indicating diminishing returns and possible overparameterization risks when data is scarce [04751abf-2].

citations.title: Sentiment Analysis in Finance: From Transformers Back to eXplainable Lexicons (XLex)
snippets:
To develop an explainable lexicon, we begin by using a transformer-based model tailored for sentiment analysis. Specifically, FinBERT is a notable model in this domain, designed explicitly for analyzing financial texts [68]. However, FinBERT is fine-tuned on a closed dataset comprising 10,000 sentences from analyst reports sourced from Thompson Reuters's proprietary Investext database. To ensure a controlled environment over the fine-tuning process, we take charge of it by using a publicly available financial sentiment dataset and one of the available base transformer models, specifically RoBERTa. According to a survey [37], the RoBERTa model demonstrates exceptional performance in various finance-related sentiment classification tasks, achieving an accuracy of 94%. Therefore, we decided to use RoBERTa as our starting model. 

To provide a comprehensive analysis, we also included results obtained using the FinBERT model. While both models produce comparable results (as shown in Table 14), the key advantage of using the fine-tuned RoBERTa model lies in the customized approach and rigorous control we have over the data and fine-tuning process, thereby boosting our flexibility to perform experiments. 

The datasets utilized for learning the explainable dictionaries are presented in Table 12, where they are labeled as "Source" datasets. The results of the XLex model are then evaluated using the datasets labeled as "Evaluation". 

To construct the sentiment dictionaries, we use SHAP to interpret the output of the pre-trained transformer model. This approach aids us in identifying individual words and classifying them as either positive or negative in sentiment. This approach is discussed in detail in Subsection III-B. 

The RoBERTa-Large model is originally trained in a self-supervised manner on an extensive corpus of English text 4 . The RoBERTa-Large model comprises 24 layers, 1024 hidden units, 16 attention heads and is based on a total of 355 million parameters. Subsequently, we fine-tune the foundational RoBERTa model using the approach outlined in [37]. The fine-tuning is conducted on a merged dataset comprising the Financial PhraseBank [69] and SemEval-2017-Task5 datasets [70]. This fine-tuning procedure ensures that the resulting model is specialized for the domain of financial sentiment analysis.

sections.title: # Data scale and pretraining: social media vs. finance
sections.text: Larger pretraining corpora and targeted fine-tuning substantially impact sentiment performance, especially on short, noisy text. Twitter-RoBERTa trained on ~58M tweets and then fine-tuned on TweetEval improves over earlier baselines by ~5 percentage points, and scaling the pretraining corpus to ~124M tweets further boosts accuracy to 73.7%, demonstrating the direct influence of data scale on sentiment accuracy [33422564-3]. In finance, combining domain-specific LLMs (FinBERT) with broad social-media–trained RoBERTa-sentiment provides complementary strengths—domain precision and linguistic breadth—enabling better aggregation than single-model pipelines without additional training [01d314b4-1]. For finance, RoBERTa-Large fine-tuned on financial phrase and review datasets provides high specialization, while FinBERT’s closed-domain pretraining yields strong accuracy and practical efficiency [01d314b4-2].

sections.title: # Multilingual and specialized encoders
sections.text: Scaling and specialization extend to multilingual settings and task-specific encoders. Aspect-based sentiment analysis models such as DeBERTa-v3-base-ABSA and FLAN-T5-large-ABSA leverage larger, task-specific variants trained on thousands to tens of thousands of annotated ABSA examples across multiple datasets (SemEval, MAMS, Television, TShirt), showing that larger, task-adapted encoders improve aspect-level sentiment extraction [04751abf-4]. sections.title: # Efficiency, overfitting, and limits to scaling
sections.text: Larger models improve accuracy but increase memory, latency, and potential overfitting risks, especially with limited labeled data. BabyLM experiments show that when pretraining data is limited, scaling up architecture size can still help, but further increasing layers (e.g., DeBERTa-XL with 48 layers) did not improve behavioral performance and was slightly worse than the large model, indicating a practical ceiling to naive scaling and possible overparameterization [04751abf-2]. In practice, RoBERTa is often preferred over BERT for peak accuracy when computational resources allow, reflecting the trade-off between model size and performance [12a89f23-0]. In finance, FinBERT can be smaller than RoBERTa (~417.8MB vs 1.32GB) while delivering competitive speed and accuracy, offering an efficiency-conscious alternative when production constraints matter [01d314b4-0].

4) DeBERTa: Decoding-enhanced BERT with Disentangled Attention, DeBERTa takes the transformer's self-attention mechanism a step further by separating (disentangling) the representations of content and position [9]. snippets:
Table 17 shows that the FinBERT model leads to better execution speeds than the RoBERTa model. However, the FinBERT model exhibits a smaller size compared to RoBERTa. Similarly to RoBERTa, the FinBERT model also underwent testing on a GPU, resulting in a nearly 12-fold improvement in execution speed compared to running it on a CPU. As expected, the XLex-based model outperforms the FinBERT model in terms of speed. 

The second important aspect of the lexicon-based model is the size. The model size is an important factor to consider when deciding which model to be used in production  17. The difference in size is considerable. As can be seen, the lexicon-based model is about three orders of magnitude smaller than the RoBERTa transformer model. The XLex-based model exhibits an identical size for each specific source dataset, with the XLex-based model registering sizes of 363KB, 202KB, and 233KB for the nasdaq, f inancial_phrase_bank (f pb), and f iqa_f pb_sentf in_neutral source datasets, respectively. Additionally, the RoBERTa-based model maintains a size of 1.32GB, regardless of the evaluation dataset used. The size of the FinBERT model is 417.8MB. Although there are approaches to make transformer-based models smaller [74], transformers are not suitable for certain use cases, such as environments with limited computational resources or embedded devices. On the other hand, Table 17 shows that lexicon-based models have a size that is suitable for such applications. 

Another important advantage of lexicon-based approaches is their interpretability. Lexicon-based sentiment models are generally more interpretable than transformer-based sentiment models because they rely on a pre-defined set of rules that are easy to understand and interpret. In a lexicon-based sentiment model, each word is assigned a sentiment score based on its associated sentiment value in the sentiment dictionary, and the overall sentiment of the text is calculated based on the sum or average of the sentiment scores of the words in the text. This makes it easy to understand why a particular text was classified as positive, negative, or neutral, as the sentiment scores assigned to each word in the text are transparent and interpretable.

sections.title: # Practical implications
sections.text:
- Choose larger, stronger encoders for complex or noisy sentiment tasks (e.g., social media, finance), and pair with domain-specific fine-tuning when possible. RoBERTa/DeBERTa consistently outperform BERT on sentiment/regression tasks [04751abf-0] Scaling pretraining data (e.g., Twitter-scale) materially improves social-media sentiment accuracy [33422564-3] Modern LLMs outperform lexicons for financial news sentiment tied to market signals [01d314b4-3]. 
- Balance size with data and compute: avoid overparameterization without adequate pretraining/fine-tuning; consider efficient variants or ensembles when resources are constrained. Scaling can plateau or hurt with excessive depth and limited data [04751abf-2] FinBERT shows that smaller, domain-tuned models can be efficient and effective [01d314b4-0] Hybrid ensembles of large transformers can boost accuracy without additional training [33422564-4].
- In finance, combine domain-specific (FinBERT) and broad-linguistic (Twitter-RoBERTa-sentiment) experts with structured signals to enhance robustness and interpretability for forecasting tasks. FinSentLLM integrates FinBERT and Twitter-RoBERTa with structured financial semantics without retraining [01d314b4-1] This multi-model approach improves directional accuracy for stock-return prediction [01d314b4-3].

citations.title: TWSSenti: A Novel Hybrid Framework for Topic-Wise Sentiment Analysis on Social Media Using Transformer Models
snippets:
In this subsection, we demonstrate the effectiveness of our hybrid sentiment analysis framework by comparing it with existing state-of-the-art methods evaluated on the IMDB and Sentiment140 datasets. Table 4 presents a comparative analysis of various models based on their reported testing accuracies. 

Our proposed hybrid approach, which integrates BERT, GPT-2, RoBERTa, XLNet, and DistilBERT, achieves superior performance with an accuracy of 95.00% on IMDB and 94.00% on Sentiment140. This surpasses the best-performing alternative model, RoBERTa-GRU by [39], which achieves 94.63% on IMDB (+0.37% improvement) and 89.59% on Sentiment140 (+4.41% improvement). The significant increase in accuracy on Sentiment140 demonstrates the robustness of our model in handling noisy social media text. Similarly, [28] proposed a RoBERTa-BiLSTM model, which achieved 92.36% on IMDB (+2.64% improvement) and 82.25% on Sentiment140 (+11.75% improvement). While this model provides a competitive performance, its lower accuracy on Sentiment140 suggests limitations in generalizing across diverse textual sources. 

[8] experimented with multiple hybrid transformer models, including DistilBERT-BiLSTM, BERT-BiLSTM, and RoBERTa-CNN-BiLSTM, achieving maximum testing accuracies of 81.00%, 79.00%, and 77.00% on Sentiment140. Our model significantly outperforms these approaches, with an improvement of up to +17.00% over DistilBERT-BiLSTM, indicating that a deeper fusion of multiple transformers provides enhanced feature extraction and sentiment classification. [31] introduced a semi-supervised boosting framework (SSSA), obtaining 79.30% on IMDB and 80.30% on Sentiment140. While their approach benefits from semisupervised learning, its performance remains substantially lower than our hybrid method, with a +15.70% increase on IMDB and a +13.70% increase on Senti-ment140. This highlights the advantage of using fully supervised transformer ensembles for large-scale sentiment classification.

citations.title: Enhanced Financial Sentiment Analysis and Trading Strategy Development Using Large Language Models
snippets: In this study, we used LLMs to analyse sentiment in U.S. financial news. We processed a dataset of 965,375 articles from Refinitiv, spanning from January 1, 2010, to June 30, 2023. We used 20% of these articles as a test set. We measured the accuracy of each model in predicting the direction of stock returns based on news sentiment. This accuracy indicates how well the model links the sentiment in financial news with stock returns over a three-day period. We evaluated six models: OPT, BERT, FinBERT, LLAMA 3, RoBERTa and the Loughran-McDonald dictionary. Their performance in sentiment analysis is shown in FinBERT. The Loughran-McDonald dictionary, a traditional finance text analysis tool, had significantly lower accuracy. This indicates that language models like OPT, BERT, FinBert, LLAMA 3 and RoBERTa are better at understanding and analysing complex financial news. The precision and recall values further support the superiority of the OPT model; its F1 score, which combines precision and recall, also confirms its effectiveness in sentiment analysis. These findings confirm that language models, particularly OPT, are valuable tools for analysing financial news and predicting stock market trends.

citations.title: Enhanced Financial Sentiment Analysis and Trading Strategy Development Using Large Language Models
snippets: In this study, we used LLMs to analyse sentiment in U.S. financial news. We processed a dataset of 965,375 articles from Refinitiv, spanning from January 1, 2010, to June 30, 2023. We used 20% of these articles as a test set. We measured the accuracy of each model in predicting the direction of stock returns based on news sentiment. We evaluated six models: OPT, BERT, FinBERT, LLAMA 3, RoBERTa and the Loughran-McDonald dictionary. Their performance in sentiment analysis is shown in FinBERT. To develop an explainable lexicon, we begin by using a transformer-based model tailored for sentiment analysis. Specifically, FinBERT is a notable model in this domain, designed explicitly for analyzing financial texts [68]. However, FinBERT is fine-tuned on a closed dataset comprising 10,000 sentences from analyst reports sourced from Thompson Reuters's proprietary Investext database. To ensure a controlled environment over the fine-tuning process, we take charge of it by using a publicly available financial sentiment dataset and one of the available base transformer models, specifically RoBERTa. According to a survey [37], the RoBERTa model demonstrates exceptional performance in various finance-related sentiment classification tasks, achieving an accuracy of 94%. Therefore, we decided to use RoBERTa as our starting model. 

To provide a comprehensive analysis, we also included results obtained using the FinBERT model. While both models produce comparable results (as shown in Table 14), the key advantage of using the fine-tuned RoBERTa model lies in the customized approach and rigorous control we have over the data and fine-tuning process, thereby boosting our flexibility to perform experiments. 

The datasets utilized for learning the explainable dictionaries are presented in Table 12, where they are labeled as "Source" datasets. The results of the XLex model are then evaluated using the datasets labeled as "Evaluation".

(2022) further enhanced the model using an expanded training corpus of social media postings, consisting of 123.86 million tweets collected until the end of 2021, a notable increase from its predecessor's 58 million tweets. This update resulted in an improved performance of sentiment analysis, demonstrating an accuracy of 73.7% on the TweetEval dataset (Loureiro et al. 2022).

citations.title: Large language models in finance : what is financial sentiment?
snippets: Financial sentiment has become a crucial yet complex concept in finance, increasingly used in market forecasting and investment strategies. Despite its growing importance, there remains a need to define and understand what financial sentiment truly represents and how it can be effectively measured. We explore the nature of financial sentiment and investigate how large language models (LLMs) contribute to its estimation. We trace the evolution of sentiment measurement in finance, from market-based and lexicon-based methods to advanced natural language processing techniques. The emergence of LLMs has significantly enhanced sentiment analysis, providing deeper contextual understanding and greater accuracy in extracting sentiment from financial text. We examine how BERT-based models, such as RoBERTa and FinBERT, are optimized for structured sentiment classification, while GPT-based models, including GPT-4, OPT, and LLaMA, excel in financial text generation and real-time sentiment interpretation. A comparative analysis of bidirectional and autoregressive transformer architectures highlights their respective roles in investor sentiment analysis, algorithmic trading, and financial decision-making. By exploring what financial sentiment is and how it is estimated within LLMs, we provide insights into the growing role of AI-driven sentiment analysis in finance.

sections.text: Overall, empirical studies across general and domain-specific sentiment tasks show a strong positive trend: increasing model size and stronger pretraining/fine-tuning improve sentiment performance, with the largest gains on noisy or domain-specific data; however, benefits plateau and can be outweighed by overparameterization when data is limited, so practitioners should balance scale with data and compute and consider ensembles or efficient domain-tuned models for production use. sections.title: # Summary trend in Vision Transformer (ViT) image resolution
sections.text:
Early ViTs standardized on 224×224 input for image classification, often while pretraining on larger web datasets at higher resolutions (around 384). As models and datasets scaled, common input sizes moved to 512 and beyond for stronger ViT variants, and dense prediction systems adopted 1024-scale encoders based on ViT backbones. More recent methods explicitly target very high or variable resolutions with architectural and training innovations, enabling inputs up to around 896–1024 and even 1024×1333 in practice, with medical and satellite imaging pushing toward kilometric resolutions albeit with significant compute and diminishing returns at 2048+.

Concrete milestones and how they evolved:

- 224×224 as the default for ViT baselines and evaluations: Many ViT studies and derivatives use 224×224 for efficiency and compatibility, despite pretraining on larger datasets. A common setup is a ViT with 224×224 resolution and 16×16 patches for classification tasks [e65d04c9-1]. Auto-scaling ViT workbench also sets a default image size of 224×224 for evaluation while pretraining on massive corpora [e65d04c9-2]. ViT’s patch-tokenization and transfer from large-scale pretraining (e.g., JFT-300M) became the standard, with 224×224 often used for downstream tasks [e65d04c9-4].

- 384×384 as a common pretraining resolution for strong ViTs: Large-scale pretraining on web corpora frequently used 384 as the training resolution for ViT variants, while downstream evaluation often resizes to 224×224. A ViT-B distilled model on ImageNet-1k surpasses a ViT-B pretrained on JFT-300M at 384 resolution [d077ebc6-0]. Standard ViT learners in large-scale studies are often trained and evaluated at 224×224, reflecting common deployment practice [d077ebc6-1]. Practical ViT models like “vit-base-patch16-384” indicate 384 was used for pretraining while inference frequently operates at 224×224 [e65d04c9-0].

- 512×512 for stronger ViT(-H) and web-scale pretraining: As model capacity increased, higher input resolutions became feasible, especially with larger pretraining sets. A ViT-H model trained on JFT-300M at 512 resolution achieved state of the art (88.55%) on ImageNet, highlighting the benefit of higher-resolution inputs with larger models [d077ebc6-0].

- 1024-scale encoders for dense prediction and general high-res pipelines: For detection/segmentation and general high-resolution analysis, ViT-based encoders are paired with large inputs. The Segment Anything (SAM) image encoder uses a ViT-H/16 with window and global attention and accepts 1024×1024 inputs, producing 64×64 embeddings [27b9dd80-0]. An external pipeline explicitly uses a frozen SAM ViT encoder at 1024×1024 to extract embeddings and then processes multi-resolution outputs up to 1024×1024 in downstream modules [27b9dd80-3]. This 1024×1024 setting reflects a practical high-resolution sweet spot for ViT encoders in dense tasks [27b9dd80-0].

- Beyond 1024: Ultra-high resolutions and variable-size inputs. Method-focused works push the envelope. MSPE and FlexiViT/ResFormer demonstrate that a single ViT can adapt to resolutions up to 896×896 and beyond by enabling multi-resolution training and flexible patching/positional embeddings, addressing the performance drop when resizing [33a63b3d-4]. Medical imaging studies note that vanilla global attention ViTs become impractical above ~2048×1024 and that gains plateau from 1536×768 to 2048×1024, recommending inputs >1200×600 for high-resolution benefits [33a63b3d-1]. Local-global hybrid ViT designs explicitly target dense tasks that require high-resolution inputs and multi-scale features, since global attention is costly at high resolutions [33a63b3d-2].

snippets: ). This is necessary to achieve the 3 × 1024 × 1024 required input size for using the pretrained and frozen Segment Anything (SAM) [14] Vision Transformer (ViT) [8] encoder. This ViT encoder extracts a compact(256 × 64 × 64) visual embedding, an informationrich representation that ensures computational efficiency and is fundamental to the entire architecture. Real-time nearest interpolation running in the GPU is used to address training with 512 2 patches, or any input size different than 1024 2 , only for the ViT encoding step. Next, the ViT embedding is reshaped to 4 × 512 × 512. Note that this corresponds to a downsampling by a factor of two of the original input. A convolutional block combines this reshaped embedding with a downsampled version of the original 4 channel input. The output of the convolutional block is again combined with further downsampling of the input, resulting in a 8 × 256 × 256 representation that will be processed by MST++. The design intent is to ground the increasingly abstract and compressed features with residual multi-resolution versions of the original input. This compressed 8 channel representation is processed by a 6-stage MST++ [3] module, a state-of-the-art spectral upsampler with channel-wise self-attention [15] mechanisms. The MST++ module expands the input's spectral resolution to produce 61 channels. Our best model on ImageNet-1k is 85.2% top-1 accuracy outperforms the best Vit-B model pretrained on JFT-300M at resolution 384 (84.15%). citations.title: Auto-scaling Vision Transformers without Training
snippets: Settings. We benchmark our As-ViT on ImageNet-1k (Deng et al., 2009). We use Tensorflow and Keras for training implementations and conduct all training on TPUs. We set the default image size as 224 × 224, and use AdamW (Loshchilov & Hutter, 2017) as the optimizer with cosine learning rate decay (Loshchilov & Hutter, 2016). A batch size of 1024, an initial learning rate of 0.001, and a weight decay of 0.05 are adopted. 6 RELATED WORKS 6.1 VISION TRANSFORMER Transformers (Vaswani et al., 2017) leverage the self-attention to extract global correlation, and become the dominant models for natural language processing (NLP) (Devlin et al., 2018;Radford et al., 2018;Brown et al., 2020;Liu et al., 2019b). Recent works explored transformers to vision problems: image classification (Dosovitskiy et al., 2020), object detection (Carion et al., 2020;Zhu et al., 2020;Zheng et al., 2020;Dai et al., 2020;Sun et al., 2020), segmentation (Chen et al., 2020;Wang et al., 2020), etc. The Vision Transformer (ViT) (Dosovitskiy et al., 2020) designed a pure transformer architecture and achieved SOTA performance on image classification. However, ViT heavily relies on large-scale datasets (ImageNet-21k (Deng et al., 2009), JFT-300M (Sun et al., 2017)) for pretraining, requiring huge computation resources. DeiT (Touvron et al., 2020) proposed Knowledge Distillation (KD) (Hinton et al., 2015;Yuan et al., 2020) via a special KD token to improve both performance and training efficiency. In contrast, our proposed As-ViT introduces more flexible tokenization, attention splitting, and FFN expansion strategies, with automated discovery.

citations.title: Merging Feed-Forward Sublayers for Compressed Transformers
snippets:
We use a vision transformer (ViT) for our image classification experiments, with resolution of 224x224, and patch size of 16x16 (Dosovitskiy et al., 2020). ViT is a 12-layer Transformer encoder model pre-trained on ImageNet-21k, and subsequently fine-tuned on ImageNet-1k. ImageNet-1k is a classification task where images belong to one of 1000 categories (Russakovsky et al., 2015). For computing activations, we use ~10k patches from the ImageNet-1k validation set. Evaluation results are computed on original validation labels. 

We fine-tune our ViT models on ImageNet-1k for up to 50k steps with a batch size of 128, and report accuracy.

citations.title: Segment anything model (SAM) for brain extraction in fMRI studies
