citations.title: Beyond Single-Tokenomics: How Farcaster's Pluralistic Incentives Reshape Social Networking
snippets:
The emergence of Decentralized Online Social Networks (DOSNs) marks a shift in social networking, emphasizing user autonomy, data sovereignty, and censorship resistance [5,60]. Despite this, most DOSNs have struggled to incentivize high-quality content, large-scale user uptake, and sustained engagement [93,112]. Most notably, their emphasis on user sovereignty has limited the adoption of commonly used monetization models [14,68,94,112], often resulting in insufficient funding being available to compete with larger players. 

Consequently, some have attempted to integrate cryptocurrency-based token incentives to encourage participation by both content creators and infrastructure operators [23,65,101,119,120]. This, however, comes with key challenges, most notably the reliance on a single, platform-issued token incentive mechanism. For instance, Steemit [101], a token-based DOSN launched in 2016, utilizes its self-issued token for content interaction incentives. However, the failure of such a token renders the rewards worthless. Furthermore, research has revealed that Steemit's single designated token incentive mechanism is susceptible to token price fluctuations [8], and has suffered from gaming and farming (i.e. strategic interactions between colluding users designed to exploit reward systems), [66] and bot-driven adversarial manipulation [22]. This led to reward concentration among a small group of colluding users, increasing centralization and economic inequality while losing its effectiveness in promoting social engagement [52]. 

In response to this, a new DOSN called Farcaster was publicly launched in 2023 to support multiple incentive mechanisms [35]. Functionally similar to X (Twitter), Farcaster stands out from current DOSNs in two key aspects. First, Farcaster supports "modular" wallet binding -unlike platforms constrained by primary account-bound blockchain addresses [13,65,101,119], Farcaster enables users to link any external Ethereum-compatible addresses [77], functioning as on-chain transaction wallets, alongside their user accounts (termed Farcaster Identifiers (FIDs)) [33], providing greater economic flexibility and autonomy. Second, Farcaster is the first to implement a "pluralistic" token incentive ecosystem.

sections.text: Design perspectives emphasize that decentralized moderation and discovery layers (aggregators) can improve scalability and user experience while preserving pluralism, drawing on Steemit’s performance at a million-user scale under consensus to argue that comparable performance and carefully designed incentives can make decentralized social platforms competitive with Web2 incumbents Aggregators and caching can deliver performance comparable to centralized platforms, and Steemit demonstrates usability at ~1M users despite running a distributed consensus protocol [f668dd7d-4]. However, governance research underscores that theoretical social-contract ideals often lack empirical grounding in operational DAOs and governance protocols, highlighting the need for measured studies of amendment voting, proposal quality, and incentive alignment in live social networks Conceptual governance models frequently lack empirical analysis of how operational DAOs and governance protocols actually function [5ee6f025-4].

citations.title: Understanding Blockchain Governance: Analyzing Decentralized Voting to Amend DeFi Smart Contracts
snippets:
The literature on decentralized governance, social contracts, and decentralized autonomous organizations (DAOs) is extensive. 

Decentralized Governance and Social Contracts. Prior work has investigated how blockchain-based governance might serve as an alternative to traditional centralized systems. Atzori et al. examined the potential for blockchain to displace centralized societal institutions and authorities [4]. Reijers et al. analyzed the alignment between blockchain governance and classical theories of the social contract, drawing on the ideas of Hobbes [31], Rousseau [54], and Rawls [12]. Chen et al. explored trade-offs between decentralization and system performance [13]. Other comparative studies have examined governance models across public and private blockchains [3,77]. For instance, Arruñada and Garicano proposed new forms of "soft" decentralized governance [3], while Zwitter and Hazenberg offered a rethinking of governance structures tailored to DAOs [77]. While these works provide conceptual insights, they generally lack empirical analysis of how these theories play out in operational DAO systems or how real-world governance protocols function in practice.

citations.title: A Pluralist Approach to Democratizing Online Discourse
snippets:
By decoupling content and moderation, the state of online social media reverts to something akin to the early days of the Web, IRC, or bittorrent. The problems of content hosting, discovery, and aggregation, which originally motivated cloud providers, search engines, and torrent aggregators analogously necessitate a set of social media aggregators that cache, index, and present content and their associated moderation feeds to users through convenient user interfaces. 

Through caching and other standard optimization techniques, the performance of aggregators could be optimized to a point where the user experience is comparable to existing platforms in terms of performance and content. As an existence proof, Steemit [53] is a blockchain-based online social media network that is usable and performant. Although Steemit handles moderation differently from what we propose, its existence demonstrates that a P2P social media network can be performant and sufficiently usable at a reasonable scale (~1 million users), despite additionally running a distributed consensus protocol. 

Beyond performance, we posit that distributed storage infrastructures are not in mainstream use by the 'average' user because there is: a) no 'killer app'; and b) insufficient incentive. Centralized systems are attractive to users due to convenience, homogeneity, and cost [34], but given comparable performance, interacting with aggregators and client-end apps could become indistinguishable from existing platforms for average users. Additional interface elements, interactions, and incentive schemes afforded by pluralism can be experimented with in the same way that new features and platforms are introduced today.

sections.text:
Synthesis: Multilayer Security and Privacy-Aware Detection
Taken together, the literature indicates that decentralized social protocols succeed in reconfiguring identity, incentives, and governance but must contend with multilayer privacy risks and incentive gaming that can distort content and financial flows. Cross-chain and cross-platform integrations produce rich, multi-signal graphs that enable both new applications and new attack surfaces, demanding detection systems that combine temporal, textual, and transactional features. DNN/GNN methods—particularly multirelational GNNs, subgraph learning, and active learning—show promising performance on public datasets like Elliptic and offer scalable pathways for AML and abuse detection, though they face challenges with label scarcity, privacy-preserving feature engineering, and adversarial adaptation to changing incentive regimes Identity linkage across L1/L2 and platform integrations enables privacy risks and surveillance, requiring privacy-aware designs in social protocol APIs [fed4f780-1] GNN-based money laundering detection, multirelational designs with adaptive sampling, and active learning show effectiveness on public datasets and address label scarcity [2d65bf96-0] Subgraph contrastive learning provides scalable screening by predicting illicit rates at the subgraph level, aligning with blockchain transparency [2d65bf96-3] Incentive gaming and price sensitivity can shift fraud patterns, necessitating adaptive detection and continuous evaluation [f668dd7d-0].

citations.title: Bitcoin Money Laundering Detection via Subgraph Contrastive Learning
snippets:
As of 9 August 2022, the size of the entire transaction record of Bitcoin, i.e., the blockchain, is 420 GB, with an average growth rate of 129% [29]. The rule-based manual money laundering detection methods used in the industry are time-consuming and resource-intensive, and there is an urgent need for more efficient methods to detect Bitcoin money laundering. Our algorithm aims to predict the illicit rate of subgraphs, significantly reducing computational costs. Our algorithm will play a crucial role in screening the vast data flow of cryptocurrencies, and subgraphs predicted to have higher illicit rates will be added to a watchlist. 

Our proposed algorithm performs exceptionally well in experiments. As illustrated in Section 5.2, the patterns discovered can effectively distinguish money laundering groups from non-money laundering groups. The transparency of the blockchain and the general-ization ability of neural networks ensure the practical application of our algorithm. Firstly, cryptocurrency transaction information is recorded in real-time on the blockchain, with public transparency. We can obtain the initiating wallet address ID, receiving wallet address ID, and transaction record ID for a transaction on public platforms (e.g., Blockchain.com [67]). This forms the basis for further mining the original features of IDs and constructing the address-transaction heterogeneous graph, as detailed in Section 3. Secondly, in the paper, we utilized two labeled datasets to train the proposed deep learning network model, Bit-CHetG. The extensive time span covered by these datasets ensures that the model learns optimal parameters with high generalization ability. In practical applications, when dealing with unlabeled transaction graphs, after the subgraphs are sampled, we can directly calculate the illicit rate of the transaction subgraph using those retained model parameters. 

The money laundering group detection paradigm based on subgraphs, once applied in reality, will significantly reduce the complexity of cryptocurrency AML. This regulation of cryptocurrency money laundering will further maintain the stability of the global financial system, resist criminal activities, and enhance international security.

sections.text:
Open Challenges and Future Directions
- Empirical governance: Field measurements of DAO voting, proposal quality, and incentive alignment in live social networks are needed to bridge conceptual models and practical governance Empirical analysis of operational DAO governance remains underdeveloped [5ee6f025-4].
- Multilayer privacy-preserving analytics: Methods to minimize cross-layer leakage while enabling useful social protocol analytics (e.g., pseudonymous aggregation, zk-SNARK-based reporting) require rigorous evaluation for utility and privacy trade-offs Cross-platform data exchange and linkage threaten anonymity and must be constrained [fed4f780-1].
- Adaptive fraud detection: Benchmarks that incorporate evolving incentives and adversarial adaptation (e.g., token price shocks, new manipulation schemes) are needed to assess detection robustness and model update policies Token price fluctuations and collusion dynamics alter behavior and detection targets [f668dd7d-0].
- Interpretable, multi-view detection: Visual analytics and multiview interfaces can support explainability for regulators and communities, but should be integrated with rigorous privacy and access controls Multiview UIs help present detection results and related transaction data for interpretability [2d65bf96-0].

citations.title: Beyond Single-Tokenomics: How Farcaster's Pluralistic Incentives Reshape Social Networking
snippets:
In blockchain-based decentralized social platforms, Steemit [101] remains the most studied [8,22,52,66,79]. Steemit's proprietary blockchain and platform-mandated token mechanism enabled early advances in decentralized incentive design, eliminating transaction fees and facilitating highthroughput reward distribution. However, these design choices unintentionally introduced critical vulnerabilities, including susceptibility to farming and collusion [8], bot misuses [22], centralization of rewards, and exacerbation of economic stratification [52,66,79]. Research by Li et al. [66] and Ba et al. [8] indicates that successful users adapt their content strategies to maximize rewards, often focusing on content promotion rather than creation. This finding raises questions about whether financial incentives optimize for platform goals or user gaming. Ba et al. [8] further reveal strong correlations between cryptocurrency prices and user activity levels on Steemit: when token values increase, posting activity and user engagement spike correspondingly. 

These prior works have focused on examining single mechanisms. However, studies suggest that the most effective incentive systems should combine multiple types of rewards rather than relying on single mechanisms [78,89,97]. Thus, our work differs from the above in that we move beyond single-incentive vulnerabilities. Instead, our research offers the first empirical analysis of Farcaster's pluralistic incentive ecosystem-integrating multiple tokens and diverse reward mechanisms through modular wallet binding and third-party reward projects [33,35,37]. Notably, we find that despite individual mechanisms retaining some prior identified shortcomings, their coexistence and complementarity show the potential to mitigate platform-wide risks.

citations.title: Understanding Blockchain Governance: Analyzing Decentralized Voting to Amend DeFi Smart Contracts
snippets:
The literature on decentralized governance, social contracts, and decentralized autonomous organizations (DAOs) is extensive. 

Decentralized Governance and Social Contracts. Prior work has investigated how blockchain-based governance might serve as an alternative to traditional centralized systems. Atzori et al. examined the potential for blockchain to displace centralized societal institutions and authorities [4]. Reijers et al. analyzed the alignment between blockchain governance and classical theories of the social contract, drawing on the ideas of Hobbes [31], Rousseau [54], and Rawls [12]. Chen et al. explored trade-offs between decentralization and system performance [13]. Other comparative studies have examined governance models across public and private blockchains [3,77]. For instance, Arruñada and Garicano proposed new forms of "soft" decentralized governance [3], while Zwitter and Hazenberg offered a rethinking of governance structures tailored to DAOs [77]. While these works provide conceptual insights, they generally lack empirical analysis of how these theories play out in operational DAO systems or how real-world governance protocols function in practice.

citations.title: The Illusion of Anonymity: Uncovering the Impact of User Actions on Privacy in Web3 Social Ecosystems
snippets:
Following Steemit, platforms like Minds and Mirror have emerged, enabling users to produce content and monetize their contributions.Many of these platforms provide features for linking social accounts, allowing users to connect to their Web2.0social media profiles, such as accounts in Twitter (rebranded as X) and Facebook, to ease the transition to Web3.As depicted in Figure 1, most modern Web3 social applications are built on the Ethereum blockchain [6].Initially, each user must create a wallet account on the layer 1 Ethereum network.When registering an account in a layer 2 decentralized social application, the application sends a request to associate with the Ethereum account of the user through the wallet.This association with the layer 1 Ethereum account acts primarily as a safeguard against Sybil attacks [15], which is enforced by validating the balance of accounts.However, the transaction data generated during the account creation process poses significant privacy risks for users.

As decentralized social platforms attract an increasing number of users, the complexity of user interactions on layer 2 expands, creating an intricate social network.These interactions have significant privacy implications, and the data linking users is valuable to both users and network owners.Moreover, the ability for layer 2 to connect with layer 1 allows various stakeholders, such as service providers [37], data analysts [26], and government agencies, to create and examine social graphs on layer 1.This activity threatens the anonymity that is a hallmark of blockchain technology and which some users wish to maintain.For example, the friend.techinitiative by Twitter [32] connects traditional Web2.0 Twitter accounts with the decentralized Web3 environment.Given that Twitter contains extensive user data, such as geolocation, personal images, and behavioral patterns [46], transferring these social connections to Web3 could significantly undermine the anonymity that blockchain systems are known for.

snippets:
In this section, we give a quick overview of the notion of Web3 and then introduce ways of building DApps on top of blockchains. 

Notion of Web3. The concept of Web3 was first proposed by Wood [40] with an initial discussion focusing on blockchain-based digital infrastructure. Later, Weyl et al. [1] illustrate the ways of building a decentralized society by exploring Web3-related applications, requirements, opportunities, and challenges. Wang et al. [3] provide the discussion between Web3 and blockchain from the perspective of architecture design. The work has identified a total of 12 types of designs according to the data workflow of access, computation, and storage. A series of reports from Consensys [41] investigates the economic performances created by decentralized networks. Web3 economy covers many on-chain DeFi protocols [14] such as stablecoins, borrowing, lending, and leverage, distributed governance protocols (e.g., DAO) [42][43] and many innovations combined with other technologies [44,45]. These protocols are built on top of smart contracts. Liu et al. [46] explore three types of infrastructural enablers, including the single smart-contract powered chain, federated contracts, and interoperable blockchain platforms. However, Web3 sofar still confronts high-level controversies in terms of its definition and application. We, in this paper, extend our exploration by complying with its core decentralization nature guaranteed by underlying blockchain services. 

Constructing Web3 Applications. Traditional Web1 and Web2 applications rely on centralized backend servers for computations and storage. Web3 applications [3] replace these servers with decentralized blockchain platforms [6] [47]. Building a Web3 application requires three phases: (i) embedding the wallet for access, (ii) connecting frontend with blockchain platforms, and (iii) operating executions on-chain. A wallet [20][21] is backed by locally running lightweight nodes and helps Web3 users to create on-chain accounts (in the form of address [12]) as their identities. A user can initiate a request by sending a transaction from wallets to the transaction pool.

question: Advantages  of digital watermarking

sections.title: # What watermarking is and why it matters
sections.text: Digital watermarking embeds identifying or control information into multimedia (images, audio, video, text) in a way that is imperceptible to humans/clients yet durable against typical processing, enabling new capabilities for protection, verification, and management of digital assets in practice and commerce. Digital watermarking techniques embed a known message in a piece of digital data as a means of identifying the rightful owner of the data; the watermark is hidden and inseparable from the host so it survives many degrading operations, and these techniques can be used on still imagery, movies, and music [7d352b32-3] Digital image watermarking technology is a research hotspot with practical applications and considerable economic value, and is regarded as an important research direction in information security [7d352b32-0]. This has made it an enabling technology for conditional/user-specific access in e-business and for broader content protection use cases across media. Digital watermarking is an enabling technology for e-business strategies: conditional and user specific access to services and resources [7d352b32-3]

citations.title: On the Security Enhancement of Multimedia Copyright Protection for E-Business
snippets:
Digital watermarking is an efficient technique to protect intellectual property from illegal copying. It provides a means of embedding a message in a piece of digital data without destroying the value of the digital data. Digital watermarking techniques embed a known message in a piece of digital data as a means of identifying the rightful owner of the data. These techniques can be used on many types of digital data including still imagery, movies, and music. This work focuses on digital watermarking for images and in particular invisible watermarking. A digital watermark is a signal permanently embedded into digital data (audio, images, video, and text) that can be detected or extracted later by means of computing operations in order to make assertions about the data. The watermark is hidden in the host data in such a way that it is inseparable from the data and so that it is resistant to many operations that may degrade the host document. 

Digital Watermarking techniques derive from steganography, which means covered writing (from the Greek words stegano or ''covered'' and graphos or ''to write''). Steganography is the science of communicating information while hiding the existence of the communication. The goal of steganography is to hide an information message inside harmless messages in such a way that it is not possible even to detect that there is a secret message present. Both steganography and watermarking belong to a category of information hiding, but the objectives and conditions for the two techniques are just the opposite. In watermarking, for example, the important information is the "external" data (e.g. images, voices, etc.). The "internal" data (e.g. watermark) is additional data for protecting the external data and to prove ownership. In steganography, however, the external data (referred to as a vessel, container, or dummy data) is not very important. It is just a carrier of the important information; the internal data. A watermark is designed to permanently reside in the host data. If the ownership of a digital work is in question, the information can be extracted to completely characterize the owner. 

Digital watermarking is an enabling technology for e-business strategies: conditional and user specific access to services and resources. Digital watermarking offers several advantages.

snippets:
Digital image watermarking technology is a research hotspot for copyright protection of digital multimedia works. The digital image watermarking technology not only has practical applications, it also has considerable economic value. 

Different digital image watermarking algorithms have different characteristics. In practical applications, the advantages of digital image watermarking technology are fully utilized to meet different needs. There are still many deficiencies in the digital watermarking algorithm, which needs to be constantly improved in the development. 

With the wide application of digital image watermarking technology, many researchers begin to regard it as an important research direction in the field of information security, but some problems still remain unsolved. For example, the comprehensiveness of the anti-attack ability of the watermarking system, the security of tampering detection in content authentication and so on.

sections.title: # Ownership identification and proof of origin (PoO)
sections.text: A primary advantage is establishing rightful ownership and authorship for disputed content, which supports legal, licensing, and monetization workflows. Watermarks can carry identifiers (e.g., owner name/image) that persist with the content and can be extracted to characterize the owner when ownership is challenged. These techniques can identify the rightful owner of the data and are applicable across imagery, movies, and music [7d352b32-3] Digital image watermarking technology is used to protect intellectual property from illegal copying and provides a means for identifying ownership [7d352b32-0]. Fingerprinting variants further support proof-of-origin by embedding unique, customizable watermarks per recipient, enabling tracing of leakage or unauthorized redistribution. Fingerprinting embeds different watermarks customized for each recipient so the owner can identify the customer by extracting the watermark if the data is supplied to third parties [38a8dca1-0] Fingerprinting watermark embedded in the content is used to trace authorized users [38a8dca1-2].

citations.title: A DFT-DWT Domain Invisible Blind Watermarking Techniques for Copyright Protection of Digital Images
snippets:
Although the main motivation behind the digital watermarking is the copyright protection, its applications are not that restricted. There is a wide application area of digital watermarking, including broadcast monitoring, fingerprinting, authentication and covet communication [7,8,9,10]. 

By embedding watermarks into commercial advertisements, the advertisements can be monitored whether the advertisements are broadcasted at the correct instants by means of an automated system [7,8]. The system receives the broadcast and searches these watermarks identifying where and when the advertisement is broadcasted. The same process can also be used for video and sound clips. Musicians and actors may request to ensure that they receive accurate royalties for broadcasts of their performances. 

Fingerprinting is a novel approach to trace the source of illegal copies [7,8]. The owner of the digital data may embed different watermarks in the copies of digital content customized for each recipient. In this manner, the owner can identify the customer by extracting the watermark in the case the data is supplied to third parties. The digital watermarking can also be used for authentication [7,8]. The authentication is the detection of whether the content of the digital content has changed. As a solution, a fragile watermark embedded to the digital content indicates whether the data has been altered. If any tampering has occurred in the content, the same change will also occur on the watermark. It can also provide information about the part of the content that has been altered. 

Covert communication is another possible application of digital watermarking [7,8]. The watermark, secret message, can be embedded imperceptibly to the digital image or video to communicate information from the sender to the intended receiver while maintaining low probability of intercept by other unintended receivers.

sections.title: # Integrity, authentication, and tampering detection
sections.text: Watermarking supports content integrity and tampering detection, offering "digital signatures" that are inseparable from the host and resistant to lossy operations. Fragile or semi-fragile watermarks detect alterations and can localize tampered regions, with changes in the watermark reflecting changes in the content for quick integrity verification. A digital watermark is inseparable and resistant to many degrading operations, enabling assertions about the data [7d352b32-3] Digital watermarking embeds an invisible signal undetectable to humans but resistant to lossy compression and common processing; content authentication methods include watermarking-based approaches and are classified into complete, robust, and content authentication [df5f18ab-1] By embedding a fragile watermark, any tampering results in distortions to the extracted watermark enabling quick detection of integrity problems; semi-fragile watermarks can detect tamper locations and modifications [df5f18ab-2]. These capabilities are critical in sensitive domains (legal, police investigations, medical) where unauthorized modifications must be detected and forensically analyzed. Ensuring integrity is imperative in sensitive applications such as legal cases, police investigations and medical use; watermarking-based techniques detect unauthorized modifications [df5f18ab-2].

citations.title: Hybrid SVD-Based Image Watermarking Schemes: A Review
snippets:
Digital content can be easily tampered with while avoiding detection. Authentication and verification of the integrity of digital content must be performed to ensure that no unauthorized modifications are performed. It is imperative to ensure that the integrity of digital content remains intact as they are leveraged in sensitive applications such as legal cases, police investigations and medical use. Thus, various digital authentication techniques have been presented in the literature [8]. Cryptography-based measures have been widely explored to solve this problem using hash functions, message authentication code and digital signature. 

In digital image authentication, cryptography hash functions and digital signature encryption method are adopted to preserve the integrity of data content. A hash value of the digital image is computed and then is used to generate a digital signature. To authenticate a received image, a new hash value is computed using the same hash function and compared with the one being stored. If the two hash values match then the digital image is regarded as been authentic. The advantage of cryptography-based image authentication techniques is that unauthorized parties are unable to create a new signature as long as they do not have the private key. However, the main problem of the cryptography-based image authentication techniques lies in the storing location that is used to save the signature. Consequently, it becomes difficult to verify the image authenticity if the storing location is removed or altered [57], [58]. 

On the other hand, image watermarking is an alternative technique used to achieve image authentication. To detect image tampering, watermarking-based image authentication techniques have been proposed based on fragile and semifragile watermarks [59]- [62]. By embedding a fragile watermark directly into the host image, any efforts to tamper the watermarked image will result in distortions to the extracted watermark. This allows quick detection of image integrity problems. Therefore, watermarking-based authentication is more advantageous as compared to cryptography-based authentication for two reasons. Firstly, it is difficult to remove the embedded watermark and tampering attempts it will  lead to changes to the watermark itself. Secondly, the storing location is not used to save the watermark data. Semifragile watermarks that have low robustness are used to detect tamper locations, modifications, and manipulation of a watermarked image [63], [64].

sections.title: # Broadcast monitoring, tracking, and monetization
sections.text: Embedding watermarks in advertisements and media enables automated broadcast monitoring to verify placement and timing, supporting rights management and royalty verification across video and audio. Embedding watermarks into commercial advertisements allows automated systems to monitor whether they are broadcasted at the correct instants and identify where and when they are broadcasted; the same process applies to video and sound clips, and musicians/actors can ensure accurate royalties [38a8dca1-0] Watermarking is a promising tool for broadcast monitoring among other applications [38a8dca1-1]. In workflows for tracking and monetizing content, watermarking and fingerprinting are integrated to automatically track, protect, and monetize media as they move through distribution channels. Secret communication, broadcast monitoring, copyright security, and content description are applications of digital watermarks [38a8dca1-3] White paper [24] examines how watermarking and fingerprinting can be integrated into workflows for automatically tracking, protecting and monetizing content [38a8dca1-4].

sections.title: # Copy control and DRM/fingerprinting
sections.text: Watermarking supports copy control by embedding copy-protection signals that indicate copyright status and constrain reproduction; compliant removal typically degrades content to deter unauthorized duplication. Standardization efforts (e.g., CPTWG for DVDs) illustrate how watermarking underpins copy protection in practice. Copy protection uses watermarks to indicate whether content is copyrighted and to prevent removal without severe degradation; the CPTWG has defined system specifications for DVD copy protection [38a8dca1-4]. Fingerprinting further ties specific authorized copies to users, enabling accountability and tracing of leaked copies. Fingerprinting is a novel approach to trace the source of illegal copies by embedding different watermarks customized for each recipient [38a8dca1-0] Common watermarking applications include copy protection and fingerprinting [7d352b32-2].

sections.title: # Data hiding and covert/secret communication

This dual-use extends watermarking into privacy-preserving messaging and steganographic applications. Watermarking and fingerprinting integration is explored for automatically tracking, protecting and monetizing content across modalities [38a8dca1-4].

sections.title: # Applicability across media and enabling e-business/DRM
sections.text: Watermarking is not limited to copyright; it spans broadcast monitoring, fingerprinting, authentication, and covert communication, and is applicable across imagery, audio, video, and text. This breadth makes it a versatile enabler of e-business strategies involving conditional/user-specific access and rights management. Applications include broadcast monitoring, fingerprinting, authentication and covert communication [38a8dca1-0] These techniques can be used on many types of digital data including still imagery, movies, and music, and offer several advantages including enabling e-business strategies for conditional and user-specific access [7d352b32-3].

citations.title: On the Security Enhancement of Multimedia Copyright Protection for E-Business
snippets:
Digital watermarking is an efficient technique to protect intellectual property from illegal copying. It provides a means of embedding a message in a piece of digital data without destroying the value of the digital data. Digital watermarking techniques embed a known message in a piece of digital data as a means of identifying the rightful owner of the data. These techniques can be used on many types of digital data including still imagery, movies, and music. This work focuses on digital watermarking for images and in particular invisible watermarking. A digital watermark is a signal permanently embedded into digital data (audio, images, video, and text) that can be detected or extracted later by means of computing operations in order to make assertions about the data. The watermark is hidden in the host data in such a way that it is inseparable from the data and so that it is resistant to many operations that may degrade the host document. 

Digital Watermarking techniques derive from steganography, which means covered writing (from the Greek words stegano or ''covered'' and graphos or ''to write''). Steganography is the science of communicating information while hiding the existence of the communication. The goal of steganography is to hide an information message inside harmless messages in such a way that it is not possible even to detect that there is a secret message present. Both steganography and watermarking belong to a category of information hiding, but the objectives and conditions for the two techniques are just the opposite. In watermarking, for example, the important information is the "external" data (e.g. images, voices, etc.). The "internal" data (e.g. watermark) is additional data for protecting the external data and to prove ownership. In steganography, however, the external data (referred to as a vessel, container, or dummy data) is not very important. It is just a carrier of the important information; the internal data. A watermark is designed to permanently reside in the host data. If the ownership of a digital work is in question, the information can be extracted to completely characterize the owner. 

Digital watermarking is an enabling technology for e-business strategies: conditional and user specific access to services and resources. Digital watermarking offers several advantages.

sections.title: # Practical considerations and trade-offs
sections.text: Watermarking delivers value through three key factors—imperceptibility (visual/audio quality impact), robustness (survival of attacks and processing), and capacity (amount of data embedded)—which involve inherent trade-offs. Improving robustness can increase visibility, and increasing payload can degrade quality; transform-domain methods tend to be more resilient than spatial-domain methods but still face limits against sophisticated attacks and in diverse scenarios. Evaluation requires analysis of imperceptibility, robustness, and watermark capacity; improving robustness may increase visibility and increasing payload can degrade quality, reflecting inherent trade-offs [7d352b32-4] Transform domain methods demonstrate greater resilience than spatial domain techniques but still suffer from lower resistance to attacks and restricted application scenarios [7d352b32-4]. Even with progress (e.g., deep learning-based approaches), open issues remain in anti-attack comprehensiveness and security of tampering detection, underscoring the need for careful design and domain-specific robustness models. With widespread application, many problems remain unsolved, including the comprehensiveness of anti-attack ability and the security of tampering detection in content authentication [7d352b32-0] Conventional methods face limitations and trade-offs; deep learning-based watermarking is a promising alternative addressing some challenges [7d352b32-4].

citations.title: Deep Learning-Based Image Watermarking Using Catalan Transform and Non-Negative Matrix Factorization
snippets:
The creation, distribution, and consumption of digital content have been transformed by the accelerated advancements in internet and multimedia technologies. However, these developments have also introduced significant challenges in protecting intellectual property rights and ensuring the authenticity of digital media [2], [3], [4]. Digital 

The associate editor coordinating the review of this manuscript and approving it for publication was Olarik Surinta . 

watermarking has become an essential method for embedding identifying information inside digital output, maintaining its quality and usability. Despite extensive research in this domain, conventional watermarking techniques face several limitations, including low robustness against attacks, limited application scope, and trade-offs between imperceptibility, robustness, and watermark capacity [5], [6], [9]. A comprehensive classification of watermarking techniques is presented in Fig. 1, organized into five main categories: visibility, document type, extraction method, attack resistance, and processing domain. This classification highlights the diverse strategies used in watermarking technology, reflecting its complexity and versatility. Conventional watermarking methods, summarized in Fig. 2, include copyright markers by altering either the pixel values or transform coefficients of the host image. Although transform domain methods demonstrate greater resilience compared to spatial domain techniques, they still suffer from limitations such as lower resistance to attacks and restricted application scenarios [8]. The evaluation of watermarking techniques requires a careful analysis of three key factors: imperceptibility, robustness, and watermark capacity. Imperceptibility denotes the degree to which the watermarking procedure influences the visual quality of the source image. Robustness evaluates the watermark's capacity to endure diverse purposeful and inadvertent assaults, like compression, scaling, or noise introduction. The watermark capacity defines the maximum amount of information that can be embedded without compromising invisibility and durability. Fig. 3 illustrates the inherent trade-offs among these factors, highlighting the challenge of balancing them effectively. For example, improving robustness may increase watermark visibility, while increasing the data payload could degrade the host image quality. Deep learning-based watermarking methods have recently gained attention as a promising alternative, offering solutions to some of these challenges [7], [10].

citations.title: Comparison of the Schemes in Digital Image Watermarking Techniques
snippets:
Digital image watermarking technology is a research hotspot for copyright protection of digital multimedia works. The digital image watermarking technology not only has practical applications, it also has considerable economic value. 

Different digital image watermarking algorithms have different characteristics. In practical applications, the advantages of digital image watermarking technology are fully utilized to meet different needs. There are still many deficiencies in the digital watermarking algorithm, which needs to be constantly improved in the development. 

With the wide application of digital image watermarking technology, many researchers begin to regard it as an important research direction in the field of information security, but some problems still remain unsolved. For example, the comprehensiveness of the anti-attack ability of the watermarking system, the security of tampering detection in content authentication and so on.

sections.title: # Summary
sections.text: In practice, digital watermarking provides durable, imperceptible proofs of ownership and origin; integrity and tampering detection; automated broadcast monitoring and rights tracking; copy control and fingerprinting for DRM; covert/secret communication; and embedded metadata for content management—across multiple media and business contexts—while requiring careful balancing of imperceptibility, robustness, and capacity to meet application-specific constraints. Watermarking identifies rightful owners, survives many processing operations, and is applicable across media and e-business access models [7d352b32-3] Fragile/semi-fragile watermarking enables quick tamper detection and localization [df5f18ab-2] Broadcast monitoring and fingerprinting enable automated tracking and tracing of unauthorized use [38a8dca1-0] Integrating watermarking and fingerprinting supports automatic tracking, protection, and monetization workflows [38a8dca1-4] Watermarking supports secret communication and content description/metadata embedding [38a8dca1-3] Design must trade off imperceptibility, robustness, and capacity, with deep learning offering new solutions [7d352b32-4].

For example, improving robustness may increase watermark visibility, while increasing the data payload could degrade the host image quality. Deep learning-based watermarking methods have recently gained attention as a promising alternative, offering solutions to some of these challenges [7], [10].

citations.title: A DFT-DWT Domain Invisible Blind Watermarking Techniques for Copyright Protection of Digital Images
snippets:
Although the main motivation behind the digital watermarking is the copyright protection, its applications are not that restricted. There is a wide application area of digital watermarking, including broadcast monitoring, fingerprinting, authentication and covet communication [7,8,9,10]. 

By embedding watermarks into commercial advertisements, the advertisements can be monitored whether the advertisements are broadcasted at the correct instants by means of an automated system [7,8]. The system receives the broadcast and searches these watermarks identifying where and when the advertisement is broadcasted. The same process can also be used for video and sound clips. Musicians and actors may request to ensure that they receive accurate royalties for broadcasts of their performances. 

Fingerprinting is a novel approach to trace the source of illegal copies [7,8]. The owner of the digital data may embed different watermarks in the copies of digital content customized for each recipient. In this manner, the owner can identify the customer by extracting the watermark in the case the data is supplied to third parties. The digital watermarking can also be used for authentication [7,8]. The authentication is the detection of whether the content of the digital content has changed. As a solution, a fragile watermark embedded to the digital content indicates whether the data has been altered. If any tampering has occurred in the content, the same change will also occur on the watermark. It can also provide information about the part of the content that has been altered. 

Covert communication is another possible application of digital watermarking [7,8]. The watermark, secret message, can be embedded imperceptibly to the digital image or video to communicate information from the sender to the intended receiver while maintaining low probability of intercept by other unintended receivers.

citations.title: Hybrid SVD-Based Image Watermarking Schemes: A Review
snippets:
Digital content can be easily tampered with while avoiding detection. Authentication and verification of the integrity of digital content must be performed to ensure that no unauthorized modifications are performed. It is imperative to ensure that the integrity of digital content remains intact as they are leveraged in sensitive applications such as legal cases, police investigations and medical use. Thus, various digital authentication techniques have been presented in the literature [8]. Cryptography-based measures have been widely explored to solve this problem using hash functions, message authentication code and digital signature. 

In digital image authentication, cryptography hash functions and digital signature encryption method are adopted to preserve the integrity of data content. A hash value of the digital image is computed and then is used to generate a digital signature. To authenticate a received image, a new hash value is computed using the same hash function and compared with the one being stored. If the two hash values match then the digital image is regarded as been authentic. The advantage of cryptography-based image authentication techniques is that unauthorized parties are unable to create a new signature as long as they do not have the private key. However, the main problem of the cryptography-based image authentication techniques lies in the storing location that is used to save the signature. Consequently, it becomes difficult to verify the image authenticity if the storing location is removed or altered [57], [58]. 

On the other hand, image watermarking is an alternative technique used to achieve image authentication. To detect image tampering, watermarking-based image authentication techniques have been proposed based on fragile and semifragile watermarks [59]- [62]. By embedding a fragile watermark directly into the host image, any efforts to tamper the watermarked image will result in distortions to the extracted watermark. This allows quick detection of image integrity problems. Therefore, watermarking-based authentication is more advantageous as compared to cryptography-based authentication for two reasons. Firstly, it is difficult to remove the embedded watermark and tampering attempts it will  lead to changes to the watermark itself. Secondly, the storing location is not used to save the watermark data. Semifragile watermarks that have low robustness are used to detect tamper locations, modifications, and manipulation of a watermarked image [63], [64].

question: What is design fabulation?

sections.title: # What is “design fabulation”?
sections.text: Design fabulation is a practice of making and telling stories—often with speculative or fantastical elements—to re/imagine otherwise technological, social, and ecological futures, while attending to power, justice, and more-than-human relations. It draws on literary fabulation and critical theory to argue that how we narrativize systems and beings shapes what becomes possible, and it operationalizes this idea through design methods that stitch together improbable collaborations and relations across people, artifacts, and environments. Fabulation orients design towards narrative potentials, linking to fable traditions and critical fabulations that bring forth untold pasts and make space for diverse, equitable futures [b1b1e362-3] Design fabulations interconnect pasts, presents and futures, challenging dominant values by centering neglected relations and decentering the human to foster joy and care for Earth [b1b1e362-4] Speculative fabulations act as material-semiotic knots in which diverse bodies and meanings co-shape one another, “stitching together improbable collaborations” to enable slippages into new territories [48fc8029-2].

citations.title: Telling it slant with side curved head and curiosity: posthumanist/feminist materialist creative activations in university spaces
snippets:
Donna Haraway (2013) proposes speculative fabulation as figurations or narratives that act as material-semiotic nodes or knots in which diverse bodies and meanings co-shape one another; speculative fabulations 'stitch together improbable collaborations without worrying overmuch about conventional ontological kinds' (Haraway 2016, 136). Like Carstens (2020), we see speculative fabulation as a mode of 'venturesome makings-with' enabling us to further pluralize the 'I' in all manner of onto-assemblages, matter-meaning assemblages in which boundaries and conventions fray and bodies become in new relational knowings. We include below three co-composed speculative fabulations which aim to embrace 'uncomfortable yet productive tensions [activating] tactics of defamiliarization and cognitive estrangement' to enable 'slippages into [new] territories' (Carstens 2020, 76) for thinking, feeling and doing higher education differently. 

Speculative fabulation 1: Nonchalance, why not? 

We are nonchalant. And as we are nonchalant, you can be nonchalant too. 

We walk along campus paths, smiling, relaxed. 

At ease in our moving bodies. Nonchalance is an embodied practice. 

A form of Zen. 

Loafing in these campus spaces requires persistence.

citations.title: What mosses can teach us about design fabulations and feminist more-than-human care
snippets: While speculative approaches in more-than-human design are not new (Reddy et al., 2020(Reddy et al., , 2021;;Wakkary, 2021), fabulation brings a feminist sensitivity and criticality which is greatly needed for more-than-human design to deliver on its justice-oriented commitments for humans, animals, and environment alike. Fabulation draws on the literary genre of the fable; stories of talking animals serving moral lessons through mundane yet fantastical human-mimicking behaviors and satirical plots. Within HCI and design, the most renowned for her work on fabulation is Daniela Rosner, who articulates "critical fabulations" as a making and storytelling approach that can bring forth untold pasts within present day design and computer discourse, hereby making space for more diverse and equitable futures (Rosner, 2018). Linking fabulation to its literary tradition, Rosner points out "Derived from the practice of telling fables or stories, the term fabulation orients design towards narrative potentials" (Rosner, 2018, p. 17). Rosner refers to Sadiya Hartman and Donna Haraway in her use of the term fabulation. To Hartman, critical fabulation "denotes the basic elements of story, the building blocks of the narrative" (Hartman, 2008, p. 11). Hartman uses this term to describe her approach of telling lost, excluded stories about the lives of Black people who were victims of Atlantic slavery; where archives and data about enslaved people did not tell the stories of their lives and what happened to them (Hartman, 2008) but enabled violence and dehumanizing actions. Similar critical approach, building on intersectional Black feminist theory, is seen in Klumbyté et al.'s work on designing fair and accountable machine learning systems (Klumbyte˙ et al., 2022). Critical fabulations, they write, "entails speculative thought and imagination but it positions those activities against the absent imaginaries and loci of power hierarchies" (Klumbyte˙ et al., 2022(Klumbyte˙ et al., , p. 1530)).

citations.title: What mosses can teach us about design fabulations and feminist more-than-human care
snippets: Design fabulations are already emergent within feminist technoscience practice and have had impact in design research as storytelling practice interconneting pasts, presents and futures (Rosner, 2023;Søndergaard et al., 2023). Yet their connection with speculative practices and non-human actors, such as plants and animals, makes them particularly useful for more-than-human imaginaries (Nijs et al., 2020). Literary scholar Robert Scholes has described fabulations as a critical response to realism and alienation; a new genre of literature that exercises our imagination and supports our "imaginative well-being" and the re-imagination of ourselves (Scholes, 1979). Characterized as "ethically controlled fantasy," fabulation produces a joy through its form that uses satire to serve moral lessons (Scholes, 1967). Learning from my design work with mosses and microscope, the following is an open definition for how fabulations work in more-than-human design: Design fabulations as a feminist approach can aid more-than-human designers in challenging dominant values and visions of technological progress by telling stories about neglected relations and absent imaginaries. They do so by decentering (hu)man and enchanting non-human actors in embedded ecologies and affective dialogs, with directionality and purpose of fostering joy in taking care of Earth and moralizing just and vibrant futures. It is a feminist approach, not only due to the legacy from feminist technoscience where fabulations have been practiced, but because feminism itself has a tradition in strong imaginary practices. Feminists are experts in imagining otherwise; living in infrastructures and systems not built for them or sometimes built to exclude them, cisgender women, disabled people (Hendren, 2020), as well as queer and trans people, non-binary folks (Costanza-Chock, 2020), and Black, Indigenous and people of color (Benjamin, 2019), are in various, often intersecting, ways reminded that the world is not imagined for them, or by them, and that it could and should be different. Making their own objects, supporting movements, using their bodies in protests, suggesting policy-change; feminists have extensive expertise and experience in making otherwise.

sections.title: # Origins and theoretical roots
sections.text: Design fabulation is grounded in critical and posthumanist traditions. Scholars connect it to Sadiya Hartman’s “critical fabulation” (retrieving excluded lives through narrative), Donna Haraway’s speculative fabulation (figurations that reassemble entangled lives and more-than-human worlds), and Daniela Rosner’s critical fabulations in HCI (reclaiming narrative agency in design discourse). Within HCI, Rosner articulates critical fabulations as a making-and-storytelling approach to reveal untold pasts in design and computer discourse, thus opening space for more diverse and equitable futures [b1b1e362-3] She links fabulation to Hartman and Haraway, emphasizing that fabulation orients design to narrative potentials and that Hartman treats fabulation as the basic elements of story used to recover marginalized lives [b1b1e362-3]. This lineage positions design fabulation not as escapism but as a justice-oriented practice that expands ethical imaginaries beyond human-centeredness. Design fabulations are emergent within feminist technoscience and are framed as a feminist approach that challenges dominant visions of progress by enchanting non-human actors and fostering just, vibrant futures [b1b1e362-4].

sections.title: # How design fabulation works: mechanisms and methods
sections.text:
Design fabulation works by combining storying with making to surface “absent imaginaries” and refigure relations. It often employs speculative narratives (stories, scenarios, vignettes), backcasting from desired futures to current “nows,” and participatory workshops that use designed materials (prompts, artifacts, visual stimuli) to catalyze imagination. Speculative fabulation has been linked to backcasting, where “fantastical, multispecies, situated and delightfully strange fabulations” help connect imaginative futures to implementable steps in the present [4e862aab-0] Methods differentiate between speculative fabulation (story- and scenario-based) and speculative fabrication (artifact-based, e.g., design fiction), with both used to question the present through glimpses of the future [4e862aab-3]. In practice, the materiality of tools and prompts shapes participants’ imaginaries and the closure of discussions, underscoring that “tools are not neutral.” The design of backcasting exercises, prompts, images, and workshop atmosphere configure participants’ speculative fabulation experiences, influencing engagement, values, and the closure of imagined futures [4e862aab-4].

Design fabulation also functions as “venturesome makings-with,” assembling speculative assemblages that trouble conventional ontologies and invite defamiliarization and cognitive estrangement. It pluralizes the “I” in matter–meaning assemblages by embracing uncomfortable yet productive tensions and enabling slippages into new territories for thinking, feeling, and doing [48fc8029-2]. In spatial design, fabulation serves as a counterbalance to instrumental pragmatism, offering visions that critique conformity and expand interpretative frontiers of space, time, and materiality. Fictions, fantasies, and fabulations have instilled optimism, sparked alternative visions, and provided sites of critique; far from escapism, they enable speculative invention, futuring, and critical reflection [48fc8029-4].

citations.title: Variations on Piranesi’s Carceri
snippets:
While the world reels, reconfigures, and recovers from the drama and trauma of 2020, wishing to thwart the effects of grief and comprehend what was once incomprehensible, there is all good reason to turn our imagination to 'what ifs', dreams, and other speculations as an antidote to hopelessness. This issue, Fictions, Fantasies, and Fabulations, calls for contributions that consider the unlikely, improbable, or downright impossible in spatial design. In recent history, fictions, fantasies, and fabulations have offered productive opposition to the rampant instrumentality of pragmatism and functional planning. Their impact has instilled optimism, sparked alternative visions, and been sites of countless critiques of conformity and the status quo. Loosely defined impulses towards the unrealisable and the most illogical of things approached in the most logical of ways have led to unparalleled episodes of creativity in drawings, poems, and material production. From Piranesi, Peter Greenaway, Kurt Schwitters, Dora Maar, Hans Op de Beeck, Ursula Le Guinn, John Hejduk, to Daniel Libeskind, explorations of the impossible have led to new interpretative frontiers that move the limits of interiority and spatial practices. Lest we forget or become complacent with the contributory and often unrecognised impact of contemporary social media, advertisement, and technological surveillance that continues to shape interior worlds, experiences, and values. In many ways, there is as much focus on unpacking, making sense of, and disproving the dangerous impacts of fictions, fantasies, and fabulations as there is on setting the scene for dreams and magical realities. 

This issue recognises the complex story of fictions, fantasies, and fabulations in spatial design, not as counter-productive forces, but as the necessary counter-balances that offer liberty from convention, propriety, and rational assumptions about behaviour, space, time, and materialthe core elements of interior worlds. Far from retreating into solipsistic escapism, fictions, fantasies, and fabulations serve as crucial sites for speculative invention, futuring, and critical reflection.

snippets:
Instead speculative fabulation offers a serious and lively practice that invite science and the arts into making worlds, telling stories and "living lives for flourishing and abundance, especially in the teeth of rampaging destruction and impoverization" (Haraway, 2016, p. 136). 

Several design researchers have been drawn to speculative fabulation, including Forlano et al. who proposed speculative fabulation as a feminist alternative to critical and speculative design (Forlano et al., 2016), Mazé who used fabulation to complicate linear visions of progress and the future in design and counter social norms (Mazé, 2017), and Wilde et al. who linked "fantastical, multispecies, situated and delightfully strange fabulations that are restorative and inclusive" to implementable nows through backcasting techniques (Wilde et al., 2021). These and more examples (Helms et al., 2021;Tsaknaki et al., 2022) show the value that fabulations bring in moving beyond dominant user-and human-centered design. What we can draw from these important sources, from the critical to the speculative, is that design fabulation has the potential to nurture a radical inclusive and radical imaginary attention to the more-than-human, which must be considered at the core of posthumanist HCI scholarship and practice to meet the needs of an entangled world and to fabulate alternatives values, visions and ways of living and being.

citations.title: Automation Is Coming! Exploring Future(s)-Oriented Methods in Education
snippets:
Based on Michael (2021), Ross differentiates between speculative fabulation, which is linked to the creation of stories, scenarios, vignettes, and speculative fabrication connected with artifacts, and objects enticing people to explore new 'inventive problems ' Michael (2021:80), or designed artifacts in the form of design fiction (Bleeker 2009). Following such a distinction, speculative fabulation methods have, for instance, been applied in the study of datafication and automation in K-12 education (Selwyn et al. 2020); Hillman et al. 2020), and higher education (Suoranta et al. 2022;Dator 2002). Such methods often use social science or techniques from the field of literary studies. 

Speculative fabrication methods, also called speculative fiction but better known as design fiction, have been underscored by Cox (2021) in education. Design fiction aims to question the present with glimpses from the future (Bleeker 2009) and is often defined as both a method for envisioning new futures and technologies and a tool for communicating innovations to researchers and the broader public (Tanenbaum 2014). Described as 'a conflation of design, science fact, and science fiction' (Bleeker 2009: 6), design fiction can be used 'to pose critical questions about the impact of technology on society and to actively engage wider publics in how technology is designed' (Cox 2021: 2). Cox (2021: 3) underscores that design fiction 'ha[s] the potential to change the scope of the debate by shifting attention away from the existing literature and its focus on developing and testing specific AI applications (Zawacki-Richter et al. 2019) to weighing up more or less desirable directions of travel for society'. 

Design fiction has been applied by Ross (2017) via Teacherbot, an automated agent participating in Twitter conversations problematizing and intervening in automated university teaching; Artcasting, a digital mobile prototype for art evaluation; and the Tweeting book, a 'prototype created to problematize the emphasis in learning analytics on human activity and data' (Ross 2017: 222). Cox (2021) offers another example of work contributing eight design fictions about the potential use of AI and robots in learning, administration, and research.

snippets:
This echoes discussions we participated in with the teachers during the workshop about the influence of Edtech in school practices, AI determinism, and narratives of the future as 'unchangeable' (Markham 2021: 384). Markham (2021) underscores 'although the capacity for imagining something new or different resides in all of us, the available material for any imaginative act is greatly influenced by prior imaginations' (383). This often results, as Ross (2022) notes, in 'the reproduction of an understating of technology as inevitable and people as powerless to generate different kinds of futures' (65). 

In our experience with speculative fabulation, we noted that the quality of the material could have also influenced the teachers' 'discursive closure' (Markham 2021) at times; more specifically, we refer to the prompts designed to unleash their imagination and the relatively homogeneity of the group participating in the workshop. As Ross (2022) reminds us, 'when considering speculative methods in teaching and research, researchers and educators need to critically question the dynamics of voice and engagement they are mobilizing' (66). 

Fourth, we suggest materiality as the fourth quality of speculative fabulation. This quality is deeply connected to the fundamental role that the design of the backcasting exercise and prompts plays in configuring research knowledge and participants' imaginaries. Tools matter. They are not neutral (Cerratto-Pargman et al. 2015). For instance, the choice of postcards as the discursive space to shape futures and pasts, the guidelines selected to guide the participants to write the fictive narratives, and the language used in the questions formulated by the researchers to scaffold participants to discuss futures and automation, the images we pre-selected for the postcards, and the general atmosphere and safe space created during the speculative workshop are, among others, designed materials, research tools that configured the teachers' speculative fabulation experience. Such designed materials and tools are part and parcel of how the participating teachers valued the general activity and felt compelled to participate.

sections.title: # Where it is used and what it does
sections.text:
- HCI and technology studies: Design fabulation recasts design discourse by recovering silenced histories and testing alternative values and visions, especially in feminist technoscience and posthumanist HCI. It theorizes and demonstrates how technological values and visions could be different by bringing forth untold pasts and enacting feminist, more-than-human approaches [b1b1e362-3].
- Education and public engagement: Speculative fabulation and design fiction are used to surface futures of automation and datafication, engage publics, and provoke debate about desirable directions of travel for society. Speculative fabulation methods have been applied to K–12 and higher education, often integrating literary and social science techniques [4e862aab-3] Design fiction is used both to envision futures and to communicate innovations, shifting attention from narrow application testing to broader societal trajectories [4e862aab-3].
- Architecture and spatial design: Fabulation reimagines spatial and institutional environments by assembling improbable collaborations and more-than-human relations, offering alternatives to conventional planning logics. Speculative fabulation is framed as a mode of venturesome making-with to pluralize subjectivities in matter–meaning assemblages [48fc8029-2] It serves as a necessary counter-balance to instrumental planning by expanding interpretative horizons of interior worlds [48fc8029-4].
- Media/journalism adjacent practice: In media, “fabrication” denotes misleading production, while fabulation (as speculative narrative) emphasizes how storytelling constructs social reality and ethical engagement; design fabulation thus distinguishes imaginative, truth-seeking practices from deception. Storytelling is a core of journalism and creates models of social reality through interpretation and representation of meaning [9e2a70fd-1] To fabulate is not to turn away from reality or truth; it seeks correspondences between “reality which is fiction and fiction which is reality,” privileging situated knowledges and empathetic relation over universal truth claims [9e2a70fd-2] Speculative fabulation is an act of fabrication that can transform the real by re-storying protean, entangled times, resisting true/false and real/fiction dualisms [9e2a70fd-0].

Their impact has instilled optimism, sparked alternative visions, and been sites of countless critiques of conformity and the status quo. Loosely defined impulses towards the unrealisable and the most illogical of things approached in the most logical of ways have led to unparalleled episodes of creativity in drawings, poems, and material production. From Piranesi, Peter Greenaway, Kurt Schwitters, Dora Maar, Hans Op de Beeck, Ursula Le Guinn, John Hejduk, to Daniel Libeskind, explorations of the impossible have led to new interpretative frontiers that move the limits of interiority and spatial practices. Lest we forget or become complacent with the contributory and often unrecognised impact of contemporary social media, advertisement, and technological surveillance that continues to shape interior worlds, experiences, and values. In many ways, there is as much focus on unpacking, making sense of, and disproving the dangerous impacts of fictions, fantasies, and fabulations as there is on setting the scene for dreams and magical realities. 

This issue recognises the complex story of fictions, fantasies, and fabulations in spatial design, not as counter-productive forces, but as the necessary counter-balances that offer liberty from convention, propriety, and rational assumptions about behaviour, space, time, and materialthe core elements of interior worlds. Far from retreating into solipsistic escapism, fictions, fantasies, and fabulations serve as crucial sites for speculative invention, futuring, and critical reflection.

snippets:
It is impossible to not correlate storytelling and journalism. In journalism, storytelling is not just narrative technique, but the individual genre form. O. Samartsev (2009), the researcher of this problem, identifies two types of journalism type: new writing and features writing. The second type is narrative style and it includes storytelling. That is, storytelling is not only the style of telling, but also the active process of storytelling: "Storytelling is engaging the reader in empathy for the heroes, bringing the reader and actors closer together, setting problems of the work in such a way that it becomes close, understandable, appeals not only to the mind, but also to the emotions". 

Over time, storytelling in journalism becomes a more dynamic and detailed description of reality. In such way, journalism storytelling is peculiar tool to create a model of social reality. That is, the main goal is interpretation, representation and, directly, the generation of meanings, that is, narratives. In modern context of global informatisation, trust to a resource is a fundamental factor in its development and advancement. In such conditions, storytelling creates a special connection, a field to interaction between readers and journalists, editorial office of a magazine or newspaper, which is interested in a certain story. Such demand breeds supply: whole sections and columns in the journal. That is, audience requires a certain, interesting and unique content. In the modern typology of journalism genres, there are names that are close in meaning, which researchers give to texts written in the storytelling format: story, case story, history. Such names are more synonyms; their difference is in goals and tasks linked by practical focus and approximate structure. 

Modern media analytics and practitioners-journalists in reviews and articles devoted to storytelling often pay attention to the external specifics of such material. That is, an external, designer side is considered, which is in the peculiarities of the font design, selection of photos, graphic accompaniment, etc. However, practically no attention is paid to the content side. That is, the form in such cases prevails over the content.

snippets:
Based on Michael (2021), Ross differentiates between speculative fabulation, which is linked to the creation of stories, scenarios, vignettes, and speculative fabrication connected with artifacts, and objects enticing people to explore new 'inventive problems ' Michael (2021:80), or designed artifacts in the form of design fiction (Bleeker 2009). Following such a distinction, speculative fabulation methods have, for instance, been applied in the study of datafication and automation in K-12 education (Selwyn et al. 2020); Hillman et al. 2020), and higher education (Suoranta et al. 2022;Dator 2002). Such methods often use social science or techniques from the field of literary studies. 

Speculative fabrication methods, also called speculative fiction but better known as design fiction, have been underscored by Cox (2021) in education. Design fiction aims to question the present with glimpses from the future (Bleeker 2009) and is often defined as both a method for envisioning new futures and technologies and a tool for communicating innovations to researchers and the broader public (Tanenbaum 2014). Described as 'a conflation of design, science fact, and science fiction' (Bleeker 2009: 6), design fiction can be used 'to pose critical questions about the impact of technology on society and to actively engage wider publics in how technology is designed' (Cox 2021: 2). Cox (2021: 3) underscores that design fiction 'ha[s] the potential to change the scope of the debate by shifting attention away from the existing literature and its focus on developing and testing specific AI applications (Zawacki-Richter et al. 2019) to weighing up more or less desirable directions of travel for society'. 

Design fiction has been applied by Ross (2017) via Teacherbot, an automated agent participating in Twitter conversations problematizing and intervening in automated university teaching; Artcasting, a digital mobile prototype for art evaluation; and the Tweeting book, a 'prototype created to problematize the emphasis in learning analytics on human activity and data' (Ross 2017: 222). citations.title: What mosses can teach us about design fabulations and feminist more-than-human care
snippets: To fabulate does not mean turning away from reality or truth. Rather, fabulation is "an attempt to find more subtle correspondences between the reality which is fiction and the fiction which is reality" (Scholes, 1979, p. 8). It is impossible to fully understand other other, or fully comprehend the non-human, and empathy is not doing it for designers (Bennett & Rosner, 2019). Rather than the search for the universal truth of the reality of more-than-human worlds, fabulation seeks to tell the truth through flirting with fiction. In its ambiguity and openended meanings, fiction creates tensions with what is considered scientific knowledge. Instead fabulation creates relation with situated knowledges (Haraway, 1988), where storytelling practices seeking to tell the truth are done in situated and highly contextual spheres; they are embedded. Fabulation invites the possibility of seeing realities in and from new perspectives, ultimately contributing to a broader and more diverse understanding of the plurality of relations that make our more-than-human worlds. Such relations might not always be known, as they are constantly being made, and thus speculations toward what may (be)come might be more interesting than what was.

citations.title: Telling it slant with side curved head and curiosity: posthumanist/feminist materialist creative activations in university spaces
snippets:
Donna Haraway (2013) proposes speculative fabulation as figurations or narratives that act as material-semiotic nodes or knots in which diverse bodies and meanings co-shape one another; speculative fabulations 'stitch together improbable collaborations without worrying overmuch about conventional ontological kinds' (Haraway 2016, 136). Like Carstens (2020), we see speculative fabulation as a mode of 'venturesome makings-with' enabling us to further pluralize the 'I' in all manner of onto-assemblages, matter-meaning assemblages in which boundaries and conventions fray and bodies become in new relational knowings. We include below three co-composed speculative fabulations which aim to embrace 'uncomfortable yet productive tensions [activating] tactics of defamiliarization and cognitive estrangement' to enable 'slippages into [new] territories' (Carstens 2020, 76) for thinking, feeling and doing higher education differently. 

Speculative fabulation 1: Nonchalance, why not? 

We are nonchalant. And as we are nonchalant, you can be nonchalant too. 

We walk along campus paths, smiling, relaxed. 

At ease in our moving bodies. Nonchalance is an embodied practice. 

A form of Zen. 

Loafing in these campus spaces requires persistence.

sections.title: # Purposes and implications
sections.text: Design fabulation aims to expand ethical and epistemic horizons by: (a) recovering and foregrounding marginalized histories and nonhuman relations; (b) cultivating “otherwise” imaginaries that counter deterministic narratives of technological inevitability; and (c) enabling participatory speculation that links imaginative “what if” to actionable “nows.” It teaches neglected relations and de-centers the human to foster joy in caring for Earth and moralize just, vibrant futures [b1b1e362-4] It counters closure by asking researchers and educators to critically question dynamics of voice and engagement in speculative methods [4e862aab-4] Backcasting connects delightfully strange, multispecies fabulations to implementable steps, bridging imaginative futures and present-day design [4e862aab-0]. In spatial and institutional settings, it helps “stitch together” unlikely collaborations and refigure boundaries, supporting plural and more-than-human ways of being. Speculative fabulations act as material-semiotic nodes that co-shape diverse bodies and meanings, enabling slippages into new territories [48fc8029-2].
