citations.title: A novel method for intelligent operation and maintenance of transformers using deep visual large model DETR + X and digital twin
snippets: To achieve real-time monitoring and intelligent maintenance of transformers, a framework based on deep vision and digital twin has been developed. An enhanced visual detection model, DETR + X, is proposed, implementing multidimensional sample data augmentation through Swin2SR and GAN networks. This model converts one-dimensional DGA data into three-dimensional feature images based on Gram angle fields, facilitating the transformation and fusion of heterogeneous modal information. The Pyramid Vision Transformer (PVT) is innovatively adopted as the backbone for image feature extraction, replacing the traditional ResNet structure. A Deformable Attention mechanism is employed to handle the complex spatial structure of multi-scale features. Testing results indicate that the improved DETR + X model performs well in transformer state recognition tasks, achieving a classification accuracy of 100% for DGA feature maps. In object detection tasks, it surpasses advanced models such as Faster R-CNN, RetinaNet, YOLOv8, and Deformable DETR in terms of overall mAP50 scores, particularly demonstrating significant enhancements in small object detection. Furthermore, the Llava-7b model, fine-tuned based on domain expertise, serves as an expert decision-making tool for transformer maintenance, providing accurate operational recommendations based on visual detection results. Finally, based on digital twin and inference models, a comprehensive platform has been developed to achieve real-time monitoring and intelligent maintenance of transformers.

citations.title: Deep learning corrosion detection with confidence
snippets:
Corrosion of steel and other engineering alloys is an ongoing concern for society, as the resulting deterioration can result in significant consequences, environmental damage, and significant financial loss 1 . In studies that have sought to determine the annual cost arising from corrosion it is usually estimated to be between 3 and 4% of GDP 2 ; with between 15 and 35% of this amount thought to be avoidable, and a significant proportion relating to the cost of inspection 3 . 

Research into automated corrosion detection is driven by cost savings and risk mitigation, with several publications on the subject over the last decade [4][5][6][7][8][9] , prompted by improvements in deep learning, computer vision and the availability of increasing computing power. A comprehensive review of research into deep learning for materials degradation, including corrosion detection, was carried out and reported by Nash, Drummond and Birbilis 10 . Previous work by the authors demonstrated the ability of a deep learning model to produce semantic segmentation maps, labelling each pixel of an image as either corrosion, or, background 11,12 . The current state-of-the-art for corrosion detection trained three model architectures: FCN, U-Net and Mask R-CNN on a private dataset 9 . Using edge detection to refine the boundaries of detected areas the best performance was reported for the Mask R-CNN model, with an average F1-Score of 0.71. 

To date, no labelled corrosion image datasets have been openly published, and the aforementioned models are prone to misclassification of subjects that are not prevalent in the relatively small training set. In the consideration of practical (industrial) utility of deep learning semantic segmentation models to be useful, some measure of prediction uncertainty is required to avert either unnecessary or potentially costly decisions. Herein we deploy three variants of Bayesian deep learning to provide confidence estimates at the pixel level for corrosion detection. 

Deep learning model architectures such as LeNet 13 , AlexNet 14 , VGG 15 , DenseNet 16 and FCN 17 have set benchmarks in competitive computer vision exercises, demonstrating impressive gains in accuracy each year.

citations.title: Detection Transformer with Multi-Scale Fusion Attention Mechanism for Aero-Engine Turbine Blade Cast Defect Detection Considering Comprehensive Features
snippets:
As a result, CNN-based models frequently exhibit unsatisfactory multi-scale object detection capability in real industrial scenarios. 

Compared to traditional CNN-based methods, the transformer-based method has apparent advantages in global perception, long-distance dependency modeling, and multiscale detection; thus, it benefits from the introduction of innovative self-attention mechanisms. DETR [37], being the most representative work of transformer-based models, simplifies the object detection process and effectively removes some hand-designed components. As a result, this technique achieves real end-to-end object detection with the global modeling capability of transformers. For instance, Dang et al. [38] proposed an efficient and robust sewer defect localization system based on DETR, applying the transformer's self-attention mechanism to analyze sewer defect level and scope. Although object detection-based models have achieved higher detection precision and efficiency while reducing manual experience dependence due to the limitations of industrial complex environments, three crucial problems still reside in defect detection: 

(1) Due to the limited quantity of casting defects and the extremely imbalanced distribution of sample categories, it becomes challenging to collect sufficient data for model training to mitigate the risk of overfitting; (2) The complexity and variability in the size of casting defects pose significant challenges for the multi-scale object detection capabilities of existing object detection models. However, most current methods struggle with extracting multi-scale features, leading to a deficiency in mining deep semantic information and accurately locating objects; (3) Traditional defect detection methods rely on hand-designed components to improve detection precision, often based on extensive prior knowledge. However, this approach imposes significant limitations on their application across diverse industrial scenarios. 

To address the aforementioned challenges, a novel DETR technique with a multi-scale fusion attention mechanism for aero-engine turbine blade defect detection is proposed. This method considers comprehensive features, enabling multi-scale defect detection even with imbalanced datasets. A JDA method is introduced, combining Mix-Mos, Mixup, and Mosaic techniques to effectively enhance the quantity and diversity of the dataset. Additionally, an attention-based channel-adaptive weighting (ACAW) module is constructed to fully use the complementary information across feature channels, leading to the elimination of redundant feature information.

sections.title: # Takeaways and Trends (2022–2025)
sections.text:
- Hybrid CNN–Transformer segmenters and efficient transformer detectors are increasingly adopted for corrosion due to improved global context and boundary precision, with ablations showing edge-aware and multi-scale fusion modules are crucial for small pit segmentation. Edge-feature modules reduce false positives/negatives in corrosion pits [1f48817b-0]. SegFormer-based hybrids achieve ~89% mIoU with compact models [1f48817b-1]. DETR+X variants surpass Faster R-CNN/RetinaNet/YOLOv8 on complex, small-object detection tasks [4fd8c75e-0].
- Efficient, lightweight detectors (YOLOv5s derivatives, RT-DETR/DETR family with optimized backbones) are favored for deployment on drones and embedded systems, with explicit attention to compute, latency, and class imbalance. CBG-YOLOv5s targets embedded platforms [092a7b9c-2]. Data augmentation and attention modules mitigate small-sample and multi-scale issues [4fd8c75e-2]. Mask R-CNN remains a strong baseline; pixel-level accuracy demands careful model selection and hyperparameter tuning [4fd8c75e-4].
- Robust datasets and augmentation are essential; semi-supervised/representation learning and Bayesian uncertainty are being integrated to generalize across diverse environments and provide actionable confidence for industrial decisions. Autoencoder-based features enhance shallow classifiers for severity rating [092a7b9c-3]. Bayesian pixel-level confidence supports risk-aware inspection workflows [092a7b9c-4]. Collecting diverse, severe and poor corrosion cases addresses class imbalance and improves segmentation [4fd8c75e-4].

citations.title: A novel method for intelligent operation and maintenance of transformers using deep visual large model DETR + X and digital twin
snippets: To achieve real-time monitoring and intelligent maintenance of transformers, a framework based on deep vision and digital twin has been developed. An enhanced visual detection model, DETR + X, is proposed, implementing multidimensional sample data augmentation through Swin2SR and GAN networks. This model converts one-dimensional DGA data into three-dimensional feature images based on Gram angle fields, facilitating the transformation and fusion of heterogeneous modal information. The Pyramid Vision Transformer (PVT) is innovatively adopted as the backbone for image feature extraction, replacing the traditional ResNet structure. A Deformable Attention mechanism is employed to handle the complex spatial structure of multi-scale features. Testing results indicate that the improved DETR + X model performs well in transformer state recognition tasks, achieving a classification accuracy of 100% for DGA feature maps. In object detection tasks, it surpasses advanced models such as Faster R-CNN, RetinaNet, YOLOv8, and Deformable DETR in terms of overall mAP50 scores, particularly demonstrating significant enhancements in small object detection. Furthermore, the Llava-7b model, fine-tuned based on domain expertise, serves as an expert decision-making tool for transformer maintenance, providing accurate operational recommendations based on visual detection results. Finally, based on digital twin and inference models, a comprehensive platform has been developed to achieve real-time monitoring and intelligent maintenance of transformers.

citations.title: Deep learning corrosion detection with confidence
snippets:
Corrosion of steel and other engineering alloys is an ongoing concern for society, as the resulting deterioration can result in significant consequences, environmental damage, and significant financial loss 1 . In studies that have sought to determine the annual cost arising from corrosion it is usually estimated to be between 3 and 4% of GDP 2 ; with between 15 and 35% of this amount thought to be avoidable, and a significant proportion relating to the cost of inspection 3 . 

Research into automated corrosion detection is driven by cost savings and risk mitigation, with several publications on the subject over the last decade [4][5][6][7][8][9] , prompted by improvements in deep learning, computer vision and the availability of increasing computing power. A comprehensive review of research into deep learning for materials degradation, including corrosion detection, was carried out and reported by Nash, Drummond and Birbilis 10 . Previous work by the authors demonstrated the ability of a deep learning model to produce semantic segmentation maps, labelling each pixel of an image as either corrosion, or, background 11,12 . The current state-of-the-art for corrosion detection trained three model architectures: FCN, U-Net and Mask R-CNN on a private dataset 9 . Using edge detection to refine the boundaries of detected areas the best performance was reported for the Mask R-CNN model, with an average F1-Score of 0.71. 

To date, no labelled corrosion image datasets have been openly published, and the aforementioned models are prone to misclassification of subjects that are not prevalent in the relatively small training set. In the consideration of practical (industrial) utility of deep learning semantic segmentation models to be useful, some measure of prediction uncertainty is required to avert either unnecessary or potentially costly decisions. Herein we deploy three variants of Bayesian deep learning to provide confidence estimates at the pixel level for corrosion detection. 

Deep learning model architectures such as LeNet 13 , AlexNet 14 , VGG 15 , DenseNet 16 and FCN 17 have set benchmarks in competitive computer vision exercises, demonstrating impressive gains in accuracy each year.

However, most current methods struggle with extracting multi-scale features, leading to a deficiency in mining deep semantic information and accurately locating objects; (3) Traditional defect detection methods rely on hand-designed components to improve detection precision, often based on extensive prior knowledge. However, this approach imposes significant limitations on their application across diverse industrial scenarios. 

To address the aforementioned challenges, a novel DETR technique with a multi-scale fusion attention mechanism for aero-engine turbine blade defect detection is proposed. This method considers comprehensive features, enabling multi-scale defect detection even with imbalanced datasets. A JDA method is introduced, combining Mix-Mos, Mixup, and Mosaic techniques to effectively enhance the quantity and diversity of the dataset. Additionally, an attention-based channel-adaptive weighting (ACAW) module is constructed to fully use the complementary information across feature channels, leading to the elimination of redundant feature information.

sections.title: # Practical Guidance
sections.text:
- Choose Mask R-CNN or SegFormer-based hybrids for pixel-accurate corrosion maps where boundary precision matters; expect F1 ≈ 0.71 on private datasets and up to ~89% mIoU with specialized modules for pits. Mask R-CNN achieved F1 ≈ 0.71 with edge refinement [092a7b9c-4]. SegFormer variants reached 89.32% mIoU with edge/feature fusion [1f48817b-1].
- For inspection robots/drones, prefer lightweight YOLO variants or real-time DETR derivatives (RT-DETR) with efficient backbones (PVT) and deformable attention for small-object detection; quantify compute and memory constraints early. CBG-YOLOv5s emphasizes small size and high speed [092a7b9c-2]. DETR+X with PVT and deformable attention improved mAP50 and small-object detection [4fd8c75e-0]. RT-DETR targets real-time inference for industrial defects [4fd8c75e-3].
- For severity classification, combine autoencoder-derived features with SVM/RF/XGBoost to cut annotation costs while maintaining performance; consider Bayesian or ensemble methods for decision confidence. VAE features improved shallow classifiers for severity [092a7b9c-3]. Bayesian models provide pixel-level confidence for segmentation-based decisions [092a7b9c-4].
- Invest in diverse, high-quality datasets spanning lighting, angles, and corrosion progression; use mixing-based augmentation and uncertainty estimation to mitigate class imbalance and out-of-distribution risks. Diverse images across severity and conditions improve segmentation and address class imbalance [4fd8c75e-4]. JDA/ Mixup/Mosaic and attention modules help with small samples and multi-scale variation [4fd8c75e-2].

In YOLOv8, the default task is object detection, which involves detecting and localizing objects in an image or video. citations.title: Detection and recognition of metal surface corrosion based on CBG-YOLOv5s
snippets:
Currently, methods for detecting corrosion on metal surfaces can be classified into two main categories: one is based on physical or chemical principles, and the other uses computer vision technology for detection. 

Detection methods based on physical or chemical processes primarily use the physical or chemical changes that occur on the metal surface during the corrosion process to assess the condition and degree of metal corrosion. These methods include electrochemical methods, resistance methods, ultrasonic waves, and spectroscopy, among others. Compared with traditional manual visual methods, these detection methods can directly measure the corrosion parameters of the metal surface, such as potential, current, resistance, sound speed, and magnetic field and spectrum, and reflect the corrosion status of the metal surface from these parameters. However, these detection methods require professional instruments and operator. 

With the constant advancement of computer technology, computer vision has been extensively applied to the field of corrosion detection. Researchers have begun to utilise the computer vision technology for classification and object detection of corrosion images. This allows for an intuitive presentation of the corrosion morphology and distribution on the metal surface, and enables efficient and accurate processing of a large amount of image data, thereby enhancing detection efficiency and accuracy. Although traditional detection methods based on computer vision have seen some improvements, their accuracy has not yet reached the desired level, and their operation is not sufficiently convenient. Deep learning has brought new ideas to object detection. Convolutional neural networks [4] can extract high-level features, thereby significantly improving classification accuracy. However, current object detection approaches based on deep learning suffer from issues such as loss of metal corrosion information due to model training on open source datasets, large model size, and inability to meet practical application requirements. 

Therefore, we selected the most widely used YOLOv5s model in the YOLO series [5][6][7][8] as the basis and designed a more lightweight CBG-YOLOv5s object detection model. This model has the benefits of small size, high speed and high accuracy, which theoretically supports deployment on embedded platforms. 

The study's main contributions can be summarised as follows: 

1. We have developed a corrosion detection model for metal surfaces, called CBG-YOLOv5s. This model can classify metal surfaces into three corrosion levels based on their texture, colour, and depth of the corrosion.

question: Recent advancements in software defined radio

sections.title: # Overview: From Generalized Platforms to Reconfigurable Ecosystems
sections.text: Software-defined radio (SDR) continues to evolve from a flexible baseband-centric concept into a pervasive, reconfigurable platform that spans PHY-layer experimentation, multi-domain operations, and integrated network control in beyond‑5G systems. Joseph Mitola’s seminal “software radio” vision emphasized using software rather than fixed hardware to design radio systems, and subsequent surveys highlighted programmable RF modules, high-speed ADC/DAC, and the SDR developer ecosystem and challenges [5f8b655e-1]. At the same time, both radio-level and network-level functionality are moving onto software-reconfigurable platforms, with SDRs widely available off‑the‑shelf and O‑RAN driving open RAN architectures [5f8b655e-3]. Modern prototyping frameworks such as WISCANet explicitly leverage accessible SDR devices and networks to accelerate B5G/6G radio system development [5f8b655e-4]. On the application side, commodity SDR stacks (e.g., GNU Radio) and devices (e.g., USRP, HackRF, RTL‑SDR) have enabled programmable radios that dynamically switch bands and support low‑level signal processing for tasks like FMCW radar [5f8b655e-2].

citations.title: WISCANet: A Rapid Development Platform for Beyond 5G and 6G Radio System Prototyping
snippets: In this section, we briefly survey recent advances in B5G/6G technologies, softwaredefined radios, and related SDR testbeds developed by other organizations. The WISCANet software architecture was specifically motivated by the accessibility of Ettus SDR devices and similar SDR network testbeds described in Section 2.3. We further compare WISCANet to traditional approaches in Section 2.5 to highlight the advantages and acknowledge the disadvantages of our solution.

citations.title: Wireless Ranging for Contactless Cognitive Load Inference in Ubiquitous Computing
snippets:
Software-defined radio (SDR) is a concept for a programmable radio communication system and it usually consists of a personal computer with analog-to-digital converter and RF front-end (see Figure 20). This functionality produces general-purpose processor that introduces flexibility for signal processing and makes special-purpose hardware somehow obsolete. The concept is not new; however, recent evolving capabilities have led to its popularity. 

One of the most useful SDR advantages is its flexibility. Legacy radios are constrained with RF front-end and, unlike SDRs, do not have the capabilities to be arbitrarily programmed. If we look at smartphones and similar devices, they currently have many different radios optimized for signals operating on different frequency bands (WiFi, LTE, GSM, UMTS, GPS) (Stewart et al., 2015). Implementation of a single SDR in such devices could dynamically switch between various frequency bands with a software code. Some of the most popular commercially available SDR devices are USRP, HackRF and RTL-SDR. Because of its flexibility and our experimental nature of problem we decided to use SDR. One of the reasons for SDR is also FMCW radar. SDR allows us to do advanced signal processing that requires access to low-level radio data. 

We implement Wi-Mind on commodity software-defined radio software framework and using off-the-shelf hardware. Our software is based on GNU Radio (2018), a free and opensource development toolkit for SDR programming. GNU Radio applications are constructed as connected blocks known as "flowgraphs" (Figure 19). We use an FMCW radar implementation provided with a GNU Radio extension gr-radar and add the following functionalities: 

• we lock the distance to specific range (i.e. FFT bin); • we extract the phase of the received signal and timestamps for each phase sample. 

For hardware, we use Ettus Research Universal Software Radio Peripheral (USRP) B210. The product has RF coverage from 70 MHz to 6 GHz and is able to use multiple antennas. Since the nature of FMCW radar requires full-duplex transmission (radar receives the signal at the same time as it is sending signal with another frequency) we opted for USRP B210.

citations.title: Software-defined Radios: Architecture, State-of-the-art, and Challenges
snippets:
Joseph Mitola III was the first to use the term "Software Radio" in 1993, and published an important work introducing and explaining the concept of using software rather than traditionally used hardware for designing radio systems [194]. In an interesting early survey (1999) [195] on the "then" emerging technology, namely SDR, the authors made the case that SDRs have a great potential to advance and facilitate the development of communication standards such as WiFi and cellular networks. In a review published a few years later [22], the author paid close attention to the hardware component of SDRs, such as programmable RF modules and high-performance DACs and ADCs, as more technological advancement had been made. 

There are very few notable works to survey and review different SDR platforms and testbeds. One such survey is the work by [38], where the author discusses the challenges SDR developers face. These challenges include size, weight, power, software architecture, security, certification and business opportunities. While this work is important for compiling information about these challenges and presenting them in one place, it stays away from enumerating the different SDR platforms, implementation approaches and their applications in the communication standards world. 

In that regard, the authors of [196] compare the SDR platforms developed by the year 2012 and give a brief description of what each platform entails. It lacks, however, any detailed comparison based on the different categories of computational power, energy efficiency, flexibility, adaptability, and cost. It is through these comparisons that a designer is able to make an informed decision on what platform to adopt for their specific application. The authors of [197] attempt to list and review several DSP-based SDR platforms from both academia and industry, with more focus on commercial solutions, and then providing a simple comparison between them in terms of programmability, power, and flexibility. However, what this work lacks, in addition to being outdated, is the discussion of FPGAs (mentioned only one example) and hardware/software co-design solutions, and a methodical analysis of different design approaches based on a set of performance metrics. 

Authors of [198] presented a survey of a few SDR platforms that had been developed more than a decade ago.

citations.title: Challenges and Opportunities for Beyond-5G Wireless Security
snippets:
Software-Defined Radios and Networks: Both radio-level and network-level functionality are moving to platforms that can be readily reconfigured through software. The capabilities of software-defined radios (SDRs) continue to improve, and they are widely available commercially-off-the-shelf throughout the world. Software-defined networks (SDNs) are also in widespread use due to their offered flexibility in network reconfiguration. There is also the emerging open-radio access network (O-RAN) movement that may soon revolutionize how wireless networks are implemented and commercialized. 

These technology areas have led to many vibrant research directions in communications and networking. At the same time, these areas have generated unforeseen security challenges that will greatly impact radio and network operation moving forward. The vast majority of research at the physical layer has focused on optimizing performance metrics such as spectral efficiency (bits/second/Hz), network efficiency (bits/second/Hz/area), and latency (seconds), while often ignoring any security constraints that arise. 

Wireless communication and networking researchers can no longer afford to conduct research that does not consider security challenges. In this paper, we discuss the emerging security challenges of beyond-5G wireless systems, and explore research directions aimed at addressing these challenges.

sections.title: # Wideband and Multiband Operation: Radar and Communications
sections.text: Recent SDR systems increasingly target wide instantaneous bandwidths and multiband/multi-function operation to meet the demands of radar and high‑throughput communications. Commercialized, modular SDRs with tunable filters and FPGA/SoC backends have proliferated across land, air, sea, space, and cyber domains, with 6G’s multi-band needs amplifying interest in reconfigurable radios spanning 1 MHz to 30 GHz [bff28889-0]. A concrete SDR-based prototype using USRPs demonstrated sub‑6 GHz operation with a maximum instantaneous bandwidth of 160 MHz for communication-aware radar waveforms [bff28889-3]. In radar, SDR has enabled coherent multiband and multifunction capabilities by combining multiple RF carriers for short- and far‑range detection, improving robustness to weather and enhancing detection under adverse conditions. Independent hardware per band can be coordinated via software to provide reconfigurable, multifunctional sensing with a smaller footprint [bff28889-1]. These capabilities translate to high‑performance, reconfigurable MIMO radar: a 64‑channel AESA radar built on commercial SDRs operated in C‑band and supported real‑time 3D MIMO detection/localization with a 3‑second refresh rate, with orthogonalization via TDM/FDM/CDM selectable at runtime. The system’s user‑selectable parameters and rapid hardware‑free reconfiguration illustrate SDR’s value for adapting radar behavior to environment without redesign [bff28889-2].

citations.title: Dual-band System composed by a Photonics-based Radar and a Focal-Point/Cassegrain Parabolic Antenna
snippets:
Currently, most transceivers operate only in a single band. New architectures have been proposed to simultaneously operate in multiple bands, by using independent hardware for each band [1], [2]. 

Future generations of radar systems aim to meet reconfigurability, multi-functionality and small footprint characteristics in order to provide improved sensors networks [3]. In this context, in the past few years, researchers have proposed photonics-based radar technologies to achieve coherent multiband and multi-functionality capability, by applying software-defined radio (SDR) [4]- [6]. In this way, multiple radiofrequency carriers are combined for enabling short-and far-range detections.

Therefore, a multiband radar transceiver increases the system robustness in terms of climatic variations, providing enhanced detection capability even in adverse conditions. citations.title: Coexistence of Communications and Cognitive MIMO Radar: Waveform Design and Prototype
snippets:
Particularly, a set of transmit sequences is designed to focus the emitted energy in the bands suggested by the spectrum sensing module while limiting the out-of-band interference. The waveforms, along with the receive processing, are designed to enhance the radar detection performance. The designed system is then demonstrated for the representative scenario of Fig. 1 using a custom built Software-Defined Radio (SDR) based prototype developed on Universal Software Radio Peripheral (USRP)s1 from National Instruments (NI) [13], [14]. These USRPs operate at sub-6 GHz frequencies with a maximum instantaneous bandwidth of 160 MHz. 

A. Background and Related Works a) Coexistence of Communication Systems: Spectral coexistence has been found to be a promising method to alleviate the spectrum scarcity problem. For example, in the ISM band, several wireless standards operate on overlapping frequency bands such as the IEEE 802.11 (popularly known as Wi-Fi) and the IEEE 802.15.4 (popularly known as ZigBee) family of standards in the 2.4 GHz ISM band. As the ISM band does not require a license to transmit, the participating standards transmit at will (frequency and power) leading to interference and a loss of throughput [15]- [17]. Similarly, in the 5 GHz ISM band, it has been speculated that there will be interference between IEEE 802.11n/ac and Long Term Evolution (LTE) [18]. For the two aforementioned interference scenarios, several spectral coexistence methods like successive Interference Cancellation (SIC) [19], [20] for single antenna and Technology Independent Multi-Output (TIMO) [21]- [23] for multi-antennas have been proposed. 

b) Radar-Communication Coexistence: The interfered bands, including those occupied by communications, are not useful for the radar system, and traditional radars aim to mitigate these frequencies at their receivers. To avoid energy wasted due to transmissions on these bands while pursuing coexistence applications, research into the transmit strategy of spectrally shaped radar waveforms has been driving coexistence studies since the last decade [24]- [32].

snippets: Compact, modular and programmable multi-band multi-channel radios with tunable filter accessories have been commercialized. The software defined radio (SDR) paradigm has emerged and is effectively used across all domains. Studies are conducted in land [3,4], air [5,6], sea [7,8], space [6,7] and cyber [9,10] domains. The SDR and communication platforms are commercialized with field-programmable gate arrays (FPGA) and system on a chip (SoC). Advanced algorithms, edge computing and parallelism empower adaptive signal processing in near real time [11,12]. There are a number of challenges and open problems in the design of SDRs [13][14][15][16]. The 6G cellular technology requires new solutions, which amplify the use of multi-band SDRs [17,18]. An all-domain command and control framework and 6G wireless technology imply the design of next-generation communication platforms to ensure communication superiority and seamless information sharing [19]. Robust multi-band wireless cellular technologies with learning capabilities [20,21] are emerging. A consistent integration of a frontend module with a variable-gain amplifier and FPGA enables high-performance processing, networking, robustness, speed, control, filtering, reconfigurability, signal conversion and interfacing.

citations.title: Real-Time Multiple Input Multiple Output (MIMO) Radar Using Software Defined Radio
snippets: In this paper, commercially-available software-defined radios (SDRs) are used to build a 64-channel, reconfigurable Active Electronically Scanned Arrays (AESA) radar operating in C-band (NATO G-band). The SDRs are used to design and implement a 3-dimensional multi-input and multi-output (MIMO) radar. The flexibility of the SDRs has been harnessed to evaluate the performance of a linear frequency modulated continuous wave (LFMCW) MIMO radar using three different methods of achieving the orthogonality, namely Time Division Multiplexing (TDM), Frequency Division Multiplexing (FDM), and Code Division Multiplexing (CDM). In addition, the radar’s parameters are user-selectable and can be rapidly changed such that the radar can be used in different environments without requiring changes to the hardware. Measurements indicate that the radar is capable of detecting and localizing multiple targets in all 3-dimensions, including bearing, range, and Doppler. The MIMO radar operates in real-time, with a refresh rate of only 3 seconds. Experimental results are generated for the TDM mode of operation with further research reporting on the CDM and FDM modes of operation.

sections.title: # Reconfigurable Waveforms and Satellite Systems (DVB‑S2X, IoRT)
sections.text: SDR has become the backbone for deploying and validating next‑generation satellite waveforms and reconfigurable gateway functions. A closed‑loop 16×16 precoded DVB‑S2X satellite gateway demonstrator executed scrambling, encoding, framing, modulation, pulse‑shaping, and MMSE precoding entirely on‑board commercial SDRs (USRP) in real time [62b5f091-0]. An FPGA‑based DVB‑S2X transmitter implemented on a USRP Kintex‑7 demonstrated superframe structures with orthogonal Walsh pilots and SINR pilots, jointly precoded with data to evaluate multi‑beam, joint transmission schemes over a live GEO link [62b5f091-1]. Beyond performance, SDR enables rapid protocol reconfiguration: a reconfigurable satellite gateway swapped between DVB‑S2X and E‑SSA uplink/downlink in 10 s when modules were local, and performed protocol reconfiguration over a DVB‑S2X link adding roughly 6–25 s depending on module size and system steps, illustrating practical timescales for software‑driven radio resource orchestration. Such measurements quantify the latency envelope for SDR‑based protocol agility in gateway control [62b5f091-2]. On low‑frequency/line‑of‑sight links, SDR‑based OFDM testing shows that modulation choice, FFT size, cyclic prefix, and pilot placement materially affect packet error rate, with BPSK outperforming QPSK/8PSK in PER and larger FFTs reducing PER at the cost of computational complexity and ICI risk, motivating adaptive modulation and coding in future SDR designs. These results point to software‑driven waveform optimization loops that react to channel and traffic dynamics [62b5f091-4].

snippets:
To ensure that the reconfigurability mechanisms are fully functional, a set of manual tests were performed. The focus was on uploading a new satellite module which would offer support for a different set of uplink/downlink protocols. As the modulator and demodulator implementations were already available for both DVB-S2X and E-SSA protocols, a protocol swap test scenario was defined and executed. First, the DVB-S2X receiver and the E-SSA transmitter were loaded on the first USRP. Then, the zip files containing the DVB-S2X Test transmitter and the E-SSA Test receiver were transmitted via the coax link to the device under test (Fig. 11). When the confirmation was received, that the modules were successfully installed, a new System Config file was sent to the device under test in which DVB-S2X was set as uplink protocol and E-SSA as downlink protocol. While the device under test was rebooting, the first USRP was reconfigured to use the E-SSA transmitter and the DVB-S2X receiver. After the reboot was completed, a control message was sent via the DVB-S2X uplink. It was observed that the sensor node reacted accordingly and that a confirmation message was received via the E-SSA downlink. 

As for the timing, an overall reconfiguration performed with the new module available locally, took up to 10 seconds (including the time required for the configuration file to be sent over the satellite link). In case of a satellite link protocol reconfiguration, the overall duration was longer, especially for the case when the module for the desired satellite communication protocol was not available on the gateway. In this case the time required to upload the new module has to be taken into consideration. For example uploading a new module with a size of 1.5 Mb over a DVB-S2X link with MODCOD 1 (QPSK, 1/4 FEC, 400 kSym/s) selected will add an average of 6 seconds to the overall duration. Adding the installation time, configuration change and system reboot resulted in an overall duration of up to 25 seconds.

sections.title: # Digital Beamforming and Array Calibration on SDR
sections.text: At millimeter‑wave frequencies, SDR platforms support full digital beamforming and array control, enabling agile beam shaping and steering through baseband software. A 28 GHz SDR beamforming system implemented on USRP demonstrated radiation patterns that matched simulation while allowing simple beam shaping and steering by digitally controlling amplitude and phase per channel [725bdff9-2]. A complementary millimeter‑wave SDR beamforming architecture described RF front‑ends, radiating elements, and host‑based baseband processing, validating the approach in anechoic measurements [725bdff9-3]. As arrays scale, mutual coupling, component nonidealities, and environmental variations degrade beam quality unless accounted for; self‑calibration methods are needed to maintain performance. Large‑scale phased arrays for 5G/6G rely on architectures that can be active, hybrid, or fully digital, but RF component nonlinearities, phase shifters, filters, ADC/DAC imperfections, mechanical and thermal effects, and position errors cause unequal element excitation and beam degradation, motivating self‑online calibration to correct mutual coupling and channel impairments [725bdff9-1].

citations.title: Antenna Design for Microwave and Millimeter Wave Applications: Latest Advances and Prospects
snippets: Based on the flexibility of software-defined radio (SDR) techniques applied to an array of antennas, this paper [6] presented a beamforming architecture designed to operate in millimeter-wave bands (28 GHz), with possible applications in radar and 5G systems. The system structure, including its main constituents such as the radio frequency (RF) front-end modules, the radiating elements as well as the baseband processing on the host computer, were widely described. Beamforming was achieved by digitally controlling the signals that fed the antennas. The experimental measurements performed in an anechoic chamber validated the proposed approach.

citations.title: Software-Defined Radio Beamforming System for 5G/Radar Applications
snippets: In this work, a 28 GHz SDR beamforming antenna system was proposed for 5G, radar or IoT applications. All the analog and digital modules were properly developed and described, allowing us to obtain a system operating in the Ka band. The use of USRP enabled a flexible and versatile architecture since all its characteristics could be adjusted digitally. The experimental results have shown good agreement between the simulated and measured radiation patterns. It was possible to verify techniques to shape the beam of the array, as well as steering it, in a simple way, through the control of the signal amplitude and phase of each channel in the USRP. This system demonstrates great flexibility and scalability to be used in a wide range of equipment, especially in radar, mobile and satellite communication systems.

sections.title: # Software Ecosystems and Testbeds
sections.text: Modern SDR advances are enabled by mature, open software ecosystems and accessible hardware. GNU Radio provides a block‑based, open‑source framework where researchers can implement baseband flows, integrate extensions like gr‑radar, and run experiments on commodity hardware such as the Ettus USRP B210 (70 MHz–6 GHz), which supports full‑duplex FMCW radar processing for applications like contactless sensing [5f8b655e-2]. WISCANet’s software architecture explicitly leverages Ettus SDR devices and SDR network testbeds to accelerate B5G/6G prototyping, comparing to traditional approaches to highlight advantages and disadvantages [5f8b655e-4]. In communications and spectrum management, SDR testbeds have also been used to evaluate resilient, multi‑band, multi‑domain operations across HF to SHF bands with integrated FPGA/SoC backends and near‑real‑time adaptive processing. These platforms support electromagnetic spectrum evaluation and machine‑reasoning algorithms for robust communication under C/CT/CW spectrum constraints [bff28889-0].

citations.title: WISCANet: A Rapid Development Platform for Beyond 5G and 6G Radio System Prototyping
snippets: In this section, we briefly survey recent advances in B5G/6G technologies, softwaredefined radios, and related SDR testbeds developed by other organizations. The WISCANet software architecture was specifically motivated by the accessibility of Ettus SDR devices and similar SDR network testbeds described in Section 2.3. We further compare WISCANet to traditional approaches in Section 2.5 to highlight the advantages and acknowledge the disadvantages of our solution.

citations.title: Wireless Ranging for Contactless Cognitive Load Inference in Ubiquitous Computing
snippets:
Software-defined radio (SDR) is a concept for a programmable radio communication system and it usually consists of a personal computer with analog-to-digital converter and RF front-end (see Figure 20). This functionality produces general-purpose processor that introduces flexibility for signal processing and makes special-purpose hardware somehow obsolete. The concept is not new; however, recent evolving capabilities have led to its popularity. 

One of the most useful SDR advantages is its flexibility. Legacy radios are constrained with RF front-end and, unlike SDRs, do not have the capabilities to be arbitrarily programmed. If we look at smartphones and similar devices, they currently have many different radios optimized for signals operating on different frequency bands (WiFi, LTE, GSM, UMTS, GPS) (Stewart et al., 2015). Implementation of a single SDR in such devices could dynamically switch between various frequency bands with a software code. Some of the most popular commercially available SDR devices are USRP, HackRF and RTL-SDR. Because of its flexibility and our experimental nature of problem we decided to use SDR. One of the reasons for SDR is also FMCW radar. SDR allows us to do advanced signal processing that requires access to low-level radio data. 

We implement Wi-Mind on commodity software-defined radio software framework and using off-the-shelf hardware. Our software is based on GNU Radio (2018), a free and opensource development toolkit for SDR programming. GNU Radio applications are constructed as connected blocks known as "flowgraphs" (Figure 19). We use an FMCW radar implementation provided with a GNU Radio extension gr-radar and add the following functionalities: 

• we lock the distance to specific range (i.e. FFT bin); • we extract the phase of the received signal and timestamps for each phase sample. 

For hardware, we use Ettus Research Universal Software Radio Peripheral (USRP) B210. The product has RF coverage from 70 MHz to 6 GHz and is able to use multiple antennas. Since the nature of FMCW radar requires full-duplex transmission (radar receives the signal at the same time as it is sending signal with another frequency) we opted for USRP B210.

sections.title: # Integration with O‑RAN and Security‑Aware SDR
sections.text: Beyond the radio, SDR concepts are converging with software‑defined networking and open RAN to create programmable end‑to‑end systems. The O‑RAN movement aims to revolutionize wireless network implementation and commercialization, bringing software‑reconfigurable radios together with SDN/NFV control for flexible, policy‑driven operation [5f8b655e-3]. This integration has exposed new security challenges: while much PHY research optimizes spectral efficiency, latency, and power, security constraints and adversarial conditions must now be considered in SDR‑centric designs for beyond‑5G systems. The literature calls for research directions that incorporate security into radio and network operation, recognizing that SDR’s flexibility can also introduce new attack surfaces [5f8b655e-3].

citations.title: Challenges and Opportunities for Beyond-5G Wireless Security
snippets:
Software-Defined Radios and Networks: Both radio-level and network-level functionality are moving to platforms that can be readily reconfigured through software. The capabilities of software-defined radios (SDRs) continue to improve, and they are widely available commercially-off-the-shelf throughout the world. Software-defined networks (SDNs) are also in widespread use due to their offered flexibility in network reconfiguration. There is also the emerging open-radio access network (O-RAN) movement that may soon revolutionize how wireless networks are implemented and commercialized. 

These technology areas have led to many vibrant research directions in communications and networking. At the same time, these areas have generated unforeseen security challenges that will greatly impact radio and network operation moving forward. The vast majority of research at the physical layer has focused on optimizing performance metrics such as spectral efficiency (bits/second/Hz), network efficiency (bits/second/Hz/area), and latency (seconds), while often ignoring any security constraints that arise. 

Wireless communication and networking researchers can no longer afford to conduct research that does not consider security challenges. In this paper, we discuss the emerging security challenges of beyond-5G wireless systems, and explore research directions aimed at addressing these challenges.

sections.title: # Practical Performance Bounds and Trade‑offs
sections.text: Recent SDR systems quantify real‑time performance envelopes and software‑driven trade‑offs that were impractical in earlier generations. A C‑band SDR‑based AESA radar achieved real‑time 3D MIMO detection with a 3‑s refresh, demonstrating that software‑controlled waveform multiplexing (TDM/FDM/CDM) and parameter tuning can be executed without hardware changes [bff28889-2]. Satellite gateways have demonstrated real‑time execution of DVB‑S2X physical‑layer functions (scrambling, encoding, framing, modulation, pulse‑shaping, and MMSE precoding) on commercial SDRs, validating multi‑beam, joint transmission designs under realistic impairments [62b5f091-0]. FPGA implementations of DVB‑S2X transmitters on USRPs show practical pilot and superframe structures for channel estimation and SINR feedback that align with OFDM control mechanisms [62b5f091-1]. Protocol reconfiguration on SDR gateways can be completed in roughly 10–25 s depending on module availability and traffic overhead, which constrains control‑plane latency for dynamic spectrum access and service switching [62b5f091-2]. On HF NVIS links, SDR‑based OFDM optimization shows clear PER sensitivity to modulation, FFT size, cyclic prefix, and pilot placement, underscoring the need for adaptive, software‑driven waveform selection under time‑varying channels [62b5f091-4].

The flexibility of the SDRs has been harnessed to evaluate the performance of a linear frequency modulated continuous wave (LFMCW) MIMO radar using three different methods of achieving the orthogonality, namely Time Division Multiplexing (TDM), Frequency Division Multiplexing (FDM), and Code Division Multiplexing (CDM). In addition, the radar’s parameters are user-selectable and can be rapidly changed such that the radar can be used in different environments without requiring changes to the hardware. Measurements indicate that the radar is capable of detecting and localizing multiple targets in all 3-dimensions, including bearing, range, and Doppler. The MIMO radar operates in real-time, with a refresh rate of only 3 seconds. Experimental results are generated for the TDM mode of operation with further research reporting on the CDM and FDM modes of operation.

sections.title: # Outlook: AI‑Native, Multimodal, and Integrated SDR
sections.text: The trajectory points toward AI‑native SDRs that combine digital beamforming, adaptive waveform shaping, and learning‑based control within FPGA/SoC pipelines, supported by open software ecosystems and integrated with O‑RAN controllers. Near‑real‑time adaptive signal processing empowered by edge computing and parallelism is already improving resilience and reconfigurability across HF–SHF bands [bff28889-0]. Hardware trends continue to emphasize programmable RF, high‑speed converters, and FPGAs/SoCs as the backbone for SDR, while surveys catalog platform trade‑offs in flexibility, adaptability, and energy efficiency [5f8b655e-1]. As SDRs fuse with SDN and O‑RAN, the software‑defined paradigm extends from the air‑interface into network orchestration, shifting optimization toward holistic spectrum, security, and latency objectives [5f8b655e-3].

citations.title: Challenges and Opportunities for Beyond-5G Wireless Security
snippets:
Software-Defined Radios and Networks: Both radio-level and network-level functionality are moving to platforms that can be readily reconfigured through software. The capabilities of software-defined radios (SDRs) continue to improve, and they are widely available commercially-off-the-shelf throughout the world. Software-defined networks (SDNs) are also in widespread use due to their offered flexibility in network reconfiguration. There is also the emerging open-radio access network (O-RAN) movement that may soon revolutionize how wireless networks are implemented and commercialized. 

These technology areas have led to many vibrant research directions in communications and networking. At the same time, these areas have generated unforeseen security challenges that will greatly impact radio and network operation moving forward. The vast majority of research at the physical layer has focused on optimizing performance metrics such as spectral efficiency (bits/second/Hz), network efficiency (bits/second/Hz/area), and latency (seconds), while often ignoring any security constraints that arise. 

Wireless communication and networking researchers can no longer afford to conduct research that does not consider security challenges. In this paper, we discuss the emerging security challenges of beyond-5G wireless systems, and explore research directions aimed at addressing these challenges.

snippets: Compact, modular and programmable multi-band multi-channel radios with tunable filter accessories have been commercialized. The software defined radio (SDR) paradigm has emerged and is effectively used across all domains. Studies are conducted in land [3,4], air [5,6], sea [7,8], space [6,7] and cyber [9,10] domains. The SDR and communication platforms are commercialized with field-programmable gate arrays (FPGA) and system on a chip (SoC). Advanced algorithms, edge computing and parallelism empower adaptive signal processing in near real time [11,12]. There are a number of challenges and open problems in the design of SDRs [13][14][15][16]. The 6G cellular technology requires new solutions, which amplify the use of multi-band SDRs [17,18]. An all-domain command and control framework and 6G wireless technology imply the design of next-generation communication platforms to ensure communication superiority and seamless information sharing [19]. Robust multi-band wireless cellular technologies with learning capabilities [20,21] are emerging. A consistent integration of a frontend module with a variable-gain amplifier and FPGA enables high-performance processing, networking, robustness, speed, control, filtering, reconfigurability, signal conversion and interfacing.

citations.title: Software-defined Radios: Architecture, State-of-the-art, and Challenges
snippets:
Joseph Mitola III was the first to use the term "Software Radio" in 1993, and published an important work introducing and explaining the concept of using software rather than traditionally used hardware for designing radio systems [194]. In an interesting early survey (1999) [195] on the "then" emerging technology, namely SDR, the authors made the case that SDRs have a great potential to advance and facilitate the development of communication standards such as WiFi and cellular networks. In a review published a few years later [22], the author paid close attention to the hardware component of SDRs, such as programmable RF modules and high-performance DACs and ADCs, as more technological advancement had been made. 

There are very few notable works to survey and review different SDR platforms and testbeds. One such survey is the work by [38], where the author discusses the challenges SDR developers face. These challenges include size, weight, power, software architecture, security, certification and business opportunities. While this work is important for compiling information about these challenges and presenting them in one place, it stays away from enumerating the different SDR platforms, implementation approaches and their applications in the communication standards world. 

In that regard, the authors of [196] compare the SDR platforms developed by the year 2012 and give a brief description of what each platform entails. It lacks, however, any detailed comparison based on the different categories of computational power, energy efficiency, flexibility, adaptability, and cost. It is through these comparisons that a designer is able to make an informed decision on what platform to adopt for their specific application. The authors of [197] attempt to list and review several DSP-based SDR platforms from both academia and industry, with more focus on commercial solutions, and then providing a simple comparison between them in terms of programmability, power, and flexibility. However, what this work lacks, in addition to being outdated, is the discussion of FPGAs (mentioned only one example) and hardware/software co-design solutions, and a methodical analysis of different design approaches based on a set of performance metrics. 

Authors of [198] presented a survey of a few SDR platforms that had been developed more than a decade ago.

sections.title: # Key Takeaways
sections.text:
- Wideband and multiband SDRs now routinely span 160 MHz instantaneous bandwidths and support coherent multi‑carrier radar, enabling robust short/long‑range sensing with software‑controlled beamforming and MIMO operation at Ka‑band and beyond. A USRP‑based SDR prototype demonstrated 160 MHz instantaneous bandwidth for software‑defined waveforms [bff28889-3]. A 64‑channel AESA radar built on commercial SDRs achieved real‑time 3D MIMO localization with a 3‑s refresh and runtime orthogonalization modes [bff28889-2]. Software‑defined multiband radar combines carriers to improve robustness and detection under adverse conditions [bff28889-1].
- Reconfigurable satellite systems (DVB‑S2X) have been validated on‑board commercial SDRs with real‑time precoding, LDPC, and pilot design, and gateways can switch protocols within 10–25 s depending on module transfer and system steps. Closed‑loop 16×16 precoded DVB‑S2X gateways executed physical‑layer functions in real time on USRPs [62b5f091-0]. Protocol reconfiguration measurements quantified 10–25 s reconfiguration windows under realistic uplink constraints [62b5f091-2].
- SDR testbeds enable adaptive OFDM optimization across bands (HF to mmWave), with clear evidence that software‑controllable parameters like modulation, FFT size, and pilot placement drive PER and complexity trade‑offs, motivating adaptive modulation/coding strategies. Empirical tests show BPSK outperforming QPSK/8PSK in PER and larger FFTs reducing PER with added computational and ICI complexity [62b5f091-4].
- As SDR integrates with O‑RAN and SDN, security and spectrum resilience become first‑class design concerns, requiring algorithms that jointly optimize performance and robustness under adversarial and dynamic conditions. Beyond‑5G security analyses emphasize that SDR/NFV flexibility must be coupled with security constraints in PHY and network design [5f8b655e-3].

Collectively, these advancements show that software-defined radio has matured into a versatile, programmable substrate for wideband sensing and communications, with quantifiable real-time performance, protocol agility, and integration into open, software-defined networks for next‑generation wireless systems. Surveys and platform comparisons continue to document the evolving hardware/software landscape and developer challenges [5f8b655e-1]. Open-source frameworks like GNU Radio and devices like USRP lower barriers to entry, enabling rapid prototyping from FMCW radar to multi-standard communications [5f8b655e-2]. Prototyping frameworks such as WISCANet reflect the move toward integrated software-hardware testbeds aligned with B5G/6G goals [5f8b655e-4].

Particularly, a set of transmit sequences is designed to focus the emitted energy in the bands suggested by the spectrum sensing module while limiting the out-of-band interference. The waveforms, along with the receive processing, are designed to enhance the radar detection performance. The designed system is then demonstrated for the representative scenario of Fig. 1 using a custom built Software-Defined Radio (SDR) based prototype developed on Universal Software Radio Peripheral (USRP)s1 from National Instruments (NI) [13], [14]. These USRPs operate at sub-6 GHz frequencies with a maximum instantaneous bandwidth of 160 MHz. 

A. Background and Related Works a) Coexistence of Communication Systems: Spectral coexistence has been found to be a promising method to alleviate the spectrum scarcity problem. For example, in the ISM band, several wireless standards operate on overlapping frequency bands such as the IEEE 802.11 (popularly known as Wi-Fi) and the IEEE 802.15.4 (popularly known as ZigBee) family of standards in the 2.4 GHz ISM band. As the ISM band does not require a license to transmit, the participating standards transmit at will (frequency and power) leading to interference and a loss of throughput [15]- [17]. Similarly, in the 5 GHz ISM band, it has been speculated that there will be interference between IEEE 802.11n/ac and Long Term Evolution (LTE) [18]. For the two aforementioned interference scenarios, several spectral coexistence methods like successive Interference Cancellation (SIC) [19], [20] for single antenna and Technology Independent Multi-Output (TIMO) [21]- [23] for multi-antennas have been proposed. 

b) Radar-Communication Coexistence: The interfered bands, including those occupied by communications, are not useful for the radar system, and traditional radars aim to mitigate these frequencies at their receivers. To avoid energy wasted due to transmissions on these bands while pursuing coexistence applications, research into the transmit strategy of spectrally shaped radar waveforms has been driving coexistence studies since the last decade [24]- [32].

snippets:
Software-defined radio (SDR) is a concept for a programmable radio communication system and it usually consists of a personal computer with analog-to-digital converter and RF front-end (see Figure 20). This functionality produces general-purpose processor that introduces flexibility for signal processing and makes special-purpose hardware somehow obsolete. The concept is not new; however, recent evolving capabilities have led to its popularity. 

One of the most useful SDR advantages is its flexibility. Legacy radios are constrained with RF front-end and, unlike SDRs, do not have the capabilities to be arbitrarily programmed. If we look at smartphones and similar devices, they currently have many different radios optimized for signals operating on different frequency bands (WiFi, LTE, GSM, UMTS, GPS) (Stewart et al., 2015). Implementation of a single SDR in such devices could dynamically switch between various frequency bands with a software code. Some of the most popular commercially available SDR devices are USRP, HackRF and RTL-SDR. Because of its flexibility and our experimental nature of problem we decided to use SDR. One of the reasons for SDR is also FMCW radar. SDR allows us to do advanced signal processing that requires access to low-level radio data. 

We implement Wi-Mind on commodity software-defined radio software framework and using off-the-shelf hardware. Our software is based on GNU Radio (2018), a free and opensource development toolkit for SDR programming. GNU Radio applications are constructed as connected blocks known as "flowgraphs" (Figure 19). We use an FMCW radar implementation provided with a GNU Radio extension gr-radar and add the following functionalities: 

• we lock the distance to specific range (i.e. FFT bin); • we extract the phase of the received signal and timestamps for each phase sample. 

For hardware, we use Ettus Research Universal Software Radio Peripheral (USRP) B210. The product has RF coverage from 70 MHz to 6 GHz and is able to use multiple antennas. Since the nature of FMCW radar requires full-duplex transmission (radar receives the signal at the same time as it is sending signal with another frequency) we opted for USRP B210.

citations.title: An SDR-Based Satellite Gateway for Internet of Remote Things (IoRT) Applications
snippets:
To ensure that the reconfigurability mechanisms are fully functional, a set of manual tests were performed. The focus was on uploading a new satellite module which would offer support for a different set of uplink/downlink protocols. As the modulator and demodulator implementations were already available for both DVB-S2X and E-SSA protocols, a protocol swap test scenario was defined and executed. First, the DVB-S2X receiver and the E-SSA transmitter were loaded on the first USRP. Then, the zip files containing the DVB-S2X Test transmitter and the E-SSA Test receiver were transmitted via the coax link to the device under test (Fig. 11). When the confirmation was received, that the modules were successfully installed, a new System Config file was sent to the device under test in which DVB-S2X was set as uplink protocol and E-SSA as downlink protocol. While the device under test was rebooting, the first USRP was reconfigured to use the E-SSA transmitter and the DVB-S2X receiver. After the reboot was completed, a control message was sent via the DVB-S2X uplink. It was observed that the sensor node reacted accordingly and that a confirmation message was received via the E-SSA downlink. 

As for the timing, an overall reconfiguration performed with the new module available locally, took up to 10 seconds (including the time required for the configuration file to be sent over the satellite link). In case of a satellite link protocol reconfiguration, the overall duration was longer, especially for the case when the module for the desired satellite communication protocol was not available on the gateway. In this case the time required to upload the new module has to be taken into consideration. For example uploading a new module with a size of 1.5 Mb over a DVB-S2X link with MODCOD 1 (QPSK, 1/4 FEC, 400 kSym/s) selected will add an average of 6 seconds to the overall duration. Adding the installation time, configuration change and system reboot resulted in an overall duration of up to 25 seconds.

question: An academic paper that defines the purpose of "dialogue" in dialogue systems and natural language processing (NLP).

sections.title: # Summary: Defining the Purpose of “Dialogue” in Dialogue Systems and NLP
sections.text: In dialogue systems and NLP, “dialogue” is commonly defined as a structured, turn-taking interaction between a computer and a human (or between agents) oriented toward one or more purposes: assisting the user to achieve a goal, seeking and exchanging information, and sustaining social engagement. These purposes motivate different system architectures and NLP components (e.g., dialogue acts, state tracking, and policy models), and they appear in both task-oriented (goal-directed) and social/open-domain settings. Below, I synthesize representative papers and surveys that define the purpose of dialogue and show how NLP operationalizes these purposes.

sections.title: # Foundational Definitions and System-Centric Purposes
sections.text:
A widely used system-centric definition frames a dialogue system as “a computer system that can interact with a human being through dialogue in order to complete a specific task,” with dialogue strategy specifying what the system must do at each point in the dialogue; rule-based and later statistical models learn strategies from annotated dialogues to identify situations and select appropriate responses, often encoded as dialogue acts that define utterance functions with respect to the dialogue process. A dialogue system is usually defined as a computer system that can interact with a human being through dialogue in order to complete a specific task; dialogue strategy defines what the system must do at each point, with rule-based or statistical models learning to identify and react to dialogue situations, and dialogue acts labeling utterances by function [3c002ead-0]. This definition makes “task completion” the primary purpose in many dialogue systems and ties it directly to NLP via annotation schemes and statistical modeling.

Contemporary overviews categorize dialogue systems by purpose into three groups: goal-oriented (task assistance), question-answering, and social dialogue systems. According to their purpose, dialogue systems can be divided into three groups: goal-oriented, question-answering and social dialogue systems [3c002ead-2]. Within goal-oriented systems, the dialogue policy—given history and user inputs—selects the next system action in a turn-taking conversation to help the user solve a specific task. Goal-oriented spoken dialogue systems assist users in solving a particular task via turn-taking conversation, with the dialogue policy determining the next system action from transcription and state [3c002ead-2]. This purpose-driven taxonomy underscores that purpose varies by system class and shapes NLP modules (e.g., intent/slot extraction, state tracking, and response generation).

citations.title: On the Use of Audio to Improve Dialogue Policies
snippets:
A dialogue system is a computer program that communicates with a user in a natural way [1]. Typically, the communication between the user and the system is either text-based or speechbased. However, recent multimodal dialogue systems can use both, or also process input images and even body gestures [2]. According to their purpose, dialogue systems can be divided into three groups: goal-oriented, question-answering and social dialogue systems [3]. Due to the new advances in deep learning, particularly about contextualizing AI and prompting Large Language Models (LLMs), it has become relatively straightforward to build simple question-answering and social dialogue systems [4]. 

Goal-oriented spoken dialogue systems are designed to assist the user in solving a particular task, where the user interacts with the application using their voice, typically in a turn-taking conversation. This approach has transformed how users manage their daily tasks, offering a more natural and efficient experience. These systems typically consist of various modules. One of the more important modules is the dialogue policy. Given the transcription of the user's message (or variables inferred from their transcriptions) and the system's latest messages, the dialogue policy determines what the next system action should be. 

In recent years, neural networks have been increasingly utilized to design dialogue policies [5,6]. Convolutional Neural Networks (CNNs) were used to extract text features in several works [7,8]. In [9], a Recurrent Neural Network (RNN) is employed, performing a given task very competitively across several metrics when trained on only a few hundred dialogues. In [10], a more complex system is presented, with GPT-2 [11] as its core. This large language model uses the dialogue history, dialogue state history, system actions, and response vectors as inputs. Among the various outputs of this fine-tuned GPT-2 model, it also predicts the next system dialogue act. To extract text representations, word embeddings have become a common strategy in many Natural Language Processing (NLP) tasks. Word2Vec [12] and GloVe [13] are some of the most widely adopted. Nevertheless, these techniques have certain limitations when applying them to different tasks [14].

citations.title: Segmented and Unsegmented Dialogue-Act Annotation with Statistical Dialogue Models
snippets:
In the Natural Language Processing (NLP) field, one of the most challenging applications is dialogue systems (Kuppevelt and Smith, 2003). A dialogue system is usually defined as a computer system that can interact with a human being through dialogue in order to complete a specific task (e.g., ticket reservation, timetable consultation, bank operations,. . . ) (Aust et al., 1995;Hardy et al., 2002). Most dialogue system have a characteristic behaviour with respect to dialogue management, which is known as dialogue strategy. It defines what the dialogue system must do at each point of the dialogue. 

Most of these strategies are rule-based, i.e., the dialogue strategy is defined by rules that are usually defined by a human expert (Gorin et al., 1997;Hardy et al., 2003). This approach is usually difficult to adapt or extend to new domains where the dialogue structure could be completely different, and it requires the definition of new rules. 

Similar to other NLP problems (like speech recognition and understanding, or statistical machine translation), an alternative data-based approach has been developed in the last decade (Stolcke et al., 2000;Young, 2000). This approach relies on statistical models that can be automatically estimated from annotated data, which in this case, are dialogues from the task. 

Statistical modelling learns the appropriate parameters of the models from the annotated dialogues. As a simplification, it could be considered that each label is associated to a situation in the dialogue, and the models learn how to identify and react to the different situations by estimating the associations between the labels and the dialogue events (words, the speaker, previous turns, etc.). An appropriate annotation scheme should be defined to capture the elements that are really important for the dialogue, eliminating the information that is irrelevant to the dialogue process. Several annotation schemes have been proposed in the last few years (Core and Allen, 1997;Dybkjaer and Bernsen, 2000).

sections.title: # Information Exchange and Information-Seeking Dialogues
sections.text: A core purpose of dialogue is information exchange, and conversational search provides a canonical instance of “information-seeking dialogue.” Conversational search is defined as enabling information retrieval through natural-language dialogue interfaces, i.e., information-seeking dialogue; understanding its nature and properties is essential to judge success [e238e66f-0]. In this setting, dialogue is explicitly oriented toward retrieving and organizing information, and empirical analyses contrast such dialogues with chit-chat, conversational QA, and task-oriented dialogues to identify distinguishing characteristics. Information-seeking dialogues are differentiated from dialogues in chit-chat, conversational QA, and task-oriented dialogue, with the task defined by the dialogue interface for information retrieval [e238e66f-0]. This clarifies that the purpose of dialogue can be informational (gathering, organizing, and returning information) rather than purely instrumental or social.

Conversational search has been recognised as an important new frontier within information retrieval [3]. Where do conversational search and information-seeking dialogues fit in this picture? that enable information retrieval by means of a natural-language interaction, i.e., dialogue interface [30,43,44]. This type of dialogue is referred to as an information-seeking dialogue. In this way, conversational search is defined in terms of the type of dialogue it is expected to produce.

sections.title: # Social Dialogue and Human-Like Interaction
sections.text:
In social dialogue systems, the purpose extends beyond a single task to sustaining engagement and conversation, often in open domains. Non-task-oriented systems enable chit-chat in open-domain environments covering a general range of topics [3c002ead-2]. Pedagogical and human-computer interaction perspectives emphasize that dialogue can be “dialogue-based” for language learning, requiring negotiation of outcomes through open learner output, which makes the interaction complex and potentially beneficial for language development. A minimal definition of dialogue-based CALL is interaction with a computer for language learning, with “dialogue-based” distinguishing it from item-based approaches; importantly, interactions must allow negotiation of outcome via open learner output, which increases complexity and benefits language learning by enabling learners to freely build meaning [f1ddfc54-1]. This purpose—supporting learners’ meaning-making and reflection—illustrates how dialogue’s social and educational purposes are operationalized in NLP-based tutors.

Foundational models of dialogue acts provide a formal bridge between linguistic meaning and system behavior in social and task contexts. A dialogue act defines the function of an annotated utterance with respect to the dialogue process [3c002ead-0] , and widely used schemas (e.g., DAMSL, DIT++) encode communicative functions spanning interaction management, feedback, obligation, and topic control. Dialogue acts schemas, such as DIT++ with around 95 communicative functions and dimensions for feedback, interaction management, and social obligations, play a key role in dialogue studies, corpora annotation, and dialogue management [74ce9ba8-2]. These act-based definitions make social purposes (rapport-building, engagement, turn management) explicit and measurable, guiding NLP systems to generate responses that maintain coherence and mutual adaptation.

A dialogue system is a computer program that communicates with a user in a natural way [1]. Typically, the communication between the user and the system is either text-based or speechbased. snippets:
In the Natural Language Processing (NLP) field, one of the most challenging applications is dialogue systems (Kuppevelt and Smith, 2003). A dialogue system is usually defined as a computer system that can interact with a human being through dialogue in order to complete a specific task (e.g., ticket reservation, timetable consultation, bank operations,. . . ) (Aust et al., 1995;Hardy et al., 2002). Most dialogue system have a characteristic behaviour with respect to dialogue management, which is known as dialogue strategy. It defines what the dialogue system must do at each point of the dialogue. 

Most of these strategies are rule-based, i.e., the dialogue strategy is defined by rules that are usually defined by a human expert (Gorin et al., 1997;Hardy et al., 2003). citations.title: Dialogue-based CALL: an overview of existing research
snippets: It is possible to define dialogue-based CALL in a minimal way as ( 1) dialoguebased (2) interactions with a computer for language learning purposes. The second element sets us inside tutorial CALL, in contrast with computer-mediated communication, where interactions are with other humans via a computer. "Dialogue-based" makes the distinction with item-based approaches, which have been dominant in autonomous CALL applications. Nevertheless, this definition also applies to any form of interaction that takes the form of a dialogue, such as branching dialogues (conversation tree with a limited choice of utterances to select from, often used in adventure games) or systems that do not take into account what the user has previously uttered (certain question-asking systems). It is thus important to state a third characteristic: (3) the interactions must allow a certain negotiation of outcome (Young, 1988) through open learner output. sections.title: # Task-Oriented Dialogue: Coordination, Eliciting Preferences, and Joint Decision-Making
sections.text:
Task-oriented dialogue systems coordinate with users to achieve goals, often in domains like travel, restaurant reservations, or tutoring. Goal-oriented dialogue systems assist users in solving critical tasks (e.g., selecting restaurants or booking tickets) through natural language interactions, typically organized into NLU, DST, policy, and NLG modules [3c002ead-3]. More advanced settings consider multi-user, cooperative decision-making, where dialogue supports shared task coordination with agents assisting multiple participants. Task-oriented dialogues among multiple users require dialogue systems to process chats between users and make decisions together, posing challenges for traditional dialogue state tracking and necessitating annotated dialogue states and acts for training [74ce9ba8-4]. In such settings, the purpose of dialogue is joint goal pursuit: eliciting preferences, decomposing tasks, and coordinating actions.

Persuasion and negotiation further illustrate strategic, social-task hybrids where building rapport supports better task completion. Strategic dialogue tasks like persuasion and negotiation have wide applications and often contain both a specific task goal and social components to build rapport for better task completion [e238e66f-1]. This underscores that dialogue’s purpose is multifaceted: achieving outcomes while managing social dynamics.
