It has been recently proposed that when driving a macroscopic electrical current through antiferromagnetic crystals whose magnetic atoms occupy inversionpartner lattice sites (e.g. CuMnAs, Mn 2 Au), a local relativistic field is generated, which points in the opposite direction on magnetic atoms with opposite magnetic moments. The resulting field-like Néel spin-orbit torque has been demonstrated to allow for a reversible switching of antiferromagnetic moments in microelectronic bit cells by electrical current pulses of a length ranging from milliseconds to picoseconds [155,156].

citations.title: Materials, processes, devices and applications of magnetoresistive random access memory
snippets: Magnetoresistive random access memory (MRAM) is a promising non-volatile memory technology that can be utilized as an energy and space-efficient storage and computing solution, particularly in cache functions within circuits. Although MRAM has achieved mass production, its manufacturing process still remains challenging, resulting in only a few semiconductor companies dominating its production. In this review, we delve into the materials, processes, and devices used in MRAM, focusing on both the widely adopted spin transfer torque MRAM and the next-generation spin-orbit torque MRAM. We provide an overview of their operational mechanisms and manufacturing technologies. Furthermore, we outline the major hurdles faced in MRAM manufacturing and propose potential solutions in detail. Then, the applications of MRAM in artificial intelligent hardware are introduced. Finally, we present an outlook on the future development and applications of MRAM.

Schematic of our heavy metal/ ferromagnetic metal hetero-structure based domain wall based synapse is shown in Fig. 1. The operating physics of the device has been discussed extensively in [3,14,15,17]. The core physics is that of spin orbit torque driven DW motion, which has been extensively studied through simulations and experiments in the past [26,27,28,29]. When in-plane current ("write" current) flows through the heavy metal layer ("write" path), a DW in the ferromagnetic layer above the it experiences spin orbit torque. If the DW is of Neel type due to presence of Dzyaloshinskii Moriya Interaction (DMI) [26,27,30,31] at the interface, it moves even in the absence of magnetic field,as observed in several experiments [26,27,30] and also our micromagnetic simulations (Fig. 2). 

In this paper, we consider a device with lateral dimensions 1000 nm × 50 nm. Thickness of the heavy metal (Pt) layer is taken to be 10 nm, which is greater than the spin diffusion length. Hence, we can consider the vertical spin current density injected by the heavy metal layer on the ferromagnetic layer above it (J s ) = in-plane charge current density (J c ) × spin Hall angle (0.07 here, considering Pt) [37,38,39]. Thickness of the ferromagnetic layer above the heavy metal layer is taken to be 1 nm. Dynamics of the moments of this layer under the influence of this spin current is simulated using micromagnetic simulation package "mumax3" [36] to model such spin current driven DW motion inside it. We choose micro-magnetic simulation parameters for the ferromagnetic layer based on that used for Pt(heavy metal)/ CoFe (ferromagnet)/ MgO devices in the simulation study of Emori et al. [30], which is based on experimentally observed spin orbit torque driven DW motion in the same devices. The parameters can also be found in Supplementary Material (Section 1) accompanying this paper.

By changing the cooling field direction by 90° at 400 K, the antiferromagnetic spin axis is accordingly rotated by 90° at room temperature as well. As a result, high-and low-resistance states were achieved by virtue of the anisotropic magnetoresistance in antiferromagnets. This work illustrates a clear picture that an antiferromagnetic alone can work as a memory, which largely promotes the development of the antiferromagnetic spintronics. Nevertheless, the information writing process in such an antiferromagnetic memory device needs both thermal heating and a large magnetic field to switch the antiferromagnetic order parameter and hence it is not really easy for practical memory device application yet.

citations.title: Neel tensor torque at the ferromagnet/antiferromagnet interface
snippets:
Antiferromagnets (AFMs) exhibit spin arrangements with no net magnetization, positioning them as promising candidates for spintronics applications. While electrical manipulation of the single-crystal AFMs, composed of periodic spin configurations, is achieved recently, it remains a daunting challenge to characterize and to manipulate polycrystalline AFMs. Utilizing statistical analysis in data science, we demonstrate that polycrystalline AFMs can be described using a real, symmetric, positive semi-definite, rank-two tensor, which we term the 'Néel tensor'. This tensor introduces a unique spin torque, diverging from the conventional field-like and Slonczewski torques in spintronics devices. Remarkably, Néel tensors can be trained to retain a specific orientation, functioning as a form of working memory. This attribute enables zero-field spin-orbit-torque (SOT) switching in trilayer devices featuring a heavy-metal/ferromagnet/AFM structure and is also consistent with the X-ray magnetic linear dichroism measurements. Our findings uncover hidden statistical patterns in polycrystalline AFMs and establishes the presence of Néel tensor torque, highlighting its potential to drive future spintronics innovations. 

Magneto-resistive random access memory (MRAM) is a promising candidate for the nextgeneration nonvolatile memory (1,2). It manipulates magnetization for information processing and memory storage via different types of spin torques. The most common type of spin torque is the field-like torque, which is caused by the presence of an external magnetic field or the residual magnetization. However, Slonczewski predicted a different type of spin torque, called the spintransfer torque (3,4), which is caused by the interaction between the magnetization and a spin current. The spin-transfer torque is more efficient than the field-like torque and can be used to write and erase MRAM bits with less power consumption. In recent years, spin-orbit torque (SOT) MRAM is proposed (1,2), while still under development, it has the potential to be even more efficient than spin-transfer torque MRAM.

citations.title: Thermal noise induced probability switching in magnetic tunnel junction based on spin-circuit simulation
snippets:
Spin-transfer torque magnetoresistive random access memory (STT-MRAM) is emerging as a promising non-volatile memory technology characterized by low power consumption and high performance. The core structure of STT-MRAM consists of magnetic tunnel junctions (MTJs), typically composed of two ferromagnetic (FM) layers separated by a thin insulating barrier, as illustrated in Fig. 1(a). One FM layer, the free layer (FL), stores binary information via its magnetization orientation, while the other, the reference layer (RL), provides a fixed magnetization reference for reading operations. The fundamental operating principle of STT-MRAM relies on spin-transfer torque (STT), which induces magnetization switching in nanostructured magnetic materials through spin-polarized currents 1 . The dynamics of magnetization switching within the FL can be described by the Landau-Lifshitz-Gilbert (LLG) equation 2 . However, practical performance of spintronic devices, including MTJs, is significantly influenced by magnetization noise [3][4][5][6] . Particularly, under thermally activated switching conditions, thermal noise becomes the dominant factor due to its pronounced effect in modifying the effective temperature and lowering the energy barrier for magnetization reversal 7 . Thermal noise arises from the Brownian motion of electrons in conducting materials, characterized typically by a white noise spectrum and a Gaussian amplitude distribution. The crucial consequence of thermal noise is the reduction of the energy barrier required for magnetization switching. When the applied current pulse approaches the critical switching current of the MTJ, thermal noise enables probabilistic magnetization switching. Such probabilistic behavior of MTJs facilitates their application in probabilistic computing. 

However, current simulation techniques primarily employ compact mathematical models, which lack physical-level fidelity. Consequently, these models inadequately account for the influence of pulse duration and circuit density effects on switching behavior, limiting their accuracy and predictive capabilities. This work utilizes a physics-based simulation framework implemented entirely in SPICE for hybrid spintronic and conventional electronic circuits 8 . This framework offers numerous advantages, including high accuracy, fast simulation times, compatibility with existing MOS-FET SPICE models, ease of implementation, and excellent usability.

citations.title: A Compact Model for Scalable MTJ Simulation
snippets: This paper presents a physics-based modeling framework for the analysis and transient simulation of circuits containing Spin-Transfer Torque (STT) Magnetic Tunnel Junction (MTJ) devices. The framework provides the tools to analyze the stochastic behavior of MTJs and to generate Verilog-A compact models for their simulation in large VLSI designs, addressing the need for an industry-ready model accounting for real-world reliability and scalability requirements. Device dynamics are described by the Landau-Lifshitz-Gilbert-Slonczewsky (s-LLGS ) stochastic magnetization considering Voltage-Controlled Magnetic Anisotropy (VCMA) and the non-negligible statistical effects caused by thermal noise. Model behavior is validated against the OOMMF magnetic simulator and its performance is characterized on a 1-Mb 28 nm Magnetoresistive-RAM (MRAM) memory product.

snippets:
Schematic of our heavy metal/ ferromagnetic metal hetero-structure based domain wall based synapse is shown in Fig. 1. The operating physics of the device has been discussed extensively in [3,14,15,17]. The core physics is that of spin orbit torque driven DW motion, which has been extensively studied through simulations and experiments in the past [26,27,28,29]. When in-plane current ("write" current) flows through the heavy metal layer ("write" path), a DW in the ferromagnetic layer above the it experiences spin orbit torque. If the DW is of Neel type due to presence of Dzyaloshinskii Moriya Interaction (DMI) [26,27,30,31] at the interface, it moves even in the absence of magnetic field,as observed in several experiments [26,27,30] and also our micromagnetic simulations (Fig. 2). 

In this paper, we consider a device with lateral dimensions 1000 nm × 50 nm. Thickness of the heavy metal (Pt) layer is taken to be 10 nm, which is greater than the spin diffusion length. Hence, we can consider the vertical spin current density injected by the heavy metal layer on the ferromagnetic layer above it (J s ) = in-plane charge current density (J c ) × spin Hall angle (0.07 here, considering Pt) [37,38,39]. Thickness of the ferromagnetic layer above the heavy metal layer is taken to be 1 nm. Dynamics of the moments of this layer under the influence of this spin current is simulated using micromagnetic simulation package "mumax3" [36] to model such spin current driven DW motion inside it. We choose micro-magnetic simulation parameters for the ferromagnetic layer based on that used for Pt(heavy metal)/ CoFe (ferromagnet)/ MgO devices in the simulation study of Emori et al. [30], which is based on experimentally observed spin orbit torque driven DW motion in the same devices. The parameters can also be found in Supplementary Material (Section 1) accompanying this paper.

citations.title: Description of Statistical Switching in Perpendicular STT-MRAM Within an Analytical and Numerical Micromagnetic Framework
snippets: The realistic modeling of spin-transfer torque (STT)-magnetoresistive random access memory (MRAM) for the simulations of hybrid CMOS/Spintronics devices in comprehensive simulation environments requires a full description of stochastic switching processes in the state-of-the-art STT-MRAMs. Here, we compare micromagnetic simulations with an analytical formulation that takes into account the spin-torque asymmetry of the spin-polarization function by considering the mean, standard deviation, skewness, and kurtosis. We find that, while the first and second statistical moments exhibit a very similar behavior, skewness and kurtosis are substantially different and must be taken into account in order to provide an accurate prediction of the switching performance. In fact, a reasonable fit of the probability density function (PDF) of the switching time is given by a Pearson Type IV PDF. The main achievements of this paper underline the need of data-driven design of STT-MRAM that uses a full micromagnetic simulation framework for the statistical proprieties PDF of switching processes.

snippets:
Electrons' spins become aligned with the ferromagnetic layer magnetization when they travel through the MTJ. In the case of a FL magnetization misaligned with that of the pinned layer, the traveling electrons' spin follows the magnetization and rotates. The change in the spin of the electrons is transferred to the FL magnetization due to the conservation of the angular momentum. As a result, the spin-polarized current exerts a torque on the magnetization of the FL. If the current is sufficiently strong, this torque causes magnetization switching. By inverting the current direction, the sign of the torque and the magnetization switching direction can be inverted. 

STT-MRAM is a perfect candidate for future universal memory applications. STT-MRAM is fast (10ns), possesses high endurance (1012), and has a simple structure. Several solutions for embedded applications are available: An 8 Mb 1Transistor-1MTJ STT-MRAM on a 28 nm CMOS logic platform [4], a 128 Mb embedded MRAM with 14 ns write speed [5], an embedded MRAM solution compatible with 22FFL FinFET technology [6]. 

Even though the first commercial STT-MRAM-based products become available, one critical aspect of the currently used STT-MRAM technology, a relatively high switching current, has not been convincingly resolved. 

The high switching current and large writing energy may jeopardize the advantages provided by nonvolatility, therefore the current needs to be properly optimized. To do so, the torques must be accurately evaluated. We briefly describe our finite element-method (FEM) based modeling and simulation approach to evaluate coupled three-dimensional charge and spin transport and the corresponding spin-transfer torques driving the magnetization dynamics. The implementation is done by using well supported FEM libraries under open-source licenses.

citations.title: Materials, processes, devices and applications of magnetoresistive random access memory
snippets: Magnetoresistive random access memory (MRAM) is a promising non-volatile memory technology that can be utilized as an energy and space-efficient storage and computing solution, particularly in cache functions within circuits. Although MRAM has achieved mass production, its manufacturing process still remains challenging, resulting in only a few semiconductor companies dominating its production. In this review, we delve into the materials, processes, and devices used in MRAM, focusing on both the widely adopted spin transfer torque MRAM and the next-generation spin-orbit torque MRAM. We provide an overview of their operational mechanisms and manufacturing technologies. Furthermore, we outline the major hurdles faced in MRAM manufacturing and propose potential solutions in detail. Then, the applications of MRAM in artificial intelligent hardware are introduced. Finally, we present an outlook on the future development and applications of MRAM.

As a result, high-and low-resistance states were achieved by virtue of the anisotropic magnetoresistance in antiferromagnets. sections.title: # What are faceted plots?
sections.text:
Faceted plots (also called small multiples or panel plots) display multiple versions of the same plot type, each showing a subset of the data determined by one or more categorical variables, so that comparisons are facilitated by viewing variations across panels rather than by adding more encodings to a single plot. Faceting in ggplot2 generates small multiples showing different data subsets [a3f2a669-0] Faceting partitions data by categorical values and repeats a plot for each partition, producing small multiples for comparison [641e827e-1] Small multiples are plots consisting of multiple panels arranged in a regular grid; each panel shows a different subset but uses the same coordinate system and scales [641e827e-2].

In many toolchains, faceting is implemented by mapping one variable to panels arranged in rows and/or columns, often with options to vary the layout (e.g., single row, wrapped grid) and to control how variables map to axes and panel dimensions. There are three types in ggplot2: facet_null(), facet_wrap(), and facet_grid() [a3f2a669-0] Faceting partitions data by ordinal/categorical values and repeats the plot for each partition [641e827e-1] FacetGrid arranges multiple axes into a grid that corresponds to levels of variables in the dataset [c0e22855-0].

sections.title: # Pros and cons/trade-offs
sections.text:
A central advantage is consistent axes and scales across panels, which enables direct visual comparison and avoids ambiguity from varying encodings. All panels use the same scales and coordinate systems [641e827e-2]. Faceting also scales well with categorical structure, letting you examine heterogeneity across groups without cramming multiple variables into a single encoding. Small multiples are formed by repeating the same plot per partition to support comparison [641e827e-1] They are useful for distributions and relationships within subsets [c0e22855-1].

Common pitfalls include cluttered grids when there are too many categories, overplotting within facets if continuous variables are mapped to position channels without transparency or sampling, and inconsistent or misleading inferences when scales are not harmonized across panels. Good practice is to limit the number of panels, use appropriate aggregation or sampling for large datasets, and ensure that all panels share relevant scales and axes for fair comparison. Small multiples can be generated for each row/column, but care is needed in layout and interpretation [641e827e-0] Maintaining the same scales and coordinate systems across panels is key to valid comparison [641e827e-2] Faceting is most effective when the same plot is repeated for each partition, preserving comparability [641e827e-1]. More detailed guidance on multi-panel figures, including layout choices and readability, is provided by data visualization handbooks and tutorials. Claus Wilke’s Fundamentals of Data Visualization discusses multi-panel figures and small multiples [641e827e-2].

sections.title: # Scope and Definitions
sections.text: Synthetic tabular data generation (STDG) creates artificial rows that mimic the distributions, dependencies, and semantics of real tabular datasets while protecting privacy or enabling reuse in settings where revealing raw data would be risky or unethical. In this work, we present a comprehensive survey of synthetic tabular data generation, covering the end-to-end generation process and introducing a novel taxonomy to categorize existing generation methods [cd95dc7c-0]. We first introduce the definition of synthetic tabular data generation and the key challenges it faces [cd95dc7c-4]. The pipeline typically includes a generative model to capture the joint distribution of columns with mixed types and dependencies, followed by post-processing to enforce semantic and logical validity, and finally evaluations of statistical fidelity and downstream utility across tasks. We then categorize existing methods into three main classes—traditional generation methods, diffusion model methods, and LLM-based methods—and summarize post-processing techniques such as sample and label enhancement to ensure semantic correctness and data validity [cd95dc7c-4].

citations.title: A Comprehensive Survey of Synthetic Tabular Data Generation
snippets:
However, existing surveys have several limitations: (1) Some existing works are limited to specific domains or methods and lack a comprehensive overview of synthetic tabular data generation. Such as some surveys [20]- [22] focus on the use of GANs for generating medical tabular data, some surveys [23], [24] focus on class imbalance, privacy, and fairness in synthetic tabular data generation. (2) Existing work primarily focuses on the generation and evaluation of synthetic tabular data [25], [26], while overlooking the importance of post-processing after data generation. Synthetic data may match the original distribution but still violate commonsense or logical rules (e.g. negative age values or children marked as married). Post-processing is therefore necessary to ensure semantic correctness and data validity. (3) The latest advancements in LLMs and diffusion models for synthetic tabular data generation have not yet been thoroughly explored [27]. LLMs and diffusion models offer advantages over traditional generative methods-LLMs for their ability to model semantic structure, and diffusion models for their stability and representation capabilities-but current surveys lack a thorough investigation of these methods. 

In this survey, we present a comprehensive review of synthetic tabular data generation. Specifically, we first introduce the definition of synthetic tabular data generation and the key challenges it faces. We then categorize existing methods into three main classes-traditional generation methods, diffusion model methods, and LLM-based methods-and provide a detailed analysis of the strengths and limitations of each category. Furthermore, we summarize and classify the postprocessing techniques into two primary categories: sample enhancement and label enhancement, highlighting their importance in ensuring data quality and semantic consistency. We also review evaluation methodologies from the perspectives of arXiv:2504.16506v1 [cs.LG] 23  Step 1: Synthetic Tabular Data Generation Fig. 1. Pipeline of synthetic tabular data generation. The first step involves training generative models on existing tabular datasets to generate synthetic data. These models include Traditional Generation Methods, Diffusion Model Methods, and LLM-based Methods. To further improve the quality of the synthetic data and ensure alignment with human knowledge, the second step applies post-processing techniques, which include Sample Enhancement and Label Enhancement.

citations.title: A Comprehensive Survey of Synthetic Tabular Data Generation
snippets: In this work, we present a comprehensive survey of synthetic tabular data generation, covering the end-to-end generation process and introducing a novel taxonomy to categorize existing generation methods. Our goal is to provide practical guidance for enterprises and organizations seeking to adopt synthetic tabular data generation techniques. At the same time, we offer insights into the key challenges and opportunities within the field, along with a thorough summary of evaluation protocols and real-world applications. Furthermore, we highlight promising directions for future research. We hope that this work will contribute to advancing the development of synthetic tabular data generation and inspire further exploration in this rapidly evolving area.

sections.title: # 1) Traditional statistical and probabilistic methods
sections.text:
Classical approaches include Bayesian networks, copula-based models, tree-structured or rule-based generators, and density estimators like Conditional Tabular GAN (CTGAN) and Variational models adapted to tabular data (TVAE). Bayesian networks can be used for generating synthetic records by approximating the conditional probability distribution from the data [65724422-0]. Tree-based methods have been used for generating partial synthetic data, with adversarial random forest showing comparable performance to deep learning for synthetic data quality [65724422-0]. Compared to black-box deep-learning models, vine copulas are relatively easy and robust to train, and provide direct distributional representations that are interpretable and tweakable [65724422-1]. Gaussian copula methods model the joint distribution via Sklar’s theorem by combining marginals with a copula capturing intercolumn dependencies; SDV uses Gaussian copulas to model tabular data [65724422-3].

Variational and autoencoder-style methods have been adapted to tabular data using continuous Gaussian mixture modeling and categorical embeddings, often showing strong empirical performance but with assumptions about latent structure that may limit expressiveness. CTGAN is a specialized GAN designed for realistic tabular data generation, adept at handling mixed data types and complex dependencies [629636e1-1]. Variational autoencoders estimate the probabilistic distribution by finding a lower-dimensional latent representation; applications have extended to tabular data synthesis, but assumptions about the latent space can limit capturing complex dependencies [65724422-0]. A VAE enhanced with a Bayesian Gaussian Mixture model applied to the latent space improves representation of non-Gaussian structures and can outperform CTGAN and TVAE on real-world datasets [65724422-4].

snippets:

Although the use of GANs for data generation is becoming increasingly popular among the core ML community, these require multiple models to be trained, leading to difficulties and computational burden (Tagasovska et al., 2019). Variational approaches, on the other hand, make strong distributional assumptions that are potentially detrimental to generative models (Tagasovska et al., 2019). Compared to black-box deep-learning models, the training of vine copulas is relatively easy and robust, while taking away a lot of guesswork in specifying hyperparameters and network architecture. Furthermore, copula models give a direct representation of statistical distributions, making them easier to interpret and tweak after training. As such, copula-based models have been shown to be effective for generating synthetic data comparable to real data in the context of privacy protection (Patki et al., 2016).

The goal of this paper is to improve ML emulators by augmenting the physical model's inputs using copulas. We give a brief overview of methods in Sect. 2.1 with specific implementation details in Sect. 2.2-2.5. Results are shown in Sect. 3, with a focus on evaluating synthetically generated data in Sect. 3.1 and ML predictions in Sect. 3.2. We conclude with a discussion and prospects for future research in Sect. 4.

CTGAN is a specialized GAN designed for realistic tabular data generation [17], adept at handling mixed data types and complex dependencies. It employs conditional modeling, training-by-sampling techniques, and mode-specific normalization to optimize synthesis across categorical and continuous variables, thereby enhancing data augmentation and effectively addressing class imbalance. CTGAN's adversarial training framework ensures continual improvement in generating realistic samples, making it ideal for various applications needing precise synthetic data from tabular datasets. In CTGAN, the generator G and discriminator D are trained simultaneously, with the goal of G producing synthetic data that D cannot distinguish from real data. CTGAN employs mode-specific normalization using a Gaussian mixture model (GMM) for continuous variables and onehot encoding for categorical variables. Each component is characterized by its mean µ k , variance σ 2 k , and weight π k , which determines its contribution to the mixture model. citations.title: CasTGAN: Cascaded Generative Adversarial Network for Realistic Tabular Data Synthesis
snippets:
Tabular data is broadly used in regression and classification tasks, which facilitates a growing interest in tabular data synthesis for machine learning applications, especially in domains with limited training data. Bayesian networks can be used for generating synthetic records by approximating the conditional probability distribution from the data [21]. While the Bayesian networks can in practice be additionally used for exploring causal relationships between the independent variables, estimating the distributions is often built on simplifying assumptions on the data [22]. Meanwhile, tree-based methods were first utilised for generating partial synthetic data in [23], and has further explored in [24] where adversarial random forest has demonstrated comparable performance to deep learning techniques in terms of synthetic data quality. However, the privacy-utility trade-offs for synthetic data generation using tree-based density estimators is not sufficiently explored. 

Deep neural networks have been widely studied for synthetic data generation, thanks to their capabilities for handling and approximating the distributions of large datasets. Variational auto-encoders (VAEs) [25] estimate the probabilistic distribution of by finding a lower-dimensional latent representation of the data. The application of VAEs has been extended to image data generation [26], oversampling of anomaly event data [27] and tabular data synthesis [28]. An underlying limitation with variational autoencoders is the assumption of the a simple parametric form of the latent space, which leads to a difficulty in capturing complex data distributions [29]. Invertible neural networks have also been proposed for tabular data synthesis through variants based on neural ordinary differential equations [30], copula flows [31] and normalizing flows for private tabular data generation [32]. A drawback of the invertible neural network based synthesis is that extensive hyperparameter tuning is needed to achieve satisfactory classification and regression performance. 

Within deep learning based generative models, GANs are favourable due to their ability to generate complex synthetic data in an adversarial and unsupervised setting [37]. table-GAN [33] is one of the earliest generative models for producing tabular synthetic output based on adversarial training.

citations.title: An Improved Tabular Data Generator with VAE-GMM Integration
snippets: The rising use of machine learning in various fields requires robust methods to create synthetic tabular data that preserve key characteristics while mitigating data scarcity chal-lenges. State-of-the-art approaches, such as CTGAN and TVAE, face difficulties with the intricate structures inherent in tabular data, which often comprise continuous and discrete features with non-Gaussian distributions. To address these limitations, we pro-pose a novel approach based on Variational Autoencoders (VAEs) enhanced with a Bayesian Gaussian Mixture (BGM) model. Unlike other methods that alter the Gaussian prior of the VAE, our approach trains the VAE conventionally and then applies the BGM model to the learned latent space. This allows for a more accurate representation of the underlying data distribution during data generation. Moreover, our model offers enhanced flexibility by accommodating various differentiable distributions for individual features, enabling the handling of continuous and discrete data types. Thorough validation on three real-world datasets, including medically relevant ones, demonstrates significant outperformance compared to CTGAN and TVAE. Our model shows promise as a valuable tool for synthetic tabular data generation across diverse domains, particularly in healthcare.

snippets:
In this research, we'll use four different Data Generators with well-known mathematical properties: Gaussian Copula, Bayesian Networks, Conditional Tabular GAN (CTGAN), and Tabular Variational Autoencoder (TVAE). The first two are statistical methods, whereas the latter two are deep neural network techniques. Let's first examine the mathematical properties of the statistical methods. 

Gaussian copula methods model the joint distribution of a table by combining each column's marginal distribution with a copula function capturing intercolumn dependencies. The foundation is Sklar's theorem [27], which states that any multivariate distribution F (z 1 , . . . , z d ) can be decomposed as 

where F i (z i ) are the marginals and C is the copula describing their dependency structure. A Gaussian copula assumes this dependence is encoded by a multivariate normal distribution with a correlation matrix, while allowing arbitrary marginals. In practice, one first estimates each column's CDF, then transforms the data into a latent space with uniform or Gaussian marginals. First, you estimate a CDF F i for each column i of the real data. Then, transform the real data into uniform variables U i = F i (Z i ) and fit a copula C to capture their joint dependence, which for a Gaussian copula means computing the correlation matrix. Lastly, draw a synthetic sample (U 1 , . . . , U d ) ∼ C from the copula model, and invert the transform by applying the inverse CDF for each column, 

. This yields a synthetic data record in the original space. 

Patki et al. [28] introduced the open-source package Synthetic Data Vault (SDV) by using Gaussian copulas to model tabular data. In their approach, all columns are converted to a standard normal scale to remove the effect of each column distribution shape, before estimating the covariance matrix of the joint Gaussian copula. After modeling the correlations, synthetic rows are sampled by drawing from the multivariate normal and then transforming back to each column's domain.

sections.title: # 2) Generative adversarial models (GANs)
sections.text:
CTGAN and its successors address mixed types, multimodal continuous distributions, and class imbalance via conditional generation, mode-specific normalization, and sampling-based training strategies. CTGAN employs mode-specific normalization (GMM for continuous, one-hot for categorical) and conditional modeling to avoid mode collapse and handle imbalances [629636e1-1]. CTGAN overcomes issues with simultaneously modeling discrete and continuous columns, multi-modal non-Gaussian values, and severe categorical imbalance using mode-specific normalization and conditional training-by-sampling [629636e1-4]. CTGAN outperforms other generative models (CLBN, PrivBN, MedGAN, VeeGAN, TableGAN) on downstream machine learning tasks; CTAB-GAN and CTAB-GAN+ extend handling of imbalanced and skewed distributions and incorporate Wasserstein penalties and differential privacy [629636e1-2].

Recent work explores GAN variants tailored to tabular dependencies and privacy, and compares to other families. Table-GAN is one of the earliest adversarial models for producing tabular synthetic output [65724422-0]. CTAB-GAN+ stabilizes training with Wasserstein plus gradient penalty and adds differential privacy in the encoder to protect individuals while preserving aggregate utility [65724422-0]. Adversarial random forest has shown comparable synthetic data quality to deep learning while raising open questions on privacy-utility trade-offs for tree-based density estimators [65724422-0].

citations.title: Distributed Conditional GAN (discGAN) For Synthetic Healthcare Data Generation
snippets: We will use methods described in [5] to produce synthetic, single-table synthetic data. In particular, CTGAN overcomes several issues related to using GANs to generate synthetic tabular data; namely, "the need to simultaneously model discrete and continuous columns, the multi-modal non-Gaussian values within each continuous column, and the severe imbalance of categorical columns." [5] In contrast to "vanilla" GANs, CTGAN uses mode-specific normalization to overcome the issue of multi-modal, non-Gaussian distributions, and address data imbalance with a conditional generator and training-by-sampling. The overall architecture implements "fully-connected networks and several recent techniques to train a high-quality model." [5] Additionally, CTGAN addresses the issue of class-imbalanced data when training the generator, which is unusual in a typical GAN architecture. CTGAN aims to "resample efficiently in a way that all the categories from discrete attributes are sampled evenly [during training] [...] and to recover the (not sampled) real data distribution during testing." [5] Thus, the data generation is conditional on each particular column value.

snippets:
Tabular data is broadly used in regression and classification tasks, which facilitates a growing interest in tabular data synthesis for machine learning applications, especially in domains with limited training data. Bayesian networks can be used for generating synthetic records by approximating the conditional probability distribution from the data [21]. While the Bayesian networks can in practice be additionally used for exploring causal relationships between the independent variables, estimating the distributions is often built on simplifying assumptions on the data [22]. Meanwhile, tree-based methods were first utilised for generating partial synthetic data in [23], and has further explored in [24] where adversarial random forest has demonstrated comparable performance to deep learning techniques in terms of synthetic data quality. However, the privacy-utility trade-offs for synthetic data generation using tree-based density estimators is not sufficiently explored. 

Deep neural networks have been widely studied for synthetic data generation, thanks to their capabilities for handling and approximating the distributions of large datasets. Variational auto-encoders (VAEs) [25] estimate the probabilistic distribution of by finding a lower-dimensional latent representation of the data. The application of VAEs has been extended to image data generation [26], oversampling of anomaly event data [27] and tabular data synthesis [28]. An underlying limitation with variational autoencoders is the assumption of the a simple parametric form of the latent space, which leads to a difficulty in capturing complex data distributions [29]. Invertible neural networks have also been proposed for tabular data synthesis through variants based on neural ordinary differential equations [30], copula flows [31] and normalizing flows for private tabular data generation [32]. A drawback of the invertible neural network based synthesis is that extensive hyperparameter tuning is needed to achieve satisfactory classification and regression performance. 

Within deep learning based generative models, GANs are favourable due to their ability to generate complex synthetic data in an adversarial and unsupervised setting [37]. table-GAN [33] is one of the earliest generative models for producing tabular synthetic output based on adversarial training.

citations.title: Convex space learning for tabular synthetic data generation
snippets:
VAEs and GANs are two pioneering techniques in generative modeling that have significantly shaped research on synthetic data. Initially used for synthetic image generation, now they have found diverse applications across various domains [12]. This section discusses the state-of-the-art synthetic tabular data generative models. 

In 2019, Xu et al. introduced CTGAN, a method for synthesizing tabular data that effectively models both continuous and categorical columns [13]. CTGAN uses a unique normalization approach for continuous features and a strategy to handle imbalances in discrete data. Continuous features are processed using a variational Gaussian mixture model, while categorical columns are represented through one-hot encoding. The model incorporates a conditional vector to address imbalances and prevent mode collapse during training. CTGAN outperforms other generative models, such as CLBN, PrivBN, MedGAN, VeeGAN, and TableGAN, in machine learning efficacy on real datasets [13]. 

CTAB-GAN, an extension of CTGAN, was developed to address challenges with imbalanced data and skewed distributions, which are common in various datasets [14]. CTAB-GAN combines conditional generation and sampling-based training techniques to enhance class representation, particularly for underrepresented classes. The method employs logarithmic transformation to compress and reduce the distance between tail and bulk data, aiding in more accurate synthesis. CTAB-GAN introduces information loss and classification loss into the generator's loss function to ensure the quality of synthetic data. It has been shown to produce synthetic data that is statistically similar to real data and useful for machine learning tasks [15]. 

Building on the advancements of CTGAN and CTAB-GAN, Zhao et al. developed CTAB-GAN+ to address the limitations of GAN-based tabular data generators, particularly in handling variables that can be both numerical and categorical. CTAB-GAN+ incorporates the Wasserstein plus gradient penalty to stabilize GAN training and differential privacy in the encoder to protect individual data points while allowing meaningful aggregate analysis [16]. This model outperforms others in terms of machine learning utility and statistical similarity, making it a robust choice for synthetic data generation [17].

sections.title: # 3) Probabilistic graphical and copula-based generators
sections.text:
Copula-based methods explicitly model marginals and pairwise (or higher-order) dependencies, offering interpretability and flexibility across mixed types, with trade-offs in modeling higher-order structure. Coping with non-Gaussian and multimodal distributions is challenging for simple models; copulas provide direct distributional representations and ease of hyperparameter specification, and have shown effectiveness for privacy-protective synthesis [65724422-1]. Gaussian copulas assume multivariate normal dependence in latent space and are implemented in SDV; more complex vine copulas can capture richer dependencies [65724422-3].

Bayesian networks provide local conditional distributions and causal interpretability but rely on structural and distributional assumptions that may not hold in complex datasets. Bayesian networks approximate conditional distributions and can explore causal relations, but estimation often requires simplifying assumptions [65724422-0].

Although the use of GANs for data generation is becoming increasingly popular among the core ML community, these require multiple models to be trained, leading to difficulties and computational burden (Tagasovska et al., 2019). Variational approaches, on the other hand, make strong distributional assumptions that are potentially detrimental to generative models (Tagasovska et al., 2019). Compared to black-box deep-learning models, the training of vine copulas is relatively easy and robust, while taking away a lot of guesswork in specifying hyperparameters and network architecture. Furthermore, copula models give a direct representation of statistical distributions, making them easier to interpret and tweak after training. As such, copula-based models have been shown to be effective for generating synthetic data comparable to real data in the context of privacy protection (Patki et al., 2016).

The goal of this paper is to improve ML emulators by augmenting the physical model's inputs using copulas. We give a brief overview of methods in Sect. 2.1 with specific implementation details in Sect. 2.2-2.5. We conclude with a discussion and prospects for future research in Sect. 4.

In this research, we'll use four different Data Generators with well-known mathematical properties: Gaussian Copula, Bayesian Networks, Conditional Tabular GAN (CTGAN), and Tabular Variational Autoencoder (TVAE). The first two are statistical methods, whereas the latter two are deep neural network techniques. Let's first examine the mathematical properties of the statistical methods. 

Gaussian copula methods model the joint distribution of a table by combining each column's marginal distribution with a copula function capturing intercolumn dependencies. The foundation is Sklar's theorem [27], which states that any multivariate distribution F (z 1 , . . . , z d ) can be decomposed as 

where F i (z i ) are the marginals and C is the copula describing their dependency structure. A Gaussian copula assumes this dependence is encoded by a multivariate normal distribution with a correlation matrix, while allowing arbitrary marginals. In practice, one first estimates each column's CDF, then transforms the data into a latent space with uniform or Gaussian marginals. First, you estimate a CDF F i for each column i of the real data. Then, transform the real data into uniform variables U i = F i (Z i ) and fit a copula C to capture their joint dependence, which for a Gaussian copula means computing the correlation matrix. Lastly, draw a synthetic sample (U 1 , . . . , U d ) ∼ C from the copula model, and invert the transform by applying the inverse CDF for each column, 

. This yields a synthetic data record in the original space. 

Patki et al. [28] introduced the open-source package Synthetic Data Vault (SDV) by using Gaussian copulas to model tabular data. In their approach, all columns are converted to a standard normal scale to remove the effect of each column distribution shape, before estimating the covariance matrix of the joint Gaussian copula. After modeling the correlations, synthetic rows are sampled by drawing from the multivariate normal and then transforming back to each column's domain.

sections.title: # 4) Diffusion models for tabular data
sections.text:
Diffusion models, inspired by high-quality image generation, have been adapted to tabular data to stabilize training and improve global structure preservation, though tabular heterogeneity and inter-column dependencies pose unique challenges. Researchers have explored adapting diffusion models from image synthesis to tabular generation to improve quality; challenges include modeling global and regional relationships in heterogeneous features and inter-column dependencies [1f127b93-2]. TABSYN improves generality by transforming mixed-type features into a unified embedding space, regularizing the latent space (e.g., standard normal), and using a linear noise schedule to generate high-quality data in fewer than 20 reverse steps [1f127b93-2].

Architectural innovations address multimodal noise and heterogeneous features but may increase computational overhead, highlighting a key trade-off between quality and scalability. Dual-scale noise modeling improves synthetic data quality but increases computational overhead; future work is needed to reduce complexity for larger-scale tasks [1f127b93-0]. Denoising diffusion probabilistic models can generate high-quality samples but must handle complex inter-column dependencies in tabular data, motivating dual-scale noise mechanisms [1f127b93-4].

citations.title: Enhancing Tabular Data Generation With Dual-Scale Noise Modeling
snippets:
Tabular data is widely used in various fields, including finance, healthcare, and social sciences, and is often the basis for data-driven decision-making. However, generating high-quality synthetic tabular data still faces significant challenges due to the inherent complexity of tabular data. Unlike the relatively homogeneous structure of image or 

The associate editor coordinating the review of this manuscript and approving it for publication was Sedat Akleylek . text data, tabular data usually consists of multiple heterogeneous features, including continuous and categorical variables, which have different distributions and interdependencies [1]. In addition, capturing complex relationships between columns-such as dependencies between numerical features or correlations between categorical variables-makes modeling tabular data even more complicated [2], [3]. 

Traditional synthetic data generation methods [4], [5], [6], [7], [8], [9], have made significant progress in improving the fidelity and diversity of generated samples. However, these methods often struggle to handle the complex, multimodal distributions in tabular data and typically fail to preserve global structure (e.g., overall correlation between features) and local details (e.g., feature distribution). Moreover, these models often operate as ''black boxes,'' making it difficult to interpret the generated data or ensure that it accurately reflects the distribution of the underlying data [10]. 

Denoising diffusion probabilistic models [11] have emerged in recent years as a promising alternative approach to data generation, showing great potential [12], [13]. These models have demonstrated the ability to generate high-quality samples by progressively optimizing noisy data through multiple steps. However, applying diffusion models to tabular data presents new challenges due to the heterogeneity of tabular features. Unlike images, where pixel dependencies are typically local and spatially coherent, tabular data exhibits complex inter-column dependencies, requiring the modeling of global and regional relationships [14], [15]. 

In this study, we propose a novel generative framework. This dual-scale diffusion method aims to overcome the challenges of DDPM in tabular data generation by introducing a dual-scale noise-handling mechanism.

sections.title: # 5) LLM-based and rule/logic-enhanced methods
sections.text: Recent surveys highlight LLM-based and diffusion-based methods as emerging directions, alongside traditional approaches, due to their potential to model semantic structure and improve stability. Existing surveys have overlooked post-processing and have not thoroughly explored LLMs and diffusion models; LLMs offer semantic modeling advantages while diffusion models provide stability and representation capabilities [cd95dc7c-4]. We summarize and classify post-processing into sample enhancement and label enhancement to ensure semantic consistency and validity [cd95dc7c-4]. These post-processing techniques are motivated by failures of purely generative models to respect domain rules (e.g., invalid age or inconsistent marital status), which can be corrected by rule-based checks, logic constraints, and commonsense reasoning modules. Synthetic data may match the original distribution but still violate commonsense or logical rules (e.g., negative age or children marked as married), necessitating post-processing to ensure semantic correctness and validity [cd95dc7c-3].

citations.title: A Comprehensive Survey of Synthetic Tabular Data Generation
snippets:
However, existing surveys have several limitations: (1) Some existing works are limited to specific domains or methods and lack a comprehensive overview of synthetic tabular data generation. Such as some surveys [20]- [22] focus on the use of GANs for generating medical tabular data, some surveys [23], [24] focus on class imbalance, privacy, and fairness in synthetic tabular data generation. (2) Existing work primarily focuses on the generation and evaluation of synthetic tabular data [25], [26], while overlooking the importance of post-processing after data generation. Synthetic data may match the original distribution but still violate commonsense or logical rules (e.g. negative age values or children marked as married). Post-processing is therefore necessary to ensure semantic correctness and data validity. (3) The latest advancements in LLMs and diffusion models for synthetic tabular data generation have not yet been thoroughly explored [27]. LLMs and diffusion models offer advantages over traditional generative methods-LLMs for their ability to model semantic structure, and diffusion models for their stability and representation capabilities-but current surveys lack a thorough investigation of these methods. 

In this survey, we present a comprehensive review of synthetic tabular data generation. Specifically, we first introduce the definition of synthetic tabular data generation and the key challenges it faces. We then categorize existing methods into three main classes-traditional generation methods, diffusion model methods, and LLM-based methods-and provide a detailed analysis of the strengths and limitations of each category. Furthermore, we summarize and classify the postprocessing techniques into two primary categories: sample enhancement and label enhancement, highlighting their importance in ensuring data quality and semantic consistency. We also review evaluation methodologies from the perspectives of arXiv:2504.16506v1 [cs.LG] 23  Step 1: Synthetic Tabular Data Generation Fig. 1. Pipeline of synthetic tabular data generation. The first step involves training generative models on existing tabular datasets to generate synthetic data. These models include Traditional Generation Methods, Diffusion Model Methods, and LLM-based Methods. To further improve the quality of the synthetic data and ensure alignment with human knowledge, the second step applies post-processing techniques, which include Sample Enhancement and Label Enhancement.

sections.title: # Quality, Utility, and Evaluation
sections.text:
Evaluation of synthetic tabular data typically spans (i) statistical fidelity (marginal and joint distribution match, independence, and correlation preservation), (ii) functional utility (downstream model performance on tasks like classification/regression), and (iii) semantic validity (conformance to domain rules and logical consistency). There remains a challenge in proposing reliable evaluation techniques and criteria for quantifying the reliability and statistical properties of synthetic data [cd95dc7c-3]. Evaluation methodologies are reviewed from perspectives that include statistical, logical, and downstream utility checks [cd95dc7c-4].

Comparative studies and open-source libraries facilitate reproducible evaluation across methods. For example, SDV and SynthCity provide Gaussian copula, Bayesian networks, CTGAN, and TVAE baselines with documented properties and procedures, enabling head-to-head comparisons on real datasets. Open-source libraries such as SDV and SynthCity compare Gaussian Copula, Bayesian Networks, CTGAN, and TVAE, with Gaussian copulas grounded in Sklar’s theorem and SDV implementing this approach [65724422-3]. Empirical comparisons show VAE-GMM integration can outperform CTGAN and TVAE on medical and other real-world datasets [65724422-4].

Despite progress, surveys emphasize gaps in standardized benchmarks and comprehensive evaluation protocols that jointly assess statistical parity, functional utility across tasks, and semantic validity across domains with mixed data types and dependencies. An underlying challenge is the lack of robust evaluation techniques and criteria for reliability and statistical properties, particularly for hierarchical and interdependent variables [cd95dc7c-3]. Existing surveys often overlook post-processing and do not thoroughly explore LLM and diffusion methods, indicating incomplete evaluation frameworks [cd95dc7c-4].

citations.title: An Improved Tabular Data Generator with VAE-GMM Integration
snippets: The rising use of machine learning in various fields requires robust methods to create synthetic tabular data that preserve key characteristics while mitigating data scarcity chal-lenges. State-of-the-art approaches, such as CTGAN and TVAE, face difficulties with the intricate structures inherent in tabular data, which often comprise continuous and discrete features with non-Gaussian distributions. To address these limitations, we pro-pose a novel approach based on Variational Autoencoders (VAEs) enhanced with a Bayesian Gaussian Mixture (BGM) model. Unlike other methods that alter the Gaussian prior of the VAE, our approach trains the VAE conventionally and then applies the BGM model to the learned latent space. This allows for a more accurate representation of the underlying data distribution during data generation. Moreover, our model offers enhanced flexibility by accommodating various differentiable distributions for individual features, enabling the handling of continuous and discrete data types. Thorough validation on three real-world datasets, including medically relevant ones, demonstrates significant outperformance compared to CTGAN and TVAE. Our model shows promise as a valuable tool for synthetic tabular data generation across diverse domains, particularly in healthcare.

sections.title: # Privacy and Security Considerations
sections.text:
Privacy is a central driver for synthetic tabular data, with mechanisms ranging from utility-preserving probabilistic models to differentially private (DP) generators and secure pipelines. Copula-based and Bayesian methods have been promoted for privacy-protective synthesis due to interpretability and controlled dependencies, though they may be limited in modeling high-order interactions. Compared to deep models, vine copulas are easier and more robust to train, and provide direct distributional representations that are interpretable and modifiable, with effectiveness demonstrated in privacy protection contexts [65724422-1]. Tree-based partial synthetic data approaches show competitive quality but leave privacy-utility trade-offs underexplored [65724422-0].

GAN and VAE-based tabular generators have been adapted to incorporate DP and robustness to imbalance and multimodality. CTAB-GAN+ integrates Wasserstein-based stability and DP in the encoder to protect individual records while supporting aggregate analysis, reflecting a trend toward combining generative quality with formal privacy guarantees. CTAB-GAN+ incorporates Wasserstein plus gradient penalty to stabilize GAN training and adds differential privacy in the encoder to protect individual data points while enabling meaningful aggregate analysis [65724422-0]. CTGAN’s conditional modeling and normalization address mode collapse and imbalance, improving realistic synthesis for augmentation and privacy-preserving analytics [629636e1-1].

Diffusion-based tabular generators emphasize scalable training and inference but may incur higher computational costs, affecting deployment in privacy-sensitive, large-scale settings; methods like dual-scale noise modeling aim to improve sample quality while acknowledging efficiency trade-offs. Dual-scale diffusion improves quality but increases computational overhead, motivating future work on efficient algorithms for large-scale generation [1f127b93-0]. Diffusion models can preserve global structure but must overcome tabular-specific dependencies and efficiency challenges [1f127b93-4].

However, these methods often struggle to handle the complex, multimodal distributions in tabular data and typically fail to preserve global structure (e.g., overall correlation between features) and local details (e.g., feature distribution). Moreover, these models often operate as ''black boxes,'' making it difficult to interpret the generated data or ensure that it accurately reflects the distribution of the underlying data [10]. 

Denoising diffusion probabilistic models [11] have emerged in recent years as a promising alternative approach to data generation, showing great potential [12], [13]. These models have demonstrated the ability to generate high-quality samples by progressively optimizing noisy data through multiple steps. However, applying diffusion models to tabular data presents new challenges due to the heterogeneity of tabular features. Unlike images, where pixel dependencies are typically local and spatially coherent, tabular data exhibits complex inter-column dependencies, requiring the modeling of global and regional relationships [14], [15]. 

In this study, we propose a novel generative framework. This dual-scale diffusion method aims to overcome the challenges of DDPM in tabular data generation by introducing a dual-scale noise-handling mechanism.

sections.title: # Applications and Deployment Contexts
sections.text:
Synthetic tabular data supports augmentation for rare-class detection, imputation, unit testing of ML systems, data masking for analytics, and privacy-preserving sharing of statistics or model training across institutions. In healthcare, CTGAN-based generators and related methods have been used for data augmentation and validation, including rare attack detection and distributed settings. CTGAN has been applied to synthetic data generation in healthcare, designed to handle discrete and continuous features and avoid mode collapse and imbalance [629636e1-0]. CTGAN’s conditional training and normalization address multi-modal distributions and class imbalance, facilitating augmentation for applications like rare attack detection [629636e1-4].

Latent diffusion models for tabular data have been proposed for cross-silo privacy-preserving analytics and imputation/synthesis tasks, leveraging compact latent representations and efficient denoising steps to balance quality and communication costs. Tabular diffusion methods (e.g., TABSYN) support mixed-type synthesis with regularized latent spaces and fast generation in fewer than 20 reverse steps, enabling use in augmentation and imputation scenarios [1f127b93-2]. Tabular data synthesis is used for augmenting training data, protecting private instances, and imputing missing values [1f127b93-2].

sections.title: # Limitations and Open Challenges
sections.text:
- Statistical vs. semantic validity: Models can match marginals and pairwise dependencies yet violate domain rules (e.g., negative ages), necessitating rule/logic-based post-processing and commonsense alignment. Synthetic data may match distributional properties but still violate commonsense or logical rules, requiring post-processing for semantic correctness [cd95dc7c-3].
- Evaluation gaps: Lack of standardized, cross-domain benchmarks that jointly assess statistical fidelity, functional utility, and semantic validity across heterogeneous tabular schemas. Evaluation techniques and criteria for reliability and statistical properties remain underdeveloped [cd95dc7c-3]. Surveys have not thoroughly explored LLM and diffusion methods, and often overlook post-processing in evaluation [cd95dc7c-4].
- Privacy-utility trade-offs: Balancing high utility with strong privacy (e.g., DP) remains challenging; tree-based and probabilistic models offer interpretability and some effectiveness but may underperform on complex dependencies and multimodal distributions. Privacy-utility trade-offs for tree-based density estimators are underexplored, and probabilistic models may rely on simplifying assumptions [65724422-0]. Copulas are effective for privacy protection but may be limited in modeling higher-order dependencies [65724422-1].
- Scalability and efficiency: Diffusion-based generators can improve quality but increase computational overhead; scalable, efficient training/inference remains a bottleneck for large datasets and cross-silo deployments. Dual-scale diffusion improves quality at the cost of computational overhead, requiring more efficient algorithms for large-scale use [1f127b93-0].
- Hierarchical and interdependent variables: Hierarchical schemas and multivariate dependencies (e.g., categorical-categorical, categorical-continuous with skew) are difficult to model without collapsing modes or losing global structure. Limitations include sufficient analysis of hierarchical and interdependent variables, and evaluation criteria tailored to such structures [cd95dc7c-3]. VAEs assume simple latent forms that may fail on complex dependencies, and invertible neural networks demand extensive hyperparameter tuning [65724422-0].

citations.title: A Comprehensive Survey of Synthetic Tabular Data Generation
snippets:
However, existing surveys have several limitations: (1) Some existing works are limited to specific domains or methods and lack a comprehensive overview of synthetic tabular data generation. Such as some surveys [20]- [22] focus on the use of GANs for generating medical tabular data, some surveys [23], [24] focus on class imbalance, privacy, and fairness in synthetic tabular data generation. (2) Existing work primarily focuses on the generation and evaluation of synthetic tabular data [25], [26], while overlooking the importance of post-processing after data generation. Synthetic data may match the original distribution but still violate commonsense or logical rules (e.g. negative age values or children marked as married). Post-processing is therefore necessary to ensure semantic correctness and data validity. (3) The latest advancements in LLMs and diffusion models for synthetic tabular data generation have not yet been thoroughly explored [27]. LLMs and diffusion models offer advantages over traditional generative methods-LLMs for their ability to model semantic structure, and diffusion models for their stability and representation capabilities-but current surveys lack a thorough investigation of these methods. 

In this survey, we present a comprehensive review of synthetic tabular data generation. Specifically, we first introduce the definition of synthetic tabular data generation and the key challenges it faces. We then categorize existing methods into three main classes-traditional generation methods, diffusion model methods, and LLM-based methods-and provide a detailed analysis of the strengths and limitations of each category. Furthermore, we summarize and classify the postprocessing techniques into two primary categories: sample enhancement and label enhancement, highlighting their importance in ensuring data quality and semantic consistency. We also review evaluation methodologies from the perspectives of arXiv:2504.16506v1 [cs.LG] 23  Step 1: Synthetic Tabular Data Generation Fig. 1. Pipeline of synthetic tabular data generation. The first step involves training generative models on existing tabular datasets to generate synthetic data. These models include Traditional Generation Methods, Diffusion Model Methods, and LLM-based Methods. To further improve the quality of the synthetic data and ensure alignment with human knowledge, the second step applies post-processing techniques, which include Sample Enhancement and Label Enhancement.

sections.title: # Recent Trends and Future Directions
sections.text:
- Emergence of LLM and diffusion-based generators: Surveys highlight LLM-based and diffusion-based methods as promising due to semantic modeling and stability, respectively, alongside traditional probabilistic models and GANs. LLMs offer semantic structure advantages while diffusion models provide stability and representation capabilities; these are underexplored in prior surveys [cd95dc7c-4].
- Post-processing and semantic validity: Automated rule checking, logic-constrained sampling, and commonsense reasoning are increasingly integrated to ensure validity beyond statistical parity. We summarize post-processing techniques into sample enhancement and label enhancement to ensure semantic correctness and data validity [cd95dc7c-4].
- Privacy-aware generative training: Hybrid designs combine DP mechanisms, Wasserstein regularization, and robust encoders/latent priors to protect individuals while preserving utility for analytics and model training. CTAB-GAN+ adds differential privacy in the encoder and Wasserstein penalties to stabilize training and protect privacy [65724422-0].
- Benchmarking and reproducibility: Comparative libraries (e.g., SDV, SynthCity) and method-specific advances (e.g., VAE-GMM, dual-scale diffusion) are pushing standardized evaluations and reproducible comparisons across datasets and tasks. Comparative studies using SDV and SynthCity examine Gaussian Copula, Bayesian Networks, CTGAN, and TVAE with clear methodological foundations [65724422-3]. VAE-GMM integration demonstrates improved performance over CTGAN and TVAE across medical and other real-world datasets [65724422-4]. Dual-scale diffusion methods highlight quality–efficiency trade-offs and the need for scalable algorithms [1f127b93-0].

citations.title: An Improved Tabular Data Generator with VAE-GMM Integration
snippets: The rising use of machine learning in various fields requires robust methods to create synthetic tabular data that preserve key characteristics while mitigating data scarcity chal-lenges. State-of-the-art approaches, such as CTGAN and TVAE, face difficulties with the intricate structures inherent in tabular data, which often comprise continuous and discrete features with non-Gaussian distributions. To address these limitations, we pro-pose a novel approach based on Variational Autoencoders (VAEs) enhanced with a Bayesian Gaussian Mixture (BGM) model. Unlike other methods that alter the Gaussian prior of the VAE, our approach trains the VAE conventionally and then applies the BGM model to the learned latent space. This allows for a more accurate representation of the underlying data distribution during data generation. Moreover, our model offers enhanced flexibility by accommodating various differentiable distributions for individual features, enabling the handling of continuous and discrete data types. Thorough validation on three real-world datasets, including medically relevant ones, demonstrates significant outperformance compared to CTGAN and TVAE. Our model shows promise as a valuable tool for synthetic tabular data generation across diverse domains, particularly in healthcare.

citations.title: A Comparative Study of Open-Source Libraries for Synthetic Tabular Data Generation: SDV vs. SynthCity
snippets:
In this research, we'll use four different Data Generators with well-known mathematical properties: Gaussian Copula, Bayesian Networks, Conditional Tabular GAN (CTGAN), and Tabular Variational Autoencoder (TVAE). The first two are statistical methods, whereas the latter two are deep neural network techniques. Let's first examine the mathematical properties of the statistical methods. 

Gaussian copula methods model the joint distribution of a table by combining each column's marginal distribution with a copula function capturing intercolumn dependencies. The foundation is Sklar's theorem [27], which states that any multivariate distribution F (z 1 , . . . , z d ) can be decomposed as 

where F i (z i ) are the marginals and C is the copula describing their dependency structure. A Gaussian copula assumes this dependence is encoded by a multivariate normal distribution with a correlation matrix, while allowing arbitrary marginals. In practice, one first estimates each column's CDF, then transforms the data into a latent space with uniform or Gaussian marginals. First, you estimate a CDF F i for each column i of the real data. Then, transform the real data into uniform variables U i = F i (Z i ) and fit a copula C to capture their joint dependence, which for a Gaussian copula means computing the correlation matrix. Lastly, draw a synthetic sample (U 1 , . . . , U d ) ∼ C from the copula model, and invert the transform by applying the inverse CDF for each column, 

. This yields a synthetic data record in the original space. 

Patki et al. [28] introduced the open-source package Synthetic Data Vault (SDV) by using Gaussian copulas to model tabular data. In their approach, all columns are converted to a standard normal scale to remove the effect of each column distribution shape, before estimating the covariance matrix of the joint Gaussian copula. After modeling the correlations, synthetic rows are sampled by drawing from the multivariate normal and then transforming back to each column's domain.

sections.title: # Practical Guidance and Choosing Methods
sections.text: For simple schemas with strong Gaussian-like marginals and pairwise dependencies, copula-based or Bayesian network models offer interpretability and privacy benefits. Vine copulas provide interpretable distributional models and are robust to train, with demonstrated effectiveness in privacy protection [65724422-1]. Bayesian networks approximate conditional distributions but require assumptions that may limit applicability [65724422-0]. For mixed types and complex dependencies, CTGAN and related GANs, TVAE and VAE variants, and diffusion models are strong choices, with careful attention to mode collapse, imbalance, and efficiency. CTGAN’s conditional generator and mode-specific normalization handle mixed types and imbalances [629636e1-1]. VAEs adapted to tabular data can capture structure but may rely on restrictive latent assumptions [65724422-0]. Diffusion models like TABSYN regularize latent spaces and reduce reverse steps to improve speed and quality [1f127b93-2]. Where domain rules are critical, integrate rule/logic-based post-processing and, where possible, incorporate domain ontologies or learned constraints to enforce semantic validity. Post-processing is necessary to ensure semantic correctness and data validity when purely generative models fail on commonsense or logical rules [cd95dc7c-3].

sections.title: # Summary
sections.text: Synthetic tabular data generation has matured from statistical methods to powerful deep generative families (GANs, VAEs, diffusion) and is increasingly complemented by LLM- and rule-based post-processing to ensure semantic validity. A comprehensive survey outlines end-to-end pipelines, taxonomies, and evaluation protocols [cd95dc7c-0]. Key challenges include robust evaluation across statistical, logical, and utility dimensions, with post-processing to ensure semantic correctness [cd95dc7c-4]. Recent methods extend to privacy-aware training and handle complex dependencies [65724422-0]. Diffusion-based approaches improve fidelity but must address efficiency and dependency modeling [1f127b93-2]. Probabilistic models like copulas remain attractive for interpretability and privacy protection [65724422-1]. Addressing evaluation gaps, scalability, and privacy-utility trade-offs will be central to broader adoption across regulated and sensitive domains. Evaluation techniques and criteria for reliability and statistical properties remain insufficient, especially for hierarchical and interdependent variables [cd95dc7c-3]. question: What 2d barcode is resilient to compression?

sections.text:
Summary answer
- The 2D barcode most commonly cited as resilient to physical damage and compression is PDF417, due to its strong Reed–Solomon error correction and stacked, multi-row structure that tolerates partial occlusion and surface degradation in logistics environments. 2D symbologies such as Aztec Code, Data Matrix, Han Xin, PDF417, and QR Code provide this level of protection and data integrity insurance [af1e2a69-1] The use of Reed-Solomon error correction in bar code symbologies has been shown to achieve at least a 1 in 797 million error rate across Data Matrix, QR code, PDF417 and Aztec Code in large-scale scanning tests [af1e2a69-0] PDF417 uses Reed-Solomon error correction, which allows the symbol to endure some damage without causing a loss of data [f8abf24b-2] PDF417 is a multi-row, variable-length symbology offering high data capacity and error-correction capability [8887655e-3]. MaxiCode (used by USPS) is also designed for robustness in mail streams, but direct evidence here focuses more on PDF417 and general RS-based robustness. An Intelligent Mail barcode is a USPS-developed method to encode ZIP Code information on mail that can be read for sorting by automated machines [f8abf24b-0] DataMatrix, Maxicode, and QR code are representative of matrix-type symbology [c8e63e62-1].

citations.title: Improving Performance of the Decoder for Two-Dimensional Barcode Symbology PDF417
snippets:
Linear barcodes have been used globally in the various fields such as supermarkets and other stores for several decades.Usually, they do not have detailed information but just carry a key to database, because they can hold only several bytes of information.The need to increase the amount of data in a symbol brought the introduction of a new form of barcodes with much higher density called the two-dimensional (2-D) barcodes.They have been introduced since 1990's.While conventional or onedimensional barcodes usually function as keys to databases, the new or two-dimensional barcodes meet a need to encode significantly more data than the conventional codes and would act as a portable data file because the information could be retrieved without access to a database.They have additional features such as error correction and the ability to encode in various languages like English, Korean and Chinese, etc., besides their increased capacity.Thus, the traditional concept of barcode as a key to a database is changing towards a "portable data file" in which all the relevant information accompanies the item without access to a database.

There are two types of 2-D symbologies -stacked and matrix-type symbologies.The stacked barcodes, to which Code49, PDF417, etc. belong, have the structure of rectangular block comprising numbers of rows, each of which is like 1-D symbology.The matrix-type barcodes are essentially a form of binary encoding in which a black or white cell can represent either binary 1 or 0. These cells are arranged in an array structured on a grid of rectangular block.DataMatrix, Maxicode, and QR code, etc. are representative of Matrix-type symbology (Pavlidis, 1992).

In this paper, we focuss only on PDF417 (AIM USA, 1994), known as the most widely used 2-D stacked symbology.PDF417 is a multi-row, variable-length symbology offering high data capacity and error-correction capability.A PDF417 symbol is capable of encoding more than 1,100 bytes, 1,800 ASCII characters, or 2,700 digits, depending on the selected data compaction mode.Every PDF417 symbol is composed of a stack of rows, from a minimum of 3 to a maximum of 90 rows.
